articles.title: ETF inflows hit record highs as investors embrace global equities and active strategies
articles.text:
PORTFOLIO PERSPECTIVES | PODCAST – 8:56 MIN
ETF inflows hit record highs as investors embrace global equities and active strategies

By
DANIEL DORNEL, DANIEL MORRIS 15.10.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

European UCITS ETFs (EU regulated exchange-traded funds) attracted a record €125 billion in the third quarter, taking year-to-date inflows to almost €350 billion. Global equities led the way, Europe rebounded and emerging markets recovered, while Chinese equity ETFs continued to see outflows.

As Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research, explains to Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, fixed-income ETFs also attracted strong inflows, particularly into government bonds and ultra-short-duration products, despite rising yields. “Active ETFs also continued their rapid growth, which we believe highlights investors’ appetite for new strategies.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into the forces shaping ETF flows and investor positioning.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Daniel Dornel

Daniel Morris: Hello and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing the latest ETF (exchange-traded fund) fund flows. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research. Welcome, Daniel, and thanks for joining me.

Daniel Dornel: Thank you, Daniel. I’m very happy to be here.

DM: As always, Daniel, it’s been an eventful quarter. One of the key surprises has been the resilience of equity markets. When you’ve seen the big increase in yields for government bonds, typically a rise in interest rates goes with the decline in equity markets but, so far, they seem to have shrugged that off. In terms of ETF flows, what are the dynamics you’ve seen in the third quarter?

DD: It has been a remarkable period. Q3 was the strongest quarter ever, with inflows around €125 billion. What’s really impressive is that we are seeing a pattern of breaking records one quarter after another. If we look closer at the monthly breakdown, July and August were the two largest months ever recorded in the UC[ITS] ETF landscape, with July alone bringing in over €50 billion.

This momentum is carrying us into an historic year. Year to date, we have already seen almost €350 billion inflows into UC[ITS] ETF[s], which means we have already surpassed the total full-year figure from last year, €327 billion.

While the growth is broad, equity projects dominated the landscape this quarter, capturing almost €100 billion of those €125 billion of total inflows.

DM: It’s interesting that you say that because there’s been a long discussion about cash on the sidelines and whether or not investors are willing to put that cash to work. And it seems from the figures you cite for ETF flows, maybe they are. We also see the strong performance of equity markets being followed by flows into ETFs. Clearly that’s a strong support for the market. Are there any particular categories or products that stand out?

DD: Without doubt, global equities have been standing out. In Q3, they attracted just under €55 billion. This isn’t a sudden spike; it is a sustained trend we have been seeing from last year.

Just to give a few figures, the year-to-date figure for global equities is already €145 billion compared to just under €100 billion for last year. So global equities now represent about a third of all equity flows.

What is particularly interesting is the acceleration in all-country exposures – a blend between developed and emerging market equities. Historically, they have been behind developed-only global equities. But on this particular sub-category, we have seen a jump from €40 billion last year to €83 billion on a year-to-date basis. This suggests investors are looking for the more diversified product[s] they can find these days.

DM: I would imagine these inflows into global ETFs, including emerging markets, probably has something to do with the strong performance we’ve seen, particularly in Taiwan and [South] Korea, around semiconductors and tech hardware. I think investors are looking to try to tap into that dynamic. Speaking of dynamics, is there anything else that you see across equity markets?

DD: Let’s start with the US. After a very strong acceleration in Q2, the appetite for US equity remained, with €23 billion in flows in Q3, again mostly concentrated in core exposures.

Moving on to Europe, we saw an interesting rebound in Q3, with €9 billion inflows. This suggests a return in confidence from investors after a very difficult Q2 where we had around €5 billion [of] outflows. We also saw an acceleration in emerging markets, bringing in €6.8 billion, a recovery from a quiet second quarter on emerging markets.

However, it hasn’t been positive everywhere. China continues to be a challenge, and we saw another difficult quarter with €1.5 billion outflows from Chinese equity product.

Looking at sub-asset classes, sector and thematic ETF[s] brought in €15 billion, the lion’s share driven by IT and tech-related themes. But there were two interesting additional trends, with healthcare – we saw €1.5 billion inflows there – and Eurozone banks, with €1.3 billion inflows.

DM: That is encouraging that you’re starting to see inflows again into Europe. We’re seeing that all the investment that the region is putting towards strategic autonomy, defence and so on is starting to bear some fruit. It’s also interesting that, despite the inflows into emerging markets, you still see outflows from Chinese ETFs. And we appreciate that tech is a big driver for the interest in emerging markets.

I started out saying we’ve had [a] surprisingly strong performance for equity markets despite the big increase in [bond] yields. I’m curious if that increase in government bond yields has had an impact on flows for fixed-income ETFs?

DD: Fixed income had a very strong quarter as well, bringing in €27 billion. The primary engine was government bonds, with €10 billion inflows. It was a mix of all maturity exposures, especially on global and euro bonds, as well as short-term maturities, especially on US, but also on European exposures.

We also saw a significant interest in ultra-short instruments, which brought €8 billion. Roughly half of that was on overnight euro exposures and 25% in US Treasuries with a maturity from zero to one year on corporate investment grade.

We also see some flows there with €4 billion, a split between US all-maturity product and euro short term. The only area of weakness was a yield with a significant slowdown, only €500 million inflows over the quarter, primarily because of the September figures where we had very negative flows on euro high yield.

DM: The outflows for high yield are relevant, as I’ve heard from our portfolio managers. That was one of the key drivers behind the increase in yields and spreads that you saw for high yield, particularly in September. Last word on ETF flows for the quarter?

DD: I’d like to highlight the rise of active ETFs again. This is where things are moving quite rapidly. In Q3 alone we saw €11 billion of inflows. This brings us on a year-to-date basis to €34 billion, so roughly 10% of the flows and it’s already ahead of [the] 2025 figure, which was just under 30 billion.

So, the dynamic is very impressive, especially on enhanced strategies and equity income strategies. But it’s not just about the flows, it’s also about the product innovation. If you look at all the ETFs launched in Europe year-to-date, 40% were active ETF[s] – that’s already over 100 new funds this year.

DM: If I can summarise some of the key points, you said not only was the third quarter the strongest ever in terms of ETF flows, but recently almost every quarter is the strongest, so it really does seem there’s a lot of momentum behind ETFs.

You highlighted that flows are going more towards global equities, conceivably as investors are looking to tap into the tech dynamic in emerging markets. That said, you also saw a rebound of flows into Europe, so another renewed bout of optimism.

And finally, positive inflows into fixed income despite the increase in [bond] yields. But you highlighted that this is tend[ing] to be short duration, so investors less at risk of rising yields and able to pick up some income in the meantime.

Daniel, thank you very much for joining me.

DD: Thank you, Daniel. Always a pleasure.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities in ETFs, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at Viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better-informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, and Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

articles.title: Euro Tax Flash from KPMG's EU Tax Centre: 16 October 2026
articles.text:
Go back to the Euro Tax Flash homepage.

CJEU decision on the application of the anti-abuse rule under Parent-Subsidiary Directive

At a glance: On October 15, 2026, the CJEU ruled in C‑203/25opens in a new tab that the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (PSD) anti-abuse provision may apply even where the immediate parent company carries on genuine economic activities, is recognized as the beneficial owner of the dividends and is not a conduit company.Taxpayer impact: The judgment confirms that genuine economic activity and beneficial ownership at the level of the direct parent company are not, in and of themselves, sufficient to exclude a finding of abuse. Tax authorities may take into account transactions carried out in other jurisdictions, including events occurring after the dividend payment and advantages obtained by other participants in the structure, including the ultimate beneficial owner.

On October 15, 2026, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU or the Court) rendered its decision in case C-203/25opens in a new tab, on the interpretation of the anti-abuse provision in the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (the PSD or the Directive).

Key findings of the CJEU

Broad scope of the PSD anti-abuse provision and assessment of the arrangement as a wholeThe Court confirmed that the PSD anti-abuse provision has a broad scope and is not limited to situations involving conduit companies. Importantly, the existence of genuine economic activity at the level of the direct parent company is not sufficient, by itself, to rule out abuse. Tax authorities must assess the arrangement as a whole and may consider all relevant facts and circumstances across the wider chain of transactions. In the case at hand, this included the transfer of shares, loan arrangements and assignments of receivables involving entities other than the immediate dividend recipient. The Court also noted that recognition of beneficial ownership under a tax treaty does not prevent the application of the PSD anti-abuse rule.Correspondence between dividend amounts and the timing of transfers may constitute indicators of a non-genuine arrangementBuilding on its previous "Danish cases" jurisprudence, the Court confirmed that tax authorities may take into account:the similarity between dividend amounts received by the parent company and amounts ultimately transferred through the wider structure;the onward transfer of funds within the group; andthe timing and frequency of such transfers.The Court clarified that abuse cannot be presumed solely because amounts correspond or because dividends are transferred onwards. Equally, the anti-abuse rule is not limited to situations where funds are transferred shortly after receipt. Repeated transfers over a longer period may also be relevant indicators when viewed in the context of the overall arrangement.Anti-abuse assessment may extend to transactions carried out outside the Member State of the distributing subsidiaryThe Court held that national tax authorities are entitled to take a holistic view of the arrangement when applying the anti-abuse provision. This includes considering:transactions carried out in other jurisdictions;events occurring after the dividend payment; andtax advantages obtained by parties elsewhere in the structure, including the ultimate beneficial owner (UBO).The Court rejected the argument that the relevant tax advantage must arise at the level of the distributing subsidiary.The relevance of the distributing subsidiary's knowledge in assessing the alleged abusive arrangementThe Court finally addressed whether the withholding tax exemption can be denied without proving that the distributing subsidiary itself knew, or could have known, about the abusive arrangement. The Court concluded that such knowledge is not required. Whilst abuse requires both objective and subjective elements, the subjective element need only be demonstrated in relation to at least one participant in the chain of transactions or the ultimate beneficial owner. Limiting the analysis to the knowledge of the distributing subsidiary would undermine the effectiveness of the PSD anti-abuse provision.

Background

The plaintiff is a Lithuanian entity wholly owned by a Cypriot parent company (HoldCo One). In 2016 and 2017, the parent company received dividends from the plaintiff and another Lithuanian entity. The plaintiff considered that the payments were exempt from dividend withholding tax under the local rules implementing the Parent-Subsidiary Directive (PSD).In February 2017, the shares in HoldCo One were sold by a Belize company, the grandparent of the Lithuanian plaintiff, to a newly set-up Cypriot entity (HoldCo Two) while the purchase price remained payable by HoldCo Two (the loan). Despite this sale, the ultimate beneficial owner of the dividends (UBO), an individual not resident in Lithuania, who owned both the Belizean and Cypriot companies, remained unchanged. Following the sale, the Belize company assigned the loan to the UBO.In 2017 and 2018, HoldCo Two granted loans (the loan arrangements) and assigned receivables to the UBO. The combined amount of these loans and receivables was subsequently set off against the outstanding amount of the UBO’s receivable against HoldCo Two tha[t was created in connection with the sale of the shares in HoldCo One. Over that period, HoldCo Two did not pay out any dividend to its shareholder (UBO).Following a tax audit, the Lithuanian tax inspectorate concluded that the dividends paid by the Lithuanian entity to HoldCo One should not have benefited from the PSD exemption and were instead subject to the standard 15 percent withholding tax. The Lithuanian tax authorities did not challenge the beneficial owner status of HoldCo One nor did they challenge the fact that HoldCo One actually carried on an economic activity. However, they argued that the transactions involving the dividends formed part of a non-genuine arrangement aimed at obtaining a tax advantage, thus triggering the application of the anti-abuse rule under the PSD as transposed into Lithuanian law3. In particular, the Lithuanian tax authorities concluded that economically, the dividends were ultimately paid to the UBO, through a chain of artificial transactions.Following an appeal raised by the taxpayer, the Lithuanian Tax Disputes Commission (Disputes Commission) acknowledged the CJEU’s rulings in joined cases C-116/16 and C-117/16opens in a new tab, commonly referred to as the “Danish cases”. Nonetheless, the Disputes Commission noted that the case at hand is different since the dividends were paid to an entity with genuine economic activity which, in the tax authorities’ view, participated in a chain of non-genuine transactions.On this basis, the Disputes Commission expressed doubts about the interpretation of the anti-abuse provision1 of the PSD and referred to the CJEU the following questions:Is it compatible with the PSD anti-abuse provision for a national tax practice to deny a withholding tax exemption on dividends paid to a genuine parent company established in another EU Member State, on the ground that the dividend is a part of a chain of non-genuine transactions?Can a chain of dividend transfers be presumed to be artificial or abusive based solely on the similarity of amounts involved at different stages of the transactions?Is it compatible with the PSD anti-abuse provision for a national tax practice to deny tax benefits on a cross-border dividend payment based on a chain of non-genuine transactions that occurred entirely after the dividend payment and in another EU Member State?Can the tax advantage be attributed to the plaintiff if it was ultimately realized by another party – i.e., the ultimate beneficiary, through a chain of non-genuine transactions?Can the anti-abuse rule under the PSD apply if the dividends were passed over on a continuous basis – i.e., from one year to one month, instead of “very soon after their receipt” as mentioned in the Danish cases?What is the relevance of the plaintiff’s knowledge or intent to undertake non-genuine transactions when applying the anti-abuse rules under the PSD.On May 21, 2026, Advocate General Juliane Kokott of the CJEU recommendedopens in a new tab that the Court find that a withholding tax exemption under the Parent-Subsidiary Directive may be denied in exceptional cases (case C-203/25). In the AG’s view, this could apply even where the parent company receiving the dividends is the beneficial owner and carries out genuine economic activities, but it passes the dividends on to the UBO through an artificial arrangement.The AG stressed that to determine the purpose of an arrangement, all relevant circumstances must be taken into account, in particular the awareness of the person who decides to implement it, which is generally the controlling shareholder. According to the AG, an abusive overall plan exists, for example, where the PSD is used to generate income for the UBO that cannot be taxed in their hands. This could be the case where dividends are channeled through non-cooperative offshore jurisdictions, so that the UBO's state of residence receives no information about the final distribution.The AG also took the view that abuse of a Member State's national tax law does not, as a rule, constitute abuse within the meaning of the PSD. However, abuse under the PSD may exist where the subsidiary distributes profits to its parent company, which is the beneficial owner, for the purpose of evading taxes in the UBO's Member State.For more details, please refer to Euro Tax Flash Issue 580.

CJEU decision

Broad scope of the PSD anti-abuse provision and assessment of the arrangement as a wholeThe Court first focused on whether the anti-abuse provision in the PSD may apply where dividends are paid to a parent company that carries on genuine economic activities and is not a conduit company, but forms part of a broader chain of transactions containing one or more allegedly non-genuine elements. In addressing this question, the Court recalled that the PSD seeks to eliminate withholding taxes and double taxation on cross-border profit distributions within the EU. The Court then reiterated its settled case-law according to which EU law contains a general anti-abuse principle. The Court noted that the anti-abuse provision introduced by Directive 2015/1212 reflects that principle in the context of the PSD.The Court further recalled that two cumulative conditions must be met for benefits under the PSD to be denied:the arrangement or series of arrangements must be non-genuine, meaning that it is not put in place for valid commercial reasons reflecting economic reality; andone of the principal purposes of the arrangement must be to obtain a tax advantage that defeats the object or purpose of the Directive.The Court first focused on the condition related to the existence of a non-genuine arrangement. The Court emphasized that the anti-abuse provision must be interpreted by reference not only to its wording, but also to its context and objectives. In this regard, the Court reiterated its settled case law that, based on the wording, context and objectives of the provision, the PSD anti-abuse rule applies broadly to all types of non-genuine arrangements and is not limited to arrangements displaying specific characteristics. Accordingly, whether an arrangement is non-genuine must be determined through an objective assessment of all relevant facts and circumstances. Where a structure consists of several transactions or steps, the analysis cannot focus solely on a single element of the arrangement or on the circumstances existing at a particular point in time, but must consider the overall series of arrangements. The Court also confirmed that it is for the national tax authorities seeking to deny PSD benefits to establish the constituent elements of an abusive practice, although they cannot be required to produce evidence that would be impossible to obtain.Applying those principles, the Court rejected the argument that the PSD anti-abuse provision is limited to arrangements involving conduit companies. Referring to the Danish cases, the Court recalled that the interposition of a conduit entity is merely one example of a potentially abusive arrangement. Consequently, the fact that the immediate parent company carries on genuine economic activities and is not a conduit company does not, in and of itself, exclude the existence of an abusive practice.According to the Court, focusing solely on the economic activity of the immediate recipient of the dividends would be inconsistent with the requirement to assess the arrangement as a whole. Instead, all relevant facts and circumstances forming part of the broader chain of transactions must be taken into account. In the case at hand, those elements included the transfer of shares in HoldCo One and the loan arrangements and the assignment of receivables between HoldCo Two and the UBO.The Court also addressed the interaction between the PSD anti-abuse provision and the Lithuania-Cyprus double tax treaty. Referring to the OECD Commentary to the Model Tax Convention, the Court noted that beneficial ownership does not automatically entitle a taxpayer to double tax treaty benefits in abusive situations. More fundamentally, the Court reiterated that double tax treaties concluded between Member States cannot be relied upon to achieve a result contrary to EU law. Consequently, the recognition of beneficial ownership under a tax treaty does not, in and of itself, prevent the application of the PSD anti-abuse provision.The Court therefore concluded that the PSD anti-abuse provision does not, in principle, prevent a Member State from denying a withholding tax exemption where a dividend distribution forms part of a broader chain of transactions containing one or more non-genuine elements, even where the immediate parent company carries on genuine economic activities and is not a conduit company.Correspondence between dividend amounts and the timing of transfers may constitute indicators of a non-genuine arrangementThe Court also provided guidance on the interpretation of the anti-abuse provision in the PSD and, in particular, on whether the correspondence between dividend amounts transferred through a chain of transactions and the timing of those transfers may constitute relevant indicators when assessing the existence of an abusive practice.The Court recalled its findings in the Danish cases, where the onward payment of dividends, in whole or in substantial part and within a very short period following their receipt, was regarded as an indication of an arrangement aimed at benefiting unduly from the withholding tax exemption provided by the PSD. Building on that case-law, the Court held that, in assessing the existence of an abusive practice, national tax authorities may also take into account the correspondence between the amount of dividends received by the parent company and the amounts ultimately received, through the chain of transactions, by the person controlling the entities involved. The Court nevertheless emphasized that neither of these elements can, in isolation, give rise to a general presumption of abuse.The Court further clarified that, whilst a rapid onward transfer of dividends may constitute a relevant indicator, a short interval between the receipt and subsequent transfer of dividends is not required for the purposes of the anti-abuse provision. According to the Court, transfers carried out on a recurring basis over a longer period may also be relevant in assessing whether a chain of transactions contains one or more non-genuine elements.The Court therefore concluded that both the similarity of the amounts transferred through a chain of transactions and the fact that such transfers take place continuously over a certain period may constitute relevant indicators for the purposes of identifying a non-genuine arrangement, without prejudice to the need for the national tax authorities to verify, on the basis of all relevant facts and circumstances, whether the constituent elements of an abusive practice are present.Anti-abuse assessment may extend to transactions carried out outside the Member State of the distributing subsidiaryThe CJEU then examined whether the anti-abuse provision in the PSD, as interpreted in light of the principle of proportionality, precludes a Member State from levying withholding tax on dividends where the transactions deemed to be non-genuine were carried out outside that Member State and the resulting tax advantage was obtained by another person within the wider structure.The Court first noted that, when assessing whether an arrangement is abusive, national tax authorities must conduct a comprehensive examination of all relevant facts and circumstances, including transactions carried out outside the Member State seeking to deny the benefits of the Directive. The CJEU further recalled its previous case law – in particular case C-228/24 (Nordcurrent), based on which national tax authorities may also take into account events occurring after the arrangement was put in place when assessing whether it is genuine.Applying those principles, the Court held that the anti-abuse provision of the PSD does not require the tax advantage that runs counter the Directive’s objective or purpose to be demonstrated in relation to the distributing subsidiary. Instead, the advantage may be obtained by the ultimate individual controlling the group, resident in another Member State. The Court further noted that such undue advantages could not be addressed if the Member State granting the exemption were prevented from taking into account transactions carried out outside its territory using the dividends received under that exemption.The Court also rejected arguments based on the principle of proportionality. The CJEU took the view that allowing national tax authorities to assess the entire arrangement is both suitable and necessary to combat abusive structures that can only be identified through a holistic analysis of the relevant transactions. In addition, the Court reiterated its settled case-law, in particular the Danish cases, that taxpayers cannot rely on the fundamental freedoms guaranteed by the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to challenge measures that are intended to prevent abusive practices.The Court therefore concluded that the anti-abuse provision of the PSD, read in light of the principle of proportionally, does not preclude a national practice under which withholding tax is imposed on dividends where the deemed non-genuine transactions were carried out outside that Member State by non-resident individuals or legal entities, including the person who obtains the tax benefit through the dividend exemption, regardless of where in the transaction chain that benefit is obtained.The relevance of the distributing subsidiary’s knowledge in assessing the alleged abusive arrangementFinally, the CJEU examined whether a Member State may deny the withholding tax exemption under the PSD without proving that the distributing subsidiary itself knew, or could have known, that the dividend payment formed part of a chain of transactions or that some – or all of those transactions, lacked genuine commercial substance.The Court recalled its settled case-law, based on which merely classifying a subsidiary as a non-genuine arrangement is not sufficient to justify the denial of PSD benefits under the related anti-abuse provision. Instead, it must also be established that the arrangement was implemented with the principal objective, or one of the principal objectives, of obtaining a tax advantage that defeats the object or purpose of the Directive.The Court recalled that an abusive situation can be evidenced in the combined presence of:objective circumstances, in which the purpose of the EU Directives is circumvented, despite a formal observance of the conditions required for their application; andsubjective elements – the existence of a wholly artificial arrangement, as well as an intention to obtain a (tax) advantage.The Court further noted that dividend distributions may form part of a broader series of decisions taken within a corporate group. Against this background, the Court considered that limiting the assessment of the subjective element solely to the level of the distributing subsidiary – by verifying whether it knew or could have known about the existence of abuse, would undermine the effectiveness of the Directive’s anti-abuse provision. The Court therefore held that it is sufficient for the subjective element to be demonstrated in relation to at least one company participating in the chain of transactions, or the individual who ultimately benefits from the tax advantage.The Court concluded that the anti-abuse provision of the Parent-Subsidiary Directive does not preclude a national practice whereby withholding tax is imposed without establishing the distributing subsidiary’s knowledge of the abusive arrangement, as long as it is demonstrated that another group company involved in the arrangement, or the ultimate beneficial owner, knew or could have known of the existence of the chain of transactions aimed at obtaining the tax advantage.

ETC Comment:

The judgment is notable because it confirms and further develops the interpretation of the PSD anti-abuse provision established in case C-228/24. Whilst that earlier case concerned the exemption of dividends received from corporate income tax, the Court has now applied the same principles in the context of the withholding tax exemption for outbound dividends, clarifying that the broad interpretation of the Directive's anti-abuse rule also applies in the case of outbound payments.In line with the AG’s opinion, the Court clarifies that, whilst onward payments of dividends in comparable amounts and shortly after receipt, constitute an indication of abuse, such elements do not automatically establish abuse. The Court also clarifies that the distributing subsidiary’s knowledge of the existence of abusive arrangement is irrelevant, as long as it can be demonstrated that another group company or the UBO could have been aware of abuse.The judgment leaves unaddressed several important aspects of Advocate General Kokott's Opinion. In particular, the AG drew a distinction between abuse of the PSD and abuse of domestic tax rules in another Member State, suggesting that alleged abuse of domestic legislation in the state of the ultimate beneficiary should not, as a general rule, justify the denial of PSD benefits by the Member State of the distributing subsidiary. In this context, the AG placed considerable emphasis on the need for a direct link between the abusive element of the arrangement and the tax advantage granted under EU law. In the AG’s view, it is only where the arrangement is designed to obtain a tax advantage that runs counter to the purpose of the PSD itself that the source Member State may deny the Directive's benefits. While the Court confirmed that the anti-abuse assessment may extend to transactions carried out outside the Member State of the distributing subsidiary and to advantages obtained elsewhere within the structure, it did not expressly engage with the AG's distinction or provide further guidance on circumstances that could lead to a benefit contrary to the object and purpose of the Directive.The judgment is also noteworthy for its comments on the interaction between the PSD anti-abuse provision and double tax treaties. The CJEU noted that it is for the referring court to interpret national law and the relevant double tax convention, which that referring court considers must be interpreted in light of the commentary on the OECD Model Tax Convention. However, the CJEU took the opportunity to note that according to the commentary on the relevant article of the OECD Model Tax Convention (Article 10), which was published in 2014 after the conclusion of the relevant double tax treaty in 2013, the fact that the recipient of the dividends is the "beneficial owner" of the dividends does not mean that the treaty relief is automatically due, as regard must be had to whether the provision is being misused to obtain the advantage. Furthermore, the Court reiterated that tax treaties concluded between Member States cannot be relied upon to achieve a result contrary to EU law. This seems to suggest that qualifying for relief, at least if such relief provides for a benefit similar to the PSD’s benefit, under an applicable tax treaty does not preclude the application of the PSD anti-abuse provision.

articles.title: Testing times require time for testing − speech by Ruth Smith
articles.text:
Testing times require time for testing − speech by Ruth Smith

Given at UK Finance

Published on
13 July 2026

Ruth Smith reflects on the Bank’s resolvability assessments of banks and building societies, and discusses how the Bank engages with firms at different stages on the journey to resolvability. She emphasises the importance of realistic testing and ongoing maintenance of resolvability capabilities, so they are ready for use if needed.

Speech
Good afternoon. It’s a pleasure to have the opportunity to speak to you today. Thank you to UK Finance for hosting us. Resolvability is a journey that the Bank and firms are on together, and engagement with industry has been essential to the progress we’ve made so far. Resolution matters because, as we have been reminded in recent years, when a financial institution fails, resolution enables the ongoing provision of critical financial services, protects customer deposits and prevents disruption to the wider economy. Maintaining a credible, effective and responsive resolution regime is at the heart of financial stability in testing times – supporting a resilient financial sector, which in turn enables households and firms to thrive. In January, my colleague Dave Ramsden spoke about this need for responsiveness and evolution in the Bank’s approach to resolution, so the regime’s outcomes are met in an ever-changing landscape.footnote [1]
Today, I want to focus on the idea of outcomes, and the goal we as the Resolution Authority have in mind for all firms – ongoing resolvability.
I will discuss our outcomes-based approach to the assessment of different firms, how we apply the Resolvability Assessment Framework, or RAF, to different groups of firms, and how we use testing and assurance to maintain progress.
I also want to look ahead to the principles we expect to guide us in evolving our approach to assessing resolvability. While our end destination remains the same, how we get there must respond to the growing maturity of firms’ capabilities, and the changing terrain and system that they are a part of.
The Resolvability Assessment Framework
The RAF applies to our major and mid-tier banks and building societies.footnote [2] The starting point is that it is proportionate by design and inherently risk-based. Firms are different, and they pose different challenges in resolution. While our objective is for all firms to be resolvable, the path to getting there will not be the same for everyone.
That is why the RAF is focused on outcomes. As firms grow in size and complexity, we expect more from them because their failure could have a greater impact on financial stability. To maintain that proportionality, we recently updated the calibration of the framework, raising both the MREL and Resolution Assessment thresholds.
The proportionality steps are broadly:

one, the RAF applies to firms where we will use our resolution powers if they fail – typically those with more than £25 billion in assets.
two, firms with bail-in resolution strategies need more capabilities than transfer firms:footnote [3] including financial resources to enable recapitalisation and capabilities to plan for post-resolution restructuring.
and three, major UK firms – those with £100 billion or more in retail deposits – must meet the RAF reporting and disclosure requirements, providing a layer of additional, public transparency and scrutiny for both firms and the Bank.

In all cases, we expect firms to own their resolvability, regardless of where they are on their journey. This means that firms’ senior management and boards are responsible for ensuring that their firm has the capabilities necessary for resolution and that these are tailored to the individual attributes of the firm.

Chart 1: RAF overview of requirements

The RAF also sets out three outcomes we want to see for the Bank to consider a firm resolvable: firms having adequate financial resources for resolution, being able to continue to do business through resolution and restructuring, and co-ordinating and communicating effectively.footnote [4]
This is not a box-ticking exercise: each firm needs to take the necessary steps to be ready for orderly resolution. What is needed for an established G-SIB differs to a neobank. And once capabilities are in place, they should be maintained to ensure they remain ready, including as the firm and the market evolve. Ongoing testing is crucial, to ensure capabilities operate effectively and are ready for use when required.
For international firms, the Bank works intensively in BAU so we are ready to support home authorities to implement a co-ordinated resolution if needed. While we expect international firms in the UK to achieve broadly the same outcomes as our home firms, how they do this may differ as they focus on having the capabilities required to deliver their group resolution strategy.
Assessing resolvability in these cases is not a one-size-fits-all exercise. We consider the approach of the home jurisdiction, alongside each firm's own preparations and UK business model. And we maintain active, practical engagement with international authorities to ensure we are all ready to use our respective powers if required.
Maintaining these close relationships enables us to respond with speed and agility in a crisis. We did this during the failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse. Such strong co-operation and co-ordination between authorities is a lesson from the financial crisis we cannot forget. Effective co-operation and co-ordination is the core purpose of the work of the Financial Stability Board’s (FSB) Cross-Border Crisis Management group for banks, which I chair. Structures like the FSB, Trilateral Principal Level Exercises (with the UK, US and Banking Union authorities), firm-specific Crisis Management Groups and regular bilateral engagement are essential for authorities to build resilience and readiness which can be relied upon in a crisis.
Our approach to assessing resolvability to date
I’ve led the RAF journey since 2018. At this point I think it is important to reflect on what we, as an authority, have done to foster progress towards firms being fully resolvable, as well as the progress that firms have made over their own resolvability.
We’ve now completed two assessments of the major UK firms and two assessments of mid-tier firms under the RAF. These assessments provide confidence that we can manage UK bank failure in an orderly way. The findings also support the Financial Policy Committee’s judgements on the optimal level of capital needed in the banking system.footnote [5]
Our first RAF assessment for major UK firms was largely desk-based. Our focus was on the capabilities firms had built and how they assured themselves that their preparations were adequate.
Our accompanying RAF public statement in 2022 provided transparency on our resolution strategies for individual firms and the areas each of them needed to focus on. We shared thematic findings and examples of good practice.
Our second RAF assessment gave us an improved view on each firm. Our assessment approach developed from being mainly desk-based to being underpinned by targeted tests of the Adequate Financial Resources outcome, providing us with a better idea of how policy would work in practice for each firm. We found continued progress by firms along with areas for further work.
Moving to our mid-tier assessments, we have mirrored our approach to the major UK firms while keeping proportionality and specificity at the forefront of our thinking. We have used the assessments to identify areas where we need to guide firms more explicitly on what we are looking for, without undermining the principle of firms’ responsibility for their own resolvability and keeping to an outcomes-based approach.
Our second assessment of the mid-tier firms last year included targeted testing of firms’ continuity capabilities, where the ultimate aim is to ensure the continued provision of services that are critical to the economy.footnote [6] Events such as the failure of Silicon Valley Bank have underlined that continuity is essential for keeping the lights on while we execute resolution. This matters for all firms and especially for mid-tiers, which are more likely to have a preferred resolution strategy of transfer. It is also an area where we saw weakness in our first mid-tier assessment.

Chart 2: RAF timeline

All this work with firms has enabled us to fine-tune what we need from firms, for example we have been able to reduce loss-absorbency requirements for transfer firms, increase thresholds, extend the time between RAF assessments, delete reporting templates, clarify requirements and share best practice. This makes the regime more efficient and targeted and demonstrates its responsiveness.
We are also streamlining our own internal processes for reviewing resolution plans, again being responsive while maintaining readiness. For example, we are leveraging the information gained through the RAF for our statutory resolvability assessments and, where firms’ capabilities have reached a steady state, we plan to use the flexibility the Bank has in legislation to review resolution plans less frequently.footnote [7]
We are reviewing our lessons from the delivery of the RAF to make further amendments to reporting requirements. This includes reviewing Supervisory Statement 19/13 on resolution planning, where we hope to tailor the requirements for the different firms in the system, while ensuring that the Bank can deploy its resolution powers across the population of firms it is responsible for. In particular, these changes aim to enhance the resolvability of smaller firms that are not in scope of the RAF.
The value of testing
Testing – whether as part of firms’ assurance or led by the Bank – is a valuable way to enhance our collective readiness. At this point we all have a mutual understanding of what it means to be resolvable, but resolution will always be a high-pressured transaction that requires both the Bank and firm. That is why we focus on outcomes and flexible capabilities.
For the Bank, testing is crucial to assess if firms’ capabilities can deliver what we need to execute a resolution in the public interest. Our testing complements our review of firms’ assessments of their capabilities and our review of their own assurance exercises. For firms, Bank-led testing is an opportunity to understand how the Bank will engage with them in resolution and how their capabilities may be utilised.
So testing cannot be seen as a narrow regulatory compliance exercise: firms should use it to think realistically about what they would have to do and how easily they could use their capabilities at pace and under pressure in resolution.
In short, realistic testing must be a priority. By realistic I mean testing that is time-bound, end-to-end, dynamic and involving relevant decision-makers or third parties. Realistic testing ultimately forces decision-makers to exercise the muscle of making decisions in uncertainty. We have seen that firms performing more strongly in assessments are likely to have undertaken dynamic, resolution-focused, integrated fire drill exercises that test across barriers and seniority levels using different scenarios.
Questions firms should be asking themselves as part of their assurance include:

Are data and data processes operable and effective at speed under the unique stresses of resolution? Bluntly, poor data and overly manual processes hinder rapid decision-making by senior management and the authorities, introducing unnecessary risk.
Have firms engaged realistically with the uncomfortable options that may be necessary? Resolution is more than just deep recovery. Firms need to ensure they embed this reality in their capability design and assurance. We all need to be clear that resolution may result in significant business model and senior leadership changes to respond to the causes of failure.
And have previous issues been remediated? Resolvability isn’t static so we will inevitably find more issues requiring remediation. Senior management need to own remediation and track progress when issues are identified.

For major firms, we have evolved our assessments to provide firms with space to perform their own assurance and to undertake specific work at the Bank’s request. That was why we chose to delay the third RAF assessment by a year.
In our third assessment we will review the clarity of firms’ assurance plans and the outputs from the valuations and restructuring planning exercises we have asked firms to undertake. Questions we will be asking include: is the assurance provided by the firm appropriate to the scale and complexity of the firm? Does it consider interdependencies between capabilities? Is it realistic? How are findings being remediated and tracked?
For mid-tier firms, we also provided an indicative scope for undertaking a valuations exercise to help firms understand our assurance expectations. This replaced a Bank-led test we had planned for this year.
We have also shared more information on how we expect to use the Bank’s powers to help firms prepare. We recently had a helpful roundtable with UK Finance to discuss the updated operational guide to bail-in and the new operational guide to transfer resolution. We issued these guides not to establish new capabilities we are asking firms to build. But to help firms and wider stakeholders understand more about how the Bank could execute a resolution transaction and what it would involve in practice. We also engage firms in a targeted way on topics where we see a need to do so, such as the recent roundtable on resolvability for building societies which was hosted by the BSA.
Third RAF assessment: assessing resolvability with agility and precision
Looking forward, we are already well underway with our third assessment of the major UK firms focused on the Continuity and Restructuring outcome. The assessment will conclude with the publication of the findings on 10 June 2027.
As I set out in my letter to CFOs Opens in a new window in February this year, our testing and assurance work for the third assessment has evolved and is:

More agile: recognising firms are doing their own testing, we have reduced overlaps in scope and sequenced or streamlined firm-specific engagement, without compromising our thematic, cohort-based approach.
More precise: we have worked with firms, supervisors and our Resolution Procurement Framework suppliers,footnote [8] building in their feedback to ensure we test effectively and realistically core capabilities for continuity and restructuring, including how they need to work together to deliver timely and robust outputs across the different phases of resolution contingency planning and execution.
And more holistic: our testing across barriers is for the first time guided by a resolution scenario, to provide a single thread running through the different tests and enhance realism. But ultimately the scenario is a means to an end of testing the capabilities.

The path ahead – for established firms on the resolvability journey
We are now at a level of maturity with bank resolution planning where we consider the policy landscape is well-established. That doesn’t mean we won’t continue to be responsive to learnings, nor will we stop considering the efficiency and proportionality of the regime. But the outcomes we need for resolution are timeless and cater for the different firms in scope of the UK resolution regime. Where the context surrounding firms is changing, we may need to look at how that alters our view of firms’ resolvability, in line with the RAF being a point-in-time assessment.
Within the major and mid-tier cohorts there are two broad groups of firms: those established on their resolvability journey and those newly coming into scope.
For the more established firms, ongoing maintenance is a key focus. This recognises these firms are resolvable. That doesn’t mean they don’t all have areas to work on or new issues won’t be identified by testing. For these firms, we will focus on remediation of past lessons, targeted testing, and reviewing assurance. But our approach will continue evolving, based also on feedback from the industry and our internal preparedness work.
We expect these firms to increasingly take even more of a lead on testing capabilities as part of their own assurance work, with a focus on holistic and realistic testing across barriers. The Bank will support firms, but we won’t be prescriptive – and rightly so, given where firms’ capabilities are. This approach will enable firms to structure their assurance in a way that works best for them, helping management achieve business objectives.
At the end of our third assessment in summer 2027, we will ask the major firms to present testing plans to us, informed by our RAF feedback. We will then engage bilaterally in a risk-based, proportionate way as firms undertake their testing plans. Where relevant, we will also engage with host authorities bilaterally and via Crisis Management Groups. I want to be clear though that we recognise that the cost for firms of maintaining resolvability is likely lower, all else equal, than the design and build phase, and this will be reflected in firms’ assurance plans.
We are planning that the fourth RAF assessment of major UK firms will not be before 2029-30. This will allow firms to focus on their testing plans and for the Bank to engage with firms and stakeholders to plan the assessment.
We will say more next summer, but as with the third assessment, we want to keep advancing and focusing on outcomes and how the Bank expects to use capabilities in a resolution.
The content and approach will reflect the findings from the third assessment, work done by firms in the interim and the circumstances at the time. But we will have a focus on the Co-ordination and Communication outcome.
Management, communication and governance capabilities lend themselves to assessing how resolvability barriers come together as a whole through the lens of simulations and senior management and board walkthroughs. So, it is likely this will be a feature. We will also maximise efficiencies between the Bank’s plans and firms’ multi-year testing plans.
Beyond that is very much in the medium term! But my expectation is that we will continue to embed resolvability assessment within firms.
Our approach to mid-tier firms with established capabilities will draw from our assessments of the major firms. But we will continue to take a proportionate approach. We will engage firms next summer on the scope and approach to the 2028 mid-tier assessment. Firms should expect a structured information request and Bank-led tests focusing on how capabilities would be used in practice. Following the third mid-tier assessment, we will consider our future approach based on firms’ progress.
The mid-tier cohort is a broad one, especially following the PRA’s doubling of the threshold for firms to be in scope of the major firm RAF.footnote [9] So, we will increasingly take a tailored approach to assessing the resolvability of mid-tier firms, based on size, complexity and resolution strategy. More complex mid-tier firms will rightly need to do more than simpler, smaller ones.
As a final thought on established firms, it is important that firms consider not just their own resolvability but their broader role in the financial system. For example, some firms act as FMI intermediaries by providing access to clearing, settlement or payment services to other banks and building societies. In these cases, providers of the intermediary service should continue to provide services, and plan accordingly, when clients are in resolution, so long as they continue to perform their obligations. They should also make information available to support clients’ resolution planning.footnote [10]
The path ahead – for those just joining us on the resolvability journey or those with more ground to cover
I will turn now to another group of firms – those just joining us on their resolvability journey or those with relatively more ground still to cover. We recognise that these firms are at a different stage on their resolvability journey and that requires a different approach from us.
This group comprises firms in a variety of situations. First, it includes firms that are growing into our thresholds and have work to do to build up their capabilities. Building capacity for resolution is essential and there is no time to waste. We will engage in a targeted and technical way with these firms, supporting them to get up the curve as quickly as possible. These firms must own their resolvability and build quickly and effectively, making the most of our established policy landscape.
More established firms may also find themselves in this group where there is substantially more work to do on their resolvability. This could happen for various reasons such as because firms are making material changes to their business, such as mergers or acquisitions, which affect their ability to achieve the resolvability outcomes. We expect firms to consider their resolvability as they go through these changes, to update us on material changes and to remediate issues that would impede resolution. We will engage with firms closely throughout this process until they reach a steady state again. It may take time for firms to make the necessary changes. But we expect firms to demonstrate they have a plan and that they have considered the impact of any integration actions on resolvability.
Established RAF firms may also have more work to do where the issues we have identified have persisted and are not being adequately remediated. In such cases, you should expect us to co-ordinate our engagement closely with the PRA. You may also see us deploying our powers to appoint skilled persons. We will do this in a targeted way and as part of a wider engagement plan with each firm.
Testing has an important role to play for all of these firms as they build or enhance their capabilities. A common feature of our approach to all these groups is the involvement of technical, dedicated specialists to support our firm-facing teams where needed. Third-party advisers on our Resolution Procurement Framework have a crucial role to play here. You should expect us to work more regularly with them as providers of market and operational expertise to support the design of the Bank’s assessments and in undertaking skilled persons reviews if required.
Beyond banks
Banks are not the only firms with resolution regimes, as Dave Ramsden noted in January. We are building out our regime for UK central counterparties (CCPs). While the capabilities will be different than for banks, the underlying expectation of resolvability is the same. In May, we published a Discussion Paper that sets out three draft outcomes for a CCP to be considered resolvable.footnote [11] This is a first step to invite feedback from industry on our thinking. Subject to the responses to the Discussion Paper, we expect to consult later this year on more detailed resolvability expectations, which are proportionate and reflective of the risks that a CCP failure would pose.
Conclusion
So, we have collectively come a long way towards the outcome of ongoing resolvability. This matters because a credible, effective and responsive resolution regime which is proportionate underpins financial stability and supports growth. But resolvability is a journey that can never be ‘done’. Firms, whatever waypoint they have reached on their resolvability journey, need to make sure they build and maintain their capabilities, so they are prepared for resolution on an ongoing basis. Testing must increasingly be at the heart of this. And we need to remain agile and responsive, and focused on outcomes, so we are ready and able to execute a resolution if needed in testing times.
I would like to thank Adam Cull, Kat Hind, Pauline Maburutse, Jane Maxwell and Matt Wooderson for their help in preparing these remarks. I would also like to thank Andrew Bailey, Dave Ramsden, Jackie Tibbetts and Robert Zammit for their helpful comments.

articles.title: Self-reports, scenarios, and games: lessons from measuring socioemotional skills in three African countries
articles.text:
Published on
Development Impact

Self-reports, scenarios, and games: lessons from measuring socioemotional skills in three African countries: Guest post by Smita Das, Clara Delavallade, and Noël Muller

Development Impact Guest Blogger

October 21, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Socioemotional skills – those we use to manage our emotions, collaborate, and strive toward goals – are central to impactful entrepreneurship programs, vocational training programs, and safe space clubs for youth and adults. Yet capturing improvements in these latent skills is hard and telling which skills drive economic empowerment and mental health is harder. Many studies rely on a few familiar concepts (self-efficacy, locus of control, grit) that reflect neither the range of socioemotional skills nor the skills the intervention teaches, often bundled into a single “noncognitive skills” index.
The World Bank’s Africa Gender Innovation Lab (GIL) and Innovations for Poverty Action (IPA) partnered to tackle this through the ESTEEM project (Effective Socioemotional skills To gain Economic EMpowerment) and associated research agenda. An earlier post sums up the agenda and findings so far. Here we focus on the nuts and bolts: how we developed self-report and behavioral measures of 14 skills for randomized evaluations in Côte d’Ivoire, Nigeria, and Tanzania, what we dropped along the way, and what we would tell a team adding socioemotional skill measures to its next survey.
Which skills to measure
We started from a review of 81 economics and psychology studies, including how skills differ by gender and relate to labor outcomes, and drew on experts, focus groups, and the CASEL and Goleman emotional intelligence frameworks. The result is a list of 14 nonoverlapping skills for youth and adults, grouped into awareness vs. management and intrapersonal vs. interpersonal skills (Figure 1). Note that some items from these measures also map to a measure of generalized self-efficacy. Also, other soft skills concepts such as beliefs and motivation were purposefully excluded. Detailed definitions and the theory of change can be found here.
Figure 1. The 14 socioemotional skills of the ESTEEM framework

How we built and tested each measure
For each skill, we developed a self-report and at least one behavioral assessment, so we could compare the two. Working with psychologists, assessment experts, and field coordinators, we took each measure through these steps across pilots and the three evaluations.
We began by reviewing existing measures to assess their fit with our skill definitions, links to labor outcomes, and evidence of validity in Africa or elsewhere. We also evaluated feasibility, prioritizing measures that could be administered in under five minutes per skill, used offline in household surveys, and limited in their overlap with other measures.
To establish face and content validity, we used expert review, focus groups, cognitive testing with 48 people across the three countries, and careful translation reviewed by a psychologist using this rubric (p. 6). We assessed reliability and validity using inter-item correlations (>0.2, <0.8), Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega, factor analysis, item response theory, and associations with employment, decision-making power, and mental health. We treated standard cutoffs (e.g., alpha ≥ 0.7; CFI ≥ 0.95; RMSEA ≤ 0.08) as rules of thumb, retaining items essential to content validity when a scale fell just short. We also iteratively improved measures, revising and removing items across rounds of data collection.
Coverage was incomplete in two countries: while we collected for both measures and all skills at multiple time points in Tanzania, COVID-19 limited baseline data collection in Nigeria, where we also collected only 7 self-reports at endline, and in Côte d’Ivoire we collected abbreviated behavioral measures (using only one scenario) for only 9 skills.
Self-reports: cheap and familiar, but prone to bias
Self-reports aggregate answers to a few survey questions (“items”) about how people see their own thoughts and behaviors (e.g., “I plan tasks carefully,” on a 5-point Likert scale). They are cheap and easy to add to a survey, but answers can depend on the setting respondents have in mind (household, work, community), who they compare themselves to, or the time period they consider. Respondents may agree with everything, give the obviously “best” answer, or lack the self-awareness to answer accurately. And behaviors that signal a skill in Western contexts may not apply elsewhere (eye contact as a sign of listening, for example).
Many self-report measures already existed, especially for intrapersonal skills, but few had been validated in African settings. Because existing measures often combined multiple interpersonal skills into a single construct, we worked with a psychologist developed several new interpersonal scales.
Two lessons emerged from this process. First, reverse-coded items did not work. We initially mixed positively and negatively framed items to detect and control for acquiescence bias, but respondents found the variation confusing, and the two sets of items loaded onto separate factors, a pattern also documented in other studies, particularly when translated. Second, a visual response scale, designed to reduce cognitive load, saved time. When shown an image of the scale, respondents could more easily remember the full range of options and quickly point to their answer.
The final self-report items and instructions (7 to 14 items per skill) are publicly available, as is the paper on their development and validation.
Behavioral measures: what we kept and what we dropped
Past Development Impact posts have covered group exercises in Jordan, number games in Türkiye, and EEGs, facial expression readings, and games in Central America. We tested four types: performance tasks, situational judgment tests, group activities, and household informant reports (see the paper on behavioral measures (Table M1) for all those we considered).
Performance tasks. At first, we saw performance tasks as the gold standard. But many took more than five minutes or could not run offline, and a task often captures only one facet of a skill, so its content can differ sharply from a self-report measure of the same skill. Short tasks are also harder to validate, since reliability and construct validity usually require repeated attempts at the same or related tasks. We kept continuous performance tasks for self-control, a triangle counting game for perseverance, and listening comprehension prompts. Enumerators also coded active listening, attention during the survey (self-control), and open-ended answers on respondent self-awareness and how respondents would solve problems and make decisions or influence others.
Situational judgment tests (SJTs). We also developed situational judgment tests, in which respondents indicate how they would act in hypothetical scenarios. By focusing on concrete situations rather than abstract judgments about oneself, SJTs leave less room for interpretation, reducing domain ambiguity and reference bias. The desirable response is also often less obvious.
Several design choices strengthened the SJTs. We developed scenarios through focus groups and drew response options from interviews with entrepreneurs and employees, socioemotional skills curricula, and self-report items, helping maintain common content validity across measure types. Rather than asking respondents to rank actions, we asked how likely they were to take each action, reducing cognitive load and literacy demands. We also developed separate household and workplace scenarios for each skill because behavior can vary across settings. As with the self-reports, the response scale was displayed visually.
Respondents liked the SJTs: they held their interest and were easy to understand. The tests also adapted well across contexts. Changing details such as businesses, currencies, and names made it possible to localize a scenario while keeping the response options broadly similar.
Group activities and household informant reports were dropped after testing with large samples, mostly for feasibility reasons. Replicating the group exercises used in Jordan (e.g., redesigning a failing amusement park) meant costly logistics to assemble participants and evaluators, and people behaved differently depending on their group, making individual skills hard to pin down. For informant reports, the household member who knew most about the respondent’s time use and income-generating activities answered the externally observable self-report items. Finding and waiting for informants slowed the survey or led to missing data, and the data quality (judged by correlation with labor outcomes) did not justify the cost.
Does the choice of measure matter? Yes
Behavioral measures we use take about twice as long to administer as self-reports. Self-reports required 2-3 minutes per skill, whereas performance tasks and SJTs required 4-6 minutes. Both types of measures also require extensive cognitive interviewing and enumerator training when introduced in a new setting.
Measures intended to capture the same skill often disagree. Correlations depended more on the type of measure than on the skill being assessed, and two measures of the same skill were often only weakly correlated, with coefficients no higher than about 0.4. The choice of measure can also produce different conclusions about gender gaps. Among jobless youth in Tanzania, young men scored about 0.2 standard deviations higher than young women on self-reports, significant across skills, whereas behavioral measures revealed only small gaps of 0.08 standard deviations or less, significant for only a few skills. This suggests that self-reports may overstate both men’s socioemotional skills and the corresponding gender gap.
The two types of measures also predicted different outcomes. Across all three countries, both were significantly correlated with labor market, mental health, and well-being outcomes, although the results were highly context dependent. Updated results reveal that behavioral measures varied more across skills and tended to be more strongly associated with labor force participation, decision-making power, mental health, and gender norms. Self-reports were more strongly associated with income aspirations, while findings for income were mixed. Relationship management, problem solving and decision making, and emotional regulation were often among the strongest predictors of outcomes. One important caveat is that socioemotional skills may not correlate with economic outcomes in contexts where work, or certain types of work, is not considered a desirable goal.
Finally, changes in behavioral measures tracked changes in outcomes over time. In Tanzania, where most measures were collected at several points, changes in behavioral measures of socioemotional skills significantly predicted changes in employment, hours worked, decision-making power, and well-being. Changes in self-reports performed better only in predicting reported job search.
Takeaways for your next evaluation
· Measure the skills your program actually targets and report them separately rather than as one index.
· Don’t rely on self-reports alone, especially if you want to track individual progress or compare groups such as women and men.
· Spend time on socioemotional skill measures upfront: translation and enumerator practice are essential to cultural adaptation and bias reduction.
· Consider domain, as individuals will use skills differently at home, work, and in the community.
· Budget survey time and prioritize. At 2–6 minutes per skill per measure, covering many skills adds up quickly.
What’s next
ESTEEM so far shows that the choice of measure can change the answer to which skills matter. Upcoming ESTEEM papers will report on randomized evaluations that taught different sets of skills (e.g., awareness versus management), measuring impacts on labor market outcomes, mental health, and gender equity. The first are out for Nigeria and Tanzania.

Smita Das (World Bank and IPA); Clara Delavallade (World Bank), and Noël Muller (World Bank and IDB)

articles.title: Innovation Insights Quarterly: Q4 2026 | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
Sometimes, innovations realize their biggest impact outside the field that produced them. From advances in materials science that enhance electric vehicle batteries, to autonomous flights that could reshape traditional logistics, this quarter’s selections show how innovation in one field can unlock new possibilities in another.

The Brain Found to Be Two Organs, Not One

Researchers found that the brain is comprised of two distinct organs that evolved independently and later became intertwined. From a functionality standpoint, the forebrain is heavily involved in thinking and decision-making, while the hindbrain helps control movement and basic capabilities such as breathing and swallowing. Because scientists had long assumed that these parts of the brain shared a common starting point, attempts to grow hindbrain nerve cells in the lab failed, as they used the wrong precursor cells. Using the correct starting cells, the researchers successfully grew working human hindbrain nerve cells from stem cells.1

Why it matters: Growing hindbrain cells could make it easier to study diseases such as ALS, which damage the nerve cells that control movement.2 The CDC projects that about 34,720 US adults will be living with ALS in 2026.3 A reliable supply of these cells could help researchers study how the disease progresses and test potential treatments.

Two Brains Are Better Than One

A new study led by Stanford Medicine found the brain is two separate organs adjacent to one another. The finding could aid research into devastating neurological diseases.

For illustrative purposes only.

Autonomous Plane Completes First Cross-Country Flight

An electric aviation company reported that an aircraft, retrofitted with its self-flying technology, flew across the United States with no intervention from the onboard safety pilot. The system handled every major stage of the trip, from taxiing and takeoff to navigation and landing, under remote supervision. Notably, it did this on an existing aircraft, showing that autonomy can be added to planes already in service rather than requiring an entirely new design.4

Why it matters: Air cargo represents less than 1% of global trade by weight but close to one-third by value, reflecting its importance for products where speed and reliability matter most.5 Autonomous aircraft could change how valuable and time-sensitive goods move around the world. The ability to complete long flights autonomously opens a new path for making this critical transportation network more flexible.

New Extraction Process Unlocks Lithium

Researchers have developed a process for refining spodumene, a common hard-rock source of lithium. Traditional methods roast the mineral at more than 1,000°C,6 while the new process soaks it in a

reusable chemical bath at temperatures below 100°C.7 The new process breaks it apart. Along with lithium suitable for batteries, the process also produces the usable byproducts alumina and silica.8

Why it matters: Lithium is a key ingredient in the rechargeable batteries that power electric vehicles, phones and laptops. These batteries are also playing an increasingly important role in storing electricity for the grid. The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects global lithium demand to triple by 2035, but currently announced mining projects are projected to supply only about 60% of what's needed.9 If the new process holds up at industrial scale, it could widen the pool of lithium resources that can be produced economically as demand continues to rise.

Robot Draws Your Blood

The US Food and Drug Administration has authorized a robotic device that can complete a standard blood draw without a human placing the needle. Today, however, a trained phlebotomist, the specialist who normally performs blood draws, is still required to supervise. The robot uses near-infrared imaging and ultrasound to choose a suitable vein, then automatically applies the tourniquet, prepares the skin, inserts the needle, changes the collection tube and places the bandage.10

Why it matters: One phlebotomist can oversee as many as three devices, turning a repetitive procedure into a supervised workflow rather than a one-worker-per-patient task.11 This development is particularly striking because a 2025 Microsoft study placed phlebotomists last in a ranking of professions most vulnerable to AI replacement, since drawing blood is a hands-on activity.12

Paint Cools Without Power

Researchers have developed a new class of paint coatings that can keep surfaces cooler by reflecting sunlight and releasing heat as infrared radiation. The result is a surface that stays cooler without using any electricity. One coating keeps surfaces about 8°C (roughly 14°F) cooler than ordinary white paint by reflecting 93% of sunlight, compared with 84% for standard commercial paint.13

Why it matters: If these coatings can be made cheap and durable, they could be applied to roofs and exterior walls that take the brunt of the sun, easing the load on air conditioners. That matters because the IEA estimates that air conditioners and electric fans account for nearly 20% of the electricity used in buildings worldwide.14 Given how much of the world's building electricity already goes to cooling, coatings that lower that demand could ease pressure on power grids and reduce energy costs on a global scale.
