Key takeaways

The AI boom is bigger for U.S. demand than for U.S. GDP. Much of the equipment behind the AI buildout is imported, reducing the direct contribution to domestic production even as investment and rising equity wealth support the broader economy.
America invests, while a global supply chain produces. U.S. AI spending is transmitting a substantial growth impulse abroad, particularly to Asian economies deeply embedded in semiconductor and technology manufacturing.
The key risk is deceleration, not necessarily a bust. With AI now a key support to global investment, trade, industrial production, and financial conditions, even still-high capex could become less supportive of global growth if its pace of expansion slows.

In light of accelerating global fragmentation and geopolitical conflict, many governments and businesses are investing in resilience. That imperative has coincided with the emergence of AI, a technology that can expand the frontier of what is possible. As a result, technology security is becoming a pillar of national economic security strategy.
As we discuss in our latest Cyclical Outlook, “Growth Holds, Risks Widen,” the result has been an unprecedented wave of investment commitments to expand AI-related infrastructure. At the time of this writing, announced capital spending by large U.S. technology companies points to more than $1 trillion of investment in 2026, according to company filings, with roughly $1.5 trillion in additional outlays forecast thereafter.
But AI was never simply a U.S. investment story. The infrastructure buildout is supporting U.S. demand, production across the global technology supply chain, and increasingly investment in other economies. That has made AI an important source of support for both the U.S. and global expansions.
By the same token, it is also becoming an important cyclical risk. Crucially, AI investment does not have to collapse for its contribution to growth to fade. Because economic growth depends on the change in spending rather than its level, even still-high investment can provide a diminishing impulse if its growth rate slows.
Below, we highlight three observations about how the AI investment cycle is already reshaping the global economy.

AI is supporting the U.S. economy through more than just investment

First, AI investment is lifting U.S. domestic demand, but its high import content substantially reduces the direct impact on real U.S. GDP growth. Nevertheless, AI is also lifting the U.S. economy in other ways. Expectations for higher productivity have propelled the U.S. stock market and appear to have shifted consumer habits toward more spending – and this “wealth effect” is contributing to stronger demand.
Some background on how U.S. economic output is measured is useful here. GDP records where production occurs, not simply where investment spending occurs. A server or graphics card purchased by a U.S. data center raises U.S. investment regardless of where it was produced. But if that equipment is imported, the transaction also raises imports, which are subtracted in the expenditure calculation of GDP. In other words, the investment data capture the acquisition of productive capital, while the import adjustment ensures that foreign production is not counted as U.S. output.
The National Income and Product Accounts (NIPAs), published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), do not identify AI investment as a stand-alone category. Instead, AI investment spans several components of nonresidential fixed investment, including information-processing equipment, software, R&D, data center structures, and power infrastructure. By combining the main AI-related investment categories with corresponding trade and inventory flows, we can estimate the net domestic growth impulse.
From these calculations, we estimate that AI-related investment has directly contributed only about 0.4 percentage point to annualized quarterly real U.S. GDP growth on average since the beginning of 2025, out of roughly 2% overall GDP growth over that period (see Figure 1) – a relatively minor amount.

Figure 1: AI’s contribution to real U.S. growth has fluctuated and is modestly net positive

Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis National Income and Product Accounts data and PIMCO calculations through 30 June 2026

But that substantially understates the scale of the investment boom itself. We estimate AI-related investment has contributed roughly 1.2 percentage points to the 2.7% average annualized growth in U.S. domestic demand over the same period (see Figure 2). In other words, the boost to U.S. spending has been much larger than the boost to U.S. production because a significant share of that spending has been on imported goods.

Figure 2: AI has driven meaningful contributions to U.S. domestic demand

Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis National Income and Product Accounts data and PIMCO calculations through 30 June 2026

Direct investment is not the only channel through which the AI boom is supporting the U.S. economy. AI-related optimism also appears to be supporting growth through financial conditions. Expectations for higher future productivity and earnings have contributed to strong U.S. equity valuations, boosting household wealth and supporting consumption.
Using the Federal Reserve’s framework for estimating the growth impulse from financial conditions (see our 30 September 2026 Macro Signposts), we estimate that the equity wealth channel has provided roughly an additional 0.5–0.7 percentage point of support for growth – roughly 1x to 1.5x the growth impulse of the investment itself.
Taken together, these estimates suggest that AI-related forces have provided meaningful support to U.S. growth, even though the direct domestic investment effect is considerably smaller than the headline capex figures might imply.

America invests, Asia produces

Second, what leaks out of U.S. GDP through imports does not disappear from global GDP. The processors, servers, and networking equipment imported to construct U.S. data centers represent production and income somewhere else.
Robust U.S. demand (see Figure 3) has consequently provided a powerful impulse to economies embedded in the AI hardware supply chain. Our updated trade data show particularly large AI-related export exposures equivalent to roughly 30% of GDP for Taiwan and more than 15% for South Korea (see Figure 4), illustrating how large the technology cycle has become relative to the underlying economies. Mexico has also become an important part of the North American supply chain.
These measures capture gross export exposure relative to GDP, rather than the domestic value-added contribution of AI-related exports. Nevertheless, they illustrate the scale of the global supply chain exposure to the investment boom.

Figure 3: U.S. and other developed markets are importing AI-related components

Source: UN Comtrade Database and PIMCO calculations as of 30 June 2026

Figure 4: AI-related exports have become a meaningful share of key producers’ overall GDP

Source: UN Comtrade Database and PIMCO calculations as of 30 June 2026

In other words, high import content limits the direct U.S. growth contribution from AI investment, but the U.S. simultaneously exports part of the investment impulse to the rest of the world. The U.S. capex boom is therefore increasingly supporting a much broader manufacturing and trade cycle, particularly across the Asian technology supply chain.

The investment cycle is broadening beyond the U.S.

Third and finally, the U.S. is no longer the only important source of AI infrastructure demand. China was also an early mover, and other parts of Asia and the Middle East are increasingly investing in computing capacity, data centers, and the supporting infrastructure needed to power them.Footnote1 As more economies seek to build domestic computing capacity, AI infrastructure investment is increasingly interacting with broader national priorities around technology security, energy availability, and supply chain resilience.
The result is that the global AI capex cycle has become an important driver of global industrial production and trade. Even against relatively muted aggregate global industrial production growth, production of computers, electronics, and related equipment has been exceptionally strong. In other words, it is producing a distinct global industrial cycle that is helping global production, while also increasing the number of economies that could be affected by an eventual slowdown.

Figure 5: Global industrial production of computers and electronics is on a multi-year upswing

Source: Various national statistical agencies, Haver Analytics, and PIMCO calculations as of August 2026. PIMCO Global IP (industrial production) data aggregates industrial production across sectors and countries using TIVA (trade in value added) weights.

Implications: A global growth engine, and a source of risk

AI was never simply a U.S. investment story. In the U.S., the direct contribution from investment is actually much smaller than the headline spending numbers suggest because so much of the equipment is imported. But the overall growth effect is larger once the equity wealth channel is included, and what subtracts from U.S. growth is added to global growth.
AI is therefore delivering several impulses at once: investment demand in the U.S. and other economies, manufacturing and exports across the global technology supply chain, and a financial conditions impulse through equity markets. Together, these forces have become an important source of support for the global expansion.
But that support also creates a new source of cyclical concentration. For the growth outlook, what matters is not simply the level of AI investment, but how long investment can continue to accelerate. The infrastructure buildout does not need to collapse for the growth impulse to diminish. It merely needs to slow. And when it does, it would have global implications – especially if the productivity gains aren’t being realized fast enough to be an offset.
Bottom line: The same forces that have made the global expansion more resilient have therefore also created a new source of cyclical concentration. AI is supporting U.S. demand, Asian production, and global investment simultaneously. That makes the boom a powerful global growth engine, but also one of the more important downside risks to the outlook if momentum fades.

1 François de Soyres, Alex Haag, Mike Liu, and Eva Van Leemput. “The Global Trade Effects of the AI Infrastructure Boom.” U.S. Federal Reserve FEDS Notes (13 February 2026). Return to content↩

articles.title: Weekly links October 23: macro impacts of migration on poverty, big African cities and jobs, how to read a paper, and more…
articles.text:
Published on
Development Impact

Weekly links October 23: macro impacts of migration on poverty, big African cities and jobs, how to read a paper, and more…

David McKenzie

October 23, 2026

This page in:

English

English

· How Nepal reduced poverty through international migration: Mahesh Shrestha has an excellent explanation of Nepal’s use of migration in In Development “In 1995, seven in 10 Nepalis lived in extreme poverty. By 2022, fewer than one in 40 did…Compared to the giants of extreme poverty reduction — China, Indonesia, Vietnam, Bangladesh, and India — Nepal’s pace is matched only by China. The extreme poverty rate in Nepal now is lower than in the considerably richer Indonesia, India, and Bangladesh. Nepal’s journey out of extreme poverty also looked very different from that of these other countries. These countries — responsible for the global decline of extreme poverty from 43% in 1990 to 10% in 2025 — did it through sustained growth, foreign direct investment, export expansion, and industrialization. Nepal had almost none of that….Nepal’s escape from extreme poverty was built not on factories or foreign investment but on the export of labor.”
· African cities, urbanization, and jobs: This piece in the FT on Africa’s explosive growth in cities has sparked a bit of discussion. “African cities expanded by 15mn people annually in the past few years and are expected to grow by 19mn annually by 2050. That’s almost two Londons a year, or more than 50,000 new African city dwellers every day….A big question for Africa over the coming decades is whether rapid urbanisation will eventually lead to faster growth and higher incomes. Or alternatively, will overstretched cities with a desperate lack of infrastructure and few formal jobs become epicentres of poverty and popular unrest?”. The piece goes on to discuss how poor infrastructure, sprawling unplanned cities, and a lack of industrialization to accompany the growth have limited the jobs benefits. It gives a great example of someone who by survey definitions is working, but is not what most people would consider when they say they want a job “One young man patrols the streets with a pair of nail clippers, cutting customers’ nails for a few cents.”. My big problem with stories like this is that they don’t typically take the counterfactual of what people would be doing had they not urbanized. This UN report on African cities notes “This report presents compelling evidence - from 2,600 cities across 34 countries - that urbanisation in Africa contributes to better economic outcomes and higher standards of living. It shows that in most socio economic dimensions, Africa’s cities significantly outperform the countries in which they are located, and that the gap between the performance of African cities and the national averages is larger than in many other parts of the world. One of the most underappreciated achievements of African cities over the last 30 years has been that, despite growing by 500 million people, they have maintained their economic performance, providing several hundred million people with better jobs and improved access to services and infrastructure.” - we can both ask how can things be better, but also should ask “better compared to what”.
· ETRM interviews Deniz Sanin and finds out how she got her research idea in a Starbucks. Also nice advice on reading papers “I think it’s important to read a paper from the perspective of: What’s the contribution, and what’s the gap? We have a tendency to focus just on the identification and the result. But if someone has made this contribution, what’s the next step? Sometimes it can be low-hanging fruit. Sometimes it’s just a question where someone says A, another person says B, but is it A or B, or is it maybe C?”
· How well can AI do your code now? In VoxEU, Sebastian Galiani, Federico López and Raul Sosa report on a benchmark exercise of 40 econometric tasks done in Stata, R and Python with LLMs. “We built a benchmark of 40 econometric tasks covering linear regression, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, discrete choice, survival analysis, and time series. Each task states the method and comes with a simulated dataset and a reference output computed in advance….For each task, two leading models write a script, as a chatbot that never runs it and as an agent that runs and revises it. Letting the models run their code raises the share of correct results from 79% to 97% and makes the prompt and the software matter far less. The failures that remain under the agent come from scripts that run without errors but return wrong numbers, and detecting them is still the researcher’s work.”
· Subsidizing posting formal vacancies did not lead Ethiopian firms to hire more: In VoxDev, Lukas Hensel, Tsegay Tekleselassie and Marc Witte summarize an experiment they did in Ethiopia. They subsidized the cost of SMEs advertising vacancies through formal channels such as newspapers and job boards. They find firms post more white-collar vacancies as a result, but don’t increase hiring of these workers, who demand higher wages. One explanation is that inexperienced firms don’t know how expensive (in terms of wages) it is to fill these positions, learn about it by advertising, and then as a result don’t hire – but the subsidies allow them to at least test the market.

David McKenzie

Lead Economist, Development Research Group, World Bank

Global highlights of Q3’26

After three quarters, global PE investment stood at $1.5 trillionThe rolling-twelve month totals $2.1 trillion in Q3’26, despite a small dip from $2.3 trillion in Q2’26, and deal volume falling to 20,362Global carve-out deal value was $182.2 billion across 1,254 deals at the end of Q3’26At the sector level, the technology, media, and telecom sector had the greatest total investment ($479.1 billion across 4508 deals) at the end of Q3’26, followed by energy and natural resources ($243.3 billion) — which was on track for a new record, and consumer and retail ($177.2 billion).

Download the report

opens in a new tab

Global PE market remains selective but strong, with $1.5 trillion invested at end of Q3’26

Selectivity has been the key theme in the global PE market in 2026, and the results as of the of Q3’26 reflect this; after three quarters, global PE investment stood at $1.5 trillion — on pace to be the third best year of PE investment on record after 2021 and 2025, while deal volume was on pace for the slowest year since 2020 at 14,650 deals. The rolling-twelve month totals echoed this trend, with the rolling twelve month total holding strong at $2.2 trillion in Q3’26, despite a small dip from $2.3 trillion in Q2’26, and deal volume falling to 20,362 — the lowest rolling twelve month total seen since Q1’21.The continued concentration of capital on high conviction assets reflects a range of factors, from continued exit challenges to ongoing geopolitical tensions and conflicts. Concerns about energy costs, energy availability in some jurisdictions, rising inflation, and interest rate increases have also helped keep PE investors focused on top tier assets and value creation opportunities.

Americas attracts largest share of global PE investment, but ASPAC on track for best year since 2021

As of the end of Q3’26, the Americas had $854.6 billion in PE investment across 6,845 deals, putting the region well ahead of EMA, which had $521.3 billion across 6,249 deals, and ASPAC, which had $137.8 billion across 1,109 deals. The US accounted for $793.4 billion across 6,223 deals of the Americas’ total at the end of Q3’26; it also attracted the largest PE deal globally during Q3’26: the $9.6 billion buyout of the Seattle Seahawks football team.While PE investment was solid across all three regions, only ASPAC was on an upward trajectory compared to 2025, with its deal value on pace for its strongest year since 2021 and its deal volume on track to improve slightly. ASPAC’s results were propelled by several large transactions, including the $8.2 billion take private of logistics provider Qube Holdings and the $5.4 billion take private of insurance broker network Steadfast Group in Q3’26.The regional rolling twelve-month totals showed a similar, with PE investment and deals volume in the Americas dropping from $1.3 trillion and 10,115 deals in Q2’26 to $1.2 trillion and 9.414 deals in Q3’26, EMA seeing a decline from $818.1 billion and 9,251 deals in Q1’26 to $764.3 billion and 8,805 deals, and ASPAC seeing an increase in PE investment from $171 billion in Q2’26 to $181.3 billion in Q3’26 while its deal volume dipped slightly from 1,517 deals to 1,504 deals.

AI ecosystem plays see strong PE interest, energy sector on track for new record high of PE investment

Globally, AI has been a major recipient of PE attention and investment for some time now. But over the past few quarters, there has been a notable evolution in the interest of PE investors. While some are still primarily focused on the tech equation, on assessing how companies and industries will be affected by the rapid evolution of AI and on using AI to drive value creation within their portfolio companies, many are now looking at the expansive AI ecosystem for deal opportunities — from data centers and electrical equipment to power generation.The energy sector has been a major beneficiary of the growing focus in AI given its essential role in fueling AI capacity. As of the end of Q3’26, the energy and natural resources sector was at $243.3 billion in investment, within reach of a new record high. During Q3’26, the sector attracted a number of large deals globally, including the $7.7 billion take private of Ireland-based off grid energy company DCC power, the $7 billion secondary buyout of US-based energy storage and renewables company Aypa Power, the $3 billion buyout of US-based oil and gas exploration company VTX Energy Partners, the $2.1 billion buyout of Australia-based energy infrastructure firm Plus ES.

Trends to watch for in Q4’26

Heading into Q4’26 and into 2027, PE investment globally is expected to remain highly selective, with PE investors continuing to concentrate on resilient businesses, sectors relevant to the AI ecosystem — like infrastructure and energy, industrial tech, and healthcare. Take privates will likely remain a major focus for PE investors given the perceived value opportunity there, in addition to carve outs as corporates look to support their AI initiatives. Exit activity will be critical to watch, although exit volume might not rise substantively without a valuation refinement on the sell-side in order to fully reopen the sponsor-to-sponsor market. IPO markets outside of the US, Hong Kong, and India will likely also need to see a reopening. Although IPO activity in the US could be quite soft given the degree of macroeconomic uncertainty, the number of pulled IPOs late in Q3’26, and the midterm elections scheduled for Q4’26. Fundraising will likely remain soft and highly concentrated on large funds and fund managers with proven ability to return capital.

Globally, the energy sector is seeing incredible interest from private equity, driven by a combination of rising power consumption, the major demand for energy infrastructure to fuel AI, and the growing focus on energy security in different jurisdictions. And that’s on top of the energy transition and the need to upgrade aging infrastructure. As sectors go, it’s clearly
a standout.

Gavin Geminder

Global Private Capital Leader

KPMG International

The income produced by municipal bonds is typically exempt from income taxes at the federal level. Municipal bonds may also be exempt from state and local taxes based on where the investor resides.

In our view, there are many good reasons to invest in the municipal bond market now.
First, muni yields are as high as they've been in 15 years following two years of unprecedented interest rate hikes by the Fed.4
Second, municipal bonds have a long history of low defaults compared to corporate bonds because they fund essential American services.5
Third, the municipal yield curve is steeper than the Treasury yield curve. A steep yield curve means that there is value in duration. Municipal investors who own longer dated munis may be compensated much more than those in longer dated Treasuries.
Fourth, federal, state and in some places local tax rates are high and we don't see them going down. This may provide additional value to the muni tax exemption.

Our high conviction approach to investing aims to deliver a highly competitive yield by exploiting anomalies that exist in the high yield municipal market. The Invesco Municipal Bond team employs a bottom-up, research-oriented approach to generate income-driven total return. Our experienced credit research staff works to uncover value in non-rated bonds, which may offer the potential for higher yield and total return.

We believe in giving investors choices that work for their unique needs. Invesco Rochester High Yield Municipal ETF is an actively managed exchange-traded fund that seeks current income exempt from federal income tax.

We view risk from multiple lenses and manage it using both integrated and independent approaches. First, risk management is embedded within our investment process. Second, multiple governance structures provide independent oversight and monitoring. Third comes senior management and board review.

articles.title: View from the markets: Why have emerging market tech stocks been so volatile? - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

Away from European bond markets, the major story for equity markets has been renewed volatility in emerging market (EM) semiconductor and technology hardware stocks. An index of these companies has dropped back towards the lows of late July, though they are still 1.8% above that level. This leaves them 28% below the July peak but with a year-to-date gain of 47%.

While the declines from the highs are unfortunate, this level of volatility should not be surprising. Estimates of the impact of the artificial intelligence phenomenon on the economy and on corporate profits range widely. This can be seen in the rising standard deviation of estimates for EM tech hardware stocks, which has jumped from 10 at the beginning of the year to 82 today. By contrast, the variation for non-tech stocks has stayed constant at around five (see Exhibit 1).

The consequence of the current high degree of uncertainty is that any marginal information can lead to a big change in the forecast for corporate profits, which can then lead to a big change in the stock price.

The key factor for investors with a longer-term time horizon is that the earnings growth in the years ahead should nonetheless be significantly positive; current forecasts for the next two years are near 90%. If in the end it turns out to be some (modest) percentage greater or less than those forecasts is secondary.

articles.title: Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot
articles.text:
Physical shocks and economic resilience: a central bank perspective − speech by James Talbot

Given at the 2nd Annual Conference on Sustainable Finance at the Banco de México on 21 October 2026

Published on
23 October 2026

James Talbot, Executive Director for International at the Bank of England and the Bank’s Executive Sponsor for climate, explains how physical climate shocks can affect inflation and output, and how central banks can assess and respond to them. He considers two connected horizons: their near-term effects on monetary policy, and the longer-term role of economic resilience, adaptation and insurance in helping economies absorb future shocks and support price and financial stability.

Speech
Physical shocks increasingly matter for central banks
Governor, distinguished guests, I am sorry that I cannot be there with you in person at such a prestigious event. It is very much an honour and a pleasure, and my thanks to Dr. Fabrizio López-Gallo Dey for inviting me to speak today.
The physical impacts of climate change are becoming larger and more proximate, and their short-term economic impacts are also increasing. Annual global damages from weather-related events have more than doubled since the early 2000s, reaching over $200bn in 2025footnote [1].
In light of that, the economic effects of climate change are increasingly on the radar of central bankers. When extreme weather events affect production, output and inflation, that matters for our primary goal of maintaining price stability.
Let me take two examples that are close to home:
Increasingly high summer temperatures reduce water levels on key transport arteries for industrial trade, like the River Rhine in Germany. When water levels fall, ships reduce the amount of cargo they carry, disrupting the movement of goods and increasing transport costs.
Such exceptionally low water levels have become a recurring feature in recent years. The economic effects have also been material: recent research estimates that 30 days of low water on the Rhine reduces German industrial production by around 1%footnote [2].
In October 2024, extreme rainfall caused devastating flash floods in Valencia. Aside from the tragic loss of human life, economic losses amounted to over 20% of regional GDP. Spanish Q4 GDP growth was reduced by between 0.1 and 0.2 percentage pointsfootnote [3].
The economic impact would have been larger were it not for the high level of insurance protection for affected households and businesses. Around 250,000 insurance claims were filed following the floods and Spain's Insurance Compensation Consortium had paid more than €4bn in compensation by late 2025, making this the largest event the scheme has ever managedfootnote [4].
Even countries like the UK, which may be less susceptible to large physical shocks, can be affected by the impact of events abroad.
Over the past four years, as chair of the NGFS Workstream on Monetary Policy, I have worked together with more than sixty central banks to set out a framework to assess the impact of climate change on the economy, to measure its effects and to determine what monetary policymakers should do about it.
I’ll talk today about how the physical impacts of climate change can affect the economy in the near term; how we diagnose their magnitude, persistence and propagation; whether their effects belong in the central forecast or in the risks around it; and how that diagnosis informs monetary policy judgements. We set out each of these steps in an NGFS guide for monetary policymakers that we published earlier this yearfootnote [5].
I also want to look beyond the near-term policy horizon. In particular, how repeated losses, adaptation, fiscal space and insurance protection gaps shape the capacity of economies and financial systems to absorb future shocks.
I will argue that these two horizons are connected: The resilience an economy has built determines the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic impact of a shock over the monetary-policy horizon. And, in turn, repeated shocks can erode that resilience over the longer term, eventually exacerbating the effects of climate shocks when they occur.
How physical shocks transmit through the economy
Let me start with how physical shocks can affect the economy.
Physical hazards can operate through several channels at once: They can damage capital. They can reduce labour supply and lower productivity. They can disrupt transport and supply chains. They can weaken demand and confidence among economic agents, tighten credit conditions and raise uncertainty.
Importantly for monetary policymakers, those channels can interact and may also move output and inflation in different directions, making the policy response more challenging.
But different physical hazards can transmit through the economy in different ways. To give some examplesfootnote [6]:

Heatwaves transmit as a shock to productive capacity and labour supply. They push down on GDP while increasing inflation volatility, making them relevant for monetary policy even though direct physical damage is not as visible as for a flood or storm.
Droughts reduce productive capacity in agriculture pushing down on production and up on prices. They can raise inflation both through the effect on domestic production and through more expensive imports.
Floods and cyclones damage the capital stock, reducing demand and investment, which can in turn push down on output and inflation. But floods can also be inflationary where they hit food supply, logistics or essential infrastructure.

So while there is no one-size-fits-all pattern for the effects of a physical shock, there are some common themes:

Shocks are often transmitted through a disruption to production;
That usually means that output and inflation often move in opposite directions; and
Even when shocks occur overseas, these can be transmitted through changes to exports and commodity prices, particularly for open economies. Indeed, a 2022 study for the euro area showed that for every 1% unanticipated increase in globally traded food prices, overall inflation rose by 0.1%footnote [7].

This latter channel is also particularly important for the UK since we import around 40% of our food. In recent work at the Bank of England, we have looked at the impacts of extreme weather events on commodity prices and UK inflationfootnote [8]. The estimates from the model suggest that global weather-related disruption has played a non-trivial role in UK food and headline inflation over the past two decades
This makes climate-related shocks relevant to our regular inflation forecasting. Indeed, many central banks are now assessing the impact of food, energy, supply-chain, and weather-related shocks. That is because these shocks are affecting inflation and output forecasts, or the risks around them, in an increasingly meaningful way.
The NGFS note on the economic and financial impacts of extreme weather events, produced for the 2026 French G7 Presidency, uses 31 case studies to show that these effects repeatedly appear in output, employment and prices across a geographically diverse range of countriesfootnote [9]. Supply-chain and trade linkages can also propagate these shocks beyond the country or region directly affected.
With that in mind, let me turn next to consider how central banks should diagnose the shock, assess its impact on their forecasts and the risks around them and therefore their monetary policy judgements.
A framework for assessing the impacts of climate shocks
Here I will draw on the recent NGFS guide on monetary policy strategy that I mentioned earlierfootnote [10]. The report provides a five-step approach to assess these impacts: identify, assess the propagation, assess whether a trade-off arises, set policy, communicate and monitor.
Step one is to identify the nature of the shock itself: How large is it? How long is it likely to last? Which regions and sectors are affected? Is it localised or widespread? And is it a one-off event or one in a sequence of shocks?
Those distinctions matter.
A short-lived disruption affecting a relatively narrow part of the economy during the low season of economic activity poses a very different challenge from a shock affecting food, energy, or critical infrastructure, or services such as tourism during peak season. And a sequence of individually temporary shocks may have quite different macroeconomic consequences from an isolated event.
Having identified the shock, step two is to assess how it propagates through the economy.
Here, the familiar distinction between direct, indirect and second-round effects is particularly useful.
Direct – or first round – effects are the immediate relative-price effects from the shock: for example, a drought raising food prices, a heatwave reducing labour productivity, or a flood disrupting production and logistics.
Monetary policy cannot repair infrastructure, restore a harvest, or offset the initial physical damage. If the shock is short-lived and expectations remain anchored, the standard monetary policy response is usually to look through the first-round effects, because policy operates with a lag and tightening in response to a temporary supply shock can impose unnecessary output costs.
But the initial shock can spread more widely, having indirect effects, as firms pass higher input costs across supply chains. And there can be second-round effects through wages and inflation expectations. Workers may seek compensation for higher living costs; businesses may adjust their price-setting behaviour; and households and firms may revise their inflation expectations.
Food and energy prices can be particularly important here. Households observe them frequently and a well-established literature shows that they have an outsized effect on expectations about future inflation. Research conducted at the Bank of England reinforces that result for the UK, finding that more than 60% of households report that food prices heavily influence inflation perceptions. Food prices also matter significantly more for household inflation-expectations dynamics than other components, with effects at short, medium and long horizons.
Frequency of shocks matters too. An isolated rise in prices will feel different to a series of repeated upward moves. Indeed, a sequence of individually temporary shocks which arrive before the effects of previous disturbances have dissipated can look and feel like more persistent inflationary pressure. Repeated disruption can also erode fiscal buffers and weaken private-sector resilience.
Central banks should therefore focus closely on frequency, persistence and pass-through to overall inflation and inflation expectations.
From diagnosis to the monetary-policy response
Step three is next: does the identified shock create a trade-off between inflation and output?
As I noted earlier, hot and dry events provide relatively clear examples. By reducing agricultural production, a drought can weaken output while putting upward pressure on food prices. A heatwave pushing down on productivity can increase inflation volatility at the same time as hitting output. But if shocks primarily damage capital and reduce output, such as floods and storms in some circumstances, they can push down on inflation where demand effects dominate.
If you permit me a brief digression at this point, the situation becomes no easier when considering the economic impact of the policies enacted by governments to ensure that the necessary climate transition happens. These policies can also drive large and persistent relative price movements, shifts in investment and reallocation of production across sectors of the economy. Modelling the impact of these shocks is therefore no less important. Here, the NGFS and IMF published joint work earlier this year on how countries’ Nationally Determined Contributions to reducing emissions under the Paris Agreement will affect inflation and output across a range of economiesfootnote [11].
Step four is to set policy and communicate the decision.
Here, the assessment depends importantly on the wider economic environment at the point the shock arrives. If inflation is already elevated and expectations are less firmly anchored, the risk that an initial price increase develops into broader inflationary pressure may be greater, and the case for responding becomes stronger. If the economy has spare capacity and demand is weak, the case for looking through is stronger.
This is also where a central bank faces an important judgement: if the effects of a physical shock are material and sufficiently well understood, they may belong in the central forecast.
But where there is substantial uncertainty around the scale of a shock or the way it will propagate, scenarios can allow policymakers to explore and communicate risks. Scenarios can complement the central forecast by helping us explore precisely the kinds of uncertainty I have described today: whether a shock proves temporary or persistent; whether supply or demand effects dominate; and whether initial price increases generate material second-round effects.
The fifth and final step is to monitor and assess whether the economy is evolving in line with expectations and adjust policy in response to new data developments. Since there is also evidence that climate shocks can affect credit supply, collateral values or financial intermediation, central banks should also monitor the operation of the monetary transmission mechanism.
You will notice, of course, that the process I describe here is not that different to how central banks assess and respond to other economic shocks. That is because the impact of climate change is now one of the set of economic shocks that monetary policymakers consider.
From immediate shocks to the resilience threshold
Since climate shocks are likely to increase in both magnitude and frequency, another important question is whether economies and financial systems can continue to absorb rising losses from these shocks over the longer term.
The capacity of households, businesses, governments and financial systems to absorb losses is a key determinant of the recovery profile from a climate shock. Fiscal space, insurance penetration, climate adaptation, infrastructure quality, financial-market depth and institutional capacity all help to determine a country’s resilience threshold. Where those buffers are stronger, shocks are more likely to be absorbed. Where they are weaker, the effects can become more persistent and can spill into credit, financial stability and public-finance channels.
Less developed economies typically have lower resilience thresholds, meaning similar physical hazards can generate larger and more persistent macroeconomic damage. A previous study by Raddatz (2009) estimated that a climate-related disaster resulted in a cumulative per capita output loss of 0.25%, 0.5% and 1% for high, middle and low-income countries respectivelyfootnote [12].
But resilience is also not fixed. Repeated shocks can gradually erode the very buffers that help economies absorb losses in the first place, including fiscal space, private-sector balance sheets and insurance capacity. Without effective mitigation and adaptation, economies may therefore become less resilient over time, with the same physical hazard generating increasingly persistent effects on output, inflation, credit and public finances.
There is also evidence that these interactions can be non-linear. The NGFS’s 2023 work on compound risks examines precisely what can happen when shocks combine, either across time or across locations. It shows that the overall macroeconomic impact of compounding shocks can be materially greater than the sum of the partsfootnote [13].
This in turn feeds back to the short-term policy response. Resilience directly affects the scale and persistence of the macroeconomic consequences of a shock, and therefore how difficult it is for monetary policy to look through it. But if losses are absorbed quickly through insurance mechanisms or other buffers, the inflation-output trade-off may be shorter-lived.
There is therefore an important interaction between resilience and monetary policy. The more resilient an economy is, the easier it is to absorb physical shocks. As resilience erodes, the same shock can become progressively harder to look through.
Insurance protection gaps and why they matter for central banks
The provision of insurance helps economies to cushion the effect of physical shocks by pooling and transferring losses. High insurance penetration and rapid payouts can reduce household distress, firm insolvency and credit losses as well as supporting a faster recovery in output.
But as physical risks increase, rising and repeated losses could place pressure on the availability and affordability of insurance in areas exposed to these shocks. If insurance coverage falls, losses will instead fall on households, businesses, banks and governments.
Two recent events provide a sobering comparison. In Spain, public-private insurance arrangements helped absorb a significant share of losses from the 2024 floods whereas in Pakistan, following the 2022 floods, only around 1% of total damages were insured, leaving households and small firms far more exposed to income and wealth losses, generating larger macroeconomic impacts.
From a microprudential perspective, withdrawal of insurance provision may enhance the safety and soundness of insurance firms, because rising insured damages can significantly dent profitability and potentially threaten firm resilience.
As the insurance supervisor, our role is not to direct underwriting decisions by individual firms. But as a macroprudential authority, we will need to take a broader view of the implications for the financial system as a whole. Indeed, the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee highlighted this issue at its September 2026 meetingfootnote [14].
Where insurance coverage falls, uninsured risks will need to be redistributed:

For households, this means higher repair costs when physical risks strike, lower property values and potential difficulties obtaining a mortgage.
For businesses, it can mean bearing losses from the destruction of physical goods, capital and infrastructure.
For banks, it can mean weaker collateral values and higher credit losses.
For governments, it can mean more frequent pressure to act as insurer of last resort.

For the UK, Bank of England staff have modelled how a widening flood-insurance protection gap could spill over to the UK mortgage marketfootnote [15].
This analysis suggests that the share of UK mortgagors without insurance could rise from around 5% today to around 7-10% in 2050, or up to 16% following a severe flood event. The aggregate effects on house prices and mortgage impairments in that modelling are relatively small compared with the severe macroeconomic stresses against which the UK banking system is tested. But that does not mean the issue is trivial: the consequences for affected households, exposed lenders and local economies could still be significant.
There is an important lesson here: the answer cannot simply be more of the same insurance. Insurance capacity cannot sustainably compensate for underlying physical risks that continue to rise. Insurers will likely increasingly need to include risk prevention in product design, underwriting, and pricing practices.
Indeed, while a successful transition to net zero can limit the future increase in physical hazards, we will also need to consider the role of adaptation in a world where climate shocks are more frequent.
Investment in ensuring resilience to climate shocks can support insurability. This may require collaboration between businesses, households and governments. Updates to planning rules and building regulations could further mitigate the impact of increased physical hazards.
Actions to improve climate-related risk identification, measurement and modelling capabilities across the insurance sector, as envisaged under the recent update to the Bank of England’s supervisory expectations, should strengthen firms' ability to assess and price climate-related risksfootnote [16].
But the financial sector also has a long tradition of coming up with innovative solutions to difficult problems. In this regard, there may be scope for greater collaboration between insurers, reinsurers and banks to share data, develop products and risk-transfer mechanisms that support resilience and help narrow protection gaps.
International cooperation
Let me finish with a word on international cooperation. Climate change is an issue which transcends borders and cannot be fixed by one country acting alone. In recent years, great strides have been made in multilateral fora like the NGFS to assess and model the impacts of climate change on the financial system. The NGFS’ flagship climate scenarios are an important tool in underpinning climate risk assessment in the financial sector. The work of the International Sustainability Standards Board to ensure consistent and better climate disclosures is helping financial firms to better manage climate-related risks and to make better decisions on where to allocate capital.
The 2025 South African G20 Presidency focused on the issue of natural catastrophe protection gaps, drawing on joint work from the World Bank and the International Association of Insurance Supervisorsfootnote [17]. That work helped to raise our collective understanding of these issues as well as suggesting a range of approaches to tackle them, tailored to country circumstances.
In 2026, the French G7 Presidency took this work forward by strengthening the evidence on the macro-financial consequences of extreme weather, while examining how to tackle protection gapsfootnote [18]. This issue is also on our radar as the UK develops priorities for its own G20 Presidency in 2027. In my view, there is value in better understanding how insurance protection gaps affect the economic impact of extreme-weather events and in exploring what can help sustain insurability and resilience as physical risks increase.
That could include looking at what constrains insurability, which approaches appear capable of operating at scale, and the conditions needed for them to work sustainably.
Insurance cannot close protection gaps on its own. But better data, investment in adaptation and more resilient infrastructure can help sustain affordable cover. Timely mitigation also remains essential to limit the future increase in physical risk.
That brings me back to the two connected horizons. In the near term, central banks will need to understand how physical and transition-related shocks affect inflation, output and expectations in order to deliver on their price stability mandate.
Further ahead, the availability of insurance will determine both the economic impact of climate shocks and the capacity of economies to absorb the resulting losses. It will also shape the prevailing environment in which central banks will pursue their price and financial stability goals.
As macroprudential policymakers, we understand that the availability of insurance matters to the resilience of the financial system as a whole. So as protection gaps widen, addressing them will require concerted action across governments, regulators, international institutions and the private sector. Multilateral fora can play an important role in supporting that dialogue and sharing lessons on what works.
As climate change increasingly affects our economies and financial systems, central banks will need to understand these effects, just like any other shock. This will enable us to make sure that the financial system remains stable and that price stability is maintained. And in turn that can provide a sustainable platform for governments to deliver the climate transition.
I would like to thank Danae Kyriakopoulou for assistance in writing this speech. I would also like to thank Lukasz Krebel and Fergus Booker for their input and helpful comments, as well as India Rimmer, Hannah Copeland, Boromeus Wanengkirtyo, Dario Bonciani, Riccardo Masolo, Silvia Sarpietro, Nikoleta Anesti, Vania Esady, Matthew Naylor, Will Banks, Kemal Erçevik, Alex Curtis and Jemima Hall for their underlying research.

Delphi Ventures operates as an independent venture capital firm that seeks to invest in world-changing founders.The views expressed in this episode are solely those of the host and guest and do not represent the views of Delphi Ventures.Delphi Ventures is an investor in Grass and holds the Grass token. As a result, Delphi Ventures has a financial interest in Grass, and statements made in this episode should not be relied upon as impartial. Guests are not compensated for their appearance, and their statements have not been independently verified. Do your own research before making any investment decision.

From a pandemic side project to delivering exabytes of web data to frontier AI labs, Andrej Radonjic has built a data business most people have never heard of. The co-founder and CEO of Wynd Labs, the team behind Grass, joins Yan on The Delphi Podcast in Miami for a conversation about why the open internet is closing its doors to AI, what labs actually pay for when they buy data, and how millions of people sharing spare bandwidth became one of the ways AI reads the web. Andrej shares how an arbitrage bot he built during his PhD pulled him into web scraping, why Grass was built on consent, and what it took to scale to exabytes, including a co-founder who flew to Ashburn and assembled servers overnight. He also explains how robots are learning from web video, why he compares AI data to defense tech, and how the new Contents API turns any public web page into a single API call. The conversation closes with the ownerless Grass Foundation behind the recent revenue attestation, what a moat really is, and his vision for Grass to become the way AI accesses the world’s information.

articles.title: Money and power: lessons from history for stablecoins and US dollar dominance – speech by Carolyn Wilkins
articles.text:
Money and power: lessons from history for stablecoins and US dollar dominance – speech by Carolyn Wilkins

Given at Queen’s University, Belfast

Published on
15 September 2026

In her speech, Carolyn Wilkins draws on historical experience of private money issuance to explore whether private digital money can operate safely at scale. She also considers what could happen if US dollar stablecoins become widely used, and what that could mean for the future of international monetary power.

Speech
Introduction
Thank you for inviting me. It is a pleasure to be here at Queen’s University in Belfast to talk about payment innovations, and what they mean for international money and power.
I’ll focus on stablecoins. They have some affinities with the local banknotes issued here. And while stablecoins are often presented in very dry terms - blockchains, tokens, settlement layers - the bigger questions are about money and power.
Payment means and systems are like electricity grids. When they are working, they are in the background, and when they are not, there can be widespread disruption. And, payment systems can be used by governments to enforce economic sanctions, as we saw after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. They can also be used to monitor financial flows and to project influence. That has made the infrastructure of money and payments an increasingly important part of economic statecraft.
The strategic issue here is what role stablecoins will play in a system where money, payments and geopolitical power are becoming increasingly intertwined. We want to know which forms of digital money will ultimately succeed, and which currencies and institutions will become embedded in the next generation of payment infrastructure. It is early days, so the answers are honestly unknown. But we can learn a lot by considering three questions.
First: can private digital money work safely at scale?
Second: what happens if US dollar stablecoins really do scale?
Third: what would that mean for international monetary power?
These questions are top of mind for me because the Bank of England recently published a framework for systemic sterling-denominated stablecoins.footnote [1]
1. Can private digital money work safely at scale?
Let me start with what a stablecoin is.
A fiat-backed payment stablecoin is a privately issued claim designed to maintain a fixed value against sovereign money - usually one stablecoin for one dollar.
There is a familiar analogue here in Northern Ireland. Private banks issue their own sterling banknotes, which circulate pound-for-pound with other sterling money and are fully backed by ring-fenced assets, but the basic monetary promise is familiar: a privately issued claim that people expect to maintain its value at par.
One way to see what stablecoins add is to compare them with Bitcoin. Bitcoin showed something fundamental: value can be transferred globally and continuously without a central intermediary. Bitcoin is not backed by reserve assets, and its value can move enormously.
In 2010, two pizzas were actually bought for 10,000 bitcoins - about $40 at the time. Today, 10,000 bitcoins would be worth about $770 million. Those are probably the most expensive pizzas in history.
Figure 1 shows the underlying problem more systematically. Bitcoin is far more volatile than the major payment stablecoins, making it poorly suited to everyday payments.
Stablecoins were designed to address that problem by backing the monetary promise of a stable value with reserve assets, while retaining some of the features of crypto technology. Transfers can take place continuously, often across borders, and transactions can be programmed using smart contracts.

Figure 1: Volatility of Bitcoin, USDT and USDC

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

There is a real demand for this innovation, particularly where payments systems are slow, expensive and difficult to access.
For now, they are used mainly inside the crypto ecosystem, as a settlement asset for trading and lending, as collateral, to provide liquidity, and as a way of moving between crypto markets and conventional money.
The market has grown very quickly. Stablecoins in circulation reached roughly $300 billion by mid-2026, up from less than $5 billion at the beginning of 2020 (Figure 2).

Figure 2: Stablecoins in circulation by market capitalisation

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

As much as the blockchain technology seems avant-garde, the economic structure of stablecoins is very familiar.
Private institutions have issued money-like claims for centuries. Those systems repeatedly had to solve the same basic problems: can the issuer make good on the promise to redeem; will claims issued by different institutions be accepted and settled at the same value; and what happens when many people want to redeem at once?
The nineteenth-century history of private money is a useful place to start.
In the United Kingdom, private banknotes circulated alongside Bank of England notes. Scotland developed a relatively stable system built around large branch networks, stronger shareholder liability and regular clearing among banks. If a bank issued too many notes, other banks returned them for settlement and it lost reserves. That imposed discipline in normal times.
England had a more fragile structure. Many country banks were small and poorly diversified. This weakness was reinforced by the Bank of England's monopoly on joint-stock banking within London, which limited the development of larger banking institutions. Dozens of banks failed in the crisis of 1825. Parliament responded by allowing larger joint-stock banks outside London.
But stronger banks did not solve the problem of liquidity in a crisis. Reserves and crisis management became increasingly concentrated around the Bank of England. The Bank Charter Act of 1844 tied note issuance more tightly to gold, yet crises followed in 1847, 1857 and 1866. Each time, the statutory limit on note issuance was temporarily relaxed so that the Bank could lend into the panic.
So the UK experience points to two conditions for success. Private money needs mechanisms that keep different claims trading at par in normal times. And it needs a way to provide liquidity when the system comes under stress.
The United States learned much the same lesson, but through a more turbulent route.
During the Free Banking era, banks issued their own notes, and those notes did not necessarily trade at face value. Their value depended on the assets backing them, the reputation of the issuing bank and even the distance from the place of redemption. There were catalogues telling people what different banknotes were worth.
So a dollar was not always simply a dollar.
The National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864 tried to fix that problem by requiring national banknotes to be backed by US government bonds. The notes became more uniform and the collateral improved.
But another problem remained. The supply of currency could not expand easily when demand for liquidity rose. The panics of 1873, 1893 and 1907 exposed that weakness.
Private clearinghouses tried to fill the gap by providing emergency settlement liquidity. In 1907, J.P. Morgan and others also organized extraordinary support. But the system still depended on improvised private cooperation.
The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 eventually put those crisis-management functions on a permanent national footing.
Across these historical experiences, several conditions for success stand out.
Private money needs credible convertibility, so holders are confident they can redeem at par, and high-quality, transparent backing that makes that promise believable. It also needs a sufficiently uniform regulatory perimeter, so that similar monetary claims are subject to consistent standards, and clearing and settlement arrangements that keep those claims exchanging at par. Finally, there must be credible arrangements for crisis management and loss allocation when the system comes under stress.
Together, these conditions support what Gary Gorton and Jeffery Zhang call the “no questions asked” property of money.footnote [2] A monetary claim works well when people can accept it at face value without having to assess the issuer every time they use it.
Stablecoins have already provided a useful test of that principle.
When Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023, Circle - the issuer of the stablecoin called USDC - had about $3.3 billion of reserves deposited there.
Holders suddenly had reason to question whether USDC could still be converted into one dollar. Redemptions accelerated and USDC lost its peg (Figure 3). The peg recovered after US authorities guaranteed all of Silicon Valley Bank’s deposits.footnote [3]

Figure 3: USDC around the failure of Silicon Valley Bank
Deviation from par value (per cent)

Footnotes

Source: Defillama.

The episode showed how a weakness in the institutional structure behind a stablecoin can quickly affect confidence in the token itself.
Regulatory frameworks are now trying to address those weaknesses.
In the US, Congress passed the GENIUS Act in July 2025, creating a federal framework for all payment stablecoins.footnote [4] The Act sets rules for who can issue a stablecoin, what assets must stand behind it, and what happens when a holder wants their money back.
It requires at least one dollar of eligible reserves for every dollar of stablecoins issued. Those reserves can include Treasury securities, bank deposits and other short-term liquid assets. It also strengthens disclosure and gives stablecoin holders priority in insolvency. One implementation challenge will be maintaining consistent standards across its federal and state regulatory regimes.
That goes a long way toward answering one question: are the assets there? The trickier question is: can they be turned into cash quickly when everyone wants to redeem at once?
We saw why that distinction matters during the “dash for cash” at the onset of the pandemic in March 2020. Even the US Treasury market came under severe strain, and the Federal Reserve had to intervene on a very large scale. Assets that are safe and liquid in normal times can become much less liquid in a crisis.footnote [5]
The Federal Reserve has also proposed a new, limited form of account that would allow eligible firms to connect more directly to its payment system. That could make day-to-day settlement more reliable. But it would not allow them to borrow from the Fed, which means there is no pre-established source of emergency liquidity in a run.
The Bank of England’s framework for systemic sterling-denominated stablecoins, which will be finalised at the end of this year, goes further on some of these issues.footnote [6] It is more restrictive about reserve assets and puts more weight on liquidity contingency planning, payment-system access and arrangements for failure. It also allows for the possibility of central-bank liquidity under appropriate conditions.footnote [7]
This framework applies only to systemic stablecoins and is more demanding than the US framework. I think this is appropriate because it gives greater weight to the liquidity and crisis-management problems that recur in the historical record.
Let’s not forget that cross-border use makes these issues even harder. In some regimes, a stablecoin may be issued in one jurisdiction, hold its reserves in another, use a custodian in a third and serve holders in many more.footnote [8] Redemption rights, insolvency treatment, supervision and crisis-management responsibilities do not automatically travel with the token.footnote [9]
International banking spent decades developing home- and host-country responsibilities, common standards and supervisory cooperation. That said, stablecoins may become global much faster than the institutional framework around them.
So, my answer to the first question is a qualified yes. Private digital money can work at scale, but the historical record is clear about the conditions required to make that possible.
2. What happens if dollar stablecoins really do scale?
This brings me to the second question.
Today, about 98 percent of stablecoin value is denominated in US dollars.footnote [10] The dollar therefore has a considerable first-mover advantage as stablecoins move beyond their original role in crypto markets.
The US administration sees this as a strategic opportunity. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued explicitly that dollar stablecoins can reinforce the dollar’s international role and increase demand for US Treasury securities.
There are three main channels through which wider use could matter.
The first channel is settlement. Stablecoin transactions can take place around the clock and cross borders without passing through every link in a correspondent-banking chain. They do not eliminate intermediaries, but they can reduce reliance on traditional banking links. Recent work presented at Jackson Hole just a few weeks ago argues that this could make settlement faster or cheaper where cross-border banking is slow or costly.footnote [11] In 2024, sending a USD 200 remittance cost around 6.4% on average globally, while costs in Sub-Saharan Africa averaged about 8.5%.footnote [12]
The second channel is digital dollarisation. If your local currency is unstable or access to dollar banking is difficult, a dollar stablecoin can put a dollar-linked asset on your phone without requiring a US bank account. Recent work finds that the advantage can be significant in some emerging-market payment corridors with capital controls or segmented foreign-exchange markets, although limited liquidity still constrains scale.footnote [13] This could extend the use of the dollar into new digital markets.
The third channel is demand for US safe assets.
Stablecoin issuers hold reserves against their liabilities, and the GENIUS Act requires reserves to be held in specified highly liquid assets, including short-dated US Treasury securities.footnote [14]
USDT and USDC together held almost $150 billion in Treasury bills at the end of 2025. Their net purchases in that year were around $33 billion (Figure 4).footnote [15]

Figure 4: Holdings of US T-bills Q4 2025, US$ Billions

Footnotes

Source: Ahmed, R. and Aldasoro, I. (2025, revised 2026), Stablecoins and Safe Asset Prices, BIS Working Papers No. 1270; authors' calculations.

Those amounts remain small relative to the Treasury market as a whole, but they make the largest stablecoin issuers meaningful participants in the short-term market.
That additional demand can affect Treasury prices. Recent evidence suggests that stablecoin inflows put modest downward pressure on short-term Treasury yields, consistent with issuers adding to demand for safe and liquid assets.footnote [16]
Of course, the overall effect will depend on where the money comes from. If investors move from a Treasury money-market fund into a stablecoin whose issuer then buys Treasury bills, the net increase in demand for US safe assets is limited. If stablecoins attract funds that would otherwise be held in another currency or another asset class, the effect is larger. If stablecoins instead draw materially from bank deposits, they could also affect bank funding costs and credit supply.
At sufficient scale, these channels could reinforce one another – creating a positive feedback loop. Greater use of dollar stablecoins expands dollar settlement. Issuers hold more Treasury securities. Deep and liquid dollar markets make dollar stablecoins more attractive to users and platforms.

Figure 5: Positive feedback loop

But the same balance sheet can work in reverse. Inflows mean reserve purchases; redemptions mean asset sales.
Remember, like deposits or money market fund investments stablecoins are demandable claims. They can trade around the clock, and holders can seek redemption quickly. Issuers therefore need to turn reserve assets into cash when redemptions rise.
If several large issuers had to sell Treasury bills at the same time, particularly into an already stressed market, they could amplify moves in yields and market liquidity. We saw a similar feedback mechanism in the UK gilt market during the LDI episode in 2022.
And the stress need not begin with the stablecoin. Concerns about US inflation, fiscal sustainability or institutional credibility could weaken demand for dollar assets, with stablecoin redemptions adding to the selling pressure.

Figure 6: Negative feedback loop

The stablecoin sector is not currently large enough for this mechanism to pose a major threat to the Treasury market or a material financial stability risk in UK. However, a major de-pegging episode could also damage confidence in regulated stablecoins more broadly.
US policy is intended to provide space for the sector to grow substantially. If successful, the balance-sheet link between stablecoins and the rest of the dollar system will matter more over time.
Scale therefore brings both benefits and vulnerabilities. Dollar stablecoins could extend dollar settlement, support digital dollarisation and add to demand for safe US assets. At greater scale, they would also create a stronger link between confidence in privately issued money and conditions in the markets where the reserves are held.
3. What would that mean for monetary power?
That brings me to the third question.
When I talk about monetary power, I do not mean only the dollar’s share of reserves or international trade.
I mean control of the system itself. Who provides the monetary anchor, who provides liquidity in a crisis, who writes and enforces the rules, and who can control access to the financial network.
By conventional measures, the dollar remains in a strong position in global finance, although its share of global reserves has declined since the beginning of the century.footnote [17] Its share of disclosed foreign-exchange reserves has fallen from a little over 70 percent around 2000 to about 57 percent in the first quarter of 2026. The decline has been gradual and spread across a range of currencies. The euro remains near 20 percent, while the renminbi accounts for a much smaller share. At the same time, the dollar was on one side of 89.2 percent of over-the-counter foreign-exchange trades in April 2025.footnote [18]

Figure 7: Official Foreign Exchange Reserves by Currency

Footnotes

Source: IMF Currency Composition of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves (COFER) Survey.

Since the end of Bretton Woods in the early 1970s, there has been no promise to convert dollars into gold. The anchor instead has rested on confidence in the fiscal and monetary policies of the United States, as well as in its institutions and legal systems and judiciary.
The sheer economic and geopolitical weight of the US has traditionally reinforced those advantages.
Network effects have made the US more powerful. Firms tend to invoice in currencies widely used by their counterparties. Financial institutions value currencies with deep markets and liquid hedging instruments. US Treasuries provide a large stock of safe assets that are used as reserves, collateral, stores of value and pricing benchmarks.
That safe-asset advantage has historically been valuable to the United States. Investors have been willing to accept lower yields on Treasuries because they are safe and liquid; one influential estimate put that advantage at about 70 basis points.footnote [19] But recent evidence suggests it has weakened. The advantage attached specifically to Treasury securities has fallen sharply, even turning negative at longer maturities, while the broader international advantage of the dollar remains strong.footnote [20]
This financial infrastructure also gives the United States strategic leverage.
Because many international transactions depend on institutions subject to US jurisdiction or on access to dollar markets, US authorities can monitor financial flows, impose sanctions and restrict access to important parts of the financial network. Secondary sanctions can extend those effects beyond US institutions.
The sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine made the strategic importance of financial infrastructure particularly visible. More broadly, the use of financial sanctions has strengthened the incentive for some governments to develop alternative channels for international payments.
China is the most important example. This is not because the renminbi is close to displacing the dollar, but because China has the economic scale to develop alternative infrastructure.
It has expanded the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, or CIPS, for renminbi-denominated international payments. China has also participated in mBridge, which has experimented with cross-border settlement using wholesale central-bank digital currencies.
These arrangements remain much smaller than the dollar-centred financial system. Their importance lies in the development of additional payment routes that rely less heavily on traditional dollar-based correspondent banking.
This points to an important distinction: the currency and the rails can change at different speeds.
The dollar could remain the leading reserve and financing currency while more cross-border payments move through regional or digital networks that are less centred on the United States. This form of monetary multipolarity does not require another currency to replace the dollar. But it could still reduce US direct control over the infrastructure through which some international payments are made.
Stablecoins can contribute to both sides of this process. Dollar stablecoins can extend dollar settlement into new digital networks. Other countries can use digital currencies, stablecoins or new payment platforms to develop alternative networks.
This competition can improve efficiency and encourage innovation. It can also create fragmentation if systems are not interoperable or if legal, regulatory and liquidity arrangements diverge sharply across jurisdictions.footnote [21]
The strategic question therefore concerns both the currency people choose to use and the infrastructure through which they use it.
The US position remains strong because no competitor currently offers the same combination of deep and liquid capital markets, a large supply of safe assets, convertibility, legal credibility and established global use.
History nevertheless shows that network advantages are persistent rather than permanent.footnote [22]
Sterling is the clearest example.
Before the First World War, sterling bills financed international trade far beyond transactions involving the UK. London was the leading international financial centre. Imperial trade links and the sterling area reinforced a powerful network even after the UK’s relative economic position had begun to weaken.
The transition away from sterling took decades.
War debts strained the UK’s fiscal capacity. The commitment to gold became harder to sustain. Britain’s relative economic weight declined, and its ability to provide international liquidity weakened. At the same time, the United States became a larger economic and financial power.
The shift reflected changing economic strength and changing confidence in the institutions supporting the currency.
That history matters for the current questions about stablecoins and US dollar dominance.
Network effects can reinforce an international currency for a very long time. But, ultimately, they sit on top of fundamentals.
For the dollar, as for any currency, those fundamentals are the same ones I mentioned earlier: sustainable fiscal capacity; credible institutions and policies, including monetary policy; predictable legal institutions and the rule of law; deep and liquid capital markets; and a demonstrated ability to provide liquidity when the financial system is under stress.footnote [23] General government gross as a percent of GDP has been on an upward trend and is projected to increase further, particularly in the US and China (Figure 8).
These are fairly old-fashioned foundations of monetary power. Digital technology does not make them less important.

Figure 8: General government gross debt (per cent of GDP)

Footnotes

Source: International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Economic Outlook Database, April 2026. Chart shows total gross general government debt on an internationally comparable basis. Separately published country measures can use different methodologies.

4. Conclusions
Let me close by returning to my three questions.
First, can private digital money work safely at scale? Yes. History shows that it can, but only when the institutions around it make redemption credible, support exchange at par and provide a way to deal with stress.
Second, what happens if dollar stablecoins really do scale? They could extend dollar settlement, deepen digital dollarisation and add to demand for US safe assets. But greater scale would also create stronger links between stablecoins and the markets in which their reserves are held. This could create financial stability risks that extend past US borders.
And third, what does this mean for international monetary power? History shows that network effects can sustain a dominant currency for a long time, so stablecoins could help reinforce the dollar. At the same time, global payments systems could become more multipolar. But technology cannot secure dollar dominance on its own. As sterling’s experience ultimately showed, that rests squarely on monetary credibility, fiscal capacity, deep capital markets and the rule of law.
