articles.title: The Model Assistant in action: What would an escalating Iran war mean for bond yields?
articles.text:
Blog

20 Oct 2026

The Model Assistant in action: What would an escalating Iran war mean for bond yields?

In Part 1 of this series, we introduced the AskOEAI Model Assistant, the world’s first AI assistant for scenario modelling, and explained why we built it. In this post, we put it to work on a question many of our clients are asking right now: what would a renewed escalation of the war in Iran mean for the global economy, and for government bond yields in particular?

The question: what if the war in Iran escalates again?

The war in Iran has already pushed up energy prices and unsettled financial markets. Renewed attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure in the Gulf have lifted oil prices, and global bond markets have sold off sharply. The US 10-year Treasury yield has climbed above 5% for the first time since 2007, and the Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September for the first time since 2023, as we discuss in our latest analysis of the bond sell-off.

Our baseline forecast already reflects the conflict and the market moves seen so far. What many clients want to know is what happens if the war escalates again: how far could energy prices rise, how would inflation and central banks respond, and how much higher could bond yields go? So we asked the Model Assistant, walking through four simple steps:

Describe your scenario in your own words, as broadly or as specifically as you like.

Research the scenario with the assistant, drawing on Oxford Economics’ analysis to propose shocks, their timing and the reasoning behind each.

Review and adjust inputs as required, then run the scenario through the GEM with a single click or message.

Analyse the results through charts and explanations, then refine your assumptions and re-solve as often as you need.

Describe the scenario in your own words

We started with a single prompt: “Model a scenario of new and sustained escalations in the war in Iran”

We didn’t specify any indicators, shock sizes or timings. In its first response, the assistant pulled in the most relevant Oxford Economics research and set out a complete first draft of the scenario.

The assistant based its calibration on the downside case from our research on a prolonged Iran war, which points to sustained energy disruption, higher inflation risk premia and increased long-term borrowing costs. It translated these channels into four shocks, starting in Q4 2026 (Table 1).

Table 1: Scenario inputs proposed by the Model Assistant

InputAssumptionRationaleBrent crude oil price+$37 from 2026Q4-2027Q4The elevated oil price path supported by prolonged-war downside caseEuropean gas price+$5 from 2026Q4-2027Q4Sustained LNG disruption and tighter European supplyAsian gas price+$10 from 2026Q4-2027Q4Asian LNG markets’ greater exposure to prolonged disruptionSupply chain stress+1.0 from 2026Q4-2027Q4Sustained disruption to shipping, logistics and refined-fuel movements

Source: Oxford Economics AI Model Assistant

Each input comes with a short rationale and a preview chart showing how the scenario path compares with our baseline.

Run the scenario and review the results

Once we’re happy with the inputs, a single click on Solve runs the scenario through the GEM. The shocks feed through trade, prices, financial markets and policy responses across economies, and the results are automatically benchmarked against our latest baseline.

Once the scenario had solved, we asked for the impact on US yields, and the assistant returned a chart and a short summary. In our scenario, US 10-year government bond yields are 0.78 percentage points above baseline at their widest gap, in 2028Q2. Higher energy prices and supply-chain stress create inflation pressure and prompt a tighter monetary policy stance, keeping risk premia elevated, lifting yields and tightening financial conditions.

Understand what is driving the results

The assistant’s analysis pointed to a tighter monetary policy stance as a key factor behind the initial rise in yields.

To understand this better, we asked the Model Agent: “How does the Fed react?”

Based on our initial assumptions, the assistant gave a concise description of the Fed’s “stagflationary trade-off”, along with further research to review. Higher inflation creates pressure to raise rates, while weaker growth and a softer labour market subsequently lead to rate cuts. This Taylor-rule mechanism drives policy-rate dynamics in the GEM, but users can take their own view and add a new assumption.

Refine the scenario through conversation

A scenario is rarely complete in one go. Having reviewed the results, we assumed a more hawkish Fed reaction: “Assume the Fed is more hawkish, raising rates by 50bps above the baseline until the energy shock subsides.”

The assistant added a fifth shock, raising the US policy rate by 0.5 percentage points above baseline from 2026Q4 to 2027Q4, until the energy shocks fade.

Adding the assumption means solving the scenario again, which takes a single click, and each version is traceable in the chat.

With a more hawkish Fed, US bond yields rise more quickly and stay higher for longer than in our first run. Comparing the two gives a range of ‘what-if’ outcomes under different assumptions, all built through conversation with the Model Assistant.

From economic question to modelled insight

In four steps, we went from a topical question to a fully modelled scenario grounded in our research, complete with charts and an explanation of the results. We didn’t need to know which variables to shock, by how much, or how to set up the model inputs. Every assumption was transparent and open to change, so we could question the results, adjust the shocks and re-solve within the same conversation.

The Model Assistant is designed to make scenario analysis quicker and open to more people, with economic judgement staying firmly with the user. To find out more about the problem it solves and what sets it apart from general-purpose AI tools, read part 1 of the series.

The Model Assistant is available as an add-on to the Global Economic Model. To see it in action, click here to request a demo.

Security and Fraud Awareness
KKR prioritizes the security of our clients’ information and assets and is committed to ensuring that clients and employees are made aware of fraudulent schemes and activities when communicating with KKR. Fraud is an issue that companies may face regardless of size, industry, or country.
While we maintain robust cybersecurity measures, cyber criminals may seek to impersonate or claim affiliation with KKR and create fraudulent websites, email domains, applications, and social media accounts. Fraudsters may pose as legitimate organizations and send emails or make phone calls to extract personal data that can be manipulated for the use of financial crimes. These scams are complex as the perpetrators may use real employee names and replicate proprietary documentation.
KKR encourages clients to be aware of the different types of fraud and to exercise caution when disclosing personal information. To help improve awareness and knowledge, we offer the following information about cyber threats and guidance to help protect from falling victim to a cyber-attack or scam.
When communicating with KKR please note:
KKR does not engage in cold calling or in sending unsolicited messages or emails to clients. KKR only contacts people from official kkr.com e-mail addresses. articles.title: Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks -  speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
Financial resilience in an age of repeated shocks - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at the Central Bank of Turkey, İstanbul Economic Forum

Published on
08 October 2026

Andrew Bailey says that although the financial system has remained resilient through repeated geopolitical and economic shocks, weaker growth, persistent supply disruptions, rising sovereign debt, leveraged markets and expanding AI-related exposures create risks. Policymakers should therefore pursue sustainable growth, maintain credible monetary and fiscal frameworks, and strengthen core financial markets so they can absorb future shocks without amplifying them.

Speech
The financial system has so far weathered the latest period of uncertainty. But lower growth, repeated supply shocks and changing market structures mean that resilience cannot be taken for granted.
The conflict in the Middle East has created major uncertainty about growth, inflation and interest rates. Existing vulnerabilities in sovereign debt markets, credit markets and asset valuations could crystallise together. The rapid expansion of financing connected with artificial intelligence has created new exposures, while incidents involving frontier AI have underlined the associated operational, cyber and financial risks.
However, an important part of the story so far is economic resilience in the sense that recent supply shocks have hit the world economy at the same time as the potential growth dividends from AI have become clearer.
Moreover, the story of the financial system so far has been one of resilience. Banking systems generally remain well capitalised and we are not seeing funding stress. Despite a succession of economic shocks and heightened volatility, most financial markets have continued to function without a major breakdown in liquidity or trading conditions.
Financial markets have so far withstood significant increases in sovereign bond yields, and most market adjustments have remained orderly. This resilience owes much to the reforms introduced after the global financial crisis. Those reforms are sometimes criticised as burdensome. Today, their value is clear.
But we cannot be relaxed. Experience teaches us that specific problems can emerge even when the wider system appears stable. The lesson of the global financial crisis is that such problems are much easier to manage when the wider system is resilient and the authorities are committed to keeping it that way.
The deeper economic challenge
Behind the immediate risks lie two longer-term developments.
The first is weaker potential growth, driven in many economies by slowing productivity, which determines how rapidly national income and living standards can rise.
The second is the frequency of large negative supply shocks. Covid, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East have each disrupted the supply capacity of economies. Covid was also both a supply and demand shock, with the balance changing over time. But all these episodes were exceptionally large, and they followed one another with unusual speed.
Are repeated shocks the new normal? Central bankers should be wary of becoming political soothsayers. But a more multipolar world, in which economic policy is increasingly an arena for geopolitical competition, may produce more frequent disruptions. We should therefore prepare for a world in which larger shocks are not rare exceptions.
This creates a particular difficulty for monetary policy. A negative supply shock pushes inflation and output in opposite directions, producing weaker output but higher inflation.
The textbook response is to look through a one-off increase in the price level. Interest rates cannot produce more oil or gas, and monetary policy affects the economy with long lags. But looking through a shock is possible only if inflation expectations remain well anchored.
If households and businesses begin to incorporate higher inflation into wage demands and pricing decisions, a temporary shock can become persistent. These second-round effects are slower to emerge. Central banks must make forward-looking judgements and update them as the evidence changes.
The difficulty becomes greater when shocks arrive in quick succession. A recent history of higher inflation can cause people to expect further inflation. The sequencing of Covid and the invasion of Ukraine have made this risk particularly acute.
The interaction with financial stability
Supply shocks can also create tension between monetary and financial stability. Interest rates may need to rise even as economic activity weakens. Debt-servicing costs increase just as household incomes and corporate earnings come under pressure. Asset prices can fall, reducing the value of collateral and restricting the supply of credit.
This is why resilience before a shock is so important. Strong banks and sound household and corporate balance sheets give policymakers room to respond without turning an economic adjustment into a financial crisis.
Fiscal policy faces a related challenge. Lower growth and repeated supply shocks weaken the public finances while increasing pressure on governments to provide support. Higher borrowing costs and weaker growth raise debt-to-GDP ratios. If markets begin to doubt the fiscal trajectory, bond yields can rise further, tightening monetary and financial conditions.
Governments can ordinarily use their balance sheets to cushion a severe downturn and rebuild fiscal space when conditions improve. That is the principle of countercyclical policy. But when shocks become more frequent, underlying growth is weaker, and the succession of shocks leads to a higher level of government debt, this becomes much harder to sustain.
A changing market structure
Global government bond markets have also changed profoundly. They were once dominated by long-term investors, often described as “real money” and “price insensitive”. Today, leveraged investors play a much larger role, while traditional demand for long-duration debt has declined, partly because of changes in pension provision and ageing populations.
This new structure has so far increased the capacity of markets to absorb the additional supply of government debt. But greater absorption has come with greater fragility. Leveraged positions can be unwound rapidly. Losses can trigger margin calls, model-driven repricing and stop-outs, producing further forced selling that can amplify market moves. The buyers are typically more price sensitive.
The same funds may hold large leveraged positions across several countries and asset classes. Deleveraging that begins in one market can therefore spread quickly to others.
The policy response must have several parts.
First, we must pursue sustainable growth. There is no single solution, but major technological advances have historically lifted productivity. Artificial intelligence and robotics can drive scientific discovery, improve efficiency and raise prosperity. Financing that investment is essential. But greater financial exposure to AI also creates risk. If earnings expectations or confidence in the pace of AI adoption were sharply revised, the consequences could spread through equity, credit and sovereign markets. AI safety and financial stability are therefore becoming increasingly connected. Safely deployed, we should see AI as a growth opportunity.
Second, monetary and fiscal frameworks must remain credible. For monetary policy, that means an unwavering commitment to returning inflation to target. I remain sceptical of unconditional promises about future interest rates. The world is too uncertain. But central banks should explain clearly how policy would respond under different economic conditions.
Fiscal policy must likewise be directed towards stability and be seen by markets as credible. Clear frameworks, including fiscal rules, can help contain risk premia when shocks occur.
Third, we must strengthen the resilience of core markets. Greater central clearing, appropriate minimum haircuts and stronger risk management all merit consideration.
There is no quick fix. But the direction is clear: raise sustainable growth, maintain credible policy frameworks, and ensure that financial markets can absorb shocks without amplifying them.
The system has been resilient. Our task is to make sure it remains so.
I would like to thank Nat Benjamin, Sarah Breeden, Karen Jude, Andrea Rosen, Vicky Saporta and James Talbot for their assistance in preparing these remarks.

Andrew Bailey
Governor, Bank of England

The onchain options sector is the largest whitespace in crypto today. This makes it the most compelling sector to allocate capital towards. Retail demand is already proven at massive scale in TradFi. And onchain, the binding constraints are no longer regulation or infrastructure. Maker liquidity is improving rapidly in tandem.
When looking at the TAM and sizing the opportunity, it’s a matter of when, not if, onchain options take center stage. The final evolution of every mature financial market is expansion into options, and crypto has reached this inflection point.
As this nascent sector is heating up, it’s finally primed to take on its ultimate challenge: cracking distribution to hit escape velocity by onboarding non-toxic (retail) taker flow at scale.

Retail Demand for Options Is Massive. Around The Globe.
There are many misconceptions around options trading, and the evidence for massive retail demand is so clear that it would be a disservice to you as a reader and investor not to spend time highlighting it. In our distribution section, we spend ample time arguing how important it is to onboard non-crypto native retail to crypto.
That’s because no global financial market hit escape velocity in its options sector until retail arrived. Funnily enough, the most persistent and totally incorrect claim you hear spouted on CT is: “retail doesn’t understand options, so they will never trade them onchain.”
Crowned strawman argument of the year, because all evidence points to the opposite. Does it take time to comprehend the greeks and the payoff structure? Absolutely, but the complexity of pricing theory doesn’t diminish interest in product demand.
In reality, options are retail traders’ favorite derivative. When access isn’t limited and UI sleek, retail trades options at outrageous scale. For the non-believers, please consult the exhibits below:

Exhibit A: U.S. Options contract volume more than tripled since 2017, driven by retail.
No need to look further than the U.S. Prior to and between 2014 and 2017, institutions dominated options volume. Retail participation was negligible. As a result, growth was stagnant, hovering around 4B annual contracts traded. In December 2017, Robinhood launched commission-free options and many brokers followed suit.
Then COVID hit and the stars aligned.
Everyone was stuck at home, waiting for things to reopen and life to continue. Asset prices cratered on the initial shock news and everyone turned to investing. Drumbeat marketing coupled with newfound retail interest in finance conjured up the perfect storm. Retail onboarded to finance apps at scale, and options volume followed suit.

Elon Musk’s gas strategy shows how the US market is changing
SpaceX is building pipelines to secure fuel supplies for its rockets, as the industry shifts from supply-push to demand-pull

19 October 2026
9 minute read

Email
Share by email

Ed Crooks
Vice Chair Americas and host of Energy Gang podcast

In Star Trek, spaceships are propelled by warp drive. In The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, it is the Infinite Improbability Drive. In the real world, Elon Musk’s Starship uses LNG.
Previous generations of rockets, including the Saturn V that put a man on the moon, have used kerosene and/or liquid hydrogen, along with liquid oxygen. LNG burns more cleanly than kerosene, and is easier to manage than hydrogen, and so has become SpaceX’s favoured option for its new Starship rocket, again along with liquid oxygen.
It is a significant development for North American natural gas markets. Not so much because of the scale of the demand for Starship fuel – which is relatively small today – but for what it indicates about strategies for securing supply.
The first Starship was launched in 2023, and last month it passed another milestone, entering orbit and deploying a payload for the first time. After some well-publicised failures, SpaceX is making progress in tackling the technical challenges it faces.
Musk has big plans for Starship: he has suggested that by 2030 there could be 30 or more launches every day, and he dreams of future versions of the rocket carrying humanity to other planets. But even if those more grandiose ambitions are not realised, Starship can still make an important contribution to space development.
Because of its size, and the intended reusability of both the main spacecraft and the Super Heavy booster used for liftoff, Starship could reduce the cost of delivering objects into orbit by orders of magnitude.
For now, the volumes of gas needed by the rocket are relatively small. Each launch uses about 1,000 tons of LNG, which is about 48 million cubic feet (mmcf) of gas. SpaceX has asked the Federal Aviation Administration for approval for up to 456 launches a year, equivalent to five every four days. Even if it hits that pace, its total demand would be about 60 mmcf/day, equivalent to only about .07% of total US gas consumption.
However, if Musk’s dream of 30 launches a day is realised, SpaceX’s demand would become significant. At that rate of activity, Starship would account for about 1.7% of US gas consumption. The company would then be using about 11 million tons per year of LNG, in the with the output of some of the large plants along the Gulf coast.
That ambition explains SpaceX’s recent moves to secure its natural gas supplies. The company has filed for approvals to build an eight-mile gas pipeline called Starpipe, which will connect a new liquefaction plant at its Starbase facility in south Texas to the nearby Bay Runner pipeline.
Bay Runner is an extension of the Whistler pipeline, forming a system to bring gas from the Permian basin to the NextDecade’s Rio Grande LNG and other facilities in the Brownsville region.
Separately, SpaceX last month filed for an approval to build another new pipeline, a 32-miles connection to bring gas from the Florida Gas Transmission system to its other launch site at Cape Canaveral on the east coast of Florida.
The company has also been recruiting a gas trader, to build a team to manage its growing demand for gas for both rocket fuel and power generation.
If SpaceX’s business develops as Musk hopes, its operations in energy markets will become an increasingly critical part of its supply chain.
The Wood Mackenzie view
Although SpaceX’s demand is currently not material for North American gas markets, and will remain that way for the near-term future, its strategy is an indication of a significant shift in the market, Wood Mackenzie analysts say.
SpaceX’s moves to invest in its own pipeline and liquefaction infrastructure, and to develop its trading capabilities, reflect a wider trend.
For most of the past 20 years, the North American natural gas market has been characterised by abundance. Pipeline investment reflected supply-push goals, as producers tried to open up new markets for their gas, says Kristy Kramer, Wood Mackenzie’s head of LNG strategy and market development. In the past couple of years, however, that has been changing.
The abundant gas resource base is still there. Production has been hitting record highs. But with US gas demand surging, both for LNG exports and for power generation, customers have started to think more actively about securing supply.
Historically, end users have often been reluctant to fund new pipeline capacity, in part because of uncertainty over the long-term outlook for gas demand. But now, having access to dedicated supply with discounted prices and year-round firm capacity have become top priorities for LNG producers and power generators. Like SpaceX, they have been supporting infrastructure development to meet those objectives.
Wood Mackenzie analysis of new pipeline capacity being added in the US over 2025-31 shows that the majority is being driven either by LNG plants or by power generators needing supplies.
Similar motives have also been driving deals for upstream assets, such as Japanese buyers’ acquisitions of US gas production. These are different types of deal, but the underlying logic is the same: securing supplies and hedging price exposure in a market that is set to tighten over the next few years.
Elon Musk built his reputation through electric vehicles and batteries, and he has been a strong supporter of solar power. He has not been a pioneer in natural gas in the same way: he is keeping up with where the sector is going, not ahead of it. But his next moves in the industry are going to be well worth watching.
Iran claims hits on two VLCCs as attacks on Gulf shipping escalate
Iran said two Very Large Crude Carriers were on fire in the Gulf after hitting mines. Iran’s official Islamic Republic News Agency said the tankers, each with capacity to carry 2 million barrels of oil, had hit mines while attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz with their Automatic Identification System transponders switched off.
As of Sunday evening, the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center (UKMTO) did not have a record of either incident. It has recorded 11 other attacks on shipping in the Gulf region over the past week.
Vice-President JD Vance said that the US needed to maintain its presence in the Gulf to prevent worse disruption to global energy supplies. "If we just… left, and we let the Iranians control shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz, what that would mean is you would pay a lot more for gasoline,” he told a town hall hosted by CBS News. The vice-president added that gasoline prices would fall “when this conflict is over”.
Brent crude rose close to US$110 a barrel last week, its highest level since May.
In brief
A former officer in the Ukrainian army has gone on trial in Germany over the sabotage to the Nord Stream gas pipeline system in 2022. The bombings, which damaged three of the system’s four lines, remained mysterious for years. But in July Serhii Kuznetsov, who was a Ukrainian special forces officer at the time of the attacks, was charged with intentionally damaging civilian infrastructure, a war crime. His lawyer argued in court this week that the case should be dismissed because the pipeline was a legitimate military target. “Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?” he asked the court.
Microsoft has withdrawn from a plan to build a new AI data centre in England, after being warned that the project could not secure a power supply until the 2030s. Microsoft had been working with Nscale to develop a GBP 2 billion data centre in Loughton, Essex.
But it emerged last month that UK Power Networks, which operates the local electricity distribution system, had warned Nscale that it could not provide an adequate grid connection until the early to mid-2030s. Nscale said it remained committed to the Loughton project despite Microsoft’s withdrawal, adding that the “unfortunate London-wide grid issue” would not have any impact on its other developments. Nscale and Microsoft are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the US.
Other views

Reducing oil imports reflects a major power's energy responsibility – Economic Daily
Quote of the week
“To put it very simply: The ban on combustion engines is now history.”
Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz welcomed an agreement with his French counterpart President Emmanuel Macron to relax climate regulations for the EU’s car industry. The revisions will make it easier for European manufacturers to continue to sell internal combustion engine cars after 2035.
Car manufacturers in Europe have been under pressure from surging sales of Chinese EVs.

Longer duration storage is growing rapidly, driven by higher penetration of intermittent solar and wind generation, falling battery costs, data centre growth, and policy incentives.

articles.title: European strategic autonomy: a €1.8 trillion investment opportunity - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
Europe is embarking on a far-reaching drive to strengthen its strategic autonomy, reducing dependence on external partners across critical areas including defence, energy, technology, healthcare, food security and industry.

For investors, the scale of this transformation could be significant. As Lazare Hounhouayenou, Portfolio Manager, tells Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, around €1.8 trillion of investment is expected to be deployed by 2035 under major European and national initiatives.

The spending could create powerful long-term opportunities for European companies exposed to these strategic sectors, potentially supporting growth and corporate profitability. Defence is already seeing increased investment, while measures to protect strategic industries and accelerate investment in space and technology point to a broader industrial policy shift.

Progress, however, is unlikely to be linear. Differing national priorities, regulatory hurdles and Europe’s complex decision-making processes could generate short-term volatility. “Yet the direction of travel is becoming clearer: Europe is recognising its vulnerabilities and taking concrete steps to address them.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast to discover how European strategic autonomy is opening new horizons for investors.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Lazare Hounhouayenou

Daniel Morris: Hello and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode will be discussing European strategic autonomy. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Lazare Hounhouayenou, Portfolio Manager. Welcome, Lazare, and thanks for joining me.

LH: Happy to be here.

DM: We’re all aware of the capex that’s being devoted to the development of artificial intelligence technologies – trillions in the US but significant amounts of money elsewhere, certainly in Europe. But we may not be quite so aware of what is going on in Europe around strategic autonomy initiatives. I hear that there’s supposed to be about €1.8 trillion devoted to this theme in the years ahead. Let’s get back to basics. To begin with, could you give us a simple and concise definition of strategic autonomy?

LH: Strategic autonomy refers to the ability of a state – or a group of states such as the EU – to act independently on the international stage and defend its interests against the world’s major power[s] in areas considered essential.

The means used to achieve these objectives, as well as the assessments criteria for sovereignty, evolve over time. In the ’60s, a state’s sovereignty was measured by its industrial and military power. Today, with the rise of AI, it is also determined by data centres, AI models.

This evolution raises new questions such as ‘has the control of [micro]chips and data centres replace[d] the control of physical borders?’ Or ‘does the state still maintain its cultural and political sovereignty when its citizens access information, communicate and form opinion[s] through AI algorithm[s] developed under a different jurisdiction?

In this polarised world, what is Europe’s position and where the region can create value according to its strengths in the long term? We think that regaining sovereignty is an absolute necessity for Europe, which must reposition itself within this new geopolitical landscape.

This requires reducing its dependence on partners and former partners across a number of sectors. Defence is one of them, but energy resources, industry, technology, healthcare and food security must also be mentioned.

DM: That sounds quite comprehensive. Can you make the connection, though, between these initiatives, and why Europe undergoing this shift to greater strategic autonomy is important for investors?

LH: Since 2022, the European Union and several European countries have launched a number of major initiatives involving significant level of investments aimed at strengthening Europe’s autonomy in sectors consider strategic and essential. Looking at the main programmes alone, we estimate that nearly 1.8 trillion of investment will be deployed by 2035.

Naturally, European industrial companies with exposure to these sectors are expected to benefit from this powerful long-term investment trend. In this context, investors have an opportunity to position themselves for the long term by investing in sectors with strong growth prospects while at the same time supporting Europe’s strategic autonomy agenda.

DM: When you look at these initiatives, are you seeing practical consequences from Europe’s decisions? That is, are you seeing progress or, conversely, obstacles, delays, rivalries that justif[y] some people’s scepticism and arguably could generate volatility in the short term?

LH: Europe is moving in the right direction, even if progress is never fast enough. Given the urgency of the situation, Europe is reconsidering its governance framework and recognises that its decision-making process[es] are not sufficiently agile.

Recently, Germany and France proposed to create a new cooperation format bringing together the European Union’s six largest economies. This is intended to overcome the slow pace of decision-making within the EU and allow the core group of countries to make faster progress on economic and strategic priorities.

At the same time, Europe has taken concrete measures in defence. For instance, we are seeing EU member states accelerating spending to meet NATO targets of three and a half [per cent] of GDP for core defence expenditure by 2035. The NATO summit held in Turkey last June just confirmed this trajectory.

Europe protected its steel industry through a protectionist steel action plan, reflected in a 50% increase in tariffs and a 47% reduction in import quotas.

And in the crucial space sector, the European Space agency has approved €22 billion for [20]26 to 20. This is an increase of nearly 30%. The objective is to strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy in space technology and mission[s].

This non-exhaustive list of proposals and decisions clearly show that Europe is advancing its thinking and governance and taking concrete action. However, Europe has still many challenges to overcome as interest[s] and priority[ies] differ from one country to the other, which is only natural when 27 countries are involved. These disagreements will create volatility around strategic autonomy themes.

But we believe it is important to take a step back and focus on the medium and long-term trajectory, which appear[s] to be moving in the right direction.

DM: Lazare, if I can summarise some of the key points that you shared with us? You explained that simply, European strategic autonomy is a group of policies/initiatives that enable Europe to act more independently on the international stage, with a focus on many sectors – industrial policy, defence, AI, to cite just a few. You highlighted that we’re talking about €1.8 trillion planned to be invested in the years ahead.

The significance of this for investors is simply that a lot of that money will flow to companies and ultimately should drive corporate profits. You acknowledge that it’s not as smooth or quick as we might like, but the important thing to keep in mind is that Europe is moving in the right direction. It does recognise the problems it’s facing and is working to tackle those problems. Well, Lazare, thank you very much for joining me.

LH: Thank you, Daniel. It was a pleasure to have the discussion with you.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities around European strategic autonomy, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com.

We recommend subscribing to Talking Heads on your favourite podcast channel, such as YouTube or Spotify. You’ll receive your podcast episodes every week. If you like Talking Heads, leave us a positive review and a nice rating.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, and Lazare Hounhouayenou.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

Africa: A refining boom on borrowed time

Africa’s oil refining sector is evolving amid geopolitical shifts and expansion efforts

Africa’s oil refining landscape is undergoing significant changes, driven by recent geopolitical events and ambitious expansion plans. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has led to sharp increases in fuel prices across the continent, highlighting the urgent need for enhanced domestic refining capacity.

The continent’s reliance on imported refined products remains a concern, as many countries struggle to meet emergency oil stock benchmarks set by the International Energy Agency. By 2030, Africa’s refining capacity could reach approximately 5.5 million barrels per day in an optimistic scenario, on par with the continent’s projected demand for refined petroleum products.

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote is at the forefront of this refining boom, with plans to expand his Lagos refinery to 1.4 mbpd and establish a new facility in Lamu, Kenya. However, challenges such as legal disputes and competition from cheaper imports could hinder progress.

articles.title: Do we finally agree on overcapacity? Now what? | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Do we finally agree on overcapacity? Now what?

Kari Heerman

Kari Heerman

Director
- Trade and Economic Statecraft,

Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

October 22, 2026

Shutterstock / metamorworks

9 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

It’s been a busy few weeks for the trade-policy naming industry. We’ve had a Franco-German “non-paper,” a Milwaukee “comprehensive framework,” and a “joint ministerial statement” bringing together 15 economies around an initiative championed by the office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) during the U.S. G20 presidency. Structural excess capacity, overproduction, global macroeconomic imbalances, industrial shocks, non-market policies and practices, or what some of the best trade nerds call overcapacity—the terminology alone has kept trade officials and experts occupied for years. Add this to the anxiety surrounding possible imminent action in USTR’s Section 301 investigation under the remarkably expansive definition of “acts, policies, and practices of certain economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors.”
The latest pronouncements, however, may signal a move from collective hand-wringing to collective action around a real challenge for the open global market economy. China’s large-scale industrial policy can sustain investment and production even when weak demand and low returns would ordinarily force firms to scale back or close. That support can force producers elsewhere to absorb more of the adjustment, losing sales, jobs, and the ability to sustain production capacity. The concern is not simply that producers elsewhere lose market share, but that state-supported expansion can concentrate entire industries in China, potentially giving Beijing market power it can use to shape commercial outcomes in pursuit of national objectives, including those that go beyond commercial competition. Whether these pronouncements ultimately lead to meaningful action against the distortions created by China’s strategic industrial policy or simply provide a common justification for protectionism is as much a political test as an economic one.
Where is the overcapacity?
China’s gaping manufacturing trade surplus has become a symbol of overcapacity concerns. It has reached an eye-popping $2 trillion in nominal terms, driven by a near-relentless rise in exports paired with much slower import growth. While consistent with concerns about state-supported industrial expansion, a trade surplus is not proof of economic malfeasance, as better economists than me rightly warn. Treating it as such risks turning an effort to preserve competition into a license for protectionism—undermining the very benefits of open markets that governments are supposed to be defending. Recent research finds that much of China’s export growth is concentrated in a relatively small number of products, underscoring the need to look beyond aggregate trade figures. Alas, no single indicator definitively establishes whether state support is sustaining industrial investment and production that would otherwise contract under normal commercial conditions, much less whether the resulting expansion threatens to drive out competitors and leave China with market power. Making the case requires a veritable cornucopia of evidence on subsidies, investment, profitability, capacity utilization, and more.

Figure 1

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

The challenge of distinguishing the effects of overcapacity from ordinary comparative advantage—the very mechanism that delivers the benefits of trade—is more than academic hair-splitting. It has been a genuine obstacle to effective action by governments, individually and collectively. International trade rules, along with the national laws that implement them, are designed to allow countries to impose tariffs or other trade defenses against import surges and unfair trade practices, but only if the countries meet demanding evidentiary and product-specific requirements. These constraints aren’t simply an expression of “neoliberal” devotion to free trade. They were designed to guard against arbitrary protectionism—and for good reason, since it undermines the benefits of open trade and imposes costs on the consumers and taxpayers who ultimately pay for it. Yet rules built to constrain arbitrary protectionism are poorly suited to addressing the scale and global reach of China’s strategic industrial policy.
The recent Franco-German proposal recognizes this gap and signals agreement between Europe’s two largest economies that the EU needs faster and stronger defenses against market-distorting industrial policies that threaten European competitiveness and could give foreign governments market power over strategically important industries. But national defenses can only do so much. Restricting imports in one market may simply redirect exports elsewhere. That’s part of what happened when the United States raised tariffs on imports from China beginning in 2018. Since then, China’s manufacturing trade surplus with the EU has soared even as its surplus with the United States has declined (Figure 2). Empirical research finds that U.S. tariffs contributed to redirecting Chinese exports toward other markets, including Europe. And even if national defenses successfully limit import competition in domestic markets, they leave firms to compete against production benefiting from Beijing’s support in third-country markets. In industries where scale and continued investment are essential to competitiveness, losing ground in those markets can make it difficult for firms to become—or remain—globally competitive.

Figure 2

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Beyond national defenses?
Meanwhile, an interesting development has emerged in the perennially trade-challenged steel industry. Finding a beacon of light in steel trade policy is a bit of a shock, but that’s where we are these days. Governments have been wrestling with global excess capacity in steel since long before electric vehicles and semiconductors entered the conversation. Years of Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) monitoring have established both the scale of the problem and China’s outsized role in it. Steelmaking capacity has continued expanding even as demand has contracted, leaving global excess capacity in 2025 exceeding the entire steel production of OECD countries by more than 200 million metric tons. Government subsidies are an important part of the story, and nowhere are they more extensive than in China. Detailed work by intrepid OECD researchers finds that steel production in China receives substantially more subsidies than elsewhere (Figure 3). In 2024, the median Chinese steel firm received 15 times as much in subsidies, relative to its assets, as the median firm elsewhere.

Figure 3

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

On September 30, members of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity (GFSEC), meeting in Milwaukee under the chairmanship of U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, adopted the Milwaukee Comprehensive Framework for Joint Action, outlining how they intend to coordinate their existing policies and trade defenses to tackle global excess capacity. Although the framework doesn’t establish binding obligations, it lays out concrete steps members intend to take and what meaningful coordination could look like. Members propose to coordinate their trade defenses, including by monitoring whether restrictions in one participating market redirect steel into another and considering appropriate responses. The framework also proposes sharing “melt-and-pour” information to help trace steel to its original source and prevent circumvention of trade restrictions through processing in third countries—no small task in modern supply chains. Looking beyond direct competition from excess-capacity steel, the framework proposes that members investigate and consider responses to export restrictions on critical steelmaking inputs that could undermine their competitiveness. If governments follow through on the Milwaukee framework, coordinated action could make their national trade defenses more effective against import competition from excess capacity steel. GFSEC members account for more than half of global steel imports. If they can coordinate restrictions, they could make it harder for China and other sources of excess capacity steel to replace sales lost in one country with sales elsewhere. It might even change the incentives for China and other countries to continue expanding excess capacity in steel.
Where could this lead?
The October 7 ministerial statement signed by 15 trade ministers following the G20 meetings in Milwaukee raises the possibility of extending the framework’s approach to sectors beyond steel. The signatories agreed to establish sectoral platforms to examine and address structural excess capacity in autos and EVs, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors, and solar panels. These sectors are familiar from China’s earlier industrial priorities. Their economics differ considerably from steel—and from one another. The OECD’s technical expertise could help governments distinguish genuine distortions from ordinary competitive success and develop responses suited to each industry. A credible diagnosis of excess capacity may also help persuade countries without an immediate defensive interest that coordinated action is warranted.
Even if countries agree that structural excess capacity is distorting trade, they may not agree that trade defenses are in their own interest. In steel, governments have established industries, workers, and political constituencies that may be pressing for protection. In other sectors, interests are more varied: some countries want to preserve production, others want to establish new capabilities, and still others may decide that the benefits of inexpensive imports outweigh the costs of distorted competition.
The politics make cooperation even harder. China has shown itself willing to retaliate against countries that challenge its policies, while the United States is making demands of the very partners whose cooperation it needs, without giving them much confidence that they won’t be its next target. Building an effective coalition may therefore require a bargain that allows countries to make trade-offs across sectors, gaining enough where they see benefits to justify cooperation elsewhere, even when the political and economic risks are substantial.
Preserve competition, not just production
Concentrating collective efforts on responding to the consequences of China’s past industrial policy risks missing the bigger challenge. Coordinating national defenses against structural excess capacity addresses only one way that large-scale industrial policy can undermine competition. China’s industrial policies can also help China gain control over critical inputs or establish market positions that become increasingly difficult for competitors elsewhere to challenge—even without a flood of inexpensive imports.
Coordinating national trade defenses is a start, but we shouldn’t mistake the means for the end. The real prize would be international responses that preserve competition, allow countries to benefit from specialization and innovation, and prevent state intervention from systematically eliminating competitive alternatives. The recent pronouncements are a long way from that ambition. The Milwaukee framework offers a glimpse of how countries might begin turning shared concerns into coordinated action. The question is whether, over time, they can build coordinated responses that preserve competition rather than simply coordinate protection.

articles.title: China And St. Augustine
articles.text:
China And St. Augustine

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 23 Oct 2026

Back in the summer of 2015, the Chinese government decided that equity markets had risen too far, too fast. The rug was pulled from under margin lending and various restrictions were put in place that brought the unfolding raging equity bull market to an abrupt end. By January 2024, the Chinese government reversed course and decided that Chinese equity prices had fallen far enough. Beijing intervened in the market (see Chinese Policies And Chinese Equities) and put a floor under domestic markets. Equities duly rallied, delivering very solid returns for 2024 and 2025. However, over the past year, Chinese equity market returns have been fairly dismal. In fact, Chinese equity markets have now fallen for 10 consecutive weeks, a feat they had never achieved before. This in spite of the fact that (a) excitement over all things “artificial intelligence” has been a key driver of global equity market performance and that (b) China is one of the few countries outside of the US actually registering notable gains on the AI front. In short, Chinese equities have had a very disappointing month, quarter, year-to-date and 12 months and what had been steady outperformance has now melted away like snow in the sun.

articles.title: The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick
articles.text:
The PRA’s second decade − speech by Katharine Braddick

Given at Mansion House

Published on
22 October 2026

In her first Mansion House speech as Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), Katharine Braddick sets out her vision for the PRA's second decade. She outlines plans for a new five-year strategy centred on four priorities: resilience, growth, innovation and transparency, alongside a series of reforms to strengthen operational resilience, streamline regulation and improve regulatory processes for firms.

Speech
Lady Mayor, thank you for inviting me to speak this evening. It is an honour to address you and your guests and a pleasure to be speaking alongside Nikhil, who I have known for many years and who I look forward to working with in this new role.
When I joined the PRA in July I joined an organisation that in a little over a decade had succeeded decisively in its initial core mission, a mission that is vital to the success of the United Kingdom and its economy: to restore the resilience of the financial sector, so that it can properly support businesses and households across the nation.
Thanks to the work of the PRA, and significant effort by industry, that resilience has not only been restored but significantly strengthened. This hard-won stability is a source of advantage for our financial sector and this country, and it underpins our position as a leading and trusted financial centre. It is also the principal legacy of my predecessor Sam Woods: we might all wish to say we had achieved such a thing in our careers.
In that decade or so the world has also, of course, changed. Security threats increase, exacerbated by a more fractured geopolitical landscape. Interconnected financial vulnerabilities are arising from stretched sectoral valuations, rising sovereign debt levels and increased market leverage. Technology presents extraordinary opportunities and material and novel risks. And society demands accountability and transparency from its public institutions to maintain their legitimacy.
A new long-term PRA strategy
In this context, then, our task is to determine what the PRA must deliver in its second decade and how to create the regulator the UK will need for the future. Next year I will publish for the first time a five-year strategy for the PRA. The strategy will set out how we intend to deliver four priorities I believe are central for the PRA’s future success:
Resilience
The first priority is resilience. Maintaining the resilience of the UK’s banking and insurance sectors is the foundation of our mission; the PRA identified early on that the need to address operational resilience as well as financial resilience is a prudential matter. Addressing non-financial resilience is an ever wider and more complex task, not least as the frequency and materiality of cyber incidents grows. Firms need to continue to invest in their capabilities, not only to prevent incidents, but to ensure they can respond to and recover from severe disruption.
The PRA similarly needs to evolve. We will significantly increase our focus on firms’ operational and cyber resilience. The cyber challenge, in particular, is an area where we can and do partner effectively with industry and our international counterparts to progress our understanding of both risks and mitigants. We will create a new PRA directorate, reporting directly to me, to act as a centre of excellence for operational and cyber resilience. We will also consult jointly with the FCA on a new supervisory statement by the end of the year, clarifying our expectations of firms as we develop our experience and understanding.
Growth
Our second theme is growth. Achieving sustained and sustainable growth is the key economic policy question of this moment and regulation has its part to play, even if it is rarely the determinative factor.
In the coming period we will further develop our framework for the secondary competitiveness and growth objective. It will address not only the costs and benefits of regulation, but how our work influences the investment environment, the availability of capital for the firms we regulate and the pricing of the services they provide. We will set out how that framework is embedded in our day-to-day decision-making, and how we will track the effect our work is having on the growth and international competitiveness of the UK.
This framework will help ensure our regime remains relevant, effective, and proportionate. We will engage industry and Parliament as we shape, use and learn from it. It will enable us to be clear and confident about our role, and articulate a well-founded understanding of our contribution to the economy. This is not just a means to deliver against the secondary objective but is ultimately a foundation for good regulation.
Of course, the PRA has already taken steps to keep our regime up to date, most recently working with our FCA colleagues to devise a new captive insurance regime to enable innovation and growth in the insurance market. And to remove barriers to growth and provide predictability, we consulted earlier this month on a framework to automatically index our regulatory thresholds with nominal growth, a first among major financial regulators.
As a next step, we have today set out with the FCA a second set of significant reforms to streamline the Senior Managers and Certification Regime. These proposals reduce the number of senior management functions requiring pre-approval and remove requirements relating to the certification regime, halving its regulatory burden on firms whilst retaining clear accountability of their senior leaders.
Innovation
Our third priority is innovation. The PRA is a world-class regulator. To continue to be so, we must become a world leading technologically enabled regulator. Working with industry, we will go further in refining the data we collect and how we collect it to ensure we can react to emerging issues and risks in a timely manner, while shrinking the need for ad hoc collections and removing collections whose benefits are not justified. We will take feedback from you on this as we go, refining our approach and prioritising the changes that add the most value.
We will accelerate our deployment of data analytics and new technologies, enabling supervisors to rapidly identify emerging themes and trends in risks. Working with industry, we will make it easier and more efficient to work with us by taking innovative approaches to data collection and enhancing the clarity and accessibility of our rulebook and supervisory guidance, streamlining communications so that firms can quickly and easily understand what we expect.
Transparency
And our fourth priority is transparency. A sound understanding of the intentions and priorities of the regulator is crucial for firms to be able to effectively plan and manage their risks. And a stable and predictable business environment is essential to enable investors to deploy capital in the UK economy. So we will provide a clear and transparent line of sight to firms, Parliament and society about our plans and priorities, not least through the publication of and reporting on the new strategy. That will provide the means for us to be held accountable for meeting our commitments and demonstrate that we are a listening and learning organisation.
As an early example of this approach, we will take decisive steps to improve the experience of banks and building societies in relation to internal models for residential mortgages. This has been a source of particular difficulty for many firms, and we need to learn the lessons of this experience.
The PRA has already improved the approval process for firms, and we will go further by providing additional transparency about our operational performance. We will consult in Spring next year on material policy changes to improve firms’ access to a modelled approach. These proposals will be subject to challenge by an independent panel of industry and regulatory experts to ensure their feasibility, learning the lessons of the past to ensure our future policy is grounded in operational realities. Working with our colleagues in the wider Bank, we will also examine the interactions between hybrid mortgage models and stressed buffer requirements.
And we will conduct an independent review of the UK’s implementation of hybrid mortgage model requirements to identify tangible ways to assist firms as they maintain and develop their models. The work of that review will be sequenced to ensure it does not jeopardise the delivery of ongoing model approval and policy work.
Delivering the strategy
The delivery of our strategy will rely on the considerable strengths that characterise the PRA: our deeply expert and purpose-driven people; our comprehensive knowledge of the firms we regulate; and our established approach to supervision – judgement-led, forward-looking and focussed on key risks to safety and soundness. That work has underpinned the success of the PRA’s first twelve years and must never be taken for granted.
As we take the PRA into its second decade, we will build on our strengths and track record by evolving our approach to meet the challenges of today and of tomorrow. We will ensure the financial sector remains resilient to the increasingly volatile environment we now face. We will set out clearly and confidently how we contribute to growth. We will exploit technology to retain our position as a world-leading regulator and supervisor. And we will operate transparently to underpin confidence in our work and thereby in our financial sector and economy.
The PRA in 2032 will be a forward-looking regulator that is respected and trusted. A regulator that is recognised for its work supporting a resilient, competitive and innovative financial system that in turn supports a thriving UK economy. I look forward to working with my PRA colleagues, and importantly also with you all, to deliver that vision.
Now, would you please join me in raising a toast to the Lady Mayor and the Mayoral Consort.

Katharine Braddick
Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation and Chief Executive Officer of the Prudential Regulation Authority

articles.title: Agents of change − speech by Sarah Breeden
articles.text:
Agents of change − speech by Sarah Breeden

Given at ECB Sintra Forum

Published on
30 June 2026

Sarah Breeden sets out how AI is reshaping finance at speed. She explores how agentic AI is transforming cyber risk, markets and payments – and why central banks must adapt fast, strengthen resilience and cooperate globally to ensure the next technology surprise does not become a test of financial stability.

Speech
It’s a privilege to be here to discuss AI and financial stability. It’s hard to imagine a more timely or important issue. AI is reshaping finance at speed. And it’s on us to ensure that the next technology surprise does not become a test of financial stability.
For some years, central banks, including the Bank of England, have worked to promote responsible AI adoption in the financial system.footnote [1] And since AI looks likely to be the next ‘general purpose technology’ and a key source of long-term economic growthfootnote [2], it’s in all our interests to do so.
But the apparent acceleration in AI capabilities, even compared with six months ago, creates a double challenge: not only enabling responsible adoption and managing risks, but also recognising that AI should transform how central banks do that job. We need to think as hard about the latter as the former.
How the technology is evolving
In 2019, the length of software task the latest AI models could complete doubled roughly every seven months.footnote [3] In 2024, that had sped up to around four months.footnote [4] Major advances this Spring in models for identifying cyber vulnerabilities suggest it may now be faster still.footnote [5]
So an already exponential increase in capability appears to be accelerating.footnote [6] We were surprised this Spring, and we should be prepared for further technology surprises.
These advances also suggest an inflection point. Around the start of this decade, generative AI systems created content on request. From late 2024, they were explicitly trained to reason through requests.footnote [7] Now with agentic AI, systems can autonomously chain together sequences of actions.
The financial system looks likely therefore to evolve quickly into one that operates more autonomously, at scale and speed: AI agents transacting on behalf of consumers and merchants; devising and executing trading strategies in financial markets; and identifying and chaining together cyber vulnerabilities.
Drivers of the transition and its financial stability risks
That will of course require central banks to respond. But before turning to that, I wanted to highlight that this transition is already macro-relevant, inherently uncertain and carries risks of its own. Four interdependent channels will shape its nature, scale and timing.
The first is AI’s capability: for example, whether progress in recursive self-learning allows models to improve autonomously.
Second, capacity: whether compute keeps pace with capability and demand.
Third, diffusion: where adoption takes hold across sectors and tasks.
Fourth, how debt and equity finance fund this historically unprecedented pace of investment.
The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee will publish its updated assessment on 7 July, so I won’t front-run that. But I will note that in April, we concluded that while to date AI infrastructure investment had thus far mostly been financed by large technology companies’ cash flows and equity, debt financing was rising rapidly, and in some new and complex ways. We therefore judged that the financial stability consequences of any fall in AI-related asset prices could well increase.footnote [8]
Financial stability implications of an agentic system, and how central banks should respond
Cyber capabilities
My most proximate financial stability concern however is what the UK Government’s AI Security Institute has described as a step change in agentic AI’s cyber capabilities.footnote [9]
In the hands of defenders, these tools strengthen cyber resilience. But, in malicious hands, they materially increase the chance of attacks that could harm financial stability. And so, the immediate challenge is to maintain the advantage of cyber defenders as these capabilities continue to evolve, particularly in an increasingly severe cyber threat environment including from geopolitics and ransomware.
Cyber resilience has been a priority for the Bank of England and our G7 colleagues for over a decadefootnote [10], and the Bank has worked closely with other UK authorities, Government and the National Cyber Security Centre. In May, the Bank, FCA and HM Treasury set out practical steps for financial institutions to prepare for these frontier AI-related cyber risks.footnote [11] Getting the fundamentals of cyber hygiene right is more important than ever.
But this gives only limited comfort. AI is uncovering many vulnerabilities to patch, including as global software providers and key UK financial institutions use the latest models. For financial stability, patching must happen quickly – across the financial sector, key
third-party technology providers, and wider national infrastructure such as energy and telecoms. That is no small task.
It’s also an urgent one. As the heads of the Five Eyes cyber security agencies said last week, “the timeline is not years, it is months”.footnote [12] Open source models may lag the most advanced closed models by only four to eight months, and their safeguards can be breached.footnote [13] If patches are released but not swiftly implemented, malicious actors can reverse engineer the vulnerabilities they address.
For central banks, this increases the onus on a system-wide approach to operational resilience.footnote [14] Stronger firm defences are essential, but not enough. Firms must also respond to and recover from disruption quickly – whether from successful cyber attacks or from patching itself causing operational disruption, as the faulty CrowdStrike update did in 2024.footnote [15]
Authorities should place higher likelihood on simultaneous multi-firm disruption, enhance tools to stress test that impact ex antefootnote [16], and strengthen mechanisms with industry to coordinate ex post.footnote [17]
We should also consider whether regulated firms need enhanced recovery options for core systems. In the event of financial failure, we have deposit insurance so customers can still access their money, and bail in-able debt so the largest firms can continue to provide services. In a cyber context, do we need systems that allow one institution to pick up another’s basic functions during disruption, as in Ukraine’s “Power Banking” programme launched in 2022?footnote [18] Or requirements for key firms to have completely separate fail-over capabilities or to be able to rebuild compromised core systems quickly from “bare metal”? These are big questions, but they are the right ones.
Agentic trading in financial markets
Turning to agentic trading in financial markets, evidence suggests that for now, trading firms mostly use autonomous AI for lower-risk operational tasks, such as research.footnote [19] But that could change quickly.
If AI agents respond similarly to the same prompts or triggers, they could amplify volatility in stress – especially if their objectives drift from original goals or public policy objectives, in a manifestation of the misalignment problem that can arise with some AI models.footnote [20]
The financial stability question therefore broadens from whether firms can use models well to whether the system can also observe and contain their resulting behaviours.
We have experience of structured, multi-round stress simulations focused on how financial market participants behave as they learn of each other’s actionsfootnote [21]. AI increases the importance of such work - and it should transform how we do it. We are experimenting with the BIS Innovation Hub and the Bundesbank on simulation methods to understand which aspects of agent design could drive herding behaviour.footnote [22]
That work can also explore mitigants: whether markets using AI agents are resilient enough; whether agents’ objective functions could incorporate public policy objectives; and whether guardrails are needed, analogous to circuit breakers or kill switches that would limit or stop trading market-wide if faulty AI models cause market meltdown.
More broadly, AI should transform central banks’ monitoring and risk assessment. Agentic technology could combine a wide range of qualitative and quantitative data to generate insights and scenarios for how the current conjuncture could go wrong, potentially using a ‘digital twin’ of the financial system to simulate interactions between participants.footnote [23]
Agentic payments and commerce
Turning lastly to e-commerce and payments, consumers and merchants have so far mainly used AI agents in recommendation mode, with humans still executing transactions. But as agentic technology advances, tech firms, payment systems and merchants are working to automate that final step (such that I could ask an AI agent to ‘book my holiday’, ‘refill my fridge’ or ‘refresh my wardrobe’).
That matters for central banks. In the UK, the Bank is leading a public-private partnership to design the next generation of retail payments infrastructure, ensuring it can support agentic payment journeys and expand choice and functionality for users.footnote [24]
But the biggest issues are likely to be for regulationfootnote [25] and industry standards: how users securely give consent and authorisation to agents, especially for multiple transactions; how disputes are settled and liability assigned for erroneous or fraudulent transactions; and how authorities avoid fragmentation and walled gardens as AI firms and payment systems all develop protocols for agents to interact with themselves and merchants.
What these two examples – agentic commerce and agentic trading – both highlight is that, as AI capabilities increase, we must keep asking whether existing, technology-agnostic regulatory frameworks remain sufficient. Our frameworks were not built to contemplate autonomous agents, and relying on a human in the loop for all agent actions is unlikely to be realistic. More sophisticated governance and accountability frameworks may be needed.footnote [26]
Conclusion
To conclude, AI capability is accelerating and becoming increasingly agentic. The financial system is likely to evolve into one that operates more autonomously, at scale and speed. The transition is uncertain and will bring risks of its own to monitor. And a more agentic system means central banks must think hard not only about how finance harnesses the opportunities and mitigates the risks, but also about how new technological possibilities should change how we do our own job.
We need policy frameworks, internal skills and institutional structures ready for more frequent technology surprises. Cyber risks, agentic trading and agentic payments and commerce are the applications on my radar today. But that list could look different in a year, if not sooner.
Scenario analysis, and how we prepare now in light of it, will be key. What if the next surprise puts the latest capabilities in bad actors’ hands, or models develop in ways that are harder to evaluate and control, given evidence that some behave differently in testing compared to real-life scenarios?footnote [27]
Cooperation with other parts of the official sector is vital – for example, drawing on AI security institutes’ model testing and strengthening resilience through domestic AI capabilities and capacity.
The same applies internationally, including in the Financial Stability Boardfootnote [28] and the G7.footnote [29] The global financial crisis underlined how interconnected finance is – the FSB came out of that.
The challenge of AI is similar. The impact of new AI capabilities can spread across borders through common technology dependencies, globally systemic financial institutions and market infrastructure.
We shouldn’t wait for a crisis to build the cooperation we need. With other central banks, regulators and finance ministries, the Bank of England will do our part to ensure responsible AI adoption and, through it, sustainable economic growth.
I would like to thank Kimberley Moran and Michael Yoganayagam for their assistance in drafting these remarks, and Owen Lock, Irina Mnohoghitnei and Andy Walters for their helpful input.
