There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesArtificial IntelligenceHow Small Business Owners Are Using AI to Help Propel Growth Oct 22, 2026ShareMarie Hunter, president of KRG Oil Company and 2016 graduate of 10,000 Small Businesses Small business owners are increasingly using AI to propel growth and develop new products, according to the Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses program’s report, The AI Economy is a Small Business Economy. 42% of the program’s graduates who responded to a survey say they use AI for financial analysis and business planning, which is more than double the rate in 2024. More than 85% of 10,000 Small Businesses graduates who responded to a survey say they use AI in some form. When Marie Hunter and her colleagues hit on a new idea earlier this year for her fuel distribution firm, she used an artificial intelligence (AI) agent to crunch the numbers.
She wanted to add solar panels to the tanks to help power their pumps and make other modifications. Rather than analyzing the cost of customizing a few fuel storage tanks for select customers, the agent delivered an ambitious blueprint for a new business.
“It came back with a plan to upsell a new product line of tanks with additional services,” says Hunter, the owner and president of KRG Oil Company, a small family firm outside Atlanta. The agent “is my force multiplier,” says Hunter.
She jokingly named the agent Billi Jean, her take on the name of one of her favorite songs. Hunter developed the agent with a colleague and originally used it to help manage emails. It also analyzes finances and prepares strategic growth plans in line with Hunter’s vision for the company.
In the last two years, small business owners such as Hunter are increasingly using AI to help shape the fortunes of their enterprises, according to a report released this month by Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses, an education and support program that has helped thousands of enterprises grow and create jobs. Hunter and the other 10,000 Small Businesses alumni interviewed in this article have been independently exploring and integrating AI into their companies.
In a survey of graduates of the program, 42% of respondents say they use AI for financial analysis and business planning, which is more than double the rate in 2024. And more than half of respondents say they use the innovation to develop or research new projects and products, according to the report, The AI Economy is a Small Business Economy.
How are small businesses using AI?
Small business owners are rapidly putting AI to work. More than 85% of survey respondents say they use AI in some form. Accounting for 43.5% of US economic output, small businesses are responsible for 61% of net new job creation, according to the US Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy. Small businesses are poised to play a significant role in the dissemination of AI.
Asahi Pompey, global head of the Office of Corporate Engagement and chair of the Urban Investment Group, says the new Goldman Sachs Small Business AI Institute is designed to support small business owners as they navigate changes brought about by AI. The Institute will help guide entrepreneurs through AI adoption and integration, positioning them to push their businesses into this new frontier.
“It is clear that AI is already changing how small business owners are making decisions, serving customers, and planning for growth,” she says. “The challenge is no longer whether small businesses will adopt AI. It is how they harness it fully and turn experimentation into lasting results.”
Interviews with graduates of Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses show just how dynamic their AI applications are, and how strategically they have designed and deployed their own AI agents.
The business owners are using AI to manage customer service at campgrounds, assist control rooms in petrochemical plants, and help design Spanish language lessons for online education. These businesses all share a common goal: using AI to get the most out of their businesses.
Using AI on the shop floor
Automation is nothing new for Bob McClure, the co-owner of McClure’s Pickles in Detroit. As the producer of more than 3 million jars of pickled cucumbers, onions, and peppers annually, the firm has long used industrial robots to label, pack, and stack its inventory. What is new is applying AI to the company’s critical functions, says McClure.
Bob McClure, co-owner of McClure’s Pickles and 2014 graduate of 10,000 Small Businesses Take food safety. Nothing is more important in his business, McClure says. The company constantly runs tests of its reporting system in the event of a food recall. In the past, employees manually entered information on the origins of the raw ingredients used to make pickles in a database, and it took 30 to 45 minutes to run a trace.
After McClure integrated professional versions of large language models (LLMs) into the firm’s enterprise resource management program, the system could show the journey the ingredients took from their source to the jar in less than two minutes. It provides an online dashboard to show where the pickles were shipped, how much of the batch is left in the warehouse, and even its pH or acidity levels.
McClure also used AI to create a maintenance application to automatically monitor production equipment, an accounting app to draft accounts payable for suppliers, and another app to review jar labels for accuracy.
Integrating LLMs into business systems has its challenges
There are challenges. Writing instructions for the LLMs takes finesse and sometimes a few “iterations” are needed to get it right. And sometimes there are bugs to work out. Because McClure, a former actor with no code training, can use natural language to engage the models, he says he does not need to license software or pay a technician. He can do it himself.
Even better, he says he can apply the AI models to multiple tasks without paying more for their services. “I think AI is uniquely suited to small business entrepreneurship because you are so strapped for resources in terms of time, people, and money,” McClure says. “I now need to hire humans to manage my AI.”
Naomi Stone, the owner and CEO of an environmental engineering consulting firm in Hermosa Beach, California, has gone a step further. She has made an AI application the cornerstone of a new venture, a company called Enso.
Can AI connect producers and consumers?
Companies already pay to dispose of their surplus materials, and Stone says Enso is designed to turn that expense into a new revenue stream. The firm uses AI to match companies holding surplus materials and industrial byproducts with buyers who can put them to work. Some byproducts, like coal ash, have long been used to strengthen building materials. Other byproducts, from packaging to equipment to manufacturing scrap, simply need the right buyer, she says.
For Stone, putting waste materials back to work advances the circular economy, a key tenet in sustainable finance. AI can facilitate matches between coal ash producers and buyers at a speed and scale Enso would have a hard time doing on its own.
“It makes matches we haven’t even thought of,” says Stone. “And the best part is it can help our clients convert waste from a cost into a new revenue stream.”
AI’s potential to illuminate unforeseen opportunities is a theme that comes up regularly among small business owners. Back in Roswell, Georgia, Marie Hunter says she has considered focusing more on her coaching business for entrepreneurs. So she gave her AI agent new instructions: to compile M&A data and prepare KRG Oil for an exit. “What does that look like, and what do I need to think about?” Hunter says. She adds that she’s ready to aspire to get her company to “the multiple it deserves.”

It Is Less Sure About U.S. Conditions.Rubio’s recent visit brought welcome attention, but more capital requires governance changes that may be a hard sell for regional governments.Link CopiedBy Jennifer B. MurtazashviliPublished on Oct 21, 2026On Monday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio made his first official trip to Central Asia for a meeting with his counterparts from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. He was accompanied by more than 200 U.S. business leaders, and the region’s capitals hoped the trip was laying the groundwork for a presidential visit next year. (No sitting U.S. president has ever visited Central Asia.)For more than two decades, security and the war in Afghanistan defined American interests in the region. But U.S. influence faded after the chaotic 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan, which did not reflect well on Washington in regional capitals. Now, Washington is working out how to update those interests for the current era. Weak governance across the region makes Western investors wary, and limited connectivity makes moving goods in and out of the landlocked region costly.In addition, Central Asia has experienced significant changes: A quarter-century ago, its five states were barely ten years into independence, with weak economies and little leverage. Today, Kazakhstan, the largest economy in the region, is home to two-thirds of foreign investment in Central Asia. It is the largest uranium producer in the world and supplies more than a quarter of U.S. uranium imports. Uzbekistan, the most populous country and the largest market in the region, has opened its economy—and because it borders every other Central Asian state, that opening has transformed connectivity across the region. Governments of the five countries now meet regularly among themselves and court many global partners, including neighboring Russia and China.Now, Rubio has the opportunity to offer Central Asia something the region wants: capital, trade, and investment in transit routes. But those offers of investment and support to connectivity will mean little unless Central Asian governments do their part. Even so, the region’s governments may bristle at the strings attached to the U.S. offers.The biggest obstacle to American investment lies in the region itself: Governments remain unreliable partners. Throughout Central Asia, courts remain weak, state enterprises tend to dominate and report to presidents directly, and deals often depend on personal ties. Foreign investors have occasionally faced serious whiplash from local governments, which change their minds on a whim. American capital will not flow at scale until contracts are more enforceable and terms are public. U.S. financing via the International Development Finance Corporation, access to Western capital, and a place in Western supply chains all require better governance and improved transparency.Those changes are a hard sell when Russia and China are neighbors and convenient partners. They do not press for reforms, disclosures, or shifts in how enterprises are governed. Central Asian governments will gladly take American investment, but American investors will not commit to them without significant improvements in the rule of law and a sound investment climate. As a result, in its quest for influence, Washington is competing against ease just as much as it is competing against capital.Geography also is a huge constraint, as all five states are landlocked—Uzbekistan doubly so. This makes connections a true matter of survival. The Middle Corridor—the multimodal trade and transport route that runs from China across the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus to Europe—avoids Russia. The new American-backed link—a proposed route across southern Armenia that could connect Azerbaijan to the Nakhchivan exclave, called the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP)—is intended to complete the Middle Corridor. However, even optimistic planning puts construction more than a year away for TRIPP, and the Middle Corridor is costly and not economically competitive.Central Asia is also looking south. Uzbekistan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan signed a framework to study a railway that would cross Afghanistan and give Central Asian cargo access to ports in Pakistan. But financing—and stability in Afghanistan—remain a long way off. On the other hand, the construction of a China-Uzbekistan-Kyrgyz Republic railway is underway.Both the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine and the war with Iran have underscored Central Asia’s urgency to build new connections to and from its markets. Kazakhstan exports most of its oil through Russia, leaving it exposed to the war in Ukraine. The Caspian Pipeline Consortium, which ends at the Russian port of Novorossiysk, has been the site of multiple Ukrainian drone strikes. Chevron and ExxonMobil are among the biggest investors in Kazakh oil, so these strikes hit American companies too. Signals from Washington have also been mixed: Recent U.S. attention has focused on Ukrainian strikes against refineries rather than export terminals. Either way, Astana must treat the targeting choices made in Kyiv as a risk to its own economy.Critical minerals have been the subject of investment discussion between Central Asia and the United States. Although Central Asia is eager to court American investment, the United States only receives about 2 percent of Central Asian mineral exports. A summit in Washington last year produced a memorandum on critical minerals with Kazakhstan, but this announcement has not yielded results.Deals announced since then do not fare well under scrutiny. The Financial Times reported that Trump’s sons held indirect stakes in a company set to merge with Cove Kaz Capital, an American firm that in April took a 70 percent stake in tungsten deposits in Kazakhstan alongside the state mining company. The White House announced the deal with great fanfare and promises of U.S. financing, but the mine itself remains years away. Central Asian governments understand the appetite in Washington for quick deals and have tailored their outreach to satisfy it.Washington has a smaller irritant of its own to remove, one that dates to the Cold War. The 1974 Jackson-Vanik Amendment, meant to pressure Moscow to let Soviet Jews emigrate, still denies permanent normal trade relations to several of the Soviet Union’s successor states.Since 1997, successive administrations have found Kazakhstan in compliance with the law, but the amendment remains on the books. Mining projects require decades-long commitments, and the amendment makes that trade less predictable. In Congress, both Democrats and Republicans support pending legislation to repeal the law for Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. Repeal would not unlock a wave of investment, but it would remove an irritant that costs Washington almost nothing to fix.Renewed U.S. attention to Central Asia is welcome, but expectations should be modest. Rubio pledged support for the Middle Corridor and offered partnerships in critical minerals, infrastructure, and advanced technologies that respect both sovereignty and the rule of law. Uzbekistan announced nearly $12 billion in agreements and prospective projects, while President Shavkat Mirziyoyev promised more predictable conditions for American investors. The test now is whether Tashkent and its neighbors can capitalize on these investment promises by enforcing contracts made on transparent terms. Rubio also said that enhanced U.S. attention to the region does not require Central Asia to stop working with other partners. Washington cannot compete with Russia and China on proximity, but it can compete on the quality and credibility of what it offers.Get more news and analysis fromEmissaryThe latest from Carnegie scholars on the world’s most pressing challenges, delivered to your inbox.About the AuthorJennifer B. Higher Yields And Corporate Profits

Tan Kai Xian

Gavekal Research | 22 Oct 2026

Equity investors were served a morsel of optimism Wednesday, as Meta’s chairman Mark Zuckerberg claimed the company’s AI investments “are paying off,” and raised guidance for total 2026 capital expenditure after third-quarter earnings beat estimates. Yet after a sharp sell-off in the shares of indebted AI names such as neocloud company CoreWeave, many investors remain jittery. They fear that with equity market performance powered heavily by the AI capex boom, higher yields will erode US corporate profits, triggering a broader sell-off. However, there are several good reasons to believe that the rise in yields so far is unlikely to inflict significant damage on US corporate profits.Add to personal dashboardInteractive chart

Summary

In the US, AI is likely to have a sequential impact on inflation. Strong demand will push inflation higher first, while productivity gains should become more disinflationary over time. Together with geopolitical and energy pressures, this is likely to keep inflation above central bank target.

The IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1%, up slightly from July, with 3.4% projected for 2027 — driven largely by the AI investment boom. Resilience is still the key message, but it is not unlimited. The IMF suggests a shift from coping to rebuilding, with a focus on supply-side resilience, fiscal repair and price stability.Looking ahead, supply resilience and policy discipline will drive growth, inflation and asset allocation.

The IMF held its Annual Meetings in Bangkok this week, releasing its World Economic Outlook. The Outlook highlights that the global economy has remained resilient, albeit unevenly, but the room for further adjustment is now more limited. Potential constraints could emerge in energy and other commodities, which have benefited so far from rerouting, substitution and efficiency gains, as well as technology-related investment. This could lead to more persistent inflation. Looking ahead, the IMF stresses the need to move from coping to rebuilding, in terms of supply-side resilience, restoring fiscal space and keeping monetary policy focused on price stability. It also warns that the financial system needs to be reinforced to create buffers against future shocks. Over the medium term, the IMF suggests that greater resilience will require more technological and trade diversification, as well as stronger supply buffers in critical sectors such as energy.

This week at a glance

Global equities had a mixed week as investors rotated away from the AI trade. Among emerging markets, Indonesia suffered on Friday after MSCI proposed removing the country from its EM classification. Bond yields fell despite a hotter-than-expected US inflation report mid-week. Oil rose for a second consecutive week on Middle East supply concerns, while gold posted a weekly loss. The dollar softened late in the week as concerns about further rate rises eased.

Amundi Investment Institute Macro Focus

AmericasUS inflation surprises to the upsideConsumer prices rose 3.7% year on year in September, reaccelerating and surprising to the upside. The increase was partly driven by energy prices, as expected, but core inflation also picked up, with the index rising 2.6% year on year. Strength was relatively broad-base across both core goods (vehicles, both new and used, recreation goods, and apparel) and core services (driven by shelter). Overall, the report leaves the Fed questioning how much progress is being made on underlying inflation, keeping further rate hikes on the table.EuropeECB Keeps the Door Open to Rate HikesSeveral members of the European Central Bank’s Governing Council, speaking at the IMF meetings in Bangkok this week, indicated that further interest rate rises may be necessary. Germany’s Bundesbank president said another move cannot be ruled out, while Belgium’s central bank governor said the ECB will “probably” have to hike again. ECB President Lagarde noted that energy-driven inflation has not yet spread broadly through the wider economy. AsiaMSCI proposes stripping Indonesia of its emerging market status on a standalone positionThis would be a double downgrade that would bypass frontier status entirely — citing persistent concerns over market transparency, suspected coordinated trading, and weak enforcement of reforms. The announcement triggered Indonesia's worst stock market session in nearly three decades on Friday, with the Jakarta benchmark index falling more than 11%. MSCI will decide by end-June 2027. Consultations could be launched after the mid-November review.

Transcript:
Kelly Evans: Let’s begin with one of the standout bank names so far this earnings season. Increasingly so, as we see the raft of results today: Goldman Sachs. Yes, it’s down 2% in sympathy with other financials, but they reported their second-highest quarterly revenue ever yesterday. Earnings per share were $2 higher than the highest Wall Street estimates. Equities trading, investment banking, and wealth management all posting big year-over-year gains. Joining us now to weigh in on that, on what’s happening with AI financing, perhaps inflation, and so much else, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon. And amid some speculation about his potential replacement, by the way, he’s out at Goldman’s Builders and Innovators Conference in San Francisco with that lady right there, Kate Rooney. Kate, over to you.
Kate Rooney: Kelly, thank you so much. We are here with David Solomon. It’s great to see you in person. Thanks for having us. We’re at the Builders and Innovators Summit. You were just saying, 15 years now. Is this the 15th year?
David Solomon: Well, first of all, Kate, thanks for being here. And this is a pretty great spot. It’s a nice place for you and I to have a day to be here and do this. But a little more than 15 years ago, we created this conference. The idea was to bring together really interesting entrepreneurs that were doing fascinating things and building interesting companies. I go back 15 years and I think about Travis Kalanick from Uber. I think about Dropbox. I think about Matthew Prince from Cloudflare. Drew Houston from Dropbox. These were some of the early entrepreneurs. They built great big companies. And here’s another class of 150 that are coming today. Some of these will be companies that, 10 years or 15 years from now, we’ll talk about. It’s been a fascinating place to see innovation and kind of the real engine of the U.S. economy and U.S. innovation.
Kate Rooney: We want to get your take on the pipeline. It’s a great setup. But Kelly mentioned earnings. You guys are coming off one of your strongest earnings reports in the firm’s history. I wonder about durability, though. You talked on the analyst call about volatility helping you guys, this tech supercycle as you described it. What is the earnings engine going forward for Goldman if things start to change or rates really start to take a bite here?
David Solomon: I think one of the things that’s missed in the narrative of day-to-day reporting and trading is that we’ve been working for eight years to really grow our franchise and increase the durability of our revenues and the diversity of our business. When we started eight years ago, we had a little less than $5 billion in management fees in our asset and wealth management business. We had $3.6 billion this quarter. We’re on a run rate of $15 billion in management fees. We have built now a firm where 45% of revenues are considered durable, recurring revenues.
Now, of course, when you look at IPOs and M&A activity, there’s a little more cyclicality around those activities. But go look at M&A revenues for the last 15 years. Every year there’s M&A revenue, some years more than others.
So we have a big, durable, diverse business in global banking and markets and asset and wealth management. And what we’ve done strategically as a firm is we’ve significantly lifted the floor of our business, both in terms of the revenue base and also the returns. I think investors are seeing that and rewarding that, and we feel very good about it.
I can’t tell you what’s going to happen in the next three months or six months. I actually look out and see some very big equity deals coming. I see some potentially very big IPOs coming. I look at our M&A backlog. We said on the call yesterday our backlog is still at very, very robust levels. I feel very good about revenue accruals we have coming in M&A. I also see the strategic activity and dialogues that are going on, and I feel pretty good about it.
Counter to that, we saw a slightly hot inflation print today. There are obviously four interest-rate hikes baked in. When you look forward, the 10-year Treasury has moved kind of 75 basis points in the last quarter and people are concerned about that. But we can operate in this environment pretty well, and we are operating well. We’ll just have to keep, quarter after quarter after quarter, showing people that our firm is a big, diverse, durable firm.
Kate Rooney: Well, one of the things you said on the call was that 5% on the 10-year didn’t scare you. What is the number that would make you nervous?
David Solomon: It’s all got to be put in context. But my point was, if you step back, the anomaly is the last 15 years after the financial crisis.
Kate Rooney: The record low.
David Solomon: Interest rates. That’s the anomaly. I mean, I’ve been around for 64 years. The anomaly is zero interest rates, not a 5% 10-year Treasury. Obviously, significant moves when they happen quickly upset markets and can have an impact. But you’re seeing the world absorb this move in the 10-year Treasury reasonably well.
Now, if you continue to have pressure because of deficits, the fact that there is big demand for capital, I think one of the things that’s going on is there’s a lot of demand for capital for this AI cycle, and that’s also competing with the fact that governments have borrowed very aggressively. There’s a lot of demand for capital for government. So there is some pressure around that that affects rates.
But I’m not scared about all this. This is the environment we live in and we operate in.
Kate Rooney: Well, one of the things that is different, I mean, you look back 20 years and sure, rates were the same, but the amount of AI capex that is now reliant on debt is very different than what we’ve seen in the past. We had Broadcom’s CEO recently saying that he thinks capital could be the biggest constraint and really a potential choke point for this entire buildout. What do you make of that?
David Solomon: I saw his comments. I have a different point of view. My point of view is there’s a lot of capital in the world. Think of the size of the market cap of public equities in the world. Think about all the savings that exist in the world. Think about the wealth that exists in the world. There’s a lot of wealth in the world.
That doesn’t mean that everybody that has an idea, everybody that has a data center, everybody that has a chip, can have unlimited capital at a very, very low cost to pursue their aspirations.
At the end of the day, capital is disciplined. It looks for returns. It goes to the best opportunities.
I would just say there’s a lot of capital out there. The financing markets, particularly in this country, the capital markets are extraordinary and developing new ways to access capital and package capital. I think some of the things we’re talking about doing right now, and our partnership with NVIDIA around compute, are super interesting.
Is there a crowding-out effect that at the margin affects the cost of capital a little bit? Absolutely. But that doesn’t mean the capital is not available. For good projects and good returns and good opportunities, there’s plenty of capital in the world.

articles.title: Managing our Environmental Impact
articles.text:
Managing our Environmental Impact. Our Commitment. Our Targets. Our Progress.

Man Group is committed to reducing its absolute carbon footprint and to being consistent and transparent about the progress we are making. As a key part of our Corporate Sustainability strategy, you can read more about how we manage our environmental impact in our Corporate Sustainability Brochure.

We continue to implement changes to our operations to ensure we are on track to meet our emissions reduction target set for 2026 and are on the strategic pathway to net zero carbon in our global workplaces by 2030.

Environmental Policy

Our Environmental Sustainability Policy Statement focuses on: using natural resources responsibly; minimising the environmental impact of our activities through maximising energy efficiency; reducing greenhouse gas emissions and; recycling and / or minimising waste. We also commit to at least annual reporting of our environmental targets, data and any issues we encounter. In 2024, we achieved ISO 14001:2018 for our London office.

Board Oversight of Environmental Matters

Our Man Group Board has responsibility for Man Group's environmental impact and ensures that Man’s Environmental Sustainability Policy Statement is implemented and reviewed. The Board has a collective role in providing environmental leadership throughout Man's global operations and is committed to continual improvement in environmental performance.

Environmental Risk Management

Man Group considers operational climate risks 15+ years into the future. It does this through multi-disciplinary company-wide risk identification, assessment and management processes. The types of risks considered include current and emerging regulation, technological changes and upgrades, market risks, reputational risks, acute and chronic physical operational impacts as well as upstream and downstream risks.

Green Buildings

Minimising our environmental impact is at the centre of our real estate strategy. We occupy eight buildings certified by LEED (Leadership in Energy Efficiency and Design), one by Energy Star and one by NABERS (National Australian Built Environment Rating System), accounting for 92% of our global headcount. Man Group’s largest office, Riverbank House (RBH) in London, has a Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM) ‘Excellent’ rating.

Riverbank House - London

Riverbank House is rated “Excellent” via the Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM). The building has a green roof, rainwater harvesting and solar power generation.

Pfäffikon - Switzerland

Our Pfäffikon office is a short walk from Lake Zurich and is powered by renewable hydro-electric energy.

Environmental data compilation systems

We strive to deliver clear and transparent reporting that captures the measurable elements within our control. We monitor and track our global environmental impact using specialist specialist tracking software and an energy services consultancy which help us to mitigate risk, maximise opportunities and reduce our carbon footprint.

Responsible Procurement

Man Group’s offices procure goods and services that are in line with our environmental objectives. We utilise ISO standards and ratings systems (such as energy star for IT equipment and green star for paper supplies) to assist us in choosing sustainable products. We also ensure all our equipment complies with the Restriction of Hazardous Substances EU Directive.

Man Group’s Supplier Code of Conduct

As a condition of supplying services to Man Group, our suppliers are directed to adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct. This code outlines the minimum standards Man Group expects of its suppliers, regarding economic activity, impact on the environment, as well as engagement with wider communities.

Man Group intends to lead by example, and we endeavour to work closely with our suppliers to rise to the opportunity of addressing the global, social and environmental challenges that we all currently face.

Environmental Improvements

Man Group’s largest office, Riverbank House, is continually assessed for energy and air-conditioning efficiency. The recommendations inform our investments.

During 2024, we achieved ISO14001:2018 for our Riverbank House office.

Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD)

Man Group is a supporter and signatory of the TCFD, and is committed to taking action against climate change. The Board oversees the development of our climate-related financial disclosures which cover governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets, as described in our Annual Report.

Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change (IIGCC)

Man Group is a signatory to the Institutional Investors Group on Climate Change, the European membership body for investor collaboration on climate change.

UN Global Compact

We are also proud, active signatories of the UN Global Compact, supporting the Ten Principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption.

Environmental Training and Awareness

Environmental awareness campaigns are run in offices focusing on areas such as increasing recycling, reducing energy use, cycling to work and removing single use plastics.

We have run a number of sustainable volunteering activities across our offices including litter pick-ups, local garden and park maintenance as well as educational awareness events.

articles.title: CIO Perspective: Asking Better Questions | BlackRock
articles.text:
Fixed Income

Oct 15, 2026

Rick Rieder

"Judge a man by his questions rather than his answers." - Voltaire
Voltaire probably didn't have the 10-year Treasury in mind, but the principle translates. The Federal Reserve (Fed) raised rates this month, bringing the policy rate to 3.75%-4.00%, and every commentator within earshot has an eight-word explanation for what it means. Markets in September 2026 are drowning in answers: the energy shock, fiscal deficits, higher-for-longer Fed policy, Treasury supply, the next consumer price index (CPI) print, and the next jobs report. What almost nobody is doing is asking the questions that actually determine investment returns from here. We think the best investors don't have more answers; they ask better questions. The structural questions facing us today are unusually clear and important and, for those willing to act on them, potentially well-compensated.
U.S. economic growth: Strong headline, fractured underneath
Is the economy strong? Yes. Is it uniformly strong? Not even close. Corporate profits are growing at a rate consistent with 7% nominal GDP growth, a level that points to strong expansion.1 But peel back one layer and the picture changes dramatically. Growth is increasingly concentrated in rate-insensitive services and nonresidential investment, particularly AI-related capital expenditure. Computers and peripheral equipment represent roughly 1% of GDP but have generated approximately 27% of recent growth.2 That is not broad-based growth; it is a capex boom channeled through an extraordinarily narrow pipe.
Meanwhile, sectors most sensitive to financing costs, housing chief among them, remain in something resembling a recession. The income needed to qualify for a median-priced home has reached $125,000, nearly double the median household income, while the average age of a first-time homebuyer has climbed to 40.3 For the first time on record, households in the fourth income quintile may not be able to afford today's median-priced home.
Chair Warsh said this week that policy is "not restrictive" given the headline strength of the economy, and the aggregate data supports that view. But the composition says something far more useful for investing: monetary policy is biting hard in some places while barely touching others.

Source: Bloomberg, Bureau of Economic Analysis, as of June 30, 2026

Inflation and Fed policy: The wrong question is “how high?” the right one is “how responsive?”
This month's 25-basis point rate increase was widely anticipated, while the updated Summary of Economic Projections leaned hawkish. The 2026 median dot now implies two hikes (4.125%), with 2027 and 2028 medians each raised by 50 basis points, suggesting policy remains on hold next year before a cut in 2028. The Fed also revised 2026 core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation a tenth higher to 3.4%, though we suspect officials did not incorporate expected negative methodology revisions due later this month, that could lower the reported number. Chair Warsh was clear in his press conference: progress on underlying inflation has been "inadequate," and he views the economy as strong enough that policy is not yet restrictive.
We agree that the economy has appeared remarkably resilient at the aggregate level, and that modest further rate increases may not put overall growth at risk. But the more important question for portfolios is not the level of inflation; it is its sensitivity to rates. The drivers of today's inflation are increasingly acyclical: energy, insurance, healthcare, education, and products tied to chips and asset prices. The San Francisco Fed's acyclical versus cyclical framework illustrates the divergence. Cyclical components have normalized toward long-term averages, while the acyclical portion continues to push headline inflation higher.
Acyclical components are driving more of today's inflation

Source: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, as of Aug. 31, 2026.

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, as of Aug. 31, 2026.

The Fed is committed to returning inflation to its 2% target, and inaction is clearly not its preferred route. Yet higher rates bite hardest in the housing and consumer borrowing channels that are already under stress, with the 90-day credit card delinquency rate at 12.9%.4 Higher rates do relatively little to slow the AI-fueled investment cycle or global energy dynamics driving the acyclical components. It is the equivalent of turning down the thermostat in one room and wondering why the other room isn't getting cooler. For investors, understanding inflation composition matters far more than tracking the headline number. We don't think this rate increase necessitates a long series of further increases, particularly with employment growth having weakened materially from the pace of recent years.
AI productivity and the labor market: Profits without paychecks
The labor market shows why the right question matters. Is employment strong? At 4.1% unemployment, sure. But the hires rate is at its lowest since 2010, and private-sector wage growth has cooled to 3.1%. Strip out healthcare, and average monthly payroll growth over the past year is just 6,000 jobs.5 Economy-wide profit per employee is growing faster than at any point in the last 25 years (outside the rebounds following the global financial crisis and COVID), while many industries are growing output without hiring at all.
Productivity was rising well before AI, which is now accelerating the trend. The right questions for investing are: how durable is this corporate profit cycle, how much will AI amplify it further, and what happens to economy-wide consumption when the winners and losers diverge this sharply? These are not questions the market can answer with a single payroll print or a Fed dot plot. They are structural, and the portfolio implications extend well beyond the next meeting.
Profit per employee is growing at a historically strong pace

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, as of Aug. 31, 2026.

Retail investing and market structure: The fantasy football problem
Sports betting is now a $17 billion revenue industry in the U.S., up 23% in 2025, and that same impulse is increasingly visible in financial markets.6 Zero-day-to-expiry options continue to take a larger share of total U.S. options volume. Leveraged ETF launches have surged, with almost 200 new ones this year carrying an average AUM of just $3.9 million.7 The dynamic resembles fantasy football: the game outside the arena can become bigger than the game itself. The obsession with what happens in the next minute, hour, or day can undermine the discipline of compounding capital over years. The structural questions, not the daily answers, are what generate returns.
Fixed income yields: The math has rarely been this powerful
For all the debate about current rate levels, the more useful question for investors is: What return can be generated from this starting point? The answer is compelling. What makes today’s opportunity unusual is that investors do not need to reach very far for that income. It’s now possible to build a diversified fixed income portfolio yielding more than 7%, with less than three years of duration and an average credit rating of A-.8 That combination of income, quality and limited interest-rate sensitivity is historically unusual, particularly as inflation continues to moderate.
US 10Y Treasury Average 1Y Forward Returns since 1995 by Starting Yield

Source: Bloomberg, as of Sept. 11, 2026.

In fixed income, the math is unusually transparent: return equals carry plus price change. Carry today provides a substantial cushion against price volatility. This does not mean rates cannot move higher in the near term; they can. It means pulling the bowstring back further only increases the forward return embedded in the entry point. Real yields are at historically attractive levels, pension funding ratios are high enough to create durable demand for long-duration assets at these levels, and the volatility required to build a portfolio with a 7% return target is the lowest it has been since before the financial crisis (2.6% annualized for a hypothetical A-rated portfolio today, versus 11.1% in 2021).9

Moreover, the ability to source yields above 6% across a range of sectors, not just high yield or emerging markets, changes the calculus. Bespoke, well-structured financing assets, including data center asset-backed securities (ABS), whole-business securitizations, and private placements, offer more yield and considerably stronger structural protection than traditional credit. When yield meaningfully exceeds volatility, optimizing portfolios for the prevailing regime can be particularly powerful. Today's environment offers just that opportunity.

Source: Bloomberg, as of Sept. 11, 2026.

Equities: Earnings growth matters, but so does the entry level
For equities, the starting multiple tells us little about future returns. The R-squared between forward price-to-earnings (P/E) and one-year returns is just 0.07. Strong earnings can continue to support equity returns. The AI ecosystem still has the fundamentals to do so. Data center infrastructure and semiconductor companies show expected earnings growth above 25%, while multiples have de-rated 10 to 13 turns from their year-to-date peaks. A meaningful share of that future growth is already under contract.10 The entry point today, after the recent pullback, looks more attractive than it has in months.
But the range of outcomes has clearly widened. From today's starting point, equities could plausibly return anywhere from -5% to +20% over the next year depending on whether earnings deliver and multiples hold or compress. With fixed income able to fund a larger share of portfolio return targets, equity risk can be spent more selectively. The trailing two months tell the story: the S&P 500 returned 1%, while stocks characterized by high free cash flow returned 16%, those with stable sales growth returned 9%, and those with low capex-to-sales returned 8%.11 Cash flow durability and capital efficiency are the filters. This is not the market to own beta for the sake of it.

Source: Citi, as Sept. 4, 2026.

U.S. government debt and fiscal risk: The elephant in the room
Before leaving the discussion on portfolio allocations, it is worth confronting a risk that underlies all markets, one that the rate increase makes more urgent. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) baseline projects debt-to-GDP reaching approximately 120% by 2036, assuming 3.9% nominal growth and a 3.7% average cost of debt. Higher funding costs make that trajectory considerably worse: a sustained 1% increase in the cost of debt adds 8 percentage points to the terminal debt burden; a 2% increase adds 16 percentage points and implies roughly $7.5 trillion in additional net interest expense through 2036.12
Nearly half of marketable Treasury debt matures within two years, and 89% of issuance is concentrated at the front end. Higher rates feed directly into the government's interest bill.13 Refinancing that short-term debt at rates just 1 percentage point lower would generate $144 billion in annual savings, enough to fund the combined FY 2027 discretionary budgets of the Departments of Health and Human Services, Agriculture, Treasury, Labor, and Commerce.14 The arithmetic of this fiscal trajectory makes managing fixed income volatility and optimizing portfolio construction not just sensible, but urgent.
Bottom line: From explaining markets to building better portfolios
The framework is simple and powerful: the edge does not come from having more answers. It comes from asking the five structural questions that actually matter.

What return do we need over the next three to five years, and how much of that can today's starting yield deliver without reaching for additional risk?
With real yields at historically attractive levels, how much interest-rate risk do we actually need to own when carry alone can do so much of the work?
In credit, where is the yield coming from, and where do leverage, refinancing, and rollover risk make the incremental spread not worth taking?
In equities, which earnings growth is durable, cash-generative, and not already fully reflected in the entry price?
As yields reset higher, how quickly should we add duration, and where on the curve do supply and the carry cushion justify that risk while fiscal pressures remain unresolved?

The direction of travel is clear even if the pacing is hard. When a diversified fixed income portfolio can yield more than 7%, carry less than three years of duration and maintain an average A- credit rating, the portfolio math changes materially. If inflation continues trending toward a 2% range, that income becomes even more meaningful in real terms. Equities still matter for long-term growth, but investors no longer need them to carry as much of the return burden. Built deliberately, that combination can create a portfolio that does not depend on the next payroll print, the next CPI surprise, or the next geopolitical headline..

Sources: Bloomberg, BlackRock, as of Sept. 12, 2026.

Markets will keep generating noise, headlines, and reasons to wait. But the math of starting yields, the breadth of investable debt, and the narrowing path to strong equity returns all point in the same direction: investors should focus on the right structural questions, rather than chasing the next data print. In today's markets, the edge comes from asking better questions.

Global Markets and EconomyIndustry Perspectives Episode 3GROWTH: Conflicts, Supply Chains and ResilienceIndustry Perspectives • Podcast • October 22, 2026View TranscriptIn continuing our Industry Perspectives podcast series, hosts Amanda Hale and Andrew Newson of Citi’s Global Trustee & Fiduciary Services are joined by Citi colleagues Rob Rowe, Interim Head of Research and Nathan Sheets, Global Chief Economist.We now turn to the topic of growth. In this, our latest episode, we begin by looking at how resilient the global economy is despite challenges such as the Russia-Ukraine War, inflation, rapid rise of central bank rates, US tariffs and more recently the war in Iran. We also look at current geopolitical and macroeconomic effects and how these may be shaping growth in both the short and long-term.Amanda Hale, Director & Head of Regulatory Services, Global Trustee & Fiduciary, CitiAmanda has over 40 years of experience in the investments industry and has been with Citi since 2008. Prior to joining Citi, Amanda worked in the CIS Policy Team at the Financial Services Authority (FSA), now the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) after having been with HSBC for 26 years in various areas such as Trustee and Depositary Services, Custody, Settlements, Corporate Actions and Income. Amanda currently represents Citi on external industry committees and panel discussions as well as chairing various internal Citi regulatory committees. She demonstrates an excellent understanding of the financial services’ regulatory environment. Andrew Newson, Senior Regulatory Technical Analyst, CitiAndrew has 27 years’ experience working in financial services. Joining Citi in 1999, Andrew worked as a Valuations Officer in the Citibank Private Bank before moving to Switzerland to become a Fund Management Support Manager in Zurich, where he managed a small team. On his return to London, Andrew joined Citibank Global Asset Management as Manager of the Fiduciary department, leading a team conducting post-trade compliance monitoring of private bank portfolios, institutional and sovereign wealth mandates, and Luxembourg Mutual Funds. In 2006, Andrew stepped into the funds business as a Fiduciary Relationship Manager, entrusted with managing key client relationships spanning both UK authorised and unauthorised fund structures. Since 2014, Andrew has been a driving force within Citi's Regulatory Services team, where he plays a pivotal role in preparing and delivering high-impact regulatory updates to clients, translating complex regulatory change into clear, actionable insight. Andrew has also represented Citi as its Technical representative at the UK Depositary Association.Rob Rowe, Interim Head of Research, CitiRob Rowe is the Global Head of Citi Research’s Global Strategy & Macro Group (GSMG) as well as Head of Research for the Americas. GSMG unites all of Citi’s Economists with Fixed Income, FX, Equity and Commodities strategists to create a common team providing research on the world’s major economies and asset classes. Rob has been with Citi for well over 30-years serving in various capacities within markets and research. He originally joined Smith Barney Harris Upham & Company in 1989 working in Investment Banking, Fixed Income sales and Research. He has worked in the past as a rates and agency debt strategist and continues to provide portfolio strategy for select clients as part of his previous role overseeing the Global Bond Portfolio Analysis team. He has written numerous articles and publications on fixed income and portfolio strategy.Nathan Sheets, Global Chief Economist, CitiNathan Sheets, Ph.D., is Global Chief Economist at Citi Research. In this role, Nathan leads Citi’s surveillance and forecasting of the global economy and directs the analysis of the firm’s economics team. He interacts closely with Citi’s major institutional clients and internal risk takers and publishes research on cross-cutting themes shaping the global economy and financial markets.Most recently, Nathan was Chief Economist and a member of the senior investment team at PGIM Fixed Income. He also has served as Under Secretary of the U.S. Treasury for International Affairs, representing the U.S. government on international economic issues. Previously, he held positions with Citigroup, as Global Head of International Economics, and with the Federal Reserve Board, as Director of the Division of International Finance and FOMC Economist. In addition, Nathan was a senior advisor to the U.S. Executive Director of the International Monetary Fund and a visiting fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. articles.title: Reporting on nature
articles.text:
Highlights

– What is the ISSB proposing?– What would the proposals mean for companies?– Practice statement or standard – what is the difference?– What’s next?– Actions for management

Companies applying IFRS® Sustainability Disclosure Standards can expect greater clarity on how to identify, assess and disclose nature-related risks and opportunities (NROs) under the International Sustainability Standards Board’s (ISSB) proposed practice statement.The proposals would introduce guidance on areas including location-specific analysis, connections between nature and climate and the use of information gathered through engagement with affected stakeholders.The proposed practice statement could influence how companies identify, assess and disclose nature-related information in practice. Comments on the proposalsopens in a new tab are open until 19 February 2027.

Barbara Zonneveld

Sustainability Reporting Director

KPMG International

mail

These proposals would not create a separate nature-reporting framework, but they could change the depth of analysis and evidence needed in practice. Companies can use the consultation period to assess how their existing processes, data and controls may need to evolve.

Barbara Zonneveld

Sustainability Reporting Director

What is the ISSB proposing?

The proposals build on IFRS S1 General Requirements for Sustainability-related Financial Information to assist companies in disclosing information about NROs. They also complement IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures. The table below summarises the key proposals.

Area  Proposal  Location-specific aspects  Consider the appropriate geographical scale for identifying and disclosing nature-related information about specific sites, regions or parts of the value chain. For example, information may need to be disaggregated by site rather than a jurisdiction to adequately explain NROs. Connecting nature and climate Identify connections between nature- and climate- related risks and opportunities, including synergies and trade-offs when assessing NROs and developing strategies and actions. Interactions with affected stakeholders Consider interactions and engagement with indigenous peoples, local communities and other affected stakeholders when identifying, assessing and managing NROs. Scenario analysis and resilience  Use scenario analysis to assess the resilience of the strategy and business model, proportionate to a company’s circumstances. Metrics and targets Collect sufficient data and undertake appropriate analysis to quantify the exposure to NROs. This includes the amount and percentage of assets or business activities vulnerable to nature-related risks or aligned with nature-related opportunities.

What would the proposals mean for companies?

The proposals build on the recommendations of the TNFD1 and have been developed to inform and be applied alongside ESRS2 and GRI3. A company already reporting on nature under these other frameworks could leverage existing reporting and use the proposals to identify any gaps in their nature-related reporting. However, a company may need to enhance their existing processes and data to apply the proposed requirements. The extent of the changes would depend on the maturity of its current nature-related practices.A company new to reporting on nature would be able to use the proposals to better understand how to identify NROs. The proposals would also allow it to understand what information would be needed and identify any gaps in its current processes.

Practice statement or standard – what is the difference?

If a company intends to state compliance with the practice statement it would need to apply all its requirements. However, it would not need to apply the proposed requirements in the practice statement to comply with IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards. Regulators and jurisdictions could also refer to or mandate the application of the practice statement in local requirements.

What’s next?

The consultation is open until 19 February 2027. The ISSB will consider the feedback received before deciding in what form to finalise the proposals. Our forthcoming New on the Horizon publication will provide analysis and practical examples to support companies applying IFRS S1 and IFRS S2.

Actions for management

Take this opportunity to have your sayopens in a new tab by 19 February 2027.Speak to your usual KPMG contact for further information on the proposals and visit IFRS Sustainability for the latest news and discussion.

1 Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures2 European Sustainability Reporting Standards3 Global Reporting Initiative Sustainability Reporting Standards

articles.title: Cut demand or cut supply? Rethinking climate policy | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary

Podcast
Cut demand or cut supply? Rethinking climate policy

Listen on

Apple Podcasts

Spotify

YouTube

Pod.link

More

Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity

Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity

Hosts:
Janice C. Eberly and

Janice C. Eberly

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

Jón Steinsson

Jón Steinsson

Nonresident Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

Interviewer:
Sanjay Patnaik

Sanjay Patnaik

Director
- Center on Regulation and Markets,

Bernard L. Schwartz Chair in Economic Policy Development,

Senior Fellow
- Economic Studies

Guest:
Ryan Kellogg

Ryan Kellogg

Ralph and Mary Otis Isham Professor and Deputy Dean
- University of Chicago

October 22, 2026

The economics points to a portfolio of climate policies rather than an either/or choice: pricing both emissions and fossil fuel extraction limits how much emissions “leak” abroad, since direct trade in fossil fuels exceeds trade in carbon embedded in goods for most countries.
Blocking specific pipelines and export terminals often fails to keep fossil fuels in the ground. Had the Dakota Access Pipeline been blocked, 82% of its oil would have moved by rail instead.
Broad clean energy subsidies are less promising than targeted policies, such as reforms that enable long-distance electricity transmission and public support for clean energy innovation.

Oil refinery terminal. Shutterstock/UNIKYLUCKK

24 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

Should cutting greenhouse gas emissions target the consumption of fossil fuels or their extraction? A new BPEA paper argues the answer is a portfolio of policies, not an either/or choice. Because fossil fuels are traded globally, pricing both emissions and extraction can limit how much emissions “leak” to other countries, and the paper makes the case for public support of clean energy R&D to reduce emissions abroad. On this episode of the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity, Sanjay Patnaik talks to the paper’s author, Ryan Kellogg of the University of Chicago, about the tradeoffs between demand-side and supply-side climate policy.

Related Content

Economics of demand-side and supply-side climate policies

Climate Policy

Economics of demand-side and supply-side climate policies

Ryan Kellogg

September 23, 2026

Listen to the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity on Apple, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you like to get podcasts.
Learn about other Brookings podcasts from the Brookings Podcast Network.
