Send feedback email to podcasts@Brookings.edu.

Transcript

[music]
EBERLY: Welcome to season nine of the Brookings Podcast on Economic Activity. I’m Jan Eberly, the James R. and Helen D. Russell Professor of Finance at Northwestern University. And this season, we’ll be listening to discussions about papers from the fall 2026 Brookings Papers on Economic Activity conference, hosted by Brookings in September.
STEINSSON: And I’m Jón Steinsson, Marek Professor of Public Policy and Economics at the University of California, Berkeley. We are the co-editors of the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, a semi-annual conference and journal that pairs rigorous research with real-time policy analysis to address the most urgent economic challenges of the day.
EBERLY: Once again, we have a great lineup of timely topics, energy markets, inflation, migration’s effects on labor and housing markets, financing AI, and more. Over the course of this season, we’ll hear a lot more about the conference papers and importantly, how decision-makers should be thinking about the topics they explore.
[1:10]
STEINSSON: This episode wades into a debate that’s been dividing climate advocates for quite some time. Should we focus on cutting fossil fuel demand or cutting fossil fuel supply? Sanjay Patnaik, director of the Center on Regulation and Markets at Brookings, speaks with the author Ryan Kellogg of the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy on his new paper, “Economics of Demand-Side and Supply-Side Climate Policies.”
EBERLY: This maps into a real debate happening right now in the U.S. and globally. Keep it in the ground and reduce supply? Or shift the incentives so that consumers instead demand more clean energy?
Kellogg’s answer is refreshingly practical. It’s not either/or. He argues for a portfolio approach and shows that trade is key. Because countries trade fossil fuels directly, reducing extraction in one location raises prices and encourages extraction elsewhere. That’s what they call “leakage” in the paper. So, it’s more effective to shift consumption toward cleaner fuels together with a reduction in extraction. One tool in one country is just not effective in a global economy. Otherwise, emissions leak through other markets and other countries.
STEINSSON: One particular tactic that he discusses is blocking specific pipelines or export terminals to keep oil in the ground. An example of this is the Dakota Access Pipeline. Kellogg finds that blocking this pipeline would not have kept much oil in the ground at all. Most of it would have just moved to railroads instead, actually increasing local pollution rather than reducing it.
EBERLY: And the paper also has a genuinely surprising detour into China, where Kellogg argues that the country’s green industrial policy, heavy government support for solar, batteries, and EVs may have actually paid for itself economically along the lines of an infant industry before you even count the climate benefits.
STEINSSON: Let’s hear more from the author. Over to Sanjay.
[3:22]
PATNAIK: Thanks so much, Jan and Jon. Hi, Ryan. Thank you for talking with me about your paper today.
KELLOGG: Happy to be here, Sanjay. Thank you for taking the time.
[3:29]
PATNAIK: Let’s dive right in. There’s a real debate between keep it in the ground and abundance- style climate policy. Where does the economics actually land on that debate?
[3:39]
KELLOGG: So, the economics actually lands on, I would call it an all of the above strategy, for reasons that are not actually terribly obvious ex ante. Like, if you think about the the simplest possible model you could think of about the economics of climate change and reducing emissions, like, the sort of model you would teach undergraduates in a intro to microeconomics class, that model would point to saying that really all you need to do here to deal with this problem—the fact that burning fossil fuels to get the energy that people need, releases these emissions that cause climate change—there’s one simple trick to solve it. All you need to do is put a tax on emissions.
That is basically you need to price carbon, probably do it on the demand side, not the supply side. And that’s the one simple trick you need to do to solve all your problems. That’s like the very EC 1 model of of the problem.
And then you call it a day and said, you’re done. We’ve solved the problem. We’ve priced emissions. That’s going to drive emissions down, and we’re going to, you know, solve the climate change problem that way.
That model is, like, really elegant and really simple, but it misses a lot of the complexities that are part of the real world that really call for a portfolio of climate policies, not just a simple carbon pricing fix.
[4:55]
PATNAIK: Can you elaborate a little bit more on those complexities?
[4:58]
KELLOGG: So, I think the biggest one, really, comes from the fact that a lot of climate policy is local. It’s city level, state level, even national level, even the EU, a collection of nations. They have a very vibrant emissions trading system. They price carbon emissions.
In some sense, even that I would think of as being a local policy relative to the global problem. And the climate problem is global simply because, and this is just a fact about the way the climate works, when a ton of CO2 gets emitted from burning oil, gas, and coal and goes up into the atmosphere, the climate does not care at all whether that ton of CO2 came from a tailpipe where I’m sitting here in Chicago, whether it came from a tailpipe in London or Paris, or whether it came from a tailpipe, say, in Cape Town, South Africa. All causes the same climate change; it all causes the same climate damages.
An implication of that fact is that, whenever you’re a climate policymaker trying to implement some local climate policy, the thing you should be thinking about constantly is how does the policy I implement here at home affect emissions everywhere else in the world? And then once you actually really do internalize that, that really has a profound effect on should I be doing demand-side policy? Should I be doing supply-side climate policy? Or should I be doing a combination of both?
And that’s going to come as a consequence of, from the fact that the world is interconnected. We trade fossil fuels; we trade goods and services. So, anything I do at home is going to change trade balances and affect emissions everywhere else in the world. And things I do at home might also have an effect on technology that might be adopted elsewhere in the world.
[6:40]
PATNAIK: Great. And you point out that countries trade a lot of oil and gas directly, not just goods made using energy. Why does that matter for climate policy?
[6:48]
KELLOGG: Yeah. So, let’s think about it that way. Suppose I’m the U.S., and the U.S. starts to aggressively price carbon emissions, with a carbon tax, a cap-and-trade program. Parts of the U.S., in fact, already do this. California has had a vibrant cap and trade program for several decades now, as have the northeastern states. Canada has done this on and off as well.
If you start pricing emissions, what is that going to do? Well, it’s going to drive down the demand for carbon. People are maybe going to drive less, maybe they’re going to substitute to electric vehicles. Electric generators are going to substitute away from coal and natural gas to renewables, maybe more nuclear, et cetera. You’re going to drive down the demand for fossil fuels.
But the three major fossil fuels, coal, oil, natural gas, they’re all traded in global markets. And we’ve seen a ton of evidence for that throughout 2026, and particularly if you think about the oil market, once the conflict between the U.S. and Iran began in the winter, in February, that closed the Strait of Hormuz, that didn’t just affect local oil markets and markets for diesel and gasoline in the Persian Gulf. That affected worldwide oil and gas markets. Prices for fuels went up all around the world.
Turning back to climate policy, if we do emissions pricing in the U.S., it’s going to have the opposite effect. That is going to push down prices of fuels throughout the world. Where that leads to a problem for, say, an emissions pricing only policy comes from the fact that if the price of oil, the price of coal, the price of gas falls everywhere else in the world, consumers there are going to demand more of those fuels. They will start burning more of those fuels, some of which will be coming from exports from the U.S. And those basically emissions increases everywhere else in the world are going to offset, at least in part, the emissions decreases in the U.S., and that’s something that climate policy people and economists call emissions leakage.
[8:36]
PATNAIK: That’s very interesting. Can you talk a little bit about leakage?
[8:39]
KELLOGG: Yeah. So, leakage is a problem, and this comes about in a lot of ways when one jurisdiction implements a climate policy of its own through trade linkages everywhere else in the world, you get offsetting emissions increases up elsewhere. Some of that comes directly through trade and fossil fuel itself. If I do carbon pricing, that pushes down the price of fossil fuels, oil, coal, and natural gas, that’s going to increase emissions elsewhere. Some of it also comes through trade and energy intensive goods, steel, aluminum, cement— products made from the, made from those basic raw materials.
If the U.S. does emissions pricing or if the EU does emissions pricing, that’s going to put its manufacturers at a competitive disadvantage relative to manufacturers elsewhere in the world—China, India, Latin America, you name it. And what winds up happening then is that those other manufacturers start to actually be the ones who start producing more of the cement, the steel, the aluminum, all of those goods that actually involve quite a lot of carbon use.
And say the U.S. as the sort of the country or the local region implementing climate policy is going to start importing those goods from the rest of the world, and that those emissions increases everywhere else are going to offset the reductions at home.
[9:52]
PATNAIK: Great. Thank you for that. The U.S. also hasn’t really tried taxing carbon extraction directly. So, what would that actually look like, and why might it be more effective than just taxing consumption?
[10:03]
KELLOGG: So, I’ll start with the second of those questions, like why tax carbon extraction? And just as sort of a statement of fact, if you look around the world at carbon pricing programs that exist, they pretty much all focus on taxing emissions. That’s what the EU Emissions Trading System does. By far the most prominent system out there. Nobody’s really taxing extraction.
Taxing extraction can be useful because instead of pushing down the price of fossil fuels, taxing extraction reduces supply, and it’s going to push up the price of fossil fuels, oil, coal, and gas, basically countering the price depression that you get from taxing emissions.
The policy that actually really works to combat leakage involves a combination of both emissions pricing and extraction pricing. Basically, what you want to do is you want to use both policies, tax emissions, a demand-side policy, and tax extraction, a supply-side policy. Do some of both so that you’re not really moving around global coal, oil, and gas prices too much, and that’s how you solve the leakage problem, or at least a big part of it.
Ideally you want to be doing some of both. Nobody out there is really taxing extraction. In principle, like administratively, it’s actually not something that’s terribly hard to do. Basically what it would involve, say, say we did that in the U.S., all that would mean is simply whenever, say, a ton of coal comes out of the ground, or a barrel of oil, or 1,000 cubic feet of natural gas, find the first point of sale, and simply apply a sales tax at that point of sale, regardless of whether that point of sale is to a domestic customer or to an international customer, say if the oil’s being exported.
It’s a relatively straightforward tax to implement. Actually, state governments more or less do this kind of tax all the time., Even if you say think about Texas, a lot of oil and gas production in Texas is coming from privately owned land. Nonetheless, the state of Texas imposes a, what they call a severance tax. A lot of states do this on produced oil and gas, even when it comes from private land. It’s not a big tax. It’s not a tax that has anything to do about climate change. It’s about collecting revenues.
But it’s basically a tax that’s applied at the first point of sale whenever oil and gas come out of the ground. An extraction tax, a broad extraction tax would work in exactly the same way.
[12:17]
PATNAIK: So, you’re suggesting basically to come at it from both sides of the market, from the demand and the supply side?
[12:22]
KELLOGG: Exactly. And again, really all you’re trying to do is, like, solve the problem that a demand side, demand side carbon pricing on its own, whether it’s a carbon tax or pricing that comes from cap and trade, leads to leakage because it pushes down global prices of coal, oil and gas.
An extraction tax on its own would also have a problem. It would push up the prices of coal, oil and gas, and you’d lead to leakage just from the opposite direction. You’d induce producers elsewhere in the world to produce more. You solve the problem by doing some of both. So, you’re not moving around the prices of coal, oil, and gas too much.
[12:56]
PATNAIK: Well, that’s super interesting. You’re pretty skeptical of a popular tactic, blocking pipelines and export terminals to keep it in the ground. Why doesn’t that work as well as people think it does?
[13:05]
KELLOGG: So, the problem there is, like, what you’ve described is sort of an alternative type of supply side climate policy, where we want to keep it in the ground, but we’re not going to price extraction broadly in the way that sort of I described as being useful for a way to help solve the leakage problem.
Instead, what you’re going to do is target very specific infrastructure, blocking pipelines, blocking liquefied natural gas terminals, LNG terminals, and that sort of thing.
And the problem you run into in the economics if you use sort of that more sort of narrow supply side approach of targeting transportation infrastructure in particular, is that you’re not sort of broadly targeting extraction. You’re targeting sort of a narrow choke point. And the economics of getting oil and gas out of the ground and consumers are just such that there’s just so much value there that producers are going to really try to find a way to find substitutes to get to market.
So, for instance, if you think about blocking a pipeline, say Keystone XL, which has been successfully blocked, or the Dakota Access Pipeline— this is a pipeline that was in fact completed in 2017; it moves oil about half a million barrels a day, so a lot, from North Dakota to the U.S. Gulf Coast. This is coming from the Bakken Shale in North Dakota.
Had that pipeline been blocked, the oil moving through that pipeline, half a million barrels a day, it wouldn’t just be bottled up and stay in the ground. Instead, most of that oil would instead be coming out through another means, namely railroads. It’s a tool that exists. It’s easy for transporters, for oil producers to use.
Yes, it’s a little bit more expensive than pipelines, but not that much more, and producers would in fact use it, and in fact did use it before the Dakota Access Pipeline was completed.
So, I have a paper on this with my co-author Tom Covert, and basically what we find is that if you had blocked that pipeline, about 80% of that half million barrels a day that’s currently flowing through it would not stay in the ground. It would just come out through the railroads instead. Which actually causes all sorts of other problems because you have these trains running down the railroad, basically mile-long unit trains of nothing but crude oil being pulled along by big diesel locomotives. Those diesel locomotives emit a lot of local air pollution like nitrogen oxides and things like that.
The locomotives also kind of by design, where do we put railroads? We put them through urban areas so that you have basically diesel locomotives emitting a bunch of nasty stuff now going through urban areas instead of oil going through a pipeline, which is much cleaner.
[15:43]
PATNAIK: No, that’s actually very ironic, and I’m really glad you’re making that point because I think oftentimes when you look at the debate, people forget that if you try to block supply, that doesn’t mean the demand goes away. Right? And so there will be other ways where this demand will be met, and in your case, as you said, it will be transported in different ways that are even more environmentally damaging.
[16:01]
KELLOGG: Exactly. And, the way to do supply side policy, so you don’t get these sort of nasty substitution problems is to… like, you don’t want to be sort of narrowly targeting, all right, we’re going to block this pipeline, or we’re going to block this export terminal, or we’re only going to stop drilling on federal lands, but do nothing on state and private lands. If you want to be successful on supply side policy, it really, really, really needs to be broad.
That is, you need to be pricing carbon extraction wherever it comes out of the ground and for every single fuel: coal, oil, gas. Otherwise, these substitution problems really make it hard for those kinds of supply side policies to be effective.
[16:39]
PATNAIK: I want to shift gears a little bit for my final question, which is China has become the dominant global producer of solar panels, batteries, and EVs largely through government support. They have huge subsidies for a lot of their industries. Is that a model other countries, including the U.S., should be following? We’ve seen these arguments quite a a lot in the public sphere. Is that something that is feasible, that is realistic, that is a good use of taxpayer money?
[17:03]
KELLOGG: At the very least, it’s something we should be thinking seriously about. Like, if I start to think about, like, what has, what have been the major developments in energy and climate over the over the past 20 years, I can think of a handful of things. You know, one I think of kind of pushing in the anti-climate direction but a big issue in energy has been the shale oil and gas boom in the United States, and how that’s really revolutionized fossil fuel markets.
And the other is what you mentioned, which is, the the just unbelievable rise of China as this manufacturing and export powerhouse for solar PV, for batteries, and for electric vehicles, EVs.
And that exporting powerhouse has come about through a lot of government support. Some of it direct subsidies, a lot of it sort of more implicit types of subsidies, loan guarantees. There’s a lot of research and development support that’s been done in China. And all of that has just massively driven down the costs of production of PV, of batteries, and electric vehicles.
From the perspective of the climate, all of that work, and this may sound trite, but it’s not crazy to describe it as just this massive gift to the world, in the sense of, like, all of a sudden, PV in a lot of places is cost competitive with electricity generated by fossil fuels, at least up to a point. The intermittency problem with solar is still an issue, and battery technology still needs to get better for that to work effectively as a reliable source of power.
We are seeing massive increases in electric vehicle penetration in the parts of the world that have opened themselves to electric vehicles from China, and that includes low-income countries and rich countries. So, you’re starting to see a lot of EVs get imported to, like, low- and middle-income countries in Latin America. There was an article, it was in The New York Times or Wall Street Journal in September, that pointed to Australia, which doesn’t really have an auto industry of its own, is really starting to ramp up its imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
[18:57]
All of that is serving to reduce emissions and doing it in a very substantial way and sort of ties into this idea that the climate change problem really is global. And what China is doing is not just reducing its own carbon emissions by its own adoption of its own PV and electric vehicles, it is pushing down emissions everywhere else in the world.
I do think there’s a big open question, and researchers are starting to get at this, of whether all the public spending that China did to build these industries actually paid off within China itself. There’s starting to be some evidence that the answer might actually have been yes. But even putting that aside, it is 100% clear to me that Chinese public industrial policies for green technologies have had massive benefits for the global climate and certainly for global energy consumers.
Other global producers of solar PV and batteries and electric vehicles might have something else to say about it. They’re getting pushed out. But from the consumer’s perspective and the climate perspective, it’s been a massive, massive win.
[20:01]
PATNAIK: What about the national security and economic security perspective? Because a lot of countries then actually might become dependent on Chinese suppliers, and and this causes a lot of geopolitical problems by swapping out dependence on, on Middle Eastern oil, for instance, for EVs or, solar panels from China. How do you think about that?
[20:19]
KELLOGG: Yeah. So, the single sourcing issue is indeed a problem. Basic energy resources, solar photovoltaics, PV, electric vehicles, they’re pretty critical to, you know, just the functioning of economy. I do think this is something importers are really going to have to wrangle with and think about how do we get to a point where the world is not simply dependent on China for these technologies.
I do want to highlight, like, one important difference between, say, oil dependence versus dependence on China as a supplier of equipment for PVs and EVs and batteries. If you think about oil dependence, a big reason why oil shocks have historically been so painful, and we’ve seen evidence of that throughout 2026 for oil and gasoline and diesel consumers throughout the world, is that oil is consumed as a flow commodity. The world goes through about 100 million barrels of oil a day, you know, give or take.
And, like, if we suddenly cut that flow off, there’s a lot of very acute pain that takes place. You can’t transport people and materials to where they want to go because we’re just continuously burning through this massive amount of oil every single day.
PV and EVs are different because they are capital goods. You don’t flow consume them. What that means is that if all of a sudden we face a disruption in the supply of solar PV or electric vehicles, that doesn’t really necessarily lead to the same amount of immediate pain. Eventually it does because you start to reduce the turnover in the EV fleet. You can’t start putting up more solar farms, all of those kinds of things, but it doesn’t lead to the same immediate acute pain that, say, a cutoff of oil production would lead to.
PATNAIK: Great. Wonderful. This is super interesting. I want to thank you so much for taking the time to speak with us today and sharing this fascinating research. All the best for your future endeavors.
KELLOGG: Thank you so much, Sanjay.
[music]
STEINSSON: Once again, I’m Jón Steinsson.
EBERLY: And I’m Jan Eberly.

RESEARCH BRIEFING

22 Oct 2026

US Holiday cheer, at a higher price

This holiday season will remain deeply bifurcated. High-income consumers will keep a floor under spending, helped by the surge in equities this year.

We forecast holiday retail sales to rise 4.2% in dollar terms and 2.2% in volume after adjusting for inflation. That would beat last year’s volume, when tariffs hurt sales and shifted purchases forward into October, but it trails a typical holiday season, reflecting the hit to spending power from higher energy prices.

High inflation is holding down real disposable income growth, high diesel prices are raising shipping costs, and Federal Reserve rate hikes are raising borrowing costs for those planning to spend by credit card.

This holiday season will remain deeply bifurcated. High-income consumers will keep a floor under spending, helped by the surge in equities this year. Our research shows recreational goods and services, household furniture, and clothing will likely benefit most from a positive wealth effect.

articles.title: European strategic autonomy: a €1.8 trillion investment opportunity - BNP Paribas Asset Management - Corporate English
articles.text:
Europe is embarking on a far-reaching drive to strengthen its strategic autonomy, reducing dependence on external partners across critical areas including defence, energy, technology, healthcare, food security and industry.

For investors, the scale of this transformation could be significant. As Lazare Hounhouayenou, Portfolio Manager, tells Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, around €1.8 trillion of investment is expected to be deployed by 2035 under major European and national initiatives.

The spending could create powerful long-term opportunities for European companies exposed to these strategic sectors, potentially supporting growth and corporate profitability. Defence is already seeing increased investment, while measures to protect strategic industries and accelerate investment in space and technology point to a broader industrial policy shift.

Progress, however, is unlikely to be linear. Differing national priorities, regulatory hurdles and Europe’s complex decision-making processes could generate short-term volatility. “Yet the direction of travel is becoming clearer: Europe is recognising its vulnerabilities and taking concrete steps to address them.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast to discover how European strategic autonomy is opening new horizons for investors.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Lazare Hounhouayenou

Daniel Morris: Hello and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode will be discussing European strategic autonomy. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Lazare Hounhouayenou, Portfolio Manager. Welcome, Lazare, and thanks for joining me.

LH: Happy to be here.

DM: We’re all aware of the capex that’s being devoted to the development of artificial intelligence technologies – trillions in the US but significant amounts of money elsewhere, certainly in Europe. But we may not be quite so aware of what is going on in Europe around strategic autonomy initiatives. I hear that there’s supposed to be about €1.8 trillion devoted to this theme in the years ahead. Let’s get back to basics. To begin with, could you give us a simple and concise definition of strategic autonomy?

LH: Strategic autonomy refers to the ability of a state – or a group of states such as the EU – to act independently on the international stage and defend its interests against the world’s major power[s] in areas considered essential.

The means used to achieve these objectives, as well as the assessments criteria for sovereignty, evolve over time. In the ’60s, a state’s sovereignty was measured by its industrial and military power. Today, with the rise of AI, it is also determined by data centres, AI models.

This evolution raises new questions such as ‘has the control of [micro]chips and data centres replace[d] the control of physical borders?’ Or ‘does the state still maintain its cultural and political sovereignty when its citizens access information, communicate and form opinion[s] through AI algorithm[s] developed under a different jurisdiction?

In this polarised world, what is Europe’s position and where the region can create value according to its strengths in the long term? We think that regaining sovereignty is an absolute necessity for Europe, which must reposition itself within this new geopolitical landscape.

This requires reducing its dependence on partners and former partners across a number of sectors. Defence is one of them, but energy resources, industry, technology, healthcare and food security must also be mentioned.

DM: That sounds quite comprehensive. Can you make the connection, though, between these initiatives, and why Europe undergoing this shift to greater strategic autonomy is important for investors?

LH: Since 2022, the European Union and several European countries have launched a number of major initiatives involving significant level of investments aimed at strengthening Europe’s autonomy in sectors consider strategic and essential. Looking at the main programmes alone, we estimate that nearly 1.8 trillion of investment will be deployed by 2035.

Naturally, European industrial companies with exposure to these sectors are expected to benefit from this powerful long-term investment trend. In this context, investors have an opportunity to position themselves for the long term by investing in sectors with strong growth prospects while at the same time supporting Europe’s strategic autonomy agenda.

DM: When you look at these initiatives, are you seeing practical consequences from Europe’s decisions? That is, are you seeing progress or, conversely, obstacles, delays, rivalries that justif[y] some people’s scepticism and arguably could generate volatility in the short term?

LH: Europe is moving in the right direction, even if progress is never fast enough. Given the urgency of the situation, Europe is reconsidering its governance framework and recognises that its decision-making process[es] are not sufficiently agile.

Recently, Germany and France proposed to create a new cooperation format bringing together the European Union’s six largest economies. This is intended to overcome the slow pace of decision-making within the EU and allow the core group of countries to make faster progress on economic and strategic priorities.

At the same time, Europe has taken concrete measures in defence. For instance, we are seeing EU member states accelerating spending to meet NATO targets of three and a half [per cent] of GDP for core defence expenditure by 2035. The NATO summit held in Turkey last June just confirmed this trajectory.

Europe protected its steel industry through a protectionist steel action plan, reflected in a 50% increase in tariffs and a 47% reduction in import quotas.

And in the crucial space sector, the European Space agency has approved €22 billion for [20]26 to 20. This is an increase of nearly 30%. The objective is to strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy in space technology and mission[s].

This non-exhaustive list of proposals and decisions clearly show that Europe is advancing its thinking and governance and taking concrete action. However, Europe has still many challenges to overcome as interest[s] and priority[ies] differ from one country to the other, which is only natural when 27 countries are involved. These disagreements will create volatility around strategic autonomy themes.

But we believe it is important to take a step back and focus on the medium and long-term trajectory, which appear[s] to be moving in the right direction.

DM: Lazare, if I can summarise some of the key points that you shared with us? You explained that simply, European strategic autonomy is a group of policies/initiatives that enable Europe to act more independently on the international stage, with a focus on many sectors – industrial policy, defence, AI, to cite just a few. You highlighted that we’re talking about €1.8 trillion planned to be invested in the years ahead.

The significance of this for investors is simply that a lot of that money will flow to companies and ultimately should drive corporate profits. You acknowledge that it’s not as smooth or quick as we might like, but the important thing to keep in mind is that Europe is moving in the right direction. It does recognise the problems it’s facing and is working to tackle those problems. Well, Lazare, thank you very much for joining me.

LH: Thank you, Daniel. It was a pleasure to have the discussion with you.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities around European strategic autonomy, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights at viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com.

We recommend subscribing to Talking Heads on your favourite podcast channel, such as YouTube or Spotify. You’ll receive your podcast episodes every week. If you like Talking Heads, leave us a positive review and a nice rating.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, and Lazare Hounhouayenou.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

articles.title: Solana Alpenglow Upgrade Ships. Adoption is the Real Test
articles.text:
Insights / Research / Solana Alpenglow Upgrade Ships. Adoption is the Real Test

Written by:

Lucas Tcheyan
Vice President, Research

Topics

Solana

research • October 23, 2026

Solana Alpenglow Upgrade Ships. Adoption is the Real Test

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com.WHAT HAPPENEDOn Wednesday, at slot 459,653,000, Solana activated the long-awaited Alpenglow update to mainnet, changing Solana’s consensus protocol for the first time since its launch.Heralded as “the biggest upgrade in Solana’s history” by Solana’s core developer lab Anza, the upgrade improves both finality and the network’s fault tolerance model. Transactions on Solana are now designed to finalize in roughly 150 milliseconds instead of the 12 seconds required under Solana’s previous TowerBFT consensus mechanism. The upgrade also introduces a new “20 + 20” resilience model, remaining secure against 20% hostile stake while tolerating up to an additional 20% of stake going offline, for a combined 40% of stake that can be unavailable or adversarial. This differs from the traditional Byzantine fault-tolerance assumptions used by many other chains, which are typically resilient only to 33% on both counts.The Alpenglow update is staged across three phases. Wednesday’s activation introduced phase 1 through Votor, which moves validator voting offchain and removes Proof of History from its previous role in consensus. Moving votes offchain frees up blockspace previously consumed by vote transactions and makes it available for user transactions. Phase 2 is expected to improve the leader handover process so the next leader can begin constructing blocks more quickly, while Phase 3 will implement Rotor, a new block-propagation design intended to replace Solana’s Turbine mechanism and reduce the number of hops required to distribute block data. For a more in-depth overview of the upgrade’s technical details and roadmap refer to our prior coverage here and here.Alpenglow arrives as part of a broader set of performance upgrades Solana has been rolling out in parallel over the past few months. Most notably, the network recently completed a staged reduction in slot times from 400 milliseconds to 200 milliseconds, increasing the frequency of block production. Together with Alpenglow’s faster finality, the shorter slot times are intended to tighten the gap between transaction submission, inclusion, and irreversible settlement, while later phases of Alpenglow (fast leader handover and Rotor) are designed to reduce remaining sources of latency in block construction and propagation.OUR TAKE Protocol upgrades on par with Alpenglow, for example Ethereum's "The Merge," have historically been important milestones that draw external interest in blockchains. They demonstrate novel technical innovation and a level of competency from core developers. That dynamic has shifted as crypto markets have matured. The reason is simple. Technological innovation alone is no longer enough. Adoption and real use are the most important metrics.That doesn’t mean upgrades like Alpenglow are insignificant. Far from it. General-purpose smart contract platforms like Solana are built to perform on par with centralized financial markets and need to continually evolve to remain competitive. Even the most established smart contract platform, Ethereum, is nowhere close to a place where it can ossify. Doing so would risk leaving any chain in the dust to existing alternatives or new entrants. Protocol updates not only demonstrate core developer technical capability, but the ecosystem’s ability to anticipate and adapt the underlying chain to changing use cases that drive real demand.In that context, Alpenglow is an important step forward for Solana. Shortening finality improves performance for trading venues, bridges, and payment applications (among many use cases). Coupled with other changes to the protocol across slot times and tokenomics, it continues to position Solana as one of the few high-performance decentralized blockchains with an organic user and developer base. As I wrote following Solana’s Accelerate conference in May, for the past year or so Solana has been “building backwards,” trying to recapture market share in verticals like perpetuals, prediction markets, and DeFi, where others clearly lead. Alpenglow is a step toward reversing that dynamic.Whether this technical progress translates into real growth depends on where Solana decides to compete. While Solana may be able to regain some market share in verticals where it already lags, it will be incredibly hard to become the default venue. As our quarterly Solana updates show, despite extensive efforts, the chain has largely failed to penetrate perpetuals or prediction markets (although it is still early on that journey). For Solana, the golden ticket so far has largely been the meme economy, which despite poor external optics, has been an incredible success from a fee and revenue standpoint. It is also competing aggressively to be a leader in the tokenization boom. But perhaps the most overlooked vertical is a growing cohort of real businesses that are using the chain for capital formation and as their operational infrastructure. Those are the green shoots that, when complemented with a world-class and driven group of core developers, can accelerate Solana’s adoption and growth. Devs are shipping. Do not fade them.

articles.title: Getting the foundations right: How South Asia can make AI work for growth
articles.text:
Published on
Voices

Getting the foundations right: How South Asia can make AI work for growth

Johannes Zutt

October 21, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Harnessing AI’s potential could help South Asia ensure sustained growth and jobs for the future. Photo: K M Asad

Two forces are currently reshaping the global economy.
The first is high energy prices, resulting from the conflict in the Middle East. South Asia is particularly vulnerable. It is one of the most energy-dependent regions in the world, and it relies more heavily on shipments through the Strait of Hormuz than other regions.
The second is the rapid advance of artificial intelligence (AI). Countries that produce AI-related goods have been propelled forward by rising exports and investment.
So far, South Asia has largely missed these AI gains. Yet the region continues to grow faster than other regions, and growth is projected to remain steady near 7 percent in the coming years.
What explains this continuing resilience?
A key contributor has been the long-term structural reforms that South Asian governments have implemented steadily over the past decade. In India, this has involved consolidating the labor code, rationalizing the goods and services tax, adopting free-trade agreements, and increasing spending on public infrastructure. In Sri Lanka, it has been mobilizing revenue, transforming utilities, and rationalizing tariffs. In Bhutan, it has been liberalizing foreign direct investment.
These reforms take time to bear fruit. Their impact is gradual and cumulative. But the benefits can now be seen in South Asia’s robust domestic demand, despite slowing growth in the rest of the world.
South Asia needs to sustain this momentum and invest in new drivers of growth. Just as today’s resilience is a product of yesterday’s reforms, future resilience will be a product of the reforms being undertaken today.
This is where South Asia can harness the opportunities provided by AI.
The potential is there. Far more South Asian workers stand to gain from AI than to lose to it. Only 7 percent of jobs in the region combine high AI exposure with low human complementarity, compared to 15 percent elsewhere. Currently, only about one in four Indian firms use AI—compared to one in two in the United States—and Indian firms tend to do so in less sophisticated ways. But adoption is accelerating fast, and for good reason: positions requiring AI skills already command a wage premium of nearly 30 percent.
South Asia is also already being pulled into the AI economy through its global supply chains. American firms that have adopted AI heavily are deepening their ties with South Asian suppliers rather than cutting them. Following the launch of ChatGPT, a one-standard-deviation increase in a U.S. firm's AI exposure has been associated with a 27 percent larger rise in its customer links with South Asian firms, and that effect more than doubles when the South Asian supplier is itself in a sector that is highly exposed to AI. In short, AI is not replacing South Asia in global value chains. Instead, it is deepening linkages.
The technology is also beginning to show up in the daily work of doctors, farmers, and teachers. In Telangana, India, AI-based weather forecasts are saving smallholder farmers up to $560 per season by improving planting decisions. In Bangladesh, AI-assisted retinal screening has increased the number of patients checked for diabetic complications by 40 percent per day. These are early signals of what broad AI adoption could do for productivity and living standards.
But AI cannot outrun the foundations on which it depends. To fully reap the benefits of AI, countries need to address foundational gaps by enriching workforce skills, strengthening the business-enabling environment, and improving physical and digital infrastructure. Governments are sometimes tempted by flagship projects — building frontier AI models or funding showcase data centers. Our evidence points elsewhere. South Asian firms themselves identify digital infrastructure and tertiary education as the two biggest constraints on AI adoption. In South Asia, reliable electricity, strong education systems, and digital connectivity will do more to spread AI's benefits broadly than any flagship project.
For most of South Asia, the gains lie in adopting and adapting existing tools to local conditions, languages, and connectivity constraints. This means emphasizing "small AI": practical applications adapted to specific tasks and local contexts, running on basic devices in low-bandwidth environments. These applications can increase productivity and incomes in the sectors that employ the most people.
South Asia region has demonstrated remarkable resilience in the face of persistent shocks. By harnessing AI’s potential and investing in foundational reforms, the region can ensure continued growth and jobs for the future.
Read more in our latest South Asia Economic Update: Adopting AI for Growth.

articles.title: Can the EU and Canada forge a new partnership?
articles.text:
Blog Name

RealTime Economics

Can the EU and Canada forge a new partnership?

Cecilia Malmström (PIIE) and

Inu Manak (PIIE)

Date
October 19, 2026 9:00 AM

Photo Credit: REUTERS/Yves Herman

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Body
In an apparently impromptu gesture, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, welcomed Canada as an "associate member" of the European Union in her annual State of the Union speech(link is external) in September. But while Europeans are nearly unanimously in favor of more cooperation with Canada on such issues as defense and climate change, making Canada an associate member would face many obstacles.
A summit between Canada and EU leaders at the end of October may clarify and deepen the new relationship. An anodyne draft joint statement is already circulating. But taking those ties to new heights will require addressing old objectives that remain unfulfilled.
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada was in attendance as a guest of honor for von der Leyen's speech in Strasbourg, but her invitation seemed to catch him by surprise. The term "associate member" does not exist. It has no legal definition in the treaties that make up the body of EU law. The surprised reaction from EU member states and Carney himself was understandable. The idea was not mentioned in the draft circulated the day before the speech.
The term "associate member" may have been borrowed from a similar call by Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany last year to offer Ukraine an "associated membership" to fast track the country´s accession to the European Union, but without voting rights or access to the bloc's common budget. Ukraine and several member states rejected his offer. Ukraine seeks full membership, nothing less. But Canada is not and will not become a candidate country to the European Union, nor does it want to be. But there are still strong prospects for deepening EU-Canada ties.
Best friends forever…
Canada and the European Union have a close and trusting relationship anchored in an ambitious Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA(link is external)) and a strategic partnership since September 2017. They share values, a belief in multilateralism, and support for Ukraine. Under economic and political pressure from the United States, Carney has sought to broaden Canada's alliances, diversify trade relations, and establish Canada as a leader of the world's middle powers(link is external) playing a greater role in upholding international rules and institutions.
But the CETA trade agreement still has untapped potential. It covers all fields of trade, eliminating 99 percent of all tariff lines, increasing access to each other's markets, and facilitating worker mobility. Trade in goods and services between Canada and the European Union has increased by 81 percent since 2016, or €131 billion, a clear sign of the agreement's success.(link is external) Total trade in goods was around €92 billion in 2025, only a fraction of Canada-US total trade(link is external) that amounted to $880 billion in the same year—but this is to be expected, with Canada geographically linked to the United States. There is still more that Canada and the European Union can do to expand trade ties. For example, a Canada-EU digital agreement, aimed at facilitating trade in services, is now also being negotiated.
One way to further CETA's potential is to fully ratify it. As it stands, the agreement is only provisional. While the European Union negotiates trade agreements for its members, the individual countries still need to approve them through their domestic processes. To date, 10 countries have still not ratified the agreement. As a result, several agreed upon rules, on investment and investment protections, are still not applicable.
Accordingly, if von der Leyen's sentiment is shared across the continent, member states should finalize their legal commitments to CETA as a natural first step in building closer relations with Canada. But since elections loom in several of the concerned countries (France, Greece, and Poland), this finalization is not likely to happen soon. As always, concerns about agricultural competition worry some countries. For its part, Canada has not managed to fill its agreed upon quota of beef exports to the European Union because of EU regulations on hormone treated meat. Overall, the European Union has an agricultural trade surplus(link is external) with Canada, though Europe's farmers are not likely to be assuaged by this fact.
CETA does not give Canada full access to the single market in Europe because it is a traditional free trade agreement. Such access is granted only to countries applying to the European Union and members of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA)(link is external) community. Neither Canada nor the European Union has expressed ambitions in this regard, even if further trade facilitation and alignment will be considered on a sectoral basis. A major complicating factor, if Canada were ever to show such interest, is that it would have to fully align with the EU body of laws, referred to as the "acquis," on standards and regulations, which is not in the cards because of Canada's close regulatory alignment with the United States.
As proof of the close relation, however, Canadian ministers have regularly been invited to European Council meetings. Canada is the first non-European country to participate in an economic instrument supporting EU member states that seek to invest in defense industrial production through common procurement, called Security Action for Europe, or SAFE(link is external). Canada has also been invited to join the biannual meetings of the European Political Community,(link is external) an intergovernmental forum established after the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It has 44 European countries participating.
What comes next?
The EU leaders and Carney will meet in Montreal for a summit on October 29-30, the first opportunity to touch base since the full trade war broke out between the United States and Canada this summer and since von der Leyen's promise of associate membership.
A bland preliminary joint draft statement(link is external) for the meeting is circulating, and it does not contain the term associate member. Instead, it focuses on concrete steps to further deepen relations and on generalizations about a partnership rooted in trust, economic ties, shared values, and support for multilateralism and reforms at the World Trade Organization. It then goes on to cover basically every possible area of cooperation from sustainable supply chains, investment mobilization, energy, artificial intelligence (AI), carbon pricing, the Arctic, military cooperation and support to Ukraine, critical minerals, student exchange, public health, and cybersecurity.
The stated aim is to build "an alliance for the future," a phrase that Carney used in his own speech to the European Parliament(link is external). Yet while the list of action items proposes to build upon the success of CETA, it fails to mention the fact that 10 EU member states still have not ratified that agreement.
A potentially significant way for Canada and the European Union to achieve progress in their relationship would be to build on an agreement signed earlier this year to strengthen cooperation on critical raw materials and rare earths. Canada´s resources can be pooled with European processing capacities, building scale and secure supply. But these efforts will require more long-term actions, such as joint risk assessments and financial investments to back them.
The draft joint statement suggests that the EU-Canada partnership "may become a model for other countries seeking friendship in a challenging world." A natural next step for the European Union would be to join Canada and other Asia-Pacific countries in the Compressive Progressive Agreement for Transpacific Partnership (CPTPP)(link is external) signed in 2018. A few meetings on a ministerial level between the 12 CPTPP members and the EU trade commissioner have been held, but nothing concrete has happened since early summer. Canada and the European Union could take their new strengthened partnership into that venue as well, where there has already been talk of strengthening the institution by establishing a permanent body(link is external) to support the implementation and updating of the agreement.
In his speech to the European Parliament, Carney wittily disavowed creation of "a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival—only with better manners." Deciding what to call the EU-Canada partnership matters less than the concrete actions that they take to create the type of international order they want to see. The European Union and Canada may just be getting started in redefining their relationship, but much can be done to strengthen and build upon their existing bonds as a first step.

articles.title: Market update - October 16th 2026 | CoinShares
articles.text: Market update - October 16th, 20262 min readDataFirm inflation and resilient spending reprice the Fed, and Bitcoin feels it firstThe macro backdrop has become less supportive for digital assets this week. September CPI rose 0.6% month-on-month and 3.7% year-on-year, with the annual rate landing above the 3.6% consensus.¹ Energy did much of that work: gasoline prices rose 9.1% over the month and accounted for around half the headline increase. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose 0.3% on the month to 2.6% year-on-year, firm enough to reinforce the Fed's concern that inflation is not yet under control.¹At the same time, the US economy continues to prove resilient. September retail sales rose 0.8% against expectations of roughly 0.3%, following an August figure since revised up to 1.3%.² Some of that strength reflects higher gasoline prices, with gasoline station sales up 6.4% on the month, but even allowing for this, the broader run of economic data suggests activity is holding up better than expected. That leaves the Fed with an uncomfortable combination: inflation remains elevated while demand has not weakened enough to remove the need for restrictive policy.Bitcoin and the broader digital asset market have moved lower on the resulting hawkish repricing, a reminder of how sensitive Bitcoin remains to monetary policy over short horizons. Higher expected rates lift real yields and the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset, while tighter financial conditions shrink the liquidity available to risk assets generally. Flows have followed. Global digital asset investment products have seen $434M of outflows so far this week, a clear deterioration in sentiment since the CPI release.Markets still do not expect the Fed to raise rates at the October meeting. Polymarket put the probability of no change at roughly 75% on 15 October, against around 25% for a 25bp increase.³ Futures have nevertheless moved considerably more hawkish since the CPI print, and expectations for another increase before year-end have risen substantially. What has shifted is the expected timing, not the direction.There is an important nuance in the retail sales data. Strong nominal spending partly reflects consumers paying more for energy rather than an acceleration in real consumption. Excluding gasoline, September sales rose only 0.2%, down from 1.0% in August.² If higher energy costs keep squeezing household purchasing power, today's resilient consumption data could give way to weaker demand later in the year.For Bitcoin, the near-term setup is therefore difficult rather than fundamentally bearish. The market needs either clearer evidence that inflation is cooling or enough weakness in activity to remove the threat of further tightening. Until one of those arrives, every stronger-than-expected macro release is likely to generate fresh rate volatility. The US economy is resilient enough to tolerate restrictive policy, while inflation is too high for the Fed to declare victory. For investors, that argues for reading the coming weeks as a data-driven range rather than a trend, and for sizing digital asset exposure against a strategic allocation rather than against this week's print.Sources1 US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index, September 2026, released 14 October 20262 US Census Bureau, Advance Monthly Retail Trade Report, September 2026, released 15 October 20263 Polymarket, Fed decision in October 2026 market, odds as at 15 October 2026Published onOct 16th, 2026WriterJames ButterfillHead of ResearchFormer Head of Research at ETF Securities, James leads CoinShares' Research department with deep expertise in equity and fund management.
