articles.title: Building Canada's next 50 years of energy infrastructure | RBCCM
articles.text:
Against the backdrop of Canada's most significant energy and infrastructure expansion in decades, Dokainish BUILD '26 brought together leaders from district energy, long-duration storage, nuclear generation, and project finance to discuss how the country can balance growth with long-term resilience. I had the opportunity to join the panel "What's Next for Canada's Energy and Infrastructure" alongside Carlyle Coutinho, CEO of Enwave; Jon Norman, President of Hydrostor; Jack Tasker, VP Finance of Bruce Power; and Annette Verschuren, Chair and CEO of NRStor. Our discussion covered trade and supply chain pressures, capital formation, regulatory clarity, and the collaborative culture that distinguishes Canada's approach to building major projects.
Here are the key takeaways:
Capital is available – but only for projects that can be delivered
Trade dynamics are reshaping cross-border investment patterns, and Canada stands to benefit from the shift. At the recent Canada Investment Summit, international investors from countries such as Norway and the U.K. actively sought to understand Canada's infrastructure landscape and identify where they can participate. Global investors are now differentiating Canada from the United States in their allocations. The message was straightforward: capital is available for projects that can be delivered.
Delivering them, however, requires long-term planning. The power sector requires long lead times to develop projects, is capital-intensive, and its assets take years to build. Nuclear plants take 10 to 12 years. Gas turbines currently have lead times of at least five years. In the West, Saskatchewan and Alberta are transitioning from coal to nuclear, targeting a 2035 to 2040 timeframe. In the East, conversations are advancing around interconnecting the Atlantic provinces and managing the power coming out of Newfoundland.
Compounding the challenge is uncertainty around future demand, which developers cannot manage on their own. Demand curves shift constantly, driven by data centers, the electrification of buildings and vehicles, and economic cycles. The growth potential in power demand, amplified by AI, has accelerated attention to these issues, yet it still takes years to bring any project to fruition.
Collaboration is Canada's real competitive edge
Meeting the country's energy needs will require a grid built for both redundancy and flexibility. The country's energy needs cannot be met by any one source – solar, wind, gas, nuclear, and hydro each have a role to play. In the West, strong wind resources warrant significant development, alongside natural gas. In the East, there is greater technological capability around nuclear. Ontario is starting to make progress with long-lead-time procurements that provide the contracts needed to bring financing to the table.
Canada's collaborative culture is a real differentiator. The Calgary oil patch is a market leader in technology and advanced drilling, an intellectual resource well regarded around the world. That collaborative instinct is a meaningful advantage Canada should leverage more deliberately. Partnerships such as deep lake water cooling have worked for 25 years, and what sustains them is not contracts but trust. On the nuclear side, the close collaboration between Ontario's two major operators, OPG and Bruce Power, on refurbishments has delivered rare success in an industry where it is uncommon. The two operators share lessons learned, staff, and coordinated schedules.
Areas for improvement remain. Innovation is one: the safety culture in nuclear creates a natural hesitation, but refurbishments are ripe for automation. Affordability, ultimately, is the biggest question the industry must address.
Canada needs to accept more risk to get things built
For those approaching capital providers, the key is to understand what kind of capital is needed, because capital comes in a wide variety of forms and risk profiles. This discipline extends to project preparation more broadly. A project with long-term off-take contracts or power purchase agreements, will attract a different capital profile than one without the same contractual support.
The broader challenge is that Canada needs to accept more risk to get things built. The market is small, and companies that succeed here must export to scale. There is also a lingering hesitation around private-sector involvement in public goods, which is critical in the power sector. There are many examples of successful private capital deployment in the industry; the greater risk is not building at all.
The capital is available, the collaborative culture is a proven advantage, and the demand is real. The question is whether Canada can translate planning into execution quickly enough to seize the moment.

articles.title: Types of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks
articles.text:
Financial Stability

What Is Financial StabilityTypes of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks Monitoring Risk Across the Financial System Proactive Monitoring of Markets and InstitutionsFinancial Stability and Stress Testing

Types of Financial System Vulnerabilities and Risks

Related Content

Financial Stability Report

Monetary Policy Report

Financial Stability Monitoring (PDF)

Mapping heat in the U.S. financial system

Federal Reserve staff regularly and systematically assess a standard set of vulnerabilities as part of their periodic review of financial stability. These assessments generally are provided to the Board and Federal Open Market Committee four times per year. Using a range of data sources as well as insights gained from discussions and engagement with domestic and foreign counterparts, staff regularly monitor vulnerabilities in four areas:

1. Elevated valuation pressures are signaled by asset prices that are high relative to economic fundamentals or historical norms and are often driven by an increased willingness of investors to take on risk. As such, elevated valuation pressures imply a greater possibility of outsized drops in asset prices.

2. Excessive borrowing by businesses and households leaves them vulnerable to distress if their incomes decline or the assets they own fall in value. In the event of such shocks, businesses and households with high debt burdens may need to cut back spending sharply, affecting the overall level of economic activity. Moreover, when businesses and households cannot make payments on their loans, financial institutions and investors incur losses.

3. Excessive leverage within the financial sector increases the risk that financial institutions will not have the sufficient capacity to absorb losses when hit by adverse shocks. In those situations, institutions will be forced to cut back lending, sell their assets, or, in extreme cases, shut down. Such responses can substantially impair credit access for households and businesses.

4. Elevated funding risks can occur when financial institutions raise funds from the public with a commitment to return investor money on short notice, but those institutions then invest much of the funds in illiquid assets that are hard to sell quickly or in assets that have a long maturity. This liquidity and maturity transformation can create an incentive for investors to withdraw funds quickly in adverse situations, commonly referred to as a “run.” Facing a run, financial institutions may need to sell assets quickly at “fire sale” prices, thereby incurring substantial losses and potentially even becoming insolvent.

These vulnerability assessments inform internal Federal Reserve discussions concerning both supervision and regulatory policies and monetary policy. Two times a year, the Federal Reserve publishes its Financial Stability Report summarizing its current assessment of these vulnerabilities, the salient risks to the financial system originating in the United States and abroad, and how they might interact. A shorter summary of current vulnerabilities is included in the twice-yearly Monetary Policy Report to Congress. They also inform Federal Reserve interactions with broader monitoring efforts, such as those by the Financial Stability Oversight Council and the Financial Stability Board.

Asset Valuations and Risk Appetite

Asset valuations are the prices of assets after accounting for economic fundamentals, such as future expected cash flows and interest rates. Valuations that are high relative to history or to economic fundamentals constitute a vulnerability because the unwinding of high prices can be destabilizing in the financial system and economy. Moreover, stretched asset valuations may be an indicator of a broader buildup in risk appetite leading to investors taking on higher levels of risk, or new risks that are not fully understood.

This dynamic can be more concerning when (1) the assets are widely held and the values are supported by excessive borrowing, (2) the maturity of the asset is significantly longer than the maturity of the liability financing that asset, or (3) there is a lack of publicly available information about the asset.

However, it is very difficult to judge whether an asset price is overvalued relative to fundamentals. As a result, analysis typically considers a range of possible valuation metrics, as well as developments in areas where asset prices are rising especially rapidly, the size and pace of inflows to an asset class, or the implications of unusually low or high levels of volatility in certain markets.

Borrowing by Businesses and Households

Excessive borrowing by businesses and households leaves them vulnerable if their incomes decline or the assets they own fall in value. In the event of such shocks, businesses and households with high debt burdens may need to cut back spending sharply, affecting the overall level of economic activity. A default can significantly limit their ability to obtain credit in the future. Moreover, when businesses and households cannot make payments on their loans, financial institutions and investors incur losses.

Leverage in the Financial System

Highly leveraged financial system intermediaries—those with significantly more debt than equity—can amplify the effect of negative shocks in the financial system and broad economy. For example, if highly leveraged institutions collectively respond to a negative shock in the economy (e.g., a sharp decline in house prices) by tightening lending standards and shrinking their balance sheets more than called for by the shock itself, perhaps because outsized credit losses threaten their solvency, the resulting contraction in credit will aggravate the decline in economic activity resulting from the shock.

Sufficiently large losses for highly leveraged institutions, especially if those institutions have a significant share of short-term funding, can lead to “fire sales,” where assets are unloaded quickly at extremely low prices. These fire sales then reduce the value of similar assets held by other financial institutions, potentially leading to a negative feedback loop.

The Federal Reserve monitors leverage in the banking sector with the help of an extensive data collection program. This includes the data collected in support of the Dodd-Frank Act stress tests for large banking institutions, the quarterly Reports of Condition and Income for all banks, and the Consumer Credit report. Additionally, periodic surveys of nonbank providers of leverage, such as the Senior Credit Officer Opinion Survey, as well as collaboration and data sharing among all the financial regulatory agencies offer valuable insights on nonbank financial leverage.

Funding Risks and Maturity Transformation by the Financial System

One key benefit provided by the financial system is to aggregate short-maturity liabilities so that they can be used to fund long-maturity assets. This function has historically occurred primarily in the traditional banking system or other depository institutions, which use deposits from consumers as part of the financing to provide multiyear auto or mortgage loans. In recent decades, nonbank financial institutions have grown substantially. For example, mutual funds offer their investors the convenience of daily withdrawals even though they invest in longer-term debt instruments.

However, as seen during the 2007–09 financial crisis and the outbreak of COVID-19 in March 2020, the mismatch between long-term assets and short-term funding creates systemic vulnerabilities that can threaten the functioning of financial markets and the broader economy. This manifests when a large fraction of those investors withdraw their funding suddenly in response to an increase in risk aversion after a negative shock.

Deposit insurance provides some protection against this vulnerability within the traditional banking system. However, firms that use short-term liabilities such as repurchase agreements (or “repos”) or commercial paper, and the financial institutions that invest in them, like money market mutual funds, are also prone to run risk. Indeed, money market mutual funds came under considerable pressure during both the 2007–09 financial crisis and the pandemic in 2020. For this reason, the Federal Reserve actively monitors—as best it can, given available data and measurement—both liquidity risk and the degree of maturity transformation in the financial system.

News Release
China's CMRG targets greater control over iron ore price discovery

22 October 2026
4 minute read

Email
Share by email

China’s purchasing power has long shaped iron ore prices, but CMRG aims to influence how they are set
By integrating procurement, inventory and transaction data, trading platforms and benchmarks, CMRG is building virtual vertical integration without owning mines or replacing traders
For Japan and other buyers outside China’s system, the risk is becoming a price taker twice over

China’s state-backed China Mineral Resources Group (CMRG) is shifting from a centralised purchasing role to a potential force in global iron ore price formation, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest research. Founded in July 2022 to centralise purchasing, negotiate prices, and manage strategic inventories, CMRG now aims to influence price discovery. It plans to do this by capturing transaction data, steering liquidity, and shaping benchmark references through a state-backed platform.
According to the report, China's CMRG: From Demand Centre to Market Governor, commodity power lies not only in owning mines or controlling physical volumes. It also resides in the ability to decide which transactions are visible, which inventories are accessible, which benchmarks are embedded in contracts, and which participants can intermediate the market. CMRG appears to be assembling all five layers of that capability: purchasing coordination, strategic inventory management, a proprietary trading platform, domestic price indices and long-term contract architecture.
Information as the most valuable asset
Wood Mackenzie notes CMRG's most strategically significant asset as information rather than volume. "By channelling transactions through its own platform, CMRG is gaining greater visibility into mill restocking, cargo rerouting and immediate order flows", says David Cachot, Head of Steel, Iron Ore and Alloys Markets at Wood Mackenzie. "This could also give it a clearer view of whether benchmark prices reflect the transactions that matter most to the market. These are insights that have traditionally been held by miners and international trading houses."
China’s journey from demand dominance to market governance

A looser market strengthens the buyer's hand
CMRG's emergence coincides with a structural shift in iron ore supply fundamentals. New volumes from Guinea and Brazil are arriving as Chinese steel demand matures, creating conditions of marginal surplus. Wood Mackenzie argues that a centralised buyer has considerably more leverage in a market with marginal surplus than in one where mills compete for scarce tonnes, because credible alternatives matter before mills fully exercise them.
The Simandou project reinforces CMRG's position in three ways:

it diversifies China's supply base
introduces high-grade blendable material
deepens China's participation in an important new supply chain

However, the project does not remove dependence on Australia and Brazil, and its ramp-up will be gradual, but it raises the credibility of CMRG's threat to delay, redirect or segment purchases at precisely the moment CMRG is consolidating its negotiating authority.
Japan: secure in tonnes, exposed in architecture
The report identifies Japan's strategic vulnerability. Japanese steelmakers benefit from strong bilateral supplier relationships, well-managed obligations, and support from trading houses with upstream equity, freight, and financing capabilities, which together reduce physical supply risk. However, Wood Mackenzie cautions that Japan could still face price-taking situations on two separate occasions.
"Japanese buyers could continue sourcing from the same miners while their landed cost becomes more sensitive to Chinese port inventories, RMB conditions, domestic sentiment and CMRG's procurement rhythm," Cachot states.
The next contest: green iron units
Wood Mackenzie identifies steelmaking decarbonisation as the next frontier for market governance. As scarcity shifts toward qualified high-grade concentrates, pellets, direct reduced iron feed, and low-carbon metallics, these less liquid, more technically specific markets will depend on long-duration partnerships rather than spot-driven price discovery.
The report states that governance of the green iron supply chain is still evolving. Buyers can strengthen their bargaining position by specifying demand, qualifying feedstocks, co-investing in beneficiation and pelletising, supporting low-carbon ironmaking, and committing to long-term offtake agreements. In this emerging market, the critical asset is not simply iron ore, but ore that is technically qualified, carbon-accounted, pelletised, financed, and delivered for use in low-carbon steel production.
"China spent two decades becoming the indispensable buyer of iron ore," says Cachot. "CMRG suggests that the next ambition is to become indispensable to how the market is organised. The physical market will still impose discipline, but within that envelope, CMRG can influence who sees the market first, who negotiates from a position of patience and who captures the value between benchmark and realised price."

articles.title: AgriConnect and Djibouti: Creating jobs and boosting food security in a resource-constrained region
articles.text:
Published on
Perspectives: MENA, Afghanistan, and Pakistan

AgriConnect and Djibouti: Creating jobs and boosting food security in a resource-constrained region

Meskerem Brhane

Yosuke Kotsuji

Fatou Fall

October 22, 2026

This page in:

English

English

Across the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan, food insecurity remains a major challenge. One in six people in the region faces food insecurity, while 42 percent cannot afford a healthy diet.
As populations grow and incomes rise, food demand is projected to rise by 67 percent by 2050, widening the gap between what the food sector needs to deliver and what it can currently provide. At the same time, climate change, water scarcity, and conflict are making it increasingly difficult to produce enough food sustainably.
But the region does not need to choose between producing more food and conserving scarce resources. The World Bank Group’s Building Food Security, Creating Jobs report points to a different path: transform agrifood systems to produce more food, create jobs, and use scarce resources more efficiently.
Achieving this will require reducing food loss, adopting climate-smart technologies, improving water productivity, strengthening storage, logistics, and trade, and creating stronger links between farmers and markets. In the process, it will also mean creating a better business environment and mobilizing more private investment.
This approach matters not only for food security, but also for jobs. The agrifood sector already supports 63 million jobs across the region, nearly three in ten workers. With the right investments and reforms, it could generate millions more, particularly by strengthening value chains and creating opportunities beyond primary production.
AgriConnect is the World Bank Group’s approach to turning these priorities into action. It brings together public policy, investment, private finance, and partnerships around value chains with the greatest potential for advancing food security and jobs.
Djibouti offers a compelling example of what this approach can look like in practice. The country imports 90 percent of its food, but by focusing on strategic agrifood opportunities, it can create more and better jobs and strengthen food security. Djibouti has a real chance to turn scarcity into opportunity by investing in what it can grow competitively.
The stakes are high. In 2026, 16 percent of Djibouti’s population faced acute food insecurity, a share expected to rise to 25 percent by year-end. Unemployment remains at 39 percent despite a decade of solid growth. Agriculture contributes only 4 to 5 percent of GDP, but it is a lifeline for rural communities. Farmers and pastoralists operate under exceptionally difficult conditions. Water and arable land are scarce, annual rainfall is low and erratic, and climate shocks are becoming more severe. Weak infrastructure and technical skills, limited access to finance and markets, and an underdeveloped regulatory environment further constrain productivity and private investment.
The Djibouti AgriConnect Compact, the first in the greater region, lays out a path forward for the country. Aligned with the government’s Vision Djibouti 2035, it brings together investment, financing, and structural reform around three strategic value chains:
Livestock remains the backbone of Djibouti’s agricultural economy. It accounts for three-quarters of agricultural GDP and supports livestock transit and re-exports to Gulf markets. In 2024, the livestock terminal at the Port of Djibouti handled more than 1.2 million animals while operating at less than 20 percent of capacity. High-yielding breeds, better feed, veterinary services, processing, and cold chains could increase productivity and capture more value locally.
Horticulture offers an immediate domestic market opportunity. Local production meets only 10 percent of demand, while vegetable imports exceeded US$35 million in 2021. Climate-smart greenhouses and water-efficient production could enable year-round supplies. Tomato yields, for example, can reach 300 tons per hectare under greenhouse cover, compared with 40 tons in open fields.
Dates are the smallest value chain today but offer substantial scope for growth. Djibouti produces only about 110 tons annually while importing roughly 2,300 tons. The plan is to reach 5,850 tons after 2030, enough to reduce the import gap and position Djibouti as an exporter.
Across all three value chains, the constraints are similar: weak connections between producers and buyers, limited cold-chain and processing capacity, uncertain land tenure, and scarce credit. Nearly three-quarters of Djiboutian households lack access to banking services, while lenders often view agriculture as inherently risky.
AgriConnect addresses these constraints together rather than separately. It aligns shared infrastructure with reforms to land, licensing, certification, skills, and finance. This shift means livestock can gain value in feedlots rather than losing value in transit, and tomatoes and other crops can earn more when grown and ripened in a greenhouse rather than in drought-stressed fields. And in the process, young Djiboutians have more opportunities to build careers in the agritech sector.
Many of these solutions are already being tested under World Bank Group-funded projects. The Agri-Food Value Chain Development Project is investing in basic infrastructure and access to financing for producers and enterprises. Under the DRIVE project, the goal is not simply to help pastoralists survive the next drought but to give them the financial tools to protect their animals, earn more, and invest in healthier, more productive animals. It is also reinforcing Djibouti’s role as a regional livestock trade hub.
At the same time, IFC, the World Bank Group’s private sector arm, is helping to strengthen the foundations for private investment. At the port, it is advising Tiryaki Agro, Türkiye’s largest agri-food exporter, on a new grain storage facility to ease bottlenecks for staple commodities passing through Djibouti. On finance, it is working with the Central Bank of Djibouti on reforms to the movable collateral-registry and leasing framework so small businesses can access the finance they need to procure logistics equipment more easily.
Scaling these efforts will require significant resources and sustained coordination. An estimated US$185–245 million is needed across the three value chains by 2030. The ambition is to reach 10,000 farmers and pastoralists and create and improve at least 5,000 jobs.
Across the region, targeted World Bank Group-supported investments are addressing this challenge and already delivering results, providing a foundation for AgriConnect.
In Afghanistan, the Food Security Project is supporting 15 agri-SMEs, reaching over 7,000 farmers, linking them to formal market contracts, and generating over 1,000 jobs. In Morocco, productive alliances enabled 730 producers, 40 percent of whom are women, to access more reliable, higher-value markets while reducing their dependence on intermediaries. In Pakistan’s Punjab province, large-scale investments in irrigation infrastructure are already helping more than 100,000 farmers gain more equitable and reliable access to water, increase yields, and shift to higher-value crops. In Yemen, investments in fisheries have supported nearly 4,000 fishers and fish processors, including 800 women, and created or improved more than 11,000 jobs.
The lesson is clear: raising production alone is not enough. Farmers need markets; businesses need infrastructure and finance; investors need predictable policies; and countries need resilient trade and water management systems. AgriConnect brings these pieces together around the value chains with the greatest potential for food security and jobs.

articles.title: A New Solution for Fragmented Markets: The Integrated Post-Trade Operating Model | BNY
articles.text:
Transforming post-trade

A New Solution for Fragmented Markets: The Integrated Post-Trade Operating Model

As market complexity increases, connecting clearing, settlement, collateral and liquidity can help firms reduce operational friction and put capital to work more effectively.

alarm

10 minute read

calendar_today

19 Oct, 2026

Post-trade fragmentation is becoming a growing drag on capital, liquidity and operational efficiency. Discover how a connected operating model can help firms streamline workflows, mobilize collateral faster and prepare for T+1 settlement, tokenization and continuous markets.

Key Takeaways

Market fragmentation is becoming a direct constraint on capital efficiency, liquidity mobility and growth.An integrated post-trade operating model can reduce handoffs, simplify workflows and improve settlement efficiency across markets.Unifying clearing, settlement, collateral and payments on a common data foundation can enhance transparency and automation.Greater collateral mobility and real-time liquidity visibility can help firms reduce prefunding needs and put capital to work more effectively.A connected operating model creates a practical foundation for T+1 readiness, tokenization and future 24/7 market structures.

For banks, investment firms, broker-dealers and other global market participants, market expansion compounds post-trade complexity. Every additional clearing venue, settlement location, collateral pool, currency and time zone increases operational interdependency across securities and derivatives transactions. Firms must also navigate faster markets, regulatory change, tokenized assets and continued pressure to improve capital and liquidity efficiency. Together, these developments are turning fragmentation in post-trade execution from an operating challenge into a direct constraint on capital efficiency.
Although specific post-trade circumstances vary by market, firms operating across jurisdictions face the same underlying challenges to coordinate securities, cash, collateral and liquidity across market infrastructures that were not designed to function as a single operating model.
Europe’s repo market provides a particularly visible example of this global challenge. Outstanding volume rose 24.6% year over year to EUR 13.7 trillion, according to the International Capital Market Association’s (ICMA) European Repo Market Survey conducted in December 2025,[1] increasing the volume of securities and cash that firms must coordinate across clearing, settlement, collateral and payment infrastructure.

Figure 1: European Repo Market Growth

Source: ICMA European Repo Market Survey No. 50, conducted December 2025 and published March 2026 | Units: EUR trillions outstanding.

At the same time, the European Union, United Kingdom and Switzerland are set to move to T+1 settlement on 11 October 2027, compressing the time available to allocate securities, fund cash obligations and resolve exceptions across time zones. Regulatory change is adding further pressure. European Market Infrastructure Regulation (EMIR) 3.0 is reshaping the derivatives clearing regime, while the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), is tightening requirements for managing cyber threats, technology disruptions and third-party dependencies.
Given such complexity, many firms are reaching the same conclusion: as markets become more connected, managing fragmentation is no longer enough to achieve sustainable growth. Although Europe makes the challenge especially visible — with 28 central securities depositories and international central securities depositories (CSDs and ICSDs) and 14 central counterparties (CCPs) in the EU and European Economic Area (EEA) alone — fragmentation is not region-specific. It emerges wherever firms must connect multiple clearing venues, settlement locations, collateral pools, currencies and time zones so a different operating model integrating every post-trade requirement is now a necessity. This new operating model for post-trade requirements should reduce external handoffs, release trapped capital, improve balance-sheet efficiency and support growth without adding proportional operational complexity.

What an Integrated Post-Trade Operating Model Requires

Traditionally firms have responded to fragmentation by adding interfaces, reconciliations and operational layers, then absorbing the cost as fixed overhead. A more effective response is to remove securities and derivatives fragmentation from the operating model itself. That means creating a model that can extend across markets efficiently and consistently. Integrating assets, data, collateral, cash and liquidity also creates a practical foundation for introducing tokenized instruments without building a separate operating environment.
Five principles define an integrated post-trade model that can be applied across markets while accommodating differences in local infrastructure, regulation and operating practice:
One relationship, multi-market access: A single connection to coordinate clearing, settlement, payments and financing across CCPs, CSDs, ICSDs and bilateral venues, enabling expansion into new markets without the cost and risk of building separate local capabilities. The same model should also accommodate both established and evolving market infrastructures, including the gradual adoption of tokenized assets and extended-hours or always-on settlement and financing models.End-to-end processing on one data layer: Clearing, settlement, custody, collateral and reconciliation that operate on a common architecture with consistent, validated outputs, eliminating operational handoffs and giving clients straight-through processing across asset classes.Intelligent automation with real-time transparency: AI-enabled workflows, exception handling and reporting delivered through dashboards and APIs to provide real-time visibility into positions and settlement status across transactions, reducing reliance on end-of-day reconciliations.Unified collateral insights: Cleared and uncleared obligations are able to be optimized against a single visible pool of eligible assets, with automated allocation, substitution and recall that help put idle capital back to work.24/7/365 visibility of cash, credit and liquidity across positions: Payments, intraday credit financing and FX are ideally connected and respond to real-time securities and cash positions, enabling efficient real-time currency conversion while improving liquidity visibility and mobility, reducing prefunding needs and strengthening working capital efficiency as settlement cycles compress.
As settlement cycles shorten and tokenization and always-on models reshape how assets may be issued, mobilized, financed, and settled, continuing to manage fragmentation rather than reducing it will become increasingly costly. The next question is how to put these principles into practice on infrastructure that operates across markets today.

Achieving a More Integrated Model

The value of a connected operating model is measured in outcomes — fewer handoffs, faster collateral deployment, lower liquidity buffers, and the ability to add markets without adding complexity.
BNY’s Integrated International Settlement and Collateral Management Operating Model (Figure 2) brings together settlement, global custody, collateral, payments, intraday credit and financing as connected elements of a scalable multi-market model rather than separate capabilities layered together.

Figure 2: BNY’s Integrated Post-Trade Operating Model
In an integrated model, clearing, settlement and collateral operate on one platform, so assets move internally rather than across providers internationally.

Enlarge

At its core is an integrated custody account that connects clearing and collateral activity, creating the foundation on which payments, intraday credit and financing can interoperate against a consolidated view of positions. The model builds on an approach operating at scale in the United States and extends that architecture across Europe and other international markets. Clients retain control of trading and books and records while benefiting from:
Scale without repeat implementation: Financial firms can extend into new markets through existing infrastructure rather than rebuild it each time. A multi-market foundation provides a more consistent path into Europe, Asia-Pacific and other regions as their market access priorities evolve.Processing without external friction: A street-facing trading, settlement and custody account and an internal collateral account operate on a single platform, enabling internal transfers that reduce third-party realignments, prefunding costs, instruction matching, settlement fails and CSDR penalty exposure. A single high-quality dataset lowers reconciliation friction and strengthens governance.Faster workflows, clearer visibility: AI, data and analytics across an integrated model and platform reduce manual intervention and accelerate workflows. APIs and real-time analytics replace fragmented reporting with an integrated view of asset eligibility and availability across the collateral pool.Increased collateral mobility: 23x5 collateral mobility across BNY’s global custody and triparty networks, supported by real-time processing, makes securities available for margin, financing and settlement. Extended operating hours provide greater flexibility for just-in-time liquidity.Liquidity that moves with the markets: Linking intraday credit to real-time positions across consolidated settlement, collateral and payment accounts improves liquidity visibility and mobility while reducing prefunding needs across venues. This more responsive approach can release working capital as settlement cycles compress.
Repo provides a practical example of how the above integrated operating model can reduce fragmentation across the post-trade lifecycle.

A Practical Example: How an Integrated Post-Trade Model Transforms Repo

A repo transaction provides a useful global illustration because the same need to coordinate securities, collateral, financing and cash arises across markets, even where local infrastructure and settlement practices differ. In today’s fragmented model, the required collateral may be held at a local CSD or ICSD through one custodian, while the repo is managed by a different triparty agent and the cash leg is settled through a separate bank.
Mobilizing the collateral can require an external transfer or realignment between custodians, accounts or depositories before it can be financed. Each handoff introduces delay, cost and settlement risk, while fragmented reporting makes it harder to establish a complete intraday view of available inventory, funding requirements and settlement obligations.
In an integrated model, clearing, settlement and collateral management are coordinated through a common platform and data backbone. The repo can be matched against real-time inventory held across the firm’s settlement and collateral accounts, with eligible collateral selected and optimized across trading and collateral requirements. Where assets are already held within the provider’s network, they can be transferred internally from the settlement account into triparty without external custodian transfers or CSD realignments. This makes the collateral available for financing, margin or settlement in near-real time, while reducing settlement costs, late-settlement penalties and fail risk.
As positions change, intraday credit and financing can respond to actual asset and cash balances. Collateral substitutions, recalls and adjustments can be processed throughout the day, while cash and liquidity are managed against a current view of obligations rather than separately prefunded across multiple custodians and venues.
At maturity, the cash repayment, collateral return and release of financing are processed through the same infrastructure, creating a consistent record and a single real-time view through dashboards and APIs.
An integrated operating model also provides a practical pathway to tokenization. Traditional and tokenized assets can be viewed and mobilized within the same portfolio, allowing firms to adopt tokenization progressively without creating separate operating models or isolated liquidity pools.
The result is faster collateral mobility, lower liquidity and capital drag, fewer external movements and reconciliations, and higher settlement efficiency.

A Post-Trade Operating Model Assessment

Understanding the impact of fragmentation starts with a simple self-assessment.
These ten questions apply across jurisdictions, regulatory regimes and settlement timelines, helping to clarify where the current model is creating friction and where an integrated approach would deliver the most value.
External handoffs: Does the post-trade model depend on asset movement between separate external settlement, custody and collateral providers? What friction, fail exposure and penalty risk is embedded in each transfer?Data consistency: Do clearing, settlement, collateral and reconciliation functions run on a common data architecture with consistent, validated outputs — or are you reconciling across fragmented systems and multiple vendors?Real-time visibility: Can front office, treasury and operations teams access real-time positions, settlement status, margin calls and fails through a single pane of glass in real-time or are they still relying on end-of-day reports to understand the firm’s exposure and position?Asset mobility: When securities and cash need to move between settlement, custody, margin and financing purposes, how long does that take and how many external parties, realignments, payments and settlement cycles are involved?Intraday liquidity: Is intraday credit and funding tied to real-time asset visibility across a consolidated post-trade position, or does it depend on prefunding schedules maintained separately across multiple providers?Automation and exception handling: How much of post-trade processing, including exception management and regulatory reporting, is automated, and how much still relies on manual intervention and workarounds?Operational resilience: As regulations such as DORA raise the bar on digital operational resilience, can the current operating model withstand and recover from information, communication and technology disruption across all of your post-trade providers and vendors or does that resilience depend on stitching together multiple third parties?Scalability: When you enter a new market, add a CCP, or onboard a new product, how much of your operating model do you have to rebuild? Does expansion multiply handoffs and fragmentation faster than it creates opportunity?Digital asset and continuous-market readiness: Does your operating model provide the common data, custody, collateral, cash and liquidity foundation needed to introduce tokenized assets and 24/7 market models progressively, or would adoption require separate systems, accounts and processes?Regulatory and market-structure readiness: As settlement cycles shorten and clearing, resilience and market-structure requirements evolve across jurisdictions, is your operating model designed to absorb change, or will each new rule and market requirement add another layer of interfaces, reconciliations and operational workarounds?
Answers to the assessment questions are meant to help reveal whether a firm's operating model is built to adapt to change, reduce fragmentation and create value across the business to unlock capital and increase liquidity, strengthen resilience and time to market.
As market infrastructure continues to evolve, management teams that identify and quantify the cost of infrastructure constraints in preparation for a more integrated post-trade operating model could avoid critical operational and capital inefficiencies piling up in favor of capturing its capital, liquidity and growth benefits.

Related Reading

Collateral Management in an Always-on Market explores how evolving market structures, settlement acceleration, collateral mobility and digital asset innovation are reshaping the future of collateral optimization.

articles.title: Daily: Higher oil and AI concerns drive risk-off move
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: CIO Monthly | Mark Haefele on AI earnings, energy prices, and interest rates (4 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Why bank stocks are falling amid rising rates (6 mins)Video: The AI Show |The AI trade's two-sided test (4 mins)Podcast: Across the Pond: Europe’s bond stress test, on Apple , Spotify (22 mins)Thought of the dayTechnology shares fell on Thursday as investors focused on the financing and potential returns from the next phase of the AI buildout. The Nasdaq fell 2.6%, its steepest one-day decline since 5 June, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 6.7% to its lowest level since July. Meta's shares declined 7% following its results, reversing an initially positive after-market reaction as concerns grew over the company’s rising capital expenditure plan. But two-thirds of S&P 500 constituents advanced on the day, and the equal-weighted index gained 0.8%, suggesting the equity weakness remained concentrated in technology. Brent crude also rose 4% to a five-month high of USD 113/bbl amid renewed concerns over energy supplies. The resulting risk-off move pushed the 10-year US Treasury yield down nearly 17 basis points to 4.95%, its largest daily decline since August 2024.But the latest moves do not alter our view that robust earnings should continue to support equities. AI demand remains strong, current bond yields provide attractive income, and geopolitical developments alone do not justify a broadly defensive investment stance.Strong earnings growth extends beyond technology, although greater selectivity is needed within the AI ecosystem. We expect third-quarter S&P 500 earnings per share to grow 28% from a year earlier, driven by AI demand, an improving industrial cycle, and resilient higher-income consumers. Semiconductor profits are expected to contribute around half of that growth, while average cloud revenue growth is forecast to accelerate from 48% in the June quarter to 58% year over year in the September quarter. That said, risks are rising among specialized AI computing providers known as neoclouds, whose single-product business model focuses on renting compute capacity. In these more capital-intensive parts of the AI buildout, funding pressures and execution risks could reinforce each other. We therefore continue to limit exposure to neoclouds and favor well-funded hyperscalers for their better risk-reward. Beyond technology, nine consecutive months of expansion in the new-orders component of the ISM Manufacturing Index and 6% year-over-year growth in September US retail sales support our view that cyclical parts of the market should also see robust earnings growth.The bond market repricing in recent months has restored meaningful return potential to high-quality fixed income. The 10-year US Treasury yield reached 5.36% in early October, its highest level since 2002, before falling to 4.95% during Thursday’s flight to safety. We continue to rate fixed income as Attractive, with current yields offering an appealing income cushion. For capital losses to offset one year of income, two-, five-, and 10-year Treasury yields would need to rise by around 246, 109, and 63 basis points, respectively, from current levels. We consider increases of this scale unlikely and expect a moderate decline in yields over the next 12 months. We continue to favor selective exposure to medium- and longer-duration high-quality bonds. By contrast, we are cautious on the longest maturities given fiscal concerns and elevated issuance.While higher energy prices pose risks to growth and inflation, the global energy system is continuing to adapt to disruption. Middle East crude and refined-product exports recovered to around 80% of pre-conflict levels in September, supported by a partial restoration of flows through the Strait of Hormuz and rerouting through pipelines. However, in October geopolitical risks have intensified, with increased Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the failure of Russia and Ukraine to agree to a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, pushing energy prices higher again.The impact on global GDP growth from higher oil prices has so far been limited. Oil prices have risen by around USD 40/bbl on average compared with last year. In isolation, we estimate such a price increase could reduce global GDP growth by 0.3-0.5 percentage points, with the amount varying for each economy depending on how much energy they import. But the AI investment cycle and the strength of household balance sheets have enabled consumption to remain resilient. Moreover, following the 2022 oil shock, economies have become more adaptable to rising energy prices. Looking ahead, energy prices will likely continue to present a headwind for the global economy, but barring a significant and sustained rise from here, this should fade over the next 12 months.So, we remain positioned for market gains through diversified exposure to cyclical and structural growth opportunities while reducing concentrated single-stock positions. Within AI, we favor well-funded hyperscalers, high-quality semiconductor and hardware beneficiaries, and defensive technology companies over more capital-intensive neoclouds. We also favor medium- and longer-duration high-quality bonds, while broad commodity exposure can improve portfolio diversification and provide protection against a prolonged energy-supply disruption.

articles.title: Solana Alpenglow
articles.text:
Insights / Perspectives / Alpenglow: What We Learned Running Solana's Biggest Consensus Change

Written by:

Nitish Manivannan
Solana Engineer

Theo Bolognini
Solana Engineer

Will Campbell
Solana Engineer

Products & Services

Staking

perspectives • October 20, 2026

Alpenglow: What We Learned Running Solana's Biggest Consensus Change

TL;DR: Alpenglow, scheduled to go live on Solana mainnet on Wednesday, October 21, changes how validators agree on blocks. Votes move off the chain, finality is designed to drop from seconds to around 150 milliseconds, and a flat 0.8 SOL per-epoch fee replaces per-vote costs. Nothing changes in how stake earns rewards. Galaxy has run Alpenglow on the community test cluster since June 2026, through six re-geneses and the first successful migration, and our validators are ready.Galaxy has operated a validator on Solana's Alpenglow test cluster since June 2026, through six re-geneses (each wiped the chain and restarted it from a fresh genesis block), a migration that failed network-wide, and a rollback. This is what that taught us.Alpenglow is the largest change to Solana's core protocol since the network launched. Designed by Anza, Solana's core development team, it replaces the way validators vote on and finalize blocks, and it is scheduled to activate on mainnet on Wednesday, October 21, at the start of epoch 1064.
How Galaxy Took PartA consensus rewrite cannot be validated on paper. It has to be started, broken, restarted and broken again. That is what Solana's Alpenglow community cluster exists for.It launched in early May 2026 with around 50 independent operators and has since grown to roughly 100 validators. Everyone taking part is a volunteer, running their own hardware across different datacenters and time zones, which surfaces problems that no controlled environment produces.Along the way, we rehearsed failovers between machines in both directions under Alpenglow's stricter rules on double voting.

Figure 1. Galaxy's validator on the Alpenglow community cluster, from joining on June 18, 2026, through six re-geneses, the first successful migration and the first rollback.
What ChangesSince launch, Solana has used TowerBFT, where validators vote by submitting transactions to the chain itself. Vote transactions account for roughly three quarters of everything the network processes and before the recent slot-time reductions, a block took about 12.8 seconds to reach full finality, about 6 seconds at today's 200ms slots. Alpenglow changes both, with a finality target of around 150 milliseconds.Votes leave the chain. Validators exchange votes directly with each other rather than submitting them as transactions. The votes are signed with BLS, so many signatures aggregate into one compact certificate proving that enough stake voted, and that certificate goes into the next block in place of hundreds of individual vote transactions. If 80% of stake votes to notarize a block, it finalizes in a single round; if participation is lower, a second round finalizes it once a 60% notarization certificate and a separate 60% finalization certificate both exist. Both paths run concurrently, and whichever completes first decides.Proof of History retires once the migration completes, because votes now arrive in a single network hop and the chain no longer needs a shared cryptographic clock.A flat fee replaces per-vote fees. Each validator burns a Validator Admission Ticket from its vote account every epoch. SIMD-0357 sets it at the commonly quoted 1.6 SOL, a figure specified against the original 400ms slot and 48-hour epoch. Because the charge scales with slot time, it works out to roughly 0.8 SOL per day at every step, and now that mainnet has reached 200ms, the ticket at activation will be 0.8 SOL per epoch against an epoch of about 24 hours.The fault model changes. Alpenglow is built for what its designers call “20 plus 20”: fewer than 20% of stake actively misbehaving, plus a further 20% simply crashed or offline.TowerBFTAlpenglowByzantine stake tolerated (safety)up to 33%up to 20%Offline stake tolerated on top (liveness)none; the chain can stall above 33% unresponsivea further 20%, so 40% combinedThe total budget rises from 33% to 40%, but the share that may be actively hostile falls from 33% to 20%. That is the tradeoff: less stake is needed to threaten safety, in exchange for tolerating more stake going offline. The designers accepted it because Solana's outages have come from bugs, congestion and correlated crashes rather than coordinated attacks.
Is Voting Cheaper?It helps to separate Alpenglow from the slot-time cuts that finished on October 9. Faster blocks and shorter epochs came from those; Alpenglow brings faster finality, votes off the chain and the flat admission ticket.For the vote itself, the answer is yes. Under TowerBFT, a validator pays a fee on every vote, once per slot, so the slot-time cuts pushed that bill up: about 1 SOL a day at 400ms and about 2 SOL a day at 200ms. The admission ticket replaces it with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch, roughly 0.8 SOL a day, which is less than half of what validators pay to vote today. Anyone reading the rising vote costs of the last two months as an Alpenglow effect has it the wrong way around: the slot-time cuts raised the cost, and Alpenglow brings it back down.

Figure 2. What a validator pays per day to vote at each slot-time step, against the flat admission ticket that replaces it. Each step is labeled with the date and epoch it took effect on mainnet.The saving is not the whole picture. Half of every vote fee went to the leader of the block that included it, so validators that produce many blocks also collected vote fees, and that income goes away along with vote transactions. The net effect for any one validator depends on how many blocks it produces. And this upgrade is about the cost of voting; the larger costs of running a validator, such as hardware, bandwidth and hosting, are a separate matter.SIMD-0326 does not change how vote rewards are earned. What changes is the accounting: vote credits are now derived from BLS certificates rather than from vote transactions on chain, and on the cost side the admission ticket replaces per-vote fees and is charged to the vote account.
What It Means in PracticeFor anyone building on or settling through Solana, the change that matters is not the headline number but how quickly a transaction becomes safe to rely on. Applications that waited seconds for finality can treat a transaction as final in a fraction of that. For stakers, nothing changes in how stake earns rewards. For validator operators, the cost of voting moves to the vote account.Moving votes off the chain also returns a large share of block space to user activity, and the flat admission ticket gives validators a predictable cost in place of a fee that scaled with how often they voted. A vote account that cannot cover the ticket at an epoch boundary is excluded from consensus for that entire epoch, so the funding operators used to keep in their identity accounts will now belong in the vote account.At Galaxy, an automated top-up service refills each vote account well before it approaches the admission threshold, and balances are continuously alerted on.
The Migration Itself Runs on AgaveValidators have been asked to run an Agave-based client through the migration. Operators on Firedancer can fail over to Agave beforehand and return afterwards, since Firedancer's 26.10 release supports Alpenglow. Frankendancer will not be supported once Alpenglow is active. Galaxy's validators will run Agave through the migration and return to Firedancer once it completes.
What Comes NextAlpenglow is arriving in phases:Phase 1: Votor, the voting change described here.Phase 2: A fast leader handover, letting the next leader start building optimistically rather than waiting for the previous window's decision.Phase 3: Rotor, which flattens block propagation into fewer hops.Slashing for validators that vote twice for conflicting blocks is well defined but deliberately not enabled in the first iteration.Galaxy is one of the largest Solana validator infrastructure operators globally and has tested Alpenglow on the community cluster since June 2026. Our staking and infrastructure solutions give institutions secure, high-performance access to Solana. Get in touch here .

Energy companies use sensors and AI to anticipate equipment failure. Can the same predictive approach protect the people operating that equipment, without turning safety systems into a new form of workplace surveillance? As AI moves from screens into robots, control rooms and industrial sites, that question is becoming practical, not theoretical.
Host Ed Crooks is joined by Olivier Oullier, a neuroscientist, investor and AI entrepreneur whose work focuses on how people and machines interact. Olivier argues that AI can improve operator safety and productivity at once through neuroadaptive systems that use signals such as brainwaves, facial expression, eye movement and voice to detect fatigue, stress, distraction or cognitive overload.
In energy operations, those systems could adapt control-room dashboards to foreground the information that matters, or help collaborative robots respond when an operator is tired or distracted. Olivier says pilots are already underway in energy operations in Mexico, Australia and the UAE. Drawing on lessons from surgery and transport, he describes this as an extension of predictive maintenance: moving from monitoring equipment to anticipating human needs, or what he calls predictive care.
That promise rests on a sensitive trade-off. Continuous physiological monitoring could support safer work, but it also raises concerns about consent, autonomy and employee surveillance. Olivier says programs should be voluntary, transparent and compliant with regulation; the discussion tests what responsible deployment needs to look like and whether better outcomes can justify collecting such intimate data.
The conversation also ranges from the risks of poorly supervised AI agents and the skills needed to use AI well to the next phase of physical AI. Olivier points to world models, which aim to help robots understand and act in physical environments, while cautioning against precise long-range predictions about jobs. For energy companies, the near-term challenge is to deploy systems that improve safety and performance without losing sight of the people they are meant to serve.

articles.title: The role of research in Prudential Regulation − speech by David Bailey
articles.text:
The role of research in Prudential Regulation − speech by David Bailey

Given at IFABS 2026 London

Published on
15 July 2026

David Bailey sets out why research is central to prudential policymaking and how it informs the PRA’s approach to competitiveness and growth. He emphasises that the relationship between regulation, competitiveness and growth is complex, and argues that continued collaboration between policymakers and researchers is essential to deepen understanding, strengthen the evidence base, and refine the PRA’s approach over time.

Speech
Introduction
Good morning and thank you for the invitation to speak today. It is a pleasure to join the IFABS conference and to contribute to the discussion.
This year’s conference is titled Financial Regulation, Innovation, and Growth: Building the Foundations for a Resilient Future. It is a title that resonates strongly with our work at the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA). Our role is to provide the core foundations of a trusted, efficient and proportionate regulatory framework that keeps the financial system resilient while enabling innovation and growth to flourish.
I am therefore delighted to be here among researchers, policymakers, and practitioners to explore how regulation and innovation can together support medium to long-term productivity and sustainable growth, both in the financial sector and in the wider economy. In that context, I want to use this speech to set out how research sits at the heart of our policymaking, and in particular how it shapes our approach to competitiveness and growth.
When I refer to research, I mean work that brings academic rigour to policy questions – so more than just evidence for the decision in front of us, but analysis that can contribute to the wider debate on how regulation affects firms, markets and the economy. And let me be clear at the outset about the purpose of what I will say today. This is not a presentation of new policy developments, nor does it provide definitive answers on the links between financial regulation and growth. Instead, it attempts to explain how rigorous research – as conducted by our researchers, often in collaboration with external academics – helps us make better informed and grounded policy decisions in a way that is consistent with our statutory objectives.
In my view, there are at least two reasons why policymakers should be deeply interested in research. First, research helps to shed light on and often quantify the mechanisms through which policy operates, providing a more structured understanding of cause and effect and helping policymakers to identify and assess the trade-offs inherent in different policy designs. This in turn helps us set policy priorities effectively.
Research also informs our assessment of risks, shapes our understanding of how firms are likely to respond to policy, and underpins some of our cost-benefit analysis. Earlier this year, we published our macroeconomic CBA methodology for banks, which is underpinned by our research, and we are now developing an equivalent framework for the insurance sector.
Then, post-implementation, research can help us to evaluate whether some of our policies have delivered the intended outcomes.footnote [1] It allows us to test our assumptions, to identify unintended consequences, and to adjust our approach over time, ensuring in this way that our rules remain proportionate, effective and aligned with our objectives.
We have set out our approach to reviewing PRA Rules publiclyfootnote [2] and research is an important input into that process. It helps build the evidence base that allows us to assess what is working well, and where change may be needed.
The second reason, and equally importantly, as Catherine Mann mentioned in a recent speech, “good research lends credibility to the institution”. And for a central bank and a regulator, credibility underpins the effectiveness of its policies and anchors its legitimacy.
Against that backdrop, I want to frame the rest of this speech around how we use research to advance all of our objectives, but in particular our secondary competitiveness and growth objective (SCGO) as that is core to the theme of this conference. I will begin by briefly recalling the framework we have put in place to understand the impacts that as a prudential regulator we can have on competitiveness and growth, before turning to three specific areas where research has played a key role.
A reminder of the SCGO framework
The relationship between regulation, competitiveness and growth is complex. There is no single measure of competitiveness, and no simple mapping from regulatory choices to economic outcomes, although some researchers have begun to explore this complex relationshipfootnote [3].
Therefore, to guide our approach to advancing the SCGO, we have developed a framework that sets out how regulation can facilitate competitiveness and growth. It is built on three foundations:

Maintaining trust in the UK financial system and its resilience so that firms, domestic or international, have the confidence to invest and build their businesses;
Operating efficiently, so that regulatory requirements and processes are timely, proportionate and cost-effective for firms to engage with; and
Being responsive to new developments, and in doing so supporting the safe adoption of innovation across the financial services sector directly, and the provision of new and more dynamic services to the customers it supports.

In turn, these foundations support growth and competitiveness by improving the efficient allocation of capital, attracting financial sector business to the UK, and supporting the ability of UK firms to sell their services abroad. These are all crucial channels through which our work supports the UK’s role as a major global financial centre.
Research has been central to how we calibrate policies across each of these foundations and has provided useful tools to help us navigate the complexities inherent in policy making. I will take them in turn.
Foundation one: Maintaining trust in the UK financial system
Trust is our starting point.
We are required to pursue our secondary objective – facilitating competitiveness and growth – subject to, and not at the expense of, advancing our primary objective of safety and soundness.
This is not simply a legal formulation. It reflects an economic reality. A financial system that is not resilient will not support long-term economic growth. Research suggests that the average net present value cost of a financial crisis, even if well managed, is around 43% of GDP.footnote [4] Trust in the regulatory framework is therefore a precondition for supporting sustainable growth and attracting investment and businesses in the UK.
For that reason, maintaining trust is at the core of our prudential framework and our first foundation of the SCGO. And trust, among other things, is underpinned by policymaking that is grounded in evidence, as well as expert judgement.
One clear example of this is the work that informed the Financial Policy Committee’s decision to update its benchmark for capital requirements in December 2025. As part of a broader body of evidence and analysis, Bank staff reviewed over 70 academic studies to identify the optimal level of capital requirements that maximises long-term growth. This built on, and updated, the earlier Brooke et al. (2015) analysis. The updated benchmark, which the FPC reaffirmed last week, represents its judgement as to the sector‑wide capital requirements that will best support long‑term UK growth as measured through GDP. It does this by balancing the benefits of capital in reducing the risks of financial crises and the costs of capital in making it more expensive for banks to lend and support their customers’ needs. Simply put, too little capital increases the risk of a financial crisis to an unacceptable level, and too much capital can be detrimental by constraining the supply of financial services to households and businesses.
Because the various academic studies used different approaches and assumptions, their results were not directly comparable. So our colleagues recalibrated them onto a consistent basis to produce a robust estimate. Further details are set out in the December Financial Stability Report.
Building on this, the FPC published a further update last week, setting out how we intend to make adjustments to the capital framework - including through targeted reforms to the leverage ratio framework and measures to improve buffer usability.
To inform the latter, bank researchers have analysed the presence of capital buffer usability frictions, as well as the benefits of releasability, during the Covid-19 shock. They found that releasing buffers can help mitigate buffer usability frictions and procyclical deleveraging.footnote [5] These are good examples of how research informs policy development. But sometimes, for new, innovative and fast-moving market developments, we do not have ready-made research to draw from, and we need to rely on other sources of evidence to inform policymaking, such as supervisory information, third-party analysis and our own modelling.
This was the case with our recent proposals on the use of Funded Reinsurance, which represents another key initiative that we are taking forward to maintain trust in the financial system. We expect benefits from these proposals in the form of improved sector resilience and enhanced UK financial stability (with evidence gathered from stress-tests) and costs to insurers and, indirectly, through corporates (modelled using information provided by insurers).
Research was therefore an important input, alongside other sources, for the analysis of the costs and benefits of the proposals. We would welcome research contributions in this area.
Foundation Two: Operating efficiently and ensuring proportionality
The second foundation is efficiency and proportionality.
Regulation inevitably imposes costs on firms. Those costs are justified where they help us advance our objectives – the benefits outweigh the costs if you like. But they can also affect competitiveness and the ability of firms to innovate. Therefore, we want to ensure that our regulation is well‑targeted and proportionate, avoiding costs for firms where they do not add sufficient prudential value.
Research is central to achieving this. It helps us to distinguish between measures that are necessary to achieve prudential outcomes, and those that may impose unnecessary or unintended constraints.
One example often cited is the work that informed the reforms to remuneration rules, and in particular removal of the so-called ‘bonus cap’, which was a policy we inherited from the EU. It capped the ratio of variable to fixed pay for bank managers.
Our research, alongside others, found that total compensation growth did not slow down following the reform. Instead, compensation structures adjusted, with remuneration packages shifting towards higher fixed pay and lower variable pay.footnote [6]
This adjustment was an unintended consequence of the policy, as it weakened the link between managerial pay and risk-taking incentives. We therefore removed the cap when we were able to.
The reforms were informed by a combination of academic expertise in causal inference and policy experience in remuneration regulation, including a detailed understanding of the evolution of remuneration rules over time, as well as access to unique firm-level regulatory data.
Foundation Three: Responsiveness and enabling safe innovation
The third foundation to the SCGO is responsiveness, and in particular enabling safe innovation.
This is an area where it is important to be candid. We do not have all the answers for any of the channels I have been discussing, but that is especially true for this one. The relationship between regulation and innovation is complex and, by definition, innovation involves the provision of new products and services on which limited data and evidence may be available. What we can do, however, is to identify the key mechanisms through which regulation affects innovation, and incentivise researchers to explore them.
I would highlight three such mechanisms.footnote [7]
The first is uncertainty. Regulation can reduce uncertainty about the future policy and risk environment. When firms have greater clarity about the rules of the game, they are better able to invest, to plan and to innovate. Conversely, uncertainty – whether about policy direction or supervisory expectations – can act as a barrier to innovation.
We have seen this pattern play out repeatedly over time. In the 19th century, banks had no clear understanding of when, or how, the Bank of England would intervene in a crisis. That uncertainty mattered. As Bagehot put it, it made banks “timid and cautious”, constraining lending and slowing financial development.footnote [8] His 1873 articulation of the lender of last resort principles changed that by establishing a more predictable framework. With greater certainty came greater confidence, and with that a more innovative and effective financial system.
And we see it again in more recent history. The slowdown in financial innovation following the global financial crisis is well documented. Heightened uncertainty dampened long-term investment, in turn weakening R&D funding and innovation.footnote [9]
The second is the degree of prescription. Outcome‑based approaches, which focus on the description of the world once risks have been managed rather than the precise means of managing them, tend to leave more room for firms to innovate. Highly prescriptive rules, by contrast, can narrow the set of possible solutions and may crowd out innovation. The challenge is to strike the right balance between clarity and flexibility. So, referring back to my earlier example, whilst greater certainty might have worked in the 19th century, it might not always be the answer in the 21st.
Take AI as an example. Our approach to date has been open, flexible and technology‑agnostic, grounded in extensive engagement with industry and other stakeholders. We already have established frameworks in areas such as model risk management, operational resilience and third-party outsourcing, and our view is that these can, in large part, be applied to AI just as they are to other technologies and processes. On that basis, we have not so far concluded that there is a need for detailed, AI-specific rules as the technology – and its use by banks and insurers – continues to evolve. But we continue monitoring developments closely, especially given rapid developments over the course of this year in the capabilities of Frontier AI models.
The third mechanism is risk measurement. Innovation often follows when previously hard‑to‑measure risks become quantifiable and integrated into decision‑making frameworks. Tools such as stress testing and regulation on modelling risk‑sensitive capital requirements can play a role here. By bringing risks into the realm of measurement and management, they can facilitate new products and new business models.
Conclusions
Let me conclude.
The central message of this speech is that rigorous research matters for the PRA. It is integral to how we make policy and how we evaluate outcomes. It helps us to make choices that are credible, transparent and grounded in evidence.
In the context of our SCGO, research is particularly important. Competitiveness and growth are complex, multifaceted concepts. They evolve over time and they are influenced by a wide range of factors beyond regulation. Research provides the tools we need to navigate that complexity.
The examples I have discussed today illustrate how research informs our approach in practice. It supports the calibration of policy, the assessment of trade‑offs, and the evaluation of outcomes.
But there is much more to learn. The relationship between regulation, competitiveness and growth is not fully understood. Particularly through innovation. Continued collaboration between policymakers and researchers will be essential if we are to deepen our understanding, to challenge our assumptions, and to refine our approach over time.
To incentivise collaboration, we publish our priority research questions as part of the PRA Business plan. These include the barriers to entry in banking and insurance, the link between competition and efficient capital allocation, measuring the financial sector’s contribution to GDP, and the impact of prudential regulation on the UK’s position as a global financial centre. Typically, collaborative research projects start organically through conversations between our researchers and external academics, often at conferences and workshops, like this one.footnote [10] So I hope the conference this week won’t be an exception.
For our part, we remain committed to embedding research at the heart of our work. We will continue to draw on the best available evidence, to engage with the academic community, and to contribute to the development of new insights.
In doing so, we aim to support a financial system that is resilient, efficient and dynamic, and a regulatory framework that maintains trust, is proportionate and enables innovation, contributing to the long‑term growth of the UK economy.
Thank you.
I would like to thank Elisabetta Vitello, Benjamin Guin, Mahmoud Fatouh for their assistance in preparing these remarks, and to Walter Beckert, Nat Benjamin, Phil Evans, Felipe Netto, Tamarah Shakir, Alan Sheppard, Vicky White for valuable comments.

There is broader academic literature showing the impact of regulation on innovation. In particular:
Porter & van der Linde (1995) argue that well-designed regulation can stimulate innovation by encouraging firms to identify inefficiencies and develop new products, processes and technologies.
Acemoglu et al. (2012) show how policy can redirect the direction of innovation by changing incentives and making particular technologies or activities more attractive.
Aghion, Bergeaud & Van Reenen (2023) provide an opposing view – they show that some forms of regulation can also reduce innovation, highlighting the importance of regulatory design and incentives.

Charts of the Week: VC Vital Signs

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com.Pre-seed deals’ share of crypto and blockchain venture capital investments grew to 25% in Q3 2026, while later-stage investments slipped to 24% of completed transactions. We track pre-seed transactions’ share to gauge entrepreneurial behavior and investor risk appetite. Later-stage deals’ share of the total remained elevated compared to the historical norm, reflecting the market's growing maturity.

Meanwhile, VC-backed crypto company valuations (bars, left-hand vertical axis in the chart below) rebounded to a new all-time high of roughly $90m in Q3 2026, as valuations across the broader VC complex outside of crypto also rose to a new high. In Q3 2026, the median crypto deal size (feverline, right-hand axis) fell sharply from Q2’s all-time high of $5m to roughly $3m.
