Corporate Law and Transformation

Group reorganizations and transformations come in many forms, domestic or cross-border, transaction-driven or strategic. EY Corporate Law and Transformation teams help businesses design and provide legally robust, commercially efficient structures, combining corporate law knowledge with multidisciplinary delivery to achieve value-added and integrated transformation outcomes.

Related topics

Law

Tax

Tax compliance

The team

Craig Stevenson

EY Global Corporate Law and Transformation Leader

What EY can do for you
Corporate transformations and reorganizations can present huge opportunities for groups with common objectives, including the need for an optimal pre-deal transaction perimeter, a value-additive post-deal integration, a tax-informed reorganization, an operating model redesign to align with a new business strategy, group-wide legal entity rationalizations to cut cost, simplify structures and improve governance and so on.
Some of the triggers for transformation can involve:
Complex and fragmented group structures that are difficult to manage and tough to align with business strategyTransaction-driven change requiring pre-deal business separation or post-deal integration, often involving mixed business units in cross-border structures and tight timelinesEvolving regulatory, legal and tax expectations across multiple jurisdictions driving changes to group structuresInefficient group structures with redundant or duplicative entities, often the legacy of deal activityThe need to simplify operating and legal entity models ahead of significant events such as ERP implementation or new go-to-market strategies
EY Corporate Law and Transformation teams routinely help organizations navigate this often-complex environment by providing comprehensive, integrated support across the overall transformation lifecycle. EY professionals and teams provide corporate law offerings alongside tax, accounting and other capabilities under one coordinated approach, across the world. Our core services span the overall range of corporate law and transformation needs, supporting robust, practical, broader execution across jurisdictions in areas including:
Group reorganizationsPre-deal carve-outsPost-deal integrationLegal entity rationalizationOperating model redesign and corporate governanceCross-border mergersProject management supportCompany law advisory
Supporting every stage of your transformation journey
Through all these services, our teams provide overall legal support throughout the transformation lifecycle in all relevant jurisdictions, working closely alongside all other EY workstreams to cater to the multidisciplinary services these projects commonly demand. Our corporate law and transformation services help provide:
Input into feasibility assessments, design of the target structure, and full drafting and implementation supportLocal law support delivered by one of the largest global legal networksExperienced project management teams who routinely lead and coordinate some of the most complex, highest-value reorganizations for some of the largest groups in the worldClose collaboration with other EY teams helping identify and resolve issues early and efficiently, lowering project risk and adding valueRobust execution of complex transformations by corporate lawyers who routinely undertake such projects, supported by consistent, coordinated delivery across countries and with deliverables and advice aligned with your other EY engagement teams
Why EY
Our Corporate Law and Transformation lawyers regularly advise on complex, high-value, multinational carve-out transactions and are consistently recognized by leading legal directories, with many practitioners receiving individual market accolades. We combine deep legal experience with a multidisciplinary approach, working closely with EY professionals across tax, accounting, strategy and valuation to help deliver transaction objectives. Our teams are supported by technology-enabled solutions that help reduce risk, streamline processes and accelerate execution, allowing us to focus on the issues that matter most and deliver greater value.
With more than 3,000 lawyers and legal professionals across 75+ countries, supported by legal managed service delivery centers, we bring a coordinated global approach to international transformations. We also adapt our support to each client’s needs, from strategic advice through to the design, coordination and implementation of complex cross-border projects.

articles.title: One Health through the lens of today’s investment megatrends - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
By Alex Bernhardt, Global Head of Sustainability Research; Rachel Crossley, Head of Stewardship, Europe; and Robert-Alexandre Poujade, Head of Nature

The One Health concept recognises that human health is inextricably linked to the health of animals and the environment, moving beyond a narrow medical perspective to a systemic view of health-related value and risk

Assessing One Health through the lens of four megatrends – geopolitics, innovation, demographics, and the environment – helps to identify impacts on worker productivity, supply chain reliability, and market growth

For long-term investors, health determinants are viewed as material factors that can influence corporate earnings, sovereign credit, and labour markets, helping to identify risks that may currently be underappreciated by the market

The forces shaping human health outcomes are far broader than hospitals, pharmaceuticals and medical devices. Human health is dependent upon animal health and the health of the environment. Together the health of these three systems are inextricably intertwined, creating the One Health concept (Exhibit 1).

For long-term investors, these health determinants are not peripheral; they shape and are shaped by productivity, labour participation, the resilience of communities and economies and other social systems.

While the pathways for One Health impacts are not always linear or clear, they can nevertheless be material to economic and financial outcomes for investors. Indeed, understanding how corporate investment can drive negative or create positive health outcomes for its stakeholders – employees, customers, communities, plants and animals – will be increasingly important in an increasingly interconnected world.

The One Health theme, grounded in preceding work by the World Health Organization and other supranationals, therefore gives us a useful frame for moving from a narrow sector view of health to a more systemic view of health-related value creation and risk.

It recognises that a workforce’s health can affect operating performance; that the health of consumers can influence the growth of markets; and that the health of ecosystems can determine the reliability of supply chains; the quality of natural inputs and the exposure of communities to disease.

Companies do not operate outside these systems. They depend on them and affect them.

This does not mean treating every social or environmental issue as a health issue. A disciplined One Health approach should improve, not dilute, investment analysis. The challenge is to identify where health determinants are financially material for a sector, issuer, or asset and through which transmission channels. To support related analysis BNPP AM’s megatrends provide a useful framework:

Geopolitics: Global health outcomes depend on food security, access to medicines, resilient supply chains and international cooperation on health and environmental risks. Geopolitical fragmentation can increase vulnerabilities while cooperation can improve system resilience

Environment: Human, animal and ecosystem health are deeply interconnected. Environmental pressures such as pollution, climate change, biodiversity loss and water stress affect public health, productivity and economic stability

Demographics: Ageing populations, urbanisation and changing disease patterns are reshaping demand for healthcare, nutrition, housing and care services. Understanding demographic trends is essential to improving long-term health and economic resilience.

Innovation: Breakthroughs in biotechnology, diagnostics, precision agriculture, data analytics and preventative care can improve health outcomes across interconnected human, animal and environmental systems. Innovation expands the range of investable health solutions

Geopolitics: Health security, resilience and strategic dependence

Access to healthcare and other social determinants of health – notably housing, food and water – is increasingly shaped by geopolitics. At the multinational level, restrictive trade policy, increased conflict, and decreased cooperation all serve to heighten the risk of future pandemics, worsening climate-related health impacts, and medicine or food shortages.

At the national level, shifts in the political landscape can result in declining quality of public services which can have cross-border effects. For instance, softening vaccine requirements could result in greater incidence of preventable disease.

Moreover, loss of public benefits like food or housing assistance can increase the public burden of disease which can have many knock-on effects for communities beyond the added frictional costs of increased emergency health treatments.

A One Health perspective shows that company resilience is dependent to a significant degree upon public institutions. This creates risks for companies dependent on vulnerable global supply chains, low-cost labour, or weakened public systems, but it also creates opportunities in healthcare security, diagnostics, and other solutions that support preparedness without simply shifting costs to consumers or governments.

Innovation: new solutions, new dependencies and new questions of access

Innovation is central to One Health because it changes what can be prevented, detected, treated and measured. Advances in medicines, environmental monitoring and AI-enabled discovery can improve health outcomes and strengthen resilience.

They can also help investors identify companies whose products and services reduce preventable harm while addressing structural demand. Healthcare innovation remains important, but the investable universe is broader than healthcare alone. It includes technologies and business models that improve the health of people, animals and ecosystems together.

At the same time, innovation can create new dependencies and unintended consequences. Digital health tools may improve access but raise questions about privacy, exclusion and quality of care.

Artificial intelligence can accelerate drug discovery, diagnostics and environmental monitoring, but it can also increase energy and water demand and concentrate benefits among firms with data, compute and distribution advantages.

Agricultural technology can reduce chemical and antibiotic use, but it can also deepen dependence on proprietary inputs. The investment question is therefore not whether innovation is positive in general, but whether the business model, governance, affordability, lifecycle impacts and measurable outcomes support durable value creation.

A One Health lens helps distinguish innovation that genuinely improves resilience from innovation that merely increases efficiency while shifting health or environmental costs elsewhere.

Demographics: Demand, vulnerability and health’s social determinants

Demographics are reshaping One Health considerations with different trends driving different outcomes. Ageing populations, particularly in developed markets, create significant risks if the transition is unmanaged.

But well managed, it can create huge opportunities for investments in the care economy including long-term care, mobility solutions and age-friendly housing.1

Urbanisation, particularly pronounced in emerging markets, increases the importance of sanitation, air quality, housing quality, green space, transport design and heat resilience.

Migration and regional demographic divergence influence labour availability, fiscal capacity and the vulnerability of communities to public health and climate shocks. Labour market participation and socioeconomic inequality can create political risk and shift aggregate demand patterns.

Environment: Ecosystems as health infrastructure

Environment is perhaps the most intuitive One Health lens because air quality and ecosystem health are a foundation for human and animal health. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and water availability all influence exposure to disease, heat stress and unsafe living conditions.

An estimated nine million premature deaths each year are caused by pollution and 90% of the global population is exposed to ambient concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) above the WHO annual air quality guideline.2 Additionally, over 60% of emerging infectious diseases originate in animals.3

Perhaps one of the most trenchant examples of the human health and animal health connection is antimicrobial resistance. It arises when bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites evolve to resist the medications that once effectively treated infections.

And its rise in humans can largely be traced to the overuse of antibiotics in livestock. Understanding the societal ramifications of consumer preferences for meat and business preferences for efficient solutions to problems (in this case, animals often living in close-quarters getting sick) is supported by a One Health perspective.

Why investors should care

Within BNPP AM’s Global Sustainability Strategy, One Health therefore sits alongside Transition and Sustainable AI as part of our forward-looking research agenda. One Health matters for investors because it connects health outcomes to the systems that sustain long-term economic value.

It broadens the investment lens from healthcare spending to the determinants of health that for example shape worker productivity/availability and supply-chain reliability. It also helps identify risks that markets may underprice because they sit between sectors, time horizons or asset classes.

Antimicrobial resistance, unsafe food systems, pollution exposure, heat stress, biodiversity loss, weak health access and social isolation may each appear narrow at first, but together they can affect corporate earnings, sovereign credit, labour markets and long-term market performance.

The investor implications are practical. First, One Health supports better risk identification by linking health determinants to financially material transmission channels such as input costs, workforce productivity and tail risks.

Second, it supports opportunity identification by clarifying where durable demand may emerge for prevention-oriented healthcare, affordable housing, climate adaptation and nature-based solutions.

And third, it supports stewardship by helping investors ask whether companies are reducing preventable harm, strengthening resilience and measuring outcomes, rather than relying on broad claims.

Measurement will be central. One Health is powerful because it captures interdependence, but that also makes it vulnerable to over-claiming. Investors need fit-for-purpose indicators that distinguish inputs, outputs and outcomes; recognise time horizons; and avoid overstating causality. We will continue our work on this over the years to come.

[1] https://www3.weforum.org/docs/WEF_The_Future_of_the_Care_Economy_2024.pdf

[2] Global Environment Outlook 7 | UNEP – UN Environment Programme

[3] Editorial: Zoonotic diseases originating from wildlife: Emergence/re-emergence, evolution, prevalence, pathogenesis, prevention, and treatment – PMC

articles.title: The State of Crypto Leverage – Q4 2025: Surviving a Stress Test
articles.text:
Insights / Research / The State of Crypto Leverage – Q4 2025: Surviving a Stress Test 

Research • March 06, 2026 • 20 mins
The State of Crypto Leverage – Q4 2025: Surviving a Stress Test 
Onchain lending slid with market prices and yields, but CeFi lenders held strong in the wake of a historic liquidation event.

Zack Pokorny
Research Associate

Share on Twitter

Share on Facebook

Share on Linkedin

Email

Topics

Bitcoin

Cryptocurrency

DeFi

Ethereum

Lending

Introduction  Crypto-collateralized lending dropped 9.81% in Q4 2025 from the all-time high set the previous quarter, a decline entirely due to a drawdown in onchain borrows. Onchain borrow activity, and borrow activity generally, is reflexive to prices and market activity. However, the introduction of looping strategies bound to market yields (e.g. funding rates) has brought onchain a new cohort of borrow activity that is sensitive to downturns in price, trading activity, and yield compression. Onchain borrows have continued to decline through the first quarter of 2026, falling 40% from the daily all-time high of $47.12 billion on Sept. 19, 2025. The bigger story in Q4 is the divergence between onchain reflexivity and offchain resilience. This is something we noted could happen in a market downturn on the Galaxy Brains podcast and in an interview with Market Watch. Despite the largest onchain liquidation event in history happening in October, there are few visible signs of stress in centralized finance (CeFi) loanbooks across the fourth quarter. That outcome is consistent with the structural shift we highlighted in our report on Q3 2025, when outstanding loan balances pushed to new highs: borrowed-funds use cases have generally de-risked, un(der)collateralized credit and rehypothecated collateral have been largely self-regulated out of common practice (and was effectively never an option onchain), and collateral asset quality has improved, leaving lenders and borrowers better positioned to absorb volatility without forced deleveraging or loss of funds. Coinbase’s quarterly filings are a testament to this. Despite negative price action through the quarter and the largest liquidation event in crypto history, Coinbase reported that “no cumulative realized gains or losses occurred during the period presented as no Crypto assets held as collateral were sold or rehypothecated." At the same time, onchain borrowing remains more rate-, yield-, and price-sensitive, particularly among the looping cohort tied to funding rates and market yields. As price, market activity, and yields compress, these positions can become uneconomical quickly, leading to sharper drawdowns in onchain borrows even when offchain loanbooks appear stable. The one caveat here is timing. The lack of observable CeFi stress in Q4 does not preclude pressure emerging with a lag, and a sustained price drawdown and the dust from Oct. 10 settling in Q1 could still translate into slower deterioration in CeFi credit metrics and risk appetite in subsequent quarters. Nonetheless, a major player like Coinbase growing its book and improving its collateralization ratio is a positive signal. Even in a downside scenario where CeFi credit metrics deteriorate with a lag, a gradual unwinding of loan books is a fundamentally different risk profile than what played out in 2022, when opaque, undercollateralized lending by the likes of Genesis, BlockFi, and Celsius led to overnight insolvencies, permanent loss of customer funds, and cascading contagion. In the background, the crypto futures market saw a significant drawdown in open interest and is showing few signs of recovery. After the largest liquidation event in perps market history taking place on Oct. 10, futures open interest has collapsed below $100 billion for the first time since April 2025 and is 33% lower than it was on the day President Trump was inaugurated for his second term. Still, perps are proving to be a valuable product. Hyperliquid’s HIP-3 has brought equity, commodity, and forex perps onchain, allowing users to trade these markets 24/7. These products have gained meaningful mindshare and adoption amid the Q4 2025/Q1 2026 geopolitical and market volatility, offering onchain users a way to express macro views without relying on traditional exchange hours or intermediaries. Traditional markets have proven (yet again) that they can't efficiently price events that break on weekends or overnight, while onchain perps can. Recent events have made that structural advantage tangible. In a world where information flows endlessly at the speed of light, we should have markets that never close. Onchain perps make this possible. As crypto lending and leverage markets mature and add step function improvements to traditional markets, their evolution is increasingly likely to mirror traditional credit infrastructure: tranched debt, fixed-rate loans, termed facilities, and more structured risk segmentation. Institutional entrants will accelerate this shift, bringing demand profiles distinct from the more cyclical and price-reflexive strategies that historically dominated onchain activity. On the derivatives side, synthetic perps are demonstrating the value of always-on markets, but they're ultimately limited by the traditional rails they reference. As onchain adoption deepens, the pressure on legacy markets to extend trading hours and modernize infrastructure will become harder to ignore. The result is a market that could look fundamentally different in the coming quarters, one that is less reflexive to crypto-native cycles and more integrated with broader capital markets. Taking this possibility into consideration, the next chapter of onchain-native leverage is being written now even as apathy and emotional despair plague the crypto community.
Key Takeaways  All told, crypto-collateralized lending contracted by $7.55 billion (-9.81%) in Q4 2025 to $69.55 billion. This is 6.79% lower than the Q4 2021 high of $74.62 billion. The dollar-denominated value of outstanding loans on DeFi fell meaningfully in Q4, contracting by $10.66 billion (-24.15%) to $33.5 billion. Galaxy Research is tracking more than $14 billion in debt outstanding used to directly buy or supplement the treasury strategies of digital asset treasury companies (DATs). The debt outstanding stagnated through the fourth quarter. Futures open interest (OI), including perpetual futures (perps), declined 39.09% QoQ from $197.18 billion to $120.11 billion at the end of the quarter. This decline was due, in part, to the largest perps liquidation event ever occurring on Oct. 10, just 10 days into the start of the quarter.
Crypto-Collateralized Lending  The market map below highlights some of the major past and present players in the CeFi and DeFi crypto lending markets. Some of the largest CeFi lenders by loan book size crumbled in 2022 and 2023 as crypto asset prices tanked and liquidity dried up. These lenders are flagged with red caution dots in the map below. Since Galaxy’s last crypto leverage report, we have added one new DeFi app and six new instances of DeFi apps already covered in past reports. We also added one new CeFi lender.   The additional DeFi apps are:    Loopscale on Solana. Miscellaneous Ethereum-based applications found on DeFiLlama The additional CeFi lender is: Milo - Founded in 2019, Milo describes itself as "a licensed digital lending company pioneering the intersection of crypto and real estate finance. Milo created the crypto mortgage category in 2022 and has remained the category leader ever since. The company has raised $24 million from leading venture investors and offers crypto mortgages, allowing borrowers to use their digital assets as collateral to purchase property as well as crypto-backed loans. To date, Milo has originated over $300 million in total loans, including more than $100 million in crypto mortgages, reflecting strong and growing demand for crypto-native financial products.”

CeFi  The table below compares the CeFi crypto lenders in our market analysis. Some of the companies offer multiple services to investors. Coinbase, for example, primarily operates as an exchange but also extends credit to investors through over-the-counter cryptocurrency loans and margin financing. The analysis shows only the size of their crypto-collateralized loan books, however.

As of Dec. 31, Galaxy Research tracked $27.56 billion of open CeFi borrows. This represents quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) growth of 11.66%, or $2.88 billion, and $20.23 billion (+282.37%) growth since the bear market trough of $7.21 billion in Q4 2023. Still, CeFi borrows outstanding are 25.58% below their Q1 2022 all-time high of $37.08 billion. Even so, CeFi loans outstanding grew for the eighth straight quarter in Q4 2025. The fourth quarter saw most non-stablecoin issuer lenders’ books remain flat to slightly down. However, Coinbase posted its largest quarter of loanbook growth by absolute change. Through Q4, Coinbase added $438.69 million in net new loans outstanding, representing +47.89% change.

Tether is the dominant lender in our analysis, commanding a 61.84% share (up 267 basis points from last quarter) of the CeFi lending market. Add in Maple, which entered the top three in the fourth quarter (6.62% market share, up 33 basis points from the third quarter), and Galaxy (6.51% market share, down 78 basis points), and the top three tracked CeFi lenders control 74.98% of the market (down 18 basis points). When comparing market shares, it’s important to note the distinctions between CeFi lenders. Some lenders only offer certain types of loans (e.g., BTC-collateralized only, altcoin-collateralized products, and cash loans that do not include stablecoins), only service certain types of clients (e.g., institutional vs. retail), and only operate in certain jurisdictions. The combination of these factors allows some lenders to scale more easily than others. 

The table below details the sources of Galaxy Research’s data about each CeFi lender and the logic we used to calculate the size of their books. While DeFi and onchain CeFi lending figures are retrievable from onchain data, which is transparent and easily accessible, retrieving CeFi data is tricky. This is due to inconsistencies in how CeFi lenders account for their outstanding loans and how often they make the information public, as well as the general difficulty of obtaining this information.  Note: Galaxy Research has not formally vetted the values supplied by private third-party lenders. 

CeFi and DeFi Lending The dollar-denominated value of outstanding loans on DeFi fell meaningfully in Q4, contracting by $10.66 billion (-24.15%) to $33.5 billion. Combining DeFi apps with CeFi lending venues, there were $61.06 billion of outstanding crypto-collateralized borrows at quarter end. This represents a reduction of $7.79 billion (-11.31%) QoQ, predominantly driven by compression of onchain borrows. On a combined basis, DeFi lending app and CeFi loans outstanding are still above the 2020-2021 cycle high of $58.69 billion. Galaxy Research sees a few contributing factors to the contraction in DeFi lending against the growth in CeFi lending: Looping becoming less economical: As market yields compressed and funding rates normalized after Oct. 10, the spread between borrow costs and yield earned on looped positions narrowed meaningfully. Ethena’s sUSDe (commonly used as collateral for looping strategies and in Pendle PT token collateral) yield fell from the 5%-7% range to 3.5% while USDC and USDT borrow costs sit between 3.75% to 4.15%. This dynamic flipped looping strategies on their heads, incentivizing users to close out their positions. Negative price action: The Oct. 10 liquidation event and subsequent price drawdown mechanically reduced DeFi borrowing in two ways: falling collateral values forced borrowers to repay or be liquidated, and risk appetite for new leveraged positions dried up in the aftermath. Historically low CeFi borrow costs: CeFi proxy rates used in our analysis fell below onchain borrow rates during Q4. This is an uncommon inversion of the typical dynamic where CeFi rates are higher or about equal to those of DeFi. Historically low absolute rates created an opportunistic borrowing window for CeFi counterparties, and the fact that offchain rates were cheaper than onchain only underscored how attractive the environment was for CeFi borrowers. Note: There is potential for double-counting between total CeFi loan book size and DeFi borrows. This is because some CeFi entities rely on DeFi applications to lend to offchain clients. For example, a hypothetical CeFi lender may pledge its idle BTC to borrow USDC onchain, then lend that USDC to a borrower offchain. In this scenario, the CeFi lender’s onchain borrow will be present in the DeFi open borrows and in the lender’s financial statements as an outstanding loan to its client. The lack of disclosures or onchain attribution makes filtering for this dynamic difficult. 

As a result of the quarter-over-quarter decline in outstanding borrows on DeFi lending applications, their relative lead over CeFi lending venues collapsed to Q1 2025 levels. At the end of Q4 2025, DeFi lending app dominance over CeFi lending venues stood at 54.86%, down from 64.24% at the end of Q3 2025.

The third leg of the stool, the crypto-collateralized portions of collateral debt position (CDP) stablecoin supply, increased by $262 million (+3.18%) QoQ. Again, there is potential for double-counting between total CeFi loan book size and CDP stablecoin supply, because some CeFi entities might rely on minting CDP stablecoins with crypto collateral to fund loans to offchain clients. All told, crypto-collateralized lending contracted by $7.55 billion (-9.81%) in Q4 2025 to $69.55 billion. This is 6.79% lower than the Q4 2021 high of $74.62 billion.

At the end of Q3 2025, DeFi lending applications represented 48.17% (-920 basis points from Q3 2025 share) of the crypto collateralized lending market, CeFi venues captured 39.62% (+768 basis points from Q3 2025 share) of the market, and the crypto-collateralized portion of CDP stablecoin supplies held 12.21% (+152 basis points from Q3 2025 share). Combining DeFi lending apps and CDP stablecoins, onchain lending venues held a 60.38% dominance (-768 basis points from Q3 2025 share) over the market.

Additional Views of DeFi Lending   Outstanding borrows on DeFi lending applications have seen material deterioration since reaching an all-time high of $47.12 billion on Sept. 19, 2025. Sitting at $28.17 billion as of February 16, 2026, onchain lending has collapsed by $18.94 billion, or 40.2%. Ethereum has seen a $16.02 billion decline in open loans on the chain since reaching its all-time high of $37.52 billion.

Stablecoins  The weighted average stablecoin borrow rate remained largely flat over the quarter, declining 28 basis points between Oct. 1, 2025 and Dec. 21, 2025. This is in line with our expectation that stablecoin interest rate volatility will remain tame and borrow costs will not exceed 10% through DeFi applications in 2026. This figure is calculated by blending the costs of borrowing from lending protocols and CDP stablecoin mint fees, weighted by outstanding borrows.

The following breaks out the costs of borrowing stablecoins through lending applications and minting CDP stablecoins with crypto collateral. The two rates track each other closely, although CDP stablecoin mint rates are typically less volatile because they are manually set periodically and do not move in lockstep with the market. Both rates have used the Fed Funds Rate as a floor for the last 18-plus months.

Benchmark over-the-counter (OTC) interest rates for USDC decreased 300 points through the quarter, falling from 6.5% to 3.5%. Since then, however, the rate has remained flat. For the first time in nearly two years offchain stablecoin borrow rates trended below that of onchain, presenting a unique opportunity to offchain borrowers. OTC interest rates are often quoted in bands depending on collateral or borrower creditworthiness. The middle band is the market rate while the top and bottom bands mark the range interest rates are quoted between. This is also true for all OTC rates shown in the following sections.

The chart below tracks the same rates as above, but for USDT lending. The onchain rate for USDT has been more in line with the OTC mid-rate than that of USDC.

Bitcoin  The chart below shows the weighted borrow rate for wrapped bitcoin (WBTC) on lending apps across several applications and chains. The cost of borrowing WBTC onchain is often low because wrapped bitcoin tokens are primarily used for collateral in onchain markets and are not in high demand for borrowing. In contrast to stablecoins, the cost of borrowing BTC onchain remains stable, because users borrow and repay it less frequently. The rate to borrow BTC onchain increased from 0.22% at the end of Q3 to 0.44% at the end of Q4.

The historical divergence between onchain and offchain (over-the-counter) borrow rates for BTC persisted throughout the fourth quarter, though offchain BTC borrow rates came down slightly and onchain rates increased slightly. In the OTC market, BTC borrowing demand is driven primarily by two factors: 1) the need to short BTC and 2) the use of BTC as collateral for stablecoin and cash loans. The former is a source of demand not commonly found in onchain lending markets, hence the spread between onchain and over-the-counter BTC borrow costs.  OTC rates for BTC declined 25 basis points over the quarter from 1.25% to 1%.

ETH and StETH  The chart below shows the weighted borrow rate for ETH and stETH (staked ether on the Lido protocol) on lending apps across several applications and chains. The cost to borrow ETH has historically been higher than for stETH because the former is in greater demand. Users repeatedly borrow ETH to fuel looping strategies to gain leveraged exposure to the Ethereum network staking APY – using stETH, the token they receive for staking ETH through Lido, as collateral. As a consequence, the cost of borrowing ETH fluctuates within 50 basis points of the Ethereum network staking APY on average. This strategy becomes uneconomical when the cost to borrow exceeds the staking yield, so it is uncommon for the borrow APR to clear the staking APY for extended periods of time. As with WBTC, the cost of borrowing stETH is often low because the asset is primarily used as collateral and not much else. 

By using liquid staking tokens (LSTs) or liquid restaking tokens (LRTs), both of which earn yield, as collateral, users borrow ETH at low, often negative, net interest rates. This cost efficiency fuels a looping strategy where users repeatedly use LSTs and LRTs as collateral to borrow unstaked ETH, stake it, and then recycle the fresh LSTs and LRTs to borrow even more ETH, thereby amplifying their exposure to the ETH staking APY. This strategy only works so long as the borrow cost for ETH is below the staking APY achieved on the LSTs and LRTs. Most of the time, users have been able to conduct this strategy without a hitch outside of a few notable periods.

ETH Over-the-Counter Rates  As with bitcoin, borrowing ETH through onchain lending apps has been historically cheaper than borrowing it over the counter. This is driven by two factors: 1) as with BTC, there is demand from short sellers through offchain venues that is not as common onchain and 2) the Ethereum staking APY serves as a floor rate for offchain borrowing because there is little incentive for suppliers to deposit assets with offchain venues, or for offchain venues to lend assets out, at rates below the staking APY. So, with ETH, the floor rate for offchain lending is often the staking APY while onchain the staking APY is often the ceiling rate.   

Corporate Debt Strategies  Since the last report we have made some amendments to the logic defining what a DAT is. To get the most accurate representation, we now define DAT as publicly traded companies whose main business may or may not be crypto-related but either way have a strategy to put crypto assets on the balance sheet. Given this amendment and greater access to public company data, the company mix used in the analysis may look different from previous reports. In addition, this quarter we started tracking Strategy’s preferred debt issuances. As a result, the amount of outstanding debt in this report is elevated compared to past ones. We are now tracking more than $14 billion in debt outstanding used to directly buy or supplement the treasury strategies of DATs. The debt outstanding stagnante through the fourth quarter.

The following timeline details the earliest maturity, call, or put date of DAT-issued debt looking forward from January 2026. Even with the expanded data set, most of the DAT debt is due, at the earliest, between June 2027 and October 2028.

The following details the effective quarterly interest due on DAT-issued debt. These values changed only marginally quarter-over-quarter and VFH Parent LLC (a subsidiary of Nasdaq-listed Virtu Financial) still holds the largest quarterly interest burden.

Total crypto-related debt outstanding, including the debt taken on by DATs, came down slightly quarter-over-quarter. After reaching an all-time high in Q3 of $91.6 billion, total outstanding debt through onchain and offchain channels sits at $84.37 billion (an 7.89% decline quarter-over-quarter).

Futures Market  Futures open interest (OI), including perpetual futures (perps), declined 39.09% QoQ from $197.18 billion to $120.11 billion. This decline was due, in part, to the largest perps liquidation event in history occurring on Oct. 10, just 10 days into the start of the quarter. Over the course of Q4: Bitcoin futures open interest decreased $27.44 billion (-34.2%) to $52.8 billion and stood at $43.97 billion as of Feb. 22. Ether futures open interest decreased $18.18 billion (-34.22%) to $34.95 billion and stood at $23.21 billion as of Feb. 22. SOL futures open interest decreased $5.28 billion (-46.42%) to $6.1 billion and stood at $4.26 billion as of Feb. 22. The futures open interest of all other crypto assets decreased $26.16 billion to $26.26 billion (-49.91%) and stood at $24.24 billion as of Feb. 22. It’s important to note that the entirety of the futures open interest figure does not constitute an absolute amount of leverage. This is due to the fact that some portion of the open interest figure can be offset by long spot positions, giving traders delta-neutral exposure to the underlying asset, and the total leverage ratio of the market is not directly observable from open interest alone.

CME’s share of open interest, including perps and non-perps, stood at 13.9% on Dec. 31, down 91 basis points QoQ. CME’s share of total ether OI (calculated as CME ETH OI divided by total market OI) stood at 15.44% as of Dec. 31 (down 210 basis points QoQ), and CME’s share of total bitcoin OI stood at 17.52% as of Dec. 31 (down 345 basis points QoQ).

Binance occupied the largest share of the perps market measured by OI with a 20.22% share on Dec 31. It was followed by CME with a 13.04% share and Gate with a 10.49% share. At the end of Q4, Hyperliquid held $7.47 billion in OI and commanded 6.22% of the total futures market (a 48-basis-point decrease from the end of Q3).

Perpetual Futures  Perps OI stood at $96.56 billion as of Dec. 31, declining by $61.75 billion (-39%) from the end of Q3. As of Feb. 22, perps OI was stood at $75.7 billion, representing a 56.91% decline from the all-time high reached in early October.

Perps OI dominance was 80.4% as of Dec. 31 and has increased 11 basis points from the end of Q3.

Conclusion Q4 2025 stress-tested the structural improvements in crypto credit markets, and the results were encouraging. CeFi loanbooks absorbed the largest liquidation event in crypto history without visible signs of contagion, while onchain lending behaved as expected, contracting reflexively with prices and yields. The divergence between the two lending markets validates the de-risking that has taken place since 2022. Looking ahead, the infrastructure for the next phase of growth is taking shape with talk of more structured credit products, institutional demand profiles, and real-world asset derivatives markets that never close. The next chapter of crypto leverage is being written now, even if sentiment hasn't caught up.

articles.title: State Member Banks Supervised by the Federal Reserve
articles.text:
State Member Banks Supervised by the Federal Reserve

This page shows the commercial banks supervised by each of the 12 Federal Reserve Banks across the country. The Reserve Banks supervise and operate under delegated authority from the Federal Reserve Board in Washington, DC.

In general, this page will be updated biannually, at the end of Q2 and Q4. Updates and revisions may post without advance notice.

Can AI improve safety without compromising privacy?

Energy companies use sensors and AI to anticipate equipment failure. Can the same predictive approach protect the people operating that equipment, without turning safety systems into a new form of workplace surveillance? As AI moves from screens into robots, control rooms and industrial sites, that question is becoming practical, not theoretical.
Host Ed Crooks is joined by Olivier Oullier, a neuroscientist, investor and AI entrepreneur whose work focuses on how people and machines interact. Olivier argues that AI can improve operator safety and productivity at once through neuroadaptive systems that use signals such as brainwaves, facial expression, eye movement and voice to detect fatigue, stress, distraction or cognitive overload.
In energy operations, those systems could adapt control-room dashboards to foreground the information that matters, or help collaborative robots respond when an operator is tired or distracted. Olivier says pilots are already underway in energy operations in Mexico, Australia and the UAE. Drawing on lessons from surgery and transport, he describes this as an extension of predictive maintenance: moving from monitoring equipment to anticipating human needs, or what he calls predictive care.
That promise rests on a sensitive trade-off. Continuous physiological monitoring could support safer work, but it also raises concerns about consent, autonomy and employee surveillance. Olivier says programs should be voluntary, transparent and compliant with regulation; the discussion tests what responsible deployment needs to look like and whether better outcomes can justify collecting such intimate data.
The conversation also ranges from the risks of poorly supervised AI agents and the skills needed to use AI well to the next phase of physical AI. Olivier points to world models, which aim to help robots understand and act in physical environments, while cautioning against precise long-range predictions about jobs. For energy companies, the near-term challenge is to deploy systems that improve safety and performance without losing sight of the people they are meant to serve.

Insights / Perspectives / Crypto Markets Recover as Rates and Lending Conditions Shift

Written by:

Max Bareiss
Head of Lending

Hannah Kip
Institutional Lending

Yoojeong Lee
Institutional Lending Associate

Kenzie Yang
Lending Analyst

Topics

DeFi

perspectives • September 17, 2026

Crypto Markets Recover as Rates and Lending Conditions Shift

In this report:Tokenized equities move onchain as collateralRobinhood Chain Brings Tokenized Equities and Lending OnchainMorpho Brings Fixed-Rate Lending OnchainCompound Targets Institutional Growth with $52M InitiativeArc Goes Live, and Credit Starts in Dollars
Lending Market UpdateJune through mid-September marked a clear transition from deep correction to recovery and, more recently, consolidation in crypto. June was the weakest stretch, with BTC testing multi-month lows around $58k in late June before stabilizing through July in a range roughly between $56k and $64k. In August, BTC rose 25% and briefly traded above $82k in early September before retracing to around $76k as of September 16 amid a more challenging macro backdrop. A notable catalyst was a reversal in ETF flows, where August saw $3.52B of net inflows, the strongest month of 2026, against just $172M in July and $4.5B of outflows in June. The rally was also coincided with the expansion of U.S. Treasury long-end bond buybacks, which initially pushed longer-dated yields lower and weakened the dollar, creating a more supportive backdrop for BTC and contributing to a sharp short squeeze. ETF flows have since become more mixed in September as momentum from August moderated. Optimism around the CLARITY Act also supported sentiment, though the bill failed to advance in the Senate on September 15, falling short of the 60 votes needed in a procedural vote and adding to regulatory uncertainty across the industry.

CME annualized basis broadly moved with the recovery. After troughing near 3.8% in late June, basis widened through July and August, peaking around 6.7% in late August. Basis has since moderated and become more volatile in September, generally trading in the 5 – 6% range and ending the period around 5.3%. Meanwhile, Treasury yields moved meaningfully higher, narrowing the pickup offered by CME basis over risk-free rates. With Treasury yields moving closer to basis levels, the trade appears relatively less attractive despite the recovery in crypto markets.

The lending market remained orderly, with deleveraging continuing across platforms. Galaxy Research’s The State of Crypto Leverage Q2 2026 report showed that the total crypto-collateralized lending market fell to $56.16B (down $11.33B QoQ, and down 40% from the Q3 2025 peak of $78.7B), with Q2 the first quarter since Q4 2022 in which all three legs declined together- CeFi, DeFi, and the crypto-collateralized portion of CDP stablecoin supply. On the DeFi side, borrows dropped 27.61% to $20.43B, roughly 3x the pace of CeFi's 9.62% decline to $22.98B. The net effect was CeFi gaining relative share even as the overall market contracted, the first quarter since Q3 2023 that CeFi loans outstanding exceeded those of DeFi lending apps, with Galaxy Research reporting that Galaxy, Coinbase, Ledn, Arch, Sygnum and Milo all growing their books. Notably, the contraction has been stepwise rather than cascading- three consecutive quarters of 10%, 5% and 17% declines, against a 55% single-quarter collapse in Q2 2022, which pointed to gradual risk reduction rather than forced liquidations.

Key trends
Tokenized equities move onchain as collateralCoinbase recently launched tokenized U.S. stocks natively on Base on August 24, beginning with NVDAc, METAc, AAPLc, and GOOGLc. Each token is a direct 1:1 claim on a real share, where institutional market makers buy the underlying stock, Alpaca Securities custodies it in segregated accounts, and Coinbase Onchain SPV Ltd holds it as bare trustee in a bankruptcy-remote structure. The tokens are composable across Base DeFi, with other protocols like Aave, Morpho and Euler live for lending and borrowing. The significance for credit markets is that this is the first time a major regulated issuer has put genuine equity claims into open lending rails, extending on-chain collateral beyond just digital assets. The implication is that on-chain credit could broaden from crypto’s own market cap toward the equity and fixed income complex, potentially making lending activity less dependent on the crypto cycle, which is a structural counterweight to the kind of collateral contraction seen this quarter where the decline from peak reflected asset prices. It also raises a topic that needs further clarification from lenders, as equity collateral carries different liquidity and settlement characteristics from BTC or ETH. Coinbase’s product is currently restricted to non-U.S. persons, and Chainlink’s feeds run 24/5 against tokens that trade continuously, meaning weekend collateral is marked to Friday’s close.
Robinhood Chain Brings Tokenized Equities and Lending OnchainRobinhood recently launched its own Arbitrum-based Ethereum L2 on its public mainnet on July 1, built for tokenized real-world assets and shipped with Uniswap, Morpho, Chainlink and BitGo integrated at launch. Stock Tokens went live for 24/7 trading (currently only available for non-U.S. persons), deployable into lending pools and usable as collateral across DeFi, alongside Robinhood Earn. Robinhood Earn is a Morpho-powered product offering roughly 7% on USDG. An important thing to note is a TradFi platform with nearly 28 million funded users choosing to operate its own settlement layer rather than route through existing chains, funded in part by a $2B convertible note priced in June. For lending markets, this matters in two ways. First, distribution: potentially routing ~28 million retail users into DeFi lending brings a scale of deposit supply that on-chain credit has not previously had access to. Secondly, the structure differs from a tokenized share, as Robinhood’s Stock Tokens are tokenized debt securities issued by a Jersey entity, conveying price exposure without ownership, voting rights or direct dividend entitlement, and Robinhood operates the sole sequencer and controls issuance. As equity collateral migrates on-chain, the underlying legal structure on whether a token represents a share or a claim on the issuer, becomes a central input to how these assets are evaluated.
Morpho Brings Fixed-Rate Lending OnchainIn a continued effort to bring traditional credit markets onchain, Morpho launched Morpho Midnight, giving lenders and borrowers access to fixed-rate, fixed-term lending. Much of onchain lending relies on variable rates and open tenors, which can make it difficult to plan around a known cost of capital or return. Midnight is designed to address this challenge, and its customizable KYC gating can further help to attract institutional participants.Existing attempts at fixed-rate markets are built on top of variable-rate markets rather than as a native primitive, where fixed rates are achieved by wrapping or tokenizing exposure to an underlying floating-rate pool. This can introduce basis risk against the underlying source, add a layer of risk on top of the base market, and can fragment liquidity. Morpho Midnight, by contrast, introduces fixed-rate lending at the protocol level rather than synthesized from a floating-rate position.Defined rates and maturities align more closely with institutional credit markets than the utilization curve model most DeFi lending uses. The initial launch features a single cbBTC/USDC market on Base, with a roadmap that includes expansion into financing backed by real-world assets (RWAs). In the meantime, Morpho sits alongside existing Morpho Blue markets: lenders can earn variable rates on Blue while quoting fixed-rate offers on Midnight, capital is only committed once matched so it doesn’t sit idle while it waits.
Compound Targets Institutional Growth with $52M InitiativeCompound is also making a concerted push to attract institutional capital, beginning with a new leadership team and a $52 million budget approved by the DAO. The initiative follows a decline in the protocols TVL which has fallen from $12B in 2021 to roughly $1.2B today. The program aims to draw institutions by introducing RWA products and building infrastructure for the likes of banks, asset managers, and fintech companies.Of the $52 million, $14 million is released at the onset, with the remainder held in reserve until the Foundation reaches specified development goals. The move positions Compound to compete with other protocols that have already established RWA lending markets.
Arc Goes Live, and Credit Starts in DollarsCircle brought Arc’s public mainnet live on September 16. The chain is EVM-compatible, gas is paid in USDC, and settlement is built for sub-second finality. A permissioned validator set is producing blocks, including BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, Mastercard, ICE, and Galaxy. Circle also minted 10 billion ARC tokens around launch, while saying that is not a commitment to sell the token to the public.Lending was on the network from the start. Aave, including a V4 market, Morpho, and Uniswap opened with the chain, and tokenized cash such as BUIDL and USYC is being lined up as collateral next to cirBTC. Galaxy curated two Morpho vaults on Arc – one USDC and one EURC – and Morpho on Arc took in more than $150 million of deposits on day one. There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesThe MarketsWhy Investors Are Reducing AI ExposureOct 23, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptMarkets are scrutinizing the crowded AI trade as investors reassess technology infrastructure spending plans and factor in rising capital costs, says Rich Privorotsky, head of European Equities Trading within Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. Third-quarter earnings from mega-cap tech will be critical, Privorotsky says on The Markets podcast. Investors are not only watching hyperscaler investment plans but looking for evidence that the spending is translating into revenue growth. He also describes a “seismic shift” from a savings glut to a spending glut, which along with high energy prices is lowering investor risk appetite.
Transcript:
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, October 22nd. And I'm joined from the Goldman Sachs trading floor in London by Rich Privorotsky, who is head of European Equities Trading within FICC and Equities.
Privo, thanks so much for joining us.
Rich Privorotsky: Thanks for having me, Hussey.
Chris Hussey: All right. Let's jump into it because I've been reading everything you've been writing about, and you made a great point, which was that earlier this summer, the pain trade, the trade that people were having to chase was long AI, short everything else.
It had become a little bit of one big trade. Now that seems to be unwinding as we go into third quarter earnings season. What's going on? How do you see it playing out from here?
Rich Privorotsky: There's just been an immense amount of concentration in the equity market, and I got to say that the past few weeks have been particularly painful for those types of consensual trades.
People were very concentrated within AI, within semis, within hyperscalers. And I would say that there are probably three different issues the market is kind of grappling with right now. One is obviously we've had a spillover in terms of the cost of capital, and I think we're seeing that pretty much everywhere. Whether it's triple C spreads, sovereign spreads in Europe, but also at the very pointy end within some of these more levered parts of the AI trade and the neoclouds really stand out.
And so that's become a question of supply. You know, will those corporates have struggle to find financing to deliver all this AI spend? The second point being on supply, that we've had questions about the ability to actually energize and deliver gigawatts, and the spread is kind of 20 at 40, 50 gigawatts for next year.
So if you can't get the power to actually energize a data center, will you actually be able to consume the chips you've already forward ordered? So those are concerns that are floating around the market. And then on top of that, you have more competition at the model layer and all of that is just compounded to a point where people have been in a de-risking mentality. And the nature of that has been taking growth expectations down via the AI trade and AI CapEx trade. And on the flip side of that, bonds have been rallying as growth expectations come down and that was on no one's bingo card.
Chris Hussey: Okay, a lot to unpack there. Let's focus though on the immediate future and actually the present, which is the third quarter earnings season. We're in the middle of it already. We've had some of the big mega cap tech stocks report, but we got a lot more to go. What are you watching for most carefully out of the third quarter earnings season?
Rich Privorotsky: Yeah, I think we're going to head into the meat of the hyperscaler numbers, and I think it's going to be really important to see not only that the CapEx is sustaining at the high levels and the market is kind of at $1.1 trillion for next year, but most importantly see continued cloud growth and monetization.
So, it's not enough just to say that you're spending a lot of money, but you also need to demonstrate that backlog is converting into revenues in a meaningful capacity. And so, I think that's going to be really critical for the market. I think the nature of how quickly their bridge to free cash flow break even occurs relative to market expectations could have a big implication on the credit markets, which have become acutely sensitive.
And so, really for me, there's a lot to look for I would say from the rest of the economy, but I think that the market's focus is really going to be on hyperscalers and then really the quality of the delivery, not just the spend.
Chris Hussey: It's a heck of a bar to have to scale for these companies. They have to keep pushing CapEx at the same time as they show you returns on that CapEx. It's not an easy setup, is it?
Rich Privorotsky: No, it's not. But, but look, I mean, the backdrop is one such that you see compute prices literally making new highs every day in the spot market. There is insatiable demand for what they have for sale. And so, I would say with a bit of a glass half full view, they should have a pretty good story to tell.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Rich, it's been a minute actually since we've had you on the call. You last joined us way back in January, but throughout the year you've been one of the guys with the mantra, "As goes oil, so goes everything else." Is that still the mantra?
Rich Privorotsky: Yeah. I think we've had a immensely problematic backdrop in energy. And I think the market, the equity market I think has done its best to really ignore and compartmentalize the rise in energy.
But that's not really fair because the S&P has done a great job compartmentalizing, but the median equity has in fact gone down well in excess of 10%. And so that has had an impact on rates. It has an impact on FCI. In fact, we've had a massive FCI tightening, and that has in a sense also pushed the Fed to do more, and we've repriced an entire hiking cycle.
So I think energy has been a big part of that. I think we still have a lot of risk premium because of energy and obviously now the next couple of weeks of how these things are going to play out is going to be really critical for broader risk, and I think my optimistic view is that we'll get some sort of resolution in the next few weeks. But, I have to admit, I've been kind of a little bit wrong thinking that would've happened a month or two ago.
Chris Hussey: I think we all have. And by FCI, of course, you're referring to the Financial Conditions Index, which is kind of a measure of tightening or loosening of the economy, of all the economic impulses. It's not just about rates. Sometimes it could be oil, sometimes it could be stocks as well when you're looking at an FCI. All right, good point on the oil side.
Also tied to that oil trade, though, was a comment you made back at the beginning of the year, which is, "I want to be long nominal assets. In an expanding world where GDP growth is strong, and GDP growth is looking still very strong, and inflation is high, I just want to be long those types of thing," which is a lot of commodities.
Where do you see that nominal asset trade today? Is it still a place to be?
Rich Privorotsky: I think in order to answer that question, I have to kind of answer the trillion-dollar question, which is what's going to happen with AI spending and how sustainable is it relevant to market expectations? Because the reality is that as we reprice that, we've repriced everything, including commodities, including nominal assets.
My gut is that we've kind of thrown the baby out with the bathwater, and we've certainly begun to worry about every dimensionality. And to kind of put that in context, I met investors this week who said, "I'm worried about the inability to deliver compute, and that scares me." And then I met another set of investors that said, "I'm worried we're going to over-deliver compute, and that scares me."
And it's somehow we've had two mutually exclusive outcomes that are both the summation of the market's worries. So, I think nominal assets are big picture where you want to be, unless we go into a disinflationary bust, right? Which is CapEx slows, everyone has to retrench, we have a proper credit cycle. And I would've said three months ago the risk of that was low, and now certainly it's a lot higher.
But my gut is that's still where you want to be over the medium and long term. But I think now perhaps a bit more of a barbell in the portfolio would be a bit more sensible.
Chris Hussey: So, it sounds like what you are saying is, whereas before it may have been as goes oil, so goes everything else, it's now as goes AI, so goes everything else. Is that right?
Rich Privorotsky: I think at the risk of being overly reductionist, that's probably about right.
Chris Hussey: Rich, thanks for being overly reductionist. I am Mr. Overly Reductionist, so I love that you were able to go there.
All right. You also mentioned that part of this, of course, would be a big credit cycle.
And that three months ago you weren't worried about a credit cycle, now you are a little bit more. Talk to us about that. Are you seeing credit cracks? Are you referring to the issues that are going on with sovereign bonds in Europe, or are you referring more to the credit issues that we see at the corporate side?
Rich Privorotsky: I've spent my entire career in what you could probably describe as a savings glut. We had more money in the system than we knew what to do with and really in the last year we're projecting to spend in excess of a trillion dollars on AI CapEx. Most governments around the world are running fiscal deficits.
We are in a spending glut, and this is a really big seismic change in terms of the way things work and what the cost of capital becomes. And so I think that is naturally pushing out borrowers who are at the fringe, who are not the highest of quality. I think you've seen it in CCC spreads, which is, in fairness, a bit idiosyncratic given the composition of what's occurred there, but they have moved a lot and that's spilled over a little bit into broader parts of credit.
And then obviously you have French sovereign concerns, which as a sovereign with a large fiscal deficit in this environment, they all get pushed out. So I think all these things are kind of having an impact and we go back to the oil trade simultaneously, as long as energy prices are high, it just kind of lowers the risk appetite and I think it is kind of a buyer's market for those types of assets.
Chris Hussey: Yeah, what a great way to crystallize it. From a savings glut to a spending glut. It's so true, and that savings glut was only five years ago. It's amazing how we've shifted. All right. A lot going on. You just told us. Let's put a bow on it. What's the trade?
Rich Privorotsky: It's a bit messy, and I would say conviction is not super high. But I think that there are pockets of electrification that we think look really interesting. They've derated a ton, and I still think there's plenty of visibility into 2027 that gives you a big margin of safety. I think there's lots of aerospace assets that have come off that, particularly on the civil side, again, equally incredibly attractive to us.
And then even parts of transports, quite frankly. If you do get any kind of energy resolution, there's a lot of, I would say, convexity in that trade given how low nets have become, how much selling we have seen in the past few week. I mean, for context, it was the biggest selling of tech we've ever seen in our prime book last week.
So, I think there are plenty of reasons to worry and I don't want to be too dismissive, but I kind of like try to be cautiously optimistic at this point.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Rich, let's fast-forward to next week. What are you watching for that's going to impact the markets in the week ahead?
Rich Privorotsky: I think it's going to be at numbers, hyperscaler numbers as we discussed. I think let's see the monetization. Let's see the CapEx figures. I think this is going to be really critical for the tape.
I think how that progresses will shape how people feel about the credit, how people feel about the underlying demand and whatever else we get, you know, in terms of data points coming from all the labs and all the providers.
Chris Hussey: Rich, always a wealth of information. Thanks so much for joining us today.
Rich Privorotsky: All right. Thanks, Chris. Thanks for having me.
Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening.This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, October 22nd. And I'm joined from the Goldman Sachs trading floor in London by Rich Privorotsky, who is head of European Equities Trading within FICC and Equities.
Privo, thanks so much for joining us.
Rich Privorotsky: Thanks for having me, Hussey.
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, October 22nd. And I'm joined from the Goldman Sachs trading floor in London by Rich Privorotsky, who is head of European Equities Trading within FICC and Equities.

News Release
Asia’s search for long-term, lower-carbon LNG supply puts Canada in focus but competition is intensifying
LNG Canada's Phase 2 FID adds momentum to Canada's LNG ambitions as Asian buyers seek diversified supply amid growing global competition

20 October 2026
5 minute read

Email
Share by email

Asia's long-term energy security will increasingly depend on diversified, reliable and lower-carbon LNG supply. As buyers look beyond traditional sources, Canada is emerging as a compelling long-term supplier due to its proximity to the Asian market, as well as its lower carbon intensity.
Canada's LNG sector is entering a new phase of growth. LNG Canada reached a final investment decision on its Phase 2 expansion in September 2026, doubling the facility's capacity to 28 mmtpa and reinforcing Canada's potential as a significant long-term supplier to Asian markets. Together with Woodfibre and Cedar LNG which are currently under construction, Canada looks to export 33 mmtpa of LNG by end of this decade.
Even with the addition of projects such as Ksi Lisims LNG, Canada remains well below Prime Minister Mark Carney's long-term ambition of achieving 100 mtpa of LNG export capacity under his "energy superpower" agenda. Meanwhile, global competition for LNG investment is accelerating as a growing number of projects compete for scarce capital and seek to reach FID. Consequently, Canada's opportunity to secure a larger position in the next phase of global LNG supply growth may be limited in both time and scale.
In this context, a whitepaper, prepared in collaboration with Energy Asia by PETRONAS and Wood Mackenzie, assesses Canada's prospects for capturing a greater share of Asia's expanding LNG demand. It also highlights the evolving needs of Asian buyers and investors, offering insights into the conditions required for LNG-exporting nations to attract investment and successfully advance new projects.

Source: Wood Mackenzie
"For Asian buyers, Canada offers something that is increasingly rare in global LNG markets: a combination of resource scale, Pacific Basin access and a short shipping routes," said Joshua Ngu, Vice Chairman, Asia Pacific at Wood Mackenzie. "That is a compelling proposition. But buyers are also weighing cost, timeline and execution risk against alternatives that are already further advanced. Canada's resource advantage is real, but realizing its full potential will depend on competitiveness, execution and timely project delivery."
A structural shift in global LNG markets
Repeated geopolitical disruptions have exposed the risks of overreliance on concentrated sources of supply, prompting Asian buyers to reassess their long-term LNG procurement strategies. As a result, supply diversification across geography, counterparties and carbon intensity has become a strategic priority for governments, utilities and LNG buyers across the region.
According to Wood Mackenzie, Asian LNG demand is expected to double from approximately 260 mtpa today to around 500 mtpa by 2060. Critically, a significant share of this future demand remains uncontracted, creating opportunities for new LNG suppliers to secure long-term market access.
South and Southeast Asia are expected to account for much of the growth in future LNG demand and are likely to be key destinations for new long-term supply agreements. However, many of these markets are highly price sensitive and have limited capacity to absorb sustained high energy costs, despite LNG's important role in supporting economic growth, industrialisation and energy security.
As a result, buyers are increasingly seeking supply portfolios that balance security, affordability and sustainability. For LNG exporters, competitiveness on delivered cost is becoming just as important as supply reliability and emissions performance.
Canada's momentum and the competition it faces
The FID for LNG Canada Phase 2 represents an important milestone in Canada's efforts to expand its LNG export capacity, while Ksi Lisims LNG continues to advance toward a final investment decision and build commercial momentum. However, Canada is competing for both investment capital and access to a rapidly growing, yet very price-sensitive, Asian LNG market.
Competition is intensifying as buyers evaluate long-term LNG offtake opportunities across a growing range of global supply options. In 2026 alone, CP2 LNG, Commonwealth LNG and Delfin FLNG 1 reached FID in the United States, while projects across Africa, Australia and Latin America continue to progress toward sanction.
The contracting and investment decisions made over the next three to five years will help shape Asia's LNG supply landscape for decades to come.
What Canada needs to do
The white paper identifies four priorities for Canada to derisk projects and attract the scale of capital required:

Improve cost competitiveness: High labour costs, substantial infrastructure requirements and constraints in the skilled labour pool risk placing Canadian LNG at a disadvantage relative to competing projects globally. Addressing these structural challenges will be critical to improving project economics and maintaining competitiveness in Asian markets.
Strengthen regulatory certainty: Investors and LNG buyers require predictable, transparent and time-bound permitting and approval processes. Reducing regulatory uncertainty will be essential to improving investor confidence and advancing projects to sanction.
Develop innovative financing solutions: The scale of capital required for Canada's next wave of LNG projects may necessitate new financing approaches, including government-supported mechanisms, credit enhancements and public-private partnerships capable of attracting institutional and international investors.
Deepen government-to-government engagement: Long-term LNG relationships are built not only through commercial agreements but also through strategic partnerships between governments. Strengthening energy diplomacy and economic cooperation with key Asian importing countries can help support investment, facilitate long-term contracting and reinforce Canada's position as a reliable energy supplier.

"Canada's resource advantage is significant, but its success will ultimately depend on its ability to translate that advantage into competitive, investable and executable projects that can secure long-term buyers and attract capital ahead of rival LNG developments," Ngu concluded.

articles.title: Flash Insights: Resilient Growth, Sticky Inflation | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
Last week saw a further deterioration in the inflation outlook, while the Federal Reserve (Fed) appears increasingly reluctant to tighten again immediately. The September headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.6% month/month (m/m) and 3.7% year/year (y/y), while core inflation increased 0.3% m/m and accelerated to 2.6% y/y from 2.4%. Energy accounted for more than half the headline increase, but the underlying picture was not particularly reassuring: Shelter inflation accelerated to 0.4% m/m, while several services and goods categories also recorded increases. The more concerning signal came from the Producer Price Index (PPI), which surged 1.3% m/m and 6.3% y/y, its strongest monthly increase since March 2022. Although energy was the main driver, prices excluding food, energy and trade services rose 0.5%, while import prices increased another 1.1%. The risk is increasingly that elevated energy and input costs feed through into broader consumer inflation, rather than remaining a temporary headline shock.

The growth picture remains resilient, but the divergence between nominal spending and underlying consumer purchasing power is becoming more pronounced. September retail sales increased a stronger-than-expected 0.8% m/m, but excluding gasoline stations, sales rose only 0.2%. Higher prices are therefore accounting for a meaningful portion of the increase in spending. The latest Federal Reserve’s “Beige Book” report reinforced this divergence: Most districts reported little change in consumer spending, with growth increasingly concentrated among higher-income households. Meanwhile, real average hourly earnings are now down 0.7% y/y and stagnant for the past six months. This is worth watching because it suggests household purchasing power is weakening despite relatively healthy aggregate consumption. However, initial jobless claims remained exceptionally low at 199,000, indicating that the labor market continues to suffer more from weak hiring than rising layoffs.

The industrial sector remains an important source of strength. September industrial production rose 0.7% m/m, exceeding expectations, although manufacturing output increased by a more modest 0.3%. Utilities production jumped 3.5%, consistent with continued strong electricity demand associated with artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure investment. This reinforces the theme that AI-related investment continues to support economic activity, even as higher energy prices and interest rates weigh on other sectors. The expansion is therefore becoming more dependent on a relatively narrow set of growth drivers.

The Fed is facing a more difficult policy trade-off, but an October pause remains the most likely outcome. The latest inflation reports strengthen the argument for additional tightening, while softer payroll growth, weaker real earnings and uncertainty around the consumer argue against moving too quickly. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh offered little indication of the Fed's intentions during his October 16 remarks, reiterating his reluctance to provide forward guidance ahead of policy decisions. Markets ended the week assigning roughly an 85% probability to rates remaining unchanged on October 28, despite the upside inflation surprises. We retain our view that the Fed will pause later this month, while a December hike remains firmly in play. The more important question is whether the Fed can afford to remain patient if higher input costs continue passing through into consumer prices. The September Beige Book offered little reassurance on that front, with four districts reporting an acceleration in price increases and firms anticipating further increases as existing contracts expire.

Despite the upside inflation surprises and another deterioration in the fiscal outlook, the sharp selloff in AI-related equities triggered substantial safe-haven demand for Treasuries. The Financial Times reported that America's unprecedented AI infrastructure expansion is encountering increasingly serious financial and operational constraints. At least 47 major projects have been delayed, withdrawn or blocked in 2026, while Bernstein research analysts estimate that only 35% of the announced US data-center pipeline should be treated as credible. Higher interest rates and weakening investor confidence are making financing more difficult for AI infrastructure developers, while electricity constraints, construction delays and local opposition are creating additional obstacles. While this does not yet imply that the AI investment cycle is reversing, it does introduce a new risk to both growth and financial markets. The same investment boom supporting US economic outperformance could become a source of vulnerability if financing conditions tighten further.

Growing concerns about the sustainability of AI-related investment sparked demand for duration (table below), with the 2-year and 10-year curves flattening by 9 basis points (bps). The rally was driven predominantly by declining real yields (10-year real yields fell 17 bps to 2.74%) rather than a significant reassessment of inflation expectations. The rally was particularly notable given that the fiscal year 2026 deficit widened to US$1.99 trillion from US$1.78 trillion, with debt-service costs reaching a record US$1.36 trillion. While investors became more comfortable owning duration at elevated yields, particularly following the improvement in auction demand the week of October 5 and weaker risk sentiment last week, we remain cautious about extrapolating the rally given persistent inflation, heavy Treasury financing requirements and still-elevated term-premium risks.
