What do you need to know?

The International Monetary Fund raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% from the 3.0% it projected in July but kept its 2027 forecast unchanged at 3.4%. Meanwhile it expects global inflation to increase to 4.7% this year from 4.1% in 2025, before easing back to 4.1% in 2027. The global economy has remained resilient thanks to the re-routing of energy supplies, mitigating the impact of geopolitical conflicts, as well as an artificial intelligence investment boom, the IMF said. However, it warned that countries need to rebuild financial reserves and shore up capacity to withstand future shocks.

Around the world

US annual inflation rose more than expected in September, increasing to 3.7% from 3.4% in August. The rise was primarily driven by higher gasoline and energy prices. Core inflation, which excludes more volatile food and energy costs, rose to 2.6% in September, from 2.4% in August. The data raised expectations that the Federal Reserve could hike interest rates further, prompting stock markets to fall before later recovering. The S&P 500 was flat in the week to Thursday’s close while the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 2%. Europe’s STOXX 600 gained 2%*. Elsewhere, Eurozone annual inflation was confirmed at 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% in August.

*In US dollar terms. Source: FactSet, data as of 15 October 2026

Figure in focus: Four years

The current bull market – a period when share prices are rising – marked its four-year anniversary last week. The rally began in October 2022 as stock markets rebounded from their lows, which were brought on by central banks aggressively hiking interest rates following the post-pandemic inflation spike. The MSCI World and S&P 500 have each climbed nearly 120% since then, according to reports. The strong performance has been driven by corporate earnings growth and optimism over artificial intelligence, though some investors have questioned how long the upward trend can continue. A bull market is considered to have ended when the index falls at least 20% from its peak.

Chart of the week

US business activity’s fastest rise in more than five years is helping investors remain optimistic about the outlook for stock markets. The S&P Global US Purchasing Managers’ Index – which measures the private sector’s economic health across manufacturing and services industries – rose to 58.4 in September from 56 in August. A reading above 50 marks expansion. Growth accelerated across both manufacturing and services, indicating broad-based strength in the US economy. AI investment and defence spending boosted the manufacturing sector, while inventory stockpiling resulted in higher orders and output. This positive backdrop continues to support equities and other risk-based assets, despite expectations of higher interest rates.

Words of wisdom: Microeconomics

How individual consumers or businesses make economic decisions, such as what to purchase or setting prices for their products. Two US professors won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences last week for their work on microeconomics. Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford developed new models showing how the combined actions of individual households and businesses affect the economy. Their models have helped central banks deal with shocks like energy crises, by using monetary policy to stabilise economies.

What’s coming up?

On Monday, China publishes its third quarter GDP growth rate and Canada reports September inflation data. The UK follows with its own inflation figures on Wednesday. On Thursday, the Eurozone publishes its latest consumer confidence survey. Friday sees Japan report inflation data while a series of Purchasing Managers’ Indices are released, covering business activity in the Eurozone, US, UK and Japan.

articles.title: The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland
articles.text:
The importance of public engagement in maintaining trust in banknotes - Speech by Victoria Cleland

Speech at the Intergraf Currency & Identity Conference, Denmark

Published on
15 October 2026

Maintaining trust in banknotes is crucial to their continued demand and relevance. This requires more than robust security features and resilient infrastructure. Victoria Cleland explores how communications and public engagement can help build and maintain confidence and trust in cash.

Speech
Trust is essential to everything the Bank of England (the Bank) does. It underpins all our activities, from setting Bank Rate to operating payment settlement systems and much in between. And banknotes are among the most visible manifestations of that trust.
The Bank is the second oldest central bank in the world and issuing banknotes (originally promissory notes) was one of its earliest functions. Historically, confidence in banknotes was linked to their convertibility into gold. You can still see the words ‘I promise to pay the bearer on demand’ on our banknotes. While the nature of that promise has evolved over time and our notes are now indirectly backed by UK government bonds,footnote [1] the principle remains the same: banknotes derive their value from trust, and that trust must be maintained.
Every time someone accepts a banknote, they trust that it is authentic and worth the value stated. They have to be confident that it can be used again in the future: whether to spend it, save it or bank it. Without that trust, a banknote is simply an object, albeit with a beautiful design. With it, households spend, businesses trade and economies function.
Central banks play a crucial role in maintaining this trust in banknotes. We do so by ensuring banknotes are available, that the cash industry remains effective, resilient and sustainable, and that banknotes remain a secure method of payment.
Communicating openly with businesses and the public so that they can recognise and easily authenticate banknotes is also an essential part of maintaining this security. The Bank has engaged extensively with the UK public on the imagery for our next series of banknotes to ensure our banknotes remain recognisable as national symbols. This culminated in last week’s announcement that the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will feature as the central imagery on our next series of banknotes.
I will now dive deeper into the Bank’s work to ensure this essential trust in our banknotes through availability, secure design and public engagement.
Ensuring trust through availability
The public need to trust that banknotes will be available when required. The Bank does not, and cannot, do this in isolation. Just as a beehive depends on its community of different bees performing complementary roles, maintaining trust in banknotes requires organisations across the cash ecosystem to work together.
Central banks, printers, cash centre operators, cash-in-transit companies, financial institutions and retailers are all important members of this ecosystem. They all play crucial and complementary roles in ensuring that the public can continue to access and use banknotes so that cash remains a trusted source of payments. At the Banknote Conference earlier this year,footnote [2] I spoke about the importance of preserving choice in payments and the role of cash in preserving choice. Ensuring that choice remains requires the whole industry to work together like an efficient beehive.
For the Bank, this includes issuing banknotes to meet public demand. The use of cash for transactions has declined over recent years, accounting for 8% of all transactions in the UK in 2025, down from 45% a decade earlier.footnote [3] But according to our research, cash is still the preferred payment method for one in seven people and, is used at least once a week by almost a quarter of the public. It is essential for some people and is seen as an important contingency by many.
And the value of Bank of England notes in circulation has continued to increase, reaching £91.5 billion at the end of February 2026. This demonstrates the enduring importance of cash to our economy and our society.
We are committed to meet the demand for our banknotes and to ensure that the right banknotes are available, in the right places at the right time. It is important to us that people and businesses who want to use cash can continue to do so. We do this by monitoring payment trends and a range of economic factors to inform demand forecasts and contingency requirements, and to help us decide how many banknotes we need our printer De La Rue to produce.
Authorities and industry must work closely together to ensure the cash cycle as a whole remains effective, resilient and sustainable. The wholesale cash distribution market is the underlying “plumbing” that gets cash to where it is needed, via cash centres through to ATMs and retailers. Last year, the Bank took on a new role to supervise firms in the wholesale cash industry who operate cash centres and their backing FIs.footnote [4] In addition, the Financial Conduct Authority has powers to protect retail access to cash for consumers. Together, these regimes will help ensure that cash will be available and accessible.
Ensuring trust through design
Another key component of trust in banknotes is counterfeit resilience: the public and businesses must be confident that the banknotes they receive are genuine. We do this by incorporating sophisticated security features into the design: these need to be both hard to counterfeit and easy to authenticate. For trust in the security of banknotes to endure, it is important that central banks change the design from time to time to incorporate the latest security features. This requires suppliers and manufacturers to innovate and invest in developing new technology and more resilient features. To maintain trust in banknotes, it is essential that this innovation continues.
When you picture a puffin, you may think of its distinct colouring including its bright orange beak. Did you know their beaks glow under UV light, just like our banknotes? These markings and photoluminescence are not purely about aesthetic appeal but also serve a functional purpose in helping puffins lure prey, deter predators and attract mates. Similarly, at the Bank, we need to design banknotes that are not only attractive but also designed with function, particularly security, at their heart.
Our next series of banknotes (Series H) is currently being designed. The driver, as with any new series, is to further enhance counterfeit resilience. And following public consultation, the new notes will celebrate UK wildlife. Images of wildlife will also support resilience, enabling us to incorporate intuitive movements into the security features which are engaging and easy for the public to recognise and distinguish.
Trust also stems from our notes being accessible to all. We are continuing to invest in banknote accessibility, running research on how people with disabilities use cash today and including tactile features to help people with visual impairments differentiate between denominations.
Ensuring trust through communication and engagement
Trust in banknotes is founded on availability and effective design, but sustaining it requires engagement – with businesses, law enforcement and the public. Even the most sophisticated security feature is only effective if people know how to use it to verify a banknote. And so public engagement and communication are a pivotal part of our anticounterfeiting strategy.
The Bank provides free educational materials, such as booklets and posters to help businesses and the public to authenticate banknotes. We also provide online training and run a free Banknote Checking Scheme to help businesses keep a watchful eye out for counterfeits: a vigilance one could compare to the barn owl which will feature on our next series. This Scheme has grown considerably, now covering over 50,000 business locations.
Recently, we have supplemented this by launching a communications campaign aimed at businesses. This campaign shows business owners talking about their own experiences and how using best practice banknote checking has enhanced their trust in banknotes. We also engage closely with law enforcement, including the National Crime Agency and local police forces, to help them investigate and prosecute potential counterfeiters.
Incorporating images that resonate strongly with the public and which they can easily recognise is also a key part of banknote authentication and maintaining trust. So last year, we launched a two-stage process to engage the public in the choice of imagery for the next series of banknotes.
In July 2025, we announced that we would introduce a new series of banknotes with even more robust security features. A new series necessitates changes to the imagery, so we launched a consultation asking the UK public which theme they wanted to see featured in the design. The Bank has been celebrating historic figures on our banknotes since 1970. However there are many ways to represent the UK so we wanted to hear the views of the public, the users of our banknotes.
Around 60% of respondents chose nature as one of the themes they wanted to see featured with many nominating specific native animals. And this March, we announced that in the light of feedback from the consultation, images of UK wildlife would feature on the next series of our banknotes. We worked closely with a panel of wildlife experts to create a shortlist of native UK animals and in June we launched a second consultation asking the public to help us choose which of the shortlisted animals to feature as the central imagery on the next series. We were delighted by the scale of the response, with almost half a million people participating.
The Bank’s overarching objective is to increase counterfeit resilience through secure design, and for this to be effective, it is also important that the new series represents the UK and resonates with the users. After all, banknotes are not just a means of payment, but also a shared symbol of national identity. This helps to promote trust and security, as familiar imagery which resonates with the public will mean they look more closely at their banknotes.
The importance of awareness and familiarity is not new. In 1797, when the Bank rushed to issue new £1 and £2 banknotes following gold shortages, counterfeiting surged as counterfeiters took advantage of people’s unfamiliarity with new banknotes. The lesson remains relevant today: when introducing a new series, issuers must bring the public along on the journey to ensure they can recognise and authenticate the notes.
To do this successfully and inclusively, central banks need to engage people through different methods including the platforms they use every day. To help publicise our most recent consultation, the Bank used an integrated communication strategy which included press, social media, engagement with schools and visiting local communities around the UK. We also collaborated with influencers to help us reach young people and audiences who may not have engaged with the Bank’s work in the past.
We opened the consultation with a launch event at the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT) London Wetland Centre to celebrate the shortlisted animals and give journalists an opportunity to ask questions – both to me and the wildlife Expert Panel who helped us develop the shortlist of animals. This provided an engaging backdrop to create content about wildlife to help raise awareness and encourage participation in the consultation.
To sustain momentum, we produced a variety of engaging and accessible content with the aim to appeal to different audience groups and help convey our broader message. This included factsheets on each of the animals and educational posts showing how banknotes have evolved over time, as well as some more fun posts.
Alongside the formal consultation, we also visited schools and ran a design challenge for children across the country to give young people a voice in shaping our next generation of banknotes. And we held a number of in-person Youth and Citizens’ panels in communities including Llandudno and Devon. These were a great opportunity for the Bank to learn directly from people about the role that cash continues to play in society as well as their views on the shortlisted wildlife.
Conclusion
Trust in banknotes begins with secure design but only endures if banknotes are available and recognised. Keeping banknotes trusted and relevant requires innovation and strong collaboration across the whole of the cash industry. And this must be coupled with communication and engagement to enable businesses and the public to understand, recognise and trust the banknotes they use.
Our recent consultation gave people a voice, helping them connect with the banknotes they use and have a meaningful say about their future design. There will now be a quieter period in our communications about the next series, while our design work continues in the background, with security at its heart. Like the hedgehog emerging after its winter retreat, we will return when we are ready to unveil the first denomination.
I would like to thank Elijah Lee, Zahra Damji, Nick McLaren, Ellen Caswell, Stuart Cooper, Lauren Murphy, Kiran Keer, Millie Rettie and Lisa Young.

articles.title: Negative return in the third quarter | Norges Bank Investment Management
articles.text:
Return on the fund’s equity investments: 0.5 percent
Return on fixed-income investments: -3.5 percent
Return on unlisted real estate investments: 0.4 percent
Return on unlisted renewable energy infrastructure: 7.5 percent

The fund’s return was 0.18 percentage points lower than the return on the benchmark index.
“The fund’s return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments. Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell,” says Deputy CEO Trond Grande of Norges Bank Investment Management.
The fund’s value fell by 670 billion kroner in the third quarter. The accounting return was -278 billion kroner. The krone strengthened during the quarter, which reduced the fund’s value by 472 billion kroner. In the third quarter, 80 billion kroner was added to the fund after management costs.
The fund was valued at 22,014 billion kroner on 30 September 2026. Of this, 72.1 percent was invested in equities, 25.8 percent in fixed income, 1.6 percent in unlisted real estate and 0.5 percent in unlisted renewable energy infrastructure.

FAQs

Can I purchase Allianz Motor/ Electric Motor Protect if I am not a Singaporean?

Yes you can, as long as your car is legally registered in Singapore under the relevant Singapore Road Traffic Act.

In which countries am I insured to drive?

Singapore, West Malaysia, and Thailand (within 80km of the border of Malaysia).

Who should I contact in case of an emergency?

In case of emergency, Allianz helpline is available 24/7 at +65 6222 1919.

View all FAQs

How does your ‘Lifetime Warranty On Repairs’ work in event of an accident?

For any defective workmanship in your accident repairs done by any of Allianz’s authorized workshops, you may proceed back to the same authorized workshop for repairs for as long as you are insured with Allianz.

How does your 24 months ‘New for Old’ replacement car work?

In the event that your car is damaged beyond repair within the first 24 months of its first registration in Singapore, Allianz will at their option:

Replace it with a new car of the same make, model, and engine capacity as your car; or
If a new car of the same make, model and engine capacity is not available, replace it with a new car of a similar make, model, and engine capacity as your car; or
Pay such cash equivalent in lieu of points (1) and (2) immediately above.

How can I get a courtesy car in the event my car is undergoing repair after an accident or breakdown?

Allianz authorized workshops will assist you in liaising with their vendor to arrange for a courtesy car if the repairs to your car requires more than 24 hours.

Can No Claim Discount (NCD) be transferrable?

No, NCD is not transferrable to another person except to your spouse, provided your spouse is purchasing a new Allianz Motor / Electric Motor Protect. This is a one-time transfer and it is non- reversible. After the transfer, your NCD for your existing motor insurance policy will become 0%.

Are my windscreens covered?

There is coverage if the windscreen is cracked, chipped or broken. An excess of S$100 is applicable for each windscreen replacement.

What is the benefit of adding named drivers to my motor insurance policy?

By having named drivers in your motor insurance policy, your named drivers will enjoy the same lower excess as you. Excess is the amount the policyholder is required to contribute before they can make a claim.

What should I do if I am involved in an accident?

Exchange particulars of all involved parties including name, NRIC/FIN, telephone number, address and insurer. Take note of the vehicle license plate(s) and take digital photographs and keep any in-car camera footage of your car, the other vehicle(s) and the surroundings, which can be included during the e-filing of accident reports later.
Call Allianz hotline for a tow truck or for further advice on the accident.
Report and bring your car (whether damaged or not) to the approved reporting centre/authorized workshop within 24 hours or by the next working day.
Avoid all unauthorized tow truck operators or repair workshops. You may refer to the Motor Claims Framework at www.gia.org.sg which will provide clear and common procedures for the reporting of motor accidents.

What do I do if the accident happens in Malaysia or Thailand?

Exchange particulars of all involved parties including name, NRIC/FIN, telephone number, address and insurer. Take note of the vehicle license plate(s).
Take pictures of your car’s damages and the damages of the other damaged vehicle(s) involved. Capture all vehicles’ license plate(s).
Take pictures of the accident location, capturing the surroundings and the vehicle(s) in its/their stationary position before moving it/them.
Call the local police if there is any injured party. (999 for Malaysia / 191 for Thailand)
Make a police report in the country where the accident occurred. Upon returning to Singapore, regardless of whether your car was damaged or not, report the accident to the Allianz authorized workshop together with your car within 24 hours or the next working day. If you have an in-car camera, please submit the video footage as well.

Will my electric components be insured?

Yes, electric and electronic components such as high and low voltage cables, battery, electric engine, and electronic control units will be covered under Allianz Electric Motor Protect.

Will my electric vehicle be protected against cyber hacks?

Under Allianz Electric Motor Protect, we will cover losses or damages to your vehicle by malicious cyber acts, even when your electric vehicle is operated under Advanced Driver Assistance Systems.

In this week's edition, Alex Thorn explains why some blue-chip companies opted out of the NYSE’s stock tokenization initiative; Thad Pinakiewicz breaks down this week’s top cyber scare; and Lucas Tcheyan revisits Solana’s Alpenglow upgrade, now live.Find all our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com. We’d love to hear from you.
PHPeril: Never Send a Human to Do a Machine’s JobWHAT HAPPENEDThe team maintaining scripting language PHP rushed out emergency patches Wednesday for two decade-old bugs that let anyone on the internet run code on millions of servers without permission. The rest of the internet spent the day discovering how many other things were also on fire.The bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, affect nearly every PHP version back to 5.4 (released in 2012). PHP quietly holds up WordPress, Drupal, Magento, and by some estimates, around 70% of the web. Cybersecurity firms Wiz and Calif found the bugs with help from OpenAI, and OpenAI says Calif found the bug with GPT-5.6 Sol, a generally available model. The plan was a tidy coordinated disclosure, and everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth. Details leaked, Amazon's honeypots logged an exploit attempt four days before the disclosure, and Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince reported thousands of exploit attempts in the 10 hours before the patch release and millions by the evening.The NSA and FBI told organizations to go offline if they couldn't patch, Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi urged site operators to act that night, Finland and several other European governments pulled sites preemptively, and the St. Louis Fed's FRED site went dark. PHP was merely the headliner. This week's full lineup of cyber scares included a CVSS 10.0 GitLab bug, Railway pausing all deployments after someone got into its environment-variable store, Node.js patches, Plex servers exploited to mine crypto, SafePay ransomware, and eMudhra, an Indian certificate authority whose private keys were small enough to guess. One of them was the number 4. (Yes, that was the whole private key; easy to remember, but...)OUR TAKEThe most worrying part of this story is that this internet-breaking exploit didn't come from those scary frontier models. The PHP Foundation worked with outside firms to scan its code with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos this year, but this exploit was only discovered in early August as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program. Even more shockingly, the exploit was discovered using GPT-5.6 Sol, a model you can pay for today, not one of the unreleased or cyber-specialized variants the labs keep caged up like a James Bond supervillain. Despite earlier testing with Claude Mythos, the vulnerability was identified through separate research using other AI models. Instead, it took a researcher’s intuition guiding a commodity model, and attackers have both.The pace at which attackers tried to utilize the exploit is like nothing ever seen before. That is the new norm. Announcing a patch in advance is supposed to get administrators ready, but it also fired a starting gun for every bad actor racing to find the bug before the fix landed. That tension between preparing defenders and tipping off attackers was always delicate, and with more cyber-capable open AI models around, the announcement window will continue to compress toward zero. Threat intel and incident response firm Mandiant already puts mean time-to-exploit at negative seven days; attackers typically strike a week before a patch exists. The zero-day clock has struck midnight, and had an integer overflow as it kept going. What this means is that human-only cybersecurity is truly obsolete, and untenable. Security in an agentic world must also be agentic; Hugging Face was the preview in July, breached by OpenAI’s own models during testing, and this is the new reality with broad access to capable coding agents. Machine-speed attackers need machine-speed defenders."Zion, hear me! It is true, what many of you have heard. The machines have gathered an army and as I speak, that army is drawing nearer to our home." – Morpheus ... or your dramatic IT security lead during an all-handsYou should be a little scared, I am. A lifelong nerd, I ran a personal server in high school, and in the late 2000s I had to learn some security practices because my little experimentation box was getting bombarded by automated SSH password-guessing, port-scanning, and general exploit attempts a full decade before the first GPT paper in 2018. The spiders were already probing everything. LLMs cranked that dynamic up to 11, then ripped the knob off. I turned off my home server on Wednesday and unplugged most of my IoT devices until I have time to use the best available model to help me patch, replace, or reflash each one. If I write something testy about the DPRK, should I worry about them flipping my smart switches until something shorts? Do I have to root my Roomba to keep it from being taken over and trying to boop the power button on my PC? Most IoT software is forgotten after creation (when did you last patch your smart fridge?), and Anthropic's red team just ran a 26-billion-parameter model across 15 $55 Android TV boxes. With a long tail of vulnerable devices, botnets of hacked devices may graduate from DDoS attacks to distributed inference for whoever controls them.All software stacks have been non-consensually thrown into the Thunderdome, but this is only the beginning of the battle. More exploits are coming, probably worse ones, but every serious patch and every agent-reviewed release strengthens the code the world runs on. A more secure internet is being born from its parents' death, like the Olympians descending to overthrow the Titans.Some code is already ready for that world. Bitcoin Core is among the most heavily reviewed codebases on earth, and no comparable compromise has been reported. Most of these exploits exist because no human can hold an entire codebase in their head; almost nothing outside TempleOS was written by one person, and even that wouldn't guarantee spotting every step of an exploit chain. Agents, with long context and a shared, eidetic memory, can do the comprehensive reviews that human teams struggle with.Modern cryptography held: nobody broke the algorithms the internet relies on. eMudhra fell on its face generating keys, not at math. At the peak of the panic, I recommended that our clients verify instructions by signing from their wallets, an additional safeguard against compromised intermediaries.Security through obscurity is finished. There will be a culling of unmaintained websites, projects, and blockchains. It is not going to be pretty, but what survives will be an internet worth trusting. Just don't make your private key 4. Educate yourself, protect yourself; it is going to get more dangerous before it gets safer. Put on your helmets, man the trenches with your agents, and hold the line. Don’t give the clankers an inch. – Thad Pinakiewicz
Issuers Object to OKX-ICE’s Stock Tokenization PlansWHAT HAPPENEDAt least 16 issuers opt out of OKX-ICE’s tokenized stock platform. Microsoft, Apple, Google, Goldman Sachs, CoreWeave, and Broadcom are among at least sixteen issuers that have notified OKXICE TSV, a joint tokenized stock venture between crypto-exchange OKX and NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange, that they object to their stocks being tokenized. The full list of issuers who have opted out: Microsoft, Apple, Google, Goldman Sachs, CoreWeave, Broadcom, UnitedHealth Group, Rocket Lab, Qualcomm, Caterpillar, McDonald’s, Western Digital, Nasdaq, Verizon, Cerebras Systems, and Applied Optoelectronics. The Securities & Exchange Commission released its “innovation exemption” on September 17 shortly after the CLARITY Act’s failure to advance in the U.S. Senate. The exemption creates a pathway to allow for legal, regulated secondary trading of tokenized securities outside of the Reg NMS system by allowing for the creation of Tokenized Securities Venues (TSV), a new type of onchain trading venue. Under the innovation exemption, the TSV must enact trading volume limits, enforce market-wide halts, and ensure that security tokenholders have performed know-your-customer (KYC) onboarding. So far, at least three separate entities have notified the SEC that they intend to launch TSV: Canton (with “TSV LLC”), Perpetuals.com, and OKXICE.OUR TAKE For years, crypto and blockchain advocates have pushed for the ability to trade stocks onchain, and in September the SEC finally delivered a pathway, but one that has set up a new battlefield with several fronts.Third-party sponsored vs. Issuer-sponsored. The issuers who opted out are utilizing an escape valve the SEC allowed when it included the right for third parties to tokenize securities, not just their original issuers. Proponents of third-party tokenization, whether by utilizing swaps, a debt-security structure, or some type of SPV wrapper, argue that they provide what investors want most: access to economic exposure in many investments. Firms like Kraken (xStocks), Ondo Finance, Coinbase, Robinhood, and OKXICE have pursued this path; all but Ondo are exchanges. On the other side, firms like Superstate, Securitize, Figure, and Bullish (Equiniti) argue that third-party issued tokens do not convey all the features of a security, such as legal, economic, and governance rights. We’ve written about this dispute extensively, and the 16 opt-outs from OKXICE’s third-party tokenization is just the latest salvo. DeFi vs. TradFi. The innovation exemption also draws a fascinating middle ground between DeFi and TradFi. What the innovation exemption allows for is more aptly described as onchain finance than decentralized finance. The TSV, whether comprised solely of one AMM or a conglomeration of AMMs, issuers, transfer agents, or other involved parties, must notify the SEC of its intentions, provide certain reporting, and crucially perform certain responsibilities that can only be performed with a level of control. The TSV is not quite an exchange or an ATS, but it’s also not quite DeFi in the commonly understood sense. Trade halts, KYC, and volume limits are not things that permissionless DeFi can perform today. The requirement that trading be limited to those who have been KYC’d, in particular, will make legal, American tokenized securities substantially less composable in the broader onchain environment, at least in the near term. But the TSV can ultimately allow for trading outside the Reg NMS system and does not need to register as a national securities exchange or alternative trading system (ATS). Not quite DeFi, but not quite TradFi.An interesting aspect of the approach taken by the SEC is that the “innovation exemption” offers exemptive relief in an unconventional way. The Commission did not look at an entity or set of entities and say “you’re exempt for these reasons.” In fact, the term TSV was invented by the SEC in the order itself, and no “TSV” exists yet. So, rather than a typical exemptive relief, the Commission has presented a new pathway, one that seems to thread the needle between rules, statutory authorities, and a maze of stakeholders. Whether this approach can be successful in promoting an innovative and experimental new environment for securities trading remains to be seen, and the answer to the question will ultimately determine the outcome of the third front in the tokenized securities battle.Onshore vs. Offshore. Onshore tokenized securities under the innovation exemption face an uphill battle in the market. If they cannot deliver a better product and comparable user experience to an offshore, third-party issued tokenized security that is fully composable in DeFi once accessed via VPN, then the whole experiment could fall flat. It’s very early still in the application of the innovation exemption, and we and many others will have more to say and announce in the coming weeks and months, but it is crucial that the innovation exemption yields tangible benefits, at least in actionable learnings to inform next steps in designing a viable onchain securities market, if that onchain securities market is to be built in the United States and not in Malta, Abu Dhabi, or the Caymans. – Alex Thorn
Solana Alpenglow Upgrade Ships. Adoption is the Real TestWHAT HAPPENEDOn Wednesday, at slot 459,653,000, Solana activated the long-awaited Alpenglow update to mainnet, changing Solana’s consensus protocol for the first time since its launch.Heralded as “the biggest upgrade in Solana’s history” by Solana’s core developer lab Anza, the upgrade improves both finality and the network’s fault tolerance model. Transactions on Solana are now designed to finalize in roughly 150 milliseconds instead of the 12 seconds required under Solana’s previous TowerBFT consensus mechanism. The upgrade also introduces a new “20 + 20” resilience model, remaining secure against 20% hostile stake while tolerating up to an additional 20% of stake going offline, for a combined 40% of stake that can be unavailable or adversarial. This differs from the traditional Byzantine fault-tolerance assumptions used by many other chains, which are typically resilient only to 33% on both counts.The Alpenglow update is staged across three phases. Wednesday’s activation introduced phase 1 through Votor, which moves validator voting offchain and removes Proof of History from its previous role in consensus. Moving votes offchain frees up blockspace previously consumed by vote transactions and makes it available for user transactions. Phase 2 is expected to improve the leader handover process so the next leader can begin constructing blocks more quickly, while Phase 3 will implement Rotor, a new block-propagation design intended to replace Solana’s Turbine mechanism and reduce the number of hops required to distribute block data. For a more in-depth overview of the upgrade’s technical details and roadmap refer to our prior coverage here and here.Alpenglow arrives as part of a broader set of performance upgrades Solana has been rolling out in parallel over the past few months. Most notably, the network recently completed a staged reduction in slot times from 400 milliseconds to 200 milliseconds, increasing the frequency of block production. Together with Alpenglow’s faster finality, the shorter slot times are intended to tighten the gap between transaction submission, inclusion, and irreversible settlement, while later phases of Alpenglow (fast leader handover and Rotor) are designed to reduce remaining sources of latency in block construction and propagation.OUR TAKE Protocol upgrades on par with Alpenglow, for example Ethereum's "The Merge," have historically been important milestones that draw external interest in blockchains. They demonstrate novel technical innovation and a level of competency from core developers. That dynamic has shifted as crypto markets have matured. The reason is simple. Technological innovation alone is no longer enough. Adoption and real use are the most important metrics.That doesn’t mean upgrades like Alpenglow are insignificant. Far from it. General-purpose smart contract platforms like Solana are built to perform on par with centralized financial markets and need to continually evolve to remain competitive. Even the most established smart contract platform, Ethereum, is nowhere close to a place where it can ossify. Doing so would risk leaving any chain in the dust to existing alternatives or new entrants. Protocol updates not only demonstrate core developer technical capability, but the ecosystem’s ability to anticipate and adapt the underlying chain to changing use cases that drive real demand.In that context, Alpenglow is an important step forward for Solana. Shortening finality improves performance for trading venues, bridges, and payment applications (among many use cases). Coupled with other changes to the protocol across slot times and tokenomics, it continues to position Solana as one of the few high-performance decentralized blockchains with an organic user and developer base. As I wrote following Solana’s Accelerate conference in May, for the past year or so Solana has been “building backwards,” trying to recapture market share in verticals like perpetuals, prediction markets, and DeFi, where others clearly lead. Alpenglow is a step toward reversing that dynamic.Whether this technical progress translates into real growth depends on where Solana decides to compete. While Solana may be able to regain some market share in verticals where it already lags, it will be incredibly hard to become the default venue. As our quarterly Solana updates show, despite extensive efforts, the chain has largely failed to penetrate perpetuals or prediction markets (although it is still early on that journey). For Solana, the golden ticket so far has largely been the meme economy, which despite poor external optics, has been an incredible success from a fee and revenue standpoint. It is also competing aggressively to be a leader in the tokenization boom. But perhaps the most overlooked vertical is a growing cohort of real businesses that are using the chain for capital formation and as their operational infrastructure. Those are the green shoots that, when complemented with a world-class and driven group of core developers, can accelerate Solana’s adoption and growth. Devs are shipping. Do not fade them. - Lucas Tcheyan

Later-stage deals’ share of the total remained elevated compared to the historical norm, reflecting the market's growing maturity.

Meanwhile, VC-backed crypto company valuations (bars, left-hand vertical axis in the chart below) rebounded to a new all-time high of roughly $90m in Q3 2026, as valuations across the broader VC complex outside of crypto also rose to a new high. In Q3 2026, the median crypto deal size (feverline, right-hand axis) fell sharply from Q2’s all-time high of $5m to roughly $3m.

News Release
Jackdaw field consent is correct for UK climate targets and the economy, Wood Mackenzie analysis shows

21 October 2026
3 minute read

Email
Share by email

The UK government has granted fresh consent for the Jackdaw gas/condensate field in the North Sea. OPRED and the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero confirmed the decision on 21 October 2026, with first gas possible within weeks.
The decision ends a process dating back to January 2025, when a judicial review suspended the original 2022 development consent on the grounds that scope 3 emissions had not been fully considered. The regulator accepted Adura’s submission that Jackdaw's climate impact is not significant and will not materially affect the UK's climate change commitments. Wood Mackenzie's P50 estimate puts total greenhouse gas emissions over the field's nine-year life at 24 MtCO2e, equivalent to 1.8% of remaining UKCS emissions.
Jackdaw is a 68 mmboe gas/condensate field 225 kilometres east of Aberdeen, the biggest pre-production asset on the UKCS after Rosebank and Cambo. It is 100% owned by Adura, a 50/50 joint venture between Shell UK and Equinor UK, with £1.2 billion invested to date. We forecast gas production in 2027 to average 140 million cubic feet per day, or 6% of UKCS gas supply.
The emissions case rests on what domestic production displaces. The UK's gas demand is more than double UKCS supply, and the country will remain a net gas importer across all future scenarios, including net zero. Replacing Jackdaw's output with an equivalent volume of US LNG would have resulted in a net increase of 3.5 MtCO2e in scope 1 and 2 emissions. The UK Climate Change Committee is clear that meeting carbon budgets requires reducing fossil fuel demand through accelerating the uptake of EVs, heat pumps, and wider electrification. Blocking domestic gas supply would not have advanced that objective.
The decision arrives as energy prices have moved sharply higher. NBP gas prices have climbed to over 200 pence per therm, the highest since 2022, while Brent has again surged past US$100 per barrel. Under our Q4 2026 base price assumptions, Wood Mackenzie estimates that government tax receipts from Jackdaw could total £1.5 billion (nominal), representing a 69% share of the remaining undiscounted pre-tax cash flow. Eighty per cent of this sum could accrue in this parliament.
For Adura, we estimate Jackdaw will generate £430 million of post-tax cash flow in 2027 alone, while the higher prices help lift the project IRR from 9% to over 14%.
The stakes extended well beyond a single field. Had approval been withheld, Wood Mackenzie assessed that over £20 billion (real terms) of future UKCS greenfield investment would very likely have been lost, along with the industry's confidence in the consent process. Jackdaw and Rosebank together are expected to support over 800 jobs and deliver a combined 20-year gross value add of over £25 billion to the UK economy. Jackdaw alone will account for 11% of Adura's net production over the project’s lifetime.
Gail Anderson, Research Director, North Sea Upstream at Wood Mackenzie, said: "Blocking Jackdaw would require the UK to import more emissions-intensive LNG to meet UK gas demand. We estimate that would have increased net emissions by 3.5 MtCO2e, not reduced them. The correct way to tackle the climate crisis is to reduce demand for oil and gas.
At current prices, Jackdaw could generate £1.5 billion in vital tax receipts for the Treasury. Blocking it would have seen these revenues go elsewhere, while over £20 billion of future greenfield UKCS investment would very likely be lost. These are compelling reasons why North Sea production should remain a vital part of the UK's energy mix."

Staying Invested: After The Worst Day, The Best Day May Come Quickly

The S&P 500’s worst day and the best day that followed
have something in common: you can’t predict either one.

October 2026

The S&P 500’s worst day and the best day that followed have something in common: you can’t predict either one. The table below underscores the risk of stepping out of the market during periods of heightened volatility. While selling after a sharp decline may feel like a way to avoid further losses, some of the market’s biggest gains have historically occurred soon after its biggest drops. For example, in 2020 and 2025, the S&P 500’s best day after the year’s worst came just six and three trading days later, respectively.
Not every major downturn is followed by a quick rebound — some recoveries take much longer. In 2018, the best day came more than ten months after February’s big drop. The real takeaway is that investors rarely know when a rebound will come, which makes timing an exit and re-entry very difficult. Successfully avoiding the worst day and re-entering at the ideal moment means being right twice. Staying invested helps ensure participation in the recovery, which can be critical to long-term returns.
