articles.title: Europe’s T+1 journey: towards 90% global alignment – Deutsche Bank
articles.text:
Trust and securities services, Macro and markets

Europe’s T+1: towards 90% global alignment

21 October 2026

When the EU, UK and Switzerland move from T+2 to T+1 settlement in October 2027, most of the world’s major markets will be aligned on a one-day settlement cycle. Reporting from Sibos Miami 2026, flow explores why a successful transition will depend on the collective efforts of the entire post-trade ecosystem

10 min read
Reading time could not be calculated{{@root.language.[rwd.flow.readingTime.error]}}

At Sibos Miami 2026, Swift set out a vision of “a new frontier of trust, speed and transformation”, one in which the financial community comes together to tackle the shared challenge of moving money faster.
That message resonates strongly in the securities services industry, where markets around the world are navigating the shift towards globally aligned T+1 settlement (trade date plus one).
While the topic of T+1 settlement has featured in several preceding Sibos events, it was the immediacy of Europe’s pending transition to T+1 that brought an intensity to panel and client discussions in Miami.
Shorter settlement cycles are, as the US Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation puts it, driving the need for robust post-trade automation “to enable faster post-trade processing, ensure compliance, and strengthen operational resilience in an increasingly connected marketplace.”1 However, getting the world’s market infrastructure participants to align on a joined-up move has been easier said than done.
“Today roughly three quarters of the world’s equity market capitalisation – so some US$114trn – already settles on a T+1 basis or faster. That includes the US, Canada, and India – with China already running on a T+0 cycle,” said Emma Johnson, Head of Industry Advocacy & Insight at The ValueExchange, as she moderated the panel ‘T+1 and the race for global settlement alignment’.
In less than a year, 30 markets across the EU, UK and Switzerland will move to T+1 settlement, increasing that share of global market capitalisation from 75% to around 90%. While on paper this looks like a global alignment, Johnson cautions that “when you get under the bonnet it’s far from it.”
Based on insights from two Sibos panels, this article examines the progress made and remaining hurdles as Europe enters the final stretch of its T+1 transition.

Fragmented but mobilising

The EU T+1 Industry Committee’s second market-wide Readiness Survey, conducted by the ValueExchange and published in July 2026,2 indicated accelerated preparations for the October 2027 transition with “strong engagement” from the industry, but identified “clear gaps in vendor guidance, fund share-dealing readiness and operational dependences”.3 The complexity of the alignment across different countries and market infrastructure segments is underlined in the survey’s summary of response sources. See Figure 1.

Figure 1: Europe’s T+1 journey in Q2 2026: a fresh snapshotSource: EU T+1 Industry Committee Readiness Survey (Q2 2026), The ValueExchange

Hannah Elson, Global Head of Custody at J.P. Morgan, sees the EU+ journey as “fragmented but mobilising”. The difference between this migration and those that preceded it (such as India and North America) is “the sheer number of market infrastructures, currencies, and regulators we are trying to align around one single day and point in time”. Euroclear’s Head of Market Liquidity, Mike Reece, added that while the actual direction of travel was aligned, “the operational reality remains fragmented and as markets accelerate at different paces we are going to have to continue living with that friction”.

‘T+1 and the race for global settlement alignment’: Left to right: Emma Johnson, Head of Industry Advocacy & Insight, The ValueExchange; Vijay Chandok, CEO, National Securities Depository (India); Dimitri Pattyn, Deputy Director General for Market Infrastructure and Payments, European Central Bank; Hannah Elson, Global Head of Custody, J.P. Morgan; Sachin Mohindra, Executive Director, Goldman Sachs; and Mike Reece, Head of Market Liquidity, Euroclear

Panellists agreed that inconsistent regulatory requirements in the region were “worrying”. The last time the bloc pulled together on a comparable regulatory requirement was the implementation of the Central Securities Depositories Regulation’s (CSDR) Settlement Discipline Regime. Introduced on 1 February 2022, the regime brought in a suite of measures aimed at reducing settlement fails and improving settlement efficiency across European markets.
Elson said one of the learning points from SDR was the disruption caused by a lack of regulatory harmonisation across jurisdictions, which resulted in chaos for those first few weeks in terms of reporting and data and standards. This translated into a lot of operational risk. With market participants now operating in an environment of settlement penalties, the impact of any disruption could be amplified unless it is effectively mitigated. As a result, readiness cannot be confined to market infrastructures alone; all participants across the settlement chain must be fully tested, prepared and aligned before the move to T+1.
An example of the impact when readiness is uneven across communities is the controlled extension of Standards Release 2026, which was announced by Swift shortly before Sibos.4 This postponed the move from unstructured to structured postal addresses for ISO 20022 payment processes, which was originally scheduled for November 2026 (see the flow article ‘Building on today’s payment foundations’). The securities element is being decoupled from the broader release and will go live in June 2027, given the T+1 migration target in October of that year. See Figure 2.
The industry must now absorb two distinct Swift releases in a single calendar year. The June 2027 release is critical. It represents the final messaging baseline before Europe adopts T+1 in October 2027. Several readiness milestones depend on SR2026 changes, and it now adds pressure to the project agenda for firms in 2027 as they prepare for the T+1 transition.

Figure 2: Swift’s Standards Release 2026 – decoupled securities-related changesSource: Swift, Deutsche Bank

Working together

Dimitri Pattyn, Deputy Director General for Market Infrastructure and Payments at the European Central Bank (ECB), agreed that the move to T+1 in Europe is more complex than that of other jurisdictions. He noted that a successful T+1 needs the reach of stakeholders and coverage in terms of processes. This was why the European Securities and Markets Authority, the ECB and the European Commission established a governance structure with the EU T+1 Coordination and EU T+1 Industry Committees. The EU T+1 Industry Committee launched a roadmap in July 2025.5 This body has been fundamental to coordinating the EU’s go-live preparations.

‘Making T+1 a reality: standards, data and collaboration’: Left to right: Jennie Baisch, Director, Global Securities Strategy, Swift; Ruchi Saraswat, Head of Technology Funding & Payments, Royal Bank of Canada; Daniel Clark, Global Head of Depositary Receipts, Head of Trust & Securities, APAC and MEA Deutsche Bank; Laura Cote, Senior Vice President, U.S. Bank; and Camille Papillard, Deputy Head of Financial Intermediaries & Corporates Client Line for Securities Services, BNP Paribas

The points about collaboration within the industry, alignment and testing were developed further in the ‘Making T+1 a reality’ panel. “T+1 is mostly about collaboration from different angles,” commented Camille Papillard of BNP Paribas.
Firstly, this must be within organisations because “you need to make sure that internally you have the systems that interconnect and teams that talk to each other much more than they used to,” she continued. Papillard’s point was that before there were 12–14 hours to manage a settlement, but with T+1 this is reduced to 3–4 hours. The batch approach with separate teams no longer works.
Secondly – as illustrated in the Readiness Survey (see Figure 1) – collaboration must be across the whole value chain. She highlighted that 64% of respondents had said that “counterparty, intermediary and tech provider dependency” were their biggest hurdles to success. She continued, “You need to know how your broker, your custodian and the central securities depositories (CSDs) are going to behave and adapt when working on your own readiness.” Furthermore, given the number of CSDs (Europe’s network comprises more than 30 national and international CSDs) it will be “very challenging” to manage testing if each CSD has their own testing plan.

Learning points from live T+1 markets

Although North America’s migration to T+1 in 2023 was much simpler than the current European journey, it was agreed there are some useful learning points. Laura Cote from U.S. Bank said that while collaboration was key to the outcome in the US, education and automation also “really enable success”. In her opinion these two factors will be key to success in Europe “because of the number of players in the mix”.
Ruchi Saraswat of the Royal Bank of Canda reflected on the need for “collaboration across counterparties” in addition to automation and strengthened tech infrastructure, given there are “so many areas which require each one of them to step in and have a human intervention”.
Asset managers want their allocations much earlier and while straight through processing (STP) without manual intervention made this possible in 2023, for 2027 there needs to be further compression. Pre-trade settlement instructions need to be available earlier. Across the transaction lifecycle, she said, “there is no room for errors or delays, and it all has to be automated; there cannot be any gaps in communication”. In her view, despite the successful North America migration, there were too many exceptions in the system requiring manual intervention. “Rather than just having a protocol to align and manage our exceptions, we need to start building a centralised system,” she argued.
Turning to Asia, Deutsche Bank’s Daniel Clark emphasised the importance of collaboration between regulators, market infrastructures, CSDs and industry participants, noting the value of constructive industry engagement during consultation periods to help shape practical and resilient market frameworks.
The bank’s white paper, ‘Asia T+1: speed without fragility’ (September 2026) sets out a potential toolkit for consideration as markets across the region assess the transition to T+1. It recognises the complexities of Asia’s diverse market landscape, including multiple time zones and currencies, varying levels of market maturity, market fragmentation and distinct regulatory frameworks.
China Northbound Connect, continued Clark, “has been in operation for more than 10 years and was designed around a highly controlled pre-trade framework, with securities settlement effectively operating on T+0 and cash settlement on T+1”. This model requires investors to confirm securities availability before entering a sell trade, reflecting the market’s specific settlement structure and controls.
“India, by comparison, adopted a different transition approach by moving to T+1 in January 2023, implementing the change through a phased migration across different market segments. This required market participants to manage both T+2 and T+1 processes during the transition, highlighting the operational considerations involved in a market-wide settlement cycle change.”

Enriching the data

“Data is critical and enriching the data is equally important,” Clark concluded, noting this was particularly evident during India’s transition. “The adoption of foundational data standards has helped improve transparency across the transaction lifecycle. From our perspective stronger and more consistent data supports more effective tracking, facilitates investigation and repair processes, and can help reduce settlement exceptions by enabling participants to identify issues across the value chain.”
J.P. Morgan’s Elson had made a similar point in the other ‘Race for global settlement alignment’ panel, explaining that the data provided “a much greater level of visibility and transparency around where trades are in the lifecycle, what the causes of failures are, and what the interconnectivity is between all the different points”. This helps her operations teams and clients “understand the efficiencies and inefficiencies in their flows”.
By the time the Sibos community reconvenes next year there will be just days to go until the T+1 transition in Europe. The discussions at Sibos 2027 in Singapore therefore look set to take on a rather different tone...

articles.title: The US should consider allowing Chinese production of electric vehicles in America under certain conditions
articles.text:
Publication Type
Policy Briefs

The US should consider allowing Chinese production of electric vehicles in America under certain conditions

Alan Wm. Wolff (PIIE)

Policy Brief 26-18

October 2026

Photo Credit: China Daily via Reuters

XLinkedInBlueskyEmailShare

Key Takeaways

The US could replace the blanket ban on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) with a phased, conditional approach that allows Chinese automakers to produce in the US, within clear limits, as long as they source substantial US local content, create American jobs, and transfer Chinese technology—in short, provide measurable benefits to the US economy.
National security risks would have to be managed, including by establishing strict rules on vehicle data privacy, supply chain transparency, oversight of Chinese state subsidies, and protection against data weaponization.
Past US experience with international industrial competition in color televisions, semiconductors, solar panels, and wind turbines offers practical lessons on designing policies that encourage domestic innovation, job creation, and fair competition.
Carefully regulated Chinese investment in the US could lower EV prices, accelerate climate goals, and help ease US-China tensions.

Body
In September 2026 President Donald Trump suggested he is open to Chinese automakers building cars in the US. The administration can and should explore ways to ease or remove the barriers to Chinese investment in EVs in the US. China's EV capabilities are formidable, so any policy to allow Chinese EV investment should carefully consider the perceived benefits to the US economy while focusing on guardrails to protect US jobs and national security.

articles.title: Japan's low-leverage economy should withstand rate hikes
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

21 Oct 2026

Japan’s low-leverage economy should withstand rate hikes

The rate hikes we expect over the next few months are unlikely to derail Japan’s economy from its modest but steady growth path. Most firms and households will be able to withstand a rise in interest rate costs thanks to their healthy balance sheets.

Most companies will likely maintain a reasonable spread between return on assets and interest rate costs thanks to their low leverage and rising profitability. However, an analysis of small firms shows that a 1ppt rise in effective interest rates could increase the share of loss-making small firms from 27% to 31%.

On aggregate, the Japanese are net savers and rate hikes will have a net positive impact by raising deposit rates. However, people in their 30s and 40s tend to be net debtors due to large, overwhelmingly floating-rate mortgages, making them vulnerable. Although higher rates will weaken already stagnant residential investment, their impact on overall economic growth should be limited.

The economy’s overall resilience to higher interest rates may allow the Bank of Japan to hike its policy rate beyond 1.75% to prevent further weakening of the yen and/or the de-anchoring of inflation expectations driven by prolonged cost-push inflation. However, the potential damage to vulnerable small firms and stretched household finances could make the government more cautious, exerting pressure on the bank.

articles.title: The surprising case for investing when the Fed’s raising rates
articles.text:
Markets and Economy

The surprising case for investing when the Fed’s raising rates

•
Chief Global Market Strategist and Head of Strategy & Insights

October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

Historically, the stock market performed better over the subsequent 1-, 2- and 3-year periods following rate hikes than it did following rate cuts.

The Fed generally raises interest rates when nominal economic growth is strong and cuts rates when economic conditions are deteriorating.

Rather than viewing every Fed hike as a warning to pull back, history suggests investors may want to consider a different response.

Few things get investors' attention quite like a Federal Reserve rate hike.
Every Fed meeting is dissected. Every word from policymakers is parsed. Every move in the bond market is treated as a potential signal of what comes next. And lately, the message from the 2-year US Treasury yield has been hard to miss. It has climbed meaningfully, suggesting the market believes the Fed may have more rate hikes to go.
That naturally raises the question. Should investors be worried?
At some point, Fed tightening has helped bring most economic cycles to an end. But as we like to say, it’s often not the first-rate hike that matters. It’s the last one. For now, it’s difficult to see the Fed being forced to raise rates to a level that meaningfully derails economic growth. Inflation expectations remain relatively contained, while the labor market is generating only modest job growth. The Fed may have more tightening ahead, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s on a path toward ending the cycle.
But that is here and now. Let's step back from the Fed watching and put rate hikes into a much broader market context.
We looked at every Fed rate hike and every Fed rate cut since the launch of the S&P 500 Total Return Index in 1989. The results may surprise investors. Historically, the stock market performed better over the subsequent 1-, 2- and 3-year periods following rate hikes than it did following rate cuts.

Stocks gained more after rate hikes than rate cutsBar chart with 2 data series.S&P 500 Total Return Index: Annualized returns following Fed rate hikes and rate cuts. Sept. 1989 to Sept. 2026Source: Bloomberg, L.P. Sep. 24, 2026. Indices cannot be purchased directly by investors. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Sep. 1989 is the start date of the S&P 500 Total Return Index.The chart has 1 X axis displaying categories. The chart has 1 Y axis displaying Values. Data ranges from 0 to 0.Chart annotations summaryNumber of rate hikes: 52Number of rate cuts: 60Created with Highcharts 11.4.8ValuesChart context menuS&P 500 Total Return Index: Annualized returns following Fed rate hikes and rate cuts. Sept. 1989 to​Sept. 2026Source: Bloomberg, L.P. Sep. 24, 2026. Indices cannot be purchased directly by investors. Past performance does not​guarantee future results. Sep. 1989 is the start date of the S&P 500 Total Return Index.Number of rate hikes: 52​Number of rate cuts: 60Raise ratesCut ratesStocks gained more after rate hikes than rate cutsEnd of interactive chart.

Why? The Fed generally raises interest rates when nominal economic growth is strong. Those environments have also historically been supportive of corporate profitability. Rate cuts, by contrast, often occur because economic conditions are deteriorating and the Fed is responding to that weakness.
Maybe the better question isn't whether investors should fear rate hikes, but what they should do when they happen.
Investing during rate hikes
A $10,000 investment in the S&P 500 Total Return Index in September 1989 would have grown to more than $462,000 by September 2026. Now imagine an investor who started with the same $10,000 but also invested an additional $1,000 the day after each of the Fed's 52 rate hikes over that period. That portfolio would have grown to more than $962,000, more than twice the value of the original investment.
Of course, that strategy involved investing substantially more than the original $10,000, but that’s precisely the point. There were 52 rate hikes over our period of analysis, meaning the investor put an additional $52,000 to work, roughly $1,000 every 8.5 months. The lesson isn't that investing the day after a Fed rate hike is the best possible strategy. It's that consistently adding investments when the Fed is tightening has historically been a good one.

Investing during rate hikesLine chart with 3 lines.S&P 500 Total Return Index: Buy and hold vs. adding over fixed periods vs. adding when Fed raises rates Sept. 1989 to Sept. 2026Source: Bloomberg, L.P. Sep. 24, 2026. A hypothetical example not intended to depict or predict the performance of any strategies. Indices cannot be purchased directly by investors. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Sep. 1989 is the start date of the S&P 500 Total Return Index.The chart has 1 X axis displaying categories. The chart has 1 Y axis displaying Values. Data ranges from 0 to 0.Created with Highcharts 11.4.8ValuesChart context menuS&P 500 Total Return Index: Buy and hold vs. adding over fixed periods vs. adding when Fed raises​rates Sept. 1989 to Sept. 2026Series 1Series 2Series 3Investing during rate hikesSource: Bloomberg, L.P. Sep. 24, 2026. A hypothetical example not intended to depict or predict the performance of any strategies. Indices cannot be purchased directly by investors. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Sep. 1989 is the start date of the S&P 500 Total Return Index.End of interactive chart.

Rate hikes are often evidence of a strong economy
So, should investors fear Fed rate hikes?
History suggests no. Rate hikes can eventually become restrictive enough to end an economic cycle, which is why we pay close attention to how far the Fed ultimately needs to go. But a rate hike itself is not inherently bad news for markets. Quite often, it is evidence of an economy strong enough to warrant tighter policy.
Rather than viewing every Fed hike as a warning to pull back, history suggests investors may want to consider a different response. Sometimes a rate hike isn't a reason to get out. It may be an opportunity to put more in.

Podcast
What agency means and looks like to girls – and why this matters

Listen on

Embedding Equality in Education

Embedding Equality in Education

Hosts:
Jennifer L. O’Donoghue and

Jennifer L. O’Donoghue

Deputy Director
- Center for Universal Education,

Senior Fellow
- Global Economy and Development

Edem Dorothy Ossai

Edem Dorothy Ossai

Africa Regional Coordinator
- NORRAG,

2021 Echidna Global Scholar
- Center for Universal Education, Brookings Institution,

Founder
- MAYEIN

October 21, 2026

Agency is lived, not something you have (or don’t have). Girls described agency in terms of freedom, identity, aspiration and action, courage, and perseverance. To them, it is something practiced and exercised every day and something that shifts with context, situation, and relationships.
Agency is both/and. Agency is individual and relational, contextual and situational, everyday and extraordinary, and about skills and systems.
Skills alone are not enough. Girls named confidence, problem-solving and leadership, but they were also clear that poverty and social norms limit what they can do. Supporting agency means we need to focus not only on skills and knowledge, but also on the relationships and systems around girls, with girls leading that change.
How we define agency shapes how we act. Moving away from one-size-fits-all approaches means designing work that reflects local realities, involves families, communities and institutions, and shifts from acting for girls to acting with them.

Girls in Kano, Nigeria, engage in community mapping exercise as part of LAAGA research. (Photo by Isa Wali Empowerment Initiative)

32 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

On this fourth episode of Embedding Equality in Education, Jenn O’Donoghue and Edem Ossai look at what LAAGA learned from girls about agency itself, drawing on definitions from more than 400 girls across multiple contexts. They explain how LAAGA’s framework for transforming systems with and for girls’ agency grew out of listening to girls and show why agency should be understood as multidimensional, dynamic and rooted in girls’ everyday lives.

TRANSCRIPT

[music]
OSSAI: Hello, everyone. Welcome to Embedding Equality in Education: Research and Action for Gender Just Futures. In our first season, we’ve been exploring the four key lessons from the work of the Learning and Action Alliance for Girls’ Agency. Our fourth episode will be focusing on what agency means and looks like for girls and why this matters.
My name is Edem Ossai. I’m your co-host, and I join you from Nigeria. In the third episode, we focused on how girls are centered as co-creators. Today, we’ll be moving on to discussing what we’ve learned from girls themselves about agency. So, what this means is that in this episode, you’ll be hearing about girls’ lived experiences directly from girls themselves. Isn’t that exciting?
I’ll hand over now to my co-host, Jennifer, who will let you into the next part of the conversation.
[0:59]
O’DONOGHUE: Thanks, Edem. And hello everyone, and welcome back to our 3Es podcast, Embedding Equality in Education. As Edem said, my name is Jenn. I’m Jennifer O’Donohue, senior fellow and deputy director here at the Center for Universal Education at Brookings, joining you from the Brookings podcast studio in Washington, D.C.
And it is great to be back with you again. I am really excited for these next few episodes where we’re really gonna start to unpack this framework that has developed through LAAGA’s work with girls around, as Edem said, how to engage girls’ agency to transform systems.
And, you know, before we we really start to dig into this framework, just a note on how we developed this framework. And I think this is really important for us because in the last episode we talked a lot about co-creation and what that process looked like of really starting with girls and and not going in with sort of preconceived ideas or preconceived definitions.
And this was really the same with the framework itself. So, we didn’t start with a framework, but rather approached this research and this work with girls with the idea that perhaps we could create a framework and create a framework with girls.
[2:07]
And so again, there was no sort of predefined model. We didn’t go in with a master plan of what we thought this was going to look like, but rather approached this in a way that was iterative, it was guided by the girls, and it was really about seeing what emerged as we took that first step forward with girls and talking with girls and understanding with girls, you know, what agency meant and looked like to them.
And then really taking our lead from the girls about what needed to happen next after that. And actually, I would love to bring in the voice of our our colleague, Jamila Razzaq from Pakistan, who was part of LAAGA’s work on the ground in Pakistan in South Punjab there, and really, I think does a great job of talking about this process of how the the work and the framework began to emerge with girls.
[2:54]
RAZZAQ: So first it was a bit distant from them, but similar to them, like, the girls from their communities. And then we provided a structure where they could discuss it among themselves. They reflect on it. And through discussions, they they formed their way of expression, like, how they understand and express their agency and understanding of agency and share it with us.
One thing, which was very surprising for me, which came as a surprise in this process was that how clear the girls were. I have done a lot of work on girls’ empowerment, where the girls are taken as passive recipient of the training or skills, which we go as as experts and share it with them.
But when we opened up the space where they could share their knowledge, their understanding, and their solutions, that was very surprising for us as researchers to see that girls were very clear what they want to be and what their future trajectory would be and who are the people who can support them, and where are the bottlenecks and barriers?
And then within the groups, when they discussed their strategies that how they navigate, they learn from each other so much.
[4:20]
O’DONOGHUE: So, as we heard from Jamila there, you know, really when we went into this work, the plan was to listen to girls, to follow girls where girls led us, and to adapt so that our work would adapt and be driven by the girls themselves. And so, if anything, I would say, the master plan in this framework creation for us was really to listen to girls. And that was where it it took off.
[4:44]
OSSAI: Thank you so much, Jenn. It’s so interesting to see what, you know, the picture that unfolds in this conversation when girls really share their perspectives. And just like you said, girls have led us into, you know, different aspects of their lives, starting with their communities.
So, the first place that girls took us to was their communities. And it’s so interesting what happens there. Girls identify key actors from families to teachers, community leaders to local authorities. Through our colleagues’ work in Vietnam, we had insights from girls around how their families play key roles in the exercise of their agency. Let’s listen to this perspective from this amazing girl’s voice in Vietnam.
[5:32]
GIRL 1 IN VIETNAM: {translated} My hardest decision is whether to continue pursuing my dream. It’s tough because my parents don’t agree with it. I want to become a lawyer, but my parents think that’s a difficult job and only boys can do it well. That’s been the hardest decision I’ve faced up to now.
[5:50]
OSSAI: You’ve just heard the voice of that girl in Vietnam, and how parents play a very pivotal role in the exercise of her agency. Making a decision about whether to continue her education or what choice of career to, you know, embark upon rests really, really strongly on parents’ approvals. So, it’s very key to understand the situations and the context and the environments that girls find themselves in, and the key actors and how they enable or confine girls’ actions or girls’ decision-making and dreaming.
And we have to emphasize at this point that the network of relationships we find ourselves, you know, surrounded by are so critical to our lives. It influences our aspirations. The the entire scope of our dreams are influenced actually by our peers, our parents, our teachers, what we see on the TV, our leaders, and this plays out every day in the lives of girls.
Through approvals and disapprovals, girls are able to pursue or prevented from pursuing many of the dreams that they have, that they reflect on and that, you know, grips and arrests their their hearts every day.
So, it’s very important, and in LAAGA, we take a very critical approach to moving from individual focus to systems and ecosystems. We recognize that many of the things we’re experiencing, or girls are experiencing are very systemic. And none of these things, issues or, you know, barriers, as we call them, can be solved by addressing them on our own.
[7:30]
O’DONOGHUE: Yeah, you know, I think this piece around the move from the, the shift really from that individual focus on a girl and her agency in particular, to really looking at ecosystems and, you know, who are those people around girls and and systems, what are those structures, and systems that exist around girls, was one of the key things that we learned from, you know, taking the step of really starting with girls and listening with girls.
And so, I think that that is something for us to hold in mind and we’ll continue to, to return to as we really move into talking about what girls showed us about agency. And just to to ask all of you, you know, as you’re listening, I think you’ll be able to hear with the girls, and from the girls here this connection between what a girl’s individual experience is like and how that individual experience fits within a system, you’ll hear girls talk about things like poverty, about educational opportunities.
And you’ll also hear the talk about the ecosystem. That’s, you know, of course, a technical word that we use, but they don’t necessarily talk about the ecosystem in that language. But they will talk about all of those people and those different actors that are around them.
So as we move forward into that I just want to remind everyone, I think we’ve talked about this in in some of our earlier episodes around methodology, but, you know, when we talk about listening to girls’ voices, we are talking about listening to more than 400 girls in our first round of research, and more than 100 girls in our second round of research.
So, let’s hear from some of the girls. In this next clip, we’ll hear from a girl in Vietnam and two girls in Nigeria as they talk about what agency means to them.
[9:09]
GIRL 2 IN VIETNAM: {translated} Agency means taking charge of yourself like doing your homework, keeping clean, working well with others, and joining school activities. It helps us become more independent, make friends, learn new things, and grow into our best selves.
[9:32]
GIRL 1 IN NIGERIA: {translated}  Agency means a courageous, resilient woman, and courage and resilient means, for example, someone who can speak their mind without fear or reservation.
[9:44]
GIRL 2 IN NIGERIA: {translated} What agency means to me is that I want to be a boss and own a big shop and also have employees that will work for me. I also want to help people around me.
[9:56]
O’DONOGHUE: So, you know, here this is really listening from over 500 girls in eight different country contexts, in Asia and Africa, in America and the Caribbean in particular, and Jamaica, as well as listening to over, you know, nearly a thousand community members from girls’ ecosystems.
So now, you know, I would love to to move us forward into really unpacking the definitions. What does agency mean to girls as they practiced agency, as they exercised that, as they expressed it? And again, to remind everyone that when we talk about agency here, we’re talking about dreams, aspirations, decisions, and actions. Those three Ds that we talked about in an earlier episode of dream, decide, and drive.
And so, Edem, would love to turn over to you to sort of share with us what were some of the common themes that we saw in girls’ definitions across these eight different country contexts.
[10:53]
OSSAI: Thanks, Jenn. And, you know, I’m so excited to have actually listened to many of these, you know, perspectives from the girls themselves.
And one thing that Jenn stresses is how, you know, we didn’t come with any preconceived definitions, so all of these perspectives were rooted in girls’ own words and experiences.
And another important thing that’s shown clearly for us was that there’s no single universal definition. Right? If you heard the quote from the girl in Vietnam, agency meant pretty much, like taking charge of her life and doing her homework. The ability to exercise, you know, that decision about when to do her homework, where to do her homework was for her, you know, a very strong expression of her agency.
Choosing, you know, who to join her in cleaning up, whether in school activities, like, who to form a team with. Right? And also listening to the girls from Nigeria about how agency was really exercising courage in the everyday decisions of their lives. Courage to, you know, perhaps answer a question in class, courage to, you know, go somewhere that maybe ordinarily she would have gone with her parents, accompanied by her parents.
[11:56]
Like, these very simple, mundane things are showing clearly how girls are moving from dreaming to decision-making and actually taking action, and it’s so powerful. Some of the powerful themes that emerged in these definitions was just the freedom to make choices, whether it’s from making the choice of, you know, where to sit down at home to do your homework, what time to make, do the homework, or where to go or who to spend time with, who to choose as a friend. That’s some kind of freedom that girls expressed in their definitions.
Identity. You know, the girls in Nigeria really emphasized on courage, the idea of that courageous woman. That empowered woman for them was the woman who was daring, audacious, courageous. Right? And so that formed a sense of identity.
And of course, the ability to move from aspirations to action. So, looking at the environment, surrounding environment, and its limitations or its strictures. those spaces that best enable them to move from dreams and desires in their heart to act them out, you know, allow for better expressions of their agency or for them reflect those moments where they’re best exercising agency.
And of course, again, courage, the courage to speak up. I think a lot of the girls, that was a common strand or theme that emerged in many of their responses: courage. And so, it tells you about environments that stifle that for them, and it’s so important for girls to be able to express that. They feel their freest, they feel their, they identify with their core most when they’re able to act courageously.
And of course, perseverance, working towards their dreams in spite of difficulties, negotiating barriers. These were many themes that emerged in girls’ definitions of agency as rooted in their own lived experiences. So, Jenn, what are your next thoughts about, you know, all of these findings that we’ve teased out?
[13:50]
O’DONOGHUE: When we think about these five common themes that you just talked about, that girls mentioned. Right? That agency is about freedom, it’s about identity, it’s about aspiration and action, it’s about courage, and it’s about perseverance.
Like, girls are experts on their communities. Girls are experts on their context. Girls are experts on their family life and their cultural identity and all of that, and they are the ones who are navigating these different spaces and structures, and they are the ones who are, who are making decisions and really, you know, leading the way in thinking about how we expand space for agency.
And to me, that seems really critical that girls were so aware of that cultural context for them. They’re so aware of the lived experience of this. They’re so aware that agency is not just about an individual. And I think in that sense, what we are seeing, at least so far in our work with LAAGA, is that we haven’t been running into that sort of tension that can exist when we go in and and communities might feel like, you know, someone is trying to change a community from the outside or is talking about something that is sort of external to their lived reality, because this is girls talking about their own lived realities.
So, you know, I think what we, what we see in these five common themes that, Edem, that you’ve really laid out is that they really reveal something deeper about agency, and that is that agency is not one-dimensional. Right? That agency is complex, it’s dynamic, it’s multidimensional. And and maybe with that, we can sort of segue into talking about what were the four dimensions of agency that emerged from LAAGA’s work?
[15:24]
OSSAI: I think you perfectly, you know, sum it up. When we think about going beyond, you know, just one dimension, and also going beyond something that’s theoretical to something that’s, you know, lived, practiced, and exercised every day.
One of the dimensions that stuck out, obviously, was the relational aspect of it. You know, it’s way beyond the individual. It it has to do with people around them and the web of very complex relationships that define our lives.
Another dimension that was very important was obviously how really contextual, or another word we can use is how very situational, you know, agency is. And so, for the girls in Pakistan, agency looks very different from how it looks like for the girls in Vietnam, for instance, or the girls in the Karamoja region in, you know, Kenya and Uganda. It’s so situational. It’s so tied to the lives that they live daily, the qualities, the characteristics, you know, the everyday affairs that play out in those, in those contexts.
And everyday agency is also really an everyday thing. It’s not something that’s momentous or, you know, something that’s such a milestone or a major event in your life happens and that’s when you exercise it. It’s happening every day in a very granular way, and it really goes beyond skills. It encompasses skills, it encompasses systems, and we must never lose sight of these dimensions when we’re talking about agency.
[16:45]
O’DONOGHUE: Yeah, and I think, you know, you laid them out for us, I think, in a in a way that was really crisp and and clear. And one thing for me about these dimensions is just remembering, right, it’s not an either/or. So, when you say it’s it’s not individual or it’s not relational, it’s both, right? It’s individual and relational.
So, it is this piece of a a person recognizing themselves as sort of capable of of independent thought, capable of independent action, and that that happens within a network of relationships. Right? So, they are doing things for themselves, and they’re being done with and for others. That they are setting aspirations by seeing the people around them and thinking about, “What does this mean for me? What does it mean for my family?”
That they are taking decisions, especially some of those, what girls talked about as, like, bigger decisions around education or career or family life, that they are reaching out to others to make these decisions, that they are negotiating with others, that they’re co-deciding with others.
And that when they’re taking action, they most frequently are not taking action alone, that they are really practicing that action with others, and that that action is often very collective. And I think our colleague Tran from Vietnam has a great example of what this looked like on the ground in Vietnam.
[18:03]
TRAN: Agency is not individual. It is shaped by relationship. And for that, we focused on three important groups. First one is of course girls themself, and they are not just participant, they are the central actors. They they shape the conversation in those spaces by sharing their own perspective. Also questioning, challenging the assumption. That is one group.
Second the people around them in their daily life, like the parents, the teachers, and also their peers, because our research showed that these relationship is very important to shape girls’ choices and also girls’ lives. And many girls also share with us that they tend to turn to their parents and teachers, when they need to make decision and move forward.
And third, institutional actors. And this includes the local government, the women’s union representative. And also, the development partners like, like us, because these are the people who influence the policy and the resources that can support girls.
[19:14]
OSSAI: I I just love how, you know, that piece really emphasizes that individual relational piece. And in that fluidity comes also the everyday nature of it. From how much money you’re gonna spend out of your pocket money, how much money you’re gonna keep to, like, when you’re filling your application forms, what choice of course will you study in the university? To where you’re gonna spend your weekend? Which auntie will you visit? Like, it’s so granular. It’s so, tied to how we, you know, show up in the world, and we show up in the world in very multidimensional ways.
[19:50]
So, I love how these dimensions really frontline for us the everyday sequence of agency.
[19:58]
O’DONOGHUE: Yeah, and I think, too, you know, and this is a point that you made in one of our previous episodes about the ways that sometimes pushing girls, right, into very public and and sort of extraordinary acts of agency like getting on stage and speaking out publicly about something, can be unsafe. Right?
And and I think one thing we’ve learned from the girls in this research, and this goes back to this contextual situational dimension, that you mentioned earlier, right, is is that in contexts where girls don’t feel that their voice is as welcome in public spaces, or in contexts where there may be real, very real security concerns that girls recognize those everyday moments of exercising their agency as acts of resistance. Right?
And, and that that is something that becomes very important to them, to seeing themself as a person who is exercising agency in these certain ways. And those ways might be ways that are not, again, seen by everyone, are not seen, you know, in these big public moments, but it become extremely important to girls and also to the people around them.
And and, you know, I want to return a little bit to this dimension and this relationship between the contextual and the situational, because to me, this is something that also has emerged from this this work and is so important to understand.
We often talk about, and I think we touched on this in an earlier episode as well, but this idea of, like, context as monolithic and, and unchangeable. Right? But really what we saw is that, yes, there are broader contextual pieces. Right? And these can include things like community structures, or or governance, basic services, access to health and education. Like, those are contextual factors. Gender norms. That’s also, you know, a contextual factor.
[21:42]
But those change, and those change in many ways because of the exercise of agency. So, what we saw is that, you know, when space was created to listen to girls’ voices. Right? So, like, when safe spaces were created, that that meant that girls could step into that space. Girls could more fully exercise their agency in that space. They would see themselves exercising their agency more. The people around them would see them exercising agency more.
And then that space would, would grow. There was, you know, an example that actually is not from our work, but from some colleagues who are working in in Turkey from a group called Sunun Kızları, where they talked about girls doing community mapping and doing this in sort of public spaces. And in the initial feeling of others, adults, being like, “Well, but girls don’t go around in these public spaces and do this type of community mapping.” And the group said, “Well, why don’t we just try?”
And so, once the girls did it, right, the context changed. And so now it’s a context where the girls are out, and they are in those communal spaces because they did the mapping. They’ve done the work around the safe spaces.
And so, again, this is sort of that interplay between this everyday extraordinary, the context that exists, and how do we create situations. And again, I’ll bring in the relations here. Right? How do people around girls work with girls to create situations that expand space for agency within a given context, so that those everyday acts of agency are sort of accumulating and becoming something extraordinary that is changing, that is changing context and that is, can change systems.
[23:16]
OSSAI: Yeah. You know, as you were talking, Jenn, like, what came to mind instantly was the example from Pakistan. Because I feel like in, you know, your last comment, like, really highlights a lot of themes. So, I recall that our colleague in, you know, Pakistan shared how rather than they themselves approaching the stakeholders, they invited girls to, you know, go home and approach stakeholders or key actors themselves with certain questions that they had, you know.
So, girls were the ones who were interviewing their aunties, their grandparents, and their mothers, asking them questions, right, to better understand the reasons behind their actions. And by just simply framing it differently.
So, these are everyday conversations that girls have in their lives, but girls don’t see the power that they’re exercising because perhaps people around them haven’t defined it, you know, or or labeled it appropriately.
But by just letting girls know that they were doing research, they were researchers themselves, it changed the, you know, picture entirely. Girls felt even more empowered. You know, there was more dignity to the status. So, they were as much as researchers as our colleagues who visited them and were consulting with them.
[24:19]
And it also, like you say, changes how girls are viewed by the key actors around them, who see these mundane actions of girls every day and just tend to casualize it or just trivialize it or just take it as like, “Yeah, yeah, there’s no big deal to it.”
But suddenly they’re seeing girls in a different light, that by asking those questions, girls gathered insights that became relevant for framing next steps in terms of what needs to be transformed. And suddenly the insights generated from these girls are forming the foundation of plans for transformation. Everybody respects, looks at the girl differently. Right?
So that example really illustrates for me the points that you just mentioned. It’s such an everyday thing, and these simple acts are actually extraordinary. They’re moving us forward every day. But because they’re repetitive, we think that they’re nothing. They are repetitive, but they’re propelling us to greater versions of ourselves. And it would be great if girls, you know, had a proper vocabulary to label themselves by, and if people around them also, you know, used the more respectful vocabulary for girls when they’re carrying out all these activities or decisions every day.
[25:23]
O’DONOGHUE: Yeah, and I, and I think, too, this piece around what it takes to really strengthen girls’ sense of agency, and that, you know, how, how that often gets tied to life skills curriculum, for example. And the girls here were very clear that, yes, like, being able to step into these spaces to, you know, to take these acts of both every day and extraordinary agency. Right? That that that does require skills, that that does require confidence. It requires skills around goal setting, around problem-solving, interrelational skills, negotiating, leadership.
So, girls were very, very clear and and, you know, very skilled, let me use the word skilled. Excuse the redundancy, but very skilled at identifying what were these skills that they felt they had, or that they felt that they needed to strengthen in order to more fully exercise that agency.
But importantly, the girls really emphasized that those skills by themselves were not enough. Right? And so, they, you know, they talked about all of these systems that they are really navigating that— and again, you know, to remind those of you who are listening, in episode two, we really dig into what it means to work with girls in marginalized contexts.
And so we are talking about working with girls who live in very highly marginalized contexts, you know, where systems like poverty, where systems like insecurity and and the inability, right, of of government and, and others to really respond to situations of insecurity, to respond to the climate crisis, to ensure that all girls have access to education and to learning, and and, you know, among other things. Those are some of the main ones that girls pointed out.
That that really means that agency work has to be about both understanding all of these things that are are sit within girls around skills, and really engaging those to move into action to transform systems. And so, I would love to ask you, Edem, to to sort of help us, and this is a teaser for what’s coming in in upcoming episodes, but, you know, this work that we have done to unpack these dimensions of agency is not just about naming something. Right? It’s not just a, an intellectual exercise, but it’s really about how do we understand this concept so that we can more effectively take action.
So, what what do these dimensions mean for you in terms of taking action?
[27:51]
OSSAI: You know, as you were asking that, I I I was recalling you know, the the perspectives shared by girls in Nigeria, you know, through the work of our colleague in Nigeria, Adefunke, where the girls, many of whom were teenage mothers, you know, were trying to reenter schooling and education again.
And they also stressed, you know, how moving from all of these findings through research to actual transformation really rests on both capability and structures. You know, for them, they emphasized, for instance, that, “Oh, getting us back to school, that’s nice, but who takes care of our babies.” Right? “What’s the affordability of schooling? How do we earn an income, you know, outside of the classroom to support ourselves and our babies?”
So, all of these things, you know, get us to really think about actionable steps. Right? And that brings us back to the framework. You know, if we want to transform systems with and for girls’ agency, we can’t just be comfortable with naming the problems, with saying, “Oh, they don’t have enough skills to negotiate,” or “Oh, there’s not enough, you know, after-school programs or childcare programs.”
What are we actually going to do about it? And also recognizing that it’s never going to be a one size fit all approach, especially given what we earlier emphasized about how situational these challenges are. So, you know, the priorities in one community may be vastly different in another community.
And the teaser, what we need to look forward to in the next episodes, is that, you know, we’re gonna be looking at local realities, how work is carried out across levels, whether individual level, relational level, like we stressed in this episode, and even the systemic levels. We’re gonna be seeing how to engage ecosystems, and these ecosystems, you know, really encompass families, communities, institutions, and even girl peer groups.
You’ll recognize in the next episodes how girls are exercising everyday agency. And don’t forget, in all our episodes, you can look forward to us centering girls as co-creators and decision-makers. So, from acting for girls, you, wherever you are and through the work that you do, you will learn and be able to act with girls.
[29:56]
O’DONOGHUE: Yeah, and I think speaking of acting with girls, we have a great example of that from our colleague Armene Modi in India.
[30:05]
MODI: You know, there are several examples and stories in our Ashta No Kai project where girls really took the lead, surprisingly so for us. And let me give you the first example. The first was about nine girls who had received bicycles through our bicycle bank project. This was an initiative to enable girls to access distant school, high schools, and high schools in India are from eighth to 10th grade. And the reason it was called a “bank” was that the girls had to return the bicycles after 10th grade, and then we would give them to other girls to use.
But the nine of these girls came to us at the end of 10th grade and said, “Can we keep these bicycles? We’d like to go to 11th and 12th grade,” which in India is junior college. We were of course delighted but realized that parents would find it difficult to fund their education, so we decided to establish a scholarship program.
So had it not been for these girls, we might have just felt okay sending girls to, you know, access high school. That means they wouldn’t get married at least until 16, 17, although the legal age for marriage in India is 18. For girls to articulate their desires, you know, and especially a desire to pursue an education we thought was something we need to support wholeheartedly.
[31:44]
O’DONOGHUE: I love this clip from from Armene where she talks about the surprise. Right? Armene talks about the the surprises that she experienced by engaging girls and engaging girls agency in this in this way. And I think, Edem, that really links up to what you were saying and and some of the key things that we need to hold in mind as we move from just talking about agency as a concept into what does it mean to take action for agency.
Agency is lived. It is not something that is just abstract or theoretical. It is complex. Right? It is dynamic. It’s multidimensional. And that it is something that girls exercise already every day in their lives. And how do we learn from that and expand the space with girls, with others around them, expand the space for the exercise of that agency, expand commitment to the exercise of agency, expand capacity for the exercise of agency, and really, you know, expanding and promoting our understanding of what agency means and looks like, and what that means that we need to do.
So again, our sort of tagline in LAAGA is that our research is about changing the world with and for young people. And so, you know, towards that end, looking forward to our next episode, and invite you all to join us for episode five, where we will move from girls to girls with communities, and really explore the question of how we have been working with girls and their communities to co-construct understandings of girls’ agency, of some of the challenges to agency in those communities, and of the solutions.
So, we look forward to having you join us in episode five. And thank you so much for joining us today on behalf of myself and my colleague.
OSSAI: Thank you for joining us. And if you want to access any of the resources we’ve published in the course of our work, just simply click the link in the description.
[music]
O’DONOGHUE: Thank you for listening to Embedding Equality in Education, a podcast from the Gender Equality in and through Education team in the Center for Universal Education at Brookings. Our sincere thanks to all the LAAGA members and others who contributed to this episode.
OSSAI: The show is produced and published by the Brookings Podcast Network. Thanks to the production team, including Ike Blake, supervising producer; Fred Dews, senior producer; Arushi Sharma, co-producer; Daniel Morales and Teddy Wansink, video producers; and Chris Chang, audio and video producer. Plus, thanks to Benji Aliaga and Madeline Chandler for their contributions to the show.
O’DONOGHUE: Daniel Morales also designed the show’s artwork. And a very big special thank you to our former senior project assistant and co-producer, Anya Kasubhai, who did so much to get this show launched.
OSSAI: Finally, our thanks to the productions team in the Office of Communications at Brookings.
O’DONOGHUE: Brookings gratefully acknowledges the support provided by Echidna Giving, Stone Family Foundation, and The LEGO Foundation in support of this work.
I am Jenn O’Donoghue.
OSSAI: And I am Edem Ossai.
O’DONOGHUE: Thank you for listening.

By

Aliya Robinson

What the regulatory backdrop means for private assets in DC plans

Explore how ERISA’s fiduciary framework applies to private assets.

October 2026, Retirement

Key Insights

The Labor Department’s 2026 proposal maintains ERISA’s asset‑neutral approach, neither endorsing nor prohibiting any particular asset class in DC plans.
The proposal’s process‑based safe harbor may ease concerns over private assets, but certain investment traits still warrant extra attention in ERISA contexts.
Any private asset allocation must result from a prudent, informed, and well‑documented process conducted solely in plan participants’ best interests.

Recent policy shifts and evolving investment capabilities have opened the door for greater use of private assets in defined contribution (DC) plans. However, fiduciaries continue to operate in a litigation‑sensitive environment, raising concerns that legal considerations may be unfairly outweighing the investment case for private assets.

As DC plans navigate this complex backdrop, we detail the following considerations for those assessing the potential benefits and risks of private asset investments:
Key factors influencing the debate over private assetsThe Employee Retirement Income Security Act’s (ERISA’s) fiduciary framework and requirements for investment selectionsPotential implications of the Department of Labor’s (DOL’s) proposed regulation, Fiduciary Duties in Selecting Designated Investment Alternatives1

Setting the stage: What’s driving momentum for private asset inclusion?

A growing number of plan fiduciaries, policymakers, and investment professionals are evaluating whether private market investments can play a prudent role in DC plans, particularly given private assets’ potential to enhance diversification and long‑term returns. This question has gained urgency as private markets have expanded rapidly (Fig. 1) and as public markets have reached historic levels of concentration.2

Private markets have grown much faster than public markets in recent decades
(Fig. 1) Assets under management by private asset class (USD billions)

Sources: Preqin, SIFMA Research: 2026 Capital Markets Fact Book, Bank for International Settlements, World Federation of Exchanges, T. Rowe Price.
To avoid double counting of available capital and unrealized value, fund of funds and secondaries are excluded.

However, unlike traditional public market investments, private assets often involve limited liquidity, less frequent or model‑based valuation, higher fees, more complex structures, and additional administrative demands. Those features require careful analysis in a DC environment—where plans often include default investments and typically offer daily valuation to support participant‑directed transactions.

Due in part to these complexities, the DC community continues to debate the merits of private asset implementation. Yet the debate is moving from whether private assets may be considered to how fiduciaries can assess them in a way that aligns with the goal of improving participant outcomes.

Two key factors are driving this shift:

1. The evolution of target date strategies

The widespread adoption of professionally managed target date strategies as qualified default investment alternatives, or QDIAs, has fueled interest in incorporating private assets into DC plans.

Whereas DC plans historically have faced operational hurdles in meaningfully implementing private assets, defined benefit (DB) plans have used them regularly throughout the life of ERISA. This reflects DB plans’ longer investment horizons, ability to manage liquidity at the total‑plan level, and centralized decision‑making by institutional investors.

Similarly, as target date strategies have evolved to include highly sophisticated designs and a broader range of asset classes, many investment professionals have also come to view them as a compelling option for private markets exposure,3 particularly given participants’ multi‑decade investment horizons.

Moreover, because target date and other diversified strategies can address liquidity, valuation, and portfolio construction more holistically, DC‑focused investment professionals generally have advocated for private asset allocations within these strategies rather than through stand‑alone options. This approach seeks to provide participants with institutional‑quality investment opportunities while minimizing the complexity associated with direct participant investment decisions.

Diversification capabilities continue to evolve
(Fig. 2) Stages of diversification in the target date industry

Source: T. Rowe Price.

2. Policy developments

Recent steps by federal policymakers—most notably the regulatory proposal from the DOL—have also driven interest in private market access. If approved, the regulation would establish a process‑based fiduciary safe harbor framework for the selection of designated investment alternatives, including those with exposure to private asset classes.4

(See details in the sections titled “How do private assets fit within the ERISA framework?” and “What are the potential implications of the DOL proposal?”)

How should plan investments be evaluated from a fiduciary perspective?

For DC plans, the key question remains whether private assets can be incorporated in a manner that both enhances retirement outcomes and satisfies ERISA’s demanding fiduciary standards.5

ERISA has roots in trust law, and trustees are held to a higher standard than those operating in a normal market transaction. In fact, ERISA’s fiduciary duty is recognized as the “highest known to the law."6

Core requirements under ERISA
(Fig. 3) Responsibilities on behalf of participants and beneficiaries

Duty of loyalty
Duty of care
What this means
Fiduciaries must act solely in the interests of the plan's participants and beneficiaries and for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits and paying only reasonable plan expenses—a standard often referred to as the "exclusive benefit rule."
Fiduciaries must act "with the care, skill, prudence, and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a prudent man acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would use in the conduct of a like character and with like aims." This standard is known as the "prudent person rule."
What else?
When it comes to investment selection, ensuring that the plan pays only reasonable expenses can also take into account the total costs of participation to participants—inclusive of investments and plan administration, whether paid for separately or through revenue generated by plan investments.
The prudence requirement focuses on the fiduciary's decision-making process rather than the ultimate performance of a particular investment.

Analysis by T. Rowe Price.

Ultimately, the fiduciary framework governing ERISA DC plan investments emphasizes procedural prudence, ongoing oversight, and participant protection. Fiduciaries are expected to employ a disciplined and well‑documented investment process that balances risk, return, diversification, cost, and operational considerations. They must also follow plan documents and diversify the plan’s investments so as to minimize the risk of investment losses.7

...ERISA does not require fiduciaries to select the cheapest possible investment.

ERISA does not prescribe a single investment lineup or prohibit fiduciaries from considering more complex or less traditional strategies. Instead, it focuses on fiduciary obligations and the prudence of the decision‑making process. Furthermore, ERISA does not require fiduciaries to select the cheapest possible investment.

Digging deeper into ERISA

Regarding the prudence requirement (i.e., the duty of care), courts have consistently recognized that fiduciaries are not guarantors of investment success. Rather, fiduciaries must undertake an objective investigation of available investment options, evaluate their risks and expected returns, compare costs and fees, and determine whether each investment is appropriate in light of the plan’s objectives and participant population.8

The duty of prudence is accompanied by a duty to diversify plan investments. Unless clearly imprudent under the circumstances, fiduciaries must diversify plan assets to minimize the risk of large losses.9
In the DC space, this obligation extends not only to the plan’s overall investment menu, but also to the design of professionally managed investment options, such as target date strategies, that may serve as participants’ default investments.Diversification requires fiduciaries to evaluate how individual investments interact within a portfolio rather than assessing each investment in isolation.

ERISA also imposes a duty to ensure that plan expenses are reasonable. Fiduciaries must carefully evaluate investment management fees, administrative expenses, revenue‑sharing arrangements, and other costs because excessive fees can significantly diminish participants’ retirement savings over time.

The Supreme Court has emphasized that fiduciaries have a continuing obligation to monitor plan investments and remove imprudent options, including investments that were appropriate at the time of selection but later become unsuitable.10
This ongoing duty requires periodic review of investment performance, fee competitiveness, manager qualifications, and changing market conditions.

For participant‑directed individual account plans, ERISA provides fiduciaries with limited protection from liability for participants’ investment decisions if the plan satisfies specific regulatory requirements.11
To qualify for this protection, participants must be provided with a broad range of investment alternatives, sufficient information to make informed investment decisions, and the opportunity to exercise meaningful control over their accounts.Although this provision may shield fiduciaries from losses resulting directly from participants’ own investment choices, it does not relieve fiduciaries of their responsibility to prudently select and monitor the investment options offered under the plan.

How do private assets fit within the ERISA framework?

Importantly, ERISA does not endorse or prohibit investments in private markets—or in any particular asset class. Private assets should be analyzed through the same fiduciary lens as any other investment12 but with heightened attention to certain features that are especially relevant in a DC context.

In its proposal, the DOL states:
[P]roviding guidance only with respect to those asset allocation funds that invest in alternative assets could create the impression that those asset allocation funds are either favored or disfavored. They are not. They are subject to the same requirements as any other investment. This is consistent with the Department’s historical practice of providing neutral guidance that does not favor or disfavor any particular type of investment or investment strategy.13

Despite potential investment benefits and an expected safe harbor, many DC plan sponsors continue to express concerns about the inclusion of private assets, especially regarding higher fees and reduced liquidity (Fig. 4).

Fees remain the biggest barrier to private asset integration
(Fig. 4) Top reasons preventing implementation in DC plans

Sources: T. Rowe Price’s 2026 Defined Contribution Consultant Study and 2026 DC Plan Sponsor Retirement Trends (see Appendix).
Note: Respondents were asked to select their top two reasons. Other responses from consultants/advisors: highly complex; need to evaluate emerging options; lack of plan sponsor interest; one‑sided risk/reward—advisors take fiduciary liability while fund companies get majority of revenue; transparency and regulatory guidance needed; value‑add to justify operational/valuation/fee concerns; who owns the design within a partnership.

Because investment costs directly impact participants’ retirement savings, ERISA fiduciaries must carefully evaluate whether the anticipated benefits justify the additional expense. Failure to prudently assess investment fees, liquidity constraints, or valuation methodologies may expose fiduciaries to potential liability for breach of their duties of prudence and loyalty under ERISA.

What are the potential implications of the DOL proposal?

Under the Labor Department’s proposed regulation, the distinctive features of private asset investments (and all other investment options) would be addressed through a process‑based fiduciary framework rather than any categorical judgment on their use in DC plans.

The proposal expressly states that ERISA Section 404(a)(1)(B) “does not require or restrict any specific type of designated investment alternative,” including asset allocation funds with exposure to alternative assets, provided the fiduciary follows a prudent process. To that end, the proposal identifies performance, fees, liquidity, valuation, performance benchmarking, and complexity as core factors fiduciaries must “objectively, thoroughly, and analytically consider” when selecting a designated investment alternative.

Analyzing the proposed safe harbor

While the safe harbor is still in proposed form and cannot be relied upon unless it is included in a final rule, its six core factors give a good indication of the DOL’s perspective and could serve as a road map for analyzing DC plan private asset investments.

1. Performance

Diversification is a key consideration in the evaluation of investment performance. The proposal emphasizes that fiduciaries should assess performance on a risk‑adjusted basis and consider how a private asset sleeve—when included in a professionally managed, multi‑asset solution—may improve overall portfolio efficiency rather than focusing solely on stand‑alone returns.

2. Fees

Cost considerations also warrant added attention, as private investment vehicles frequently charge higher management fees and performance‑based compensation than traditional investment products.

The existence of higher fees does not necessarily render a private investment imprudent. However, fiduciaries must determine whether the anticipated benefits—including enhanced diversification, improved risk‑adjusted returns (net of fees and expenses), or access to unique investment opportunities—reasonably justify the additional expense.

The DOL proposal validates this assertion, adding that fiduciaries must compare a reasonable number of similar alternatives.

3. Liquidity

Recognizing that DC plans involve withdrawals, loans, reallocation activity, and possible plan‑level redemption demands, the proposal requires fiduciaries to evaluate whether the investment can meet both participant‑level and plan‑level liquidity needs.

While target date solutions and other multi‑asset portfolios can manage liquidity within a diversified framework—i.e., portfolio inflows and outflows may not necessitate transactions in the private allocation—fiduciaries should carefully evaluate whether the liquidity profile of an investment option with private market exposure is compatible with the plan’s operational requirements.

4. Valuation

The valuation uncertainty14 generally associated with private asset investments complicates the daily pricing of the investment alternative and participant transactions that characterize DC plans.

The proposal requires fiduciaries to determine that a designated investment alternative has adequate measures to ensure it can be timely and accurately valued in accordance with plan needs.

For private assets, the proposal points to conflict‑free, independent valuation processes as a positive example, while warning against conflicted proprietary valuation methods, such as those used in certain continuation fund structures.

5. Performance benchmarking

Consistent with performance‑related considerations, the proposal requires fiduciaries to determine that a designated investment alternative has a meaningful benchmark15 and to compare the investment’s risk‑adjusted expected net returns with that benchmark.

This requirement reflects the principle that fiduciaries must use a comparator that meaningfully corresponds to the investment under review rather than relying on a generic or mismatched index. Thus, a broad public equity index may be unsuitable for a target date or asset allocation vehicle whose objectives, glide path, or risk exposures differ materially from that index.

By contrast, a custom composite benchmark may be appropriate where it reflects the designated investment alternative’s actual asset mix and strategy, including where the investment includes both public market exposures and a private asset sleeve. In that context, the proposal recognizes that fiduciaries may rely on qualified investment professionals in benchmark construction and analysis, provided the fiduciary reads, critically reviews, and understands the analysis offered in support of the benchmark.

6. Complexity

The proposal likewise recognizes that private assets and other alternative strategies may involve a degree of structural, operational, and analytical complexity beyond that of traditional public market investments.

It provides that fiduciaries must appropriately consider the complexity of the designated investment alternative and determine whether they have the skills, knowledge, experience, and capacity to understand it sufficiently to discharge their obligations under ERISA and the governing plan documents. If they do not, they must seek assistance from a qualified investment advice fiduciary, investment manager, or other appropriate professional.

This principle is particularly important if the investment involves specialized fee arrangements, private market valuation methodologies, bespoke benchmark construction, or implementation features that require careful oversight.

The relevant inquiry is not whether the investment is sophisticated, but whether fiduciaries can demonstrate that it has been evaluated with the rigor, expertise, and documentation that ERISA requires.

Additional considerations

While the proposal gives a strong indication of how the DOL is thinking about the inclusion of private assets in DC plans, it only addresses the duty of care and not the duty of loyalty or the duty to monitor. As such, fiduciaries may also consider the following:

(Fig. 5) Practical issues for fiduciaries

Topic
Key questions
Plan alignment
Do the plan documents permit this type of investment, and is the contemplated use of private assets consistent with the plan’s stated investment objectives, mandates, and fiduciary framework?
Fiduciary process
Has a regular, disciplined, and well‑documented process been established for evaluating whether private assets are appropriate for the plan?
Operational feasibility
Are the operational demands—including administration, recordkeeping, custody, valuation, and daily participant activity—manageable for the plan?
Ongoing monitoring
What monitoring framework will be used on an ongoing basis, and how frequently will fiduciaries review the investment?
Participant communication
How will the plan communicate the investment’s features, risks, liquidity characteristics, and expected role in the portfolio to participants?
Participant interests
Does the use of private assets support better retirement outcomes in a way that is prudent, understandable, and implementable?

Source: T. Rowe Price.

Final thoughts

As investment opportunities continue to evolve, ERISA’s principles of prudence and loyalty remain the central legal standards by which fiduciary decisions are evaluated.

The DOL’s 2026 proposal reinforces those principles by applying a neutral, process‑based framework that requires fiduciaries to evaluate performance, fees, liquidity, valuation, benchmarking, and complexity with rigor and care.

For some plans, a limited allocation to private assets—particularly within professionally managed, diversified vehicles such as target date solutions—may be capable of satisfying ERISA’s standards and improving long‑term participant outcomes. For others, the operational burdens, cost structure, or participant profile may counsel against inclusion.

The bottom line for DC plans is that the path forward is defined by process rather than labels. It is up to fiduciaries to thoughtfully assess private market opportunities while maintaining a clear focus on participant interests, reasonable costs, effective oversight, and the long‑term purpose of retirement investing.

Aliya Robinson
Director, Congressional Affairs
