articles.text:
Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation Disclosures

Integration of Sustainability Risks into Investment Decision-Making ProcessAs a global macro multi-asset manager, our investment process is rooted in a deep understanding of how economies and markets work. Because environmental, social, and governance dynamics often impact global economies and markets, we deeply research these issues and integrate that research into our investment process in a manner that is consistent with our systematic way of managing money. Our approach seeks to understand how ESG considerations impact the financial objectives of return and risk. As a result, any research insight related to environmental or social issues that we believe would have material impact on financial performance flows through to each portfolio consistent with its objectives.Our research process is designed to continually adapt to include and prioritize new topics as they arise. The list of environmental, social, and governance dynamics we are looking at, and our assessment of their materiality continues to develop and evolve. Below we provide examples of different ESG topics with clear macro implications that we’ve researched and how we’ve incorporated the insights from that research into our investment decision-making with the aim of increasing returns and reducing risk.Remuneration PolicyBridgewater’s remuneration policies are consistent with its approach to the integration of sustainability risks into the investment decision making process. As sustainability risks can be a type of financial risk, Bridgewater acknowledges that failure to consider such risks could have an adverse impact on the performance of investments. Pursuant to its remuneration practices, Bridgewater typically awards fixed and variable remuneration to staff. Variable remuneration is awarded on a discretionary basis and takes into account the performance of an individual employee and the performance of the strategies managed by Bridgewater. Accordingly, to the extent that sustainability risks have an adverse impact on performance of the strategies that Bridgewater manages, this is likely to be reflected in the overall level of variable remuneration awarded to staff.Principal Adverse Impact PolicyBridgewater does not consider the principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factors as contemplated by article 4 of SFDR, as the nature of these investment products do not provide for the consideration of such adverse impacts. However, as noted above Bridgewater does incorporate so-called sustainability factors that it believes have material financial (risk/return) relevance into its investment process for all products it offers.EngagementBridgewater’s Stewardship and Corporate Engagement Policy is set, implemented, and overseen by the Sustainable Investing Committee, and it covers our approach to proxy voting, corporate engagement, industry collaborations with a broad range of industry actors, including data providers, research institutions, industry partners, and our clients, as well as external affiliations. The policy adheres to the guidelines of the Principles for Responsible Investing (PRI) and aligns with the recommended framework of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).Bridgewater Associates, LP — 2022 Statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factorsBridgewater Associates, LP — 2023 Statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factorsBridgewater Associates, LP — 2024 Statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factorsBridgewater Associates, LP — 2025 Statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factors

articles.title: What’s driving the municipal market’s remarkable growth? | RBCCM
articles.text:
The following conversation was recorded on September 29th, 2026.
Despite recent volatility, what is the outlook for U.S. Municipal Finance?
Bob Spangler: Rates are obviously up pretty dramatically but, fundamentally, the market remains strong.
We’re currently at $476 billion of issuance in our market. About $125 billion of that is refundings, which leaves new money at around $340 billion, and I think we will reach around $585 billion for the calendar year.
So, we're in a market now that's grown quite a bit. Part of that is a reflection of state and local governments’ responsibility in building infrastructure in the U.S, and part of it is inflationary.
Will rising rates slow refunding activity?
Spangler: 30% of the issuance year to date has been refunding. That compares to 25% on average over the last five years. We’ve had a run-up in refundings up through September but, with rates having risen as much as they have, we’re not anticipating that level of refundings going forward.
Do you expect new issuance to continue to grow?
Spangler: This is a $4.2 trillion market with more than 50,000 municipal issuers in the U.S.
Local governments continue to face ongoing funding needs for schools, roads, water and sewer systems, and other essential projects.
Local governments set out capital expenditures and project out what they need for three, five, 10 years out. So many of those capital needs will have to get funded no matter what. With that as a backdrop, the notion of us being in a market where we have elevated issuance for the next three to five years, if not beyond, is very real.

"The notion of us being in a market where we have elevated issuance for the next three to five years, if not beyond, is very real."
Bob Spangler, Head of U.S. Municipal Finance, RBC Capital Markets

Where are issuers deploying capital today and looking beyond traditional structures?
Spangler: In the current environment, issuers that compete against the taxable market are likely to be among the most active. We continue to see strength in single-family mortgage revenue bond issuance as the spread between tax-exempt and taxable funding has widened. Affordable housing, workforce housing and first-time homebuyer programs are all areas of continued focus.
We're also seeing significant activity in power and prepaid energy financing. Growing electricity demand from data centers is increasing the need for new generation capacity, while prepaid energy structures can help deliver meaningful savings directly to consumers. Prepaid gas deals now total more than $33 billion year to date, representing roughly 7% of the municipal market and already exceeding last year's volume.
Healthcare is another area of growth. Issuance is already running ahead of last year as providers look to improve efficiency and invest in their operations. We are also seeing growing interest in energy efficiency projects and industrial development bonds tied to reshoring and other public policy priorities.

"We’re also seeing a lot of focus on power. With all the data center buildout, this country needs every electron it can find."
Bob Spangler, Head of U.S. Municipal Finance RBC Capital Markets

Why has the market absorbed record issuance so well?
Keith Solomon: Despite increasing supply, the municipal market has benefited from a healthy supply-demand dynamic for several years.
Reinvestment cash continues to flow back into the market, while municipals have remained attractive to investors relative to other asset classes.
More recently, rising Treasury yields, inflation concerns and heavier new-issue supply have put pressure on municipal valuations. Yet that has also created opportunity.
As yields have moved higher, municipal bonds have become increasingly attractive to retail investors and crossover buyers evaluating relative value versus Treasuries. The result is renewed investor interest despite recent market volatility.

"Despite record supply, the muni market has remained remarkably resilient — reinvestment cash and steady inflows continue to support demand."
Keith Solomon, Head of Municipal Products, RBC Capital Markets

Has anything changed in relation to borrowers and their approach to capital?
Spangler: Our bread and butter remains state and local governments – schools, water and sewer, a lot of local transportation. Those will stay as long-term fixed-rate 20-, 25-, and 30-year bonds.
But what we’re starting to see is that those with a more dynamic revenue stream and cost basis are looking to be as creative as they can in finding products and reaching different investors.
How are investor expectations evolving?
Solomon: Investors are increasingly looking to get involved earlier in the process and seeking more customized opportunities.
Particularly within private capital, investors are looking for structures that better suit their needs while helping issuers access financing more effectively. That trend is creating greater flexibility in how deals are brought to market and funded.
How are we adding strategic value for issuers and investors?
Spangler: We’ve maintained a presence in the local markets where we've historically had strength.
That includes Texas, where we're currently the number one underwriter and represent roughly 15% of the market year to date.
We've continued investing in our core markets, including Colorado, Arizona, New Mexico, California, Illinois, Ohio and New Jersey, while combining that local presence with national sector expertise.
Our bank commitment to the municipal market, whether it be investors on third-party TOBs or directly as issuers, will exceed $25 billion by the end of this year.
This bank appreciates the market, appreciates the infrastructure and the vital nature of what we're funding, and appreciates that it is really the backbone of the U.S.
Solomon: We've maintained market share north of 10% in the new-issue market and have worked over the last three years to strengthen our position in the secondary market as well. By allocating more balance sheet to sales and trading, we've become a larger liquidity provider and a more meaningful counterparty for investors.
We've also expanded our high-yield capabilities, allowing us to pursue opportunities where other firms have pulled back or reallocated resources. As investors look for yield and more specialized opportunities, that part of the market has become increasingly important.
What is the outlook for municipal finance?
Solomon: While recent volatility has pressured the market, municipal bonds have historically proven resilient. Higher yields are attracting investor attention, and the market continues to benefit from strong long-term demand fundamentals.
Spangler: While refunding issuance may slow, the underlying need for capital remains. Infrastructure investment, housing, healthcare and other essential services will continue to require funding, supporting elevated issuance levels in the years ahead.

articles.title: Daily: Higher inflation need not derail US assets
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Market Playbook | Asia beyond the AI trade (6 mins)Video: The AI Show | Is the AI trade under strain? (4 mins)Thought of the dayUS equities fell on Wednesday after September inflation came in higher than expected, increasing expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes. Headline inflation accelerated to 0.6% month over month from 0.4% in August, driven largely by a 9.1% rise in gasoline prices. More importantly, core inflation rose 0.3%, above the 0.2% increase consensus forecast for a second consecutive month, while the annual rate rose to 2.6% from 2.4%.Price pressures also extended beyond energy, with increases in shelter, airfares, vehicles, apparel, and technology-related goods. Markets raised the probability of an October hike to around 40% from about 20% before the release.The breadth of the increase makes the latest inflation strength hard for the Fed to dismiss. We now expect the Fed to raise rates in December and March, following its September move. We have also raised our end-December forecast for the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.9%, from 4.6% previously.But this remains below Wednesday's closing level of 5.19%, and we do not expect the revised rate and yield outlook to undermine the positive outlook for US assets.The economic strength driving the Fed to raise rates is also supportive for equities. US GDP growth was close to 2.5% annualized in the first half of the year and likely near 3% in the third quarter, underpinned by a healthy labor market. While September payroll growth slowed to 29,000, the three-month average of 51,000 remained broadly in line with estimates of the pace needed to keep unemployment stable. Initial unemployment claims also recently reached a 10-week low, with no broad increase in layoffs, while the ISM manufacturing index remained firmly in expansion at 54.5 in September. This combination gives policymakers greater scope to focus on inflation without creating a high near-term risk of recession. For investors, the same resilience should support household income, consumer spending, and company profits, helping equities absorb moderately higher rates.Markets are pricing a more aggressive rate path than we expect. Investors are pricing roughly 3.5 further hikes, in addition to the one in September, while we expect just two more increases. Recent Fed communication also supports a more measured path: New York Fed President John Williams has said there is “no need for urgency,” although back-to-back higher-than-expected core inflation readings make October a closer call. We expect hikes in December and March, and then for rates to remain on hold until late 2027. The gap between market pricing and our forecast leaves scope for Treasury yields to decline if the Fed waits in October and subsequent data indicate that inflation pressures are stabilizing.Another strong earnings season should help equities withstand moderately higher rates. We forecast S&P 500 earnings per share growth of 28% for the September quarter, supported by AI demand, improvement in cyclical industries, and resilient consumer spending. We expect AI-related capex to rise 84% this year to USD 900bn, while semiconductor profits are expected to account for about half of the S&P 500 earnings growth in the third quarter. The earnings contribution should also extend beyond technology: The new-orders component of the ISM manufacturing index has remained in expansion for nine consecutive months, supporting the outlook for industrial profits. Notably, equities have historically performed well after the start of Fed tightening cycles. Across the 16 Fed hiking cycles since 1954, the S&P 500 gained an average of 10.8% in the year following the first increase, although past performance is no guarantee of future returns.So, we remain positioned for further equity gains while emphasizing broad diversification across sectors and regions. Strong economic growth and earnings should help equities withstand moderately higher rates. We also continue to see value in fixed income: Higher starting yields provide attractive portfolio income, while our expectation for the 10-year Treasury yield to decline to 4.9% by the end of December leaves scope for capital gains. We continue to favor a combination of cyclical and secular equity exposure alongside quality fixed income.

articles.title: Daily: Strengthen portfolio defenses as volatility rises
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioPodcast: AI demand remains the signal amid neocloud noise, on Apple , Spotify (6 mins)Podcast: Across the Pond: Europe’s bond stress test, on Apple , Spotify (22 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Why bank stocks are falling amid rising rates (6 mins)Video: The AI Show |The AI trade's two-sided test (4 mins)Video: Data with Donovan | The Fed's rate path ahead (5 mins)Thought of the dayMarket volatility has increased over the past week as investors weigh questions about AI profitability in a higher-rate environment, while geopolitical conflicts remain unresolved. Brent crude oil was up 0.9% to nearly USD 110/bbl at the time of writing.With the third-quarter earnings season now in full swing, further volatility is likely. Markets will be assessing hyperscalers’ ability to generate returns on their substantial AI investment, the financing and execution risks associated with the AI buildout, and whether higher interest rates are weighing on business activity and consumer spending.We still expect a robust reporting season, with AI-related growth helping drive overall S&P 500 earnings growth of 28%. But increasingly concentrated market performance and the potential for stock-specific volatility reinforce the importance of portfolio resilience. We see ways investors can further diversify their sources of return and strengthen portfolio defenses.Structured strategies can tailor equity exposure to different market outcomes. Investors concerned about a correction but keen to retain equity exposure can consider put warrants, which may help limit losses on stocks they already own. For those looking to add exposure cautiously, capital preservation strategies can provide participation in a market recovery while seeking to protect some or all of the initial investment at maturity. Income-seeking investors may consider reverse convertibles in parts of the equity market where implied volatility remains elevated. These strategies can be tailored to investors’ outlook, objectives, and risk appetite, but they carry risks including issuer default, limited liquidity, and potential capital losses.Hedge funds may add differentiated sources of return as market dispersion increases. Higher interest rates can widen differences among companies, economies, and securities, giving active managers more opportunities to identify relative leaders and laggards. This may benefit equity market neutral strategies, while diverging central bank policies can expand the opportunity set for discretionary macro managers. Uneven moves across yield curves may also create opportunities for fixed income relative value strategies. We therefore believe diversified exposure to select hedge fund strategies can complement traditional portfolios, although manager and vehicle selection remain important given risks including leverage, limited transparency, higher fees, and illiquidity.Commodities can diversify portfolios and provide insulation against supply-driven inflation. Their historically low correlations with equities and bonds can offer a differentiated source of return, while exposure to energy may help protect against supply disruptions and the resulting inflationary pressures. The longer-term outlook for broad commodities is also supported by rising power demand, AI infrastructure investment, electrification, and constrained supply across several markets, particularly copper. We favor diversified exposure across precious metals, energy, industrial metals, and agriculture, with an actively managed approach helping to navigate shifts in market leadership.While we remain constructive on equities and believe investors should retain diversified core exposure, the case for broadening portfolio sources of return has strengthened amid concentrated market leadership, higher financing costs, and ongoing geopolitical risks. Investors should also take into account their objectives, risk tolerance, and liquidity needs.

articles.title: Protecting our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
articles.text:
Protecting our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
Across the industry, we are seeing an increase in bad actors impersonating and misusing corporate brands to get access to personal information and funds from unsuspecting individuals. These activities may involve individuals acting as company representatives and may include fake websites, social media inquiries, or communications that closely resemble official channels.
Please read the below for important reminders that can help protect you from potentially fraudulent activity.
We strongly caution against providing personal data or transferring funds in response to unsolicited requests. For your safety, always verify the authenticity of communications claiming to be from Lazard by contacting us through our official website or known contact points.
Specifically, Lazard will never engage in the following activities:

Sending unsolicited investment proposals or requests for personal information from nonverified persons.
Requesting payments to bank accounts in the names of individuals, third parties, unknown company names, or through payment intermediaries.
Offering unrealistically attractive returns that seem too good to be true.
Expressing urgency to complete an investment or make a payment.
Requesting additional payments to release investments that have already been made.
Requesting money to be sent via social media messaging apps and/or platforms.

If you believe that you have fallen victim to fraud, please contact your bank immediately. Additionally, you should report the incident to law enforcement in your jurisdiction as soon as possible.
The safety and protection of data and information is a priority for Lazard, and we appreciate your careful attention and diligence.
***
Lazard cannot accept any responsibility for any loss, damage, or claims arising from fraudulent activities. Please fully read account disclosures and related policies.

Capital Solutions: Five Questions Investors Ask Most Regularly

October 2026

6 minute read

Jennifer Box

Blaine MacDougald

Several years ago, we identified an emerging, secular opportunity to deliver ‘Capital Solutions’ at scale, to both companies and investors, in a way that aligned with our unique skills and capabilities.
Since then, we’ve been on a journey to help expand this market in partnership with a broad range of companies (sponsored, family/founder owned and listed), advisors, and investors.

SUBSCRIBE TO INSIGHTS

At KKR, Capital Solutions are bespoke, partnership-oriented financings we provide to fundamentally healthy, large, growing businesses to help them unlock value through active management.
As investors consider Capital Solutions for a permanent role in their asset allocation framework, they are asking us thoughtful questions about portfolio fit, return drivers, and opportunity set.
This is the first of a series of articles that will address questions we hear regularly from investors. Below are the five questions we’ve heard most frequently over the last year.
Capital Solutions have features of both debt and equity. Where do they fit in my portfolio?Why would a company accept the higher cost of a Capital Solution when it could access cheaper debt financing?How do you structure to mitigate downside risk, and is it similar to a credit investment?How large can the Capital Solutions market become?How has demand for Capital Solutions evolved in today’s volatile market?

Capital Solutions: One Approach, Two Perspectives
The Company View: Whether a large multi-national corporation or a family-owned business, the appeal of a Capital Solution lies in the ability to design flexible financing that is purpose-built for their objectives, whether that is funding growth, facilitating a shareholder realignment, or optimizing the capital structure. With structured capital, owners of growing businesses can retain control, while still accessing the benefits of private equity-style alignment and hands-on value creation.
The Investor View: Capital Solutions present an opportunity to compound capital through a portfolio of instruments anchored in contractual, debt-like characteristics, while still achieving equity-like returns. We often say at KKR that we like to ‘make our own luck.’ In Capital Solutions, that comes down to three things we believe we do well. First, we leverage our unique model to originate differentiated opportunities. Second, we structure and align our capital with the majority owners and management teams. Third, we identify ‘controllable’ operational levers in businesses and then lean into our value creation toolkit to unlock equity upside through those levers.

1. Capital Solutions have features of debt and equity. As such, where does this belong in my portfolio exactly? How do you see other allocators approaching this?

In short: Capital Solutions fits within a credit, equity, or dedicated private markets allocation. The right home depends on the investor’s objectives, the structure of their asset allocation, and available capital.

We believe Capital Solutions can play an accretive role in any investor portfolio, whether as part of the credit allocation, the equity allocation, or a flexible private markets allocation.
The right ‘home’ for Capital Solutions ultimately comes down to the investor’s goals for their total portfolio and allocation framework.

Regardless of where Capital Solutions might ‘sit’ in an asset allocation, we believe the strategy can provide attractive diversification to a portfolio as well as a compelling risk-reward that complements existing debt and equity exposures. Companies choose a Capital Solution for its flexibility when compared to traditional debt financing, while also benefitting from the same value-add partnership they would get in a control private equity deal. Therefore, we believe we are building a portfolio of unique assets that an investor could not otherwise access in a traditional credit or private equity offering.
Several of our clients look to Capital Solutions for return enhancement of their credit portfolios. These allocators typically have meaningful exposure to yield-oriented strategies such as senior direct lending and asset-based finance. These strategies comprise the ‘core’ income ballast of the credit portfolio. A Capital Solution strategy can complement such yield-oriented credit strategies by offering a total return anchored in contractual return that compounds over time, augmented by the potential for equity upside participation. The result is a potentially higher overall multiple on invested capital.
Equity investors are increasingly turning to Capital Solutions as a downside-mitigating, lower-volatility way to access equity-like returns, but with a more credit-like risk profile. Capital Solutions investments differ from common equity strategies in three key ways. First, they generally provide a 'day-1' contractual return component. Second, shorter deal duration typically allows capital to be returned faster. Third, fees are typically charged on invested capital rather than committed capital. The combination of these factors can help mitigate the J-curve and accelerate DPI (Distributions to Paid-In Capital) in comparison to common equity.
As the graphic below illustrates, when compared to common equity, Capital Solution transactions will participate in upside convexity, albeit typically to a lesser degree than straight common equity given the downside protection features.
Finally, we are seeing a number of allocators start to build dedicated portfolio allocations to capture the unique risk-reward of Capital Solutions. In doing so, these allocators transcend the traditional asset allocation silos of equity and credit—the same way the companies who use this financing move beyond the binary choices of equity or debt.
EXHIBIT 1: Capital Solutions Return Profile Illustrated

Note: As of June 30, 2026. There can be no assurance that the trends above will persist. Downside protection is no guarantee against future losses. No strategy can completely eliminate risk and past performance is not indicative of future results. Downside protection is no guarantee against future losses. (1) Assuming a 5-Year exit.

2. Why would a company accept the higher cost of a Capital Solution if it has access to cheaper debt capital?

In short: Many owners are not just looking for cheap, passive capital. Rather, they are looking for a strategic partner who can help them execute an ambitious growth plan, while retaining control of their businesses.

When we meet business owners, they are often undergoing, or about to undergo a period of sustained organic and/or inorganic growth. Therefore, to preserve operating flexibility, these businesses are often under-levered and not interested in maximizing financial leverage during such a phase of growth and transformation. Instead, many of these owners are weighing whether to sell control or remain invested and bring on a sophisticated capital partner to help finance strategic objectives and execute a 3- to 5-year growth plan. A Capital Solution offers an alternative to equity capital — which would be more expensive, result in a loss of control, and entail a heavier governance burden — while still delivering the same value-added resources and alignment as control equity.
In our experience, companies that can access comparatively cheaper debt financing are often pleased to take our more ‘expensive’ capital during a critical growth period. They believe they will be better positioned to meet their strategic goals with our hands-on aligned capital, versus cheaper passive debt capital that burdens their free cash flow generation. This is the essence of what partnership capital means: it is not merely a financing arrangement or a passive relationship. It is a true partnership where the company gains access to the full breadth of KKR's resources, from operational expertise and talent networks to strategic counsel, alongside capital that compounds with the growth of the business.
For example, in 2024, we partnered with a successful industrials business that manufactures highly precision-engineered parts for the U.S. fire and water safety market. The company’s management and owner, a mid-market private equity firm, selected KKR as the partner of choice, even though we were not the cheapest cost-of-capital option. Both management and the owner saw significant go-forward value potential for the business, but recognized the criticality of identifying the right, well-resourced, aligned partner to bring this potential into reality. Within months of investing, we helped hire a best-in-class CFO through our advisor network and developed a detailed integration plan for a major acquisition.

3. How do you structure for downside risk mitigation in your investments? Is it similar to a credit investment?

In short: The downside risk mitigation features of our Capital Solution investments are similar to those of a traditional Credit investment, while also benefitting from governance rights given the equity partnership nature of the capital.

A core tenet of our investment philosophy is to aim to structure Capital Solution investments with multiple layers of downside protection.
Downside risk management starts with asset selection, which for us entails a focus on high-quality, large, growing businesses with strong management teams and leading competitive positioning in their respective industries. To quantify this, our portfolio companies have average EBITDA of approximately $300 million and average enterprise value of approximately $3.5 billion. These are market-leading businesses with meaningful scale.
From there, we develop tight transaction structures to further mitigate downside risk.
A critical element of our approach is our position within a company's capital structure. We invest senior to the common equity, with significant equity value beneath us to absorb downside. In a typical investment, our capital sits at the ~25% to ~55% loan-to-value level. From an economic risk perspective, this means our businesses are minimally, or even under-levered. It also means the enterprise can sustain nearly 50% of value degradation, and our principal and contractual return remain protected.
EXHIBIT 2: Capital Solutions: Representative Capital Structure
Representative Capital Structure1,2

Note: As of June 30, 2026. There can be no assurance that the trends above will persist. Downside protection is no guarantee against future losses. No strategy can completely eliminate risk and past performance is not indicative of future results. (1) Figure is for illustrative purposes and does not represent a specific investment. (2) Based on weighted average across current Capital Solutions investments in KKR Opportunities Fund II, a representative Fund, including unfunded commitments. Adjusted for a 25% discount to the strike price, where applicable.

We also structure our Capital Solution investments to include a host of governance rights that are often superior to traditional creditor rights. For example, we look to secure exit rights, board seats, and veto rights over major capital and financing decisions.
This is the central feature of our investment approach: a typical investment structure is grounded in a meaningful degree of contracted return. Roughly 50% to 70% of total expected return is contractual and credit-like in nature, providing a significant floor regardless of equity outcomes. We can build this contracted return using a number of levers, from a coupon (paid-in-kind or cash), preferred dividend, Original Issue Discount (OID) or a liquidation preference/minimum return on our capital.
We are often asked if we have a preference in the exact format of our downside protection, as well as the specific instruments in which we are willing to invest. We are agnostic about the exact legal structure of the security. At our core, we are credit investors, and rigorous credit selection is our north star. What we care about is quality of business and leadership, our position in the capital structure, our governance rights package, the potential for meaningful upside participation potential, and our ability to influence the outcome as a partner to the owners and management teams.
For us, two different Capital Solutions might be economically equivalent and yet these solutions may resonate differently with our partner companies. For example, a ratings-sensitive company or a family-owned business may strongly prefer a structured equity solution to traditional debt financing, where we would invest in a lowly-levered (or sometimes fully unlevered) business, capturing preferred equity returns for what is de facto senior debt risk.
For example, in 2023, we partnered with a family-owned business and leader in large-scale events as it embarked upon a transformative acquisition to meaningfully accelerate its growth trajectory. The company’s management recognized that the acquisition would require not just capital, but a partner with deep expertise in unleashing the expected synergies from such a transaction. Given the owners’ preference to avoid ‘debt’ on the balance sheet, we structured the capital as ‘Preferred Equity’, attaching at ~5% loan-to-value (LTV), and detaching at ~40% LTV. The instrument carried a low double-digit annual cash yield, OID, and call protection. In our view, this is ‘debt’ in all but name, and our flexible approach to structuring solved an important objective for the company. In addition, our investment included warrants, a board director seat, a board observer seat, and a host of other protections. The flexibility of our solution met important objectives for the company, while also satisfying our requirements for attractive risk-reward skew in a Capital Solution investment.
4. How do you think about the potential size of the Capital Solutions market?

In short: We believe the Capital Solutions market is still in its infancy, and with ample room to grow given the secular demand drivers for partnership-oriented capital. We also believe the supply/demand backdrop is favorable for capital providers who are well-equipped to source a broad set of high-quality opportunities and take businesses to a new operating level.

Unlike traditional debt or equity capital markets that are well-established and clearly defined, the Capital Solutions market is one we are building from the ground-up with each bespoke transaction we execute. For example, we recently executed our largest European Capital Solution transaction in partnership with a leading, global flight technology platform. The transaction sparked an influx of inquiries from European companies and sponsors intrigued by the strategic possibilities that such flexible capital allows.

More recently, we have partnered with a leading enterprise IT solutions company, following longstanding dialogue. Our investment takes the form of a newly issued convertible instrument, structured alongside a broader partnership that gives the company access to our value creation resources. In this instance, the potential to collaborate with us on areas such as M&A, strategic growth opportunities, capital allocation, and operational improvement, is even more critical to the company than the capital itself.
With our transactions, we have witnessed a ‘flywheel’ effect that generates new opportunities, contributing to the steady growth of the Capital Solutions market overall.
We believe the secular demand for partnership-oriented capital is further augmented by other durable market themes, such as sponsors facing elongated hold periods for assets. A capital solution can be structured to facilitate an ultimate exit via sale, IPO, partial exit via a fund-to-fund transfer, a continuation vehicle, or a return of capital through shareholder realignment. The owner can therefore hold a scarce, high-quality asset for longer and continue to build value.
Given their inherent hybrid, multi-asset nature, we believe Capital Solutions are poised to continue taking market share from both traditional equity and credit markets.
5. How has the demand for Capital Solutions evolved in the recent volatile market environment?

In short: Market volatility has amplified the demand for Capital Solutions, as companies and sponsors increasingly seek flexible capital, and hands-on strategic support when traditional financing and exit paths are less reliable.

We believe the secular case for Capital Solutions is only reinforced in volatile markets. General market uncertainty and volatility can render typical exit paths, such as M&A and IPOs, less reliable for private companies. This market dynamic provides a constructive backdrop for Capital Solutions because it encourages sponsors and owners to seek flexible, creative financing solutions to hold high-quality businesses longer, unlock liquidity, or continue to fund growth without sacrificing control.
For investors in Capital Solutions, we believe this source of active management and value creation can provide a unique source of alpha. This is particularly relevant in today's environment, where we expect forward-looking returns across public equities and broader markets to continue to compress, making active management and hands-on value creation an increasingly essential driver of differentiated performance. Moreover, in a volatile investing environment, we value the downside return protection afforded by a meaningful base of contracted return. Taken together, we see potential for an attractive asymmetry between downside protection and upside potential.
Finally, we believe the favorable supply/demand imbalance in the Capital Solutions market is likely to become exacerbated, which should only create a richer, more attractive investing environment.

RELATED RESOURCES
For a deeper primer on Capital Solutions, we encourage you to visit our 2025 piece, ‘Reinventing Corporate Capital’.

NDR: All eyes on earnings season

Strong earnings growth has helped offset macro headwinds this year, including higher oil prices, elevated bond yields, and renewed Fed tightening, and investors will look to Q3 results to see if that support can continue.

While earnings growth is expected to remain historically strong, attention is increasingly shifting toward 2027 guidance, where the key question is not whether earnings will grow, but how much growth will decelerate. The backdrop for profits remains the most favorable in four years, but investors tend to reward earnings acceleration more than growth alone.
After an exceptional Q2 reporting season, when 85.5% of S&P 500 companies beat analyst estimates (chart above) and beat rates for mid- and small-cap stocks reached multi-year highs, companies may face a higher bar as earnings season begins in earnest with results from several major banks. One-time factors helped make Q2 particularly strong, raising questions about how repeatable that performance will be in the quarters ahead. News Release
Wood Mackenzie: Geopolitical supply shocks and AI power crunch collide across global base metals

22 October 2026
8 minute read

Email
Share by email

Geopolitical disruptions, resource nationalism and an escalating power crunch are reshaping global base metals markets, according to Wood Mackenzie's latest analysis. As the global data centre pipeline surpasses 250 GW, demand for power infrastructure is accelerating competition for copper, aluminium and other strategic materials.
The metals impact of AI extends well beyond data centres themselves. Transmission networks, substations and dedicated power generation can require three to four times more metal than the facilities they support, creating a new source of structural demand alongside electrification and energy security investment.
Yet upstream investment is struggling to keep pace. Despite elevated commodity prices, project sanctioning remains below expectations as permitting delays, geopolitical uncertainty and increasing project complexity weigh on investment decisions. The challenge comes as governments place greater emphasis on supply-chain resilience and critical mineral security.
"Data centres represent an economy-wide power infrastructure challenge, but the bigger story is the collision between accelerating demand and increasingly complex supply delivery," said Lindsay Grant, Vice President of Metals and Mining Research at Wood Mackenzie. "High prices should trigger investment, yet project sanctioning remains below expectations. Without faster approvals and investment commitments, the industry cannot deliver the mine supply needed to support future growth."
Wood Mackenzie's analysis highlights four structural themes shaping metals markets and investment decisions through 2036.
Wood Mackenzie's analysis identifies four structural data points shaping base metals markets through 2036.

Copper: Record prices of US$14,759/t reflect severe refined market dislocation, with US stockpiling pushing domestic cover above 170 days while leaving the rest of the world in a 460 kt deficit. While Chilean mine output falls 5.2% in 2026, global mine supply is set to expand by more than 5% next year, ending three years of stagnant growth.
Aluminium: A supply shock from Middle East smelter damage cut almost 2% of global primary output, driving a 1 Mt deficit in 2026 despite Chinese operating rates reaching 99% and Indonesia producing 1.3 Mt. While the market is projected to return to surplus in 2027 as Indonesian output scales toward 3 Mt by 2030, underlying fundamentals remain supportive.
Nickel markets are expected to rebalance in 2026 as Indonesian supply restrictions curb production, with Class 2 supply tightening from 2027. Despite Class 1 oversupply and weak battery demand, prices are forecast to recover towards US$19,000/t by 2030, subject to Indonesian policies and sulphur supply disruptions.
Lithium and energy storage: lithium carbonate prices up approximately 130% from mid-2025 lows, yet raw lithium carbonate represents just 2% to 3% of turnkey storage project costs; US$60 billion invested in the lithium supply chain over the past decade, with US$150 billion to US$250 billion more required through the 2050s.

Electrification, geopolitics and AI: the demand context
Wood Mackenzie is tracking more than 250 GW of data centre projects globally, over three times the pipeline a year ago. AI data centre electricity demand is forecast to increase fivefold between 2025 and 2030 and exceed 1,000 TWh by 2035. In Asia Pacific, demand is projected to nearly triple by 2030, while grid constraints are increasingly forcing operators to consider higher-cost microgrid and off-grid power solutions. In Japan, data centres come online in less than five years against upwards of ten for grid upgrades, driving adoption of microgrids and off-grid generation at two to three times the cost of grid-connected power.
Copper: Supply constraints and inventory hoarding mask underlying demand
Physical copper markets remain distorted by US stockpiling and trade policy, which have pushed inventory cover above 170 days domestically while leaving the rest of the world with just 48 days and a 450 kt deficit. Although global mine supply is expected to grow by more than 5% next year, the longer-term challenge is investment. Wood Mackenzie estimates the industry must deliver approximately 850 ktpa of new greenfield copper supply annually over the coming decade, yet permitting, geopolitical risk and increasing project complexity continue to constrain development.
Aluminium: primary deficits and grid substitution
The aluminium market faces a supply shock this year after attacks in the Middle East damaged two of the world's largest smelters, knocking out almost 2% of global primary production and pushing the 2026 balance into a 1 Mt deficit. High aluminium prices and premiums, combined with low alumina costs, encouraged smelters worldwide to ramp up capacity and restart idled electrolytic cells. This was particularly evident in China, where operating rates reached 99% and output slightly exceeded the national capacity cap.
However, this additional volume and Indonesia's rapid growth (reaching 1.3 Mt in 2026 and scaling to just under 3 Mt by 2030) were not enough to eliminate the shortfall. While the market is projected to return to surplus in 2027 as prices soften, medium-term fundamentals remain supportive, leaving faster-than-expected Indonesian expansion and broader economic weakness as the only notable downside risks.
Nickel: structural bifurcation between Class I and Class II
The nickel market is returning toward balance in 2026 following several years of oversupply, with global refined output contracting by 2% in the first annual decline since 2015. However, this headline stability masks a deep structural bifurcation. The Class II segment faces widening deficits from 2027, as Indonesian NPI production consolidates below its 2025 peak under the weight of tighter RKAB mining quotas, falling ore grades, and recent El Niño-related drought disruptions.
In response, Chinese stainless steel mills are structurally increasing their use of scrap and Class I cathode in melt mixtures to hedge against shrinking NPI availability. Conversely, the Class I and chemical segments face ongoing surplus from expanding Indonesian HPAL projects and Chinese refining capacity, though localised sulphur supply constraints and power bottlenecks continue to present operational risks to new project delivery.
Battery technology and energy storage: LFP dominance and the chemistry transition
LFP will dominate the mass battery market through 2030, driven by Chinese exports, rapid gigafactory expansion and significant advances in charging speed. CATL's third-generation Shenxing battery targets a 10% to 80% charge in under four minutes. European automakers are pivoting toward LFP to preserve margins as global EV adoption accelerates across Europe and emerging markets, though subsidy changes have stalled US momentum.
Beyond LFP, alternative chemistries are advancing on distinct timelines. In April 2026, CATL secured a three-year, 60 GWh sodium-ion supply agreement with HiTHIUM Energy Storage, marking the technology's transition to industrial-scale commercialisation, with large-scale shipments in China beginning in Q3 2026. Wood Mackenzie projects battery module cost parity between sodium-ion and LFP by 2035. Solid-state battery mass-production timelines have compressed toward 2030, supported by strong Chinese policy backing.
Lithium and storage economics: capital requirements and price dynamics
Lithium carbonate prices fell to a multi-year low in mid-2025 before rebounding approximately 130% by 2026, but this volatility does not translate directly into higher project costs. Raw lithium carbonate represents just 2% to 3% of total costs in a typical 100 MW, four-hour turnkey storage system. An 83% price rise in Q1 2026 translated to only a 9% increase in LFP cell prices and an approximate 10% rise in turnkey system costs. Reference price lags of four to eight months provide further insulation, though cell offer validity periods have tightened to as little as two weeks.
Investors have deployed US$60 billion in the lithium supply chain over the past decade, supporting a tenfold increase in global refined chemical supply. Meeting demand through the 2050s will require a further US$150 billion to US$250 billion. Chinese developers achieve significantly higher capital efficiency than Western counterparts, meaning equivalent investment delivers proportionally more production capacity. Western markets need to broaden their capital pools to support ex-China supply chain development and safeguard domestic automotive manufacturing.
Across copper, aluminium, nickel and lithium, the common thread is that future supply depends on investment decisions being made today," Grant added. "Markets are adapting to a world where security of supply, energy availability and geopolitical considerations increasingly sit alongside cost competitiveness in shaping investment outcomes.

Background
These findings were presented at the Wood Mackenzie LME Forum in London on 21 October 2026, which examined the impact of geopolitics, decarbonisation and AI on electrification and base metals markets. Australia has separately legislated that large-scale data centres must return as much renewable energy to the grid as they draw from it. Wood Mackenzie subject matter experts are available for interview across copper and aluminium markets, critical minerals policy, battery technology and energy storage, rare earths, and AI data centre power demand. Please contact Wood Mackenzie’s global communications team to arrange interviews.

articles.title: Searching for signposts − speech by Alan Taylor
articles.text:
Searching for signposts − speech by Alan Taylor

Given at the 2026 Dow Lecture, National Institute of Economic and Social Research

Published on
29 September 2026

In this speech, Alan Taylor discusses a key macroeconomic challenge facing the Bank of England: the risk that higher energy prices generate persistent inflationary pressures through expectations and so-called “second-round” effects. He examines the balance of risks, how the Bank monitors these effects, and how the current restrictive monetary policy guards against inflation persistence.

Speech
It is very much an honour and a pleasure to be here with you today at NIESR, and my thanks to David Aikman for inviting me to give the 2026 Dow Lecture.
I am conscious that I follow in the footsteps of a number of my esteemed current and former colleagues at the Bank of England, including Swati Dhingra, James Talbot and Silvana Tenreyro. The Dow Lecture has provided an important forum for thinking seriously about the major macroeconomic challenges facing the United Kingdom, and I am grateful for the opportunity to contribute to that tradition.
Today I want to focus on one such challenge facing monetary policy right now: the ongoing and still unpredictable energy shock.
I should emphasise that this is only one of the challenges currently facing policymakers. The world economy is again being shaped by geopolitical uncertainty, by shifts in global trade and production, and by changes in financial conditions. But time is scarce, so I will not spend this lecture trying to predict geopolitical events or venturing too far down those other avenues.
Instead, as we look down the macroeconomic road ahead, I want to ask a narrower but, in my view, more tractable question: how do inflationary energy shocks pass through the economy; how far and wide do their effects subsequently persist; what role do expectations play in that propagation process; and what does all of this mean for monetary policy?
Unfortunately, that road ahead is not clearly illuminated, even at the best of times. The signposts policymakers would like to rely on are often sparse, partial and difficult to interpret. That is especially true after a large inflation shock, when the accumulated evidence can point in different and sometimes contradictory directions and the distinction between temporary pressure and longer-term persistence is hard to draw in real time.
So where should we look?
The answer, I will argue, is not to search for a single decisive indicator that will reveal the route ahead. Rather, the better approach is to look across a set of imperfect signposts: the initial energy-price impulse; the response of inflation expectations, especially among households and firms; the extent to which those expectations feed into wages and prices; and the wider state of demand, slack and policy credibility that will shape that transmission. Together, this array of signposts can help us judge whether an energy shock is likely to fade, or whether it risks becoming embedded in more persistent inflation.
A useful starting point is to recap the distinction the Bank has often drawn between so-called direct, indirect and second-round effects in the transmission of energy price shocks.
The direct effects are the mechanical impact of higher energy prices on headline CPI. For example, increases in petrol prices, household gas and electricity bills feed directly into measured inflation as faced by consumers in items they directly buy.
The indirect effects occur when higher energy prices raise the costs of producing and distributing other goods and services, leading firms to pass some of those costs through to consumers. This is particularly likely in energy-intensive sectors or where margins are under pressure. These effects can be powerful, but they are still relatively easy to conceptualise. They tend to work through the economy over a fairly short horizon, and input-output tables give us a benchmark for judging the relative magnitude of the pass-through.
The more difficult issue concerns the second-round effects. This phrase is often used rather broadly, even loosely. I think it best to use it narrowly and precisely to describe the behavioural, general-equilibrium dynamics that can follow an initially temporary rise in inflation and make the inflation process more persistent.
These dynamics should not surprise us. Most of the prices and wages in our economy are largely determined by private decisions without policy intervention. If inflation rises sharply, workers may seek higher nominal wages to recover lost real income. Where labour demand is strong, firms may have to accept those costs to recruit and retain workers. Firms may also raise prices not only because their own input costs have risen, but because they expect competitors, suppliers and customers to behave differently in a higher-inflation environment.
The key policy question is not whether these dynamics exist, but how large and persistent they are likely to be, for a given shock, and how monetary policy should respond.
Our flexible inflation-targeting mandate is central to that judgement. Like most central banks, we have not been assigned a price-level target; our task is not to reverse the increase in prices caused by an energy shock, but to return the rate of inflation to target.
And the flexibility embedded in the mandate instructs us to do so over a period that avoids undesirable volatility in output. Together with the lags in monetary transmission, this means that policy can ‘look through’ short-lived relative-price shocks, which is the relevant case for most external commodity price shocks in the most normal times.
But monetary policy cannot look through the emergence of more persistent inflationary pressure. Here, its influence lies not in reversing the original price-level increase, but in preventing that shock from propagating into an ongoing inflation process.
The question is therefore how much policy should lean against that risk, given uncertainty about its magnitude and the trade-off between stabilising inflation and real economic activity.footnote [1] This is the nature of the policy problem created by second-round effects that we now face.
And inflation expectations are central to that problem. If households and firms expect a rise in inflation to be short-lived, they are less likely to respond in ways that sustain it. If instead they expect inflation to remain high, workers may seek greater compensation for future price increases and firms may raise prices to protect their margins. Those responses, all else equal, can then make the original shock more persistent, making matters worse.
This is why inflation expectations matter for second-round effects. Let me now make it concrete with an example.
The experience of 2022 is instructive. If we look first at the evolution of headline CPI and energy CPI, the basic pattern is clear (Chart 1). Headline inflation initially moved with energy inflation but remained persistently high even as energy inflation dropped sharply. That divergence is important. It suggests that the initial shock was doing more than mechanically raising the energy component of CPI. Rather, broader forces were contributing to a more persistent inflation process that unfolded gradually in waves (Taylor, 2025; Ramsden, 2024).

Chart 1: Headline and energy CPI inflation
12-month rates

Footnotes

Notes: 12-month rates, monthly, January 2020 to August 2026. The headline rate is the published 12-month rate; the energy rate covers motor fuels as well as household electricity and gas. The two series are drawn on different scales. The zero line and the direction of every move are therefore common to both, but the vertical size of a move is not comparable across the two lines. The 2% target refers to the left-hand axis. Latest observation: August 2026. Source: ONS.

We can see the same pattern more formally by decomposing the drivers of inflation over this period (Chart 2). Using the Bank’s forecast, we can separate the contribution of direct and indirect energy-price effects from the broader general-equilibrium dynamics that followed. The decomposition suggests direct and indirect effects (orange bars) account for much of the initial rise in headline inflation. But they cannot fully explain the persistence of inflation through 2023 and into 2024. Beyond additional global supply disruptions (light blue), contributions from persistence judgments (purple), slack (green), and the unaccounted-for component (pink) are consistent with broader general-equilibrium dynamics having played a material role.

Chart 2: Bank of England forecast decomposition
2020-2026

Footnotes

Notes: Contributions to the deviation of four-quarter CPI inflation from the 2% target, quarterly, 2020 Q1 to 2026 Q2. The white line is the published total; the bars are the thirteen components and sum to it. The chart stops at the last quarter for which CPI has actually been published. Source: Bank of England. Latest observation: 30/06/2026

So, what drove those general-equilibrium dynamics? They reflected the interaction of the original shock with wage and price-setting behaviour, inflation expectations, slack in the economy, and the stance of monetary policy. No single factor explains the persistence of inflation. Rather, the key point is one of state dependence: the effects of an energy shock depend not only on the size of the shock itself, but also on the economic environment into which it arrives.
In other words, the economy responded as an interconnected system in which households, firms and financial markets, in the UK and globally, formed views about what that particular shock meant in that particular context, and acted on those views.
That experience points to the first major signpost: inflation expectations. What do economic actors think is coming?
During the 2022 energy shock, expectations among financial markets, firms, and households rose markedly. Chart 3 compares CPI inflation expectations among households and firms, and a market-implied measure of inflation compensation over the coming year.footnote [2]
We see that the inflation expectations evolved differently across agents. Market implied expectations normalised relatively quickly as energy prices fell and policy tightened. By contrast, firm and household expectations, declined more slowly and remained elevated for longer. The heterogeneity in dynamics across measures shown in Chart 3 is therefore important not simply because expectations rose, but because it illustrates that expectations can move at different speeds and remain elevated even after the original shock begins to unwind.

Chart 3: Inflation expectations across agents
1 year ahead in

Footnotes

Notes: Expected CPI inflation one year ahead. Households are the Citi/YouGov survey measure; firms are the weighted median response to the Decision Maker Panel's 1-year-ahead CPI question; financial markets are the 1-year spot inflation swap rate, averaged from daily quotes to a monthly mean. Each measure is plotted over its own full available sample and no attempt is made to align them, so the number of series shown varies across the horizontal axis. Coverage: Households (Citi) Nov 2005-Aug 2026 (250 observations); Firms (DMP) May 2022-April 2026 (48 observations); Financial markets (1-year swap) April 2004-July 2026 (268 observations). Latest observation: July 2026. Source: Citi/YouGov; Decision Maker Panel; Bloomberg L.P.

So, what do these indicators on that first signpost tell us? Well, most models, even those that are purely statistical, attribute a role to inflation expectations in explaining inflation persistence. For instance, a machine-learning model produced by Buckmann et al., (2025), summarised in Chart 4, attributes a notable share of the persistence in inflation, reflected in a relatively slow-moving trend component, to what we might call the inflation-expectations channel.

Chart 4: Boosted Inflation Model Decomposition
Short-term expectations explaining inflation

Footnotes

Note: Near-term predictive contribution to CPI inflation from a trend component capturing expectations, wages and services-related inflation components. The model also separates demand- and supply-related contributions, not shown. Latest observation: July 2026. Source: Buckmann et al., (2025) Boosted Inflation Model.

The sceptic would call that a black-box explanation, and I would not want to overstate the precision of any single model-based decomposition. But together the divergence between energy and headline inflation, the Bank’s forecast decomposition, the behaviour of expectations and the statistical evidence suggest that the 2022 shock propagated well beyond its direct and indirect effects.
But a model decomposition does not reveal the mechanism. Expectations rising is not the same as expectations becoming inflationary in practice, in a causal sense. To affect realised inflation, they must change wage bargains, spending or price-setting, and the ability of households and firms to act on them will depend on labour-market conditions, demand, competition and margins.
This is why the second major signpost we come to is transmission: whether expectations actually feed into realised behaviour.
For monetary policy today, that distinction is central. The UK is again facing an energy shock, but in a different environment from 2022: the labour market is looser, excess demand has given way to excess supply, and monetary and financial conditions are restrictive. Those conditions may not fully eliminate the risk of second-round effects, but they should serve to limit their magnitude.
In the remainder of this speech, I assess the evidence across the two stages of the expectations channel. Stage 1 asks how inflation expectations did, and likely will, respond to the ongoing energy shock. Stage 2 asks whether those expectations are likely to be transmitted through into wages, prices and other economic decisions, making inflation more persistent. I then sum up by considering the implications, in my view, for policy strategy, given the evidence and uncertainties.
Stage 1: Drivers of inflation expectations and dynamics
Inflation expectations are relatively easy to obtain, but much harder to interpret. They matter for policy not simply because people report a number in a survey, but because those numbers may shape the decisions households and firms go on to make. So let me begin with the first part of the mechanism: how expectations are formed.
Over the past decade, we have learned much more about how different groups form inflation expectations. A key message from that work is that financial markets, professional forecasters, firms and households are not simply interchangeable sources of the same signal (Coibion Opens in a new window & Gorodnichenko, 2025 Opens in a new window; Weber et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., 2024 Opens in a new window; Reis, 2023) Opens in a new window. They pay attention to different information, update at different speeds, display different biases, and bring different experiences to bear when thinking about inflation.
Financial markets are, in some sense, the easiest case to understand. They are strongly incentivized to process information as quickly and as accurately as possible. They react to data releases, central bank communications, geopolitical developments, changes in the expected path of policy, and form expectations that are, by construction, highly forward-looking and information-sensitive.
In levels, households and firms look rather different to financial markets. Both form expectations that are highly dispersed in the cross-section, and importantly they tend to biased upwards with a skew (Chart 5). This upwards bias translates into means that typically sit above realised inflation, at least in the pre-2022 period, and since 2024. For households, this caveat applies not only to expected future inflation but also to perceptions of inflation today. Those perceptions also tend to be biased upwards, meaning that expectations are formed from a subjective starting point rather than directly from the same benchmark as official statistics (D’Acunto & Weber, 2026 Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., May 2024 NBER Opens in a new window).

Chart 5a: Households’ 1-year expectations of inflation

Footnotes

Notes: Individual respondents' expectations of CPI inflation one year ahead, from the Inflation Attitudes Survey, quarterly. The line is the equal-weighted mean. The bands are, from darkest to lightest, the 25th-75th, 10th-90th and 1st-99th percentiles of the cross-section. Quarters with fewer than 10 responses are dropped. The dashed line is realised 12-month CPI inflation at the same date, that is, what inflation actually was when the expectation was formed, not the outturn the expectation was about. Latest observation: January 2026. Source: Inflation Attitudes Survey; ONS.

Chart 5b: Firms’ 1y-ahead CPI expectations

Footnotes

Notes: Firms' expectations of CPI inflation one year ahead, from the Decision Maker Panel, monthly. This is the DMP's CPI question, not its own-price question. The line is the weighted mean across firms. The bands are, from darkest to lightest, the 25th-75th, 10th-90th and 1st-99th percentiles of the cross-section. The dashed line is realised 12-month CPI inflation at the same date, that is, what inflation actually was when the expectation was formed, not the outturn the expectation was about. Based on 641 to 848 responding firms a month. Latest observation: April 2026. Source: Decision Maker Panel; ONS.

Of course, these surveys are not perfect instruments; responses are noisy, question wording matters, and the average can conceal a great deal of disagreement (Assenza et al., 2026 Opens in a new window; D’Acunto et al., 2024 Opens in a new window). But that is precisely why the distribution of beliefs, not just the mean, might be informative.
For policymakers, however, the key signal may lie less in the level of expected inflation than in how expectations respond to shocks over time. On this dimension, we can see that firms appear closer to households than to financial markets, while still occupying an intermediate position.
Neither households nor firms, in general, continuously process every piece of macroeconomic news in the same way as financial market participants. One of the key lessons from recent research is that they often use relatively accessible information when forming and updating expectations. That is not irrational. Attention is scarce and information is costly to acquire and process. And, for most households and firms, the returns to doing so are much smaller than for financial markets, particularly in a world with low and stable inflation.
Indeed, low attention to inflation is not a failure of credibility; but a reflection of it. One of the achievements of the inflation-targeting era was that inflation became sufficiently stable that most people did not need to think about it very much.
Whether the recent inflationary episode disrupted that low-attention equilibrium is an empirical question to which I will return. To interpret that evidence, however, we first need to understand how households and firms form expectations when inflation does attract their attention.
Households appear to pay particular attention to price changes in salient items of the consumption basket, rather than headline CPI per se. Food, energy and fuel prices are clear examples: they are visible, often purchased or closely noticed, and feature prominently in people’s sense of the cost of living (Anesti, Esady, Naylor, 2025; D’Acunto et al., 2021 Opens in a new window; Coibion & Gorodnichenko, 2015 Opens in a new window).
This indicates that the effect of inflation on expectations may depend on where that inflation shows up. An increase in the price of something households buy frequently may shift expectations more than an equivalent increase in a less visible component of the index (D’Acunto et al., 2021 Opens in a new window). A risk is that expectations may respond asymmetrically to changes in inflation in these components: rising quickly when visible prices increase but falling slowly when those prices stabilise (Anesti, Esady, Naylor, 2025). In that case, a temporary shock can leave a longer imprint on beliefs than its direct arithmetic contribution to inflation would suggest.
Firms, too, appear to respond to realised inflation, but with a greater focus on Headline CPI. Recent high-frequency evidence from the UK Decision Makers’ Panel (DMP) finds that firms’ inflation perceptions and expectations respond around official CPI releases (Chart 6). Those responses appear related to the reported change in CPI inflation, with little evidence of an additional response to the surprise relative to expectations, such as professional forecasts.

Chart 6: Firms’ responses to CPI news from Yotzov et al., (2025)

Footnotes

Notes: This figure plots the impact of CPI inflation changes on one-year ahead (Panel A) and three-year (Panel B) CPI inflation expectations based on the methodology outlined in Section 3. The omitted category is the day before the CPI release. (0% confidence intervals are reported around the point estimates. Source: Yotzov et al., (2025).

Putting these pieces together, we see a common theme. While financial markets are more forward-looking, both households and firms form expectations partly by looking backwards — to realised inflation, to perceived current inflation, to observed price changes (with a bias toward salient ones), and to the economic environment they have just experienced. That distinction captures an important contrast between “Wall Street” and “Main Street”.
That backward-looking behaviour is not necessarily mistaken: where inflation itself has a (possibly time-varying) inertial component, recent inflation contains information about its likely path.
In the UK data, this backward-looking component shows up clearly (Chart 7). A one percentage point increase in perceived inflation is associated with a rise in expected inflation one year ahead of around 0.4 to 0.5 percentage points. Put differently, expectations appear to be partly conditioned by what households and firms believe inflation to be today, with the implication that biases in the latter can be passing through into the former.

Chart 7: Pass-through of perceived to expected inflation versus inertial component inflation

Footnotes

However, expectations are not only backward-looking. Experimental evidence shows that both households and firms do update their inflation expectations when they are provided with clear forward-looking information, including information from central banks (Coibion Opens in a new window, Opens in a new windowGorodnichenko Opens in a new window & Weber 2022 Opens in a new window; Coibion, Gorodnichenko & Kumar 2018 Opens in a new window).
That matters for monetary policy communication. It tells us that economic agents are not unreachable. But it also tells us that communication must compete with expectations that may already have taken shape from subjective experience, media coverage and observed prices. The question is not whether central bank information can matter. It can. The question is how much it matters relative to the information people have already gathered from what they see around them.
A simple way to frame this is as a competition between signals from the recent past and signals about the likely path ahead. The UK evidence is consistent with financial market expectations being more strongly associated with forward-looking information, and households and firms responding to elements of both channels (Chart 8).

The balance also varies within groups. That cross-sectional variation is important. Among households, those with more accurate perceptions of current inflation appear more responsive to both backward- and forward-looking information, while those in the tails respond less to macroeconomic signals. The distribution may therefore contain information obscured by the average.
For policy, the distinction between attentiveness to backward- and forward-looking signals matters: the backward-looking component may warrant particular attention. If a temporary increase in inflation leads households and firms to revise up their expectations persistently (Stage 1), and those expectations then feed through into wage and price-setting (Stage 2), the original shock can become more persistent and the force of transmission could mean that perceptions self-validate.
So did the inflationary episode of 2022 disrupt that low-attention equilibrium and take us some way down that path? There are reasons to think that it did, and that expectations may now be more sensitive to inflation shocks than before 2022. Whether that makes them more useful as a guide for policy is less clear.
That 2022 inflationary surge was large, visible and prolonged. It not only affected prices across the economy; it also generated intense media coverage and made inflation a normal topic of conversation again. We see this behavioural shift through online data; with Google searches and media references to inflation rising sharply in 2022 (Charts 9a and 9b).
