articles.title: Learning about earnings: Can we rely on labour market slack to mitigate the latest supply shock? − speech by Megan Greene
articles.text:
Learning about earnings: Can we rely on labour market slack to mitigate the latest supply shock? − speech by Megan Greene

Given at London School of Economics

Published on
20 October 2026

The extent to which the latest energy price shock feeds into more persistent inflation through second-round effects remains a key consideration for policymakers. The presence of slack in the labour market could suggest that wage pressures will remain contained, limiting the scope for second-round effects. But is this likely to be the case?
In this speech, Megan challenges this argument, drawing on a wide range of wage indicators to assess recent developments in pay growth and the likely path ahead for wages and domestically-generated inflation. She then turns to broader measures of labour market slack to examine whether current conditions are likely to restrain second-round effects via the wage-setting channel.

Speech
Introduction
Thank you for inviting me to the LSE to speak. It’s nice to be back here—I often studied in your library when I was an undergraduate in the US working in London for the summer. Come to think of it, I may have snuck in so please don’t alert the authorities.
Over the past few months, a lot has happened in the world of geopolitics…and yet very little has fundamentally changed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains beset by attacks and potential new chokepoints in shipping have emerged such as the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Although Middle Eastern oil flows have at times returned to near pre-war levels, expensive and inefficient workarounds have kept energy prices high (Figure 1). Wholesale gas prices are close to triple their level at the start of the year, with oil spot prices just under double their early-January level.footnote [1] And the prices for refined products have remained elevated despite volatile spot prices. Even if the conflict in Iran ends tomorrow, we have already been hit by a protracted energy shock.

Figure 1: Evolution of energy prices since start of 2026
Index, 100 = price at 1 Jan 2026

Footnotes

Source: ONS, Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.

(a) Dashed vertical lines denote selected key events. Dates may not be exact due to frequency of data. Latest datapoints are for 19 October 2026.

I have previously laid out the various avenues via which such a negative supply shock can propagate through the UK economy, highlighting the important role of second-round effects in embedding inflation in the economy. As I set out in my last speech Opens in a new window in June, they can take hold through the price- or wage-setting channel, or both. For today’s purposes, I will focus specifically on the wage-setting channel.
Wages represent a material cost for firms, particularly in the services sector where labour accounts for a large share of total costs. Wages are also a significant determinant of incomes, thus underpinning consumption. As a result, measures of wage growth offer useful insight into domestically-generated inflation. Of course, not all wage growth is inflationary. If wages rise because productivity improves, the implications for inflation may well be limited. But wages can also act as the mechanism through which temporary negative supply shocks become embedded in domestic inflation, particularly when workers seek to protect real incomes and firms then raise prices to protect their margins.
The MPC has judged that there is slack in the labour market, as evidenced by the ratio of vacancies to unemployment relative to equilibrium (Figure 2). Some of my colleagues and I have argued that the wage-setting channel poses a smaller risk of generating second-round effects than the price-setting channel. If firms are facing higher costs and have experienced years of margin compression, they are likely to pass on some of their higher costs by raising prices. This is consistent with intelligence that we’re hearing from our Agents. But if there is slack in the labour market, worker power is relatively weak. Even if workers demand higher pay as their costs go up, employers may deny that request given the large pool of talent from which to choose.

Figure 2: Vacancy-unemployment (V-U) ratio and V-U equilibrium
Ratio(a)

Footnotes

Source: Advertising association/ World Advertising Research Centre Expenditure Report, ONS and Bank calculations. Latest data point is for 2026Q2.

(a) The equilibrium V/U ratio is estimated using an error-correction model over the period 1982–2024. The real cost of vacancy posting and hourly labour productivity are included as long-run determinants for the level of vacancies. The model also includes controls for short-term movements in these variables (Stelmach, Kensett , & Schnattinger, 2025 Opens in a new window)

Given our monetary policy strategy has relied partly on slack mitigating the impact of second-round effects, it’s worth exploring how much labour market slack there really is. The wider economy has proved surprisingly resilient, implying there is less slack than some labour market indicators suggest. If so, there is a greater risk of second-round effects emerging through the wage-setting channel than we initially thought.
We may not have a clear steer on whether the shock from the Iran conflict gives rise to material second-round effects through wage- or price-setting until early next year when our Agents’ pay survey is out in February and the brunt of 2027 pay settlements are agreed in January and April. But if we wait for this evidence to lean against second-round effects with a tighter monetary policy stance, we will already be too late given the lags with which monetary policy affects the economy and inflation.
As outlined in our Forecast Evaluation Report and the Macro-technical paper Opens in a new window alongside it, predicting wage growth has been a challenge for the Bank, particularly since the Global Financial Crisis. As shown in Figure 3, Bank forecasts tended to systematically predict higher wage growth than what we experienced until the Covid period, after which our forecasts systematically underestimated the strength of wage growth.footnote [2]

Figure 3: MPR forecasts and outturns of wage growth(a)
Annual growth (%)(a)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) The grey lines show forecasts from different vintages. The aqua line shows the outturns k=12 quarters after the first data release.

Our suite of wage models, like many macro forecasting models, are largely driven by historical relationships. The recent persistent undershooting of wage growth forecasts may suggest something structurally shifted in the labour market during the pandemic. As I argued in my 2024 speech (Greene, 2024), this could reflect reduced matching efficiency, lower search intensity, labour hoarding, persistent recruitment difficulties and weaker participation. It could also reflect stronger real wage resistance following the 2022 energy shock than historical relationships have implied (Pill, 2025). Wage growth has generally decelerated since 2023, suggesting these upward pressures have been unwinding, but they may not have unwound entirely.
Models inevitably simplify reality, and their performance depends critically on the quality of the signals they are trying to capture. One important development over the past decade has been an expansion in the range of wage indicators we look at, reflecting efforts to measure underlying wage pressures from multiple perspectives.
But this richer information set has brought its own challenges. At the moment, wage data are like a Rorschach Test; they can be used to confirm anyone’s preconceived view of slack in the labour market because they are giving mixed signals (Figure 4). Different indicators often tell different stories, reflecting differences in coverage, frequency, composition and methodology (Villar, Moyon, & Ahn, 2025 Opens in a new window). The task for policymakers is therefore not simply to monitor wages, but to understand the dynamics underpinning different metrics.

Figure 4: Measures of private sector wage growth
Annual growth (%)(a)

Footnotes

Sources: Bank of England settlements database, DMP survey, HMRC, Indeed, ONS and Bank calculations.

(a) The private sector regular pay growth line shows the ONS measure of private sector regular AWE growth, measured as the three-month average on the same period a year earlier. The DMP lines show average realised pay growth and average expected pay growth (shifted 12 months forward) from the DMP survey on the same basis. The HMRC RTI line shows a proxy of growth in median pay in the private sector, also measured as the three-month average on the same period a year earlier. Bank staff construct the HMRC RTI measure by taking median pay for each industry – excluding public administration and defence, education, health and social work – and weighting them by industry shares in payrolled employment. Annual growth is then calculated using the Laspeyres formula, holding industry weights fixed at their levels a year earlier to reduce the effect of changes in workforce composition. The Indeed Wage Tracker line shows annual average job title matched pay growth for UK job vacancies. The latest data points are for the three months to August 2026 for private sector regular pay and the Indeed Wage Tracker and September 2026 for the HMRC RTI private sector median, BoE settlements and the DMP survey.

This brings me to my main focus today. Given the importance of understanding wage-setting behaviour and what it might mean for slack and second-round effects, I want to dig into some of our key wage indicators to parse signal from noise. I will start by examining how these indicators differ and where in the wage-setting process they are likely to be most informative. I will then consider what they can tell us about the recent developments and what signal we might glean about wage dynamics going forward. Finally, I will examine how confident we can be that a material degree of slack will restrain second-round effects and inflation via the wage-setting channel.
Getting into the weeds isn't always glamorous, but in policymaking as in gardening, sometimes you just have to get your hands dirty.
Measures of wage growth
When confronted with a range of indicators, it is often useful to take a step back and consider exactly what information each one conveys. After all, wage indicators measure different things and are collected in different ways. This is a feature, not a bug - the differences between measures allow us to build a richer picture of wage developments within the domestic economy to assess the degree of current and emerging wage pressures.
In light of this, Table 1 brings together some of the key metrics used by the Bank of England to monitor UK wage growth. While not exhaustive, the selection illustrates the breadth of information available to policymakers and the different insights a variety of measures can provide, as demonstrated by the range of questions presented in the second column: each of these metrics has something different to offer when it comes to understanding wage pressures.

Naturally, some measures receive more attention than others. Chief among these is the average weekly earnings (AWE) series, which helps us answer the question “what is the growth of the average wage?”. AWE is an accredited official statistic published with a two-month lag by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), derived from the Monthly Wages and Salaries Survey (MWSS).footnote [3] The MWSS is issued to around 9,000 businesses and covers approximately 15 million employees across Great Britain. While adjustments are made to account for smaller firms, the survey includes only businesses with 20 or more employees. Nevertheless, AWE provides a broad measure of the change in pay levels across the economy and is thus useful for gauging domestic inflationary pressures stemming from changes in wages.
At the Bank, we tend to focus on private sector regular AWE growth as opposed to the whole economy (including the public sector) for a few reasons. Private sector pay feeds more directly into the CPI measure of inflation, particularly when it comes to services, where labour costs make up a large chunk of total costs. In addition, UK public sector pay is often determined by government policy decisions. As such, wage-setting in the private sector is generally more closely tied to labour market conditions, whereas institutional pay setting arrangements and fiscal constraints can often influence public sector pay outcomes. Monetary policy therefore has more influence over private sector pay. Furthermore, private sector regular pay excludes volatile bonuses while they’re included in total pay. For these reasons, I’m going to focus on private sector regular AWE pay growth for the rest of this speech.
Pay As You Earn (PAYE) Real Time Information (RTI) data provides an alternative read on wage growth. This is published by the ONS on a monthly basis, in conjunction with HMRC, and can be used to help answer the same question as the AWE: “what is the growth of the average wage?”. Median estimates of the data are available with less of a lag than the official AWE measure, though they are often heavily revised. In addition, its production does not rely on survey responses. Instead, the information comes directly from HMRC’s PAYE RTI system, which covers the whole population of employees payrolled by employers, allowing for more detailed breakdowns of the data. The data is presented as gross pay, which includes bonus pay and other one-off payments (but not pension contributions) unlike private sector regular AWE. Arguably, this can make it harder to gain a clear view on wage growth and makes it more difficult to compare RTI and AWE.
We can also draw on wage growth measures derived from responses to the Decision Maker Panel (DMP) survey to answer the question “what assessment do firms make of their own wage growth?”. The DMP is a large, monthly panel survey of Chief Financial Officers from small-, medium- and large-sized UK businesses. Since 2022, the survey has included a number of questions focused on firms’ wages. This means that the back data available for wage analysis is limited. In 2026, the survey included wage growth data from approximately 700 firms, covering around 300,000 employees each month. Responses are used to construct measures of both realised and expected wage growth. The former tells us what has actually happened to firms’ own wage growth over the last year, while the latter gives us an idea of what firms anticipate will happen to their wage growth over the next year. Forward-looking indicators are hard to come by – an unfortunate truth for those of us in the forecasting business – but they are particularly useful given that both shocks and monetary policy take their time to work their way through the economy. As such, I am monitoring this measure closely as the current shock unfolds.
Pay settlements data can also provide us with a glimpse into the future path for wage growth. Such data allows us to shed some light on the pay decisions firms are making with regard to their current employees, helping us answer the question “what pay increases are firms agreeing for their existing employees?”. However, settlements data captures changes in basic pay and does not capture all sources of earnings growth, such as progression, merit and performance-related pay, or bonuses. We can access pay settlements data through the Bank of England’s settlements database. This database brings together information collected from businesses across the UK economy by the Bank’s Agents and external data providers, collected at various frequencies. Given that these figures can be updated retrospectively as more settlements are finalised, they are subject to some revision. We also get a sense of how pay settlements are likely to evolve over the next year in the Agents’ pay survey, released in February but with intelligence coming in from our Agents in the lead up to that.
Settlements data can only tell us so much. By its nature, its focus is on those workers already employed. But what are firms willing to pay new hires? The Indeed Wage Tracker provides insight into this, measuring the median annual change in advertised wages and salaries found on the Indeed platform across job title, region and salary-types. The sample size of each is reliant on a number of different factors, including the amount of total job vacancies, the proportion that is posted online and the share of these postings that contains wage or salary information (Adrjan & Lydon, 2023 Opens in a new window). This data is collected in the UK and a range of developed countries, allowing for cross-country comparison.
This is a whistle-stop tour of wage growth metrics. Each tells us something slightly different about wage growth pressures in the economy. I’ll now put them to use to explore present and future developments in wage growth.
Recent and current wage growth: two measures, different stories
Having gone through the various wage metrics, let’s use them to try to work out how much slack there is the labour market now and whether the wage-setting process has changed. For this, I’ll look at private sector regular AWE and its median RTI equivalent (proxied for the private sector), which both answer the question “what is the growth of the average wage?”. The good news is that both metrics show wage growth broadly continuing to moderate since recent peaks in 2023 (Figure 5). But these two indicators tell very different stories about the extent of that progress.

After almost 3 years of gradual easing, recent AWE data broadly suggest a further and more rapid leg down in wage growth, coming in at 3.0% in August (the aqua line in Figure 5). In contrast, our primary RTI metric of private sector wage pressure – growth in median pay – remains at a considerably higher rate of 4.4% in September (the orange line in Figure 5). Historically, these measures have tracked each other reasonably closely, albeit over a relatively short sample given RTI data are only available from 2014. Since early 2026, the divergence between them has become unusually large by historical standards.
RTI and AWE measures are answering the same question and both are constructed using sectoral wage growth and weighted according to the level of employment.footnote [4] So what's behind their divergence now? To decompose the wedge between these different measures, I’ll use a measure of mean pay growth derived from the RTI data (showing annual wage growth of 5% in August), which is more comparable to mean private sector regular pay growth from AWE (showing annual wage growth of 3% in August).
The wedge between these measures is explained primarily by three factors:

Differences in wage growth within industries: for a given industry wage growth in AWE is different to that in RTI. This is possible due to the different data underlying the two (a survey in the case of AWE, administrative data for RTI).
Between-industry compositional effects: This arises because the industry shares underlying the two differ and can change over time as employment shifts between industries.
Differences in flexible pay such as bonuses: AWE regular pay doesn’t include bonuses and arrears, whereas RTI does.

Differences in wage growth between industries and within industries can both help us understand underlying wage dynamics. Wage growth driven by changes in industry shares has implications for aggregate wage pressure and can give us a sense of overall slack. Wage growth within sectors reflects firms’ pay-setting decisions and can reveal whether they have changed in the face of a shock.
Figure 6 isolates the contributions to the wedge from the three sources. In August the wedge was 2 percentage points and has grown since late 2025 due to steadily rising compositional differences (pink area), fluctuating contributions from within industry differences in pay growth (purple area) and bonuses (blue area).

Of the three main components explaining the wedge between AWE and RTI, let’s first address the easiest to interpret: flexible pay. AWE private regular pay data exclude bonuses and arrears, while private sector RTI data include them. We want to compare apples-to-apples when we are gleaning signals from the two series. To do this, we assume that the bonuses (and arrears) captured in the AWE measure of total pay are also present in the RTI data and subtract their contribution from the RTI measure. This is necessarily a simplifying approximation and so the results should be interpreted with some caution. Bonuses and cost of living payments played a significant role in explaining the wedge between the two series in 2022-23 and earlier this year before waning more recently. During 2022-23 bonuses and one-off payments were common across sectors, whereas more recently these have been concentrated primarily in finance and professional services.
Now let’s turn to the role of compositional effects in creating a wedge between AWE and RTI. We can do this by comparing the changes in sectoral employment weights in private sector AWE and private sector RTI over the past year (Figure 7). This chart shows the year-on-year changes in the latest data, but it reflects trends that have persisted throughout 2026. AWE shows employment shifting towards lower-paid sectors, with rising weights for industries such as accommodation and food services and falling weights for higher-paying sectors such as financial and professional services. RTI, however, paints the opposite picture, with employment shifting slightly away from lower-paying sectors towards higher-paying ones.

What signal can we draw from this? There is really no silver bullet here, and this is exactly why we look at multiple indicators to get a complete picture of the labour market. But on balance, I’d put slightly more weight on the compositional story from the RTI. The RTI series is drawn from administrative data rather than a survey. RTI doesn’t require imputing employees who work in small firms (under 20 employees) as the AWE series does. Finally, the narrative from the RTI data chimes with the Labour Force Survey (LFS), which also indicates that employment has shifted to higher paid industries over the past year. There are reasons to treat the LFS with caution; it suffers from low response rates and the industry classifications are self-reported and may not always be accurate. On balance, I place slightly more weight on the RTI’s narrative that workers are shifting towards higher paying industries. This means that the AWE may be giving us an artificially low reading of wage growth because of the specific compositional effects it incorporates.
Let’s now take a look at differences in pay growth within industries in the AWE and RTI series. Figure 8 shows wage growth within various sectors in the latest AWE and RTI releases. The AWE data suggests that, on balance, wage growth in lower paying sectors was running hotter than for higher paid sectors. The RTI data, however, suggest wage growth was faster in higher paying sectors.footnote [5] For the reasons I’ve just explained, I have a bit more faith in the RTI data. But again, these discrepancies point to the importance of making use of a range of metrics.

Where does this leave us? Our adjusted measures of wage growth remain above levels consistent with our inflation target of 2%. The most frequently cited indicator that we use, private sector regular AWE, seems to have been consistently undercooking actual private sector wage growth since late-2025.
Looking ahead: what can guide us?
Over the past year, different metrics of wage growth have told different stories. However, there is strong evidence to suggest that underlying wage growth is higher than that reported by private sector regular AWE. What we ultimately want to know, however, is how wage setting will evolve going forward, particularly in light of yet another negative supply shock. For this, I’ll look at some forward-looking indicators—specifically the DMP, pay settlements and the Indeed Wage Tracker.
The DMP has been an invaluable source of information on wages since wage questions were introduced in 2022. The survey directly asks firms about wage changes for their employees, and so arguably provides the clearest window into firms’ wage-setting processes. Realised wage growth has broadly tracked the trends in AWE and RTI, though there have been some periods of divergence. The DMP recorded a lower peak in 2023 and indicated more gradual moderation in wage growth thereafter. We can see this in Figure 10, which plots DMP realised wage growth and one-year ahead expected wage growth, at the time of the survey, alongside the RTI and AWE measures.

The noticeable gap between private regular AWE and pay settlements over the past five years can be explained by the state of the labour market. Faced with recruitment difficulties and elevated staff turnover, firms had stronger incentives to raise pay to attract and retain workers. As a result, there was ‘pay drift’; actual wage growth often exceeded that implied by pay settlements, reflecting pay for new workers, retention-related pay increases and other adjustments outside formal settlement rounds. This is consistent with academic literature that finds that workers achieve faster pay growth when outside job opportunities improve, and that the threat of higher turnover can prompt firms to raise pay more broadly across their workforce (Jäger, Roth, Roussille, & Schoefer, 2024 Opens in a new window) (Sokolova & Sorensen, 2021 Opens in a new window).

As I outlined in a recent speech (Greene, 2026), the labour market is considerably weaker now than it was in 2022. As aggregate demand has softened, demand for labour has also eased, reducing recruitment difficulties and, in turn, the pressure on firms to grant large pay increases. Expected pay settlements may therefore provide a more reliable guide to future wage growth than they did during the post-pandemic period.
At present, our Agents report that expected settlements for 2027 will be similar or only slightly lower than in 2026, suggesting the wage disinflation process may be stalling. For the past two years, actual settlements have come in above what was projected in the Agents’ pay survey (4% in 2025 vs 3.7% in the pay survey; current estimate of 3.6% in 2026 vs 3.4% in the pay survey), so I expect the risk to the latest guidance is to the upside. Moreover, the vast majority of pay settlements will be agreed between January and April (Figure 15), when we expect inflation to be above 4%. This is well above the threshold in which households are more sensitive to inflation outturns in forming their expectations.

Finally, the Indeed Wage Tracker offers a highly forward-looking and high frequency insight into wage pressures. The Indeed Wage Tracker captures the pay firms are willing to offer new recruits and therefore captures those workers that the pay settlements data omits. Their main limitation is that they – typically – represent a small proportion of the work force who have in recent years made a relatively small contribution to overall wage growth. However, as retention pressures have eased and firms are less reliant on large pay increases to retain staff, wages offered to new recruits may play a somewhat larger role in explaining overall wage developments as they did in the years before the pandemic.
Since late 2023, the Indeed Wage Tracker has tended to imply slightly higher wage growth than private sector regular AWE (on average about 0.8pp) (Figure 4). In August, the UK Indeed UK Wage Tracker stood at 4% (Figure 15) and while UK wage growth remains high relative to many of its peers, it has become less of an outlier in recent months. However disinflationary wage momentum here also seems to be levelling off, with the wage tracker remaining stuck at around 4% since the turn of the year.

Taken together, I place considerable weight on the DMP and pay settlements, while monitoring the Indeed Wage Tracker as a higher frequency indicator of broader labour demand conditions. Collectively, these measures suggest that the wage disinflation process is stalling out with pay growth likely to stabilise over the coming year closer to 3.5% than 3%. I believe this remains above levels consistent with our inflation target and suggests there is less labour market slack than we thought.
What will I be monitoring for the emergence of second-round effects?
There is a plethora of wage growth indicators that can help inform our view of slack in the labour market. Our investigation of these different measures leads me to believe that underlying wage growth is running above rates consistent with our 2% inflation target and this looks set to continue. This suggests there is not as much slack as we had expected, and so there is a greater risk of second-round effects emerging from the wage-setting channel.
But we need not only focus explicitly on wage measures in making our assessment of slack. Other labour market and activity measures can provide insights on the degree of slack in the economy, and as I have demonstrated previously Opens in a new window, wider economic conditions play a role in determining the extent to which second-round effects are likely to take hold. Taking stock of these conditions suggests that it may be unwise to assume that labour market slack and weak demand will mitigate the risks. Other labour market indicators also suggest there is less labour market slack than we thought and that it may have peaked. As with wages, there is no one perfect metric of employment growth – particularly in recent years given issues with the Labour Force Survey. Bank staff produce an estimate of underlying employment growth drawing on a range of surveys and hard data. Figure 17 shows that employment growth was essentially flat in 2025 and below the rate of population growth—consistent with a degree of slack opening up. However, underlying employment growth has been steadily rising this year. This has recently been corroborated by the KPMG/REC jobs report, according to which measures of employment and labour demand have risen above pre-conflict levels.

Meanwhile, there are other signs that labour market slack may have peaked: the unemployment rate has fallen from 5.2% in the three months to January 2026 to 4.7% in August; redundancies have come down from their peak of 150,000 in the three months to October 2025 and are currently running at just above 100,000, in line with the average observed since 2012; and vacancies show signs of stabilising.
A stable or slightly improving labour market is consistent with more resilience in activity than we and other forecasters had been expecting. In April, HM Treasury’s summary of independent forecasts for the UK economy showed a median GDP forecast of 0.7% in 2026, roughly in line with our middle projection (Scenario B) in April of 0.8% growth this year. By September, HM Treasury’s summary of forecasts showed median growth of 1.3% this year and our central projection in July predicted 1.1% growth in 2026 . There has been a trend towards revising UK GDP forecasts for this year up, particularly as stronger-than-expected data has come in.
Surveys of firms and consumers tell a similar story. September's flash PMI ticked down modestly but remained in positive territory, reflecting an expansion of output. Purchasing managers are reasonably positive about the future as well, with the future output index at 67.4, just a little below the long-run average of 68.2.
The economy has proven surprisingly resilient even in the face of tighter financial conditions. Since the outbreak of the Iran conflict, financial conditions have tightened largely as short-term interest rates and mortgage rates have increased. But while the price of credit has risen, the impact on credit volumes has been muted. Although mortgages for home purchases have fallen since the conflict began, overall gross mortgage lending was £23.6bn in August—slightly below pre-conflict levels (an average of £24bn in the second half of 2025), but above the average level since 2024 (£21.9bn). Monthly consumer credit (credit cards, car finance and other non-mortgage credit) hit a high of £2.5bn in August, and over the past 6 months monthly net finance raised by corporates has remained above the average level since 2024. It is not obvious to me from this data that our monetary policy stance is meaningfully restrictive.
Meanwhile, household and firm inflation expectations remain elevated. As I have previously argued Opens in a new window, attentiveness to inflation has risen after over five years of inflation remaining above target. Inflation is also currently already within the threshold at which outturns impact expectations. Greater inflation attentiveness is reflected in an increase in the frequency of UK Google searches for a variety of inflation-related terms in recent years (Figure 18).

Conclusion
Our monetary policy strategy since the outbreak of the Iran conflict has relied to some degree on labour market slack mitigating the risks of second-round effects taking hold. But not all of our wage metrics support this argument. A closer look at the two main metrics we use to understand the recent evolution of wage growth—private sector regular AWE and private sector RTI—suggests wage disinflation has stalled at levels above those consistent with inflation at 2%.
If getting a better handle on the evolution of wage growth to date is tricky, devising a clear view of the future is trickier. The forward-looking indicators we consider—the DMP, pay settlements and the Indeed Wage Tracker–all point to wage growth that is likely to plateau closer to 3.5% than 3% over the coming year. The risks to this are skewed to the upside, in my view. Not only have we tended to underpredict wage growth since the pandemic, but realised pay settlements have been above those predicted in the Agents’ pay survey the past two years. Furthermore, the majority of 2027 pay settlements will be agreed at a time when inflation is above 4%.
Our broad range of wage indicators suggests there is less slack in the labour market than we thought and it may have peaked. This is reflected in broader indicators for the labour market and activity. All together, this suggests the risk of second-round effects taking hold is higher. This is even more so the case as energy prices have remained high and volatile for longer. In my view, this makes a risk management approach to our monetary policy strategy even more appropriate.
When it comes to managing risks around second-round effects, we face two main scenarios. In the first one, we proactively lean against second-round effects by hiking interest rates and later discover this was unnecessary and adjust our policy stance. In the second one, we are too sanguine about second-round effects and set policy accordingly before course correcting. I believe the evidence laid out in this speech shows the risk of second-round effects is greater than we thought. Furthermore, staff simulations suggest setting policy as if you were in a stronger second-round effects scenario and then adjusting policy upon learning you are in a minimal second-round effects scenario leads to better outcomes than doing the opposite. I therefore continue to believe we should proactively lean against the risk of second-round effects.

In practice, and as discussed later in this speech, the MPC often focuses on private regular pay but results are broadly invariant to that distinction.

The AWE measure is also used to calculate earnings growth under the current Triple Lock framework.

The RTI data provides mean and median figures, AWE provides only the mean.

Another reason weekly (as measured by AWE) or monthly pay (as measured by RTI) could be changing is due to changes in hours worked. If pay is rising because people are working more hours that has different implications for wage pressure than if their hourly pay is rising. The LFS is the only timely source of data on hours worked but comes with an additional health warning. The ONS recently explained Opens in a new window that declining response rates on the LFS, coupled with the non-response imputation method and reliance on respondent recall, had led the LFS to overstate hours worked on average. Nevertheless, across the whole economy, the LFS suggests average hours worked for employees increased from 31.8 to 32 per week in the year to the second quarter of 2026. In some sectors where pay growth has been weak according to the AWE data – such as accommodation and food services – average hours worked have fallen. Similarly, in some sectors where the RTI data suggests monthly pay growth has been strong – such as finance and insurance – there has been a rise in average hours worked. Overall, we can tentatively conclude that shifts in hours may account for a marginal part of changes in wage dynamics over the past year.

The ONS provides its own decomposition of private sector regular average weekly earnings. In August it estimated that the wages contribution was 3.4%.

The wage growth consistent with an inflation target of 2% depends on labour productivity growth, the share of imports in consumption and import price inflation, and margins. As set out in the February 2026 Monetary Policy Report, labour productivity growth of 1%, imports’ share of consumption of 25% and import price inflation of 1%, with growth in margins of 0% gives target-consistent wage growth of 3.25%. I think that labour productivity growth is likely to be lower and import price growth higher than 1% and so my estimate of target-consistent wage growth is closer to 3%.

Motoring along: how Chinese EV production is powering the battery sector

View Milan Thakore's full profile

High fuel prices are good news for electric vehicle (EV) sales, a theme we’ve been monitoring closely since the start of the Iran war. France, UK, Sweden, Australia, Norway and China are among those reporting record EV penetration in September, while sales in Southeast Asia and Latin America are also surging.
But the global picture of switching from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to electric is far from uniform. I asked Milan Thakore, Principal Analyst in our Electric Vehicle and Battery Supply Chain team, how he sees things playing out.
Where have EV sales surged?
The global trend is up, with global EV (including battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle) sales increasing 14% year-on-year to end August. EVs now represent nearly one in three new car sales globally. However, at a regional level, the picture is patchy. In Europe and most emerging markets, Chinese EVs have set the benchmark in terms of affordability, and this is reflected in strong sales numbers in those markets.
The US has still not recovered from the withdrawal of supportive policy and EV penetration is down. Even ‘difficult-to-electrify’ markets like India are now overtaking the US in percentage terms. The surprise is China’s own domestic sales. Despite EV penetration approaching 70%, EV sales are down by nearly 1 million units from last year’s peak of 9 million.
What’s holding EVs back in China?
The entire vehicle market in China is tanking, with light vehicle sales across all power trains falling by 3.6 million units year-on-year. ICE vehicles account for the biggest share of the drop – more than double the hit to EVs – with the main factors high fuel costs, a shrinking pool of legacy replacement buyers and a weaker macroeconomic outlook. This twist has unexpectedly lifted EVs’ penetration rate almost to the country’s 2030 EV target four years ahead of time. High fuel costs are also changing consumer behaviour – owners with two vehicles are unsurprisingly favouring their EV and leaving the ICE car at home.
Will Chinese EVs manufacturers ramp up exports?
Big time, as they look to offset slowing growth domestically. More Chinese brands are coming to the market, with ever-improving vehicle designs and performance. Critically, they are priced very competitively to entice customers to often unheard-of brands. One such brand is Leapmotor, which has partnered with Stellantis, the world’s fifth-largest automaker.
Leapmotor’s B05 model sells at around €30,000 for which the buyer gets up to a 300-mile range and a wide array of features as standard, including ventilated seats, panoramic sunroof and the whole suite of safety features. A comparable German ICE model could cost up to €5,000 more once you’ve added on all the ‘extras’.
Could ‘NextGen’ batteries be transformational?
Yes. The latest LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries will hit international markets at the end of 2026. The largest battery makers, CATL and BYD, are amongst those pushing the technology, and others will follow. These will dramatically speed up charging from up to 30 minutes today to below 10 minutes. Charging infrastructure will have to move from kilowatts to the megawatt-level to achieve ‘flash’ charging. BYD doesn’t see this as a challenge.
Is Europe about to be swamped by Chinese exports?
Europe has the highest EV penetration outside China, with sales pushing towards 40%. Sustained subsidy support, abundant model availability, and high retail gasoline and diesel prices drove record September sales in most European countries.
Policymakers need to balance climate goals with defending European manufacturing and employment by supporting a local EV and battery manufacturing value chain. Chinese automative companies are already building manufacturing capacity and battery supply chains in Europe so European-made Chinese EVs will eventually replace imports. European OEMs are also investing heavily but will need to keep advancing to protect market share.  
Where else are EVs flourishing?
Sales in South America and Southeast Asia have all but doubled, driven primarily by a flood of imports from China. As in Europe, these regions want to keep manufacturing local, and Chinese automakers are already building out that capacity. East Asian BEV growth has also doubled as South Korean manufacturer Hyundai-Kia attempts to offset the drop off in US EV demand with sales into its home market.
Are we at an inflection point for EVs? There’s a good chance we are for two reasons. First, the evolving attractiveness of EVs as a product, particularly the quality of vehicles on offer, longer battery range and speed of charging all of which will continue to improve into the future. Secondly, the soaring cost of gasoline and diesel fuel in 2026 has shifted running costs massively in favour of EVs in all markets.
Our sense is that the Iran war will be seen as an inflection point, accelerating a trend already well underway, with EVs eating into ICE vehicles’ market share in many markets. The duration of both the conflict and high pump prices will determine how soon it unfolds – and how much road fuel demand is eroded. 
It’s possible that Wood Mackenzie’s base case assumption that global passenger EV penetration hits 50% by 2035 arrives a few years earlier.

articles.title: ETF Technology Advancements, Automation & Convergence | BNY
articles.text:
ETF Corner series

The Next Frontier in ETF Technology: The Convergence of Servicing and Trading

As ETFs scale toward USD 30 trillion, the next advantage is the connected infrastructure behind them — not the wrapper itself.

alarm

6 minutes read

calendar_today

23 Oct, 2026

Note: Adapted from a recent BNY Consultant Webinar Series session, this article summarizes perspectives shared by BNY specialists from Asset Servicing and Markets on ETF market trends, growth opportunities and evolving operating models.

Key Takeaways

Global ETF assets are projected to exceed USD 30 trillion by 2030, driven by active ETFs and fund conversions1.The primary market — not the wrapper — is where the ETF operating model is now being tested.Cross-border growth demands multidimensional connectivity across settlement cycles, currencies, venues and counterparties.FX execution timing directly drives tracking quality; treating it as an afterthought compounds variance over time.

The global ETF market is growing rapidly and becoming more complex. Assets, flows, product launches and investor adoption continue to reach new milestones, while the product set expands beyond traditional passive exposures into active, options-based, fixed income, digital asset, alternatives and multi-asset strategies. In a recent BNY webinar, our experts highlighted that global ETF assets are expected to exceed USD 30 trillion by 2030, with active ETFs, fund conversions and precision portfolio construction among the key forces driving growth.

But as ETFs scale, the conversation is shifting. It is no longer enough to ask whether an investment strategy can be put into an ETF wrapper. The more important question is whether that ETF can operate efficiently in the market every day, across primary and secondary market activity, across currencies, venues, counterparties and settlement cycles.

That is where ETF technology and automation are becoming central to the next phase of market development. The ETF industry has long focused on the investor-facing benefits of the wrapper: transparency, liquidity, tax efficiency, access and cost. Less discussed is the technology infrastructure that underpins the primary market, where issuers, authorized participants (APs), market makers, service providers, trading desks and FX providers must connect efficiently.

Did You Know?
BNY’s ETF platform, ETX, supports more than 2,600 funds, more than 70 ETF issuers, over USD 4 trillion in ETF assets under administration and more than 4,400 daily baskets created2.
BNY also services hundreds of new ETFs annually, with more than 14 million trades originated and settled across the platform.
Read more about ETF

For BNY, this is an increasingly important area of investment and differentiation. “The main takeaway is that the ETF industry is hitting record highs across virtually every metric we track,” said Ben Slavin, ETF Global Industry Head at BNY. “We're seeing accelerating adoption globally, continued momentum in active ETFs, growing interest in ETF share class structures, and innovation across asset classes. Taken together, these trends point to an industry that is not only growing but entering a new phase of scale and maturity.”
The challenge now is how to make that scale work operationally.

The ETF Wrapper Is Evolving, and So Is the Operating Model

ETFs are often described as simple, transparent and efficient. For investors, that can be true. But behind the scenes, ETFs are operationally sophisticated market structure products.

As Bob Humbert, Global ETF Product Head at BNY, explained: "The best way to think about ETF servicing is that it sits at the intersection of capital markets, portfolio management and fund services." Increasingly, the industry's focus is shifting from individual functions to how those functions are connected. BNY’s ETX was designed around that principle, bringing together issuers, APs, market makers, exchanges and servicing providers in a single ecosystem that helps transform investment ideas into tradable ETF products.

That connectivity matters because ETF growth brings new operating demands. Active strategies may require more customized baskets. Options-based products can introduce additional trading and settlement complexity. Cross-border ETFs may involve multi-currency execution, multiple settlement cycles and fragmented liquidity. Emerging market exposures can create specific challenges around valuation windows, liquidity timing and FX benchmarking. Issuers are also exploring dual share classes, digital assets, alternatives and more complex multi-asset exposures.

ETX: Built for Scale, Built for ETFs
ETX is BNY's ETF technology platform, bringing together portfolio construction, basket management, AP and market maker connectivity, execution workflows and servicing capabilities in a single ecosystem. ETX helps issuers, APs and market makers operate more efficiently, with a focus on smoother execution, enhanced transparency and scalability across the ETF operating model.

“ETX’s goal is to remove friction and bring together the people, workflows and infrastructure required to support ETFs at scale,” said Humbert, adding that technology will increasingly be judged not by individual features, but by how effectively it connects the ETF ecosystem.

Primary Market Technology: The Less Visible Engine of ETF Efficiency
Technology that helps Authorized Participants operate more effectively can improve execution, support liquidity and enhance the investor experience. Innovations such as BNY’s ETF Directed Trading illustrate how continued advances in primary market infrastructure can help APs gain greater visibility into execution economics, streamline cash-order workflows and exercise more control over the creation/redemption process, ultimately supporting a more efficient and resilient ETF ecosystem.

From ETF Servicing to Connected Infrastructure

As ETFs evolve, success will increasingly depend on connecting servicing, trading, liquidity and distribution. The industry is moving beyond standalone servicing models toward more integrated platforms that connect portfolio construction, basket management, execution, AP workflows, FX and post-trade operations in a seamless manner
“A lot of friction is generated when ETF flow has to transition to traditional OMS/EMS stacks,” said Humbert. “It creates inefficiencies not only for issuers but also for APs and market makers.”
This is where ETX and BNY's broader ecosystem come into play. By connecting ETF servicing, markets, distribution via BNY Pershing, FX, transfer agency and execution capabilities through a common platform, the firm is focused on reducing friction across the ETF lifecycle and helping clients move more efficiently from investment concept to market execution.
“Our vision is centred on building the infrastructure needed to support the next phase of ETF growth,” added Slavin. “Helping issuers and liquidity providers scale more efficiently, improving connectivity across the ecosystem and supporting innovation as markets continue to evolve.”
As ETFs become more trading-intensive and liquidity-sensitive, servicing technology is increasingly expected to support front-office outcomes, linking operations, execution and liquidity in a more seamless way. It is not simply about launching more funds. It is about making them work efficiently at scale.

Buy-Side Trading Solutions: Execution Expertise Inside the ETF Workflow

"BTS brings institutional trading expertise into an ETF ecosystem where execution quality, liquidity access and market structure matter”, explains Dragan Skoko, Head of Buy-Side Trading Solutions at BNY.
For ETF issuers, that means helping connect portfolio implementation, AP engagement, market-maker interaction and execution workflows. Whether supporting newer entrants building ETF operating capabilities or established issuers expanding across jurisdictions, asset classes or more complex exposures, BTS can help market participants navigate liquidity and execution considerations while supporting each fund’s investment objective. Ultimately, ETF technology is not just about automation; it is about embedding market expertise into the workflow so issuers can scale efficiently and with greater control.

FX: The Hidden Lever in ETF Performance

FX is another area where ETF automation and market connectivity can have a meaningful impact. For issuers operating across multiple markets, currencies and liquidity pools, FX has become an important component of the ETF operating model. "The U.S. market is larger and more centralized, while European markets are more cross-border, multi-currency, multi-venue and operationally intensive”, Skoko noted.
Prashant Chandrashekar, FX Product Manager at BNY, described FX as becoming more instrumental within the investment process. “ETFs are becoming increasingly global, which then means FX plays a larger role in the overall global portfolio, performance of the ETF,” he said. He noted that investors and issuers are paying closer attention to performance attribution and currency impacts.
The timing of FX execution is particularly important. Where an ETF holds international securities, those securities may be valued at specific fixing windows. If the related FX trade is executed hours or days later at a different rate, the fund may carry unintended currency exposure. That slippage can compound into tracking variance over time.
Execution timing and workflow integration can directly affect tracking outcomes. It also reinforces why FX can no longer be treated as an operational afterthought. Chandrashekar describes BNY FX Plus’s slippage mitigation feature as a core benefit to address an on-going industry challenge and support more efficient currency execution
This is the practical value of ETF tech: making it easier to execute with a service provider by connecting servicing and markets capabilities in one workflow.

The Next Frontier: ETFs Built for Scale, Speed and Precision

The ETF market has always been shaped by innovation, but the next frontier may be less about the wrapper itself and more about the infrastructure behind it.
Tech and automation will be central to this next chapter. For issuers, the opportunity is to bring products to market with greater speed and control. For APs, it is to manage execution more efficiently. For market makers, it is to quote with better information. For investors, it is to access ETFs that trade and track more effectively.
As Skoko put it, what comes next is “tighter and tighter integration with the rest of the BNY ecosystem” to make it easier for issuers and APs to achieve efficiencies.

That integration is at the heart of the ETF technology story. It is not automation for its own sake. It is automation designed to connect the ETF ecosystem, from servicing to trading, from basket to execution, from FX to settlement, and from product idea to market outcome.
For an ETF industry scaling toward its next major milestone, that connected infrastructure may be one of the most important competitive advantages of all.

T+1 Raises the Stakes for Automation
As settlement windows shrink, firms have less tolerance for manual processes, fragmented systems and operational inefficiencies. The shift is reinforcing the importance of connected operating models that link execution, FX, settlement and fund operations seamlessly across the ETF ecosystem.
Read more: Europe's move to T+1: Implications for ETF servicing models

For more insights about ETFs, visit BNY’s ETF Corner, one destination for ETF market intelligence and expertise.

Frequently asked questions

A money market fund is a type of mutual fund that invests in short-term, high-quality debt instruments like government securities, certificates of deposit, and commercial paper. It’s designed to offer stability, liquidity, and modest income.

A government money market fund is a type of mutual fund that invests primarily in short-term debt securities issued by the U.S. government, such as Treasury bills, notes, and bonds, or in repurchase agreements (repos) backed by these securities.

Prime money market funds are a type of mutual fund that invests primarily in corporate debt and other taxable short-term securities, such as commercial paper, certificates of deposit, and asset-backed commercial paper.

Ultrashort and short-term bond funds are investments that hold debt securities with short maturities, typically less than one year for ultrashort funds and one to three years for short-term funds. articles.title: What's new in the World Development Indicators, October 2026: poverty and inequality updates, new food security & nutrition data, latest energy statistics
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

What's new in the World Development Indicators, October 2026: poverty and inequality updates, new food security & nutrition data, latest energy statistics

World Bank Data Team

October 22, 2026

This page in:

English

English

On October 8, 2026, the World Development Indicators (WDI) database published new and revised data across a wide range of development topics. 

What’s New in the October 2026 Release? 
People

Food security and nutrition data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) now run through 2024, including the prevalence of undernourishment and of moderate or severe food insecurity.

Labor market indicators have also been refreshed with the latest national estimates from the International Labour Organization (ILO): employment-to-population ratios, labor force participation, unemployment, youth not in employment, education or training (NEET), part-time employment, and the share of women in senior and middle management, broken down by age and sex where available.

Prosperity

Poverty and inequality indicators are updated through 2025. They cover headcount ratios and poverty gaps at the $3.00, $4.20, and $8.30 a day poverty lines (2021 PPP); societal, national, and multidimensional poverty; the Gini index and income shares; and shared prosperity indicators tracking income growth among the bottom 40 percent.

The Worldwide Governance Indicators now include estimates and scores through 2025 for all six dimensions, from Control of Corruption to Voice and Accountability.

Balance of payments indicators have been refreshed with the latest IMF data, including foreign direct investment inflows, remittances as a share of GDP, current account balances, and exports of goods and services.

Purchasing power parity (PPP) conversion factor for households and NPISHs final consumption expenditure is updated using Consumer Price Index (CPI) data sourced from IMF

Data on military expenditure and arms transfers are now available for 2025.

Planet

New 2024 data have been published on access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking (used to monitor SDG 7.1.2) for total, urban, and rural populations.

Access to clean cooking has expanded steadily. By 2024, 75 percent of people worldwide had access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking. The remaining challenge is increasingly concentrated outside cities.Progress has been uneven. In 2024, access had reached around 90 percent in urban areas, compared with just 56 percent in rural communities.Regional trajectories vary widely. The access level in Sub-Saharan Africa remains much below that of other regions.South Asia and East Asia & Pacific have made especially rapid gains. In South Asia, rural access increased from 6 percent in 2000 to 62 percent in 2024, sharply narrowing the divide with cities. The East Asia & Pacific region has also made rapid progress.Regional averages mask substantial differences in access and speed of change. For example, both Indonesia and Viet Nam increased rural access by 82 percentage points in the span of 24 years.Select a country to see how access has changed in urban and rural areas, and whether the gap is narrowing, persisting, or widening.

Energy statistics from the International Energy Agency (IEA) have been refreshed with 2024 data for non-OECD economies and, for selected electricity indicators, 2025 data for OECD economies.

New 2024 FAO data cover fertilizer use, land use, forests, irrigation, and cereal production and yields, together with updated crop, livestock, and food production indexes.

Infrastructure

Data from the World Intellectual Property Organization on patent, industrial design, and trademark applications by residents and non-residents have been updated for 2022–2024.

Where to find it
As always, the data is available through the Open Data site, DataBank, the Data Catalog, bulk downloads, and the WDI API. The full details are in the October 2026 release note.

articles.title: Seeking Out AI’s Next Winners
articles.text:
Seeking Out AI’s Next Winners

Artificial intelligence (AI) is driving one of the largest investment cycles in
decades. The companies building the infrastructure that underpins AI — from
semiconductors and manufacturing equipment to cloud platforms and data
centers

October 2026
Author: Jay McLeod, Walter Scott Investment Analyst

KEY TAKEAWAYS

The scale of AI investment is
unprecedented, with much of
the spending directed toward
AI infrastructure.
The companies building
AI infrastructure remain
essential to the ecosystem’s
development. However,
history shows that as new
technologies mature, value
creation often broadens
beyond the businesses
supplying the tools.
Some of the most compelling
opportunities may lie with
businesses that can use AI
to strengthen established
competitive advantages,
improve customer outcomes
and enhance productivity.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is driving one of the largest investment cycles in decades. The companies building the infrastructure that underpins AI — from semiconductors and manufacturing equipment to cloud platforms and data centers — are attracting significant attention as organizations invest heavily to develop and deploy the technology.
However, history suggests that the ultimate beneficiaries of transformative technologies are not always the businesses supplying the tools. Electrification created substantial opportunities for power providers, but its broader economic impact came from the companies that successfully applied it to improve productivity and strengthen their competitive positions. AI may prove no different.
For long-term investors, the key question is where AI will have the greatest economic impact. While the foundations remain essential, some of the most compelling opportunities may emerge among businesses using AI to improve customer outcomes, operate more efficiently and reinforce strengths built over many years.
Laying the Foundations
Understanding that opportunity begins with the infrastructure enabling AI today. The scale of investment is unprecedented, with the world’s leading technology companies expected to invest approximately US$730 billion in capital expenditure in 2026 alone,1 much of it directed toward AI infrastructure. Every dollar invested creates demand across a much broader ecosystem, from semiconductor manufacturing and cloud computing to data centers, cybersecurity, industrial automation and the businesses that will use AI to operate more efficiently.
Much of the market’s attention has focused on the companies developing the technology. These businesses are likely to remain important to AI’s development, but the opportunity may extend well beyond them.
AI adoption depends on a much wider network of physical and digital infrastructure. Every new data center requires substantial investment in the facilities and systems that support its operation. Networks must be secured. As AI moves beyond the data center, intelligence needs to be embedded into factories, vehicles and industrial equipment.
From Infrastructure to Adoption
The companies building AI infrastructure remain essential to the ecosystem’s development. However, history shows that as new technologies mature, value creation often broadens beyond the businesses supplying the tools. The ability to apply technology effectively can become just as important as the technology itself.
Businesses across industries are incorporating AI into products and existing operations, using machine learning and advanced analytics to automate routine tasks, improve decision-making and increase productivity.
These applications are emerging across a range of industries, from financial software and energy to utilities, manufacturing and transportation. By embedding AI into established products and processes, companies can build on their existing strengths while improving how they operate and serve customers.
What Makes a Long-Term AI Winner?
AI is often most powerful when combined with advantages that are difficult to replicate. These include proprietary data, deep operational expertise, strong customer relationships and established market positions. Rather than disrupting such companies, it may reinforce their competitive positions by improving decision-making and enhancing customer outcomes.
For long-term investors, this reinforces the importance of looking beyond today’s headlines. In our view, some of the most compelling opportunities may lie with businesses that can use AI to strengthen established competitive advantages, improve customer outcomes and enhance productivity. Where new technology meets enduring business quality, the potential for long-term growth may be greatest.

About Walter Scott
Walter Scott is the global equities-focused investment firm within BNY Investments.

1 JPMorgan Research, June 2026

Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to computer systems that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as visual perception, speech recognition, decision-making, and language translation.

articles.title: Quantum Won’t Kill Crypto, But It Could Accelerate Wall Street’s Adoption of Blockchain | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
For many in the crypto industry, the specter of quantum computing has become the stuff of existential dread. According to popular doomer narratives, public blockchains like Bitcoin will be among the first target of quantum-based attacks that will wipe out trillions of dollars.

In this view, public blockchains most salient feature, decentralization, is an Achilles heel that will impede the implementation of defensive upgrades to protect from quantum-powered hackers. The doomers argue that networks like Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana will be helpless against a threat that will one day smash the public-key cryptography that has long made them secure.

This makes for a dramatic story, but the premise is misguided. While the threat is real, the conclusion–that quantum will kill crypto–is simply wrong.

First, it’s important to recall that it is not only blockchains that are at risk from a quantum-powered attack. Much of the internet as we know it is vulnerable to Q-day, or the moment when quantum machines finally muster the capacity to pick the locks of the world’s existing encryption defenses.

Exposed are hundreds of trillions of dollars of the world’s assets, as well as our most sensitive private data. Already, bad actors have initiated “harvest now, decrypt later” schemes to strike hard and fast when Q-day finally arrives. Alarmed, governments have responded by mandating action plans to prepare. Yet, amid this scramble to shore up our digital bulwarks, the one industry that seems to have experienced a particular sense of foreboding over quantum advancements also happens to be the most capable of meeting the challenge.

I’m referring, of course, to the crypto industry. Because of a long-held open-source ethos, public blockchains and associated infrastructure have long faced attack by malicious actors. Builders of these networks have learned to become survivors, constantly patching up vulnerabilities and both anticipating and responding to myriad other threats. Compared to other industries, the crypto industry’s response to new cyberthreats has been lightning fast and, indeed, many have already sprung to action in building defenses ahead of Q-day’s arrival.

Conversely, it is legacy financial systems that appear prone to rolling out insufficient responses to meet pressing challenges. Back in 20181, for example, the SWIFT network began a major initiative to modernize its 1970s-era global banking-transfer messaging technology. And the time it took to complete this undertaking? Seven years.

Granted, SWIFT is a sprawling network of 11,000 institutions that had to coordinate efforts across 200 countries. But the upgrade it undertook—modernizing a messaging format—was simple in comparison to the broader task at hand: swapping out the guts of decades-established cryptography layers that touch certificates, hardware, software, vendors and counterparties across the financial system.

It’s not just SWIFT. There’s a long history of significantly delayed overhauls to a wide variety of key pieces of core financial infrastructure, all of which bode ill for timely upgrades to meet the quantum challenge. A planned revamp of the Federal Reserve’s high-value wire system began in 20152, but only managed to cross the finish line in July 2025.3 In 2016, the Bank of England4 began planning an overhaul to its central ledger for handling interbank settlements. While a target completion date was set for 2021, it didn’t actually happen until 20255 (and aspects of this upgrade are still ongoing).

Even as organizations like SWIFT have announced ambitious efforts to tackle the quantum threat, history suggests that we temper our expectations that the sprawling surface area of legacy financial services, governments and other industries will be ready when Q-day arrives. According to the U.S. Government6 some of the most critical digital infrastructure must be quantum secure by 2030—that four year timeline is half of what it took SWIFT to undergo a far less ambitious upgrade.

That’s why it’s heartening to see workable solutions emerging from the cryptoverse’s many world-class cryptographers, many of whom already have gone on the quantum offensive. Indeed, leading blockchain organizations have published comprehensive plans (JJR1)7 for achieving post-quantum readiness well before 2030. Even Ethereum, known for prioritizing decentralization over speed, has moved without hesitation, laying out 2029 in the network’s roadmap8 as when it will be quantum ready.

At the same time, the crypto industry has spawned a wave of new startups that are building a wide variety of novel post-quantum picks and shovels, ranging from wallets to payment infrastructure. Resources and talent indeed are being marshalled in a profound way, and it increasingly looks as though the crypto industry might have just leapfrogged the traditional players in the broader pursuit of achieving quantum readiness.

This is encouraging and so too are the growing legions of finance professionals who see great promise in blockchain networks and tokenization. As they confront the enormous task of upgrading their outdated legacy financial infrastructure, many of these professionals instead will find it easier to simply switch over to using quantum-hardened blockchains. Follow Christopher Perkins Executive Vice President
Head of Franklin Crypto Investments More Articles From This Author Endnotes

Source: SWIFT. ISO 20022: A new era for global payments.
Source: Federal Reserve Press Release. “Federal Reserve Board invites public comment on proposal to adopt ISO 20022 message format for Fedwire Funds Service.” July 5, 2018.
Source: Federal Reserve Press Release. “Federal Reserve Financial Services completes ISO® 20022 migration for Fedwire® Funds Service, advancing U.S. payments modernization.” July 15, 2025.
Source: UK Parliament. “The Bank of England’s Real-Time Gross Settlement Renewal Programme.”
Source: Bank of England. “Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system and CHAPS Annual Report 2024/25.” August 21, 2025.
Source: U.S. Government. “Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks.” June 22, 2026.
Source: Stellar. “Introducing the Quantum Preparedness Plan.“ June 9, 2026.
Source: Ethereum. “Post-quantum cryptography on Ethereum.” September 8, 2026.

WHAT ARE THE RISKS?

All investments involve risks, including possible loss of principal.

Equity securities are subject to price fluctuation and possible loss of principal.

Fixed income securities involve interest rate, credit, inflation and reinvestment risks, and possible loss of principal. As interest rates rise, the value of fixed income securities falls.

ETFs trade like stocks, fluctuate in market value and may trade at prices above or below their net asset value. Brokerage commissions and ETF expenses will reduce returns. ETF may not readily trade in all market conditions and may trade at significant discounts in periods of market stress.

Commodity-related investments are subject to additional risks such as commodity index volatility, investor speculation, interest rates, weather, tax and regulatory developments.

Blockchain and cryptocurrency investments are subject to various risks, including inability to develop digital asset applications or to capitalize on those applications, theft, loss, or destruction of cryptographic keys, the possibility that digital asset technologies may never be fully implemented, cybersecurity risk, conflicting intellectual property claims, and inconsistent and changing regulations. Speculative trading in bitcoins and other forms of cryptocurrencies, many of which have exhibited extreme price volatility, carries significant risk; an investor can lose the entire amount of their investment. Blockchain technology is a new and relatively untested technology and may never be implemented to a scale that provides identifiable benefits. If a cryptocurrency is deemed a security, it may be deemed to violate federal securities laws. There may be a limited or no secondary market for cryptocurrencies.

Digital assets are subject to risks relating to immature and rapidly developing technology, security vulnerabilities of this technology, (such as theft, loss, or destruction of cryptographic keys), conflicting intellectual property claims, credit risk of digital asset exchanges, regulatory uncertainty, high volatility in their value/price, unclear acceptance by users and global marketplaces, and manipulation or fraud. Portfolio managers, service providers to the portfolios and other market participants increasingly depend on complex information technology and communications systems to conduct business functions. These systems are subject to a number of different threats or risks that could adversely affect the portfolio and their investors, despite the efforts of the portfolio managers and service providers to adopt technologies, processes and practices intended to mitigate these risks and protect the security of their computer systems, software, networks and other technology assets, as well as the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information belonging to the portfolios and their investors.

articles.title: The Fruit Of Tariffs Is Fraud
articles.text:
The Fruit Of Tariffs Is Fraud

Thomas Gatley

Gavekal Dragonomics | 16 Oct 2026

Trade tensions between China and the US seem to have eased a bit recently, with the two sides agreeing on a mutual reduction of tariffs on some goods after their presidential summit. Yet the environment remains hostile: the US has another Section 301 investigation underway on “structural excess capacity.” The reality, though, is that tariffs are not working very well at keeping out Chinese goods. While on the surface it appears that eight years of tariffs has led to a material decoupling of US-China trade, this is a fiction. The US continues to import huge quantities of Chinese goods, but these imports are obfuscated by widespread fraud and re-routing.According to US Customs, imports from China and Hong Kong totaled US$276bn over the past 12 months, down by half from US$550bn in late 2018. This is well below the total of imports from Canada, Mexico, Asean, or the EU, all of which used to be smaller sources of US imports than China. If this trade data was accurate, it would represent a major, rapid and historic decoupling of the world’s two largest economies. But it is not accurate. China’s exporters and US importers have found two important ways to minimize the amount of tariffs they pay, which combine to massively distort US trade statistics. The true value of Chinese-made goods flowing into the US is likely in excess of US$600bn annually, more than twice as much as US Customs reports.

Money Markets Committee and UK Money Markets Code

The Bank of England chairs the Money Markets Committee, which has endorsed the voluntary UK Money Markets Code setting out best practice for participants in the deposit, repo and securities lending markets.

In this section

Fair and Effective Markets
Foreign currency reserves
Market intelligence
Bank of England Market Operations Guide
Settlement and collateral management
SONIA interest rate benchmark
Transition from LIBOR to risk-free rates

On this pageMoney Markets CommitteeUK Money Markets Code CommitteeSecurities Lending CommitteeMoney Markets Liaison Committee and Securities Lending and Repo CommitteeUK Money Markets Code

Money Markets Committee
The Money Markets Committee (MMC) is a senior-level forum for market participants and the relevant UK public authorities to discuss issues concerning the UK unsecured deposits and funding market, the securities lending market and the repo market.
The MMC is chaired by the Bank of England.
The committee meets quarterly and also has two permanent sub-committees: the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee and the Securities Lending Committee.
Objectives of the Money Markets Committee

To discuss important domestic and global market or structural developments affecting the UK money, repo and securities lending markets.
Where appropriate, to propose responses to any issues identified.
To aid understanding and enhance monitoring of the functioning of the UK money markets.
To endorse and facilitate continuing market-wide adoption of the UK Money Markets Code, a voluntary code of good practice for the money and securities financing markets.
To identify and address any high-level issues concerning contingency planning in the UK money markets and payment systems, having regard to international developments.

Increasing diversity in our committees
The UK Money Markets Code includes an expectation that market participants will promote the development of a diverse and inclusive within their money market teams. This includes working to create a diverse pipeline of potential future Committee members.
We also aim for diversity within the Money Markets Committee and its Sub-committees, in order that they can best represent the people of the United Kingdom. Diverse membership means that these Committees benefit from diversity of thought, which bring different viewpoints and help to ensure well-informed decision-making.
We work with members from the Money Markets Committee to diversify its membership. As part of this, we provide opportunities for members to bring observers to Committee meetings, in order that these observers can gain a better understanding of the Committee, and to help identify potential future diverse candidates.
You can find out more about ‘Meeting Varied People’ – our initiative to increase the diversity of the market contacts that we engage with – on the Market intelligence page.

UK Money Markets Code Committee
The project to update and revise the former codes for non-foreign exchange market products in the UK market led by a sub-committee of the Money Markets Committee. The UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee is a permanent sub-committee of the MMC, and is co-chaired by, and made up of, senior market participants. The sub-committee meets regularly to ensure that the code remains relevant and up to date as markets evolve.

Terms of reference for the UK Money Markets Code Sub-Committee
