articles.title: Canvas Market Insights: Calm on the Surface, Steady as She Goes? | Franklin Templeton
articles.text:
For passive investors, a bird’s-eye view of third quarter equity index returns was likely pretty boring. The S&P 5001 Index rose 2.3%, bringing the year-to-date return to 12.8%. International developed markets fared less well and emerging market equities were slightly negative.2 The small cap Russell 2000 Index3 declined -7.2%. Yields soared as the Iran conflict entered its 8th month and investors demanded higher risk premiums on fixed income securities.

For active equity investors, the quarter likely felt more like a battle scene. July saw one of the most severe momentum reversals in the last four decades. Large moves in individual stocks occurred in both directions, cancelling each other out at the index level, a phenomenon we’ve dubbed The Hidden Momentum Reversal.4

A key driver was the Artificial Intelligence (AI) trade. AI beneficiaries dramatically underperformed in July while those previously perceived as vulnerable to AI disruption outperformed. In retrospect, it seems highly likely that the July episode was precipitated by the unwind of a large AI-focused hedge fund that needed to liquidate levered long and short bets on the AI ecosystem.5

The event, which partially reversed in August, left an indelible mark on thematic AI trades. This is relevant to all investors, not just the technophiles in the audience, because AI and AI-adjacent stocks currently represent about 55% of the U.S. market capitalization.6

Last quarter, we argued that AI was better understood as a capital cycle than a bubble and that elevated dispersion was increasing both the opportunities and risks beneath equity indexes. Three months later, the market provided a real stress test. July exposed how deeply AI has become embedded in market leadership, while corporate fundamentals increasingly show that sustaining the buildout requires more cash and outside capital.

As we move through a large capital expenditure cycle for the AI segment, the investment question for allocators is shifting from whether AI can drive earnings to whether the capital required to sustain those earnings will generate sufficient returns on that capital.

Calm on the Surface, Carnage in Factor Land

The hidden momentum reversal occurred within a minor drawdown at the index level. The carnage under the surface was masked by low correlations between U.S. stocks. Portfolio volatility is driven by two components: 1) the standalone volatility of the underlying holdings and 2) how correlated the holdings are with each other. For index volatility to remain calm while individual stock volatility rises, correlations between stocks must fall. That is exactly what we have observed.

Passive investors only see small ripples on the surface while a strong undertow pushes active investor positions around. This is not a problem per se, but like pressure building at a tectonic fault line, minor shifts can have unexpected and unpredictable consequences. If correlations normalize while single-stock volatility remains elevated, index volatility could rise materially even without an increase in single-stock volatility.

For the quarter, some active investors were likely very happy while others were quite disappointed. The chart below shows U.S. Large Cap active manager return dispersion over the last 20 years. When dispersion is high, the difference between the best and worst manager returns is wide. You can see on the right side that manager dispersion has soared in 2026, largely driven by whether a manager leaned into or away from AI-related names.

Dispersion in U.S. Large Cap Manager Returns

Source: Morningstar, Canvas Research. Note: Standard Deviation of manager returns, 6-month moving average. Past performance is no guarantee of future results. Please see important information at the end of this paper.

With dispersion comes another benefit for tax-aware investors. A wide return spread between winners and losers generally creates ample opportunity for tax loss harvesting, the practice of realizing losses to offset future gains within client-defined tracking error7 budgets. In the third quarter, our trading team realized approximately $300 million in gross losses across the Canvas platform for active and passive equity investors.

AI Was the Fault Line

Not surprisingly, when we drill down into systematic drivers of pre-tax returns for U.S. large cap, a similar theme is evident. Factor spreads were generally wide for the quarter.

Technology is now 38% of the Russell 1000 Index8, and as it goes so goes the broad market and factors. Selection effects within the Information Technology sector contributed -6.8% to Momentum’s performance. Coming into the quarter, high momentum stocks were overweight AI-beneficiaries

(Semiconductors, Hardware & Equipment) and weak momentum was overweight to names subject to AI disruption (Software & Services). During the July reversal, AI beneficiaries dramatically lagged while AI disruption plays soared.

The reversal matters because the stocks sitting at the center of momentum are also sitting at the center of a much larger change in corporate capital allocation.

From Software Economics to Industrial Economics

The calm at the index level is hiding a significant redistribution of capital under the surface, and AI is the driver. The AI trade is evolving from a high margin, asset-light earnings story into a capital-intensive investment cycle right at the moment that the cost of capital is rising.

While AI can easily be classified as a technology, we think a better framework is a “manufacturing of knowledge.” The industrial revolution transformed our ability to manufacture physical goods by combining energy, machines, and labor at scale. AI follows a similar architecture: data is the raw material, semiconductors and datacenters are the machinery, and foundational models orchestrate the production process to generate text, code, images, summaries, and potentially new knowledge.

Today’s models do not literally manufacture knowledge. Knowledge implies some combination of truth, context, and understanding. Current models manufacture outputs that compress, synthesize, and redistribute the accumulated knowledge embedded in training data, the rich history of knowledge that has compounded since the dawn of human existence. But they dramatically expanded access to expertise that was confined to specialists in fields like mathematics, science, and engineering.

The economic distinction from the software era is critical. Once software is developed and distributed, marginal costs can be low and margins very high (i.e. the Microsoft Office suite). AI is not software. AI is forcing a shift in the economics of technology from primarily asset-light software economics toward something resembling industrial economics.

Scaling capability requires enormous recurring investment in compute, data centers, semiconductors, energy, and model development. The estimated cost of training a frontier model has risen dramatically as complexity has increased: GPT-1 contained just 117 million parameters versus 671 billion for DeepSeek-V3.

The last decade rewarded businesses that could scale digital offerings. The AI era increasingly requires investors to ponder whether massive CapEx9 will generate adequate long-run returns.

The Capital Cycle Has Arrived

When we look at the underlying fundamentals, we are starting to see a shift in the earnings and capital structures of the AI ecosystem. To do so, we constructed a universe of large capitalization U.S. stocks and subdivided it into two groups: AI and ex-AI.10

It is no surprise that AI players have massively ramped up capital expenditures. Over the trailing 12 months, 92% of earnings have been reinvested. Reinvestment has gradually replaced share buybacks as the de facto avenue of capital allocation. As of September 2026, the AI ecosystem moved to net share issuance for the first time since 2013.

Earnings Allocation of AI Group
(% OF EARNINGS DEPLOYED)

Source: Compustat, Canvas Research.

We can see this impact through free cash flow as well. Free cash flow yield has steadily declined in recent years.11 This is not an immediate cause for concern. We view it as a nascent industry starting to mature.

Free Cash Flow Yield

Source: Compustat, Canvas Research.

Reinvesting in high return of capital projects is certainly the cornerstone of Finance 101. As investors, we just need to gain comfort that the reinvestment will result in positive economic returns and management teams are not getting too far out over their skis to capture revenues. One data point that gives us pause is the way depreciation, an income statement item, is not keeping pace with capex, a cash flow statement item. Depreciation and/or amortization are accounting concepts that allow businesses to make large up-front investments and spread out the costs of the investment over the useful life of the asset, i.e. a manufacturing plant depreciated over 30 years, so a company can have high expenditures today without the entire cost immediately reducing earnings. However, investors get the true picture of outlays via the statement of cash flows, which reflects the full investment in the period in which it occurs.

For mature firms, a depreciation-to-capex ratio of 1.0 is indicative that cash receipts and outlays match reported earnings. However, rapidly growing firms should have greater CapEx than depreciation if adding productive assets.

CapEx is increasingly running ahead of recognized depreciation for the AI group. That is consistent with a major expansion cycle, but it also means reported earnings are not a complete measure of the cash outlays needed to support rapid growth. Since late 2023, depreciation-to-capex has dipped from 0.91 to 0.66, suggesting the AI ecosystem’s earnings understate the cash required to sustain that growth.

Depreciation as a % of Capex

Source: Compustat, Canvas Research.

We are not suggesting that the AI ecosystem suddenly has weak fundamentals, but we do need to recognize that growth is consuming a larger share of those fundamentals. As the cycle matures, non-cash depreciation and CapEx will need to be reconciled.

Investors need to think hard about how much of today’s CapEx will be rewarded with attractive returns versus how much is being outlaid simply to maintain competitive position.

The Risk Has Migrated

The growth of the AI ecosystem over the last several years is quite astounding. The idea that such large firms can compound earnings at triple digits for multiple years seems to defy the laws of economics. Meanwhile, analysts continue to underestimate earnings-per-share (EPS)12 growth. Actual EPS reports have beaten estimates 95% of the time for the AI group by an average of 13% over the last five years.

The result of such strong actual earnings growth is that the AI group is now trading at a forward price-to-earnings13 discount compared to the rest of the market for the first time since 2017. Given the open questions as to the capital needs associated with the maturing AI ecosystem, we think this is a healthy development.

Forward Price-to-Earnings Ratio

Source: CapIQ, Compustat, Canvas Research.

We are also in the midst of a strong earnings estimate revision cycle. The chart below shows that analysts have increased their expectations for AI group earnings by 21% in the last 6 months.

Change in Next 4 Quarters EPS Estimate vs 6-months Prior

Source: CapIQ, Compustat, Canvas Research.

From a top-down perspective, analysts expect U.S. large cap earnings growth of 16% for the next four quarters, of which the AI group is expected to contribute a third of that growth.

The AI complex no longer looks obviously expensive on consensus earnings. However, that does not eliminate risk; it just relocates it. The market is increasingly underwriting the earnings estimates themselves at a time when earnings quality is becoming somewhat more complicated.

One driver of that complication is the cross investments within the ecosystem. Microsoft, for example, holds a 27% stake in OpenAI reportedly worth $135 billion.14 Google and Amazon hold stakes in Anthropic. These large stakes can influence the investing company’s earnings through either proportional results (as through the equity method of accounting used by Microsoft for OpenAI) or through fair value methodologies that require mark ups when new funding rounds occur (as Amazon and Alphabet do with their Anthropic holdings).

As can be seen in the chart below, non-operating income now represents 7.5% of the AI ecosystem’s 30% GAAP15 profit margin, suggesting the headline earnings could become more volatile.

Decomposition of Earnings Per Share as % of Sales

Source: CapIQ, Compustat, Canvas Research.

In summary, AI’s influence on broad market valuation, margins, capital allocation policies, expectations, and sentiment is growing at a time when the ecosystem is just beginning to mature. The key conclusion here is that valuation risk has morphed into execution and return-on-capital risk.

While we don’t necessarily share in the AI-bubble thesis at this time, there are some undercurrents to remain attuned to as we head into 2027.

Everyone Wants Capital

The post-GFC16 regime was defined by excess capital in search of assets. The current regime looks to be increasingly defined by competition for capital.

Corporations need capital for the AI infrastructure buildout. For the last 15 years companies increasingly returned excess capital to shareholders through buybacks and dividends. The current regime may increasingly be characterized by greater equity and debt issuance, a request of capital from investors.

The electrical grid and energy system need it to accommodate a step change in power consumption and to address energy supply instability. The defense sector needs capital to accommodate the changing global security landscape. The federal government needs capital to fund deficits. Mega-IPOs and private-to-public transitions want capital to monetize gains.

A greater share of capital that might otherwise have been returned to shareholders is being redirected toward investment in the real economy. The new transmission channel is likely an underappreciated driver of resilient economic growth and inflation. As of the third quarter, non-residential fixed investment (one of the avenues by which the AI buildout flows through to GDP17) increased 9.6% year-over-year. Nominal GDP is growing at relatively high persistent rates not seen since the 1990s.18

Given the above, it should not be a surprise that the price of capital is rising. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield surged 0.81% on the quarter, building on gains earlier in the year. While the impetus seemed to be continued energy supply disruptions from the Iran conflict, 10-year breakeven rates (the market’s implied compensation for long-run inflation) “only” rose 0.14%.

The larger change came from a 0.67% rise in real yields to 2.91%, the highest level since 2008. That increase breaks down to a 0.29% rise in expectations for the short-term Fed Funds rate19 over the next 10 years and a 0.38% increase in the 10-year term premium. Term premium is compensation for bearing the risk of policy rate changes, the level of future rates, as well as unexpected inflation and duration risk.

The move was not driven by a rise in inflation expectations beyond the short-term. Investors instead demanded a higher policy rate path and greater compensation for holding duration. This is consistent with a structurally higher rate regime.

Policymaker Purgatory

At this point policymakers are somewhat stuck. The lean towards deglobalization, geopolitical conflict, and the decline of energy stability are trends which monetary policy cannot address. The recent rise in oil, other commodities, and global bond yields is emblematic of this paradox.

Easing to support growth and asset values risks inflation, a weaker dollar, and potential capital misallocation. Tightening would restrain demand but do nothing to increase oil supply, electric capacity, or advanced semiconductor production. Doing nothing leaves the market to its own devices in determining the cost of capital.

The problem is that many of today’s economic constraints are real-economy constraints (energy, compute, infrastructure, and industrial capacity) that monetary policy cannot manufacture. These structural issues fall to fiscal authorities; however, they are constrained by the albatross of exorbitant and growing fiscal deficits.

One avenue where we do expect to see some activity in the coming years is on the regulatory front. The Fed and Treasury have macroprudential20 powers that could be used to relax the regulatory environment, a structural de facto easing that does not require congressional approval.

What It Means for Portfolios

Index calm does not equal low risk. Low correlations are suppressing index volatility while stock and manager dispersion remains elevated. That increases manager selection risk but also stock-selection and tax-management opportunity.

AI risk is shifting from valuation to execution. Investors should increasingly discriminate based on differences in balance sheets, cash generation, capital intensity, and returns on incremental investment rather than simply asking whether or not the AI trade is “expensive.”

Capital has a price again. Higher yields and greater competition for savings raise the hurdle rate21 for corporate projects and risky financial assets. That should favor disciplined capital allocation, broaden the opportunity set beyond mega-cap growth, and increase the value of diversification.

None of this requires investors to predict the next correction. Climbing the wall of worry is what equity markets do best and that has certainly rung true in 2026 thus far. Equity indexes may remain steady as the tectonic plates shift below the surface. But the combination of greater dispersion, a more capital-intensive AI ecosystem, and a higher cost of capital raises the importance of diversification, security selection, tax management, and disciplined capital allocation. In that sense, steady as she goes does not mean standing still. Follow Ehren Stanhope Co-Head of Investment Management, Chief Investment Strategist

S&P 500 Index: An index of 500 leading U.S. companies widely used as a measure of large-cap U.S. equity market performance.
MSCI World ex USA Index 0.89% and MSCI Emerging Markets Index -0.37%. These indexes measure large- and mid-cap stocks in developed markets outside the U.S. and in emerging markets, respectively.
Russell 2000® Index: An index of approximately 2,000 U.S. small-cap stocks designed to represent the small-cap segment of the U.S. equity market.
See our recent paper “The Hidden Momentum Reversal” for a deep dive.
It was widely reported that Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness hedge fund faced large drawdowns and collateral calls in July 2026.
Canvas Research as of 9/30/2026.
Tracking error: A measure of how closely a portfolio’s returns follow its benchmark, expressed as the standard deviation of the return differences.
Russell 1000® Index: An index of approximately 1,000 of the largest U.S. stocks designed to represent the large-cap segment of the U.S. equity market. Investors cannot invest directly in an index, and unmanaged index returns do not reflect any fees, expenses or sales charges.
Capital Expenditures (CapEx): Spending by a company to acquire, build or improve long-term assets such as property, equipment and infrastructure.
Our AI ecosystem classification includes companies with material exposure to compute infrastructure, AI enablement, automation or AI-driven disruption; the ten largest constituents, weighted by market capitalization, are Nvidia, Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, Broadcom, Meta Platforms, Micron Technology, Advanced Micro Devices, and Intel. The ex-AI group are all U.S. large capitalization stocks not in the AI group. It should be noted that this group was established with the benefit of hindsight and does not represent an investable index.
Free cash flow yield is defined as operating cash flow minus capital expenditures divided by price.
Earnings Per Share (EPS): A company’s earnings available to common shareholders divided by its number of shares outstanding.
Forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio: Share price divided by analysts’ estimated earnings per share for the next 12 months.
Microsoft and OpenAI joint announcement, October 28, 2025.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP): The standard accounting rules U.S. companies use for financial reporting.
Global Financial Crisis (GFC): The period of severe financial market stress and economic contraction from 2007 to 2009.
Gross Domestic Product (GDP): The value of final goods and services produced within a country over a specified period.
The obvious exception being the inflationary spike of 2021-2022 during the pandemic.
Federal funds rate: The overnight rate at which U.S. banks lend reserves to one another; the Federal Reserve sets its target range.
Macroprudential powers: Regulatory tools, such as bank capital and liquidity requirements, aimed at risks to the financial system as a whole.
Hurdle rate: The minimum rate of return a company or investor requires before committing capital to a project or investment.

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesEuropeGerman Exports Rebound amid Demand from the US, EU, and AI BuildoutOct 15, 2026Share Germany’s surprising performance shows a shift in the export sector’s fortunes following a long period of relative weakness. Our economists forecast “robust” German real-export growth of 3.5% in 2026 and 2.4% the following year. Revived trade with the US and the EU, plus the global AI buildout, is expected to boost German exports. Competition from Chinese exporters, particularly in third markets, is still expected to weigh on German export performance in the medium term. Germany’s exports increased in the first half of 2026 and are providing a modest boost to GDP growth in Europe’s largest economy, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
Our economists forecast that real exports will grow at a “robust” rate of 3.5% in 2026 and 2.4% the following year. Recent export strength reflects resilient foreign demand alongside modest, productivity-driven improvements in competitiveness.
Goldman Sachs Research expects German exports to increase, driven by revived trade with the US and the European Union, plus the global artificial intelligence (AI) buildout.
“Taken together, we are more optimistic about German export performance than at the start of 2026,” writes Niklas Garnadt, an economist in Goldman Sachs Research, in a report. Strong export performance in the first half of 2026 is consistent with healthy foreign demand and a modest improvement in relative unit labor costs, driven by stronger productivity growth.
Garnadt cautions that competition from Chinese exporters is expected to continue weighing on German exports in the medium term, especially in third markets.
Are German exports getting more competitive?

Still, the brighter outlook marks a shift for a sector that has been a drag on growth since the onset of the European energy crisis in 2022, writes Garnadt. Increases in relative unit labor costs and the real effective exchange rate have recently taken a toll on German competitiveness.
The near-term outlook for exports has “improved materially,” Garnadt writes. Survey-based, forward-looking export indicators have risen to their highest levels since the start of the European energy crisis. Hard data show that foreign manufacturing sales have risen since the start of the year, alongside a recovery in real goods exports. Foreign orders have increased even more sharply. This suggests further export growth in the quarters to come, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
What’s driving Germany’s export turnaround?

In addition to improved competitiveness, German exports to the US are recovering from the decline triggered last year by US tariffs. While exports in the second quarter remained materially below pre-tariff levels, the shortfall peaked in the second half of 2025 and has narrowed since then, writes Garnadt. Recent monthly economic data point to further improvement in the third quarter.
Trade with the EU is also rebounding after the slump that followed the energy crunch four years ago. “Since early 2025, EU trade has become a significant tailwind, reflected in rising manufacturing sales and orders,” writes Garnadt.
Demand for AI infrastructure boosts key German sectors

Thanks to the development of AI infrastructure worldwide, German computer, electronics, and electrical equipment companies are making meaningful contributions to export growth. AI-exposed goods have materially outperformed total exported goods over the past year, according to Goldman Sachs Research
There was also stronger growth in exports of chemicals and intermediate goods in the first half of 2026, perhaps reflecting precautionary purchases related to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz this year. Garnadt writes that this trend may partly reverse in the months to come. And Chinese competition will remain a challenge over the medium term.

Even so, Garnadt points out that Germany’s surprisingly positive performance in the first half of 2026 shows a significant shift in the export sector following a long period of relative weakness.
“Positive near-term indicators, productivity-driven competitiveness gains, stronger demand from Europe and the US, and spillovers from the global AI cycle point to healthy export growth ahead,” he writes.

articles.title: Why Bonds Respond To The Fed, Not To Inflation
articles.text:
Why Bonds Respond To The Fed, Not To Inflation

Anatole Kaletsky

Gavekal Research | 20 Oct 2026

Exactly two weeks ago, I argued that the worst bear market for bonds since the 1970s was due for at least a tactical reprieve because investors were overestimating the number of Federal Reserve rate hikes likely in the year or so ahead (see Reasons To Start Buying Bonds). By sheer good luck, the US bond market turned on that very day. The 10-year yield peaked on October 6 at 5.31%, and declined to 5.09% by last Friday in response to a series of Fed comments that proved less hawkish than expected, before rebounding slightly on Monday.Better still for the view that bond prices these days are driven almost exclusively by Fed expectations, the past fortnight’s bond market rebound has occurred in a clearly deteriorating inflation environment, as evidenced by the shockingly bad US CPI and PPI data released last Wednesday.

articles.title: Inference Market (and Micro) Structure
articles.text:
Insights / Perspectives / When Intelligence Commoditizes, Compute Becomes the Trade

Written by:

Vikram Singh
Investor

Topics

AI

Cryptocurrency

perspectives • August 11, 2026

When Intelligence Commoditizes, Compute Becomes the Trade

TLDRIntelligence is commoditizing through open-source models. Open source models are almost at parity with the frontier and usage is up 350× since January 2025. Since serving inference for open-source models is permissionless, a competitive market for inference is emerging.The inference “market structure” is somewhat like a trading venue. There are buyers of tokens (Cursor, Lovable, enterprises), a marketplace (OpenRouter), and sellers of tokens (Fireworks, Baseten, Together AI) quoting a one-sided order book on a model’s tokens.Inference providers are like market makers: they quote continuously, hold inventory in the form of compute, earn a spread, and vie for token flow. The marketplace is like an exchange: OpenRouter earns a “matching” fee (5.5% take rate) with potentially room to charge the “market makers” for token flow PFOF.GPU-hours are the homogenous input into producing every token and serve as the layer for transferring risk for inference token production. Compute futures emerge as a mechanism to manage the 130% volatility of GPU-hours and to protect inference provider’s COGSA few trends are playing out in real time:Intelligence is commoditizing and democratizing rapidly. Since GPT-4, no frontier model has held the lead for more than 100 days. New models are shipping every 41 days . Open source models are catching up to the best frontier lab models within months vs years. This changes frontier labs economics substantially since they only have 4 months to amortize training capex before spend migrates towards open source models.

Source: Epoch AI's ECI benchmark data[2] (CC-BY, credit Epoch AI)

Source: Epoch AI's benchmark data[3] (CC-BY, credit Epoch AI)
Jevons’ Paradox is playing out in real time. Cost savings achieved by switching from frontier models to open-source models are being reinvested into more token spend. Thus, token consumption compounds even if budgets stay flat. This is evidenced through OpenRouter routing 125× more tokens last week than it did in January 2025 with 75% of volume being open source models vs 27% earlier.

Source: OpenRouter datasets API, as of Jul 22 2026
The proliferation of open source models is leading to higher short-to-medium term GPU rentals. Utilization and rental prices have shot up across the Ornn H100 index after the recent open source model releases

Source: OpenRouter’s weekly rankings , Ornn’s H100 SXM index.
Venture investment in inference providers, GPU rental marketplaces, and routing platforms has heated up intensely over the last three months.

With token flows migrating to open-source models, token buyers growing more price-conscious, and inference being permissionless, a competitive market for serving inference is emerging. Competitive markets tend to develop mature market structures. The inference serving stack roughly resembles a trading venue and a deeper exploration reveals some interesting intricacies.
Inference Market StructureThere are three core participants in the inference trading analogy: Buyers of Tokens, Sellers of Tokens, and a Marketplace.

Source: https://openrouter.ai/docs/faq), (https://sacra.com/c/fireworks-ai/)
Customers/Buyers of TokensConsumers chatting with ChatGPT, engineers running Cursor, apps like Lovable and Harvey serving models behind their own features, agent fleets doing background research, and enterprises wiring LLM APIs into production workflows – all are buyers of tokens. These users are split across a distribution of token-price elasticity:15% are highly elastic. For e.g., Developer experimentation25% medium elasticity. For e.g., Consumer chat40% low elasticity. For e.g., Enterprise SaaS5% price inelastic. For e.g., Real-time response needs

Source: arXiv 2603.21690
Normalizing for the model used, elasticity is somewhat a function of who waits on the inference response. Human-facing demand is inelastic while agent-originated batch demand is elastic. For example, identical tokens cost half as much if you accept a 24-hour batch window instead of a synchronous reply.The aggregate numbers overstate how sticky demand is: a 10% price cut buys only a 0.5–0.7% bump in usage, but that average blends enterprises that will pay almost anything for mission-critical work with hobbyists and dev pipelines that flock to whatever is cheapest. Closed models serve the trusted high-cost work and open models absorb the cheap high-volume flow.As such, the average token is not elastic, but the marginal token is very elastic. Most of the volume already flowing today is bought by a person waiting on the answer: a chat reply, a Cursor completion. That buyer barely notices price and nobody switches models mid-conversation to save cents. However, the next phase of token-demand is bought by software: agent loops, batch research jobs, CI pipelines. Thus, the marginal token satisfies an objective function that maximizes quality while minimizing cost and one in which times plays a lesser role. OpenRouter already optimizes for this future demand as its default router splits a model’s traffic across providers weighted by 1/price² . Thus, a provider that halves its quote roughly quadruples its share of the flow. And since over 70% of routed tokens already come from CLIs and agents, almost all incremental token demand is likely elastic demand.
Inference Providers/Sellers of TokensThese are your sellers of tokens (Fireworks, Baseten, Together AI, and so forth). They burn GPU-hours to produce tokens and quote their token prices on the marketplace. Inference providers can differ on several price-based and performance-based axes. We will discuss them more in depth in the microstructure section.
Marketplace/ExchangeThis platform connects token buyers with inference providers and charges a fee for offering that service. For tokens, the clearest example here is OpenRouter.However, the token marketplace differs from a trading venue in that it’s not two-sided. You can buy tokens from an inference provider but you cannot sell them back to the provider or to any third party. This is inherent to the nature of the token which is manufactured on demand and consumed on delivery, which leaves nothing behind to warehouse or resell. A financial product that structurally cannot have a bid-side has limited avenues for price discovery.So, what does the absence of price discovery look like in practice?Below is OpenRouter's live provider board for DeepSeek V4 Pro. One open model, eighteen sellers, quoted simultaneously:

Three things stand out:Firstly, token quotes cluster at an administered anchor. At the bottom of the board sit five providers (Weights & Biases, Together, Fireworks, Baseten, and Parasail) quote the exact same price: $1.74/$3.48. The same pattern holds on every flagship open model. On Kimi K2.6, seven hosts quote exactly $0.95/$4.00 (including Moonshot itself):

And on GLM-5.2, six hosts quote exactly $1.400 (including Z.ai) while six more run promotional discounts off that same administered price.

Interestingly, the first-party prices are not always the floor. DeepSeek posts the cheapest V4 Pro endpoint, but on K2.6, GLM-5.2, and V4 Flash, third parties undercut the anchor.Secondly, prices can range highly and delivery quality remains questionable. In the DeepSeek example, the quotes span from $0.435 to $1.74 (a 4x gap) across 17 providers. Disclosures around quantization are self-reported and often incomplete (3/5 hosts at the same price list don’t list their quantization). Thus, a cheap quote can be confused for a degraded model vs. an efficient provider for new entrants.Thirdly, mechanisms for price convergence do not exist in token-land. Since the order book is one-sided and secondary marketplaces don’t exist tokens cannot be resold and there are no venues for arbitrage.Thus, tokens themselves are not tradeable today but exploring the microstructure for all parties in a token transaction reveals a two-sided marketplace somewhere else.
Inference Market MicrostructureBy microstructure, we mean the mechanics of the token transaction itself: what instrument each participant actually holds, how their margins are constructed, and what risks sit on their “books.”

BuyersMargin=Value created from token use-Token CostBuyers operate on a value-based business model. They ingest tokens and output a product of some value. Thus to maximize their margins, they must optimize for lower token costs. They are beginning to do this by:Efficient model routing: Coinbase has saved 90% of their dollar spend on tokens by routing prompts to OSS models , holding AI costs flat while growing token usage exponentially. Lindy cut 100% of its traffic over to DeepSeek and saved millions. Cognition and Factory already offer model routing within their harness and Cursor launched their own router yesterday to offer users 60% costs savings. This suggests, OSS models are capturing “token flow” from the frontier labs for non high-value tasks.Restructuring workloads: Batch jobs price cost half the live price , and caching helps cut costs by 60-80% for repeated prompts. For instance, Sail Research looks to solve for longer-running background agents and claims up to 12× more tokens per dollar for work that can wait minutes instead of milliseconds.Professionalizing procurement: Routing policies, model-mix budgets, and substitution playbooks are emerging as COGS management tools. Cloud spend experienced a similar transformation when AWS bills got big enough and FinOps teams emerged to manage spend. Token spend is undergoing a similar transformation
ExchangeAn exchange’s margin looks like:Margin=Spread+Fees+Axuillary SourcesFor token marketplaces like OpenRouter, the spread is non-existent since there is no markup — provider prices are passed through at list. However, OpenRouter charges a 5.5% fee when you buy credits – $1B in GPV accrues $55M in net revenue.The 5.5% is a convenience fee. OpenRouter offers model aggregation (sign up for one account, use 400+ models), easier billing, failover guarantees, strong UI/UX, and most recently it introduced intelligent model selection through openrouter/auto (similar to the model router Coinbase built internally). One of the core premise of using OpenRouter is because as a user you get all capacity available. Fallback is a big value proposition. Even if an app or company builds internal routing or aggregation themselves, providers would prioritize flow from OpenRouter.Since aggregators/marketplaces own the end user experience, they can extract those rents from both sides of the table – not only the buyers. As such, OpenRouter may charge a tax on the inference providers as well and charge them a share of their margins for providing them token flow – similar to how Robinhood charges Citadel for order flow.That said, switching costs for OpenRouter are high but not insurmountable. $10M of token spend involves a $550k rent to OpenRouter. An exchange charging 550bps per trade while taking on zero risk sounds a bit egregious and preserving such high margins while taking no principal risk may be difficult. It is not farcical to imagine loss-leading competitors arising but they will have to compete on UX.That said, there are ways for the exchange to preserve its take. Token quality is invisible at the point of purchase and OpenRouter is the intermediated trusted party between the buyers and sellers that records quantization, uptime, latency, throughput, and data usage policies across every inference provider. It can charge rent for that trust and for verification similar to how a ratings agency does.
Inference ProvidersInference providers like Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI own or rent GPUs and run model inference on them. Most inference providers can only run open-source models, while Anthropic and OpenAI inference can only be provided by the labs themselves and Infra-as-a-Service partners such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex.The margins for an inference provider look like:PNL=Proceeds from tokens sold-Cost to produce tokensA market maker quotes prices continuously, carries inventory, and earns a spread between what its inventory costs and what market orders pay. Similarly, an inference provider quotes prices for tokens they produce, holds token-production inventory in the form of GPU-hours, and earns the spread between what it costs for them to “make” a token and what the market pays for them.

Different inference providers also carry different “grades” of tokens. The same model can differ across providers on the non-price axes:Quantization (FP8 vs FP4 vs INT8): Fewer bits per weight is cheaper and faster to serve, at some cost to model quality. Time to first token (TTFT): How long before the reply starts. Important for human-facing chatTokens per second (TPS): How fast the reply streams. Important for agentic workloads.Uptime: Provider blackout during urgent requests can be quite detrimentalFor an inference provider, revenue is flow × price, and flow on a marketplace goes to the most competitive quote (sorted by 1/price² on OpenRouter). Defending margin at a competitive quote thus requires the lowest cost to produce. Since the cheapest quote gets picked off first on OpenRouter’s marketplace, loss-leader dynamics might naturally evolve if normalized for quality.To some extent, inference providers run a crack spread strategy on GPU-hours. In oil markets, a refiner’s “crack spread” is the margin between the crude it buys and the refined products (gasoline, diesel) it sells. The refiner is long crude, short products, and earns whatever the refinery in the middle can extract between the two prices. Similarly, inference providers are long GPU-hours forward, short tokens spot, with the serving stack acts as the refinery in between.We can write the inference provider’s margin per GPU-hour as:m=p⋅R⋅u-cwhere:p is the token priceR is the refining yield (tokens produced per GPU-hour)u is utilizationc is the GPU-hour costIt’s helpful to understand the above with an example. Let’s freeze our GPU/hr cost to $2.74/hr (Ornn H100 price on July 21) . A provider renting at the index and serving 1,000 tokens per second at $0.90 per million token produces 3.6M tokens per hour at full utilization and earns $3.24/hr against $2.74/hr of rent: a spread of +$0.50/hr. At 50% utilization, revenue halves to $1.62/hr and the spread turns negative to −$1.12/hr. Breakeven utilization on this “crack spread” sits at a utilization of 85%.

Two caveats. First, p and R pull against each other. Speed is sold by shrinking batch sizes, and smaller batches mean fewer tokens per GPU-hour. Serving users faster raises the price you can charge but lowers the yield you produce. That is why the same model on the same hardware sells for $0.56/M at 50 tok/s but $4/M at 125 tok/s. Providers often optimize their stack to serve a particular point on this curve.

*Anchor points from SemiAnalysis InferenceMAX[13] curve shape illustrative.
Secondly, the example’s 15% gross margin is much thinner than the reported 45–50% margin inference providers run today. They are able to:Charge higher prices (p ↑) by capturing flow from users further out on the throughput-cost curve.Compress costs (c ↓) by signing longer-term GPU commitmentsDrive utilization (u ↑) by dynamically managing or repurposing the GPU fleet (more on this below)Push yield (R ↑) with the serving-stack optimizations (more on this below)p is set by sell-side competition and c by the GPU market. R and u are the only two a provider have complete control over.As such, providers seek to maximize R and achieve differentiation on those axes against other providers. Common techniques to optimize costs and maximize R are as follows:Quantization (FP8 → FP4/INT4): Decoding a token is memory-bandwidth-bound: every output token requires streaming the model’s active weights from HBM. Quantization (using FP4 vs FP8) halves the bytes per weight and halves the bandwidth used. FP4 yields 1.8× over FP8 in production, and B200s running FP4 reach up to 3.65× the performance per dollar of H200s on FP8. However, quantization comes at the cost of model quality.Prefix/KV caching. Most tool call an agent makes resends mostly the same prompt with a little new text at the end. Rather than re-process that prompt from scratch each time, the provider stores the computation from the last call and only processes what’s new. Coding agents reuse 85–97% of their prompt this way in production, and going from no caching to 90% reuse takes roughly 10× off the GPU bill. For agent traffic, cache-hit is the most important metric in determining the compute bill.Speculative decoding: A small “draft” model guesses several tokens ahead, and the big model verifies the whole guess in a single pass. Checking is much cheaper than generating, so one read of the big model’s weights now yields several tokens instead of one.Prefill/decode disaggregation: Prefill (reading a prompt) is bound my compute decode and (generating a reply) is bound by memory bandwidth. Yet they share the same GPUs. Splitting them onto separate pools, each tuned for the respective bottleneck, allows for 10–30% improvements and up to 4.4× per GPU for large MoE models on rack-scale systems.Parallelzing MoE experts: Frontier MoE models activate only 3–5% of their parameters per token. Spreading the experts across 32–144 GPUs shrinks the weights each GPU holds, freeing HBM for larger batches, and expert load-balancing alone contributes a 1.5–2.5× throughput gain. DeepSeek runs its own fleet this way (prompts on 32-GPU units, generation on 144-GPU units ), SGLang reproduced the setup on 96 GPUs in the open-source engine, and NVIDIA’s rack-scale GB200 NVL72 systems are built around exactly this pattern.

These optimization levers compound multiplicatively. Despite models getting larger and GPU/hr prices increasing, inference costs have plummeted across generations. DeepSeek’s flagship output price fell ~8× since January 2025 (R1 at $2.19/M → V4 Flash at $0.28/M ), while the H100 index ended the same window 17% higher: $2.34 to $2.74.

Source: R1, Jan 2025 → V3.2-Exp’s −50% cut, Sep 2025 → V4 Flash, 2026 . GPU line: Ornn’s H100 SXM price index , daily, pulled Jul 21 2026.*
Inference providers differentiate by building proprietary depth in these optimization levers. Fireworks wrote FireAttention, a custom attention kernel that allows it to serve the same weights 4× faster than stock vLLM and excels at latency-sensitive flow. Together built ATLAS, a speculative-decoding system whose draft models learn from live traffic, designed to enable its speedups to compound with volume. Baseten trains custom EAGLE-3 draft heads per customer, and has excelled at dedicated deployments. SAIL tunes its whole stack for time insensitive work and has excelled at long-running background agents.However, these optimizations eventually diffuse into the open-source serving engines like vLLM and SGLang. As such, the “alpha” for an inference provider decays and the decay/diffusion rate has been accelerating. Prefill/decode disaggregation took 11–16 months, Multi-head latent attention (MLA) took 3–8 months, EAGLE-3 took 1–2 months and by DeepSeek V4 the release included the most performant serving stack out of the gate.

The edge decay is structural. Not every optimization is published but the largest ones keep arriving as papers because the labs that invent them want their models served widely and cheaply on day one. Red Hat pays vLLM’s core maintainers and NVIDIA contributes to both vLLM and SGLang.There is additional industry nuance here. Some open source labs work closely with inference clouds and let them access model weights pre-open launch in exchange for 15-30% of lifetime serverless revenue from that model. Inference providers basically give up a percentage of future revenue from that model to get a 10 day head start to optimize their gear and plan their capacity around the new model release. Providers can also unlock more storage to have higher cache hits to be able to attract more flow. Model life cycles are short and the initial surge in demand post model release is quite profitable – almost like market makers vying for flow during an IPO or a TGE.A serving-stack edge is therefore temporally short-lived and like any trading alpha must be continuously re-earned.As such, once the optimization stack (R) is exhausted, COGS management turns financial:Rebalancing capacity (u): Provider’s often split their fleets in two parts: dedicated capacity, (where a customer reserves specific GPUs for its own model) and a shared serverless pool everyone else draws from. Dedicated capacity is paid for around the clock but is rarely busy around the clock and its idle hours are predictable. The unlock is that most customer fine-tunes are LoRA adapters: small weight deltas layered on the same base model that is already loaded on the GPU. So when a dedicated customer goes quiet overnight, providers can swap that customer’s adapter out and route serverless traffic onto the reserved GPUs and swap them back on when the customer wakes up. In this manner, the same GPU-hour essentially gets sold twice — once as a reservation, once as serverless flow — pushing effective utilization from 50% to 120%. This is not dissimilar to airlines selling more seats than the plane holds, because the no-shows are predictable. Here the no-show is a dedicated customer’s idle hour.Managing compute cost (c): Compute is the largest cost item in the entire token delivery supply chain. Of every $100 of tokens created, roughly $50 is burnt in GPU-hours. As such, GPU-hours are the homogeneous input for producing any token and thus the most integral part of the entire token lifecycle. The all-in cost of an owned H100 in turn is as follows:

Today providers manage c with term contracts and short-term rental agreements while internalizing all depreciation, price and volatility risk. Financial derivatives like futures and forward curves for GPUs (and memory) can help inference providers transfer risk and manage their cost effectively.In other words, as an inference provider’s software and hardware optimizations asymptote, it’s business begins to look more and more like a trading book.
Compute Futures: The Two-Sided MarketA tradeable instrument requires standardization (one unit substitutes for another) and stability (a contract written today describes the same good at maturity).Tokens fail both today:Standardization: A token is a product tuple across model × quantization × context × latency tier. Fixing the model, one ends up with a Caretsian bundle for the model’s grades – 3 quantizations × 2 context configurations × 3 latency tiers is already 18 distinct, non-fungible products of the “same” model. Stability: The overton window for the newest model has been shrinking. New models now come out every 41 days, often rendering an entire class of older models redundant and plummeting demand for them.Could a token index repair this? Only halfway. Token prices are set at the labs’ discretion and are manipulable by construction. Even the SIT proposal , which fixes the inputs, grades the model rather than the served inference, where the quality games actually live (identical weights score 76–100% on tool calls depending on the host).As such, a token index can work as a reference rate but it cannot carry risk transfer. Risk transfer must happen one layer down in the homogenous input layer that is GPU-hours.GPU-hours already have emergent indices for standardized price discovery such as Ornn’s Compute Price Index and two-sided liquid trading venues like the Architect Innovation Exchange (both Galaxy Ventures portfolio companies)

Why an inference provider needs to manage GPU price risk? An inference provider’s entire cost side is one volatile spot input – their cost of compute. In m=p⋅R⋅u-c, the provider controls R and u and competition sets p but c floats on a spot market whose realized volatility averages 130% annualized with current realized vol sitting at 312%.

In practice a provider’s book is a blend of owned GPUs inventory, 1–3 year term commitments, and short-term rentals at prices near the spot index. Left unhedged, the blend loses in both directions.When rent spikes (May 2026: +101% off the trough), the spot leg’s cost doubles while token prices stay stagnant (token prices have been monotonically decreasing so far) and thus every marginal GPU-hour serves at a loss.

When rent collapses (the $1.63 trough), the longer-term commitments are over-paying above the spot market rate, and competitors renting at spot can quote token prices below the provider’s cost.

How would inference providers manage price risk in practice? Buy GPU-hour futures against the fleet’s forward rental needs. Locking the cost leg replaces the floating spot rent with the futures price plus the cost of running the hedge itself:m=p⋅R⋅u-(F_0+f)where F_0 is the futures price for the tenor being locked and f is the financing cost of the position (collateral tied up as initial margin plus daily variation margin). As with any future, you can have contango or backwardation. Let’s walk through with some examples of a dummy futures curve:Contango (F_0>c_spot): Futures curve slopes up, so the buyer bears carry costs — m=p⋅R⋅u-(c_spot+"carry"+f). Take the February glut: spot sat at $1.63, but our dummy futures quoted above it at $2.05 for May delivery, $2.20 for further out because the market expected rents to mean revert. A provider hedging then paid $0.40–0.60 over spot for locking in the futures price. When the squeeze took spot to $3.28 in May, the hedged provider was still paying $2 and saving the $1.28 delta in operating costs.

Backwardation (F_0>c_spot): Futures curve slopes down, so the buyer pockets a discount (positive roll) — 𝑚=𝑝⋅𝑅⋅𝑢−(𝑐𝑠𝑝𝑜𝑡−discount+𝑓). Take May’s squeeze: spot hit $3.28, but our dummy futures quoted below it at $2.90 two months out because the market expected the shortage to pass. Whoever needed a GPU that week paid the full $3.28 while a provider buying next quarter’s hours got them at a discount to the panic price.

Either way, an open price risk becomes a known, contracted cost which provides margin stability and the only risks left are the two the provider is actually able to internalize, R and u.There are still a few caveats to the above:Firstly, basis risk is not entirely removed: The contract settles on index-spec H100 hours, while a real fleet is a mix of vintages, regions, and interconnects that won’t track the index one-for-one. The hedge covers the market move, not the provider’s fleet’s spread to it.Second, locking c doesn’t lock demand: If a provider hedges more hours than they end up utilizing the position flips from a cost hedge into a directional long on compute. The hedge ratio therefore is somewhat a function of the provider’s confidence in their future projection of their u.Huge thanks to Brett and Ishanee from Architect, Kush, Wayne, and Jack from Ornn, and Vishwa from Anera in their help in reviewing and helping me with this piece. Architect and Ornn are both Galaxy Ventures portfolio companies.Sources1. https://tomtunguz.com/three-years-in/ ↩2. https://epoch.ai/data-insights/gpt-4-longest-eci-lead ↩3. https://epoch.ai/data-insights/open-closed-eci-gap ↩4. https://openrouter.ai ↩ ↩5. https://data.ornn.com ↩ ↩ ↩ ↩6. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.21690 ↩ ↩7. https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch ↩ ↩8. https://openrouter.ai/docs ↩9. https://tomtunguz.com/inflation-deflation-ai/ ↩10. https://x.com/Altimor/status/2062389885437366342 ↩11. https://x.com/SpencerFarrar/status/2070230293429244094 ↩12. https://openrouter.ai/docs/faq ↩13. https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/ ↩14. https://github.com/deepseek-ai/open-infra-index/blob/main/202502OpenSourceWeek/day_6_one_more_thing_deepseekV3R1_inference_system_overview.md ↩15. https://lmsys.org/blog/2025-05-05-large-scale-ep/ ↩16. https://pricepertoken.com/pricing-page/model/deepseek-deepseek-r1 ↩ ↩17. https://devtk.ai/en/blog/deepseek-api-pricing-guide-2026/ ↩ ↩18. https://technode.com/2025/09/30/deepseek-releases-v3-2-exp-experimental-model-cuts-api-prices-by-over-50/ ↩19. https://fireworks.ai/blog/fire-attention-serving-open-source-models-4x-faster-than-vllm-by-quantizing-with-no-tradeoffs ↩

There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesThe MarketsHow Higher Rates and AI Issuance Are Affecting Credit Markets Oct 16, 2026ShareSubscribe:SpotifyAppleYouTubeDownload TranscriptCredit markets have stayed resilient even as interest rates rise and investors scrutinize the outlook for artificial intelligence (AI), says Alex Finston, co-head of US and Asia Credit Trading in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. On The Markets podcast, Finston points out that historically, as long as the increase in rates is steady, investors have often seen rising bond yields as an opportunity. He also shares his take on higher-quality AI credit, whether investors should be hedging their portfolios, and municipal bonds.
Transcript:
Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Thursday, October 15th, and I'm here in the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Alex Finston, who is co-head of US and Asia credit trading within FICC and equities. Alex, thanks so much for joining us on The Markets.
Alex Finston: Yeah, my pleasure.
Chris Hussey: Okay, Alex, let's start with the data because it's been a big week of data with CPI out yesterday and an interesting reaction from the bond market. CPI came in hot, bond market first rates went up, then rates came down. They've come back down again today. What's going on with CPI and why the bond reaction?
Alex Finston: Yeah, look, clearly a disappointing number from the perspective of the market. Yesterday and also with the PPI data from today, I'd say there's a hyperfocus in terms of near-term inflation catalysts and the flexibility this provides the Fed.
I would say elements of higher than expected, both core and energy, created some anxiety there. But I'd say the larger theme is still what is the interplay between this and the AI growth story. So, you know, as we looked at, the reaction function in the market, I'd say the sharp decline in yields was really, the element here that the market's focused on.
And really that's just telling you how much the market is looking forward towards, like will the long-term growth story be impacted at all or is this a short-term blip?
Chris Hussey: That's a great point. So, on the one hand, you have inflation pushing up rates, but on the other hand, you have people worried that it's too much, and then growth will push down rates.
All right, let's talk about credit here because that's your real focus here, and credit is where rates maybe have the biggest impact in the corporate credit market. Yesterday, we saw a little bit of volatility in corporate credit. What's going on in the corporate credit markets nowadays? Why are people getting a little bit concerned?
Alex Finston: I would say at a high level, credit markets have been incredibly resilient throughout the course of 2026 by any reasonable historical narrative, spreads are still tight. the investment-grade index is roughly in the 10th percentile on a 20-year look-back.
Lead fin market's 25th percentile. So still very healthy. At a macro level, the story is really what's going on under the hood, and I would say I'd break that down into kind of three key elements. One has been the AI and the AI supply story. Two has been disruption from new technologies. And the third is really higher rates for longer and how that disproportionately impacts some sectors over others.
Chris Hussey: Yeah. Let's go to that higher-for-longer rates one. I want to sort of disaggregate that if I can for a second. In a higher-for-longer rates environment, do we attract more credit investors or is there a point where the rates get so high that we start to wash it out?
Alex Finston: If we look at the 20-year look-back in fixed income assets, this is an incredible time to be allocating capital to the space.
Look, largely that's a function of just pure treasury yields. But I would say foreign demand still remains incredibly robust. When we look at some of the historical narratives or periods of volatility that we've seen since the great financial crisis, slow and steady moves higher in rates have generally been met with buying and been viewed as an opportunity.
I'd say where you tend to get more, agitation is when you have violent moves in rate to fall to the upside. I'd say largely despite the degree of the move that we've seen in the past month, the market has stomached the volatility incredibly well, and I'd say via our franchise, we continue to see buyers of high-quality credits, particularly on days of weakness.
Now, the question that you pose is when does it become a problem? And I would say largely it becomes a problem when, again, we move up very quickly in a disorderly manner, or two, you know, more importantly from the perspective of the borrower, if we get absolute rates that just make it un-economic to continue to fund and finance through credit markets, you tend to get more agitation there.
Still feels like we're a long ways away from that moment.
Chris Hussey: As the co-head of credit trading, you have a unique lens into what some would call the canary in the coal mine of the economy. Do you see any canaries dropping dead in the coal mine right now?
What's going on here?
Alex Finston: Yeah, so it's a great question, and I'd kind of bring you back to maybe where we started the discussion earlier. On a macro level, markets are incredibly healthy and resilient. Under the hood there is volatility, but I think these are all stories that make sense within the context of the market.
We've seen an incredible amount of investment in the AI space via debt markets. That supply has been well absorbed at a variety of levels from a diversity of investors. There's an incredible amount of capital that's waiting to be deployed for the space. I would say as it relates to sector dispersion, there are ebbs and flows over time based on changes in the macroeconomic environment.
And again, via our franchise, I would say the depth and breadth and diversity of clients that are willing to deploy capital at different levels in these spaces, again, still remains incredibly strong.
The last point that I would make is if you look at implied volatility across most macro asset classes, it still remains incredibly low. I would say if you started to see what started as sector dispersion really create problems for unaffected industries or implied volatility extraordinarily high relative to the level of consternation at the market, I'd be more concerned. But I still think that the North Star is growth, the North Star is AI, and those are still good stories to tell.
Chris Hussey: Yeah, no, it's a great point. All right, one last question for you around the macro, and you mentioned that one of the things that sort of is elevating rates is not really the spread between corporates and the government, but it's just government bonds themselves. Let's talk about government bonds just very briefly, if we can.
Is that the canary in the coal mine? We're seeing issues in France. We're seeing a $40 trillion deficit in the United States. Does it worry you at all about that and maybe even crowding out the corporate credit markets?
Alex Finston: Look, I would say there's clearly a focus on fiscal responsibility. There's clearly a focus on capital allocation for corporates. But I'd say the more important element of this is there's competition for capital across a diversity of markets, and there are great credits at wider levels, and there are credits that will use tight spreads as an opportunity to finance their needs going forward.
I don't think it's a story of is it sovereigns or is it corporates? I think the underlying theme, again, gets us back to the dispersionary forces that we're talking about within markets at the moment. It's becoming a credit picker's market. There will be winners and there will be losers, but I think this is naturally natural and healthy over the course of a credit cycle.
Chris Hussey: Yeah, credit picking is always a great market for investors. All right, let's put a bow on it. What's the trade?
Alex Finston: So, look, I think there's three that are top of mind. The first, given the recent volatility that we've seen in the market, I think it's an incredible opportunity to be able to buy high-quality AI at wider yields than we've seen or higher yields we've seen in some time.
Two, implied volatility, incredibly low. To the extent you're looking for hedges within your portfolio, it's never been a better time.
Third, unique opportunity. Tax-equivalent yields and high-quality Munis approaching 10%.
Chris Hussey: Wait a minute. That's a buy to me. Munis.
Alex Finston: Can you believe it?
Chris Hussey: All right, talk to me about the Muni trade. Why now?
Alex Finston: Look, I'd say we've seen heightened supply over the course of the past two months in the municipal bond market, which has created an opportunity to buy highly rated credits at higher absolute yields. Again, given the backdrop of where we are in the rate environment, the ability to replicate high quality 30-year GO at tax equivalent yields of 10%, historically, pretty attractive.
Chris Hussey: Wow. I haven't heard a municipal bond get pitched in a long time. That's fantastic. All right, what are you watching for next week?
Alex Finston: Look, I think to some degree it's the same themes, right? We're looking to see if the Fed has flexibility. We're looking for whether we're going to see any large AI deals between now and the end of the year.
We're looking for the structure of those deals, the duration of those deals, where across the globe financing is being sourced from. And then, again, like, looking to make sure that the growth story is intact. All things start and end with the growth story. And again, the data so far has been pretty constructive.
Continue to be very impressed with the liquidity and capital available in markets at the moment. And it feels like we're going to get some great opportunities between now and the end of the year.
Chris Hussey: Okay. I can't believe it, but we're almost at the end of October, and the Jets are two and three. Will they finish above 500?
Alex Finston: No, they won't. But we're looking forward to a strong 2027.
Chris Hussey: We're always looking forward to a strong next year. Story of the Jets' lives. Alex, thanks so much.
Alex Finston: Yeah, my pleasure. Thank you.
Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening.

articles.title: European chemicals won the quarter, not the war
articles.text:
Blog

20 Oct 2026

European chemicals won the quarter, not the war

Since the conflict in the Middle East began, European chemical producers have widely been seen as beneficiaries of their rivals’ disruption. Earnings have picked up, but 12-month EBITDA at key manufactures remains roughly a quarter below its 2019 level. We think the gains reflect their competitors’ problems rather than any meaningful improvement in Europe’s own position, and that they are unlikely to last.

What you will learn:

The gains reflect rivals’ problems rather than Europe’s strength. With Asian producers short on feedstock and facing steeper cost increases, since their chemicals sectors rely heavily on oil and naphtha imported from the Middle East, some buyers have turned to European suppliers who could still deliver.

Our implied energy cost index shows the gap with Asia narrowing. With European gas prices rising ahead of winter and EU gas storage at its lowest level for this time of year in more than a decade, European costs are set to fall less steeply than Asia in 2027, eroding Europe’s early advantage.

We now expect European chemicals output to contract in 2027, having forecast growth of 1.4% for the year before the conflict.

Seek long-term capital appreciation by outperforming the MSCI ACWI IMI Index over a full market cycle, while maintaining a diversified portfolio of equities across developed and emerging markets.

Investment Approach
A disciplined, systematic investment process that combines fundamental and behavioural insights to identify attractively valued companies with high-quality fundamentals and improving growth prospects. Risk-aware portfolio construction seeks to translate these insights efficiently into a diversified portfolio while maintaining controlled active risk.

A diversified portfolio of large, mid and small cap equities across developed and emerging markets.
An active, benchmark-aware approach designed to serve as a consistent core global and emerging markets equity allocation.
