articles.title: No bank too big to fail, and none too small to resolve − speech by Ruth Smith
articles.text:
No bank too big to fail, and none too small to resolve − speech by Ruth Smith

Given at The Florence School of Banking & Finance Resolution Academy, European University Institute

Published on
23 September 2026

Ruth Smith discusses the Bank’s approach to managing small and medium-sized firm failure within the UK’s resolution framework. She emphasises the evolution of the resolution toolkit to ensure the regime remains robust for small and medium-sized firms, and reflects on the importance of transparency, proportionality and optionality.

Speech
Good evening, everybody. It’s a pleasure to have had the opportunity to listen to many of you over the course of today’s insightful presentations and discussions on banking resolution. Thank you to the European University Institute and Florence School of Banking and Finance for inviting me to speak today.    
Resolution is in many ways a team sport, and events like the Bank Resolution Academy are a real opportunity to learn from one another, understand the parts we each play, and look at what we can learn from a different viewpoint.    
Following on from today’s sessions on resolving medium-sized banks and the tools available to us in a resolution, I hope to provide a UK perspective on how the Bank of England prepares for resolving small to medium-sized firms.    
As you know, in the UK we have resolution regimes for banks and CCPs.  Today I am focusing on banks and will discuss what we mean in the UK when we talk about small to medium-sized firms and our approach to resolution planning for this large and varied group. I will also cover the lessons learned from the resolution of Silicon Valley Bank UK in 2023, and the new mechanisms we have added to our toolkit to improve optionality in a resolution while still seeking to lessen the burden on firms.    
Despite our recent experience of carrying out a resolution, and the improvements we have made as a result of that, there is still plenty of work to do when we consider resolution of smaller firms.   
The UK banking sector   
The UK has a diverse banking system, comprising some of the world’s large globally systemic banks right down to banks who have balance sheets in the tens of millions. This diversity requires flexibility in how our colleagues in the supervisory arm of the Bank of England, the PRA, apply their regulatory focus and equally needs us as the separate but collaborative Bank of England UK Resolution Authority, to tailor our approaches accordingly. Like any successful team, we each have distinct roles, but we are working towards the same objective of a safe and sound financial system.   
The UK remains a competitive and dynamic marketplace with multiple firms engaging in our pre-application process each year via the New Bank Start-up Unit, and the international presence remains strong, with firms of all sizes having UK subsidiaries and branches. Within the sector we see firms successfully entering, embedding their business, adapting to the demands of the marketplace, and in some cases exiting. This breadth of presence requires us, as the UK’s Resolution Authority, to be ready for those firm exits with a flexible and proportionate approach. Perhaps most importantly, we must be aligned to not only our teammates in the PRA, but where those subsidiaries and branches are part of a wider global group, to our resolution colleagues in overseas jurisdictions such as those here today.   
In practice then, what does this diversity of banking sector and tailoring our approach mean for UK resolution planning?     
We think about our banks in three broad groups,footnote [1] the first of which generally comprises our largest banks, where we plan for bail-in.    
We then have what we describe as mid-tier banks, typically with balance sheets in the £25-40 billion range, where firms can be set either a transfer or a bail-in as the preferred resolution strategy. For the firms currently in this range, we generally set a preferred resolution strategy which involves transferring these firms in resolution to a private sector purchaser, or, in the absence of a purchaser, temporarily to a Bank of England owned bridge bank – pending a further sale.    
Following an update to our policy on how much loss absorbing capacity firms must hold, or “MREL policy”, last year,footnote [2] unlike bail-in firms, transfer firms are not required to maintain MREL above minimum capital requirements. However, both bail-in and transfer firms are subject to the Resolvability Assessment Framework, or RAF. The RAF is our framework to assess UK financial firms’ resolvability and depending on the value of deposits held, some of these banks are also required to publicly disclose their own resolution self-assessment.    
In most cases, unless a firm with assets of less than £25 billion were viewed as posing a risk to financial stability, these smaller banks are then assumed to enter liquidation as a means of resolving their business if they are unable to either recover or complete a solvent wind-down. These are the firms we would use the Bank Insolvency Procedure or BIP for and do not hold additional MREL above minimum capital requirements or maintain additional capabilities to prepare for their failure.  BIP involves a rapid pay-out of depositors by the UK deposit guarantee scheme.footnote [3]  
As always there is judgement in setting a preferred resolution strategy, it is not solely based on a firm’s size and as such a transfer strategy can nevertheless be set in circumstances where the Bank assesses that a firm below the £25 billion mark would pose an unacceptable risk if it were to enter modified insolvency.    
Since the 2007-2008 global financial crisis the focus for resolution has rightly been on the largest, most systemic banks, those described as ‘too big to fail’. For these firms, the necessary team may well be large and international, and involve each person playing their role to produce the desired outcome of a smooth resolution.  And, as we look forward at an ever more interconnected system, operationally speaking, for not only our largest firms but smaller banks too, and join this together with our experiences of a small bank failure, we find ourselves working with the same teammates, and asking the same questions about stability and confidence in the wider sector as well as the impact of that failure on the bank’s customers. With this experience still relatively fresh in our minds it is this I want to speak about in depth.   
Our approach to small firms    
For our smallest banks, those typically defined as having less than £25 billion total assets, the plan for the majority of them should they fail is theoretically straightforward. Where a firm experiences severe stress which it is unable to recover from, the simplest solution is a director led solvent wind-down, allowing the firm to exit the market in an orderly manner while remaining a going concern. This enables the firm to stay in control of its own exit, minimising disruption to customers, creditors, and the wider market.    
Not all solvent wind-downs require active involvement from the resolution authority.  The PRA leads the assessment of whether a firm can continue to meet its obligations and execute an orderly exit from the market.  Where there are concerns about the firm’s ability to complete the wind-down solvently, the Bank, as resolution authority, works closely with the PRA to understand what alternative actions may be required, such as a BIP, should the firm’s plans prove no longer credible.    
Across all our work, the close relationship we have with the PRA is one of the most important aspects of our resolution framework. They are a teammate that we cannot be successful without.   
In the situation where a firm enters solvent wind-down, both authorities must be satisfied throughout that the firm’s wind down plan is credible, that it has sufficient resources to meet its obligations to depositors and creditors, and that allowing the firm to continue with their solvent wind-down plan aligns with our respective statutory objectives.  For a smaller firm, where a solvent wind-down ceases to be credible, insolvency may be the only remaining option.    
A BIP is a modified insolvency process. While the BIP shares many of the features of a standard insolvency process, it is specifically modified for deposit takers such as banks and building societies.    
Unlike an ordinary corporate liquidation, a BIP has a key objective of protecting covered depositors, which is done in two possible ways: payout or transfer. A BIP payout involves the insolvency practitioner or bank liquidator winding up the bank, whilst the Financial Services Compensation Scheme, the FSCS, carries out a rapid payout of deposits to the eligible depositors.    
Authorities in the UK have worked to significantly improve the speed and effectiveness of this payout process, learning from our European counterparts, to help ensure that protected depositors can regain access to their funds as quickly as possible. This speed of payout is important in maintaining public confidence in the efficacy of the resolution regime, and in the stability of the wider financial system.   
The second option is a BIP transfer, which involves the transfer by an appointed insolvency practitioner of the firm’s covered deposit book to another firm, with the insolvency practitioner winding up the remainder of the firm. For many of our smaller firms, the BIP provides a credible and proportionate resolution strategy.    
 So far so good and, hopefully, relatively straightforward and with minimal disruption.    
The boundary between BIP and transfer    
However, the small bank sector in the UK is highly diverse, innovative, and faces heavy competition. These characteristics have resulted in many of these smaller firms developing specialised business models which serve key customer groups, sectors, or communities that may not be well served elsewhere in the market or not be able to quickly and easily transfer their banking services to an alternative provider.   
The BIP is ultimately a liquidation procedure, and while it ensures covered depositors benefit from FSCS protection and payout, it is not designed to maintain the continuity of banking services.    
As such, customers of the failed firm may lose access to their existing banking relationships, payments may be disrupted, and those with uncovered deposits may need to wait for distributions through the insolvency procedure. For some smaller firms’ business models this may be acceptable, but for other firms, particularly where customers rely on continued access to banking services to operate on a daily basis, the impact can be significant and potentially outside the risk appetite of the collective authorities.    
This means that the picture in the UK is nuanced, requiring our assessments of whether a BIP would meet our statutory special resolution objectivesfootnote [4] to consider not only the size of a balance sheet, but also the nature of the customers it serves and the services it provides. As the Resolution Authority we need both a clear game plan and the ability to adapt it in real time.    
Lessons learned from SVB UK    
For the Bank, our experience with Silicon Valley Bank UK in March 2023 provides a powerful illustration of why flexibility in resolution planning is so important.    
At the time, SVB UK was a relatively small institution, with a balance sheet of around £12 billion and a preferred resolution strategy of BIP. Following the failure of its US parent and intervention by the FDIC, the Bank announced on Friday 10 March that, in the absence of further information, it intended to place SVB UK into insolvency.    
Based on what was known at that point, insolvency appeared to be the option that best met the public interest and the resolution objectives.   
As the situation developed over the weekend, however, it became clear that many customers relied on SVB UK not just for deposits, but for critical banking and payment services. At the same time, we needed to be cognisant of public confidence in the system against the backdrop of several other small bank failures in the US.   
We therefore kept multiple options open over the weekend, including insolvency. HSBC emerged as the credible bidder able to complete a transaction before markets opened on Monday while ensuring continuity of critical services, and with close liaison with FDIC throughout, and consultation with the PRA, FCA and HM Treasury, we concluded that a private sector transfer would better meet the special resolution objectives than a BIP.   
Unlike a BIP, the transfer provided protection for all depositors, not just those within the covered limits, ensured continuity of banking services, and most importantly protected and enhanced public confidence in the stability of the wider UK financial system in a way that did not incur costs on public funds.     
For me, this evidences that a preferred resolution strategy provides a vital starting point in contingency planning, but authorities need the flexibility, operational readiness and judgement to adapt quickly when executing a resolution as circumstances change in real-time. In the case of SVB UK, that flexibility was critical to achieving a better outcome for customers, for financial stability, and for the public interest.   
With this in mind, I want to speak to three key takeaways from this, our most recent experience of a bank resolution - transparency, optionality and international cooperation.     
Transparency   
First, SVB UK underlined the importance of a transparent resolution regime and communicating clearly and openly with markets, and authorities. The UK’s resolution framework relies not only on the Bank’s powers as resolution authority, but also on firms, investors, and other market participants understanding how these powers are used in practice, so that they can react accordingly.    
During the resolution weekend for SVB UK, both regulatory and finance ministry authorities worked together to consider multiple strategies in parallel. While this demonstrated the flexibility of the UK's framework, it also reinforced the value of ensuring there was common understanding about how different resolution options would be executed in a live event - between authorities, potential buyers, and the firm itself. Success depended on everyone understanding their role and how the wider team would operate under pressure.   
To bolster this shared understanding, in April we published the Bank’s operational guide to transfer resolution. The guide explains how the Bank would use its transfer powers in practice, whether the transfer involves selling the failed firm to a private sector purchaser, or placing it into a temporary bridge bank owned by the Bank of England.    
It aims to provide greater transparency around the key stages of a transfer, including preparatory work for both us and the firm, buyer engagement, transaction execution, and the information needed to support an accelerated sale process.    
By setting out these operational arrangements publicly and in advance of a future stress, the guide explains that transfer is not simply a theoretical power, but a credible and operationally deliverable resolution strategy. It helps firms better understand what may be expected of them, including the importance of maintaining the information and capabilities needed to support a rapid transfer if required.  It provides transparency to all potential stakeholders within a transfer, including prospective buyers, on how the bidding process would run for a transfer, improving the quality of bids, the competitiveness of an auction, and the smoothness of running the process overall.  
We applied the same learnings on transparency and communications to the Bank’s updated operational guide to bail-in resolution.  As firms grow, they face different resolution expectations. The guide provides greater clarity on how the Bank would execute a bail-in, giving firms, investors and other stakeholders a clearer understanding of the practical steps involved. In doing so, it supports preparedness, reduces uncertainty and reinforces the credibility of the UK's resolution framework across the full spectrum of firms.   
Optionality   
Moving on then to consider the optionality that our resolution framework gives us when planning for a firm failure. While the existing regime gave us an effective and flexible set of options that we were able to use to resolve SVB UK smoothly over a weekend, since 2023 we have continued to work very closely with our colleagues in HMT, our finance ministry, to introduce a new choice in our toolkit in the form of the recapitalisation payment mechanism.    
Introduced via the Bank Resolution (Recapitalisation) Act 2025, this tool is intended to cover associated losses or recapitalisation needs in a transfer via a new industry-funded safety net.    
Simply put, assuming the failing firm meets the public interest test, the recapitalisation mechanism allows us to cover certain costs associated with transferring a firm in resolution up front, be that to a private purchaser or a bridge bank, and then recover these from the industry via the financial services compensation scheme levy ex-post. This minimises the risk to public funds while providing options to use stabilisation powers to resolve a smaller firm when in the public interest.  We were fortunate that in the case of SVB UK the write-down of the regulatory capital was sufficient to enable us to transfer the firm to an interested and credible buyer – but this will not always be the case.  
Use of the mechanism may include recapitalisation of a firm during transfer due to a capital shortfall or potentially providing funds to the purchaser upfront and possibly in the form of guarantees to address any material concerns raised during the bidding process.    
For example, we recognise that the circumstances around a failing firm are often uncertain and extremely fast moving, resulting in limited time for due diligence to be conducted by interested buyers and introducing significant barriers which must be navigated to ensure a successful transfer.    
The new mechanism also gives us the space to be more proportionate in terms of what we require from small and medium-sized firms prior to a resolution. As I have noted, transfer firms are no longer required to hold MREL, in part due to the industry-funded safety net that this new mechanism provides.   
This flexibility represents a big step forward in strengthening our resolution toolkit. However, as always, we need to balance the needs of the failing firm with those of the wider financial system – recognising that any funds used to support the transfer are ultimately repaid by the wider industry.    
Importantly, it is not a replacement for BIP – an insolvency procedure is still a viable option for many firms and dependent on the scenario, may still be the right approach to take when considering our resolution objectives. While the use of the recapitalisation payment mechanism will always be situation specific, in all cases, the Bank will seek to use any funds in the most efficient and effective way possible, and the Act will not be used inappropriately to protect creditors from losses.    
This addition to the Bank’s resolution toolkit recognises that the UK runs a non-zero failure regime, and therefore it is important for firms to be allowed to grow but also be allowed to fail and exit the market smoothly – regardless of their size. It places a portion of that accountability back onto industry, not taxpayers, and ensures the Bank as Resolution authority has more options available to it and is ready for multiple failure scenarios without excessive burden on our smaller firms.   
International cooperation and coordination   
Third and finally, SVB UK underlined the importance of close coordination between authorities, particularly where a failing firm forms part of a wider international banking group.    
Effective resolution of cross-border firms requires more than financial resources and legal powers. It also depends on strong cooperation between home and host authorities, shared understanding of the firm's operational dependencies, and a common objective of maintaining critical services for customers. Like any team, it is helpful to train together before a match, and cross-jurisdictional exercises that allow us to practice and understand how we best work together are an important part of preparing for firm failure before the moment of stress arrives.    
While SVB UK involved close coordination between the UK and US authorities, the same principles would apply to firms operating across other jurisdictions.    
As banking groups become international, maintaining these relationships and coordination channels is an essential part of ensuring that resolution strategies remain credible and operationally deliverable.    
Conclusion   
What does the evolution of our framework mean in reality then? For me, it demonstrates that within the UK resolution regime, we have a robust toolkit that gives us confidence in having options to resolve small, medium and large firms.  
But looking ahead, I can still see areas of the banking sector where we could do more, particularly when it comes to small and medium-sized firms, to better prepare ourselves as authorities and prepare firms, in “peacetime”. I have spoken about how flexible options allow us to execute a resolution in more than one way for any given firm, in order to prioritise better outcomes for depositors while still protecting the public purse and wider financial stability.  
We often envisage using these options when presented with new information that challenges our original game plan during a resolution. However, I consider that we can do more to ensure we are always ready, by working with supervisors and firms to use their existing data and regulatory reporting to identify where they may be on the boundary of a BIP or transfer strategy in advance.   
As trailed in our update to the MREL policy last year, we are reviewing the indicative threshold of 40,000 to 80,000 transactional accounts as an intervention point for when a transfer strategy may need to be set for a firm under £25 billion in total assets. In part, this review is taking into account that the recapitalisation payment mechanism gives us more optionality for firms that do not hold MREL, and that consumer banking behaviour has changed since the threshold’s original implementation, making it less in step with the judgements we have to make when setting preferred resolution strategies.   
However, by removing the burden of MREL for such firms, we still need to ensure that we can execute a transfer effectively.  As part of this review, we are working with the PRA to ensure our resolution planning and reporting policies reflect these recent developments. This includes considering the information we require BIP firms to report on regularly. Are we asking the right questions? Is there existing data that firms already have through recovery and solvent exit planning that would better support our shared readiness for resolution planning as a BIP or in preparation for a transfer strategy in the future?  
With a more established resolution regime we must ask ourselves these kinds of questions to ensure we are continually improving and evolving our approach to firm resolution across the sector. I expect that we will publish our updated approach in early 2027 and look forward to hearing industry views in due course.   
A firm’s resolvability journey is never done, and as such our job as resolution authority isn’t either. No single authority can deliver resolution alone; it remains, at its core, a team effort and we will all need to remain live to an evolving sector to ensure our capabilities and policies are in step with the firms we regulate. The world rarely stays still and advances in technology, how firms operate and where the next risk may arise from is a horizon that we must keep at the front of our mind when considering barriers to an orderly resolution. Firms are a part of our team in a resolution, and I hope by continuing to work closely with one another, we can maintain readiness through a proportionate and effective resolution regime.   
I would like to thank Mala Gopalakrishnan, Kat Hind and Amanda Tennant for their help in preparing these remarks. I would also like to thank Geoff Davies, Charlotte Gerken and Dave Ramsden for their helpful comments.    

In general, for the purposes of resolution planning these three groups of firms are categorised as those with total assets of: i) £40 billion or more; ii) between £25 billion and $40 billion; and iii) less than £25 billion.

articles.title: Daily: Quality bonds for income and diversification
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Investors Club: Managing inflation, UST yields and tech pressure (6 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Asia beyond the AI trade (6 mins)Video: The AI Show | Is the AI trade under strain? (4 mins)Thought of the dayUS bond and equity markets have remained volatile over the past 24 hours as investors weigh mixed signals on the outlook for AI alongside further evidence of persistent US inflation. Chipmaker TSMC offered a more cautious outlook, while the producer price index in the US rose 1.3% in September, its largest monthly increase in four and a half years and well above the 0.5% consensus forecast. Although energy accounted for much of the rise, prices also increased across a broader range of goods and services, adding to concerns that inflation pressures remain in the pipeline. The data followed a higher-than-expected consumer price index print in the US earlier in the week.But US Treasury yields declined, with the 10-year yield trading at around 5.09% and close to its lowest level in three weeks. Equity market volatility increased risk aversion and supported demand for high-quality bonds. While further yield volatility cannot be ruled out amid elevated inflation, heavy debt supply, and persistent fiscal concerns, we continue to rate fixed income as Attractive.Current market pricing of Federal Reserve tightening remains too hawkish. We now expect the Fed to raise interest rates by another 50 basis points over the next 12 months, but this remains more dovish than the current market pricing of nearly 90 basis points more. Recent comments from several Fed officials support a more gradual tightening, with Vice Chair Philip Jefferson stating there is no immediate urgency to hike again, and New York Fed President John Williams saying he sees no need for further rate increases in 2027. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly has also signaled little urgency in adjusting policy rates. This suggests to us that Treasury yields should decline from their current levels as markets scale back their expectations, leaving scope for capital gains in bonds.Elevated starting yields offer an attractive income cushion. Elevated starting yields provide a stronger income base and have historically been a good indication of subsequent total returns. This income can also cushion portfolios against further increases in yields. Our analysis indicates that 2-, 5-, and 10-year US Treasury yields would need to rise by around 257, 113, and 65 basis points, respectively, for capital losses to offset the income earned. We therefore believe investors can benefit from attractive portfolio income even if yields remain volatile.Quality bonds offer diversification and stability in a portfolio. The latest Treasury rally underscores how high-quality bonds can help stabilize portfolios by providing diversification when risk assets come under pressure. Our analysis of US stock and bond portfolios found that a conventional 60/40 portfolio had a maximum recovery period of 4.2 years from bear market drawdowns since 1945, compared with 6.2 years for an all-equity portfolio. Medium- to long-duration quality bonds may also appreciate if tighter monetary policy slows growth or reduces longer-term inflation expectations, helping to offset weakness elsewhere in a portfolio. This combination of income, potential price appreciation, and diversification can help smooth overall portfolio returns across different market environments.So, fixed income should remain a key component in a well-diversified portfolio, and we see opportunities across regions and market segments. Investors should calibrate both credit risk and duration to their objective and investment horizons. More income-focused investors may turn to short-maturity bonds to reduce duration risk, while those who are willing to tolerate volatility may consider select tactical opportunities in medium- to long-duration high-quality bonds. We remain cautious on the longest maturities given fiscal concerns and rising AI-related issuance.

Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com.WHAT HAPPENEDAt least 16 issuers opt out of OKX-ICE’s tokenized stock platform. Microsoft, Apple, Google, Goldman Sachs, CoreWeave, and Broadcom are among at least sixteen issuers that have notified OKXICE TSV, a joint tokenized stock venture between crypto-exchange OKX and NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange, that they object to their stocks being tokenized. The full list of issuers who have opted out: Microsoft, Apple, Google, Goldman Sachs, CoreWeave, Broadcom, UnitedHealth Group, Rocket Lab, Qualcomm, Caterpillar, McDonald’s, Western Digital, Nasdaq, Verizon, Cerebras Systems, and Applied Optoelectronics. The Securities & Exchange Commission released its “innovation exemption” on September 17 shortly after the CLARITY Act’s failure to advance in the U.S. Senate. The exemption creates a pathway to allow for legal, regulated secondary trading of tokenized securities outside of the Reg NMS system by allowing for the creation of Tokenized Securities Venues (TSV), a new type of onchain trading venue. Under the innovation exemption, the TSV must enact trading volume limits, enforce market-wide halts, and ensure that security tokenholders have performed know-your-customer (KYC) onboarding. So far, at least three separate entities have notified the SEC that they intend to launch TSV: Canton (with “TSV LLC”), Perpetuals.com, and OKXICE.OUR TAKE For years, crypto and blockchain advocates have pushed for the ability to trade stocks onchain, and in September the SEC finally delivered a pathway, but one that has set up a new battlefield with several fronts.Third-party sponsored vs. Issuer-sponsored. The issuers who opted out are utilizing an escape valve the SEC allowed when it included the right for third parties to tokenize securities, not just their original issuers. Proponents of third-party tokenization, whether by utilizing swaps, a debt-security structure, or some type of SPV wrapper, argue that they provide what investors want most: access to economic exposure in many investments. Firms like Kraken (xStocks), Ondo Finance, Coinbase, Robinhood, and OKXICE have pursued this path; all but Ondo are exchanges. On the other side, firms like Superstate, Securitize, Figure, and Bullish (Equiniti) argue that third-party issued tokens do not convey all the features of a security, such as legal, economic, and governance rights. We’ve written about this dispute extensively, and the 16 opt-outs from OKXICE’s third-party tokenization is just the latest salvo. DeFi vs. TradFi. The innovation exemption also draws a fascinating middle ground between DeFi and TradFi. What the innovation exemption allows for is more aptly described as onchain finance than decentralized finance. The TSV, whether comprised solely of one AMM or a conglomeration of AMMs, issuers, transfer agents, or other involved parties, must notify the SEC of its intentions, provide certain reporting, and crucially perform certain responsibilities that can only be performed with a level of control. The TSV is not quite an exchange or an ATS, but it’s also not quite DeFi in the commonly understood sense. Trade halts, KYC, and volume limits are not things that permissionless DeFi can perform today. The requirement that trading be limited to those who have been KYC’d, in particular, will make legal, American tokenized securities substantially less composable in the broader onchain environment, at least in the near term. But the TSV can ultimately allow for trading outside the Reg NMS system and does not need to register as a national securities exchange or alternative trading system (ATS). Not quite DeFi, but not quite TradFi.An interesting aspect of the approach taken by the SEC is that the “innovation exemption” offers exemptive relief in an unconventional way. The Commission did not look at an entity or set of entities and say “you’re exempt for these reasons.” In fact, the term TSV was invented by the SEC in the order itself, and no “TSV” exists yet. So, rather than a typical exemptive relief, the Commission has presented a new pathway, one that seems to thread the needle between rules, statutory authorities, and a maze of stakeholders. Whether this approach can be successful in promoting an innovative and experimental new environment for securities trading remains to be seen, and the answer to the question will ultimately determine the outcome of the third front in the tokenized securities battle.Onshore vs. Offshore. Onshore tokenized securities under the innovation exemption face an uphill battle in the market. If they cannot deliver a better product and comparable user experience to an offshore, third-party issued tokenized security that is fully composable in DeFi once accessed via VPN, then the whole experiment could fall flat. It’s very early still in the application of the innovation exemption, and we and many others will have more to say and announce in the coming weeks and months, but it is crucial that the innovation exemption yields tangible benefits, at least in actionable learnings to inform next steps in designing a viable onchain securities market, if that onchain securities market is to be built in the United States and not in Malta, Abu Dhabi, or the Caymans.

articles.title: Daily: Strengthen portfolio defenses as volatility rises
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioPodcast: AI demand remains the signal amid neocloud noise, on Apple , Spotify (6 mins)Podcast: Across the Pond: Europe’s bond stress test, on Apple , Spotify (22 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Why bank stocks are falling amid rising rates (6 mins)Video: The AI Show |The AI trade's two-sided test (4 mins)Video: Data with Donovan | The Fed's rate path ahead (5 mins)Thought of the dayBrent crude oil hit USD 112/bbl for the first time since May and is on track for a third consecutive week of price gains as fresh attacks in the Middle East have heightened concerns about further disruptions to energy supplies. Since the start of this month, Brent crude has risen 9.4%.Saudi Arabia reported attacks on an Aramco oil field and an airport in its Eastern Province, while the US ordered diplomats to leave the country amid Houthi strikes. Separately, the New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries had developed specific plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the US midterm elections, which take place on 3 November.With the Russia-Ukraine conflict also continuing, geopolitical risks are unlikely to subside in the near term, keeping inflation concerns elevated and adding to macroeconomic uncertainty.But geopolitics are not the only factor driving market performance. Resilient economic growth, robust corporate earnings, and strong AI demand continue to underpin equity gains. Our view remains that investors should focus less on the possibility of short-term drawdowns associated with geopolitical events and more on ensuring that their portfolios can withstand periods of volatility.History suggests that geopolitical shocks are rarely a sufficient reason to stop investing. Since 1941, the S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after the start of a geopolitical crisis roughly three-quarters of the time. For diversified portfolios, the long-term cost of remaining uninvested has often proved greater than the temporary cost of living through a geopolitical drawdown.The global energy system should continue to adapt to the disruption. While still below its pre-war levels, OPEC crude production rose by 0.92 million barrels per day in September to 25.1 million, or around 85% of February’s output, according to the group’s latest Monthly Market Report. Trade routes are also shifting, while the G7 decision to release additional emergency oil stocks should provide some temporary relief. Together, these developments demonstrate the global oil market’s ability to respond to disrupted supplies. We acknowledge that the physical oil market remains tight and is vulnerable to further supply shocks, but our base case is that a gradual recovery of energy flows and production should allow oil prices to moderate into next year. This means that the impact of higher energy prices on the global economy should remain insufficient to derail growth.Exposure to commodities can help manage volatility. Instead of retreating from markets, investors can use energy exposure to insulate portfolios against such supply-driven volatility and boost diversification. In fact, we think investors should consider broad commodities as a differentiated source of return, especially as rising power demand, AI infrastructure investment, electrification, and constrained supply are supportive of an upcycle. Historically, commodities have exhibited low correlations with traditional asset classes, and we think an actively managed approach can help investors navigate across the commodity complex.So, we retain a constructive market outlook and believe investors should stay invested for further equity gains via broadly diversified exposure across sectors and regions. We also believe investors can strengthen their portfolio resilience by incorporating fixed income, broad commodities, and select alternatives according to their risk tolerance, liquidity needs, and financial objectives.

articles.title: Equities update - Week 43 - October 23 2026
articles.text: Equities update - October 23rd 20268 min readFinanceDataWeek 43 brought further volatility to the AI infrastructure trade as financing constraints and concerns over eventual overbuilding weighed on sentiment despite strong revenue growth and constructive demand forecasts. SpaceX reported robust growth, Western Digital cited demand visibility through 2030–31 across its largest customers, and Meta continued advancing its Muse AI rollout alongside substantial infrastructure investment. However, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang highlighted that capital availability is constraining neocloud expansion even as demand remains strong. This captures the central tension: accelerating demand can support infrastructure investment, but shareholder returns still depend on financing costs, delivery schedules and the price paid to build capacity. Elsewhere, demand for Treasuries pulled the US 10-year yield below 5% on the week, however, sharp upside moves in the VIX and MOVE indices reflected uncertainty across both equity and bond markets. Bitcoin and select crypto-native equities proved more resilient, with Bitcoin unchanged over the week. Corporate progress also remained constructive, Mastercard’s expanding stablecoin and agent-payment capabilities, alongside Coinbase’s partnership with Thunes, demonstrated continued investment in the distribution and services needed to turn digital-asset activity into practical financial applications.Week 43 Key Developments in Blockchain Equities:Index Performance: Index Performance: The Index declined 1.6% over the week, while Bitcoin was unchanged, against a backdrop of elevated energy prices, uncertainty over monetary tightening and renewed scrutiny of AI investment returns. The US economic calendar was relatively light this week, although weekly labour-market data remained resilient, with initial unemployment claims falling by 6,000 to 194,000, providing little evidence of an acceleration in layoffs. Expectations increasingly centred on an October Fed pause followed by a December hike; a Reuters poll found that 94 of 100 economists expected unchanged rates at the 27–28 October meeting, while all anticipated an increase in December. Nevertheless, Treasuries rallied as weakness in technology shares encouraged demand for safer assets, pulling the 10-year yield below 5% on Thursday. Gold’s weaker performance over the week highlighted the uneven response across traditional safe-haven assets, underscoring the complexity of the current market environment.Block Index Key Movers: 7-day top performers: Sony Group (+5.9%), CME Group (+5.7%), Nextera Energy (+3.7%) 7-day worst performers: Cipher Digital (-17.1%), Riot Platforms (-16.8%), Galaxy Digital (-16.2%) Mastercard’s developments this month highlight how established payment networks can capture value from stablecoin adoption while providing resilience within BLOCK amid equity market volatility - Mastercard has been a standout performer, gaining approximately 15% month-to-date and reaching new all-time highs. The company has made meaningful progress in developing its stablecoin capabilities this year, particularly through its acquisition of BVNK. This week, it launched Stablecoin Security, initially with Borderless.xyz and Keyrails, extending fraud and sanctions screening across traditional and blockchain payment flows. It also opened early access to Agent Pay for Machines, following pilots involving Coinbase, Base, Cloudflare and BVNK, allowing AI agents to purchase digital services within approved budgets and permissions.In our view, the significance lies in Mastercard broadening the services it provides around the movement of money. Banks and businesses adopting stablecoins still require conversion, merchant acceptance, local payouts and risk controls. Bringing these capabilities together could strengthen customer relationships and create opportunities to generate revenue across several stages of a payment. This builds on an established services franchise: value-added services and solutions revenue grew 18% on a currency-neutral basis in Q2, compared with 8% for the payment network. Services growth will therefore be a key metric to watch when Mastercard reports its Q3 results next week. The agent-payments initiative offers another potential avenue for growth, extending Mastercard’s spending controls and payment authorisation capabilities to software that increasingly transacts independently.For BLOCK, Mastercard combines an established earnings base with further growth opportunities in digital payments. Its strong performance also highlights the diversification available within blockchain equities as investors place greater scrutiny on the financing requirements of AI infrastructure.Earnings Recap – Key Holdings:CME Group – PositiveMeta Platforms, Nextera Energy - MixedOther news - Index constituents:Coinbase and Thunes announced a partnership on 19 October combining Coinbase’s stablecoin infrastructure with Thunes’ connections to local payment systems, bank accounts and mobile wallets. The opportunity lies in completing the payment journey: a faster blockchain transfer has limited practical value if the recipient cannot readily receive and use the money locally. Thunes could help Coinbase address this constraint across supplier payments, gig-worker payouts and remittances, extending its infrastructure business beyond exchange trading.Circle and Proof announced a collaboration on 19 October demonstrating how AI agents can present verified identity credentials and make USDC payments from a Circle Agent Wallet. The demonstration addresses a practical obstacle to agent-led commerce: establishing who authorised a purchase and retaining evidence if it is disputed.SBI VC Trade and SBI XDC Network APAC announced an agreement with South Korea’s Shinhan Card on 21 October to explore blockchain-based payments. Planned work includes testing how yen-denominated stablecoins could connect with physical merchant payments, alongside potential cross-border trade settlement. The significance is the combination of SBI’s digital-asset capabilities with established merchant-payment infrastructure, potentially addressing acceptance and conversion barriers simultaneously.Strategy’s 19 October disclosure showed purchases of 267 BTC for US$22.1m,. Taking holdings to 848,517 BTC, alongside US$93.1m of STRC repurchases. It increased its preferred-securities repurchase authorisation to US$3bn, with 1.16bn remaining. As of 18 October, its USD Reserve was US$4.83bn, with a separate US$447.3m of USD Cash.Other news – Non - Index constituents:OKXICE, the joint venture between OKX and NYSE owner ICE, filed with the SEC for a platform offering 24/7 tokenised US-stock trading. Its proposed structure uses permissioned Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on XLayer, with securities traded against supported payment stablecoins. This brings exchange infrastructure into closer competition with crypto-native trading platforms and creates another potential source of stablecoin settlement demand.Securitize launched tokenised exposure to 12 US stocks, initially on Solana, with USDC settlement. Each token is backed by a share and represents a security entitlement, with applicable economic and voting rights; holders become registered shareholders only if they convert where available. Initial trading uses its broker-dealer platform during extended hours.OCBC and Ant International launched a ‘tokenised-deposit’ solution on 7 October enabling 24/7 movement of SGD- and USD-denominated deposits between Ant’s entities in Singapore and Malaysia through WhaleRTP. The practical benefit is greater flexibility in deploying working capital outside banking cut-off times, alongside improved reconciliation. This is also relevant to the competitive landscape: banks are developing blockchain payment capabilities while retaining customer funds as commercial-bank deposits, giving corporate treasurers an alternative to transferring liquidity into stablecoins. Separately, HSBC and Ant International expanded tokenised treasury activity into the Middle East, following pilot transactions involving UAE-dirham transfers and cross-border dollar payments.Published onOct 23rd, 2026WriterSatish PatelInvestment AnalystCo-manages the Invesco CoinShares Global Blockchain ETF with expertise in payments and technology.

articles.text: On September 15, we advised investors to proceed with caution. We pushed out our 8,400 S&P 500 target from year-end 2026 to mid-2027 and set 7,900 as our new year-end target. On October 14, we reiterated our caution. Sure enough, the stock market has been turbulent since mid-September, with AI-related stocks falling sharply.We are seeing some buying opportunities, but better ones are likely after the November 3 midterm elections. articles.title: AI poses uneven opportunities and risks across APAC cities
articles.text:
RESEARCH BRIEFING

16 Oct 2026

AI poses uneven opportunities and risks across APAC cities

Investment and expansion in professional services have propelled Asia’s major cities into the ranks of the world’s most influential economic hubs. AI advances have the potential to reinforce these trends, but there are also clear risks ahead.

Investment and expansion in professional services have propelled Asia’s major cities into the ranks of the world’s most influential economic hubs. Since 2000, gross value added in these sectors has grown on average by 7.9% each year across all our Asia Pacific cities, boosting incomes and living standards. AI advances have the potential to reinforce these trends, but there are also clear risks ahead.

Cities that cater to AI-related demand have seen robust gains. Reputation, strategic policies, and a skilled and abundant workforce have supported Asia’s specialisation in producing the electronic components needed for AI systems. With AI-related exports set to boom across Asia this year, we expect strong manufacturing growth for key cities such as Hsinchu (Taiwan), Georgetown (Malaysia), and Hai Phong (Vietnam).

As AI adoption rates rise, service-centric cities will be the key beneficiaries, reinforcing the strength of the region’s major hubs like Singapore, Beijing, and Tokyo. This is because service sectors like IT and finance are the most likely to receive productivity and income gains, given their ability to leverage the technology.

However, city-level labour market responses will be complex. Although we do not expect widespread job losses from AI adoption, there will be greater exposure for specific low value-added occupations in ICT and administrative activities, which heightens the risk for outsourcing economies like Manila and Bengaluru. Developments are also likely to widen regional inequalities as more rural and industrial regions fall behind.

Policy, politicsand earnings
We retain our defensive and diversified stance across assets, sectors and regions amid near-term uncertainty around monetary policy, politics and earnings.
The next two weeks will be busy for major central banks, US political watchers and technology leaders powering the AI supercycle. We expect the Fed, ECB and BoJ to hold rates next week, but markets will focus on whether central banks are turning more hawkish due to the latest surge in fuel prices.
The US mid-term elections are expected to give Democrats control of the House and Senate, with implications for taxes and the AI-led investment boom. Meanwhile, the consensus is expecting the US tech sector to report over 60% y/y earnings growth for Q3.
Each of these three drivers has the potential to surprise markets. We close and lock in gains on our European CoCo1 bond and US 10-year government bond opportunistic ideas amid French and US political risks.

Editorial

Policy, politics and earnings

Strategy summary: We retain our near-term defensive and diversified stance across assets, sectors and regions amid near-term uncertainty around monetary policy, politics and earnings. The next two weeks will be busy for major central banks, US political watchers and technology leaders powering the AI supercycle. We expect the Fed, ECB and BoJ to hold rates next week, but markets will focus on whether central banks are turning more hawkish due to the latest surge in fuel prices. The US mid-term elections are expected to give Democrats control of the House and Senate, with implications for taxes and the AI-led investment boom.
Meanwhile, the consensus is expecting the US tech sector to report over 60% y/y earnings growth for Q3, the biggest jump in over two decades outside the post-COVID rebound. Each of these three drivers have the potential to surprise markets.
Big Three to hold monetary policy: We expect the Fed, ECB and BoJ to hold policy rates next week, after September’s hikes, as they assess whether higher bond yields have tightened financial conditions enough to offset fuel-price-driven inflation. We expect the Big Three to hike next in December as fuel prices are likely to stay elevated into early next year due to refining capacity constraints. Nevertheless, the Fed and ECB are likely to deliver less than around 60bps of rate hikes priced in by money markets over the next 12 months on the back of an eventual easing of oil and fuel prices leading to disinflation by H2 2027. This outlook means 3-7-year Developed Market investment grade bonds currently offer attractive risk-reward.
Opportunity in Australian bonds. Other major central banks, such as the Bank of England, Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of New Zealand are likely to hike rates by 25bps in the next two weeks given their focus on taming near-term inflation. However, we believe the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) is close to the end of its hiking cycle, even if it hikes one last time in the coming months (money markets give a 60% chance of a hike on 3 November). Australia’s domestic labour and housing markets and business confidence are softening after the RBA hiked its policy rate four times this year to a 15-year high.

Meanwhile, Australia’s cash rate is 60bps higher than the US policy rate, supporting the AUD. We continue to see attractive income and FX gain opportunities from AUD corporate bonds.
A ‘Blue Wave’ in the US? Prediction markets strongly favour Democrats taking the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate in the 3 November US mid-term elections. While an opposition sweep in the mid-terms has historically delivered the best 12-month returns for equities among all scenarios, partly due to the resulting policy gridlock, a decisive Democratic “blue wave” could increase longer-term risks of higher taxes and uncertainty over policy towards AI investment and data centres. With the Senate race still close and prediction markets fallible, we remain cautious on risk assets in the near term.
Closing EU bank contingent convertible bonds (CoCos1) and US 10-year government bond ideas: We lock in 2% gains in EU CoCos and 1.7% gain in US 10-year government bond ideas amid French and US political risks (page 5-6). We continue to hedge any inflation risks through inflation-protected bonds and geopolitical risk through an Overweight in gold.
Watching Big Tech earnings: Upcoming Big Tech earnings raises uncertainty as market leadership remains concentrated and share-price reactions more mixed. With valuations less likely to drive returns, earnings delivery and sustainability of AI investment, funding and monetisation and broadening out of earnings beyond tech will be critical, raising the risk of volatility and sector divergence. We remain invested but defensively positioned, favouring diversification across sectors and regions.
Staying defensive and diversified. Top client questions

What are the key takeaways from the technology sector earnings reported so far this week?

Our view: Recent technology sector earnings results point to strong compute demand and continued capex expansion, supporting our positive long-term view on the AI investment theme. However, rising funding and execution risks warrant near-term caution. We prefer to avoid increasing exposure to higher-risk areas within the technology sector for now.
Rationale: Earningsresults reported this week suggest major tech companies remain committed to expanding their AI infrastructure. While this bodes well for AI infrastructure providers, ambitious expansion plans imply that an increasing share of AI capex is likely to depend on debt financing. We expect debt-financed AI capex to rise from c.25% of AI capex in 2026 to c.40% in 2027.
Greater reliance on borrowing increases sensitivity to interest rates, while deployment delays could postpone revenue recognition amid ongoing financing costs. However, evidence of improving AI monetisation and adoption should strengthen operating cash flows and support internal capex funding. Against this backdrop, we will assess Big Tech earnings next week for greater clarity on capex guidance and funding and AI monetisation trends.
— Ryan Goh, Investment Strategist

Are you still positive on Euro area bank equities amid heightened political and fiscal uncertainty in the region?

Our view: We remain positive on Euro area bank equities, supported by resilient earnings and shareholder-friendly capital return policies. While France’s fiscal uncertainty and a softer growth outlook warrant caution, the recent pullback in Euro area bank equities offers selective opportunities. We favour well-capitalised banks with strong deposit franchises and diversified earnings.
Rationale: We expect Euro area banks’ Q3 2026 net interest income to grow 1.5-3.0% q/q, led by Spanish banks, driven by higher rates and continued asset repricing. Resilient fee income from wealth management and investment banking activity, as well as dividends and buybacks, should provide further support. Price-to-book (P/B) valuations have eased, despite expectations for healthy return on equity (ROE), thus improving risk-reward.
Fiscal uncertainty in France has widened sovereign spreads, pressuring banks’ bond holdings and funding costs. Although French banks represent 13% of the Euro area Bank Index, volatility could spread to regional financial markets. However, stress in the broader banking system appears limited, supported by strong capital buffers and ECB tools to contain disorderly market moves and sovereign market contagion. We will continue to monitor credit trends, sovereign spreads and banks’ 2027 earnings guidance.
— Robin Xie, Senior Investment Strategist

What has driven the recent weakness in China equities, and what is your outlook from here?

Our view: We maintain China equities as a Core holding, as valuations remain inexpensive. Rapid technological innovation and investment in AI localisation provide tailwinds, but the potential for a re-rating appears delayed. Investors should seek to diversify their portfolios and reduce concentration risk.
Rationale: China equities have weakened, driven by mounting scepticism over AI capex returns, structural margin compression and concerns about the country’s significant financing requirements. Another notable feature in China has been significant share issuance, which has diluted earnings per share and weighed on the MSCI China Index’s performance. These pressures have been compounded by geopolitical headwinds, restrictions on advanced chips, an enduring property sector contraction and weak domestic demand. September’s stimulus measures also disappointed markets in terms of their scale and pace of delivery.
Notwithstanding these headwinds, valuations remain inexpensive, supported by rapid domestic innovation and structural tailwinds in AI localisation, leading us to retain China equities as a Core holding. Elevated volatility reinforces the need to be defensively positioned, favouring diversification rather than relying on technology sector concentration. We also remain Overweight China’s healthcare, financial and materials sectors.
— Cindy Lam, CFA, Senior Investment Strategist

Are you still bullish on US 10-year government bonds?

Our view: We are closing our opportunistic bullish idea on US 10-year government bonds at a gain of 1.7%. The risk-reward has become less compelling after the yield broke below 5%, the lower bound of our three-month forecast range of 5.00-5.25%.
Rationale: The US 10-year yield fell over 17bps to 4.97% on 22 October – its first move below 5% since 23 September and biggest one-day drop since March 2023. A sell-off in AI-related equities and renewed Middle East tensions drove investors towards safe havens. Earlier this month, the yield hit its highest level in over two decades. The forces behind the rally are fragile, though. Oil prices remain elevated amid escalating Middle East tensions, and September US consumer inflation rose to 3.7% y/y. Fed officials have signalled there is no urgency to raise rates at the 27-28 October meeting, but persistent price pressures keep further tightening on the table. We prefer to lock in gains and close our opportunistic bullish idea on 10-year government bonds at a gain of 1.7%.
— Jonathan Liang, CFA, CIO, Fixed Income & FX

Top client questions (cont’d)

What is your outlook for French bank bonds, especially ahead of France’s upcoming sovereign credit rating reviews?

Our view: The recent sell-off in French bank bonds is a repricing of tail risks, not a credit story. We expect further price volatility until the April 2027 French presidential election, particularly at the junior end of the capital structure, so we are closing our opportunistic EU bank contingent convertibles (CoCos1) idea at a gain of 2.0%.
Rationale: We believe the recent sell-off in French bank bonds reflects domestic political and fiscal risks rather than weaker credit fundamentals. The sustained widening of the OAT-Bund spread has raised concerns about the profit and loss (P&L) impact on banks’ sovereign debt holdings. Banks provide limited disclosure on these exposures. However, banks’ investment portfolios are generally diversified, and holdings booked at amortised cost should soften the P&L impact. Near-term catalysts include the upcoming sovereign credit rating reviews. A sovereign downgrade could trigger bank rating downgrades, with domestically focused lenders potentially more exposed than regionally diversified peers. A sovereign credit event is not our base case, but we expect headline risks to persist until the French presidential election. Against this backdrop, we are closing our opportunistic EU bank CoCos idea.
— Cedric Lam, Senior Investment Strategist

Will the November US mid-term elections and European bond volatility support a sustained Swiss franc (CHF) rebound?

Our view: We expect a near-term CHF rebound, supported mainly by safe-haven demand amid European bond volatility. We believe the US mid-term elections will be a secondary driver.
Rationale: European sovereign bond volatility provides the stronger catalyst for CHF strength. The France-Germany government bond yield spread remains elevated near 160bps, reflecting heightened French fiscal concerns and reinforcing the CHF’s safe-haven appeal. The US mid-terms could provide additional support for the CHF. A Democratic victory in either chamber is expected to constrain further fiscal expansion, potentially weighing on the USD. However, this would not necessarily lead to faster fiscal consolidation.
The SNB’s 0% policy rate leaves the CHF at a sizeable interest-rate disadvantage vs. the USD, constraining sustained CHF gains. With EUR/CHF below 0.90, excessive CHF strength could also increase the risk of SNB intervention. A decisive USD/CHF break below 0.8130 would strengthen the technical case for a more sustained CHF rebound.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist— Iris Yuen, Investment Strategist

Top client questions (cont’d)

Would worsening budget deficits and political uncertainty across parts of Europe affect your view on EUR/USD and Euro area government bond yields?

Our view: Fiscal and political concerns constrain near-term EUR/USD gains, with France being the primary vulnerability. We expect EUR/USD to recover towards the 1.17-1.18 range over the next 12 months, supported by continued Euro area economic growth and an expected fading of USD support. We expect wider differentials in Euro area government bond yields, with political risk premium elevated in French government bonds (OATs) and German government bonds (Bunds) supported by safe-haven demand.
Rationale: France’s high public debt, large budget deficit and political obstacles to fiscal adjustments are weighing on market confidence, with the country’s 10-year government bond yield rising above 5%. The risk of stress spreading to Italy and Spain adds to regional concerns, although current evidence does not establish a broad European fiscal crisis. German government bonds should benefit from safe-haven demand, while fiscal concerns keep risk premia on vulnerable countries’ bonds elevated. EUR/USD remains more sensitive to US-Germany interest-rate differentials and broader market confidence than to French bond yields alone.
France’s fiscal risks, elevated energy costs and high US interest rates weigh on the EUR in the near term. Over the next 12 months, Germany’s multi-year public investment programme, resilient exports and sound banking-sector fundamentals are expected to support Euro area growth. We expect the Fed’s rate-hiking cycle to peak by mid-2027, reducing USD support and driving the EUR towards 1.17-1.18 .
The principal tail risk is fiscal stress widening government bond yield spreads and spilling over into bank funding conditions and lending activity, weakening growth and delaying the EUR’s recovery.
— Vincent Tan, Senior Investment Strategist— Cedric Lam, Senior Investment Strategist

Managing Payment Fraud Risk

Payment fraud is rising sharply worldwide1, costing businesses tens of billions of dollars2 each year.Organizations handling large volumes of financial flows are particularly targeted.In a large majority of cases, despite strengthened technical security measures, human factor remains a key source of vulnerability3. Raising awareness and training your teams are key levers in protecting against these types of fraud.Stay ahead of key fraud risks and support your organization's resilience.Main fraud scenarios observed:Phishing or smishing (email or SMS phishing)An email or text message impersonating a trusted individual or a recognized organization (bank, internet service provider, etc.) in order to collect your personal information.Fake bank advisor fraud / Impersonation scamA call or message from someone claiming to be a representative of your bank, citing technical checks or a supposed fraud attempt on your account, to pressure you into urgently approving a fraudulent transaction or handing over your bank card via a fake courier.IBAN fraud / invoice redirection fraudThe fraudulent alteration of the bank details of one of your counterparties, such as suppliers or service providersCEO fraud / Business Email CompromiseAn urgent and confidential request allegedly coming from a senior executive within your company, aimed at getting you to approve a banking transaction.Malicious QR codesQR codes that redirect users to fraudulent websites designed to collect personal information or prompt the installation of malicious software.Email account compromiseHacking of email accounts, allowing fraudsters to monitor interactions between the client and their bank and/or insert fraudulent messages. 1- Corporate treasurers report significant rise in fraud | The Association of Corporate Treasurers 2- According to World Metrics, Businesses lost $32bn to payment fraud in 2022: Payment Fraud Statistics (2026): Latest Research 3- Discover how human error and manipulation pose risks to B2B payment security and learn strategies to mitigate these vulnerabilities effectively
