Strategic Asset Allocation Market Strategy
NDR’s cross‑asset strategic allocation applies decades of quantitative research to guide investors over long‑term horizons.

NDR’s cross-asset strategic asset allocation service leverages NDR’s quantitative methodology and forty-five years of market analysis to help investors navigate a long-term investment horizon. Underpinned by NDR’s 10-year LTCMA analysis, the SAA team provides positioning optimized to a 3-5 year investment horizon for Financial Advisors from Very Conservative to Very Aggressive client risk profiles.Grounded by a robust, academically supported, methodology and simulation, the service provides long-term coverage of individual asset classes, relative positioning between TAA and SAA portfolios, dynamic allocation bands, Monte Carlo probability-of-success metrics linked directly to client financial plans, and opportunities for consultative advice including investment committee participation (dependent on service level).

articles.title: The institutional form of independent central banks: from history to contemporary challenges - speech by Andrew Bailey
articles.text:
The institutional form of independent central banks: from history to contemporary challenges - speech by Andrew Bailey

Given at LSE TRIUM Anniversary Conference

Published on
04 September 2026

In his speech Governor Andrew Bailey argues that the foundation of independent central banks rests on more than technocratic expertise alone and elaborates on the long intellectual and historical tradition of their accountability. He contends that central banks exist to protect public goods, namely stable money and a resilient financial system, by insulating key decisions from short term political pressures while remaining accountable within a democratic framework.

Speech
I would like to reflect on independent central banks as institutions, and how their authority is grounded and is challenged.
On 3rd September 1780 (246 years ago yesterday) a 23 year old aide to George Washington wrote that: “the Bank of England unites public authority and faith with private credit and hence we see what a vast fabric of paper credit is raised on a visionary basis.” That 23 year old was Alexander Hamilton.footnote [1]
The meaning of central bank independence is not just a technical point about monetary policy or financial stability, or just a point about the design of public institutions. It is about the relationship between societies and the institutions they create to serve them. This brings to mind Douglass North's definition of institutions as the rules of the game in a society or, more formally, the humanly devised constraints that shape human interaction.footnote [2]
Institutions are not just organisations. They are durable arrangements through which societies solve collective problems. To do this, they must embody understandings about how authority should be exercised, how conflicts should be managed, and how common interests should be protected.
Independent central banks are among the most distinctive institutions modern societies have created. They exercise important powers. Their decisions influence borrowing costs, saving decisions, employment prospects, investment plans and the broad stability of the financial system. Their powers, and how they are used, are always the subject of debate, and that's fair enough given the importance.
Now, there are critics of these arrangements. Some critics argue that central banks disproportionately reflect the interests of financial markets and financial institutions. In a similar, but distinct, spirit others argue that central banks are too detached from the preferences of citizens. These criticisms often differ in their origins and motivation, but they converge on a common question. Why should an unelected institution possess such significant authority?
My purpose today is not just to defend central bank independence, though you can be assured I am happy to do that robustly. Rather, it is to reflect on the deeper intellectual traditions from which it has emerged and to consider what those traditions can tell us about the challenges we face.
When economists explain central bank independence, they often begin with questions about the credibility of policy regimes and their time consistency. These arguments are important. They explain why in many countries independence emerged because governments at crucial times had demonstrated incentives to pursue short-term monetary policies that ultimately undermined economic stability, and to undercook financial stability outside more immediate proximity to a financial crisis.
But they do not fully answer a more fundamental question: why should society trust an institution that operates with a degree of independence from day-to-day political control? To answer that question, it is useful to look further back.
One important tradition begins with the French philosopher Montesquieu.footnote [3] Writing in the eighteenth century, Montesquieu was preoccupied with the problem of concentrated power. His great concern was how societies could prevent authority (in that case royal authority) from becoming arbitrary. His answer was that power should be moderated through institutions that stood between rulers and citizens.
Parliaments, courts of law and other intermediary bodies performed this role. They constrained power, not simply through legal rules but because they possessed recognised standing within society. They had identities, traditions and sources of legitimacy independent of those they were intended to restrain. For Montesquieu, these roots mattered. Institutions could not simply be invented and expected to command authority. They required legitimacy that grew over time.
At first sight, modern central banks appear rather different. A central bank derives its authority primarily from legislation. Its independence is granted through statute. It does not rest upon inherited privilege, social rank, or customary authority. Modern central banks are deliberately designed to be technocratic institutions. And yet, the questions Montesquieu asked remain relevant. His central concern was how societies create institutions capable of constraining the exercise of power for the common good. In that sense, the challenge he identified remains with us.
A second intellectual tradition is also relevant. This tradition emerged from English political thought in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and from debates about sovereignty, money and commerce. As David Hume put it, in the seventeenth century commerce, for the first time, became a “reason of state”.footnote [4]
Thomas Hobbes provided one starting point in this development.footnote [5] In the world of Hobbes, the authority to determine the value of money belonged to the sovereign. Just as the sovereign commanded armies and administered justice, so too the sovereign controlled the monetary system of the day, such as it was. Given this overriding concern with political order and stability, for Hobbes dividing authority over money risked dividing authority itself.
But this view was challenged. John Locke argued against the idea that governments should be able to alter the value of money according to political convenience.footnote [6] During the monetary controversies of the 1690s, Locke insisted that arbitrary changes in the value of money damaged trust, disrupted commerce and undermined the public faith upon which economic exchange depended.
This marked a significant intellectual shift. Money was no longer seen just as an instrument of sovereign authority. It became something that served a broader public purpose. Its stability mattered not merely because government or the Sovereign desired it, but because society required it.
David Hume developed this argument further.footnote [7] Hume observed that commerce had become central to the prosperity and strength of nations. Economic life was no longer peripheral to statecraft. It had become one of its defining concerns. Stable money and reliable credit systems became essential foundations for expanding commerce. They enabled people to transact, invest, save and plan with confidence.
In this tradition, monetary stability became a public good. It is from this intellectual lineage that modern central banking most directly emerged. The founding of the Bank of England in 1694 illustrated this evolution, reflecting two powerful forces.footnote [8]
The first was the rapid expansion of trade and commerce. As markets became more sophisticated and more interconnected, the need for a stable and reliable monetary and financial framework grew.
The second was the necessity of financing war. In 1694, England's conflict with France created urgent demands for finance. The arrangement that established the Bank of England enabled private capital to be mobilised in support of public objectives.
One of the interesting points in The Spirit of the Laws is that Montesquieu linked England's financial credibility to its constitutional arrangements (comparing it to France). In England, public credit was not merely a matter of financial technique; it depended on institutions capable of generating public trust. This interpretation is entirely consistent with the quote from Alexander Hamilton.
But the opposite view is also powerful, as set out by John Pocock and summarised by Istvan Hont:-
“The understanding of commerce and commercial society in late seventeenth century England was most advanced by just those thinkers who saw the political health of the English nation as jeopardised by the pervasive corruption that resulted from the intrusion of the demands of the war economy into the sphere of domestic politics.” There was a growing awareness of the distractions which the new of kind of war finance, the running of a huge public debt, might cause to the balance of the English constitution. A political and military regime financed by the public debt implied a danger of the rising in influence of a financier class, which could exercise power without enjoying a proper and legitimate place in the politics of the country.footnote [9]
One way to describe the importance of the growth of commercial societies is to show how they led to the emergence of some of the most profound issues of political economy, namely:

The rise of nation states as economic and commercial agents in their own right;
The need for a properly constituted system of sovereign power to settle internal and external disputes;
The demand for state finance;
The role of justice in economic distribution;
The growth of elaborate divisions among economic interests;
Greater complexity and opacity in the workings of economies; and
The development of tools for authorities to modify the workings of markets, and the risk of a variety of motives for doing so.footnote [10]

These issues remain at the heart of economic policymaking today. The early Bank of England was an important part of the development of commerce. It is however important to recognise that the original Bank of England looked very different from the institution we know today. It was not conceived as an independent guardian of monetary stability. It emerged from a partnership between government and a relatively small and concentrated group of financially sophisticated investors. And, unlike the modern institution, the early Bank was not removed from politics.footnote [11]
The origins of the Bank align as much with Mancur Olson's later analysis of organised interest groups as with any modern idea of an independent public institution.footnote [12] My point is not to criticise those origins. They reflected the realities of the time. But they do remind us that central banking did not emerge fully formed. It evolved gradually as understandings of money, credit, commerce and public authority evolved. Nonetheless, the big themes we wrestle with today were beginning to emerge at that time.
The modern central bank is therefore the product of a long historical process. On one hand lies the Montesquieu tradition, concerned with limiting arbitrary power through institutional checks. On the other lies the tradition of Locke and Hume, concerned with establishing money and credit as public goods upon which society depends.
Modern central banks bring these traditions together. Their essential purpose is to safeguard the stability of money including the resilience of the financial system. These are not interests that belong exclusively to any group. They are public goods from which society as a whole benefits.
The important distinction between the public interest and the public good, as set out by Brian Barry, is important in this respect.footnote [13] Individual citizens naturally have different preferences, priorities, and interests. Democracies exist in part to sort out those competing claims. But some goods are valuable to the public as a whole precisely because they are universally shared.
Monetary and financial stability is one such good. Whatever our views on taxation, spending, regulation or public services, we all operate within a common monetary and financial framework. The value of money is something upon which every household and every business rely. To be effective in the sense of trust and legitimacy in society, support for such a public good should come from the plurality of society rather than any single member group.
This does not mean that monetary policy and financial stability are devoid of distributional effects. Interest rates affect borrowers and savers differently. Financial stability policies can affect sectors and institutions in different ways. Public policy inevitably has consequences that are not distributed uniformly.
But recognising those consequences should not obscure the broader purpose that these policies serve. The objective is not to favour one group over another. It is to preserve the monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible.
In that sense, central bank independence represents a modern adaptation of Montesquieu's thinking. The institution exists not to accumulate or counter arbitrary power but to protect the value of money from short-term pressures that could damage the public interest. But this arrangement also creates an enduring challenge.
Unlike the institutions that Montesquieu had in mind, central banks do not possess deep social roots of their own. Indeed, they must be careful not to become identified with any single interest group. A central bank that became closely aligned with particular sectors or political movements would undermine the very rationale for its independence, and therefore its legitimacy
As John Dunn has argued, this gets us to the issue of the constitutional theory of how power can be institutionalised and thus be implemented effectively in practice. This is the critical relationship between “the constitutional order of power and the pragmatic determination of economic policy”. It’s the modern version of the problem Montesquieu identified and sought to solve. As Dunn notes, constitutional order can appear very settled and continuous, whereas economic policy can appear anything but at times. Writing in the mid 1980s, Dunn argued that a constitutional order which rendered the benign conduct of economic policy more likely than not had not yet been constructed. Solving this challenge has been critical for the legitimacy of modern central banks.footnote [14]
So where does legitimacy come from? The answer, I believe, is now straightforward. Modern independent central banks are not independent of democratic government in the important sense that their authority originates in legislation or the like enacted by elected representatives. In the Bank of England’s case, Parliament defines the objectives, establishes the powers, and retains the authority to amend the framework within which we operate. This role is critical.
This brings me to the contemporary challenge. Across many countries we have witnessed growing scepticism towards public institutions generally. In the case of central banks, as I mentioned earlier, some critics argue they are too close to financial interests and that they stand in the way of popular preferences.
This challenge is not new, but some aspects of it are sharply set out at present, particularly in the area of financial regulation. The argument goes that central bank policies affect the distribution of returns, wealth and welfare directly, which pulls economic interests back into the picture. This concern applies more to financial stability policy than to monetary policy, though monetary policy is not immune from it. One version of the criticism is that the central bank remains too close to financial interests. A central bank's usual response is that the public good of stable money substantially outweighs any distributional effects. But this response can return the argument to Olson's thinking, since the financial world does contain well organised and concentrated interests.
The irony is that central banks can, and today do, face an opposite accusation from the financial interests themselves, who argue that regulation has gone too far. So, criticism arrives simultaneously from two directions that contradict each other.
The fact that criticism can come simultaneously from opposing directions does not prove that central banks are correct. On their own, two perceived wrongs don’t make a right. But it does underline that independence often requires making decisions that do not align with the private interests of any constituency or group, and that at times resisting pressure from the concentrated interests that Mancur Olson identified is part of the task of protecting a public good like the value of money.
A second challenge comes from populist political movements. As Jan-Werner Müller has argued, populism often rests on the claim that a particular political movement alone represents the authentic will of the people.footnote [15] Put thus, the public interest is something that a single ideology can capture and deliver directly. This effectively collapses Barry's distinction between the public interest and the public good.
Any institution seen to get in the way becomes an unrepresentative elite standing between the people and their will, and thus an obstacle to popular sovereignty. This is a serious challenge. We have developed systems of government (in the broadest sense of this term) in which legitimacy rests in the plurality of society, not in the preferences of any single group within it. Courts of law, universities, regulatory bodies and central banks all derive authority through forms of democratic delegation set within a framework of that plural society.footnote [16] Maintaining the trust that goes with that delegation matters deeply.
Central banks cannot take legitimacy for granted. They must explain their decisions clearly. They must engage openly with the public. They must remain accountable to elected representatives for their statutory objectives. In our case that means the Treasury Select Committee of the House of Commons. Through this engagement and accountability, we must demonstrate how our actions serve the public good, in its traditional meaning.
Let me conclude. Institutions that exercise significant authority should expect scrutiny. Such scrutiny is a sign of democratic health. But we should also recognise what is at stake.
Sustained economic prosperity depends upon confidence in the future. Households must be able to spend and save. Businesses must be able to produce and invest. Financial markets must be able to allocate capital efficiently. All of these activities rely upon confidence that the value of money will remain stable including that the financial system will remain resilient.
Those conditions cannot be created overnight. They depend upon institutions that are trusted, durable and credible. Central bank independence does not mean detachment from democracy. It means insulation from short-term political pressures within a democratic framework. Its legitimacy derives from a parliamentary delegation and accountability goes with that independence. It is the basis on which independence legitimately rests.
In our own time, as in previous generations, the challenge is therefore not to weaken that foundation but to strengthen it: through accountability, through transparency, through public engagement and through an unwavering commitment to the public good of sound money that independent central banks exist to serve.
Thank you.

articles.title: Navigating the AI hype cycle: A case for active
articles.text:
Economics and markets

Navigating the AI hype cycle: A case for active

October 21, 2026

Commentary

Regional outlooks

Commentary

Regional outlooks

Commentary by Andrew Shuman, Director of Research, Vanguard Oversight & Manager Search
AI-related capital spending has dominated the U.S. economy and stock market. Investors have hardly had to differentiate between AI’s winners and losers as the rising tide of the data center buildout has seemingly lifted all boats across the supply chain.
Vanguard continues to believe that naively chasing the recent winners of the AI buildout creates a risk of buying high, and that companies outside traditional tech that use AI to improve efficiency and margins represent the next opportunity area. So how can investors position their portfolios for what history suggests could be a forthcoming shift in leadership?

Is semiconductor leadership poised for a shift?

Notes: This chart compares rolling three-year returns for semiconductor and semiconductor equipment companies within the Russell 1000 Index with returns for the index as a whole, which are represented by a zero baseline. Semiconductors and semiconductor equipment are as defined by the Global Industry Classification Standard. The Russell 1000 represents the 1,000 largest publicly traded stocks in the U.S.
Sources: Vanguard calculations, based on data from Bloomberg, as of September 30, 2026.

A potential echo of prior technology cycles

Thematic and sector/industry ETFs focused on semiconductors or data center construction have substantially outperformed the broader equity market in recent years (despite a 10.2% decline this month, through October 16).
These ETFs have garnered substantial inflows in the process, perpetuating their momentum. Investors pumped nearly $82 billion into technology stocks in the 12 months through August 2026, according to Morningstar. That was more than three times the net inflows into the next-leading sector, industrials. Given their cyclicality, semiconductor and semiconductor equipment stocks tend to have higher betas and volatility, often experiencing significant drawdowns—as they did in July when falling by more than 12%.
A shift in leadership would echo prior technology cycles, from the buildout of railroads in the mid-19th century to 1990s broadband. New AI-enabled business models may also outperform incumbents, as e-commerce and social media companies built atop the internet did in the 2000s and 2010s.
For investors looking to position portfolios for this potential shift in leadership, value stocks are a natural first instinct. These “old economy” companies that could benefit from AI adoption are disproportionately represented in value indexes. However, depending on the specific index, exposure to potential AI adopters may also bring exposure to companies known as “hyperscalers.” For example, Amazon and Microsoft, which are spending billions of dollars on AI data centers, are now two of the Russell 1000 Value Index’s three largest holdings.
Additionally, the productivity benefits of AI adoption among old economy or value stocks may or may not flow through to equity holders and stock prices. Potential margin gains will depend on management quality, data infrastructure, and competitive advantages. In highly competitive industries where all participants can achieve similar savings using the same AI models, competition may result in passing those savings to customers through lower prices, rather than leading to higher margins.

From hype to reckoning: Where will AI profits accrue?

Talented active managers, when accessed at reasonable costs, could prove their mettle in navigating this environment across both equities and fixed income. As the AI cycle matures and hype shifts to a real reckoning with economic profitability and return on investment, active managers could have wide scope to add alpha by identifying underappreciated long-term winners within the AI buildout, AI adopters, and AI-enabled disruptors.
Dispersion within individual stocks has widened significantly despite historically normal levels of overall market volatility, creating an ideal backdrop for stock selection.

Greater volatility within individual stocks

Note: This chart compares the Cboe S&P 500 Constituent Volatility Index (VIXEQ), which measures the implied volatility of individual stocks within the Standard & Poor’s 500 Index, with the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), which measures the implied volatility of the S&P 500 over the next 30 days.
Source: Bloomberg, as of October 8, 2026.

Likely winners and losers among the hyperscalers

History suggests that the trillions of dollars being poured into building out AI data centers could result in overcapacity that leads to broadly disappointing profits and stock returns, but it’s still likely there will be winners and losers among the hyperscalers. To some degree, the market has already baked in some of this risk, with valuations sitting around 20 to 25 times expected earnings.
Active managers can add alpha by identifying the hyperscalers that:

Offer the best potential return on investment based on their ability to build products for both consumers (such as internet search and personal agents) and enterprises (such as cloud computing).

Can deliver these products efficiently and at low cost.

Maintain strong balance sheets as they increasingly tap both public and private credit markets for capital.

Further, understanding how these hyperscalers will adapt their data center construction to work around bottlenecks and integrate leading-edge technologies to lower costs will be key to identifying the sustainable winners in the supply chain of semiconductors and industrials—versus companies enjoying shortage-driven pricing power that is likely to prove transitory.
Among AI adopters seeking to use the technology to improve efficiencies, active managers can use their knowledge of management teams, proprietary data, and industry dynamics to identify sustainable winners. This may become more important as AI token costs fall. Previously, larger companies with the biggest budgets had a clear advantage in adopting AI. As costs decrease and the ability to experiment increases, value could accrue to smaller companies with more nimble cultures and management teams willing to disrupt their existing business models.
Last but not least, active managers can seek to identify the new growth companies with business models built atop AI that are either still private or represent only very small weights in cap-weighted indexes. This is akin to investing in e-commerce or mobile internet companies whose business models would not have been possible without the dot-com bubble’s expansion of broadband internet. Ultimately, these were the most successful companies and stock market investments of that era and now sport multitrillion-dollar market capitalizations.
Active managers able to identify the Amazons and Googles of the 2030s may be well positioned to deliver attractive returns to their shareholders.

articles.title: Changes to provisions approaching the finish line
articles.text:
This article has been updated in October 2026 to reflect the decisions the IASB has made in response to the feedback received on its 2024 proposals to amend IAS 37. The related guide has not been updated and reflects the original proposals only.

Highlights

– When do you recognise a provision?– Will IAS 37 provide specific guidance for levies?– Which costs do you include in measuring a provision?– Which discount rate do you use when discounting a long-term provision? – What’s next?

With companies facing ongoing uncertainties and complexities, accounting for provisions – particularly when to recognise a provision and at what amount – has come to the fore.In 2024, the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) issued proposals to revise IAS 37 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets*. These proposals could result in a company recognising provisions earlier and for larger amounts.In response to feedback on the proposal to withdraw IFRIC 21 Levies, the IASB has decided to introduce specific guidance for levies in IAS 37. It has also clarified how the 2024 measurement proposals would apply.The IASB is planning to release the final amendments in the first half of 2027, so companies need to get ready for the forthcoming changes.

Provisions is a foundational standard, and many tend to interpret it through the lens of their local GAAP. The IASB’s project on provisions is approaching the finish line. Once finalised, the amendments would help drive consistency and clarity in financial reporting, especially in times of heightened uncertainty.

Irina Ipatova,

Associate Partner, International Standards Group (ISG)

KPMG International

When do you recognise a provision?

One of the challenging questions in applying IAS 37 is when to recognise a provision – specifically, how a company determines if it has a present obligation and what a ‘past event’ is. These questions became more prominent with the rise of climate-related commitments and threshold-based obligations. The proposals to amend IAS 37 include:three new tests to determine whether a present obligation exists; andspecific guidance for threshold-based obligations.What does this mean for companies? The impacts of these changes could be significant for some, depending on the nature of their obligations and existing accounting policies.Under the proposals, companies may need to start recognising some provisions sooner and over time. New judgements may be required.

Will IAS 37 provide specific guidance for levies?

Yes, IAS 37 will provide specific guidance for levies. The guidance will explain how to apply the three new tests and will differ from IFRIC 21.Under the new guidance, the timing of recognition for some levies – especially those that are payable only if multiple conditions or thresholds are met – may change. At present, a company recognises such a levy only when the last activity occurs. Under the new guidance, it would need to apply judgement to determine which activity the government is seeking to levy. The timing of that activity would drive the timing of recognition for the levy.

Which costs do you include in measuring a provision?

IAS 37 provides no specific guidance on which costs to include in measuring a provision. Therefore, companies’ approaches vary depending on the nature of the provision and their accounting policy.Based on the feedback received on the proposals, the IASB clarified that a company would measure a provision depending on how it would settle the obligation.For obligations to transfer cash only (e.g. to settle a legal claim), a company would include the cash amount.For obligations to transfer goods or services (e.g. to engage a third party to perform decommissioning works), a company would include all direct costs, comprising:
incremental costs; andan allocation of other costs that relate directly to settling the obligation. This may result in some provisions becoming larger.

Which discount rate do you use when discounting a long-term provision?

In applying IAS 37, the approach to determining the discount rate for long-term provisions varies between companies – i.e. some use a risk-free rate; others adjust the rate for non-performance or their own credit risk. Based on the feedback received on the proposals, the IASB will proceed with the proposed requirement to use a risk-free discount rate when measuring a long-term provision. Depending on the company’s current accounting policy, some provisions may become larger.

What’s next?

The IASB is planning to release the final amendments in the first half of 2027, so companies need to get ready for the forthcoming changes.

articles.title: Daily: AI fundamentals remain robust despite market volatility
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioPodcast: Jump Start | Earnings season in focus (5 mins)Podcast: Across the Pond: Europe’s bond stress test, on Apple , Spotify (22 mins)Video: Investors Club: Managing inflation, UST yields, and tech pressure (6 mins)Video: The AI Show |The AI trade's two-sided test (4 mins)Video: Data with Donovan | The Fed's rate path ahead (5 mins)Thought of the dayStocks of major neoclouds, specialized AI cloud computing infrastructure providers, came under intense pressure last week as investors questioned their growth models amid the prospect of higher-for-longer interest rates. These concerns helped drive a 4.5% decline in the Nasdaq, its biggest weekly loss since June. Competitive risks from China and worries over revenue growth at leading AI labs also contributed to the weakness.But the pressure on neoclouds does not undermine the broader AI investment cycle. Financing and execution risks are rising, but recent semiconductor results and GPU rental prices suggest that demand for AI compute remains robust. In our view, this supports the broader AI growth story.Neoclouds and hyperscalers have very different growth models. Neoclouds are single-product, AI-first infrastructure providers focused on renting GPU compute capacity. They therefore generally require substantial upfront investment before contracted revenue translates into cash flow. While hyperscalers are increasingly tapping debt markets to fund their AI buildout, their general-purpose cloud platforms offer a broad range of services and more diversified revenue streams. We believe hyperscalers’ cost of debt also remains manageable at 6.5-7%, particularly given that the return on invested capital from their new data center investments is around 25% or higher.The impact on overall AI-related expenditures should be limited, as compute supply remains constrained. We estimate AI capex will grow 33% to USD 1.2tr in 2027, with neoclouds accounting for less than 10% of this investment. While a further significant increase in funding costs could pose a risk to this segment of the AI buildout, the credit quality of many neocloud customers and the volume of advance orders should offer some relief. More importantly, GPU rental prices have continued to rise, pointing to robust demand for AI compute capacity amid supply constraints. The latest data show that rental rates for four-year-old GPUs have risen 7% over the past month, bringing the year-to-date increase to nearly 30%. Rates for two-year-old GPUs, meanwhile, have risen 35% so far this year.Resilient 3Q earnings should reinforce confidence in AI fundamentals. Both ASML and TSMC posted positive quarterly results last week, with an encouraging outlook for the industry. TSMC said demand remains robust and expects its aggregate capital expenditure in 2026-28 to be meaningfully higher than in 2024-26, while ASML highlighted strong order intake for 2028, with interest extending into 2030. Without taking a view on individual companies, we think these results provide further evidence that AI demand remains strong and continues to grow. We also expect incoming results from hyperscalers to show accelerating cloud revenue growth.So, we maintain our positive outlook on the structural growth of AI, while acknowledging that funding and execution risks could reinforce each other across the AI infrastructure ecosystem. Tighter credit could constrain deployment, while delivery delays could postpone the cash generation needed to service debt.For investors, this backdrop calls for a selective approach. We continue to limit exposure to neoclouds amid funding and construction pressures, instead favoring well-funded hyperscalers for their better risk-reward. We also like high-quality semiconductor and hardware beneficiaries of AI spending, and think investors should consider exposure to defensive areas of tech such as payment networks, select consumer electronics names, and select software companies.

Your wealth, your vision – expertly managed. Discover flexible strategies, tailored solutions and global insights to help you invest and manage your wealth with confidence.

Who we are

Deutsche Bank Wealth Management is a leading global wealth manager with a long‑standing presence across key markets, supporting clients worldwide. It is part of Deutsche Bank’s Private Bank, which has more than 700 billion euros in assets under management*.

How we work with you

Investment expertise, aligned with your objectives

We work with you to understand your goals and can build a tailored solution based on Deutsche Bank’s Chief Investment Office views. You can benefit from expert guidance and a disciplined, forward-looking approach with a global perspective – locally executed – as you invest and manage your wealth.

Strategic asset allocation, finding the right mix for your portfolio

To give yourself the best chance of achieving your investment goals, using strategic asset allocation to find the right mix of asset classes in your portfolio is essential.

Effective asset allocation strategies are those that take enough risk to give your portfolio the potential to grow, but not so much that you feel uncomfortable – and therefore more likely to withdraw funds at the wrong moment.

Getting this balance right, and maintaining it for the long term, can be costly and complex. This is why our robust approach to strategic asset allocation is designed to maintain your core portfolio as efficiently as possible.

A modular approach to investing, reflecting your goals

Our active, modular approach to investing blends our core discretionary solutions with advisory opportunities.

Deutsche Bank can create a portfolio that reflects your goals, combining potential market opportunities with leading solutions from our discretionary platform, including our flagship strategic asset allocation strategy.

Our modular investment approach weaves together core strategic allocation with complementary, thematic, high conviction, and liquidity solutions – creating a flexible framework tailored to your individual goals.

Working towards your long-term success

We aim to ensure your portfolio is structured to meet both long-term goals and short-term liquidity requirements.

articles.title: Daily: Strengthen portfolio defenses as volatility rises
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioPodcast: AI demand remains the signal amid neocloud noise, on Apple , Spotify (6 mins)Podcast: Across the Pond: Europe’s bond stress test, on Apple , Spotify (22 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Why bank stocks are falling amid rising rates (6 mins)Video: The AI Show |The AI trade's two-sided test (4 mins)Video: Data with Donovan | The Fed's rate path ahead (5 mins)Thought of the dayBrent crude oil hit USD 112/bbl for the first time since May and is on track for a third consecutive week of price gains as fresh attacks in the Middle East have heightened concerns about further disruptions to energy supplies. Since the start of this month, Brent crude has risen 9.4%.Saudi Arabia reported attacks on an Aramco oil field and an airport in its Eastern Province, while the US ordered diplomats to leave the country amid Houthi strikes. Separately, the New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries had developed specific plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the US midterm elections, which take place on 3 November.With the Russia-Ukraine conflict also continuing, geopolitical risks are unlikely to subside in the near term, keeping inflation concerns elevated and adding to macroeconomic uncertainty.But geopolitics are not the only factor driving market performance. Resilient economic growth, robust corporate earnings, and strong AI demand continue to underpin equity gains. Our view remains that investors should focus less on the possibility of short-term drawdowns associated with geopolitical events and more on ensuring that their portfolios can withstand periods of volatility.History suggests that geopolitical shocks are rarely a sufficient reason to stop investing. Since 1941, the S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after the start of a geopolitical crisis roughly three-quarters of the time. For diversified portfolios, the long-term cost of remaining uninvested has often proved greater than the temporary cost of living through a geopolitical drawdown.The global energy system should continue to adapt to the disruption. While still below its pre-war levels, OPEC crude production rose by 0.92 million barrels per day in September to 25.1 million, or around 85% of February’s output, according to the group’s latest Monthly Market Report. Trade routes are also shifting, while the G7 decision to release additional emergency oil stocks should provide some temporary relief. Together, these developments demonstrate the global oil market’s ability to respond to disrupted supplies. We acknowledge that the physical oil market remains tight and is vulnerable to further supply shocks, but our base case is that a gradual recovery of energy flows and production should allow oil prices to moderate into next year. This means that the impact of higher energy prices on the global economy should remain insufficient to derail growth.Exposure to commodities can help manage volatility. Instead of retreating from markets, investors can use energy exposure to insulate portfolios against such supply-driven volatility and boost diversification. In fact, we think investors should consider broad commodities as a differentiated source of return, especially as rising power demand, AI infrastructure investment, electrification, and constrained supply are supportive of an upcycle. Historically, commodities have exhibited low correlations with traditional asset classes, and we think an actively managed approach can help investors navigate across the commodity complex.So, we retain a constructive market outlook and believe investors should stay invested for further equity gains via broadly diversified exposure across sectors and regions. We also believe investors can strengthen their portfolio resilience by incorporating fixed income, broad commodities, and select alternatives according to their risk tolerance, liquidity needs, and financial objectives.

The State Of Chinese AI

Arthur Kroeber, Laila Khawaja

Gavekal Technologies: Briefing | 19 Oct 2026

The AI world suffered tremors last week, as doubts began to surface about the frontier labs’ revenue growth and the rising amount of high-priced debt used to finance the US’s data center building binge. The risks raise a question: when and if the American AI bubble pops, can China race ahead? Probably not. China’s AI ecosystem is impressive and evolving fast. But it is not positioned to overtake the US any time soon, even if American labs and hyperscalers hit serious speed bumps. This note assesses four features of China’s AI industry: the open-weight ecosystem, data, electricity and talent. articles.title: The Ultimate Contrarian Trade?
articles.text:
The Ultimate Contrarian Trade?

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 21 Oct 2026

French generals are said to spend their lives fighting the last war (i.e. the Maginot Line and all that…). The same could probably be said for European Union policymakers. Take the recent measures adopted by the EU to limit the sale of Chinese hybrid vehicles into Europe as an example (see The Cost Of Protection). On the face of it, this embrace of protectionist measures might seem to be in the “spirit of the age.” After all, today is supposed to be an age of “deglobalization” and of “great power rivalry”; an era of “reshoring” manufacturing production, and blocking of Chinese imports. However, how sustainable will such policies prove to be over the medium to long term?To answer this question, we will make like a Jesuit priest and answer with another question: specifically, what is likely to become the first concern of elected officials across most of the Western world in the coming months, quarters and years? Let me suggest this: it will be the rising cost of funding of government debt.

Trust Funds and Partnerships
Partnerships are foundational to the World Bank’s work and vital to realizing the goal of ending poverty on a livable planet. Trust Funds, Financial Intermediary Funds, and Co-Financing arrangements help the World Bank provide flexible and customized development solutions to help clients.

About

The complexity and urgency of the world’s challenges require meaningful collaboration among members of the development community and other stakeholders if the goal of ending poverty on a livable planet is to be realized. With overlapping crises threatening global development and a growing global demand for a bold and coordinated response to these crises, the World Bank is working to strengthen partnerships and utilize every resource available to maximize development impact.The Bank works with a growing array of development partners, both traditional and non-traditional, formal, and informal, to help meet our shared goals. From the ongoing partnership with our sovereign donors, through engagement with foundations and civil society, to an increased focus on leveraging private capital, the Bank recognizes how transformative partnerships can be when new ideas, perspectives, and experiences are combined with the necessary financial resources.Development partners work with the Bank through trust funds, financial intermediary funds, and co-financing arrangements:to align and pool funding support with other development partners within agreed strategic frameworks.to benefit from the Bank’s convening power, at both the international and country level, to maximize coordinated action and achieve impact at scale.to benefit from the Bank's extensive technical expertise, country experience and supervision capacity, its financial control framework, and its ability to monitor and report on results.to provide grant funding in fragile, conflict-affected, and other complex situations enabling the Bank to engage and provide critical assistance in circumstances where traditional instruments are not well-suited.to support innovative or emerging policy areas, which the Bank and Partners view as a priority.Trust FundsThe World Bank uses trust funds, a financing arrangement set up with contributions from one or more development partners, to complement core funding from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), and the International Development Association (IDA) to help attain its institutional goals. Trust funds support the achievement of these goals by providing financial resources, contributing to the knowledge agenda, and leveraging the Bank’s convening power and global and local presence to contribute to country, regional, and global development. Trust funds allow the Bank to mobilize and direct concessional resources to strategic development priorities and to mobilize the resources and capabilities of other development actors through partnership programs.Financial Intermediary FundsFinancial Intermediary Funds (FIFs) are financial arrangements that leverage a variety of public and private resources in support of international initiatives, enabling the international community to provide a direct and coordinated response to global priorities. FIFs are a key financing arrangement for the World Bank, where the Bank acts as a trustee of large multilateral financial mechanism to support global development initiatives and partnerships. As a FIF trustee, the World Bank provides financial services, including receiving, holding, and investing contributed funds, and transferring them when instructed by the FIF governing body.Co-FinancingCo-financing is an important financing mechanism of the World Bank. The World Bank works with Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs), bilateral agencies, and other development partners to allow funds to flow directly from co-financers to the recipient client country and finance activities within the scope of a World Bank operation. Under these arrangements, World Bank resources and third-party resources are deployed in a coordinated manner to World Bank operations that are led by the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) or the International Development Association (IDA).

articles.title: PHPeril: Never Send a Human to Do a Machine’s Job
articles.text:
Insights / Research / PHPeril: Never Send a Human to Do a Machine’s Job

Written by:

Thaddeus Pinakiewicz
Vice President, Research

Topics

AI

research • October 23, 2026

PHPeril: Never Send a Human to Do a Machine’s Job

This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter. Subscribe to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning. Find our past reports and newsletters at galaxy.com/research. Send feedback to research@galaxy.com.WHAT HAPPENEDThe team maintaining scripting language PHP rushed out emergency patches Wednesday for two decade-old bugs that let anyone on the internet run code on millions of servers without permission. The rest of the internet spent the day discovering how many other things were also on fire.The bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, affect nearly every PHP version back to 5.4 (released in 2012). PHP quietly holds up WordPress, Drupal, Magento, and by some estimates, around 70% of the web. Cybersecurity firms Wiz and Calif found the bugs with help from OpenAI, and OpenAI says Calif found the bug with GPT-5.6 Sol, a generally available model. The plan was a tidy coordinated disclosure, and everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth. Details leaked, Amazon's honeypots logged an exploit attempt four days before the disclosure, and Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince reported thousands of exploit attempts in the 10 hours before the patch release and millions by the evening.The NSA and FBI told organizations to go offline if they couldn't patch, Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi urged site operators to act that night, Finland and several other European governments pulled sites preemptively, and the St. Louis Fed's FRED site went dark. PHP was merely the headliner. This week's full lineup of cyber scares included a CVSS 10.0 GitLab bug, Railway pausing all deployments after someone got into its environment-variable store, Node.js patches, Plex servers exploited to mine crypto, SafePay ransomware, and eMudhra, an Indian certificate authority whose private keys were small enough to guess. One of them was the number 4. (Yes, that was the whole private key; easy to remember, but...)OUR TAKEThe most worrying part of this story is that this internet-breaking exploit didn't come from those scary frontier models. The PHP Foundation worked with outside firms to scan its code with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos this year, but this exploit was only discovered in early August as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program. Even more shockingly, the exploit was discovered using GPT-5.6 Sol, a model you can pay for today, not one of the unreleased or cyber-specialized variants the labs keep caged up like a James Bond supervillain. Despite earlier testing with Claude Mythos, the vulnerability was identified through separate research using other AI models. Instead, it took a researcher’s intuition guiding a commodity model, and attackers have both.The pace at which attackers tried to utilize the exploit is like nothing ever seen before. That is the new norm. Announcing a patch in advance is supposed to get administrators ready, but it also fired a starting gun for every bad actor racing to find the bug before the fix landed. That tension between preparing defenders and tipping off attackers was always delicate, and with more cyber-capable open AI models around, the announcement window will continue to compress toward zero. Threat intel and incident response firm Mandiant already puts mean time-to-exploit at negative seven days; attackers typically strike a week before a patch exists. The zero-day clock has struck midnight, and had an integer overflow as it kept going. What this means is that human-only cybersecurity is truly obsolete, and untenable. Security in an agentic world must also be agentic; Hugging Face was the preview in July, breached by OpenAI’s own models during testing, and this is the new reality with broad access to capable coding agents. Machine-speed attackers need machine-speed defenders."Zion, hear me! It is true, what many of you have heard. The machines have gathered an army and as I speak, that army is drawing nearer to our home." – Morpheus ... or your dramatic IT security lead during an all-handsYou should be a little scared, I am. A lifelong nerd, I ran a personal server in high school, and in the late 2000s I had to learn some security practices because my little experimentation box was getting bombarded by automated SSH password-guessing, port-scanning, and general exploit attempts a full decade before the first GPT paper in 2018. The spiders were already probing everything. LLMs cranked that dynamic up to 11, then ripped the knob off. I turned off my home server on Wednesday and unplugged most of my IoT devices until I have time to use the best available model to help me patch, replace, or reflash each one. If I write something testy about the DPRK, should I worry about them flipping my smart switches until something shorts? Do I have to root my Roomba to keep it from being taken over and trying to boop the power button on my PC? Most IoT software is forgotten after creation (when did you last patch your smart fridge?), and Anthropic's red team just ran a 26-billion-parameter model across 15 $55 Android TV boxes. With a long tail of vulnerable devices, botnets of hacked devices may graduate from DDoS attacks to distributed inference for whoever controls them.All software stacks have been non-consensually thrown into the Thunderdome, but this is only the beginning of the battle. More exploits are coming, probably worse ones, but every serious patch and every agent-reviewed release strengthens the code the world runs on. A more secure internet is being born from its parents' death, like the Olympians descending to overthrow the Titans.Some code is already ready for that world. Bitcoin Core is among the most heavily reviewed codebases on earth, and no comparable compromise has been reported. Most of these exploits exist because no human can hold an entire codebase in their head; almost nothing outside TempleOS was written by one person, and even that wouldn't guarantee spotting every step of an exploit chain. Agents, with long context and a shared, eidetic memory, can do the comprehensive reviews that human teams struggle with.Modern cryptography held: nobody broke the algorithms the internet relies on. eMudhra fell on its face generating keys, not at math. At the peak of the panic, I recommended that our clients verify instructions by signing from their wallets, an additional safeguard against compromised intermediaries.Security through obscurity is finished. There will be a culling of unmaintained websites, projects, and blockchains. It is not going to be pretty, but what survives will be an internet worth trusting. Just don't make your private key 4. Educate yourself, protect yourself; it is going to get more dangerous before it gets safer. Put on your helmets, man the trenches with your agents, and hold the line. Don’t give the clankers an inch.

articles.title: Why Canada can be AI’s democratic superpower | RBCCM
articles.text:
Canada has the talent, technology, expertise and democratic values to be a global AI superpower – offering the world an alternative to U.S. and Chinese dominance, according to the latest episode of the Disruptors podcast.
The country has already played a foundational role in the emergence of AI, through the work of Canadian “AI godfathers” Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, and as the founding home of organizations such as Cohere.
And, as global demand surges for a diversified technology supply chain, Canada – with its frontier-model LLM and its AI strategy committed to “trust, opportunity and sovereign control” – can become the “global champion” of AI development and deployment that is safe, fair and benefits all.
Canada’s approach advocates greater safeguards to ensure appropriate vulnerability tests can place alongside increasingly fast development cycles; uniform access to the most powerful tools – so everyone can defend their organizations at the same time – and the reimagining jobs rather than a destruction.

"At the moment, we see differentiated access. U.S. firms are getting selective access to the most powerful tools, while others aren’t. The world needs to think about sovereign frontier capabilities and a safe AI ecosystem."
Dave McKay, President & CEO, Royal Bank of Canada

This episode was originally published on Disruptors, an RBC podcast, on September 16, 2026. For more information, visit Disruptors podcast.

articles.title: Celebrating 20 years of the World Bank Enterprise Surveys: Insights from the first complete global cycle, 2023-2026
articles.text:
Published on
Data Blog

Celebrating 20 years of the World Bank Enterprise Surveys: Insights from the first complete global cycle, 2023-2026

Eugenia Rodríguez

Cierra Wells

Mohammad Amin

October 23, 2026

This page in:

English

English

The 2023–2026 World Bank Enterprise Surveys cover 164 economies, providing the first complete global cycle of comparable firm-level data on productivity, innovation, jobs, and the business environment. / Image: Shutterstock

Twenty years ago, the World Bank Group began asking firms simple yet powerful questions: How do firms experience the business environment in which they operate? What does it take to run a business? On May 20th, 2026, the World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES) marked two decades of doing exactly that while achieving a historic milestone: for the first time, the globe was covered in a single three-year cycle; the 2023–2026 database now spans 164 economies across every continent.
The anniversary brought together experts, researchers, and policymakers to discuss what enables firms to innovate and grow — a question the WBES has been uniquely positioned to answer since 2006. With more than 470 surveys conducted across more than 180 economies and nearly 300,000 interviews with business owners and top managers, the program has built the world's most comprehensive and freely accessible source of firm-level information on the business environment. By going directly to firms, the program captures what traditional indicators often miss: how businesses adopt new technologies, respond to competition, hire workers, and navigate their operating environment, revealing which conditions are most closely linked to innovation, productivity, and job creation.
Twenty years of consistent, comparable data have also made it possible to track genuine progress — or regression — across economies over time. The impact speaks for itself: WBES data have informed more than $90 billion in World Bank Group programs, supported over 1,300 peer-reviewed studies, provided key performance indicators for the Sustainable Development Goals, and been featured in major international analyses such as the World Economic Forum's Gender Gap Report. The data now also serve as a foundational input into the World Bank's Business Ready flagship report, helping to shape the next generation of private-sector reform.
What can we learn from the first complete global cycle (2023-2026) of our Enterprise Surveys data? Here, we highlight three findings on differences in firm performance across economies, the factors associated with innovation and productivity, and the outcomes of innovative activity.

Figure 1: WBES data coverage in 2023-2026, 164 economies

1. Higher-income economies innovate more and have a more even distribution of productivity across firms than lower-income economies.
Firms in high-income economies are not only more productive on average but also show less productivity dispersion. As shown in Figure 2, the most productive firms in low- and lower-middle-income economies are 5.9 times more productive than the least productive firms in those economies. That ratio declines to 4.1 in upper-middle-income economies and to 2.8 in high-income economies. Lower-income economies, therefore, face not only lower average productivity but also greater internal dispersion, a pattern consistent with resource misallocation and market inefficiencies that can constrain aggregate productivity and growth.
Innovation follows a similar pattern. Only 16 percent of firms in low- and lower-middle-income economies report introducing a new product or process in the past three years, as defined by the Oslo Manual, compared with 23 percent in upper-middle-income economies and 28 percent in high-income economies.
Together, these findings underscore a broader lesson from Enterprise Surveys data: firm performance is closely tied to the environment in which firms operate. Economies with stronger regulatory and institutional frameworks tend to foster innovation and spread productivity gains more broadly across firms, whereas weaker business environments often concentrate economic dynamism among a relatively small group of high-performing firms.

Figure 2: Dispersion in labor productivity by income groups

2. Better management is associated with more innovation, and aggregate gender gaps can be misleading.
The breadth and depth of the WBES data allow us to examine many factors associated with firms' capacity to innovate. One of the most important is management quality. A 10 percentage point improvement in the WBES management quality index is associated with a 3 percentage point increase in the likelihood of innovation. This relationship is even stronger in more complex regulatory environments, where the association rises to 4 percentage points, compared with just 1 percentage point in less demanding regulatory settings. These findings suggest that strong management practices may be particularly valuable in helping firms adapt, identify opportunities, and maintain the organizational capacity needed to innovate.
WBES data also reveal a more nuanced picture of gender and firm performance than simple comparisons often suggest. As shown in Figure 3, overall differences between men- and women-led firms can mask important underlying patterns. Women-led firms tend to demonstrate stronger management practices and maintain comparable overall performance despite operating in more challenging environments shaped by regulatory, institutional, and socio-cultural constraints. In other words, their performance reflects resilience in the face of additional barriers rather than the absence of them.

Figure 3: Overall gender gaps can be misleading

3. Innovation is associated with more jobs and greater resilience to informality.
The data reveal meaningful differences in outcomes between innovative and non-innovative firms. Firms that introduce product or process innovations are associated with 1.3 percent higher employment growth, a pattern that holds across all income groups. Other growth-oriented activities — including investment in fixed assets (3.1 percent), quality certification (3.0 percent), and adoption of foreign technology (2.9 percent) are associated with even larger employment gains, suggesting that innovation is part of a broader set of firm capabilities linked to growth.
Innovation is also associated with greater resilience in the face of informal competition, a persistent challenge in many developing economies. As shown in Figure 4, non-innovative firms facing informal competition experience a 17 percent decline in labor productivity, compared with 11 percent among innovative firms. While informal competition is associated with lower productivity for all firms, the productivity penalty is substantially smaller among firms that innovate.

Figure 4: Innovation can act as a shield from informal competition

These findings offer only a glimpse of what comparable, representative firm-level data can reveal. All WBES data are publicly available through the WBES website, where users can access economy-level indicators, and through the WBES data portal, which provides both economy-level and cross-economy databases for deeper exploration.
As the global development agenda grows more complex, the value of listening directly to firms — consistently, comparably, and at scale — remains as relevant as ever. Understanding what firms experience, what shapes their performance, and what enables them to grow can inform better policies and more effective programs that support a thriving private sector. As WBES marks its twentieth anniversary, it does so with the most comprehensive picture of the global private sector it has ever assembled and a continued commitment to expanding that knowledge base.
The central premise of the Enterprise Surveys remains unchanged: firms themselves are among the best sources of information about the opportunities and obstacles that shape economic development. As WBES enters its next decade, that perspective will remain essential for understanding how economies can foster innovation, create jobs, and build more productive and inclusive private sectors.

Eugenia Rodríguez

Economist, World Bank

articles.title: The Fandom Effect: Sports Urbanism 2026
articles.text:
Consulting Report

19 Oct 2026

The Fandom Effect: Sports Urbanism 2026

How Sports, Place, and Civic Joy Can Reignite Our Urban Centers

As the first phase of a multi-part study of sports-anchored mixed-use districts (SMDs) conducted by Gensler before, during, and following the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Gensler and Oxford Economics surveyed 5,858 people in 17 North American cities to understand their experiences and preferences for sports stadiums and the districts that surround them. Findings were used to establish a pre-tournament baseline to understand engagement and experiences with these venues across the host region.

The results made clear that visiting a stadium has become about much more than the game. Fans travelling from near and far want to take advantage of everything stadiums and their surrounding neighborhoods have to offer, from dining and retail to fan experiences. Visitors often turn a game into a full day out, while avid fans see a stadium not just as a place to watch sports, but as a part of a routine. Additionally, on days without an event scheduled, stadiums have the potential to draw larger audiences through communal events and family-friendly programming. Many avid fans (64%) already make use of these areas, while an overwhelming 94% of those surveyed claim they would make use of the area surrounding a stadium if their preferred programming was in place.

There are also challenges to this expanded use. Lack of safety, limited access due to inconvenient locations, and the rising costs of attendance deter many from becoming frequent visitors to these districts. 85% claim ticket prices have become too expensive, and nearly a fifth (16%) have avoided a venue in the past due to safety concerns.

Learn more about the full study and read The Fandom Effect: Sports Urbanism 2026 here.

articles.title: The Inflation Outlook and the Bond Market Sell-Off
articles.text:
19th October 2026

Written by:

Speakers:

Neil Shearing

Group Chief Economist

Download

Free trial

Get 10 publications of your choice, free for 14 days, no subscription required.Start free trial

Two themes have dominated markets over the past few weeks: the sustainability of the AI investment boom, particularly the debt financing behind it, and the sell-off in bond markets, which at one point earlier this month pushed 10-year US Treasury yields to their highest level since the mid-2000s.We will return to the AI capex boom in a forthcoming piece. For now, while we remain optimistic about AI’s potential to boost productivity, it is becoming harder to see how the returns generated will justify the scale of the investment surge over the past year. That judgement is necessarily uncertain, however, given the difficulty of assessing the technology’s future revenue potential.The outlook for bond yields is more clearly a macroeconomic question. What matters most is the outlook for inflation and, in turn, monetary policy. On this front, the latest data – including hotter-than-expected US inflation figures for September – have been troubling. But, as we set out in our latest Global Inflation Watch, while inflation is likely to rise further in the near term, we expect it to fall back in 2027.Still mainly an energy issueGlobal inflation rose from 2.6% y/y in January to 3.6% y/y in August (the latest month for which we have full data). (See Chart 1.) Chart 1: Global CPI Inflation (% y/y)Sources: LSEG Data & Analytics, Capital EconomicsBut this increase has been driven almost entirely by higher energy prices. In advanced economies, non-energy inflation was actually marginally lower in August than before the Iran war began. (See Chart 2.)Chart 2: Contributions to DM Headline Inflation (% y/y)Sources: LSEG Data & Analytics, Capital EconomicsEnergy prices will continue to push up headline inflation in the months ahead. We forecast that Brent crude will remain around $100pb into early 2027 and, just as importantly, expect refining margins to stay elevated. This will push up fuel inflation, although price caps should limit the impact in Japan and parts of Asia. Higher natural gas prices will also raise household energy inflation across most advanced economies, although not in North America, where gas prices and power generation costs have barely risen this year. Taken together, these pressures are likely to push global inflation to above 4% y/y in early 2027.The outlook beyond that will depend to a significant extent on what happens to global energy prices and, by extension, supplies from the Middle East. Our baseline forecasts assume that Middle East supply gradually improves over the first half of next year, causing Brent crude to fall to $70pb by the end of 2027 and European natural gas prices to decline to €40/MWh. This should bring down both fuel and household energy inflation.There will also be indirect effects. Higher energy costs will feed through into food prices and other energy-intensive goods and services, pushing food inflation to multi-year highs in most developed economies. But these effects should slow, rather than prevent, the decline in headline inflation as energy prices fall.Second-round effects still absentThe more important question for central banks is whether the energy shock generates second-round effects. The concern is that households and firms respond to higher prices by demanding higher wages and raising their own prices, turning a temporary inflation shock into a more persistent domestic problem.We think this risk is relatively low. Although household inflation expectations have risen, economic conditions are very different from those that prevailed during the last energy-driven inflation shock in 2022. Labour markets are less tight, limiting workers’ ability to secure compensatory pay rises. Firms also generally report that demand is not as strong, thus restricting their ability to pass higher costs on to consumers. We therefore doubt that higher inflation expectations will translate into a sustained acceleration in wage growth. This should, in turn, limit both the rise in core inflation and the time it remains elevated.Inflation dynamics will, of course, differ by country. We expect underlying price pressures to remain stronger in the US, partly because of the effect of the AI boom on consumer technology prices. But we expect core inflation to remain below 3% in the major developed economies and fall towards 2% by the end of 2027. Our forecasts for headline inflation are also below the rates implied by inflation swaps over the next two years and, in most cases, below consensus expectations for 2028. (See Chart 3.) The gap is particularly pronounced in China, where we expect the deflationary forces associated with excess capacity to reassert themselves.Chart 3: Capital Economics Inflation Forecast & 2-year Inflation Swap Rate (%)Sources: LSEG Data & Analytics, Capital EconomicsThis brings us back to monetary policy and bond yields. If inflation falls as we expect, central banks will not need to raise interest rates as far as markets currently anticipate. We expect the Fed, ECB and Bank of England to tighten policy over the coming months, but by less than markets are pricing in. (See Chart 4.)Chart 4: Policy Interest Rates (%)Sources: LSEG Data & Analytics, Capital EconomicsTo be fair, the risks to this outlook are skewed in one direction: a deeper or more prolonged disruption to energy supplies from the Gulf would push inflation higher and could force central banks to tighten policy more aggressively. But absent such a development, the recent rise in bond yields looks difficult to justify on the inflation outlook alone.In case you missed itStephen Brown argues that AI-related activity has accounted for just over one quarter of US GDP growth over the past year. This week we are hosting events on everything from Israel’s elections to the outlook for commercial real estate. Sign up here.
