The US consumer has proved more resilient than expected, supported by a constructive employment backdrop, income growth and rising household wealth. But beneath that aggregate strength, behaviour is shifting. Consumers are becoming more selective, and their ability to absorb further inflation is becoming increasingly divided by income.​
In this episode of the Barclays Brief, host Ronnie Wexler speaks with Priya Ohri-Gupta, Head of US High Grade Research and US Consumer Credit Research Analyst, about the state of US consumer resilience and why it is increasingly uneven. ​
They explore the emergence of a two-speed consumer economy, with higher-income households supported by wealth creation while lower-income consumers face greater pressure on their ability to spend. At the same time, consumers across the board are becoming more deliberate about where their money goes, seeking value and trading down.​
Ronnie Wexler and Priya Ohri-Gupta also consider the signals that could point to weakening demand, and how inflationary pressures currently being absorbed by retailers could test resilience into 2027.​
As US consumers become more selective, investors may need to follow suit. With the important holiday spending period approaching, Ohri-Gupta considers the characteristics that could differentiate consumer and retail businesses as spending patterns evolve.​
Listeners can hear more related to this topic:​​

Negative headlines, resilient markets​

US Rates: Higher for longer ​

Do high gas prices change how Americans buy cars? ​

Clients can read more on Barclays Live:​​

State of the US consumer: The consumer who won't quit​

​

Related content

Negative headlines, resilient markets

Higher yields, tighter monetary policy and elevated oil prices haven't stopped markets climbing. Ajay Rajadhyaksha explains why AI investment, earnings growth and consumer resilience still matter most.

Important Content Disclosures
This content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice or a recommendation. Views expressed are those of the speakers and may not reflect those of the firm. Any forward-looking statements are based on current assumptions and subject to risks and uncertainties.​

Transcript

00:00
Ronnie
Hey everybody, it's Ronnie. It's Monday, October 19th, and I'm here in our New York studio with Priya Ohri-Gupta. Priya heads our US High Grade Research team and is also our Credit Analyst on the US Consumer space. With all of the inflationary crosscurrents swirling right now, it felt like the exact right time to get a real time check on the state of the US consumer. So, Priya, welcome to the Brief.
00:22
Priya
Thanks Ronnie, I'm excited to be here.
00:24
Ronnie
It's great to have you here. And the timing is excellent. You recently teamed up with several other groups in Barclays Research, and you wrote a piece that examined the health of the US consumer, and then you titled it ‘The Consumer Who Won't Quit’, which is a great title that I really appreciate. Can you walk us through what is keeping the consumer, in aggregate, so strong?
00:44
Priya
Yeah, Ronnie, in short, it's spending power and it's coming in much higher than we had estimated. So our economic team has identified a few factors that are contributing to this.
First, the employment backdrop remains very constructive. We're adding about 51,000 jobs per month on average.
Second, income developments have been positive since April. So what's contributing to this? One, The Bureau of Economic Analysis has some non-wage components, those are adding about 300 billion of nominal disposable income.
01:19
Ronnie
Wow, that’s a lot.
01:20
Priya
So a lot more money for consumers to spend. And secondly payroll growth has been up 4.1% since April. And that's reasonably covering inflation that's running a little over 3%.
And then finally consumer wealth has continued to build given strong equity market performance. That's up $7.2 trillion in the first half of ‘26.
01:44
Ronnie
Let's hope markets don't perform like they did last week in order to keep that in check. But let's get back to the consumer. They have a lot of choice in this economy. Can you maybe elaborate on some of the choices they're making with these different headwinds that we're all facing?
01:29
Priya
Yeah, Ronnie, I think choice is the right word here. Consumers are not spending on everything. That was a trend we saw post-Covid, but it's definitely shifted. And companies now have to increasingly give them a reason to spend. So what we're seeing is that spending growth on new products is actually outpacing that on essentials and maintenance goods.
Consumers are being smart about where they're shopping, so they're comparing prices in dollar stores to mass merchants, to traditional grocery and online shopping is helping to add to that transparency.
Consumers are buying fewer items, but they're shopping more often. They're looking for deals. They're stretching what they have in their pantries. And we're seeing some of the classic trade down behaviour as well. So, looking for lower price per item switching from branded to private label. Eating at home over eating out at a restaurant. So those are some of the behaviours that we're seeing there.
02:53
Ronnie
So that's interesting. And kind of leads me naturally to my next question, which is higher gas prices. They're so visible. There are obviously a lot of other persistent inflation dynamics associated with that and beyond. You just kind of went through it a little bit, but can we get a little deeper into where this is showing up and what kind of divergence and bifurcation?
03:14
Priya
Yeah, this is really being underpinned by the K shaped economy. So if we think about that, the upper to middle income tiers that are driving the top of the K to the upper right are driving a lot of the spending, supported by greater wealth creation from home prices, equity market growth, as well as higher tax refunds earlier in the year. So as we think about those incomes, households earning over $100,000 per year actually account for nearly 60% of expenditures in the US. So that's really buoying what we're seeing.
And then if we think about lower income households, that's the bottom end of that K. They're seeing a lot more constraint around their disposable income from higher gas prices. So for example, households earning less than $70,000 a year account for only 30% of expenditures, with over two thirds of this spent on essential goods. And they spend about a high single digit percentage of their wallet on gasoline alone. So that's a lot more of their wallet share that goes to gas prices so you're seeing a disproportionate effect on those consumers from what we've been seeing in gas prices this year.
04:27
Ronnie
All right. That's a very good assessment of this two-speed economy. Let's walk into future risk factors. Is the consumer begins to weaken more meaningfully, where are we going to see it? Where will the warning signs show up?
04:40
Priya
Yeah. So I think there's two things that we'll start to see. First is going to be a meaningful pullback in spending. You know right now we're still seeing higher ticket spend on things like cars and travel. And we're about to go into the, you know, important holiday period so we'll start getting updates on that in coming weeks as to whether consumer behaviour is changing or not in terms of spending patterns. The other thing to look out for are higher credit card utilisation or deterioration and delinquency trends, which has also been fine so far.
You know, if we take a step back and think about what factors could lead to some of this. You know, as we talked about, the equity market performance has been really strong. So any hiccups there on a prolonged basis.
05:20
Ronnie
Not last week, but yes.
05:21
Priya
Yes, not last week. You know a continued elevated gas and diesel costs are contributing to higher transportation. So that's inflation risk for manufacturers and retailers. And one of the key questions is really how much of that gets passed on to consumers and how quickly that happens.
So far what we're hearing from manufacturers is that they themselves are starting to pass on prices to the retailers that they sell into. But the retailers are acting like a buffer. So the full effect of those price increases is not yet getting to the consumer.
But we have a Barclays cost tracker and that does suggest that we could start seeing a meaningful uptick in that inflation as we move into early 2027, which could be well ahead of the CPI figures that we're looking at so definitely something to keep an eye out on the horizon.
06:09
Ronnie
Interesting. So why don't we end on what this means for investors? It's obviously complex and multi-variable, but let's think a little bit about which companies will do best in an environment like this and which will struggle. And please help us think about that.
06:24
Priya
Yeah, this is definitely a market to be selective or ‘choiceful’ as consumers are being right now. So if we think about the types of names that our equity team prefers on the specialty retail side, we're looking for companies that have clean inventory, controlled distribution, pricing power and measurable productivity upside. These types of companies would be the off-price retailers, brand owners with scarcity and pricing power, as well as select portfolio and mono brand retailers that have category leadership. So those are going to be the winners there.
And then if we look at broad lines, hard lines and food retailing, you know, the most defensive are going to be your dollar stores. Aftermarket auto parts also have pricing power and some trade down benefits. The grocers are usually seen as a place to hide, but there's some aggressive pricing dynamics. You know, we talked about the retailers acting as a buffer for pricing, getting through consumers so that could be an effect there.
And then home improvement could be an area of gradual improvement. And valuations have become more attractive there. But if we think about home furnishings, that's an area that could see significant margin benefits just given some of the lower tariffs that we're realising this year.
07:31
Ronnie
Priya, thank you so much for joining us. Those are really fantastic insights and I'm sure our listeners will appreciate them.
07:36
Priya
Great. Thank you.
07:38
Ronnie
In summary, US consumers continue to spend, but we argue that beneath the surface they're more selective and increasingly divided by income cohort as we head into year-end for retailers and the holiday season. It's going to be very important to track how this evolves, and it will no doubt leave a lot of opportunities for investors in this space from it all.
Thanks a lot for listening to the Barclays Brief. Please remember to hit subscribe wherever you listen to your podcast. And we'll be back next week.

About the experts

Priya Ohri-Gupta

Head of US High Grade Research and US Consumer Credit Research Analyst

Priya Ohri-Gupta is Head of US High Grade Research and a Managing Director at Barclays. She also has senior coverage of the US High Grade Retail and Consumer sectors. Priya joined Barclays in May 2010 after spending one year in the Bank Supervision group at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Prior to that, she was the Senior Analyst covering High Grade Food, Beverage, Tobacco and Consumer Products at Lehman Brothers. Before moving to Fixed Income Research in 2007, Priya spent seven years in Equity Research, focused on Retail Hardlines at Lehman Brothers and Cosmetics, Household and Personal Care Products at Banc of America Securities. Her team is ranked #1 for both the Investment Grade Consumer Products and Investment Grade Retailing in the annual All-America Fixed Income Research Survey, and has been #1 or #2 since 2011. She holds a BA in Economics and South Asian Studies from the University of California, Berkeley and an MBA in Finance and Management from NYU's Stern School of Business. She is also a CFA charterholder.

Ronnie Wexler

Global Head of Equities Distribution

Ronnie Wexler is the Global Head of Equities Distribution based in New York and a member of the Global Markets Management Committee. Ronnie has more than two decades of leadership experience in the financial services industry. He joined Barclays from NYDIG, where he served as Global Head of Business Development. Prior to this, he spent 19 years at Goldman Sachs where he held several leadership positions across Securities Division distribution, most recently as Partner and Co-Head of Americas Equities Distribution & Execution. In this role, Ronnie was responsible for all client facing functions across execution services, derivatives and research sales. He joined Goldman Sachs in 2001 and was one of the founding members of their Cross-asset Sales desk. Ronnie graduated from Cornell University and serves on the Board of Directors for Teach for America New York.

articles.title: Consumer Checkpoint: Still sizzling
articles.text: David Tinsley Joe Wadford Liz Everett Krisberg Taylor Bowley Vanessa Cook Lynelle Huskey September 2026 Consumer spending remained solid in August. Total card spending per household rose 0.9% month-over-month and 4.5% year-over-year, according to Bank of America internal data. Discretionary services continue to provide a steady foundation for this growth, despite moderation in a few categories. Consumers still appear to be focused on value. Spending at general merchandise and big-box retailers continues to outperform more traditional retailers, as evidenced during the back-to-school season. This suggests households are actively seeking lower-cost alternatives while maintaining spending. Spending and wage growth have largely converged across income groups, though across generations, the largest "K" shape remains among Millennials. Household finances also remain healthy, with credit card utilization declining across most age and income cohorts. Lower- and middle-income households still hold elevated deposit balances across all age groups, suggesting spending should remain resilient. Read our full analysis for a more in-depth look at these trends. Consumer Checkpoint is a regular publication from Bank of America Institute. It aims to provide a holistic and real-time estimate of U.S. consumers’ spending and their financial well-being, leveraging the depth and breadth of Bank of America proprietary data. Any such Bank of America proprietary data is not intended to be reflective or indicative of, and should not be relied upon as, the results of operations, financial conditions or performance of Bank of America. articles.title: Lazard’s Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+)
articles.text:
Lazard’s Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+)

Lazard's Levelized Cost of Energy+ (LCOE+) analysis was originally developed in 2007 to bring clarity to the evolving cost dynamics of various generation technologies at a time when no industry standard approach existed. It remains a widely cited resource grounded in Lazard's extensive industry expertise and client relationships. This year's report explores key aspects of energy generation, energy storage and system-level considerations while reflecting on developments over the past 12 months.

Access the 2026 LCOE+ Report
Lazard's 2026 LCOE+ report highlights that, despite rising and inflationary cost pressures across all generation technologies, renewables remain the most cost-competitive form of new-build generation on an unsubsidized basis (i.e., without tax subsidies). The report also emphasizes that meeting unprecedented power demand will require both a diverse generation fleet and a thoughtful acceleration of permitting and approval processes. At the same time, rising new-build costs and execution challenges have made replacement capacity more expensive and harder to deliver while load growth drives increased utilization of existing assets, improving their marginal cost relative to new-build LCOEs. Storage costs have also risen this year, reversing recent declines.

Access Lazard's 2026 LCOE+ Report

In today's energy landscape, the relevance of data-driven cost analysis has never been greater. The LCOE+ captures a market defined by unprecedented demand growth, rising costs across every generation technology and an intensifying focus on reliability — making objective, real-world benchmarking more critical than ever for the stakeholders, policymakers and investors shaping the industry's future.

George Bilicic
Managing Director

We’ve entered a speed-to-power era—demand is outpacing supply, costs are climbing across every technology, and value is shifting to whoever can deliver capacity the fastest, renewables remain the lowest-cost and quickest to deploy resource, but meeting this moment will require a diverse generation fleet.

Samuel Scroggins
Managing Director

articles.title: Mixed signals, research findings, and policy judgements − speech by Catherine L. Mann
articles.text:
Mixed signals, research findings, and policy judgements − speech by Catherine L. Mann

Given at the Natixis CIB Private Debt Forum

Published on
02 July 2026

Catherine L. Mann highlights how disaggregated data can improve our understanding of trends in headline economic variables. She also examines how volatility in inflation and financial markets has influenced financial conditions. Catherine then explains how research about de-anchoring of inflation expectations and the speed of monetary policy transmission has underpinned her activist policy strategy.

Speech
Introduction
As I think about my recent policy decisions, my assessment has evolved with incoming data and ongoing research. At the start of this year, moderation in price and wage growth, alongside slowing activity, had brought me closer to considering a reduction in Bank Rate. However, since the onset of the conflict in the Middle East, the reemergence of the trade‑off between inflation and activity has led me to place more weight on inflation persistence, shifting my view towards a longer hold, and potentially a need to lean against that risk.
This remains my view, as notwithstanding a sporadic reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, infrastructure rebuilding, future-proofing, and restocking supplies imply that higher energy prices will likely persist. Associated firm pricing reactions are also likely to keep inflation from moderating to the two percent target within the monetary policy horizon. That said, the discussion for today addresses the timing of a hike versus hold decision. The first topic is how an assessment of disaggregated data provides important nuances to the economic picture relative to the headline numbers. The second topic is how key research findings for both inflation persistence and monetary policy transmission inform my policy strategy.
The disaggregated assessment of the data shows mixed signals across key indicators. Realized inflation and expectations differ across households, firms, and financial markets, and have been influenced in the aggregate by fiscal measures. Wage developments differ across the public and private sectors, with further variation across industries. Public sector activity growth continues to outpace that of the market sector, alongside continued government budget overruns, including on account of interest costs. Volatility in both inflation and financial conditions has increased, affecting the degree of restrictiveness as well as the signal-to-noise assessment.
Interpreting mixed and noisy signals is nothing new for central bankers, but it is more challenging in the current environment where more frequent shocks are building on already persistent inflation with embedded second-round effects, amid higher volatility with elevated uncertainty (see Mann 2024b). In this speech, I will evaluate some of these mixed signals, explain how I interpret them and how – in light of research – they have shaped my recent decisions, especially the last one in June, and what they could mean for my monetary policy strategy going forward.
Uncertain underlying trend inflation
Prior to the conflict in the Middle East, inflation – as indicated in the February 2026 Monetary Policy Report – was expected to come down to our two percent target by the second half of 2026. However, that sanguine projection masked the underlying economic patterns, as increases in administered prices and national insurance contributions (NICs), which contributed 0.7 percentage points to the inflation hump in 2025, were assumed to dissipate in Q2 2026. The projected fall in inflation also reflected the energy bills package introduced in the Autumn Budget. The latter accounted for a reduction of nearly 0.25 percentage points to CPI inflation, as Chart 1 shows. Finally, slack in the economy was projected to weigh on inflation through the projected tightening of the fiscal position. The latter two factors underscore the importance of fiscal measures in getting us back to the inflation target.

Chart 1: Contribution of budget measures to deviation from inflation target
Percentage point deviation from the 2% inflation target

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: ‘Administered prices, NICs, and electric vehicle (EV) mileage charge’ includes the estimated direct effects of changes to Vehicle Excise Duty, bus fares, VAT on school fees, and water charges. The NICs component represents Bank staff’s allowance for the effects of the recent increase in employers NICs on CPI inflation. The EV mileage charge component relates to the mileage-based charge on electric vehicles announced in Budget 2025.The ‘Energy budget measures’ bars represent the estimated direct effects of the energy bills package. The ‘Import prices’ bars includes an MPC judgement on the price of tradables (see May 2024 Monetary Policy Report) which has little effect on the profile beyond 2026. The ‘Other’ bars represent other deviations of inflation not attributable to the listed influences including the estimated effects of changes to tobacco and vaping products duties.

Of course, that projection was prior to the US-Israel-Iran war. The economy and our projections have evolved since then. For starters, the conflict resulted in a higher forecast for CPI inflation across all three scenarios presented in the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report. While outturns for price growth – so far lower than expected – continue to reflect lagged pass-through from pre-war moderation in commodity and domestic cost pressures, household inflation expectations have picked up materially since the conflict.
Because inflation shocks are amplified and attention to inflation rises when inflation is elevated – both with thresholds of around 3 to 3.5 percent CPI inflation – inflation expectations could pick up even more (Weber et al., 2025 Opens in a new window; Gaffney and Potjagailo, 2026).footnote [1] Staff research also shows that the latest rise in households’ short-term inflation expectations move back into the non-linear region, even if not quite as far as in 2022 (Buckmann et al., 2025). While the most recent observation of the Citi/YouGov measure of household inflation expectations has decreased from its April peak, it remains within the region of these non-linear dynamics, and both short- and long-term expectations remain elevated relative to historical averages and their pre-Iran war levels.
On the firm side, research surveys reveal that the recent inflationary episode spurred an increase in the share of firms setting prices in response to changes in economic conditions – so-called state-dependent pricing – instead of adjusting their prices at fixed intervals (Bunn et al., 2026a). State-dependent firms increased their prices more quickly when inflation rose but also raised their prices by less relative to time-dependent firms as inflation decreased (Chart 2) as the time-dependent firms’ adjustment caught-up. A higher frequency of price adjustments yields an upside inflation bias as well as more volatile inflation, as prices respond more quickly, more often, and more strongly to positive inflation shocks.

Chart 2: Firm output price growth by price-setting behavior
Own-price growth and expected year-ahead own-price growth, percent

Footnotes

Source: Bunn et al. (2026a).

Notes: Chart depicts trends in own-price growth (solid lines) and expected year-ahead own-price growth (diamonds), split by firms’ price-setting behavior. Firms are split into state-dependent and time-dependent pricing based on each firm’s most recent response to this question (as of April 2026). The series are three-month moving averages, with the latest data up to May 2026. Percentages in brackets denote share of firms using state- and time-dependent pricing.

To get a better understanding about the current conjuncture and prospects for nominal conditions, I look at firms’ responses to the Decision Maker Panel (DMP) survey, particularly the distributions of responses to questions about expected CPI inflation and expected one-year-ahead price- and wage-setting. Following the outbreak of the Iran war, the survey data show that firms’ CPI inflation expectations quickly responded, (left panel in Chart 3). Although the distribution has shifted to the right in the latest quarter (purple) relative to the three months preceding the Iran war (orange), it remains below 2022 (aqua) and is also much less dispersed. This implies that the pattern of firms’ responses does not yet exhibit the same degree of uncertainty about future inflation as it did during the
Russia-initiated inflation surge.
The distribution of firms’ expectations for their own-price growth in the year ahead has shifted modestly to the right, too. This is most apparent for consumer-facing firms and goods producers, while services firms and business-facing companies have adjusted their expectations by less. These changes in firms’ expectations and price-setting behavior are a key ingredient for the evolution of CPI inflation itself.
The DMP survey data also show that some firms have modestly altered their realized prices in recent months, with the distribution for goods-producing firms exhibiting a bit more mass in the right-hand side of the distribution, suggesting that there could be more inflation in the pipeline. Input and output PMIs have also been elevated.

Chart 3: Distributions of firms’ inflation and wage growth expectations
Expected one-year-ahead CPI inflation (left panel) and expected year-ahead wage growth (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: Decision Maker Panel.

Notes: Charts show kernel density plots for expected one-year-ahead CPI inflation (left panel) and year-ahead wage growth expectations for 2022, December 2025 to February 2026 (three months prior to the Iran war), and March 2026 to May 2026. Distributions are weighted by industry and employment shares.

Widening the aperture on potential wage dynamics from the firm-level survey data, current official wage statistics show mixed signals. Despite a continued easing in private sector regular pay growth (left panel in Chart 4), which is now within the Bank staff’s estimates of target-consistent wage growth, whole-economy total pay has not decelerated to the same degree. We therefore continue to see a wedge between the two pay measures, as illustrated by the right panel in Chart 4.
Over the past year, that wedge has largely been driven by stronger public sector wage growth and the impact of bonuses. In recent months, the contribution from the public sector has eased somewhat. Drawing on the evidence from February 2026 Monetary Policy Report on heterogeneity in wage setting, this pattern is consistent with stronger pay growth in sectors characterized by more structured or collective bargaining where inflation and inflation expectations play key roles. This includes the public sector and similar “union-type” segments within the private sector, as well as cost-minimizing firms, which together account for around 80% of private-sector workforce.
Pay settlements have largely been finalized for the year, and there is limited evidence (as shown in Chart 3 above) from firms in the DMP of a pick‑up in what they expect to offer their employees next year. Looking ahead, the risk is that wage pressures are deferred rather than dissipated, particularly if future pay settlements – including in these more collectively bargained segments – are set against the backdrop of higher realized inflation and elevated expectations in the second half of this year.
Furthermore, even if energy prices moderate, the temptation will be to maintain the own- price and wage strategies to partially rebuild margins, which, according to the survey data, have been absorbing the current shock (Bunn et al, 2026b Opens in a new window). All told, distributions are important indicators to evaluate whether inflationary pressures, the wage setting process, and resulting price setting feed into overall inflation.

Chart 4: Regular pay growth and contributions to the wedge between whole-economy and private sector pay growth
Three-months-on-year growth (left panel) (a) and percentage point contributions to the difference (right panel)(b)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Left panel (a) depicts three-months-on-year public and private sector regular pay growth in percent and the range of target-consistent estimates for regular pay growth. Right panel (b) depicts percentage point contributions by bonuses and public sector regular pay growth to the wedge between three-months-on-year whole economy total and private sector wage growth. Latest data: April 2026.

The trade-off re-emerges
Alongside the higher projected paths for inflation in the April Monetary Policy Report is a slower projected pace of GDP growth across all scenarios relative to February (Chart 5). The trade-off between inflation and activity has re-emerged, as I have noted in previous speeches (see Mann 2025a, 2025b).

Chart 5: Real GDP in the February and April 2026 Monetary Policy Reports
Index (2025 = 100)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Aqua line shows the forecast for real GDP from the February 2026 Monetary Policy Report. Orange, purple, and gold lines show the respective forecasts for scenarios A, B, and C from the April 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

While headline GDP growth remains subdued, looking beneath the aggregate number reveals a divergence between the role of public and private sector activity. While GDP growth has recently been primarily driven by market sector output (MSO, right panel in Chart 6), public sector output has grown by around 4.5 percent since Q4 2023, outpacing the cumulative growth of market sector output by around one percentage point (left panel in Chart 6).

Chart 6: Growth in market sector and public sector GDP and their contributions to GDP growth
Cumulative change since 2023 Q4 (left panel) and contributions to change since 2023 Q4 (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: ONS and Bank calculations.

Notes: Notes: The government sector comprises public administration, education, and health, while the market sector comprises all other industries, including agriculture, wholesale and retail trade, accommodation and food services, and other market-based activities. Latest data: April 2026.

Why do I highlight the different growth rates of government and market sector GDP? The MPC’s forecast is conditioned on announced fiscal policy, as reflected in the Office for Budget Responsibility’s (OBR’s) projections. In simple terms, fiscal policy is funded by a mix of public sector borrowing and taxes. As noted in the Bank’s recent Forecast Evaluation Report, “looser-than-expected fiscal policy has […] contributed to there being less spare capacity” (Bank of England, 2026b). As shown in Chart 7, this reflects higher outturns for public sector borrowing than embodied in the OBR’s forecasts, consistent with the OBR’s own forecast evaluation Opens in a new window (Office for Budget Responsibility, 2026 Opens in a new window). Using a structural VAR model, Brignone and Piffer (2026) demonstrate that upward revisions in inflation forecasts following the post-pandemic inflation surge can be attributed to a combination of expansionary shocks on the demand side, revisions to past shocks, and contractionary supply-side shocks. Going forward, the question is whether there will be upside surprises in fiscal policy,footnote [2] which could provide additional support to public sector activity and can have broader implications for productivity, aggregate demand, inflation, and financial conditions.

Chart 7: Successive forecasts and outturns of public sector net borrowing
Public sector net borrowing as a percent of GDP

Footnotes

Source: Office for Budget Responsibility.

Notes: Data shows successive forecasts (grey) and outturns (orange) of public sector net borrowing as a percent of GDP. Latest forecast: March 2026.

Labor market data also show a mixed picture, with implications for the strength of demand. Beneath the rise in headline unemployment in recent years and its projected increase, the dispersion in unemployment rates across industries has also increased. Chart 8 illustrates how unemployment rates across different industries have changed since 2022. The shaded area (aqua) shows that the dispersion of unemployment rates across different sectors has increased since mid-2025, suggesting that unemployment is more unevenly distributed across industries. For instance, the unemployment rate remains higher in accommodation and food services and has risen faster in that industry compared to overall unemployment since mid-2025. By contrast, the professional and technical sectors are closer to the lower end of the distribution of unemployment rates across sectors.
Some of these differences may reflect varying exposure to recent changes in fiscal policy, such as changes to national insurance contributions and the national living wage, as well as sector-specific demand conditions, including exposure to the energy shock. The result is a labor market that is far from uniform, indicating that some industries are more resilient than others, and that headline unemployment may overstate weakness in the labor market. Therefore, demand may be more resilient than projected by the aggregate numbers.

Chart 8: Dispersion in unemployment rates across industries
Unemployment rates by previous industry (percent)

Footnotes

Source: April 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

Notes: Data show ONS estimates of unemployment by previous industry. This measure will not fully capture new entrants to the labor market who do not find a job as they have no previous industry, nor will it reflect the capacity for workers to transition across industries. The shaded area shows the range of industry-level unemployment rates by previous industry over time. Given data limitations and relatively small sample sizes, it can be difficult to draw firm conclusions from changes in these data. These data are not seasonally adjusted. The latest data shown are for the three months to April 2026.

Financial conditions are volatile
I also considered financial conditions in forming my June decision, as has always been the case. Global spillovers, as discussed in one of my speeches last year, have importantly contributed to the volatility of financial market variables, particularly in a small open economy like the UK. That remains the case today (Chart 9).
Looking at the time-varying volatility of asset price factors extracted from a daily structural VAR based on Brandt et al. (2021) Opens in a new window, we see that the Iran conflict has been associated with a material increase in the volatility of international monetary policy factors but also in the volatility in the UK-specific risk factor. In fact, the UK-specific risk factor is now furthest away from its historical normal. By contrast, volatility in the model's macro factors and global risk (which is a flight-to-safety factor) is little changed. This divergence suggests that markets are interpreting the conflict less as a shock to the growth outlook and more as a source of uncertainty about inflation and the associated monetary policy response, as well as perhaps the consequence of the behavior of an evolving investor base in the gilt market, a topic I discussed in my speech on the UK's external exposures (Mann, 2026).

Chart 9: Volatility of asset price factors
Rolling standard deviation of shocks

Footnotes

Source: Mann (2025c), Bloomberg Finance L.P. and Bank calculations.

Notes: The calculations are based on a structural VAR identified using sign and magnitude restrictions following Brandt et al. (2021) Opens in a new window. The model is extended to analyze monetary policy spillovers between the UK and its two most important trading partners and dominant currency blocks, the US and the euro area (as described in Mann (2024a)).

We can also directly observe the increase in financial market volatility in how UK overnight index swap (OIS) curves have evolved since the onset of the Middle East conflict. Following the outbreak of the Iran war, OIS curves have become increasingly volatile, as the widened range in their movements post-conflict (aqua) relative to pre-conflict (purple) in Chart 10 (left panel) shows. During this period, these large increases in OIS rates have been passed-through rapidly into mortgage rates faced by households: interest rates on two- and five-year fixed rate mortgages with a 75% loan-to-value ratio have risen by 87 and 73 basis points, respectively (right panel in Chart 10). The asymmetry in price and wage developments I highlighted earlier – more robust adjustments to upside shocks and relatively slow adjustment to downside shocks – can also be observed in financial markets, as increases in OIS rates pass through to mortgage rates more quickly than do decreases.
As I noted in my 200-word paragraph in the latest MPC minutes, higher financial market volatility acts as a headwind to both consumption and investment. For firms, increased uncertainty around financing conditions raises the hurdle for investment. For households, more volatile inflation can result in uncertainty about future inflation, which tends to encourage precautionary behavior and the maintenance of higher savings buffers (Fischer et al., 2025). At the same time, my preferred measure of financial conditions (see Burr, 2023 Opens in a new window), has not tightened that much. Taken together, just like other parts of the economy, financial conditions are sending mixed signals, too.

Chart 10: Volatility in OIS curves and pass-through to mortgage rates
UK instantaneous forward OIS curves (left panel) and daily quoted mortgage rates and OIS rates (right panel)

Footnotes

Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P., Bank of England and Bank calculations.

Notes: Swathes of UK instantaneous forward OIS curves in the left panel cover an equivalent period of time. Range of moves in OIS curves pre-Iran war (purple swathe) observed from 28 October 2025 until 27 February 2026. Range of moves in OIS curves since the Iran war (aqua swathe) observed from 27 February to 26 June 2026. Right panel shows 2-year and 5-year OIS rates and 2-year and 5-year fixed rate mortgages with 75% loan to value ratios. Latest observation for daily quoted mortgage and OIS rates: 26 June 2026.

Research informs my monetary policy strategy
Against the backdrop of the data and prospects discussed above, two research strands inform my strategy. The first strand emphasizes the importance of leaning against upside risks to inflation to reduce risks of de-anchoring and to ensure that monetary policy remains credible. I’ve discussed research on persistent upside risks to inflation and the consequences in numerous previous speeches.footnote [3] The second research strand emphasizes the speed with which firms adjust their expected pricing strategies and the capacity for Bank Rate decisions to feed through relatively quickly into expectations, firms’ price-setting behavior, and overall inflation, a topic that I addressed last in 2023 (see Mann, 2023a).
Let’s look at what’s new in the first research strand. This research on de-anchoring examines how responsive medium- to long-term inflation expectations are to changes in short-term inflation expectations by regressing the former on the latter alongside a set of control variables.footnote [4] A regression coefficient close to zero indicates firmly anchored expectations – in that case, expectations about inflation in the medium- and long-term are insensitive to short-term fluctuations. By contrast, a coefficient close to one suggests that expectations are de-anchored. Chart 11 shows the analysis for households, firms, and financial markets.
Data from household and firm surveys show an increased responsiveness of their inflation expectations to near-term inflation developments since the Covid pandemic and the energy shock following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, suggesting that these two groups are not firmly anchored (left and center panel in Chart 11). Financial market participants’ expectations are more anchored relative to households and firms, despite the responsiveness of their long-term expectations to short-run expectations being more volatile (right panel in Chart 11). Taken together, these findings point to some erosion in credibility and potential risks of de-anchoring among households and firms.

Chart 11: Responsiveness of medium/long-term inflation expectations to short-term inflation expectations
Regression coefficients (percentage points)

Footnotes

Source: Bank of England/Ipsos Inflation Attitudes Survey, Decision Maker Panel, Market Participants Survey and Bank calculations.

Notes: Household measure shows the slope of 5-year-ahead inflation expectations on 1-year-ahead inflation expectations from the Bank of England/Ipsos Inflation Attitudes Survey. Firm measure shows the slope of CPI 3-year-ahead expectations on CPI 1-year-ahead expectations from the Decision Maker Panel. Financial Markets measure shows the slope of 5-year-ahead inflation expectations on 1-year-ahead inflation expectations from the Market Participants Survey. Shaded areas denote 95% confidence bands.

Staff research has also used the Boosted Inflation Model – a machine learning model based on boosted decision trees that is designed to capture non-linear relationships between a range of indicators and CPI inflation (Buckmann et al., 2025). It can decompose inflation into its underlying drivers, reflecting the price Phillips curve as well as potential drift of that curve. Chart 12 shows the model’s decomposition of predicted inflation relative to the two percent target. The contribution of the trend inflation component (aqua), which comes from elevated household inflation expectations has started to increase since the Iran war, but remains below the levels last seen in 2023 and 2024. Since household expectations can feed into both wage and price developments, this can be a harbinger of second-round effects.
These developments increase upside risks to the inflation process and raise the risk of
de-anchoring, particularly given the extended period of above-target inflation and the increase in inflation volatility. As discussed in Mann (2022), once expectations drift from the two percent target, monetary policy needs to tighten more, to both control expectations and to moderate inflation itself. So, considering this research strand alone would typically point towards a tighter policy stance.

Chart 12: Decomposition of CPI inflation from Boosted Inflation Model
Annualized and smoothed (left) and annualized month-on-month (right)

Footnotes

Source: Buckmann et al. (2025).

Notes: Colored bars show the block-wise predictive contributions to 1-month-ahead annualized month-on-month CPI inflation (white line), around 2% target. Blockwise boosted inflation model estimated via cross-validation over 1989m1-2026m5 sample. Dashed line: CPI inflation, annualized.

What’s new in the second strand of research – the speed of transmission of monetary policy. Evidence points to a relatively more rapid transmission of monetary policy to borrowing costs, but also directly to inflation expectations as compared to what is embodied in most traditional slack-driven models of inflation process. Although even the more familiar approach finds that monetary transmission to GDP has been quicker.footnote [5]
With regard to the first stage of transmission of monetary policy,footnote [6] the relatively quick increase in mortgage rates in response to the rise in inflation and market expectations of tighter monetary policy that I showed in Chart 10 illustrates a key channel through which the financial environment will affect households considering a new mortgage or seeking to remortgage by making their monthly repayments more expensive. Note as well that the moderation from the peak has been slower than the advance, pointing to asymmetry in the institutional response to the policy environment.
Besides the fast pass-through to financial variables, Brandt et al. (2026) Opens in a new window use
high-frequency credit and debit card spending data to show that monetary policy shocks can affect real economic activity very quickly, too. They show that consumer spending declines within a few days in response to a contractionary monetary policy shock, while web searches for terms related to unemployment rise. This result suggests that a fast adjustment in households’ expectations about their economic prospects can drive a change in consumption behavior.
Firm-level research by Yotzov et al. (2026) Opens in a new window also shows that firms update both their CPI inflation perceptions and expectations as well as their own-price growth expectations upon CPI releases. Specifically, the authors find that between 2022 and 2024, a one percentage point increase in headline CPI inflation raises firms’ expected year-ahead own-price growth by 0.3 percentage points. On CPI perceptions, they respond quickly within a few hours of data releases. Firms’ expected own-price growth also increases a few hours after a positive change in CPI inflation, although to a smaller extent.
Research by Di Pace et al. (2025) Opens in a new window analyses how firms update their price expectations in response to monetary policy announcements by the Bank of England. They find that within days following the Bank Rate decision, firms revise down their year-ahead price growth expectations if the increase in Bank Rate is sufficiently large. As Chart 13 shows, Bank Rate increases of 50 basis points or more result in a statistically significant and economically sizeable downward revision in firms’ expected price growth for the year ahead. While this pattern is evident across the distribution of firms’ expected own-price changes, it is more pronounced in the left tail. This means that firms revise the lower-price outcomes in their pricing plans more than the higher-price outcomes, suggesting an asymmetric updating of expectations. Chart 13 also shows that firms do not seem to significantly alter their price growth expectations in response to announcements of Bank Rate changes smaller than 50 basis points.

Chart 13: Responsiveness of firm price expectations to Bank Rate changes
Regression coefficients

Footnotes

Source: Di Pace et al. (2025) Opens in a new window.

Notes: The chart plots regression results for different moments of the distribution of firms’ price expectations on monetary policy shocks within a 5-day window around policy announcements. Monetary policy shocks are measured using actual Bank Rate changes. The series is normalized so that coefficients correspond to the response to a 25 basis point shock. BR change < 50 bps indicates a Bank Rate change below 50 basis points in absolute value. BR change >= 50 bps indicates a Bank Rate change equal or above 50 basis points in absolute value. Analysis uses data from November 2016 until December 2023. Error bars denote 95% confidence intervals.

Implications for monetary policy strategy
How do I use the underlying data and these two strands of research to inform my policy strategy? Consider the following three dimensions generally, but with specific reference to my June decision.
First, the importance of a disaggregated assessment. Disaggregated data is always key to how I evaluate the economic conjuncture. In June, these data exhibited mixed signals, which provided a more nuanced view of the inflation-activity trade-off than the macro data. Wage growth has differed between private and public sectors. Pricing behavior of firms has varied in speed of responsiveness. The administered one-off changes in prices masked underlying trend inflation. Disaggregated labor signals in some sectors were less weak than the overall unemployment rate. Tracking fiscal outturns has been important, especially given the gap between GDP and market-sector output, and the evidence from the Forecast Evaluation Report.
Second, on the topic of volatility and noise versus signals. Whereas both higher inflation and financial market volatility do make it harder to distinguish signals from transitory movements, because inflation volatility goes hand-in-hand with inflation rates, and financial volatility is reflected in risk premia, the noise contributes to the signal. It puts upside pressure on inflation and tightens financial conditions, at least in nominal terms. The source of inflation pressures – from costs versus from demand matters. The source of financial risk premia – from domestic drivers versus foreign spillovers – matters. In June, the cost-oriented inflation pressures were being offset by domestic-oriented financial restrictiveness. Bearing these factors in mind has been key to many of my policy decisions.
Third, on the topic of timing. Energy price developments, profit margin behavior, and the underpinnings of the 2027 wage negotiations will be critical in determining whether current cost pressures become more embedded. All these conditions are still unfolding. Given the seasonality of wage negotiations and their dependence on previous inflation and inflation expectations, data outturns (including the expectations for one-year-ahead) in the second half of this year are particularly important for my future decisions.
Considering my June decision, by the disaggregated data assessment, there was more upside risks to inflation compared to downside risks for activity. On that basis and considering the research about risks of de-anchoring alone, tightening Bank Rate could have made sense. But, at the time of the June meeting, financial markets had tightened considerably at least in nominal terms.
Research on the responsiveness of pricing and consumer behaviors to CPI announcements and to monetary policy shocks is clear evidence that monetary policy can have quick effects on the key variables of inflation expectations and CPI inflation, which is the Bank of England’s remit. In June, observing these forward-looking and high-frequency data in the context of both strands of the research meant that an activist hold was the appropriate decision.
Going forward, as I evaluate the disaggregated data, the sources of signal-to-noise in financial conditions, and the inputs to firms’ pricing strategies, I am confident that if outturns – especially in expectations – are unfavorable to the underlying inflation process, an activist move can bring inflation expectations and outcomes toward the two percent target.

articles.title: Efforts toward closing the gender gap: lessons from two decades of reform in Egypt
articles.text:
Published on
Let's Talk Development

Efforts toward closing the gender gap: Lessons from two decades of reform in Egypt

Julia Braunmiller

Mahmoud Elsaman

Mirey Ovadiya

October 22, 2026

This page in:

English

English

With legal reform, funding, and political will, Egypt shows that rapid progress in closing gender gaps in labor markets is possible. | © Shutterstock.com

In many countries, women get left behind in the labor market. With one of the largest gender gaps in labor force participation in the world and a sweeping new labor law enacted in 2025, Egypt is a good place to analyze what its reforms have set in motion and the lessons other countries can draw from its trajectory.
In Egypt, 20 percent of women participate in the labor force, compared to 74 percent of men. Closing that gap could do more than advance women's rights: World Bank estimates suggest it could increase Egypt's GDP per capita by 41 percent by 2050, and by as much as 56 percent in the long run.

A two-decade reform effort, in one law
Egypt has emerged as one of the world's most active reformers according to the Women, Business and the Law (WBL) 2026 report, reflected in a 10-point score increase. That score is the product of more than two decades of iterative efforts that resulted in the Labor Law of 2025, the first comprehensive overhaul of Egypt's labor code in more than 20 years. The law removed restrictions on women's night work, mandated equal pay for work of equal value, extended paid maternity leave from 90 to 120 days, introduced (limited) paid paternity leave, strengthened protections against dismissal during maternity, and enabled flexible work arrangements. The Labor Law did not stand alone. Earlier financial sector reforms introduced protections against gender-based discrimination in access to financial services, strengthened the use of sex-disaggregated data, and improved protection from gender-based violence through a one-stop center for survivors and transport safety protocols. IFC has worked with Egypt’s private sector to support women entrepreneurs and workplace equality.

Four lessons from Egypt’s trajectory for other countries:

Design reforms around evidence and maintain a dialogue. WBL data helped identify Egypt's priority areas and anchored discussions with policymakers across two decades. Equally important was the sustained dialogue that followed. A pattern seen across reforming economies is that data can catalyze reform, but only when embedded in ongoing engagement.

Sequence reforms strategically: start where movement is possible. Not all reforms are equally easy to advance. Labor market regulations are often more immediately actionable than rules embedded in personal status law or inheritance regimes, which are tied to deeply rooted social norms and require broader societal dialogue.Egypt's scores reflect this. The 2025 reforms brought meaningful progress in legal frameworks scores for Pay (81.25), Parenthood (64.25), and Work (50). Marriage (0), Mobility (25), and Assets (25) remain lowest. Early gains build momentum and create space for tackling harder reforms over time. The implication is not to avoid difficult reforms, but to sequence them within a longer-term agenda.

Pair legal change with financing instruments that lock in results. Legal change is more likely to translate into outcomes when anchored in a results framework. Egypt's experience with Development Policy Financing illustrates this: policy actions anchored commitments to financial inclusion with targets to expand women's access to non-bank financial services supported by sex-disaggregated monitoring, access to protection services, and improved transport safety. Tying disbursements to measurable targets means reforms are not only enacted but tracked.

Build implementation systems from day one. Implementation cannot be an afterthought. Egypt's WBL 2026 supportive frameworks data show where the gaps remain. Paternity leave stands at one day, with no policy incentives to encourage fathers to take it. Labor Law care provision obligations need supplementing with measures to ease the financial burden for employers and expand quality childcare. New flexible work provisions need implementing guidance before they can be used with confidence. Asset ownership, entrepreneurship, and employment can be promoted by strengthening social insurance, simplifying regulations, and expanding financial services and products. And while the National Strategy for the Empowerment of Egyptian Women 2030 sets clear targets for women's labor market access, the institutional architecture to track progress is not yet in place.

What comes next, and what others can take from it
These lessons are not unique to Egypt. Closing gender gaps in labor markets requires a combination of legal change, institutional and budgetary support, and sustained political commitment. Egypt’s trajectory shows that meaningful change at speed is possible. The next phase will determine whether that change delivers results at scale in women's economic participation.

A note from the authors
The findings in this blog are based on WBL 2026 data, which measures the legal and policy frameworks affecting women's economic participation as of a specific point in time. A higher or improving score reflects progress in legal provisions — it does not indicate that those laws are being enforced, or that women's lives have improved in practice. The new WBL 2026 Enforcement Perceptions score aims to capture precisely this gap: for Egypt, it stands at 42 out of 100, below the global average of 53, signaling women’s equal opportunity laws are enforced at less than half of their potential. We are not making a broader claim about the situation of women in Egypt. Many of the barriers women face — in Egypt and elsewhere — are not captured by any legal index. Where those gaps are visible in the data, we point to them; but readers should keep this limitation in mind when interpreting any score-based findings in this blog.

Gender

Egypt

Julia Braunmiller

Senior Private Sector Development Specialist

articles.title: Export finance – enabling trade in an uncertain world
articles.text:
Back to InsightsInfrastructure and Sustainable FinanceThe Future of InfrastructureExport finance – enabling trade in an uncertain world15 October 2026ArticleArticleShare via EmailShare on FacebookShare on LinkedInShare on TwitterIt is a time of significant change for export credit agencies, with the sector innovating in the face of a volatile macro backdrop. Such changes often outlive the crises that brought them about and ensure that large-scale trade deals go ahead.
The
ECA-backed credit market has reached record highs, reflecting a structural
shift in how governments, exporters, and borrowers approach this kind of
financing.
Reform of the OECD
Arrangement has extended repayment terms allowing for up to 22 years for
renewable and nuclear projects, with a second round of modernisation now under
consultation.
Untied financing, which is
not linked to a specific export contract, has become a fast-growing part of the
market and a route for governments to pursue industrial strategy.

In times of uncertainty, export credit agencies (ECAs) are an important source of finance. These state-backed entities provide counter-cyclical support to a country’s exporters by extending credit when commercial markets are unavailable, enabling large-scale trade deals to go ahead, which otherwise could fail due to lack of funding.
Against the backdrop of last year’s disruptions to global trade, centred around the US introducing a new wave of tariffs, and this year’s energy shock, as the Strait of Hormuz faces ongoing disruptions, the ECA-backed financing market has reached record volumes. In 2025, there was USD191 billion in financing, up 38% on the previous year1.
A recent meeting of G7 ECAs highlights how governments are leaning on ECAs to support national industrial strategies, expressing how agencies can help build resilience into supply chains, secure critical minerals, and work in emerging areas, like artificial intelligence 2.
We can see innovation taking place over the previous 18 months. In 2025, US tariffs prompted new measures aimed at helping exporters deal with the impacts of tariffs. UK Export Finance, for example, quickly announced that it was expanding its financing support for British businesses by GBP20 billion 3 (USD27.2 billion). When the Strait of Hormuz was blockaded early in 2026, Export Finance Australia was provided with new capabilities to secure critical supplies for the Australian economy 4. And the Japan Bank for International Cooperation have announced USD10 billion financial support for partnership on wide energy and resources resilience 5.
Beyond immediate reactions to pressing events, there are ongoing changes to the OECD Arrangement on Officially Supported Export Credits that governs the activities of ECAs in member countries. Also known as the OECD Consensus, the Arrangement is a framework that aims to promote the fair use of export credits, emphasising the quality of goods and services, rather than the availability of export credits.
In 2023, the Arrangement underwent a significant modernisation with a package of measures. The standout change was an increase in the maximum repayment terms to up to 22 years for projects related to renewable energy and nuclear power, with 15 years the upper limit for all other projects 6.
There is likely more change to come, as there is active consultation going on for a second round of modernisation of the Arrangement. In June, industry representatives submitted a set of priorities to the OECD consultation 7. These include revising financing terms to better reflect the current risk environment – such as increasing the maximum level of support to up to 95% of the exported content.
There is also an understanding that the nature of exports is changing, with digital goods becoming an important part of the international offering for many developed economies. As such, there are calls for the Arrangement to better support the trade of software and other digital goods, bringing them on a par with physical goods.Manav FutnaniGlobal Head of Export Finance | HSBCThis is a time of significant change for ECAs: individual agencies are spurring innovation, while the rules governing export credit are becoming more progressive. Taken together, ECA operations are evolving to better support the exporters and buyers they serve.The rise of untied financeIn terms of the kind of support that ECAs are offering, untied financing has become a growing focus. This is a form of export finance that is not linked to a specific export contract. Instead, an ECA lends in support of a strategic government priority, such as a broader commitment to source from the agency’s home country over time, securing critical resources, or encouraging inbound investment.
Untied financing is attractive because it allows the agency to get involved before a contract is in place. These deals can be easier to originate and execute, compared to traditional buyer credits.
As such, the amount of untied financing has surged in recent years – achieving around one fourth of the volumes 8. HSBC is closely involved in supporting some of the most impactful untied finance programmes – such as Italy’s Push Strategy, run by SACE, which as of 2025 had guaranteed more than EUR15 billion of loans 9. Our involvement can be seen across a wide range of major transactions.
These include: a EUR500 million facility for software company Bending Spoons 10, USD400 million of financing to major Brazilian electric utility Eletrobras 11, a USD300 million sustainability-linked loan for Bahrain’s nogaholding, now known as Bapco Energies 12, and the USD625 million untied loan of the Italian ECA to Kuwait National Petroleum Company 13.Financing future infrastructureThe world’s infrastructure needs are enormous. In financial terms, the estimated bill for new and updated infrastructure projects could be a cumulative USD106 trillion through 2040 14. Financing such a huge sum requires input from a wide variety of funding sources. ECAs are an increasingly important part of the mix, as they are able to provide long-tenor finance for projects that often take decades to become profitable.
Infrastructure accounts for the largest share of ECA medium-and long-term credit in developing countries. In the period from 2019 to 2024, ECAs issued USD74.4 billion in commitments in everything from ports to health services, with Sub-Saharan Africa taking the largest share 15.

ECAs play an important role in the energy transition, with their portfolios gradually shifting towards renewable sources. In 2025, oil and gas projects accounted for just 5% of the sector’s commitments, compared to 36% five years before. Inversely, renewables volumes amounted to 16% in 2025 compared to the 10% of the previous five-year period 16. For example, ECA financing is critical for nuclear power, particularly given extended construction periods and significant capex requirements. ECA cover is key in achieving material liquidity for these investments.

The successful funding of Sizewell C is a case in point. The new nuclear power station is a major infrastructure project for the UK, where it is expected to power up to six million homes for at least 60 years 17. The GBP5 billion loan, granted by 13 international banks, was guaranteed by Bpifrance Assurance Export, with HSBC acting as the ECA coordinator and mandated lead arranger for the French ECA 18.
As technology progresses, so too does the nature of infrastructure. In just a few years, data centres have evolved from being considered a form of commercial real estate to strategic infrastructure, as governments recognise that domestic compute capacity will determine which countries can build and run their own AI systems. And although there is currently strong appetite to fund the growth of data centres, in both public and private markets, ECAs could contribute to the financing in the years to come.

Major ECAs are already putting AI into their plans. The Export-Import Bank of the United States (US EXIM) recently announced the launch of ExportAI – an initiative that aims to accelerate the export of US AI technologies 19. In the UK, UKEF is exploring the finance models that could support the deployment of British hardware in data centres overseas 20.

Supporting data centre finance is not without its challenges. One issue is that there is a wide range of components that go into a data centre. High-end semiconductors will be the most prominent cost, but there also needs to be cooling equipment, network infrastructure, and storage systems. Each of these goods could originate from a different country, which would necessitate the involvement of multiple ECAs.

While ECAs have reinsurance and coinsurance arrangements, these do not lend themselves naturally to the kind of procurement structures that are likely to be relevant to this sector. If ECAs are going to be relevant, they will need to devise entirely new programs customised to the needs of this industry. At this time, US EXIM is the only agency that appears to have made significant progress in this respect.
The HSBC advantageAt HSBC, export finance is a core part of our global financing platform. We bring together export finance, infrastructure and project finance, and sustainability into a single client solution. For clients executing large, multi-faceted cross-border transactions, this breadth of capabilities within one bank can make a real difference.

Our network is truly global, operating across all the major trade corridors, allowing us to serve clients in all the geographies where infrastructure and sovereign financing demand is growing most rapidly, backed by the risk mitigation of ECA coverage. We also have an expanding footprint of dedicated experts in many key markets – most recently, we added new team members in Mumbai, Riyadh, and Mexico City.

In addition, our long experience in export finance makes us a trusted partner for all the stakeholders involved. By working closely with ECAs, exporters, and borrowers, we are able to co-create innovative “market first” programmes. For example, in 2025 India’s Reliance Industries signed a USD500 million untied loan backed by Korea Trade Insurance Corporation, which was the first corporate untied deal by a South Korean ECA 21. This award-winning deal sits alongside Sizewell C, which was voted as Global Deal of the Year by The Asset 22.

articles.title: Fed Thoughts: Climbing Up The Learning Curve
articles.text:
Fed Thoughts: Climbing Up The Learning Curve

Change can be difficult to navigate, especially when its
principal agent explicitly rejects prevailing norms.

October 2026

Change can be difficult to navigate, especially when its principal agent explicitly rejects prevailing norms. Less than five months into the job, Federal Reserve (the Fed) Chair Kevin Warsh has put investors in that position, which makes charting the course of monetary policy complicated. However, there are a few things we’re reasonably sure of:
The Fed will likely raise rates at least one more time this year.The Fed will likely not signal its decision going into the October meeting, as Warsh tends to avoid forward guidance to keep the “family discussion” lively.The Fed will likely present a firm stance in pursuit of price stability, imparting a hawkish skew to its message.
We are uncertain about the cadence of policy action. The group leans toward removing accommodation, but its leader, who proposed cutting the annual number of scheduled meetings, may prefer less frequent interventions. We believe these stylistic changes reflect a different worldview from his immediate predecessors. Warsh places greater faith in market mechanisms, and he would rather learn from investors than lead them, worries less about high-frequency fluctuations in the data, and may prefer less frequent intervention.
We examine these issues one at a time.
GOING WITH THE FLOW
The chair has been clear: “Forward guidance is not the business we should be in.”,1 This has been widely interpreted as learning from investors, but we think of it as working with markets in a manner best seen from first principles.
Most modern models of policy setting describe policy as attempting to improve social welfare. Given the Fed’s dual objective, this is accomplished by keeping employment at its maximum sustainable level and inflation at the goal of 2 percent. With the labor market now roughly in balance, that calculation depends on inflation’s proximity to goal. The further away inflation is from goal, the greater the loss to society. Moreover, the loss to society increases rapidly away from 2 percent.
When inflation is far from goal, the appropriate policy direction is clearer: policy tends to be easy when inflation is well below goal and tight when it is well above goal. Market participants can help the Fed by keeping inflation expectations well anchored, which the Fed encourages through forward guidance about its policy determination.When inflation is near goal, the policy tradeoff is more delicate. The correct direction depends on an uncertain outlook. Market participants can help the Fed by expressing their own view on the appropriate stance of policy. For a clean read on that opinion, however, the Fed shouldn’t put its weight on the scale and should refrain from forward guidance.
We are relatively sure that Warsh currently sees the world as in the latter, flatter part of the policy terrain, where listening to markets makes more sense than leading them. Some of his colleagues probably view that area as more circumscribed, as witnessed by the sharing of their policy views in public. But those are their own views, as Warsh is not likely to send others in his stead to shape the message to markets given his sense of the Fed’s appropriate place in the policy space, in my view.

NEWTON’S FIRST LAW
It appears that Warsh’s preference to learn from markets rather than influence them also leads him to worry less about the fluctuations of high-frequency data. His short summary from the September press conference was: “Trends matter. Data points are noisy. Data dependence is a dangerous preoccupation.”2 However, even though he wants to dial back data dependence, he also seems comfortable with gradual 25-basis-point policy adjustments.
An eighteen-month economic outlook is unlikely to change in the six weeks between FOMC meetings, and a change significant enough to alter the policy direction is also unlikely to call for just one 25-basis-point adjustment. Once such an adjustment begins, momentum takes over. The result is Newtonian, as the first law of physics states that a body at rest stays at rest, and a body in motion stays in motion (unless acted upon by an outside force), which is why we believe that the Fed is likely to raise rates further this year. The inertial body is in motion.

SETTING THE PACE OF ACTION
We are less certain of how Warsh’s medium-termism (a view of market conditions over the medium term — from the next several quarters to a couple of years) translates into the timing of decisions. He has asked the Committee to consider fewer regularly scheduled meetings. That would not necessarily mean fewer policy actions, but it would raise the institutional hurdle for frequent adjustments. As he said at his confirmation hearings, “Four is not enough,” but it seems that eight may be too many.3
Forgoing action in October wouldn’t halt the Fed’s forward motion (as we expect the messaging to be forceful about returning inflation to goal), only establish its pace. At the very least, Warsh will likely head into the meeting with no firm plan to raise rates, although the “family discussion” at the meeting could tip the scales the other way. We’re inclined to put the chances of action higher than currently in markets because action may help satisfy Warsh’s desire to be an agent of change:
Rate-increase policy reinforces his commitment to recover price stability;Unexpected action demonstrates that all meetings are live; andDelivers another blow to forward guidance from Fed officials.
We believe that medium-termism can win out and that action will likely be deferred to December, but we can’t say for certain (and neither should you).

Vincent Reinhart
Chief Economist & Macro Strategist
Vincent is the firm’s Chief Economist and Macro Strategist. In this role, he is responsible for developing views on the global economy and making relative value recommendations across global bond markets, currencies and sectors.
Previously, Vincent served as the Chief US Economist and a managing director at Morgan Stanley. For the prior four years, he was a resident scholar at the American Enterprise Institute (AEI). Vincent also spent 24 years at the Federal Reserve, holding several roles including Director of the Division of Monetary Affairs and Secretary and Economist of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). His responsibilities at the Federal Reserve included directing research and analysis of monetary policy strategies and the conduct of policy through open market operations, discount window lending and reserve requirements. Prior to these roles, he was the principal liaison with the domestic desk at
the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and was responsible for preparing a document outlining policy alternatives for each FOMC meeting. He was Deputy Director in the Division of International Finance and Associate Economist of the FOMC and spent five years at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in both the domestic and international research departments.
His academic publications primarily concern the conduct of policy and issues related to the monetary transmission mechanism as well as an analysis of alternative auction techniques and Treasury debt management. After an undergraduate training at Fordham University, he received graduate degrees in economics at Columbia University.
