articles.title: Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States
articles.text:
FEDS Notes

Twitter

Share

RSS

October 16, 2026
Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States
Katie Brinkman, Christine Dobridge, Tim Dore, Simon Glossner, Elizabeth Holmquist, Nam Nguyen, Maria Perozek, and Irina Stefanescu1
Section 1: Introduction

Over the past decade, private credit has played an increasingly important role in providing funding to middle-market businesses. While there are several definitions of private credit, here we define it as privately negotiated loans to businesses that are originated by nonbank investment funds rather than by traditional financial intermediaries such as banks.

Until now, private credit loans and the financial vehicles that originate them have not been separately identified in the Financial Accounts of the United States, largely due to the private nature of these transactions and limited available data. We now address this gap using confidential SEC Form PF data along with other data sources to compile balance sheets for private debt funds and other private credit vehicles.

Beginning with the September 2026 release, we have integrated private credit into the Financial Accounts by adding new sectors for private credit vehicles and new financial instrument tables for private credit loans and shares of private debt funds.2 Integrating private credit into the comprehensive Financial Accounts framework—rather than producing standalone tables—helps users to trace the full intermediation chain from investors through private credit vehicles to borrowers, facilitating analysis of its effects on business leverage and financial stability.

This note explains how we have incorporated private credit into the Financial Accounts and discusses implications for key balance sheet measures for businesses and households. Section 2 provides a brief overview of the U.S. private credit market. Section 3 reviews the previous treatment of private credit in the Financial Accounts. Section 4 describes the integration approach, including data sources and methodology for each private credit vehicle and new financial instrument. Section 5 discusses implications for nonfinancial business leverage and household net worth. Section 6 concludes.

Section 2: Background

The private credit market has grown rapidly over the past decade. As shown in Figure 1, assets under management in private credit vehicles have grown from approximately $350 billion in 2012 to over $2.6 trillion as of 2025:Q4, with outstanding private credit loans to U.S. businesses totaling approximately $1.5 trillion.

Figure 1. Assets of Private Credit Vehicles and Private Credit Loans to U.S. Borrowers3

Note: Data as of Q4 each year. The key identifies bars in order from top to bottom.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States, SEC Form PF.

Accessible version

Private credit is primarily provided through private debt (PD) funds and business development companies (BDCs), though private credit provided through middle-market collateralized loan obligations (MM CLOs) and interval and tender offer funds has also grown substantially in recent years.4 Most borrowers are middle-market nonfinancial firms seeking funding for acquisitions, growth capital, or refinancing. Given the scale and growth of private credit, its integration into the Financial Accounts is essential for comprehensive measurement of credit flows to nonfinancial businesses and for understanding the role of private credit in the financial system.

Section 3: Previous Treatment in the Financial Accounts

Prior to the September 2026 release, most private credit loans from domestically domiciled private credit vehicles were included as liabilities on nonfinancial corporate business balance sheets but were not identified as debt instruments, and the intermediation activities of private credit vehicles were largely excluded from the Financial Accounts. This section describes the previous treatment of private credit and explains why integrating these vehicles has effects that extend beyond the private credit sectors themselves.

The previous treatment of private credit vehicles in the Financial Accounts varied depending on whether the originating vehicle was domiciled in the United States or abroad. We already captured foreign private funds lending to U.S. businesses in the Rest of the World (ROW) sector. Therefore, we only added U.S.-based private credit vehicles as new sectors in the Financial Accounts to complete the picture.

U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles
U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles were not identified as separate sectors in the Financial Accounts. As a result, their balance sheet assets and liabilities were either missing entirely or incorrectly attributed to other sectors.

For the most part, loans originated by U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles were not recorded as loan assets of a financial sector, however, the corresponding loan liabilities of U.S. businesses, were not entirely absent.5 Private credit loans to nonfinancial corporate businesses were generally recorded as miscellaneous liabilities, while loans to noncorporate businesses were generally classified as depository institution loans. As a result, the previous treatment obscured the composition of business borrowing and understated measures of nonfinancial business debt captured by the Financial Accounts' debt instruments.

Depository institution loans issued to U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles were incorrectly attributed to foreign nondepository financial institutions. In addition, debt securities issued by business development companies (BDCs) and U.S.-domiciled MM CLOs were not previously recorded and therefore represent additions to financial sector debt outstanding in the Financial Accounts.

Similarly, equity shares issued by U.S.-domiciled private debt funds, closely held BDCs, interval funds, and tender offer funds were previously omitted from the Financial Accounts. Equity issued by publicly listed BDCs, by contrast, was already included in corporate equity issues but was attributed to the other financial business sector.

Because the Financial Accounts comprise an integrated set of sectoral balance sheets, the omission of U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles also affected the measurement of assets and liabilities in other sectors. These effects are particularly important for the household sector, for which many asset holdings are calculated residually.6 For example, when private credit vehicles hold instruments that are also held directly by households—such as checkable deposits and corporate equities—the absence of private credit vehicles from the accounts caused some of these assets to be residually attributed to households, thereby overstating measured household assets and net worth. Conversely, household net worth was understated by the omission of directly held equity shares in private debt funds, closely held BDCs, interval funds, and tender offer funds. Incorporating private credit vehicles therefore both reallocates existing financial assets and liabilities across sectors and introduces instruments that were previously absent from the Financial Accounts.

Foreign-domiciled private credit vehicles
Foreign-domiciled private debt funds and middle-market CLOs have not been introduced as separate sectors in the Financial Accounts because their transactions and positions with U.S. residents were already captured in the ROW sector. In particular, private credit loans extended by foreign-domiciled vehicles to U.S. businesses were recorded as foreign loans to U.S. corporate businesses within the "other loans and advances" instrument category but are now separately identified. Similarly, U.S. financial assets held by foreign private credit vehicles are recorded as ROW assets, with holdings of private debt fund shares now separately identified. Private credit loans extended to foreign businesses by domestic private credit vehicles are a new addition to rest of the world loan liabilities. Equity issued by foreign private credit vehicles and held by U.S. residents is included among U.S. holdings of foreign corporate equities, with private debt fund shares now shown separately.

Section 4: Integration of Private Credit into the Financial Accounts

This section describes how we integrate private credit into the Financial Accounts framework. We begin with an overall summary of the private credit market followed by a description of each new sector and financial instrument added to the accounts.

4.1 Summary of Private Credit Market
Table 1 provides a snapshot of balance sheet assets and liabilities for all vehicles that make up the U.S. private credit market. As of the end of 2025, U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles had assets under management of $1.9 trillion. At the same time, there were $1.5 trillion in private credit loans extended to U.S. businesses, including $335 billion from foreign-domiciled funds. Private debt funds and BDCs have the largest shares of the market, with each holding just under half of total private credit loans outstanding. These private credit vehicles also hold substantial amounts of corporate equity in their portfolios, including equity stakes taken in connection with lending arrangements.

U.S. private credit vehicles are primarily funded through equity issuance ($1.1 trillion), although they also access funding though bank loans ($349 billion), and debt securities ($135 billion). Foreign-domiciled private debt funds also provide a substantial share of credit in the market. We estimate that the portfolios and capital structures of these foreign funds are similar to those of U.S.-domiciled private debt funds.

As noted in Section 3, we have added U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles to the Financial Accounts. The following subsections describe each new sector and the associated financial instruments.

4.2 New Financial Sectors
Private debt funds: tables S.124.8.t and S124.8.s
Private debt funds are privately offered, closed-end investment vehicles that are typically organized as limited partnerships and managed by an affiliated investment adviser. These funds are "private funds" and thus exempted from the regulations of the 1940 Investment Act. PD funds cover different private credit strategies with various mandates and risk profiles, including direct lending, mezzanine and junior capital, distressed and special situations, asset-based and specialty finance, private real estate debt, and infrastructure debt. Capital is raised through commitments from qualified investors—such as pension funds and insurance companies—and drawn over time through capital calls to fund loan originations and acquisitions. Investors do not typically have the right to redeem fund shares before the termination of the fund.

Our primary data source for private debt funds is confidential SEC Form PF, which provides detailed balance sheet information for private funds. These Form PF data translate well into the Financial Accounts structure, as funds report levels of assets and liabilities, which we use for the balance sheet table, as well as holders of private fund shares, which we use for the instrument table.7

However, there are some measurement challenges associated with compiling these balance sheets. First, PD funds are not explicitly identified in Form PF data, so to classify funds as private debt funds, we use signals from fund strategies, fund names, and classifications that are provided in other databases, including Preqin, PitchBook, and Moody's. We merge Form PF data with fund-level information from these sources to construct comprehensive sector-level balance sheets.

Second, not all funds file Form PF on a quarterly basis; some file only annually and provide more limited information. For funds that file quarterly, we are able to estimate quarterly balance sheets. For funds that file only annually, we impute annual balance sheet data using portfolio shares from quarterly filers with similar investment strategies, then interpolate quarterly values between the annual estimates.8

The Z.1 includes data on transactions and stocks for U.S. private debt funds in tables S.124.8.t and S.124.8.s (see Table 2). U.S-domiciled private debt fund AUM have grown over time, from $180 billion in 2012 to about $940 billion as of 2025:Q4.9 Private credit loans account for about 60 percent of assets, and corporate equities account for about 18 percent.10

These shares are added as a new financial instrument "private debt fund shares" in the Financial Accounts and are shown in table F522.3.s of the release, discussed in more detail in Section 4.3.

Business development companies (BDCs): tables S.124.5.t and S.124.5.s
Business development companies are closed-end investment companies created by Congress in 1980 to channel capital to small and mid-sized U.S. businesses. BDCs elect to be regulated under Section 2(a)(48) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 and must invest at least 70 percent of their total assets in eligible portfolio companies—primarily domestic unlisted companies or certain small-cap companies. Unlike traditional investment companies, BDCs can employ substantially higher leverage, with statutory limits allowing up to 2:1 debt-to-equity ratios.

BDCs can be structured as publicly traded companies (with shares listed on exchanges), public non-traded companies (offering shares directly to investors meeting certain suitability criteria with periodic redemptions), or private companies (offering securities to either accredited or qualified investors through private placements, similar to private debt funds). All three types of BDCs are included in the Financial Accounts.

Our primary data source is BDC Collateral, a proprietary financial analytics platform and data aggregator developed by LSEG LPC. The platform extracts data from BDCs' 10-Qs and 10-Ks, which we use to estimate equity investments, private credit loans, syndicated loans, cash positions, and miscellaneous assets. The dataset includes both cost and fair value for BDCs' investments, enabling us to decompose changes in asset levels into transactions and revaluations. The BDC table includes memo items showing the breakdown of assets across the three BDC types.

As shown on table S.124.5.s (see Table 3), BDCs have AUM of about $570 billion as of 2025:Q4, up from less than $40 billion in 2012 (see Figure 1). Private credit loans account for 80 percent of assets, while syndicated loans and corporate equities each account for about 7 percent.

Interval funds and tender offer funds: tables S124.6.s and S124.6.t
Interval funds and tender offer funds are closed-end investment vehicles designed to invest in illiquid asset classes (e.g., private credit) while providing investors with limited, periodic liquidity through scheduled repurchase mechanisms. The fundamental distinction between the two structures lies in the mandatory versus discretionary nature of their repurchase obligations, with interval funds being required to redeem a certain number of shares at specified intervals while tender offer funds have more discretion over the timing, frequency, and offer size.

Registered interval and tender offer funds are regulated under the 1940 Act. Regulatory requirements include enhanced disclosure through Form N-2 registration statements and Form N-PORT reporting of portfolio holdings, adherence to leverage limitations, and independent board oversight. We use data from Morningstar and SEC Form N-PORT to construct the balance sheet.11

Balance sheet data for interval and tender offer funds appear in table S124.6.s (see Table 4), which shows combined assets of $292 billion as of 2025:Q4, up from $100 billion in 2021 (the beginning of our series). Together, private credit loans and syndicated loans (lines 7 and 8) account for nearly 30 percent of assets, while corporate equities (line 9) account for 44 percent.

Middle-market CLOs: Added to tables S125s1.3.s and S125s1.3.t
Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) are financial vehicles that issue securities backed by pools of loans. Middle-market (MM) CLOs are backed specifically by loans to middle-market companies. The loans underlying MM CLOs are often originated by direct lenders such as PD funds, BDCs, and asset managers affiliated with life insurers. These lenders, or their affiliates, also commonly serve as the CLO managers.

To estimate the outstanding value of private credit loans held by MM CLOs, we use data from Moody's Analytics Inc., Global CLO database, which includes information on CLO assets, performance of CLO tranches, and attributes of the underlying loans and loan obligors.12 We identify MM CLOs by filtering for deals and tranches identified as small and middle-market CLOs that are denominated in U.S. dollars and are backed by loans to U.S. businesses. We then calculate total quarterly MM CLO assets under management (AUM) using data on the outstanding deal value of all CLO tranches meeting these criteria.

Unlike the other private credit vehicles described above, MM CLOs are not added as a new sector but are instead incorporated into the existing issuers of asset-backed securities (ABS) sector, which captures private-label securitization activity collateralized by a variety of financial assets, most notably mortgages and syndicated loans. To do this, we added private credit loans held by U.S.-domiciled MM CLOs to the asset side of the ABS balance sheet and the same amount of corporate bonds to the liability side (shown in lines 7 and 18 of table S125s1.3.s, see Table 5). In 2025:Q4, domestic MM CLOs held $54 billion in private credit loans. MM CLOs domiciled abroad (primarily in the Cayman Islands) are included in the ROW sector.

4.3 New Financial Instruments
The private credit integration introduces two new financial instruments into the Financial Accounts: private credit loans (the loans originated by private credit vehicles) and shares of private debt funds (ownership stakes in private debt funds).

Private credit loans: table F4.4.s
As noted in the introduction, private credit loans are defined here as privately negotiated loans to businesses that are originated by nonbank investment funds. This definition encompasses corporate direct lending, asset-based and specialty finance, real estate debt, infrastructure debt, and other privately negotiated loans. It therefore does not depend on the identity of the borrower, the purpose of the loan, or the assets supporting repayment. These loans span the full range of seniority levels: some are senior secured with first claim on collateral, others are unsecured or junior claims that absorb losses earlier but expect to earn higher returns, and still others are hybrid instruments blending debt and equity characteristics.

Private credit loans originated by all private credit vehicles are reported on a new financial instrument table. This table shows both the holders (lenders) and issuers (borrowers) of the loans, providing a complete picture of U.S. private credit market activity.

As of 2025:Q4, total private credit loans outstanding across all vehicles amounted to approximately $1.5 trillion. U.S.-domiciled private credit vehicles—primarily PD funds and BDCs—account for about $1 trillion, or roughly two-thirds of the total, while foreign-domiciled vehicles (mainly PD funds) account for $376 billion in loans to U.S. businesses (see Table 6).

Section 5. Effects on Financial Accounts Measures of Debt, Leverage, and Household Wealth

Nonfinancial business debt and leverage
This section examines how adding private credit loans to the Financial Accounts affects measures of aggregate nonfinancial business debt and leverage. Private credit now makes up a substantial fraction of total business debt. As shown in Table 8, which presents components of total debt of the nonfinancial business sector as of 2025:Q4, private credit loans accounted for about 6 percent of total business debt, up from around one percent in 2012 (Figure 4).

Debt positions of nonfinancial businesses have been identified as important metrics of financial health and systemic financial risk. Measures of nonfinancial leverage based on Financial Accounts data are also used to evaluate financial stability risks in the Federal Reserve's biannual Financial Stability Report.13 Prior to incorporating private credit loans as a component of debt in the Financial Accounts, aggregate debt positions of nonfinancial businesses were understated. It is useful, therefore, to evaluate whether debt trends are meaningfully different with the inclusion of private credit in aggregate measures of U.S. business debt.

Despite the strong growth in private credit loans in the U.S. economy since 2018, the addition of private credit loans to the Financial Accounts does not substantially change the trends in business debt overall. Panel A of Figure 5 presents the ratio of nonfinancial business debt-to-GDP with and without private credit loans included in the measure of debt. The debt-to-GDP ratio is around 5 percentage points higher in recent years when private credit is included, but the ratio remains below the median as measured since 2012 and has been on a declining trend since 2020. Panel B of Figure 5 shows debt growth with and without private credit included in the measure of total business debt. Annual debt growth since 2018 is somewhat higher when private credit is incorporated but the trend is not substantially different.

Figure 5. Debt Trends for the Nonfinancial Business Sector, with and without Private Credit Loans

Note: Data as of Q4 each year. Debt is defined as loans plus debt securities.

Source: Financial Accounts of the United States.

Accessible version

Household net worth
The integration of private credit also directly and indirectly affects measures of household net worth. As discussed in Section 3, the previous treatment of private credit led to the misattribution (directly or indirectly) of certain financial assets on the household balance sheet. The integration of private credit vehicles and instruments results in more accurate measurement of household balance sheets. Additionally, we now show households' direct exposures to private credit through investment in private debt fund shares as well as their indirect exposures through important household assets such as pension entitlements.

Section 6. Conclusion

Beginning with the September 2026 release, the Financial Accounts of the United States fully integrate private credit by adding new sectors for private credit vehicles and new financial instrument tables for private credit loans and shares of private debt funds. Using confidential SEC Form PF data along with other sources, we construct comprehensive balance sheets for approximately $1.1 trillion in private credit loan activity by U.S.-domiciled vehicles. The integration helps users track the intermediation chain from investors through private credit vehicles to borrowers, with detailed data available on private credit loans across sectors.14

This integration substantially improves measurement of nonfinancial business leverage and provides more accurate measurement of household balance sheets and exposures to private credit markets. The comprehensive framework facilitates analysis of the connections between private credit and the broader financial system, enhancing the Financial Accounts' utility for assessing financial stability risks. For more detail on the institutional features of private credit vehicles and the growing role of private credit in financial markets, see the forthcoming companion FEDS note "U.S. Private Credit Vehicles: Institutional Structure and Aggregate Balance Sheets." For complete methodological details on the construction of these series, see the Guide to the Financial Accounts of the United States.

articles.title: A unique vantage point − speech by Nathanaël Benjamin
articles.text:
A unique vantage point − speech by Nathanaël Benjamin

Given at the ISDA Derivatives Trading and Treasury Forum

Published on
01 October 2026

Nat Benjamin sets out how the Bank of England has a unique vantage point from which to understand the UK’s ever more complex and interconnected financial system, and how such surveillance can be used to strengthen its stability. He then illustrates this with gilt repo market resilience as one policy area that has benefited from that mindset.

Speech
Why surveillance matters more than ever
Good afternoon, and my thanks to ISDA for inviting me to speak at this year’s London Derivatives Trading and Treasury Forum. It is a pleasure to be here.
ISDA has played a key role in shaping the modern derivatives market through its work on legal standards, market infrastructure, data, and risk management. At a time when markets are becoming more interconnected and increasingly vital for the provision of financial services to the real economy, that contribution matters more than ever.
The nature of risks to financial stability has changed a lot over the last two decades.
Before the global financial crisis, the attention of authorities was often focused primarily on individual banks. The resilience of individual institutions is still fundamental today, of course. But many of the vulnerabilities that matter today emerge not within a single bank, but from interactions across non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), markets, and funding structures.
Recent episodes have demonstrated that stress can originate in one part of the financial system and propagate rapidly through funding markets, collateral demands, margin calls, and leveraged positions. And the actions taken by individual market players can, even when rational from their own perspective, combine to amplify stress across the system. We have talked about these risks on numerous occasions – including in this forum.
As the risks have changed, so has our financial stability perspective, adopting a resolutely system-wide lens that can observe their complex interconnections and interactions.
That scrutinising lens, how surveillance is evolving, and what it can help us achieve, is the first thing I’m going to talk about today. And then I will turn to one policy area which has benefited from that mindset: the resilience of gilt repo markets.
A unique vantage point
Over the past decade, the post-crisis reform agenda has transformed the information available to authorities.
One of the shortcomings identified following the global financial crisis was the lack of visibility into activity in important financial markets, and into the interconnections between market participants. Transaction-level reporting was introduced in response, allowing authorities to better understand how markets function and how market participants interact.
Today we can draw on transaction-level reporting across derivatives, securities financing, and trading activity, together with fund-level reporting and supervisory data. We've been using these insights for years to better understand how markets function, how risks propagate, and where vulnerabilities may be building across the financial system. They have informed our analysis during episodes such as the “dash for cash” that followed the outbreak of the Covid-19 pandemic, the stresses in energy markets following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, or the 2022 gilt market disruption. Yet as the nature of vulnerabilities changes, the way we use this data has changed too. Having access to millions of transaction records is not the same as being able identify how shocks might propagate through a complex web of funding relationships, collateral chains, and leveraged investors.
No single reporting regime was designed to provide a complete view of the financial system. Each dataset offers a different lens. As the UK’s central bank with macro- and micro-prudential authority, we have a unique vantage point that allows us to bring multiple sources of data together, building out a picture of chain reactions that would otherwise be unforeseeable.
Our institutional set-up makes us particularly well placed to do so for UK markets. As a participant in these core markets ourselves, and through the gathering of market intelligence from that position, we obtain invaluable insight that brings colour and context to reporting data. And through close collaboration with our colleagues at the Financial Conduct Authority, we can bring together information from derivatives markets, securities-financing markets, trading activity, fund reporting, and prudential supervision within a shared analytical framework.
This allows us to answer questions that would have been much harder to address in the past. We are increasingly able to identify where leverage resides, how it is financed, who is providing that financing, and how funding and liquidity shocks might propagate through the financial system. These capabilities are helping us to understand the behaviour of leveraged market participants and to evaluate how changes in market structure, such as greater central clearing, broader clearing access, or minimum haircut frameworks, could affect the resilience of core funding markets.
To show what a system-wide perspective can do, let's turn to a sector where these insights have been invaluable: hedge funds.
Data, and the case of hedge fund leverage
Increasingly, hedge funds contribute to liquidity, price discovery, and risk-bearing capacity across important financial markets. The financial stability question for us is not the fact that they use leverage to support their activities – that is a commercial matter entirely up to them, and indeed well-managed leverage is a positive thing for the economy. The question is rather about where that leverage resides, how concentrated it is, how it is financed, and how it interacts with the rest of the financial system.
Those questions cannot be answered using any single dataset, or by looking at hedge funds in isolation. They require combining transaction-level data, fund-level reporting, supervisory intelligence, market engagement, and deep market expertise.
Doing so has already generated insights that would have been difficult to obtain in the past. For example, in our July 2026 Financial Stability Report (FSR) we showed that, over the past four years, hedge funds have shifted from being net cash lenders to net cash borrowers in repo markets across a range of currencies, reflecting the important role of the banks as by far the major providers of leverage.footnote [1] We were also able to show that growth in hedge funds' gilt repo borrowing has coincided with increasing futures open interest, consistent with an expansion in basis trading activity. We were able to spot and track the growth of the cash-futures basis trade in the UK over the last 18 months – which was corroborated by our market intelligence.footnote [2] These insights help us understand where leverage is being created, how it is financed, and which transmission channels may matter during periods of stress.
That said, transaction data can only tell us part of the story. They help us understand positions and interconnections. They do not necessarily tell us how firms will behave if conditions deteriorate. To understand that, we complement our datasets with analysis of behaviours and reaction functions.
That is why we have started to run system-wide scenario exercises in collaboration with the industry. Our first one, two years ago, focussed on core sterling markets. During that exercise, many hedge funds originally assumed that additional repo financing would be available if needed. But it was clear from dealer banks that this would not necessarily be forthcoming. So we shared that feedback with hedge funds and asked how they would respond if banks reduced the amount of gilt repo financing available. Many reported that they would need to unwind positions financed through repo, illustrating how pressures on dealer balance sheets could be transmitted to leveraged investors and potentially amplify market moves.footnote [3]
Hedge funds play an important role in supporting market functioning, including in government bond markets, by warehousing risk and providing liquidity. But they are also generally more responsive to changes in market conditions and financing costs. As a result, the unwinding of leveraged and often crowded positions can have a disproportionate impact on market liquidity and may amplify stress during periods of market turbulence.
This is precisely why a system-wide perspective matters. A hedge fund can observe its own financing relationships. A dealer can observe its own clients. However, only the authorities can bring these perspectives together, helping identify vulnerabilities and interconnections that may not be visible to any single firm. Publishing analysis through our Financial Stability Reports, Staff Working Papers, and other publications allows market participants to benchmark their own exposures against broader market developments, improve risk management playbooks, understand which avenues would or wouldn’t be open to them in a stress, and identify vulnerabilities earlier.
As a concrete example of this, in our Financial Stability Report we have started to publish regularly aggregated data and charts that can help market participants understand wider developments and aid their own risk management. Examples of this in our latest FSR include how the preferred maturities of the gilt investor base have changed over the past decade, investor positioning in gilt repo, and breakdowns of the term and collateral maturity of those transactions.footnote [4] As part of our ongoing market engagement we look to understand which other areas might benefit from increased transparency, such as deep dives into specific market segments like retail investors in gilt markets and transparency on basis trade dynamics.
So please do take a look at our FSRs! I am not sure all the market participants who might find this information helpful actually clocked that we had very deliberately started to publish it. So far the feedback from hedge funds about its usefulness has been positive, and our message is: please put your thinking caps on and let us know what other aggregate data you would find helpful to see for your risk management. If we have it and can share it, we will.
At its best, surveillance is not just about helping authorities understand the system, it is also about helping the system understand itself better. Equipped with better information, market participants can be a more effective first line of defence, and the market as a whole is better able to self-stabilise when shocks hit – reducing the need for us to intervene.
And because we’re better placed than anyone else to see the overall picture, assembling it and sharing it back is an increasingly important policy tool in our toolbox.
But in addition to allowing market transparency to play out more effectively and do its work, surveillance also helps us identify in a discerning way the select few areas where the structure of markets does need to evolve to enhance resilience. Which brings me to a market where we have been asking such questions: the government bond repo market.
Leverage and funding in core markets
Like much of the financial system's infrastructure, the repo market is probably most visible only if it stops working properly. But its day-to-day role is essential – it keeps cash and collateral flowing through the financial system, supports liquidity in government bond markets, and facilitates the transmission of monetary policy.
Our first system-wide exploratory scenario (SWES) several years ago illustrated the crucial role that this market plays. Its resilience has improved, as was demonstrated by the fact that it has withstood successfully all the recent shocks in a heightened global risk environment. But that improved resilience isn’t yet locked permanently into its fundamental structure – it can still not be taken for granted.
Specifically, a key issue on our radar is how leveraged positions that are extremely large, concentrated, or correlated with respect to the size of the market have the potential to amplify shocks if they are unwound abruptly. Market corrections as a result of economic fundamentals are natural and healthy. What we want to avoid is such corrections getting amplified by structural features, as happened in the 2022 LDI crisis. That does not mean eliminating risk, though. Quite the opposite. The repo market performs crucial economic functions precisely because participants take and manage risk, often in the form of leverage. In principle leverage supports market liquidity and efficient risk transfer. Margin protects counterparties. Intermediation connects investors with different funding and investment needs.
Our intention is not to reduce leverage financed through the repo market. It is to ensure that the way it is provided and accessed supports market liquidity, efficient risk transfer, and the allocation of capital in all environments – not just when the sun shines. That might require limiting the particular forms of risk-taking that make the system more fragile.
So well-managed and well-understood leverage is welcome. Out-of-control leverage is unwelcome.
The challenge for policymakers is therefore to identify the combination of measures that best strengthen the resilience and efficiency of the system as a whole, in both normal and stress times. These properties depend on the ability of the financial system to supply liquidity when it is most needed. And they depend on limiting the build-up of vulnerabilities that can generate sudden and disruptive demand for liquidity during periods of stress.
On the supply side, greater central clearing has the potential not only to reduce counterparty credit risk, but also to strengthen the resilience of the market structure itself. The benefits for risk management are well understood, including more transparent and risk-sensitive margining practices. Less often appreciated are the market-wide benefits arising from greater netting efficiencies, lower balance sheet usage and a greater capacity for intermediaries to absorb positions, warehouse risk, and supply liquidity during periods of stress. Bank of England researchers have estimated that greater central clearing could have reduced gilt repo exposures on UK bank dealers' balance sheets during the “dash for cash” by between 40% and 60%.footnote [5] So this could free up a lot of capacity.
Experiences in other jurisdictions suggest that greater use of central clearing can encourage innovation in market structure and access models. In the United States Treasury repo market, for examplefootnote [6], market structures are evolving alongside clearing reforms, with new intermediation models and broader clearing access arrangements developing over time.
This is why access models matter. Different access arrangements can broaden participation in central clearing while preserving the diversity of participants that supports market liquidity. In the indirect model, clients access the central counterparty (CCP) via a clearing member. Sponsored access allows eligible firms to become direct participants of the CCP with support from a sponsoring clearing member, typically a dealer bank. Such support might include managing the connectivity to the CCP; managing collateral and settlement processes; and funding default fund requirements. In some ‘guaranteed’ sponsored models, direct access can be extended to an even wider range of participants, supported by greater obligations of the sponsor, for example to step in and make margin payments on behalf of the sponsored member. Arrangements can therefore sit at different points along a spectrum. By allocating responsibilities differently between clients, clearing members, and the CCP, they create different trade-offs between market access, balance sheet efficiency, incentives to provide intermediation, and overall market resilience.
Improvements in access to client clearing may themselves encourage greater use of clearing and catalyse the evolution of markets over time.
The measures I have discussed so far operate primarily through the liquidity supply channel. But recent episodes have demonstrated that liquidity stress is often driven not simply by a shortage of liquidity supply, but by sudden increases in liquidity demand.
This is where margining and haircut practices become important, reducing the build-up of extreme and unmanageable leverage, strengthening counterparty risk management, and lowering the likelihood of abrupt position liquidations.
In some circumstances, zero or near-zero haircuts can be justified by risk-reducing features such as netting and portfolio margining arrangements, which lower the overall exposure of the lender of leverage to its counterparty by recognising offsetting positions across different portfolios. However, while these arrangements can explain an important share of observed near-zero haircuts, we found that competitive considerations also play a role in the setting of very low haircuts – whereby the haircut is not set on risk grounds, but to avoid losing the client to competitors.footnote [7] This matters because near-zero or negative haircuts that are not directly linked to underlying risk can facilitate the build-up of unmanageable levels of leverage at little cost, and increase vulnerabilities in periods of market stress. More broadly, these findings support ongoing efforts by policymakers to strengthen the resilience of core funding markets and reduce vulnerabilities associated with extreme leverage in non-bank financial institutions.
Considering policy across these areas inevitably involves trade-offs. Poorly calibrated measures could reduce market-making capacity, shift activity elsewhere, or create unintended incentives. Margin and collateral arrangements that limit netting opportunities or prevent the recognition of genuine risk offsets can increase funding pressures precisely when market participants are already under stress.
From a financial stability perspective, the objective is not simply to demand more collateral from market participants. It is to ensure that collateral and margin requirements reflect underlying risks while avoiding unnecessary demands on liquidity during periods of stress.
This raises an important question: can the same level of risk protection be achieved while reducing unnecessary liquidity demands? This is one reason why appropriately designed cross-margining arrangements are attracting increasing interest, as they can improve collateral efficiency and reduce unnecessary liquidity demands where genuine risk offsets exist. However, cross-margining is not a free good. The scope for recognising offsets has to be determined by genuine offsets in the risks, noting asset correlations that appear stable in normal times may become less reliable during periods of stress. Realising the benefits of cross-margining also requires effective legal and operational arrangements and close cooperation across infrastructures and jurisdictions.
No single measure is likely to be a silver bullet for the resilience of gilt repo markets.
Measures that promote the appropriate pricing and management of leverage, support clearing adoption, broaden access to central clearing, and improve collateral efficiency should be viewed as complementary rather than substitutes. Considered together, they may offset some of the costs or limitations that would arise if any individual measure were implemented in isolation.
As it happens, and thankfully, that is what system-wide surveillance is helping us understand. It will certainly inform which policy package we put forward.footnote [8] As we said in the past, doing nothing is not an option.footnote [9] We intend to publish a comprehensive update on this, including potential policy proposals, in early 2027.
Many of these issues are inherently cross-border, and we continue to work closely with international partners through the Financial Stability Board and other fora to strengthen the resilience of market-based finance globally, where surveillance is high on the agenda. We are strong supporters of initiatives such as the FSB’s Nonbank Data Taskforce to break down barriers to transparency in these inherently global markets. The changes we see to the UK’s financial system are also being seen by our fellow regulators around the world, so we are far from alone in investigating these issues.
Conclusion
Of course the challenge of interpreting vast quantities of data to make sense of complex, interconnected systems is not unique to financial regulation. Let me conclude with a famous example of system-wide thinking from history. Often, the deployment of newly invented radar technology is credited with winning the Battle of Britain. But it was not one innovation that won out: not superior radar, better guns, or faster pilots. RAF fighter command understood that it was getting the right data where it needed to go that would win the battle. It was in setting up the famous Dowding System in the 1930s – a central command that could filter thousands of data points from radar systems, civilian spotters, and reconnaissance planes, turn those observations into system-wide insight, and relay them back out to gunners and fighter squadrons, giving them the information they needed to make front line decisions – that made British air defence so effective.
They had a system-wide mindset. And that mindset is bound to be powerful as we adapt to a new era of complexity and interconnectedness in the financial system. As central banks and regulators we have a unique vantage point over the whole system. Post-crisis reforms gave us more data than ever before. But our objective is not more and more data for its own sake. It is to draw from it genuinely system-wide insight. And then to share that aggregate data and insight back with the financial system to support its enduring ability to self-stabilise autonomously.
The more reliably it does that, the more selective we can be with policy interventions.
Thank you.
I would like to thank Gerardo Ferrara, Emily Evans, Nicholas Butt, Shefalika, Waris Panjwani, Michael Wood, Bradley Hudd, Julia Giese, David Bailey, and Sasha Mills for their comments and help in the preparation of these remarks.

Europe has 99 problems, but the paucity of bearish views about the Old Continent is not one of them! And yet, somewhat shockingly, European assets have outperformed US assets over the past two years. View from the markets: A critical earnings season approaches

By
DANIEL MORRIS 16.10.2026

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

In this article
Third quarter forecastsEM tech volatility

LinkedIn
Twitter
Facebook
Email

By Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist

As the third quarter earnings season kicks off, investors are nervous given the recent sharp rise in bond yields, which have so far had only a modest impact on equities. While the MOVE index, which measures expected bond market volatility, has returned to levels last seen with the start of the Iran war, the VIX index of equity volatility is not far from the lows for the year.

Listen to the article

Play00:0005:47Volume

The dominance of technology hardware in driving earnings growth and equity price appreciation means that any disappointing announcements from these companies will likely be keenly felt. Expectations are high, with the sector globally forecast to see a doubling of earnings compared to the same quarter a year ago. For emerging markets, it is twice that.

These growth rates are substantially higher than those for other sectors, leading some to see the concentration of earnings growth this quarter as a sign of the market’s fragility. It is true that tech earnings will likely dominate the season. They account for nearly two-thirds of the increase in profits for equities globally, followed by energy stocks at 20% (see Exhibit 1).

The dominance of tech earnings, however, is not inherently bad if the other sectors are themselves generating sufficiently positive growth in profits, even if the absolute increase in profits is far less than for technology. For this quarter, however, that is only partly the case.

The median earnings growth for the remaining sectors (that is, excluding tech and energy) is 7%, which is not particularly high. The materials sector is the one expected to see the strongest growth, but most of the forecasts for the other sectors are comparatively low (see Exhibit 2). If this pattern were to continue into the quarters ahead, one would indeed expect the market to be vulnerable as technology would be practically the sole source of profit expansion.

For 2027, however, the pattern is forecast to be different. Earnings growth for the energy sector turns negative, while it moderates for the tech sector. The growth rate for the remaining sectors rises to 12%, spread more evenly across the sectors. That should be sufficient to support ongoing market appreciation.

Third quarter forecasts

The importance of the tech and energy sectors for earnings is reflected in the third quarter forecasts for country and regional indices. Growth rates for indices with a large share of tech or energy stocks are high, while excluding these sectors results in lower figures. For example, we noted that emerging market tech stocks earnings are expected to increase more than four-fold, but for the remaining sectors the forecast is just 11%. In Europe, the 29% gain expected for the index this quarter is reliant on the energy sector; if we exclude it, the growth rate drops to 17% (which is still good; see exhibit 3).

EM tech volatility

Despite the renewed increase in oil prices over the last week, and the higher-than-expected US CPI (consumer price index) inflation data, Treasury yields have dropped by more than 20 basis points from their recent peak. This has prompted a modest rebound in non-tech equities globally. The tech hardware sector, however, has seen another wave of selling, concentrated in South Korea, as it was last July.

We have always expected above-average volatility in the tech sector because of the newness and significance of the artificial intelligence phenomenon. Price gains have been so large, and earnings expectations so high, that any marginal change in sentiment has a commensurately bigger impact.

We remain positive on the medium-term outlook and see volatility along a rising trend. Nonetheless, the impact of AI investment should continue to broaden to other sectors, notably in the US, allowing for the wider breadth of earnings, as shown in Exhibit 2.

articles.title: Disaster response and resilience in rural America
articles.text:
Commentary

Disaster response, recovery, and resilience in rural America

Research summary of America’s Rural Future symposium | August 6, 2026

Compiled by:
Anthony F. Pipa,

Anthony F. Pipa

Senior Fellow
- Global Economy and Development, Center for Sustainable Development

Brent Orrell,

Brent Orrell

Senior Fellow
- American Enterprise Institute

Adam Aley, and

AA

Adam Aley

Policy Analyst
- Global Economy and Development, Center for Sustainable Development

Madeline Tong

MT

Madeline Tong

Research Assistant
- American Enterprise Institute

October 23, 2026

A review of disaster risk highlights the limits of existing measures and suggests that disaster reforms must preserve the federal role in providing financial resources to address severe local losses while also advancing state and local resilience.

Federal disaster policy remains largely reactive. Shifting toward investment in preparedness and mitigation would build lasting local capacity, especially if designed around the constraints rural communities face.

Competitive programs for disaster preparedness, mitigation, and resilience often favor jurisdictions with existing staff and resources, leaving higher-risk, low-capacity communities with limited support. This suggests improved targeting and operational shifts can help ensure federal resources reach the rural communities that would maximize the public benefit.

Members of America's Rural Future Commission meet with local emergency management and disaster recovery officials during a 2026 site visit to Hindman Settlement School in Kentucky, which is still rebuilding from the 2022 flood that swept through the region. Photo: Junjie Ren/Brookings

A partnership between

16 min read

Bluesky Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.comBluesky

This research summary draws on insights generated by America’s Rural Future: Brookings-AEI Commission on U.S. Rural Prosperity.

Executive summary

As climate-related risks intensify, rural America is disproportionately exposed to the economic and social consequences of natural disasters. Many rural communities face structural vulnerabilities that complicate disaster planning and recovery, including aging infrastructure, long distances to emergency services, limited housing supply, and less administrative capacity to access and manage recovery resources. These constraints make costly disasters consequential for long-term rural prosperity. Current attention to reforming federal disaster assistance creates an opportunity to bring rural concerns to the foreground and ensure rural realities are reflected in effective and sustainable disaster policy.
The symposium examined the federal disaster system across the full continuum, including mitigation, preparedness, and resilience in addition to immediate response and long-term recovery, which often garner the most attention. The opening session considered how disaster exposure, vulnerability, organizational capacity, climate risk, and insurance are measured, and whether those measures reflect the diversity of rural conditions. A second session examined federal policy, the changing role of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and the unresolved distribution of responsibilities among federal, state, and local governments. The third discussion explored investments, institutions, partnerships, and local relationships that can help rural communities strengthen long-term resilience. Across the sessions, participants repeatedly noted that making information and funding available is not the same as having the capacity or incentives to use these resources.
A review of disaster risk in rural America exposed the limits of existing measures. Disasters affect people and places differently, and factors such as social vulnerability and local government capacity shape communities’ ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from disasters, including their ability to invest in mitigation. Participants considered how measures such as the Social Vulnerability Index and Rural Capacity Index can help illustrate these differences and give a fuller picture of disaster risk and resilience. Participants said that no single measure captures disaster exposure across every rural community. In Glendive, Montana, decades of federal studies documented a severe flood risk without, until 2025, producing a funded solution, illustrating why measuring risk does not necessarily lead to resilience.
The discussion identified local capacity as a key determinant for evaluating risk exposure, with constraints on staff time, fiscal resources, project development, and coordination shaping how well a community can prepare for and respond to disasters. Turning to insurance and climate models responsible for communicating these risks, participants agreed that models should be fit for purpose and transparent about uncertainty but did not resolve how insurance should account for geographic specificity, data used for pricing, affordability concerns, or how technical risk information should be communicated to policyholders and policymakers.
The second session focused on federal disaster policy and the future of FEMA. The nation’s disaster system spans several federal programs, each operating under separate authorities, providing funding at different stages of disaster assistance—preparedness, response, and recovery—and distributing funds on different timelines. Declaration thresholds and damage assessments can also understate the cost of disasters in rural communities. Funding remains largely reactive rather than preventive, making it difficult for communities to invest in mitigation and preparedness efforts to reduce future disaster costs.
Recent proposals for FEMA reform emphasize shifting responsibility toward states, reducing declarations and federal spending, and changing declaration criteria. The discussion focused on how the federal government could balance its role as a backstop with a more active role in mitigation. While participants agreed that building state capacity to respond to disasters would be a worthwhile goal, they argued that the FEMA Review Council’s recommendations do not say where disaster assistance funding would come from in the absence of federal support, as costs from disasters are often prohibitively expensive for state and local governments. Participants broadly supported simpler, faster, and more consistent delivery of federal disaster aid. Differences arose over which reforms require congressional action (including amendments to the Stafford Act), which can be made administratively, and how to balance flexibility with legitimate fiduciary safeguards.
The final session examined how long-term resilience is built in practice. Recovery and mitigation planning is not a discrete project; it involves building resilience across housing, infrastructure, land management, and more. The social capital needed for this planning in rural communities is often informal and hard to build through standalone projects, so participants advocated for the creation of long-term recovery groups and related networks that can remain in place, even after disasters, so communities retain the networks and knowledge needed for long-term resilience. The discussion also considered how greater representation of local emergency managers in debates over disaster assistance reform could ensure that the specific conditions of rural communities are accounted for. Participants also noted that rural communities often possess resources and assets to improve disaster resilience, but do not know what first steps to take, or prioritize other concerns because the political and policy incentives to focus on disaster mitigation are low.
Across the symposium, a recurring theme was that many vulnerable rural communities have limited capacity for disaster resilience, making them less able to compete for mitigation funding and more vulnerable to the next disaster. Participants argued that breaking this cycle requires moving beyond reactive, project-based assistance toward sustained support for the staffing, coordination, and institutional capacity communities need to build resilience. Important questions remain about how to measure vulnerability, price and communicate risk fairly, reform federal disaster assistance, and help rural communities move from identifying disaster risks to implementing solutions.

Key insights
Participants highlighted the following as foundational elements for evaluating and improving disaster assistance in rural areas:

Disaster reform must preserve the federal role in providing financial resources to address severe local losses while also advancing state and local resilience.
Federal disaster policy remains predominantly reactive. Disaster reforms would benefit from investments that strengthen preparedness and mitigation and build durable local capacity, taking rural constraints and characteristics into account.
Rural disaster risk cannot be captured by a single measure: Separate measures of exposure, social vulnerability, and organizational capacity, along with consistent data indicators, are needed to measure preparedness and track progress.
Identifying risk is not the same as having the capacity to address it. Rural communities are often aware of their exposure to disasters but lack the resources to prepare for or respond to them.
Competitive programs for disaster preparedness, mitigation, and building disaster resilience often favor jurisdictions with existing staff and resources, leaving higher-risk, low-capacity communities with limited support, suggesting that noncompetitive assistance could better serve them.
Insurance pricing can have far-reaching implications for the affordability of living in disaster-prone rural communities. Pricing should accurately convey risk without disproportionately punishing rural residents living in disaster-prone areas.
Rural communities with limited or at-risk housing supply are especially vulnerable after a disaster. When residents cannot find local housing, they may be forced to leave, thereby weakening the local tax base, workforce, and human capital needed to recover.
Rural communities rely heavily on social capital and local organizations to sustain recovery efforts. Supporting long-term recovery groups between disasters helps preserve the resilience needed to prepare for and respond to future events more effectively.
Disaster reforms should incorporate local emergency managers’ experience, since they see firsthand where current disaster assistance systems work and where they fail.
Outside organizations and extension systems can strengthen rural resilience when they reinforce local capacity and invest in the leaders and institutions doing work on the ground.

Ongoing debates and research priorities
Symposium participants reached broad agreement on the insights above, but several tensions remain unresolved.

Measuring rural disaster resilience

Issue: A recurring question was how resilience should be defined and measured to improve rural disaster policy. Participants described the county-level baseline resilience indicators for communities spanning six capital domains—human well-being and cultural, economic and financial, infrastructure and housing, institutional and governance, community capital, and environmental. It remains unclear how these six domains should be measured, weighed against one another, and translated into resilience strategies. Another unresolved question was whether a single standardized index can capture these varied indicators without obscuring local conditions and changes over time.
Research: Given the inherent differences in exposure and vulnerability within and between rural communities, what measures can best help policymakers track rural disaster resilience? Should these six domains be weighted or prioritized differently? How can a framework enable comparisons across rural communities while accounting for local conditions and change over time?

Insurance pricing and risk communication

Issue: Participants debated how disaster risk should be measured and reflected in insurance pricing for at-risk rural communities. Insurance pricing can communicate risk, especially in rural communities in disaster-prone areas, but participants did not resolve how geographically specific premiums should be, whether forward-looking climate projections have inflated near-term risk estimates, how to weigh historical variability, or how to address affordability and financing. As risk models and insurance markets continue to evolve, the challenge is to convey risk accurately without making coverage unaffordable for rural households unable to retrofit or relocate.
Research: How can insurance data and pricing better serve rural policyholders? How should insurance risk premiums be calculated, and at what geographic scale should premiums be set? How should pricing balance historical variability and forward-looking projections? How can this information be used in a way that does not make living in rural communities prohibitively expensive?

Preserving the federal role in disaster assistance

Issue: State and local governments rely on the federal government when the financial impact of disasters outstrips their financial capabilities, so proposals to reduce federal funding and shift financial responsibility for recovery to state and local governments drew concern from participants. The challenge is not that state and local governments, including rural communities, lack the leadership capacity to lead recovery efforts, but that they need access to sufficient, predictable, and flexible funding to meet their needs. Strengthening state leadership and capacity to take on a greater role in recovery is worthwhile, but it must be balanced with adequate federal resources to address immediate humanitarian needs as well as build the resilience and preparedness to mitigate future effects. These issues raise the question of how to best strengthen state and local leadership, provide resources and incentives for mitigation and preparedness, while preserving the federal government’s role as a backstop when disasters exceed state and local resources.
Research: How should the federal government balance providing adequate resources when disasters exceed state and local capacity with creating incentives and support for state and local governments to invest in preparedness, mitigation, and long-term resilience?

Scope of disaster reform

Issue: Participants broadly agreed that disaster assistance should be delivered more quickly, consistently, and with fewer administrative burdens, since some rural communities currently wait years to receive federal reimbursement for eligible costs incurred during disasters. However, perspectives differed over which reforms require congressional action, and which changes FEMA can pursue under its existing authority without new legislation. Some said that because Congress establishes FEMA’s statutory responsibilities and appropriates disaster funding, major changes to the declaration process, funding structure, or the Stafford Act would require legislation or appropriations. Alternatively, others proposed that FEMA already has the authority to implement some of these reforms without new legislation, suggesting that these administrative reforms can begin within the agency. The Review Council’s own report states a preference for legislative action, and the Congressional Research Service (CRS) notes that executive action could carry out several recommendations, including new criteria for major disaster declarations; the bipartisan Fixing Emergency Management for Americans Act (H.R. 4669) is the main congressional vehicle.
Research: Which disaster-assistance reforms can and should FEMA pursue under its existing authority to lessen administrative burdens for rural communities and speed the reimbursement process, and which structural or funding changes require congressional action through amendments to the Stafford Act, other legislation, or appropriations? What institutional barriers limit FEMA’s use of the flexibility it already possesses?

Investments that build durable implementation capacity

Issue: Questions arose over which investments in capacity and coordination most effectively strengthen rural communities’ ability to build durable disaster resilience. Under the current federal disaster-assistance system, funding is often made available only after a disaster has occurred. The limited mitigation and preparedness programs that exist are primarily awarded on a competitive basis, often excluding low-capacity, high-risk rural communities. While participants agreed that part of the solution lies in shifting from a project-based approach to disaster assistance toward more sustained, place-based investments, it remains unclear which investments are most effective for rural communities to build the local capacity needed to prepare for and respond to disasters.
Research: What kinds of investments in disaster mitigation, preparedness, and planning are best for building capacity and reducing the long-term costs of disasters? How can assistance be offered so that lower-capacity communities can access and use funding?

Local commitment and community agency

Issue: Participants debated whether capacity is always the central obstacle to rural disaster resilience or whether local commitment and political will can be equally important. Participants pointed out that investing in disaster mitigation when disasters have not yet occurred can be challenging, as rural local officials, who are often operating within constrained budgets, may have little incentive to pursue preventive action. Since the federal disaster system is largely reactive, it provides limited funding and few incentives for communities to address risks before disasters occur. At the same time, participants cautioned that apparent inaction may reflect overall distrust in the federal disaster assistance system. The question of how to encourage communities to exercise local agency would benefit from further research.
Research: To what extent do local commitment and political will affect the implementation of disaster resilience measures? How should policymakers distinguish a perceived lack of local commitment from a lack of staff, funding, or means? How can policy encourage local agency without shifting unreasonable responsibility onto communities with limited resources?
