There is only one Goldman Sachs.Discover CareersWORKING AT GSStudentsLife at GSBenefitsFeatured OfficesOpen RolesMarketsWhy Luxury Goods Companies’ Revenues Are Forecast to ClimbOct 22, 2026Share Makers of luxury goods are poised for faster revenue growth after several years of sluggish sales. Goldman Sachs Research forecasts 7% revenue growth for luxury-goods companies in 2027, up from 6% in 2026, based on a basket of key luxury-brand stocks. This represents a solid recovery and a rebuttal of the argument by some bears “that the sector may have gone ex-growth for an extended period,” according to Goldman Sachs Research. The US has become a surprising bright spot for luxury goods, with behavior shifting in a market where buying habits have not fully reflected the significant number of wealthy consumers. The outlook for luxury brands is improving after several years of lackluster performance, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
A basket of large, publicly traded luxury-goods makers is forecast to increase revenue by 7% in 2027, Erwan Rambourg, head of Europe Luxury and Lifestyle in Goldman Sachs Research, writes in a report. This is an improvement from an expected 6% growth rate in 2026, when the sector came out of several years of weaker performance.
“We view this as a solid recovery for an industry that has faced a prolonged period of sluggish performance,” Rambourg writes.
The market capitalization for luxury-goods stocks increased in 2022, after the stock market swoon caused by the Covid pandemic. Luxury stocks benefited from “exuberant spending,” Rambourg notes, but this was followed by a period of aggressive price increases and a slower pace of innovation from the sector.
What is the outlook for luxury goods companies?

Luxury-goods makers’ share prices have fallen over the past three or four years, but so have earnings estimates, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The result is that valuations do not look particularly attractive, and they also don’t appear stretched. “But we think valuation alone is rarely a catalyst for investors to buy or sell shares in the sector,” Rambourg writes. “Instead, it is more a function of sales momentum, which we see picking up soon.”
Why luxury goods sales have been sluggish

The industry has faced multiple challenges. China’s ongoing property slump, US tariffs in 2025, jittery equity markets, upcoming midterm elections and higher rates, as well as the ongoing Middle East conflict and other geopolitical tensions have weighed on spending decisions.

“There have been many reasons for consumers to cancel or delay purchases of discretionary products,” Rambourg writes. Still, these broader factors probably haven’t been the main constraint, he says, attributing the weak performance in recent years mostly to “a degree of strategic inertia” among luxury brands.
Price hikes after the Covid pandemic, which were perceived as excessive by some observers, likely played a larger role in the slowdown in growth for luxury goods. More affordable luxury brands benefited as traditional high-end names hiked prices—estimated at around 60% between mid-2019 and mid-2026—opening space in the market that they could fill, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
“As a direct impact of elevated price points and a value proposition that became less compelling across many brands, it appears that many target consumers decided to pass on purchasing luxury goods,” Rambourg writes.
Alongside the aggressive price increases, limited innovation by the industry in the post-Covid period led to diminished consumer interest, and store traffic tailed off. That said, a number of luxury companies have new CEOs and creative directors who started presenting their collections last year. “We believe that it likely takes three to four collections for consumers to recognize—and possibly buy into—the change,” Rambourg writes.
Why the US may still be an emerging market for luxury

For many years there has been “a surprising disconnect between wealth in the US (high) and luxury demand among American consumers (low),” Rambourg points out. The market was likely restrained by a “guilt factor” or by “outlet culture,” he says. However, behaviors have begun to change since the Covid pandemic.
“The appetite of American consumers for luxury goods has picked up strongly,” he writes. Luxury brands have taken notice, and store openings are multiplying.
“While it may sound counterintuitive, we still think the US is an emerging market for luxury goods,” he adds.
Elsewhere in the world, South Korean demand growth may be somewhat fragile because it is linked to wealth in the country’s tech-heavy and volatile equity market. The importance of Hong Kong for luxury brands has diminished over time, but the market is showing signs of recovery, with both local consumers and visitors from mainland China supporting sales growth, according to Goldman Sachs Research.
The luxury goods companies Goldman Sachs Research covers have recorded average top-line growth of 6% annually over the past 25 years.
“While growth has been pedestrian of late,” sales levels exceed what a 6% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) would have implied since just before the Covid pandemic in 2019, Rambourg points out. “In other words, the bear argument that the sector may have gone ex-growth for an extended period is not one we agree with,” he writes.
What is the longer-term outlook for the luxury goods sector?

To help understand where the sector and individual luxury goods makers may be headed, the report includes a benchmarking framework. This provides a way to think about long-term growth drivers, broken down as seven Cs.
One of the Cs is clout, and Rambourg posits that “big is beautiful” in the luxury sector. He notes that bigger brands not only tend to secure better locations, but they also benefit from lower rent as a percentage of sales. Another is categories, with some consumer verticals, such as jewelry, having better growth potential than others, such as beauty products.
Other considerations in the framework include: consumer caliber, referencing the relative resilience of high-net-worth consumers, which can likewise make high-end brands more resilient; and creativity, which may be difficult for equity analysts to quantify but does come into play in assessing prospects for luxury companies.
Rounding out the list are consistency, which gets to the clarity of brand positioning; codes and icons, which are not necessarily loud logos but can be a discreet symbol, pattern, or logo only identifiable by people who know the products well; and finally, corporate considerations, as many luxury-goods companies are partly owned and run by family members.

articles.title: China’s Growing Grip On Printed Circuit Boards
articles.text:
China’s Growing Grip On Printed Circuit Boards

Laila Khawaja

Gavekal Technologies: Chips | 15 Oct 2026

China accounts for nearly 60% of the global production value of printed circuit boards, foundational components in numerous defense and civil applications. AI is driving the demand for advanced PCBs and tightening the supply of various critical upstream materials. Chinese PCB makers are investing unprecedented amounts to expand advanced capacity, while upstream suppliers allocate scarce supplies towards higher-value AI products, both of which squeeze conventional PCB manufacturers. These trends could accelerate industry consolidation and strengthen China’s leading players, at a time when foreign governments are seeking to reduce dependence on Chinese PCBs.

As the Communist Party enters its intense “campaign season” to prepare for a major political transition in 2027, reading Beijing's actions and responses may become more difficult as domestic politics weigh on its behavior more than usual.Link CopiedBy Damien MaPublished on Oct 22, 2026The weathervane of Chinese politics shifts the most in the spring and autumn. Generally speaking, spring is when major policies are decided, usually at the National People’s Congress (NPC), while autumn is when politics are front and center, typically at the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) Central Committee plenary sessions, or plenums.The Fifth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee, slated for October 26, is one of these occasions. It will likely be an unusually potent barometer of the direction of Chinese politics because this Fifth Plenum essentially kicks off the political transition that culminates in the selection of new top leaders of the CCP at the 21st Party Congress in October 2027.The coming year, then, is as close to a “campaign season” as the Chinese system has, with a hefty dose of Leninist characteristics. Personnel movements will intensify, party discipline will tighten, and political jostling and horse trading will take place. Much of that process, as is well known by now, will be predictably opaque.Outcomes may be difficult to see immediately, but the absence of observable evidence does not mean evidence of absence when it comes to Chinese politics. Personnel matters, in fact, tend to matter more than other indicators for assessing how the CCP top brass is thinking about its future.

What’s a Plenum?

Plenums are high-level political events that typically take place seven times between one party congress and the next over five years. Each plenum is headed by the CCP general secretary and convened by the Central Committee, which is selected every five years at a party congress. At the plenums, decisions are made on personnel, ideology, party discipline, and major economic policies.

The first plenum confirms the new leadership at the start of the new party congress, while the last plenum approves the work report in preparation for the next party congress. While these bookend plenums are more pro forma, it’s the second to sixth plenums that usually provide significant decisions and signals of where the political winds are blowing.

To wit, the Third Plenum in 2013 unveiled an economic reform program that gave markets the “decisive role” in allocating resources. The Fifth Plenum in 2015 approved the 13th Five-Year Plan and quietly ended the one-child policy. The Sixth Plenum in 2021 adopted a historical resolution that essentially placed Xi Jinping alongside Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping ahead of Xi’s third term.

In terms of personnel, in July 2024, the Third Plenum stripped former foreign minister Qin Gang of his Central Committee seat. The Fourth Plenum in 2025 ratified the expulsion of nine senior officials, among them Central Military Commission vice chairman He Weidong. This is especially so after a period of intense purges within the CCP and the People’s Liberation Army. The latest reported investigation of former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan, eight years after his retirement, is another case in point. Huang was of course involved in one of the most significant political crises facing the party in 2012 that also ushered in the era of Xi Jinping. This case raises the prospect that retired elites are not immune from getting caught in the politics ahead of the 21st Party Congress.Other stones will be turned and more political targets will be on the menu. But how key roles get filled between now and the March 2027 NPC will also offer important clues to how the party evaluates and selects officials ahead of the political transition. While it is far too early to speculate on the potential composition of the new top leadership at the Politburo level, it is clear that Xi Jinping intends to serve an unprecedented fourth term as general secretary through 2032.Still, major questions loom over the 2027 transition, all of which point to the essential uncertainty over Xi’s succession plan or lack thereof. As the Chinese political campaign season unfolds, we will examine this question more deeply, including a retrospective of Xi’s fifteen-year run at the helm of Chinese politics and whether that yields clues to what’s in store post-2027. But first, here’s how the upcoming Fifth Plenum matters as Chinese politics kicks into high gear over the next year.Why This Fifth Plenum Is UnusualIn the two previous party congress cycles, both Fifth Plenums focused on ratifying China’s massive economic blueprints, or Five-Year Plans. However, this October’s Fifth Plenum deviates from this pattern and is instead expected to center on politics. Indeed, on September 21, the Politburo issued the Central Committee’s Decision on Several Major Issues Concerning the Persistent Advancement of Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance, signifying that party politics will be the main theme of the Fifth Plenum.This echoes the October 2016 Sixth Plenum, which was also convened the year before the 2017 political transition in which Xi paved the way to abolish presidential term limits. At that plenum, party governance was made a central priority. It adopted and revised two documents, the “Norms on Political Life Within the Party Under the New Situation” and the “Regulations on Internal Supervision of the Communist Party of China,” reinforcing the institutionalization of political discipline and intra-party oversight. These measures helped embed anti-corruption enforcement and party self-policing more firmly in Xi-era governance.That plenum was followed by a series of high-level purges of senior party and military officials, with Sun Zhengcai, a Politburo member at the time, being the highest-profile politician to fall. All these personnel moves occurred between the Sixth and Seventh Plenums ahead of the 19th Party Congress.In contrast, the recent flurry of purges that targeted the military in particular arrived before this Fifth Plenum. Those that fell included Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli, who were charged with “seriously trampling on and undermining” the military system of ultimate responsibility. They seemed to have been accused of, more severely than usual, political disloyalty alongside corruption.Watching the Two Ps: Purges and PromotionsThe run-up to the 21st Party Congress will bring further personnel changes as the party manages its leadership ranks ahead of the 2027 transition. The key question is not whether disciplinary action will continue, but what the pattern of removals and appointments reveal about the direction of elite politics. Two indicators deserve particular attention: purges, in terms of scale and intensity, and promotions, in terms of how vacancies are being filled.Purges: Continued Enforcement of the BaselineFurther disciplinary action would be consistent with existing anti-corruption enforcement and political discipline under Xi, but would not be particularly revelatory of the personnel landscape ahead of the 21st Party Congress. A sustained change in the seniority of those targeted, the institutions affected, or the emphasis placed on political loyalty alongside corruption, would be more revealing.Such changes in the scale or character of disciplinary enforcement could therefore offer clues about how intra-party power balances are shifting, because each senior official is usually the central node of an entire political network. Purges, therefore, are as much about the individual as it is about targeting those networks and alliances.But whether purges intensify remains an outstanding question. That’s because the current cycle differs from the 2016–2017 cycle. Whereas the Sixth Plenum in 2016 preceded a series of prominent corruption cases before the 19th Party Congress, a spate of major military purges have already occurred ahead of this 2026 Fifth Plenum. This difference makes the coming months worth observing for any significant changes in the pattern.Promotions: Who Moves Up?Promotions will likely be a more revealing indicator of how the leadership is managing the transition. Disciplinary actions have left numerous senior positions vacant, so appointments will determine what experience, institutional background, and networks to the top leadership, particularly Xi himself, are elevated ahead of the transition. This is especially so for a younger generation of political rising stars that will likely do relatively well in this political transition, even if they do not climb to the apex just yet.These decisions will offer concrete evidence of how the party is managing its senior ranks leading up to the 21st Party Congress. A promotion into a senior party or military role, for example, will carry different weight than an appointment to a government ministry. Assuming that Xi remains in charge, then networks will be an important criterion for promotions, given that those currently sitting on the Politburo Standing Committee are all of the president’s men.Ultimately, the October 2026 Plenum provides a baseline for assessing how Chinese elite politics will progress and how stable the transition will be. It will not provide clear answers but will likely leave some breadcrumbs to be followed and to discern what patterns form and whether significant moves are made in personnel.As Beijing heads into its political season, reading some of its actions can become more difficult, as the proximate cause of its behavior could be due to managing domestic politics. But the heightened level of domestic uncertainty tied to the political transition also means that there’s strong vested interest for Beijing to maintain a more stable external environment during this period.AcknowledgmentsThe author thanks Hannah Zou for her research and support.About the AuthorDamien MaDirector, Carnegie China; Maurice R. Greenberg Director’s ChairDamien Ma is the director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director’s Chair of Carnegie China, an East Asia-based research center with its office in Singapore. For two decades, Damien has worked at the intersection of markets, policy, and global affairs, becoming a leading voice on China’s ascendance and U.S.-China dynamics, the most consequential bilateral relationship of the century. But turning these technological achievements into commercial success will be a greater challenge.Tong ZhaoCommentaryChina Financial MarketsThe Plaza Accord and Its Relevance for ChinaThe Plaza Accord was not an externally imposed punishment of Japan but part of a broader restructuring that Japanese economists and policymakers themselves recognized was necessary. articles.title: New Bank Start-Up Unit
articles.text:
New Bank Start-up Unit

The New Bank Start-up Unit provides information and support for those thinking of setting up a new bank in the UK.

On this pageIntroductionThinking of becoming a bank in the UK?Engaging with the NBSUNew Bank Pre-application engagementSubmitting the applicationThe application feeThe authorisation (including decision making) processRegulatory expectations as part of the assessment approachThe assessment – authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation)Life as an authorised bank (with restrictions - mobilisation)Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions)Resource links, new banks authorised since 2013 and contact details

Introduction
Firms that want to operate as banks in the UK (see ‘thinking of becoming a bank’ section) must be authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), with the consent of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
International banks seeking to establish a banking subsidiary and/or branch in the UK should, in parallel with referring to the NBSU website, consult SS5/21 (International banks: The PRA’s approach to branch and subsidiary supervision), as well as the FCA’s Approach to international firms publication Opens in a new window.
The New Bank Start-up Unit (NBSU) is a joint initiative set up by the UK financial regulators, the PRA and the FCA, to provide information and support for firms interested in, or currently applying for, authorisation as a bank in the UK.
To advance the PRA and FCA’s primary and secondary objectives (information on the PRA’s objectives, goals and latest business plan. Information on the FCA objectives Opens in a new window, both regulators will assess whether a firm meets the Threshold Conditions, which are the minimum standards that all firms must meet at their point of authorisation, and on an ongoing basis while operating as a bank.
The Threshold Conditions for the PRA and FCA (below) are set out in Schedule 6 to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 Opens in a new window.

Legal status: Deposit-takers must be corporates or partnerships;
Location of offices: A UK incorporated corporate body must maintain their head offices and, if one exists, their registered office in the UK;
Prudent conduct of business: The firm must conduct their business in a prudent manner, which includes having appropriate financial and non-financial resources;
Suitability: The firm must satisfy the PRA that they are a ‘fit and proper’ person with regard to all circumstances to conduct a regulated activity; and
Effective supervision: The firm must be capable of being effectively supervised by the PRA.

Effective supervision: The firm must be capable of being effectively supervised by the FCA;
Appropriate non-financial resources: The firm’s non-financial resources must be appropriate in relation to the regulated activities they seek to carry on, having regard to the FCA’s operational objectives;
Suitability: The firm must be a fit and proper person. The firm’s management must have adequate skills and experience and act with integrity (fitness and propriety). The firm must have appropriate policies and procedures in place, and it must appropriately manage conflicts of interest; and
Business model: The firm’s strategy for doing business must be suitable for a person carrying on the regulated activities it undertakes or seeks to carry on and must not pose a risk to the FCA’s objectives.

Thinking of becoming a bank in the UK?A ‘bank’ is an entity that carries out deposit-taking business. The PRA and the FCA glossaries define a ‘bank’ as a firm with a Part 4A permission, which includes accepting deposits and is a credit institution, but is not a credit union, friendly society, or building society.The Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 Opens in a new window defines the regulated activity of accepting deposits (see Chapter II Accepting Deposits) and stipulates that, to accept deposits, one of the following statements must be true:a) Money received by way of deposit is lent to others or;
b) A firm uses deposits to materially fund a business line.Firms must consider if their proposed business satisfies the definition of accepting deposits and be able to justify this assessment to regulators. You should also consider the following:

Firms should consider their options for accessing payment systems as early as possible and adequately reflect this in their plans. Payment systems are critical to allow the transfer of funds between people, businesses and financial institutions – new banks are unlikely to be able to operate without access to a payment system. The NBSU encourages firms to consider the guidance on payment systems access.
New banks can access a payment system in the following ways:
Full direct access – where the new bank will have a direct technical and settlement relationship with the payment system provider (PSP);
Direct technical access – where the new bank will have a direct technical relationship with the PSP but use a sponsor for settlement; or,
Indirect access – where an Indirect Access Provider (IAP) acts as the new bank’s sponsor for both technical and settlement sponsorship.
There are a variety of software vendors with products and services that may reduce the cost and complexity of the direct access option, as well as several IAPs providing indirect access offerings. Further information about direct and indirect access can be found on the Payments Systems Regulator Opens in a new window and Payment System Operators’ websites, and in the Code of Conduct for Indirect Access Providers Opens in a new window.

If the firm is already FCA solo-authorised (for example an investment firm seeking to broaden their funding base to take on retail deposits), they will need to apply to vary their permissions to add deposit-taking. Whilst this is a different regulatory transaction, the firm should follow the same authorisation process as fully unauthorised firms. In this instance, the NBSU recommends that, like unauthorised firms, the solo-regulated firm should follow the pre-application stages before applying to become authorised. In addition, the NBSU encourages FCA solo-authorised firms seeking dual authorisation to consider their capital and ownership structures and ensure that those are as simple as possible.

The use of certain sensitive words such as ‘bank’ and ‘banking’ in registered company names is controlled by legislation to prevent the public from being misled. Firms cannot call themselves a ‘bank’ until they have been authorised by the PRA. Prospective firms must take care when liaising with press, prospective investors, and posting on social media, prior to obtaining authorisation.
Firms may begin the application process as ‘Example Ltd’ but only once they are authorised as a bank can they call themselves ‘Example Bank Ltd’.
Firms must seek the FCA’s consent before using domain names that include sensitive words including ‘bank’ and ‘banking’. Further information can be found on the FCA’s sensitive business name Opens in a new window page.

Please refer to ‘Should I become a bank Opens in a new window’ guide to help firms understand whether being a bank is the appropriate model for them.
Are there alternatives to being a bank?
Yes, please refer to the ‘alternatives to being a bank Opens in a new window’ guide for further information on some of the alternatives.

The NBSU is open to listening to proposals and answering any questions you may have - before any significant work has been undertaken towards becoming a bank in the UK. If you have a proposal that you would like to raise or discuss, please email NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk with your proposal/enquiry – someone from the team will get back to you within five working days.

Engaging with the NBSUTo navigate the authorisation process as efficiently as possible and achieve their objective of setting up a bank, firms should be ready, willing and organised. We have provided below some examples of how firms can demonstrate this. Please note that this is not an exhaustive list:
Ready and thinking ahead – Firms should ensure that they have a well thought through proposition which has undergone robust challenge and consideration of the inherent risks (this should also be appropriately reflected into their key documents). Firms should ensure that they will have in place appropriately skilled staff and operational infrastructure to commence trading at the point of being authorised. This includes a robust IT framework, a robust governance framework, risk management framework, premises, and finances;
Willing – Firms should demonstrate that they have done their research, understanding not only the activities that they will be undertaking but the rules and regulations which their business will be governed by; and
Organised – Firms should ensure that they are operationally ready to carry out the regulated activities at the time of their authorisation (if successful).
We aim to have positive regulatory relationships with firms along their journey, from pre-authorisation to becoming authorised and later becoming established banks. We do this by keeping an open and constructive dialogue:

Be open and honest;
Have considered the guidance provided on this website
Provide all the necessary information to undertake our assessments
Notify us of any changes, challenges or concerns as soon as possible
Develop plans, complete the necessary work, and prepare and send materials in good time for meetings with us;
Fully consider and address the feedback we provide on key documents such as the Regulatory Business Plan (RBP)/the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP)/the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP) documents
Understand, consider and demonstrate how they will meet the required standards at authorisation and on an ongoing basis.

To clearly set out the process and requirements for setting up a bank;
To host pre-application meetings to discuss the firm’s proposals and highlight any concerns;
To provide firms with clear feedback on their proposals including formal written feedback;
We will end our pre-application engagement with firms if our feedback is not adequately addressed in the development of their proposition and key documents
To help firms understand the standards required of being an authorised bank.

New Bank Pre-application engagement
(Optional but recommended)
The NBSU offers firms a ‘complimentary service’, which includes enhanced engagement and support as firms build out their proposals before applying for a banking licence.
Although pre-application engagement is optional and not part of the statutory authorisation process, it is something that the NBSU encourages firms to take advantage of at an early stage (feedback from previous applicant banks has shown how valuable they have found it).
Early engagement allows the NBSU to provide input into the development of regulatory business plans, by guiding potential applicants towards what the PRA and FCA are most interested in, as well as helping them understand regulatory requirements. It also allows the NBSU to identify any significant issues or showstoppers at an early stage.
Pre-application engagement with the NBSU is usually focussed around three stages (although this is flexible and all three stages might not be necessary):
i. business proposition;
ii. draft regulatory business plan; and
iii. technical sessions.
If you would like to take advantage of this complimentary pre-application engagement service, then please contact NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.

Although still early in a firm’s preparations, you will have reached the stage where you can present (usually as a PowerPoint presentation) high level information on your business model, financial forecasts, governance, source of funding, ownership, controllers and risks. You should also provide an indication of the timeframes that you are working towards and indicate whether you will be applying for full authorisation or authorisation with restrictions (also known as mobilisation), as this will impact your planning, as well as the information requirements for your application.
Upon receipt of your business proposition, the NBSU will review and schedule a meeting, typically within three weeks from date of receipt (this meeting may be over MS Teams so progress can be made as efficiently as possible). You will also receive written feedback within three weeks of the meeting.

The RBP forms a critical component of the assessment of a potential application, and therefore the NBSU expects your RBP to already be at a detailed stage prior to submission and should include the following:

Business model and financials covering business strategy, route to profitability, financial projections;
Market analysis and research that underpins the business model assumptions;
Corporate governance setting out board and committee structure as well as proposed approach for recruiting senior managers;
Risk register and stress testing;
Risk management and control framework;
Funding plans, which includes details around the owners and controllers. Where funding is still being sought, you should provide details of your plan to bring in investors;
Conduct risk of harm and consumer duty (if applicable);
Financial Crime Risk Management Framework;
Operational resilience covering outsourcing, IT infrastructure timescales to implement/test and business continuity;
Details of the regulated activities you wish to undertake (please refer to the application form for further information on the regulated activities that can be applied for);
Mobilisation plan (if applicable);

Please refer to the Regulatory Business Plan guide for further information on why an RBP is important, what should be included and the common challenges.
Once you have submitted your RBP (it is useful to be notified of the planned RBP submission date two weeks in advance), the NBSU will review and schedule a face-to-face or hybrid MS Teams meeting, typically within three weeks from date of receipt. You will also receive written feedback within the three weeks following the meeting.

At this stage, the expectation is that you have addressed all the feedback provided and can submit a fully developed RBP. For UK start-ups and subsidiaries of international banks, you will also have drafted and submitted your ICAAP and ILAAP documents by this stage.
The firm’s management team should own ICAAP and ILAAP and be able to discuss these in detail at the technical session. The ICAAP and ILAAP should have gone through a full review and challenge by someone other than the author (the Board or the key guiding minds of the firm), before they are submitted to the NBSU.
At this stage, the PRA will assess the ICAAP and ILAAP, which includes engagement with the relevant technical specialists. The assessment will focus on whether the ICAAP and ILAAP meet the relevant regulatory expectations and consider whether the documents would be sufficient to set capital and liquidity requirements during an application.
The NBSU will also consider the latest RBP to assess if there is any further feedback prior to the firm submitting the application. Further, depending on the nature of the proposed business model and operational design, the FCA may also look to hold focused technical sessions on the financial crime control framework.
Following the submission of the near final RBP, ICAAP and ILAAP, the NBSU will schedule a face to face or hybrid MS Teams meeting. Typically, this will be within six weeks from date of receipt. As this review involves technical specialists, it is important to give both the PRA and FCA as much notice as possible prior to submitting, and to provide at least two weeks' notice, so that both regulators can line up the necessary resource and avoid delays. You will also receive written feedback within three weeks of the meeting.

Submitting the application
The application process commences with the submission of the New Firm Authorisation application (and supporting documentation), and the payment of the PRA and FCA’s non-refundable application fee. It is entirely up to the firm to decide when it should submit its application, but this should be at a point where the firm can demonstrate that their business is ready, willing and organised to be authorised as a bank.
There are two routes available for applying to be a bank in the UK:

Full authorisation; or
Authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation) – this route is primarily targeted at UK start-ups. Although the Threshold Conditions still need to be met, the NBSU’s approach to the information requirements will be proportionate to the restrictions that will be put in place, and therefore will likely result in a quicker authorisation (the information instead will be required during the mobilisation period and will be assessed as part of the application to remove the restrictions). Please refer to the further information on mobilisation.

The application forms
Please note, firms will need to send an email with an electronic copy of their application (and supporting documentation) to the PRA at the following mailbox: NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.
If the file size exceeds 25 MB, please use multiple emails to accommodate your submission.

Full authorisation application form (doc)

Authorisation with restriction (mobilisation) application form (doc)

Branch application form (doc)

Corporate controller form (doc)

Individual controller form (doc)

Partnership controller form (doc)
Trust controller form (doc)

Please refer to Senior Managers Regime where the Long Form A, Short Form A and Form M can be downloaded.

Please refer to Holding company approvals.

Please refer to Banking capital instruments - pre/post-issuance notification (PIN).

This form can be downloaded from the FCA website: FCA IT Controls Form Opens in a new window.

The application fee
The PRA and the FCA Regulatory Transaction fees for applications for new authorisations are payable in accordance with PRA Rulebook Opens in a new window and FCA Handbook Opens in a new window.
The total fee payable (covers both PRA and FCA fees) to seek permission to accept deposits (other than a credit union) is £56,300.
The preferred method for payment is via BACS to the FCA, who will provide a single invoice covering both the PRA and FCA fees.
Please make the payment to the FCA using the details below:
Account name: FCA Collection account
Bank name: Lloyds Bank
Account number: 00828179
Sort code: 30-00-02
Swift code: LOYD GB 2LCTY
Iban code: GB68 LOYD 3000 0200 8281 79.
When you make the payment, please reference it with the following: Title: ‘New authorisation application’ and the ‘firm name’ (name of the firm applying for authorisation).
Please then email your remittance advice and payment details to: fcafees@fca.org.uk and NewBankstartupunit@bankofengland.co.uk.
Information on how to pay the fee is also contained within the application form.
Please note that in the case of a firm withdrawing its application, and later re-submitting another application, they would likely need to pay the full fee again.

The authorisation (including decision making) process
The NBSU will acknowledge receipt of your application within two working days.
Usually, the NBSU will communicate whether your application is complete or incomplete within three weeks of receiving it (if incomplete, the regulators will inform you of any missing information).

For complete applications (i.e., the NBSU has received the application fee and all the necessary applications and supporting documents, which should be of sufficient quality and detail for completion of the assessment) – the PRA targets four months to determine the application (with a statutory timeframe of within six months).
For incomplete applications – the PRA targets 10 months to determine the application (with a statutory timeframe of within twelve months).

During the assessment period the NBSU welcomes regular dialogue and encourages you to reach out as and when you need. The NBSU will keep you informed on the progress of any reviews and proactively highlight any significant risks or issues identified. In addition, the NBSU will typically meet monthly with the firm’s senior management.
The PRA aim to issue a decision as quickly as possible, but this depends on how complete your application is and how promptly you respond to our requests for information. We may have questions or need more details from you during our assessment. Responding quickly and thoroughly will help speed up the process.
The decision-making process:

Both the PRA and FCA will independently decide whether to authorise your bank.
Without FCA consent, the PRA cannot authorise your bank

If authorised, you'll receive:

An authorisation letter
A Scope of Permission Notice detailing your permissions and any requirements
A welcome pack

Your bank’s details will be added to the Financial Services Register on the date shown in the authorisation letter.

Initial notification
If during our assessment of the application we think there are grounds for refusing your application, we'll inform you both verbally and in writing where you'll have time to address our concerns.

Minded to refuse letter
If you can't address the concerns, we'll send you a letter explaining why and which rules or threshold conditions haven't been met.

At this point you can either withdraw your application (and reapply later when issues have been addressed) or, if you want to proceed, the PRA and FCA will follow its decision-making process
Issuing statutory notices (Warning Notices and Decision Notices)
Please refer to SoP1/24 - The Prudential Regulation Authority’s allocation of decision making and approach to supervisory decisions, which sets out

the PRA’s allocation of decision-making regarding statutory notices (Warning Notices, Decision Notices, and Supervisory Notices);
the PRA’s approach to decision-making on statutory notices in relation to supervisory decisions under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000; and
the PRA’s approach to publication of decisions in supervisory cases.

Regulatory expectations as part of the assessment approachThe assessment – full authorisationThe areas that the NBSU assess as part of a new bank application are set out below but should not be considered an exhaustive list. Firms are responsible for considering in detail all relevant laws, rules and regulatory policies, and ensuring that they understand and can fully comply with them.

Read information on ‘regulatory expectations’ (including where expectations are different for branches)
The assessment – authorisation with restrictions (mobilisation)
It is up to firms to propose to the NBSU which activities they complete in mobilisation (please refer to the application form for details of the activities that can be applies for). Therefore, the key for the NBSU’s assessment is that all the design work is complete with a clear plan to deliver everything with a plausible timeframe.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Life as an authorised bank (with restrictions - mobilisation)
Once a new bank is authorised with restrictions, it enters a mobilisation period, which typically lasts no longer than 12 months. During this time, the bank's deposit-taking permission is restricted to a total of £50,000, while it completes the remaining build-out of its operations. This period allows new banks to secure further investment, recruit staff, invest in IT systems, and commit to third-party suppliers, as they are now an authorised bank.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

The PRA and FCA anticipate that new banks will want to progress quickly through the mobilisation phase. This could take as little as a few months but cannot continue indefinitely and should take no longer than 12 months. For a new bank to exit mobilisation, they should submit a Variation of Permission (VoP) application via Connect.
Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Further information is contained within the mobilisation page.

Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions)
At this stage, the firm should be fully operational and in a position to fulfil its business proposition as agreed with the PRA and FCA.

Authorisation is only the start of the journey towards becoming an established bank.
New banks must always meet their capital and liquidity regulatory requirements and the Threshold Conditions.
New banks must ensure that they submit their regulatory returns on time and keep up to date with the latest regulatory information.
New banks must ensure that risk management frameworks and controls evolve commensurately with the scale of business growth.
The PRA and FCA will assess how new banks are managing the key prudential and conduct risks, respectively, to their businesses through supervisory engagement.
Read: Life as an authorised bank (without restrictions).

Resource links, new banks authorised since 2013 and contact details

SS3/21 Non-systemic UK banks: The Prudential Regulation Authority’s approach to new and growing banks – This outlines the PRA’s expectations of firms and new banks and how those evolve throughout the authorisation journey.
Climbing mountains safely – a speech by Sarah Breeden – This speech, published alongside the CP on the PRA’s approach to new and growing banks, sets out key aspects from the consultation (i.e. what firms need to consider becoming an established bank).
PRA’s approach to banking supervision – This sets out the PRA’s approach to supervising regulated firms.
SS5/21 International banks: The PRA’s approach to branch and subsidiary supervision – This sets out the PRA’s proposals regarding its approach to supervising the UK activities of PRA-authorised banks and designated investment firms that are headquartered outside of the UK or are part of a group based outside of the UK.
Financial Services Register Opens in a new window – Where a new bank’s details will appear and includes the mobilisation restriction applied.
Read: New banks authorised since 2013.
If you have any queries about becoming a new bank, please contact NewBankStartupUnit@bankofengland.co.uk.

articles.title: What stablecoins mean for banks, rates and equities
articles.text: The four ways stablecoins reach an equity portfolio9 min readFinanceAltcoinsDataStablecoins have grown beyond a crypto-market story. They can move the earnings and valuations of listed banks, exchanges and payment networks without an investor ever buying one. When people move cash from current accounts into tokens backed by Treasury bills, banks lose cheap funding and may have to replace it at a higher cost.Do stablecoins take deposits away from banks, and which banks are most exposed?Treasury advisers flagged $6.6T of US transactional deposits as exposed in April 2025 and total stablecoin supply equals 4.6% of that figure. An IMF study with data to June 2025 found no significant share price reaction in large or community banks to stablecoin demand shocks. So far, stablecoin adoption looks more like a margin risk than a funding shock. A stablecoin works like a very simple bank. Someone hands over a dollar and the issuer keeps safe assets against it, known as stablecoin reserves. A current account is cheap, steady funding, because customers rarely move it and earn little for leaving it there. When that dollar moves into a stablecoin, the bank has to replace it with funding that costs more.The scale so far is small next to the pool at stake. Total supply stood at $305.83B on 27 September 2026, 0.8% below the $308.16B of 31 March. Two issuers, Tether and Circle, hold 84.7% of it. A static market is itself the finding: the deposit threat is a question of years and policy, not of this quarter's growth rate.Exposure is uneven. Investors can screen on net interest income as a share of total revenue: lending-heavy banks, such as US regional lenders, score higher than diversified banks or investment banks, so they have more to lose if funding costs rise. The same screen works on European financials.The policy fight sets the speed. The GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025, requires one dollar of reserves for every token and bars issuers from paying interest to holders. It does not clearly stop exchanges paying rewards on tokens held on their platforms, and many do. According to the Congressional Research Service (6 March 2026) and the Council of Economic Advisers (April 2026), banks want exchanges to stop paying rewards on stablecoins, because those rewards make the tokens compete more directly with bank deposit accounts. Exchanges want to keep offering them. It is a fight over whether a token is allowed to look like a current account, with bank equities on one side and exchange equities on the other.How do stablecoins affect Treasury bill yields and short-term rates?Stablecoin reserves sit mostly in short-dated US government instruments, so supply growth adds demand at the front end. BIS research using data through March 2026 finds that a $3.5B inflow lowers three-month bill yields by 0.7 basis points on impact and about four basis points within ten days, with a larger effect when Treasury-market liquidity is strained.A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so the effect is real but small. An earlier version found that equal-sized outflows had a larger effect. The current BIS research does not restate that comparison, so treat the asymmetry as unsettled.In its Q2 2026 attestation release of 31 July 2026, Tether reported $187.8B of total assets at 30 June, with most reserves held in US government-backed instruments and short-term liquidity facilities.For an equity investor, growth is a mild tailwind for bill prices. A shrinking market could be a sharper shock, because the stress that triggers redemptions is when the bill market can least absorb the selling. The BIS paper measures the yield response to stablecoin flows; it does not show that redemptions occur when bill-market liquidity is weakest. Treat this as a risk scenario, not an observed outcome. Redemptions on that scale have not been tested. The largest seven-day fall in supply in the past year was $3.83B, in the week to 1 February 2026.What an equity investor takes from this is not a level but a variance. Stablecoins add a little to rate swings and do not set the level, but short rates feed bank funding costs, money market fund yields and the discount rate on every other asset.How are stablecoins changing settlement and market infrastructure?Stablecoins are becoming the cash leg of on-chain settlement, so distribution and settlement revenue is now contested. Circle’s five-year agreement with Binance, announced on 22 September 2026 with a $100M Binance equity investment, shows how much issuers lean on large distributors for reach.The settlement leg is the cash side of a trade, where money changes hands as the asset is delivered. On blockchains, that leg increasingly uses stablecoins. This is the most structural channel: its importance depends less on today’s supply growth than on where tokenised assets eventually settle. Where an asset settles, in which currency and on whose rails are revenue questions for exchanges, clearing houses, custodians and card networks, all of which are listed.Two features of the plumbing matter. A dollar that settles in seconds, at any hour, can be posted, moved and recalled in ways a bank wire cannot, which lets intermediaries hold smaller buffers and changes what their service is worth. And because stablecoin settlement never closes while shares trade on exchange hours, a timing gap opens between the two markets.Ethereum’s share of stablecoin supply fell from 53.0% to 48.0% between 31 March and 27 September 2026, while Tron rose from 28.0% to 30.9%, Solana from 4.8% to 5.4% and Hyperliquid from 1.7% to 2.5%. The shift indicates which networks are gaining a larger share of stablecoin liquidity and, with it, greater economic relevance.Distribution is where the rent settles. Circle’s release describes a $100M share purchase by Binance at a 5.0% discount, and a commercial agreement under which Binance promotes USDC and Circle provides infrastructure. It gives no fee terms. With total supply broadly flat and USDC share little changed (24.7% against 25.1% on 31 March), the deal suggests distribution has become a cost of defending reach. Whether it reduces issuer margins depends on terms Circle has not yet disclosed. The question for investors is not whether stablecoins win but which listed layer keeps the margin.Why are stablecoins starting to be backed by tokenised equities?Ethena said on 25 September 2026 that Binance will be its first venue for extending USDe’s basis trade into equity perpetual futures, and The Block reported that part of the backing will be tokenised US equities. Equities are becoming collateral for instruments priced like cash, which makes the quality of that collateral a diligence question.USDe is a synthetic dollar backed by a trade rather than bank deposits. Ethena holds tokenised equities, blockchain tokens that track listed shares, and shorts matching perpetual futures, derivatives without an expiry date, so price movements are designed to offset. The remaining return is the funding rate, a payment between traders for leverage. Cash-and-carry, in other words, with equities in place of commodities.This creates a new source of demand for tokenised shares and equity perpetuals, driven by collateral needs rather than a view on the company. The key question is whether the hedge holds under stress, given that equity-perpetual markets are far thinner than their crypto equivalents. Synthetic dollars can blur the line between cash-like instruments and equity-backed collateral.Ethena deserves a fair counterweight. USDe supply fell 74.7%, from $14.83B on 4 October 2025 to $3.75B on 28 April 2026, a redemption of that size settled without the instrument breaking, which is the test the design exists to pass. It stood at $4.94B on 27 September 2026. The practical step is not to form a view on any stablecoin. It is to know where in a portfolio the exposure already sits: regional bank margins, front-end rate swings, exchange and payment network revenue, and now the collateral behind instruments treated as cash.FAQsDo stablecoins take deposits away from banks, and which banks are most exposed? Some deposits move, but supply is flat and equals 4.6% of the $6.6T of US transactional deposits flagged as at risk. Deposit-funded lenders, such as US regional banks, carry the most exposure.How do stablecoins affect Treasury bill yields and short-term rates? Slightly: BIS research finds a $3.5B inflow lowers three-month bill yields by about 4 basis points within ten days.How are stablecoins changing settlement and market infrastructure? Settlement and distribution revenue is now contested between exchanges, custodians, clearing firms, card networks and issuers.Why are stablecoins starting to be backed by tokenised equities? Equity hedges widen the pool of assets that can back a synthetic dollar beyond crypto, at the cost of tying its stability to thinner equity derivatives markets.Published onOct 23rd, 2026WriterCoinShares

articles.title: ETF inflows hit record highs as investors embrace global equities and active strategies - BNP Paribas Asset Management - United States
articles.text:
European UCITS ETFs (EU regulated exchange-traded funds) attracted a record €125 billion in the third quarter, taking year-to-date inflows to almost €350 billion. Global equities led the way, Europe rebounded and emerging markets recovered, while Chinese equity ETFs continued to see outflows.

As Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research, explains to Chief Market Strategist, Daniel Morris, fixed-income ETFs also attracted strong inflows, particularly into government bonds and ultra-short-duration products, despite rising yields. “Active ETFs also continued their rapid growth, which we believe highlights investors’ appetite for new strategies.”

Listen to the full Talking Heads podcast for insights into the forces shaping ETF flows and investor positioning.

You can also listen and subscribe to Talking Heads on YouTube, Spotify, or wherever you normally get your podcasts.

XXX

Read the transcript

Talking Heads with Daniel Dornel

Daniel Morris: Hello and welcome to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast. Every week, Talking Heads will bring you in-depth insights and analysis on the topics that really matter to investors. In this episode, we’ll be discussing the latest ETF (exchange-traded fund) fund flows. I’m Daniel Morris, Chief Market Strategist, and I’m joined today by Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research. Welcome, Daniel, and thanks for joining me.

Daniel Dornel: Thank you, Daniel. I’m very happy to be here.

DM: As always, Daniel, it’s been an eventful quarter. One of the key surprises has been the resilience of equity markets. When you’ve seen the big increase in yields for government bonds, typically a rise in interest rates goes with the decline in equity markets but, so far, they seem to have shrugged that off. In terms of ETF flows, what are the dynamics you’ve seen in the third quarter?

DD: It has been a remarkable period. Q3 was the strongest quarter ever, with inflows around €125 billion. What’s really impressive is that we are seeing a pattern of breaking records one quarter after another. If we look closer at the monthly breakdown, July and August were the two largest months ever recorded in the UC[ITS] ETF landscape, with July alone bringing in over €50 billion.

This momentum is carrying us into an historic year. Year to date, we have already seen almost €350 billion inflows into UC[ITS] ETF[s], which means we have already surpassed the total full-year figure from last year, €327 billion.

While the growth is broad, equity projects dominated the landscape this quarter, capturing almost €100 billion of those €125 billion of total inflows.

DM: It’s interesting that you say that because there’s been a long discussion about cash on the sidelines and whether or not investors are willing to put that cash to work. And it seems from the figures you cite for ETF flows, maybe they are. We also see the strong performance of equity markets being followed by flows into ETFs. Clearly that’s a strong support for the market. Are there any particular categories or products that stand out?

DD: Without doubt, global equities have been standing out. In Q3, they attracted just under €55 billion. This isn’t a sudden spike; it is a sustained trend we have been seeing from last year.

Just to give a few figures, the year-to-date figure for global equities is already €145 billion compared to just under €100 billion for last year. So global equities now represent about a third of all equity flows.

What is particularly interesting is the acceleration in all-country exposures – a blend between developed and emerging market equities. Historically, they have been behind developed-only global equities. But on this particular sub-category, we have seen a jump from €40 billion last year to €83 billion on a year-to-date basis. This suggests investors are looking for the more diversified product[s] they can find these days.

DM: I would imagine these inflows into global ETFs, including emerging markets, probably has something to do with the strong performance we’ve seen, particularly in Taiwan and [South] Korea, around semiconductors and tech hardware. I think investors are looking to try to tap into that dynamic. Speaking of dynamics, is there anything else that you see across equity markets?

DD: Let’s start with the US. After a very strong acceleration in Q2, the appetite for US equity remained, with €23 billion in flows in Q3, again mostly concentrated in core exposures.

Moving on to Europe, we saw an interesting rebound in Q3, with €9 billion inflows. This suggests a return in confidence from investors after a very difficult Q2 where we had around €5 billion [of] outflows. We also saw an acceleration in emerging markets, bringing in €6.8 billion, a recovery from a quiet second quarter on emerging markets.

However, it hasn’t been positive everywhere. China continues to be a challenge, and we saw another difficult quarter with €1.5 billion outflows from Chinese equity product.

Looking at sub-asset classes, sector and thematic ETF[s] brought in €15 billion, the lion’s share driven by IT and tech-related themes. But there were two interesting additional trends, with healthcare – we saw €1.5 billion inflows there – and Eurozone banks, with €1.3 billion inflows.

DM: That is encouraging that you’re starting to see inflows again into Europe. We’re seeing that all the investment that the region is putting towards strategic autonomy, defence and so on is starting to bear some fruit. It’s also interesting that, despite the inflows into emerging markets, you still see outflows from Chinese ETFs. And we appreciate that tech is a big driver for the interest in emerging markets.

I started out saying we’ve had [a] surprisingly strong performance for equity markets despite the big increase in [bond] yields. I’m curious if that increase in government bond yields has had an impact on flows for fixed-income ETFs?

DD: Fixed income had a very strong quarter as well, bringing in €27 billion. The primary engine was government bonds, with €10 billion inflows. It was a mix of all maturity exposures, especially on global and euro bonds, as well as short-term maturities, especially on US, but also on European exposures.

We also saw a significant interest in ultra-short instruments, which brought €8 billion. Roughly half of that was on overnight euro exposures and 25% in US Treasuries with a maturity from zero to one year on corporate investment grade.

We also see some flows there with €4 billion, a split between US all-maturity product and euro short term. The only area of weakness was a yield with a significant slowdown, only €500 million inflows over the quarter, primarily because of the September figures where we had very negative flows on euro high yield.

DM: The outflows for high yield are relevant, as I’ve heard from our portfolio managers. That was one of the key drivers behind the increase in yields and spreads that you saw for high yield, particularly in September. Last word on ETF flows for the quarter?

DD: I’d like to highlight the rise of active ETFs again. This is where things are moving quite rapidly. In Q3 alone we saw €11 billion of inflows. This brings us on a year-to-date basis to €34 billion, so roughly 10% of the flows and it’s already ahead of [the] 2025 figure, which was just under 30 billion.

So, the dynamic is very impressive, especially on enhanced strategies and equity income strategies. But it’s not just about the flows, it’s also about the product innovation. If you look at all the ETFs launched in Europe year-to-date, 40% were active ETF[s] – that’s already over 100 new funds this year.

DM: If I can summarise some of the key points, you said not only was the third quarter the strongest ever in terms of ETF flows, but recently almost every quarter is the strongest, so it really does seem there’s a lot of momentum behind ETFs.

You highlighted that flows are going more towards global equities, conceivably as investors are looking to tap into the tech dynamic in emerging markets. That said, you also saw a rebound of flows into Europe, so another renewed bout of optimism.

And finally, positive inflows into fixed income despite the increase in [bond] yields. But you highlighted that this is tend[ing] to be short duration, so investors less at risk of rising yields and able to pick up some income in the meantime.

Daniel, thank you very much for joining me.

DD: Thank you, Daniel. Always a pleasure.

DM: That’s it for this week’s episode of Talking Heads. If you would like more information about our capabilities in ETFs, please reach out to your asset management contact or check out Viewpoint, our website for investment insights, at Viewpoint.bnpparibas-am.com. Viewpoint brings commentary and analysis in a variety of formats, from investment outlooks to asset allocation videos and podcasts to help investors make better-informed decisions.

You’ve been listening to the BNP Paribas Asset Management Talking Heads podcast with me, Daniel Morris, and Daniel Dornel, Head of ETF Research.

Please do join me next week. Until then, take care.

articles.title: The Economic Impact of the Cigarette Industry in Sri Lanka
articles.text:
Consulting Report

20 Oct 2026

The Economic Impact of the Cigarette Industry in Sri Lanka

Commissioned by Ceylon Tobacco Company PLC (CTC)

This report, commissioned by Ceylon Tobacco Company PLC (CTC), examines the economic footprint of the legal cigarette industry in Sri Lanka in 2025. The analysis covers the full value chain, from tobacco leaf cultivation and manufacturing to distribution and retail, assessing its contribution to GDP, employment and government tax revenues. It also examines the impact of illicit cigarette trade on the public finances.

CTC is Sri Lanka’s sole legal manufacturer of Factory Made Cigarettes. Its operations, alongside those of tobacco farmers, distributors and retailers, support economic activity across the country, both directly and through spending with domestic suppliers and employees’ wages.

In 2025, the legal cigarette industry contributed an estimated Rs 74.0 billion to Sri Lanka’s GDP and supported around 81,400 jobs, equivalent to 1% of national employment. The industry also generated an estimated Rs 181 billion in tax revenues, accounting for 3.6% of national tax receipts. Separately, illicit cigarettes accounted for an estimated 20% of the Factory Made Cigarette market, resulting in an estimated Rs 29.5 billion in forgone tax revenue.

articles.title: Financing Europe’s Next Wave of Electrification
articles.text:
Back to InsightsInfrastructure and Sustainable FinanceGeneral SustainabilityFrom Demand to Deployment: Financing Europe's Next Wave of ElectrificationBy Seb Henbest, Randolph Brazier and Brian Peers19 October 2026ArticleArticleShare via EmailShare on FacebookShare on LinkedInShare on TwitterData centres, EVs, heat pumps and industrial technologies are driving electricity demand growth in Europe at a pace not seen this century1. While technology and capital exist to deliver this phase of clean electrification, projects must be investable to be delivered at speed and scale.
That means expanding clean power, grids, storage and end-use technologies in parallel – underpinned by predictable cash flows, clear risk allocation, robust offtake arrangements and scalable financial structures. This challenge has become more acute as the cost of capital has risen, increasing the financing burden on capital-intensive projects with long development and construction cycles.Europe’s energy transition is moving into a more complex phaseFinancing and building individual wind and solar assets are giving way to an ecosystem approach where renewables must be coupled with energy storage and grid technology to meet growing and increasingly dynamic demand from EVs, heat pumps, and data centres. The future electricity system is a network with blurred lines between generation and consumption, connecting power utilities, grid operators and energy retailers with manufacturing, logistics, real estate and consumers.
The case is also broader than emissions reduction. Greater electrification can improve energy security, reduce exposure to volatile imported fossil fuels and support industrial competitiveness. But targets alone will not deliver the necessary infrastructure. Europe must turn policy ambition and customer demand into projects with credible commercial models and financeable revenues.
Cheap, abundant and reliable electricity will be a foundation of Europe’s increasingly electrified economy. But the conditions to provide it will not be uniform. Regions with strong renewable resources, firm low-carbon generation, available grid capacity and the ability to add storage and flexibility could gain an advantage in attracting data centres, advanced manufacturing and other electricity-intensive activity. This creates strategic choices over where infrastructure and industry should be located, how far countries are prepared to depend on interconnected power markets and imported technologies, and which capabilities should be retained domestically for reasons of resilience and national security. Governments face these choices while managing constrained fiscal capacity, reinforcing the need to direct public resources towards measures that unlock private investment rather than attempting to fund the system alone.Bankable cashflow is keyClean technologies may be available, and investors may be willing to provide capital, but projects will still stall if their cashflows are difficult to understand or contain risks that no party can manage. The link between ambition and deployment is bankability.
Large grid-connected batteries illustrate the challenge. In many European markets, a battery can earn income from energy trading, capacity markets and balancing services. A diverse revenue stack can be valuable, but it can also create uncertainty over which revenues will persist, how they interact, and how exposed they are to market or regulatory change. The issue is not complexity in itself. It is whether that complexity can be translated into a transparent and credible forecast of future cashflow.
The significant increase in the cost of capital is also testing project bankability. Clean electrification assets are typically capital-intensive and can take years to develop and build, exposing their economics to rising bond yields and changing financing conditions. For projects already operating at the margin, higher funding costs can be enough to prevent investment. The critical question is who ultimately bears this risk: customers, developers, investors, counterparties or the public sector. Unless it is explicitly allocated and appropriately priced, capital is likely to remain cautious.
For businesses, this creates a more complex financing challenge. Building a data centre, electrifying a fleet or decarbonising an industrial facility increasingly depends on infrastructure and counterparties beyond the company's own boundaries. Customers therefore need financing solutions that can address interconnected risks and bring together different sources of capital. When it is unclear how an asset will operate, where its income will come from or who will bear a particular risk, even sophisticated capital becomes cautious. For capital to mobilise, it’s critical these barriers are unlocked.
Financing clean electrification also presents unique challenges when renewables, or the electrical devices they power, are small and distributed, CAPEX-heavy, disruptive to install, and are sitting with end-customers who may not typically be able to access low-cost financing.What makes infrastructure bankableThe growth of wind and solar over the past two decades provides a useful lesson. Investors did not finance renewable generation simply because governments announced targets. Capital arrived at scale when technologies became better understood and policy frameworks made future revenues more predictable.
The UK’s Contracts for Difference mechanism is a prominent example. It has not removed every uncertainty facing a renewable project. But it has provided a clearer long-term revenue framework. That has helped make the most important long-term risks visible, measurable and financeable.
Bankability is not the absence of risk. It is the point at which lenders and investors can understand how a project will operate, identify where revenues will come from, assess the strength of counterparties and allocate each material risk to the party best able to manage it. If technology performance, market access, construction delivery, regulation or customer demand cannot be translated into measurable risks and credible cashflows, capital will remain cautious regardless of the strength of the policy target.A framework for private financing bankabilityThat is where financial institutions can add value: helping customers translate demand into bankable projects and connect those opportunities with different pools of capital. A practical framework could begin with four questions:

Is there sufficient revenue certainty from creditworthy counterparties through contracts, hedges, guarantees or durable market mechanisms?
Are the technology, construction, operating and market risks transparent, measurable and manageable, and is each risk allocated to the party best able to manage it?
Can the resulting opportunity be financed through mainstream debt and equity markets rather than relying indefinitely on bespoke capital?
Can the project support the prevailing cost of debt, while still delivering appropriate risk-adjusted returns relative to global alternatives?
Financial innovation can turn demand into cashflowSound project fundamentals and creditworthy counterparties remain essential, but financial innovation can help bridge the gap between promising technology and investable cashflow. Its most useful role is not to disguise risk. It is to create contractual evidence of future demand and move specific risks to parties with the expertise, incentives and balance sheet to manage them.
Energy-as-a-Service can help overcome one of the biggest barriers to electrification: upfront capital investment. Instead of funding and operating assets such as batteries, heating systems or EV charging infrastructure themselves, customers pay a periodic fee to a specialist provider that owns, operates and maintains the equipment. This can reduce both financial and operational risk for end users while enabling broader adoption. At the same time, providers can aggregate assets across multiple sites under standardised contracts, creating larger and more diversified cashflow pools that can improve access to financing and support a wider range of customers. Similar service-based models can also be applied to transport, bundling vehicles, charging infrastructure, energy, maintenance and financing into a single offering.
Offtake monetisation offers another route using long-term contracts for low-carbon products or electricity. Where the buyer is credit-worthy and the contractual terms are robust, demand can support financing by making future revenues more visible. Aggregation, guarantees, and risk-sharing mechanisms can also help broaden the pool of viable off-takers where individual buyers cannot support the full financing requirement, or similarly on the other side of the equation where projects might be plentiful, but small.
Across these models, the common objective is to convert demand into shovel-ready projects with dependable cashflow that can attract investment.How public capital can help unlock private investmentPrivate finance will be central to Europe’s energy transition, but it cannot deliver the transition in isolation.
Energy infrastructure is shaped by policy, regulation, planning and public investment. Public resources can help to meet the financing needs of the energy transition through debt and equity funding, or by providing risk capital to catalyse and scale private finance.
There is also a question of fiscal prioritisation. The scale of investment required means governments cannot finance every network upgrade, generation asset or industrial conversion directly. Public resources are likely to have most impact where they can remove system bottlenecks, reduce risks that private actors cannot control and mobilise the greatest amount of additional private capital.
Public support is particularly valuable where technology risk remains high, a market is in its infancy, or early projects face first mover barriers or costs. Revenue stabilisation, competitive auctions and guarantees can help first-of-a-kind projects move from demonstration to deployment. Used well, these interventions establish a track record, improve the market’s ability to price risk and create space for private finance to enter.
Government and regulators also shape bankability without providing capital directly. Standards can create confidence in what qualifies as a low-carbon product. Procurement commitments can establish demand. Robust carbon prices can strengthen the commercial case for cleaner alternatives. Faster and more transparent permitting and grid-connection processes can reduce uncertainty that project sponsors and investors cannot control.
The objective should be catalytic: use public policy and capital to reduce or re-allocate the risks that markets cannot yet manage, while preserving incentives for competition, innovation and private investment.
Supporting the clean power ecosystemEnsuring that clean electrification is delivered at scale will require a whole new ecosystem covering technology providers, delivery partners, capital providers, infrastructure owners, corporates, regulators and the public sector. Assembling and co-ordinating this is as important as the financing of the end electrification assets themselves. The good news is that Europe has a track record coordinating policy and finance that can turn emerging technologies into mainstream infrastructure.
Clean electrification will require investment not only in generation, but also in the networks, flexibility, services, and supply chains that allow clean electricity to power a growing share of the economy.
Success will depend on connecting customer demand, infrastructure, technology and capital; making revenues sufficiently predictable, allocating risk to the parties best able to manage it, and creating structures that allow opportunities to move from individual projects to repeatable investment at scale. Europe's next phase of electrification will therefore be as much a commercial and financing challenge as an engineering one. articles.title: ETF tax benefits: Why ETFs can be efficient investments
articles.text:
ETF education

ETF tax benefits: Why ETFs can be efficient investments

October 23, 2026

Key takeaways

ETF creation:

In-kind ETF creation and redemption may be facilitated by authorized participants in large quantities.

Tax efficiency:

ETFs typically generate fewer capital gains than mutual funds given how they’re structured and traded.

ETF events:

Portfolio rebalancing, stock splits, shareholder redemptions, and other events often don’t lead to more taxes.

Many investors may turn to exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for more transparency1 or lower costs.2 But ETFs are also tax efficient.3 They typically generate fewer capital gains than mutual funds due to how they’re structured and traded in the marketplace. Fewer capital gains to tax means investors potentially get to keep more of their returns.
How are ETFs created?
ETF creation and redemption typically avoid the cash transactions that may trigger capital gains distributions. Generally, an ETF issuer creates and redeems ETF shares through an “in-kind” process involving large institutional investors and market makers called authorized participants (APs). The APs have an agreement with the ETF manager that lets them create or redeem ETF shares in large blocks known as creation units. A creation unit typically consists of 10,000, 20,000, 25,000, 50,000, 80,000, 100,000, or 150,000 shares.
During the creation process, when demand for the ETF exceeds supply, the AP delivers a basket of securities held in the ETF to the issuer in exchange for a creation unit. In a redemption, however, the process is reversed. The AP receives a basket of securities while the ETF manager takes back a creation unit. ETF shares can be quickly created or redeemed elastically without cash transactions to help meet supply and demand in the marketplace.
Why do ETFs have fewer tax implications?
Since these transactions happen in shares (in-kind) and not in cash, there are typically no capital gains. What’s more, current tax law states that capital gains are not recognized at the time of the transaction and thereby not considered a taxable sale. The ETF creation and redemption structure may create meaningfully different after-tax returns between an ETF and an index-tracking mutual fund — even if both track the same index.
With ETFs, capital gains and taxes are generally recognized only when investors sell their own shares. On the other hand, mutual fund investors can see gains and taxes impacted by the selling activity of the fund’s other shareholders.
How do common ETF events affect taxes?
Portfolio rebalancing
Rebalancing a portfolio is typically handled in-kind with transactions and generally not taxable for the ETF and its shareholders. If the ETF must sell securities no longer in the index and buy additional securities, though, this may be a cash transaction and a taxable event for the ETF.
Corporate events
Stock splits, mergers, acquisitions, and other corporate events are also typically handled in-kind. But if the ETF must sell or buy securities for cash, there may be a taxable event for the ETF.
Shareholder redemption
When APs redeem their shares, this is usually handled with in-kind transactions rather than cash, which helps prevent distributions and taxes for shareholders.
