Domestic Politics and EU Enlargement StrategyThu, November 5th, 20265:30 PM - 6:30 PM (GMT+1)Carnegie Europe Office & Live OnlineLink CopiedEU enlargement is at an inflection point: Between public skepticism and radical-right gains, some of the biggest obstacles sit within the union. As the publication of the bloc’s annual enlargement package refocuses attention on these concerns, addressing them has become a critical priority.Brussels has a sophisticated process to prepare candidates for membership, but nothing to align its enlargement strategy with the political realities in member states. How can the EU bridge the gap between the legalities of enlargement and citizens’ everyday lives to ensure current members are ready to welcome new ones?To discuss these dynamics, Carnegie Europe invites you to a public event with Gert Jan Koopman, director-general for enlargement and eastern neighborhood at the European Commission. He will speak with Stefan Lehne, senior fellow at Carnegie Europe, and Iliriana Gjoni, research analyst at Carnegie Europe. articles.title: Can China Turn Its Small Modular Reactor Ambitions into Commercial Reality?
articles.text: Source: GettyArticleCarnegie ChinaCan China Turn Its Small Modular Reactor Ambitions into Commercial Reality?China has showcased its engineering prowess with small modular reactor demonstration projects. But turning these technological achievements into commercial success will be a greater challenge.Link CopiedBy Tong ZhaoPublished on Oct 20, 2026This article is part of “China's Nuclear Renaissance,” a Carnegie China series examining the opportunities and challenges China faces as it seeks to lead a new wave of nuclear energy innovation and development.If it begins operation as expected by the end of 2026, the Linglong One reactor would become the world’s first commercial land-based small modular pressurized water reactor. Built in just over five years in Hainan province, the 125-megawatt electric (MWe) reactor is considered a feat of Chinese nuclear engineering and construction prowess.1 But is Linglong One merely a showpiece, a technology experiment, or does it foreshadow a broader shift in Chinese nuclear energy strategy?With roughly half of the world’s reactors under construction in China, the country is on course to becoming the world’s largest nuclear power producer. China expects to surpass the United States in installed nuclear generating capacity by 2030. Given the scale and speed of nuclear deployment in China, Beijing may also drive nuclear power innovation with new reactor designs and applications.Small modular reactors (SMRs) are one such innovation. These reactors range from 50–350 MWe in output, compared to modern standard nuclear power plants that produce 1,000+ MWe. In theory, SMRs can be manufactured assembly-line style to drive down unit cost. In other words, the hope is that nuclear power will become more compact and cheap with SMRs, making such systems readily deployable in different environments and markets.As a potential SMR builder and exporter, China has important advantages, chiefly because it has achieved a high degree of indigenization in manufacturing major components of commercial reactors, including key reactor and primary-system equipment, and has become substantially more self-reliant in specialty materials, precision instruments, and software. Bottlenecks remain, however, notably in developing the specialized fuels required by some advanced SMR designs and in managing spent fuel.Even as China has demonstrated that it can build first-of-a-kind (FOAK) SMRs, the outlook for commercialization remains far less certain. If China cannot turn the demonstration projects into standardized, repeatable, and economically competitive fleets, then the case for scaling up domestic SMR deployment will wear thin.In the first of a series that examines the realities of the nuclear renaissance, this analysis focuses on China’s challenges in realizing SMRs’ potential. It evaluates Chinese SMRs’ economic competitiveness, market potential, regulatory maturity, supply chain completeness, and social acceptance. For the foreseeable future, the overseas market for Chinese SMRs will remain limited, and therefore unlikely to significantly alter their overall commercialization prospects. A subsequent analysis in this series, focused on China’s nuclear exports, will examine the international market in greater detail.From Demonstration to Market Commodity?The United States remains technologically formidable, with one of the world’s most diverse and innovative portfolios of SMR concepts in various stages of development. China, by contrast, has prioritized consolidation and construction of large, grid-connected plants to power its growing industrial and consumer economy. While focusing in recent decades on improving and scaling up these gigawatt-scale systems, Beijing has also more recently adopted a careful and calibrated approach to SMR development, starting with demonstration projects like Linglong One.For China, as for others, the cost of SMRs is likely to be a significant factor in their commercial and export viability. Chinese analysts expect the first wave of SMR deployment globally to begin around 2030.2 But that is contingent on whether manufacturing capacity will be in place and whether SMR’s cost curve can be bent downward, as China has done successfully with solar, electric vehicles, and batteries.Due to their smaller size, SMRs will produce electricity that is estimated to roughly be 20 percent more expensive—usually measured in terms of the levelized cost of electricity—than conventional large reactors, according to Chinese experts.3 Linglong One, currently China’s most prominent SMR project, is reportedly up to twice as expensive to build per kilowatt of capacity as an average large pressurized-water reactor, and the electricity it produces is 50 percent more expensive.4 The project has also run into delays, which could push costs higher still. The high-temperature gas-cooled reactor project in Shandong Province experienced similar construction overruns and a reduction in nominal capacity for unspecified reasons. That project’s construction cost per kilowatt has been assessed at more than twice that produced by a Hualong One large reactor.5 It is tempting to dismiss these challenges as par for the course for FOAK projects. But the limited progress to date leaves much to be desired. Chinese experts recognize that to make SMRs genuinely modular for nth-of-a-kind (NOAK) deployment requires further simplification of systems and components, greater design standardization and factory fabrication, easier transportation, and faster on-site assembly.6 Reducing construction time and unit cost that will lead to repeat orders is the only viable path forward in developing a real market for SMRs, but significant progress remains elusive.To improve the economic viability, government policy support in the form of financing and regulatory changes could give SMRs a boost. The absence of substantial targeted support so far suggests, however, that Beijing has yet to make the SMR industry a policy priority. In the meantime, state-backed financing is already subsidizing large reactors, making them cheaper and squeezing out potential cost advantages for SMRs. Unless a sizable market emerges in which SMRs offer distinct advantages, Beijing may remain reluctant to subsidize SMR deployment on a large scale. For now, policy support appears to remain limited to SMR technology development and demonstration.7On the energy regulatory side, Beijing could reclassify nuclear power as renewables to include it in the Green Electricity Certificate system or make SMR projects eligible for the China Certified Emission Reduction (CCER) system. Either measure could raise project revenue, but both options face obstacles. For CCER in particular, no methodology exists for calculating emission reductions from SMR projects.Instead, Beijing has been gradually reducing preferential tax treatment for nuclear power projects in general as the broader nuclear industry matures. A late 2025 policy, for example, eliminated refunding the value-added tax for newly approved reactors while phasing it out for projects already approved.8 Unless the government introduces new SMR-specific incentives, this trend could further weaken the inherent potential of the economies of scale for SMRs.What Market?Setting aside cost challenges, the actual market for SMRs in China is uncertain. Unlike the United States, where the AI-energy thesis has prompted big technology companies to invest in SMRs as a long-term, clean option to power data centers,9 in China there does not appear to be similar interest or a perceived need for SMRs. Even as aggregate electricity demand continues to grow, China has been adding generation capacity in the form of coal, renewables, and conventional nuclear at an even faster clip. This has led to regional electricity surpluses and even production curtailment at some coal plants along with solar and wind farms.10China’s highly developed and interconnected power grid further weakens one of the standard use cases for SMRs: bringing power to rural, remote areas that aren’t connected to main grids. But China’s extensive transmission network, including long-distance and ultra-high-voltage lines, allows electricity from various energy sources to be moved across regions relatively efficiently, including to remote areas. As a result, China’s grid often favors large generating facilities, including large nuclear reactors, whose output can be absorbed over broad areas while capturing greater economies of scale.Herein lies a key paradox for SMRs: The indigenized technology and supply chains of China’s conventional nuclear fleet have allowed it to quickly develop SMRs, yet the tremendous success of China’s large nuclear plant build-out has crowded out potential use cases for SMRs. Seemingly what is left for SMRs are China’s hinterlands, but in these regions, nuclear will compete with the massive deployment of renewables that are already cheap. The renewables surplus is already driving Beijing to site more data centers in those regions under the “Eastern Data, Western Compute” (东数西算) initiative and the “green direct connection” (绿电直连) strategy.11 SMRs’ Optimal Use CasesThe most promising domestic market for Chinese SMRs may be industrial applications and residential uses, given their smaller size, potential to be sited closer to demand centers, and possible safety advantages. For instance, SMRs can combine the generation of electricity with the production of heat, steam, hydrogen, or desalinated water. With outputs typically in the range of a few hundred megawatts or less, SMRs may be better matched to the thermal needs of an industrial park than a gigawatt-scale large reactor. This could give SMRs a genuine “sweet spot” in the industrial energy market.If SMRs can be sited close to chemical complexes or industrial parks, they could reduce the losses associated with transporting heat or steam over long distances from large reactors that generally require larger safety zones. Certain SMR technologies may be particularly well suited to such applications. The high-temperature gas-cooled reactor demonstration in Shandong, for example, can produce hotter steam than conventional large pressurized-water reactors, making it more suitable for some industrial processes. Similar logic could support combined district heating and electricity supply if SMRs can be located sufficiently close to residential areas.That market proposition, however, depends not only on cost factors but also on whether SMRs can actually be deployed close to industrial users or population centers. This issue may be more political than technical in nature, depending on how Chinese nuclear regulators evaluate the safety credentials of these various designs.Regulatory UncertaintyChina has begun adapting its nuclear safety rules to be more conducive to SMR deployment. New environmental radiation rules issued in 2025 removed the previous blanket requirement that nuclear power reactors be located at least 10 kilometers from towns or cities with populations of 100,000 or more, while also reducing the minimum planning-restricted-area boundary for SMRs from 5 kilometers to 1 kilometer.12Actual restriction perimeters remain site-specific, but the differentiated and potentially much smaller siting envelope allows, in theory, for deployment closer to industrial users and population centers. What’s more, the smaller radioactive inventory and the passive safety features incorporated into many Generation III and Generation IV SMR designs can reduce the likelihood of severe accidents relative to older large-reactor designs.Regulatory guidance, however, still lags. One challenge is the overlap between safety regimes in different industrial sectors. When an SMR is co-located with a chemical plant, for example, regulators must consider both how a chemical accident could threaten the reactor and how a reactor accident could affect the chemical facility. Nuclear sites and chemical plants are currently governed by different rules, including different safety-zone and security requirements, overseen by separate authorities.13 Joint risk assessments and integrated safety rules, while underdeveloped, are necessary for such coupled projects.Even within the nuclear sector, the lack of clear, detailed, and executable rules covering the full process of planning, evaluating, approving, and managing SMRs remains a major obstacle to large-scale investment and deployment. This is largely a result of a regulatory dilemma common to new technologies: Regulatory uncertainty discourages investment and development; but because SMR technologies are not yet mature, regulators face limits on how far they can move ahead without more empirical evidence from their construction and deployment. This is observable with the National Nuclear Safety Administration issuing a limited set of “Technical Opinions” on SMR nuclear safety in August 2026.14 The document establishes useful high-level principles but stops short of the detailed licensing standards tailored to different reactor types.Constrained Supply ChainBeyond economics and regulations, China still has critical gaps in parts of the SMR supply chain, particularly the industry-wide challenge of scaling up the production of specialized fuels and managing diverse forms of spent fuel as the industry converges on advanced technology choices for both large and small reactors.Although China has limited domestic uranium resources, upstream access to uranium supplies isn’t likely to be a major challenge. China remains heavily dependent on imported uranium, but a portfolio combining expanded domestic production, stockpiling, Chinese control of overseas mines, and market purchases should keep supply for the nuclear sector broadly manageable through the 2040s and likely beyond.15The challenge will be to meet fuel needs for advanced non-light-water reactor designs, which have been championed by the industry writ large. Some of these advanced designs, including a significant share of SMRs, require high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) enriched to between 5 and 20 percent, whereas light-water reactors traditionally used low-enriched uranium containing less than 5 percent U-235. Although China already produces HALEU fuel for its high-temperature gas-cooled reactors, it still faces significant hurdles in scaling other HALEU fuel forms.China will similarly face challenges in managing used fuels from a diverse range of SMRs. Many non-light-water reactors will require new technologies in order to reprocess their spent fuel. While China’s Atomic Energy Law, adopted in 2025, reaffirmed the country’s long-standing policy of developing a closed nuclear fuel cycle through reprocessing of spent fuel, its capabilities to deal with fuel from several advanced non-traditional reactor types remain technologically immature.Chinese NIMBYismPhysical security and public acceptance present additional challenges to SMR deployment. If SMRs are co-located with existing large nuclear plants, they can benefit from the relatively high-standard security systems already in place. But that defeats the purpose of SMRs, which are supposed to be standalone and geographically dispersed. Depending on the volume of SMRs, replicating existing security arrangements at every SMR site could be economically unviable. On the other hand, proximity to end users, especially residential districts, could also make public acceptance of SMRs more difficult than for large reactors located farther away from population centers.In fact, China has experienced organized public opposition to nuclear power plants, which has delayed several proposed nuclear power projects across the country. In some cases, public opposition contributed to project cancellations.16 China’s political system may be better optimized than others to overcome NIMBYism, but that does not eliminate the problem of local distrust of nuclear facilities. Given Chinese authorities’ high sensitivity to any potential sources of social unrest, public opposition could still become a meaningful constraint on where SMRs can be built.ConclusionChina’s SMR program has crossed the threshold from concept to demonstration, but it remains far from commercial viability. Over the next decade, China will need to prove it can transform FOAKs into NOAKs to realize SMRs’ potential. That means standardizing designs, identifying sufficiently large markets, scaling factory fabrication, driving down costs, and winning public trust along the way. At the same time, regulators must establish workable proximity-siting rules while fuel-cycle research and capabilities catch up with advanced reactor designs.Here lies the paradox: Realizing cost reductions from modularization and scale requires volume, and volume requires a large addressable market. That market may be difficult to find domestically, where the commercial case for SMRs will likely remain selective and niche, focused on powering industrial heat and steam, district heating, desalination, and off-grid electricity.For now, the potential of China’s SMR industry doesn’t match the reality. The road to commercialization will likely be an incremental process of, as the Chinese saying goes, “crossing the river by feeling the stones,” an approach that centers on experimentation and ad hoc deployment before leap to scale.AcknowledgmentThe author acknowledges LLM tools were used for preliminary proofreading. articles.title: Operational resilience of the financial sector
articles.text:
Operational resilience of the financial sector

We make sure banks and financial services firms in the UK can overcome disruption

Related links

Co-ordinating the response to disruption of financial services

On this pageOverviewStrategic outcomesFirm-level outputsSystem-level outputs

Overview
Operational resilience is the ability of firms and the entire financial sector to prevent, adapt, respond to, recover from and learn from disruptions.
Financial firms and financial market infrastructures (FMIs) must have robust plans to deliver important services, no matter the disruption. This includes man-made threats such as physical and cyberattacks, IT system outages and third-party supplier failure. It also includes natural hazards such as fire, flood, severe weather and pandemic. These can affect firms’ safety and soundness, undermine policyholder protection and, in some cases, affect financial stability.
The Bank of England and our Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) carry out this work with the UK's two other financial authorities: the Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
Our approach assumes that sometimes disruptions that prevent firms from operating as usual will occur and mean they cannot provide their services for a period.

External links

Operational Resilience - Financial Conduct Authority Opens in a new window
The National Cyber Security Centre Opens in a new window

Prudential and Resolution Policy Index related links

Banking - Operational resilience
Insurance - Operational resilience

Strategic outcomes

Build firms' resilience: when severe but plausible disruption occurs, it should not affect financial stability, safety and soundness or policyholder protection. Firms must ensure high standards of IT and cyber resilience, third-party dependency risks.
Build systemic operational resilience: firms and the Bank work to ensure that when systemic operational risks crystallise, they do not impact the UK's financial stability. Third parties must be sufficiently resilient to support this outcome. It is important that firms can contribute to sector-wide incident response and can learn and evolve from failures.
Manage risks: limit the likelihood and impact of losses. Firms must set aside capital so that the crystallisation of risks is unlikely to affect firm safety and soundness.

The following outputs are designed with these outcomes in mind:

Monetary Policy Committee voting history

Firm-level outputs

Operational resilience policy
Our Financial Policy Committee (FPC) looks at the entire system. Our Prudential Regulation Committee (PRC) and Financial Market Infrastructure Committee (FMIC) focus on the firms and FMIs we regulate.
In summary, we ask firms to:

identify important business services: boards and senior management must prioritise services that, if disrupted, would affect our objectives and the public interest;
set impact tolerances: firms must say to what extent they could continue important business services after severe but plausible disruptions; and
make sure they can stay within impact tolerances: firms must map their important business services and test their capacity to continue to the agreed extent – they should address any vulnerabilities they have identified.

The operational resilience policy SS1/21 requires firms to prepare a written operational resilience self-assessment of compliance. The aim is to document a firms’ resilience journey, identifying risks that could prevent them from delivering important business services within tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios. It helps the firms’ boards and senior management make informed investment decisions to address resilience gaps.
We assess the status of a firm’s implementation of our policy. This includes reviewing:

their important business services, impact tolerances and additional metrics
scenario testing details, results and assurance that the firm can remain within impact tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios
firms’ identification of risks, threats, and vulnerabilities through mapping, testing and live incidents
response and recovery actions, remediation plans and timelines

Self-assessments allow us to identify good practices at an individual firm level while also facilitating thematic comparisons, helping us build a clearer picture of the wider systemic operational resilience picture across the industry.
Incident management and reporting
The PRA has published a policy that details requirements for reporting certain operational incidents, and notification and reporting of material third-party arrangements. It sets out expectations for regulatory reporting, which aim to enhance the PRA’s understanding of firm and sector threats and vulnerabilities.

CP17/24 – Operational resilience: Operational incident and outsourcing and third-party reporting

Third-party management
The PRA’s current policy is set out primarily in Supervisory Statement (SS) 2/21: Outsourcing and third party risk management, which was published in March 2021. The Bank has a near-identical set of policies for FMIs, such as clearing houses and payment systems.
Operational risk framework
Our role is to assess whether a firm's operational risk management framework allows them to effectively identify, assess, monitor, report and manage material operational risks to which it is or might be exposed, in line with board-approved strategy and risk appetite.
We are also responsible for assessing whether firms hold sufficient capital to mitigate the impact when operational risks crystallise.
This supports the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Rules, which require us to assess whether firms’ own funds and internal capital is adequate to cover the level of the risks to which it is or might be exposed and is reflective of the firm’s operational risk profile.
Cyber resilience
Firms and FMIs should assess their cyber risk and build adequate resilience capabilities to prepare for, and respond to, potentially disruptive cyber incidents. To maintain the financial sector's cyber resilience and to support our supervisory oversight, we have developed cyber assessment tools. They include CBEST, STAR-FS and CQUEST.
CBEST
This provides a framework for regulators to work with firms using a simulated cyberattack. This allows firms to explore how to counteract an attack on the people, processes and technology of cyber security controls. We base the simulated attacks on present threats.
The aim is to test:

a firm's defences
its threat intelligence capability
its ability to detect and respond to external and internal attackers

Firms use the assessment to plan how they can strengthen their resilience.
An accredited service provider carries out the simulation, acting within legal, ethical and moral constraints. It aims to get through a firm's defences using the cyber kill chain. They also assess if the confidentiality, integrity or availability of systems and processes that deliver a firm's important business services can be compromised.

CBEST Threat Intelligence-Led Assessments

CBEST thematic review
The annual CBEST thematic is intended to inform the sector on the findings and lessons learned from our CBEST programme, which assesses the cyber resilience of key financial institutions through security testing performed in ‘live’ corporate environments.

2023 CBEST thematic findings
2024 CBEST thematic findings
2025 CBEST thematic findings

STAR-FS
STAR-FS (simulated targeted attack and response assessments for financial services) is part of the PRA and FCA supervisory toolkit, to assess the cyber resilience of firms' important business services. This allows regulators and firms to better understand vulnerabilities and take remedial actions, thereby improving their resilience and, by extension, the wider financial system.
It promotes a threat-led penetration testing approach that mimics the actions of actors' intent on compromising an organisation's important business services as well as the technology assets and people supporting them.
An implementation guide and supporting templates are available. If your firm is interested in conducting a STAR-FS please contact your supervisor. It aims to provide:

an outcome-based assessment of financial institutions' protection, detection and response technical capabilities against cyber-attacks;
an approach, conducted through a firm-led delivery model, that can identify cyber resilience vulnerabilities within systems, people and processes;
reduced regulatory and firm effort relative to other supervisory technical assessments such as CBEST;
levels of independent technical assurance beyond those ordinarily included in firms' own penetration testing programmes; and
a testing approach accessible by a larger number of financial institutions to experience and learn from.

STAR-FS Implementation guide – Threat Intelligence Led Penetration Testing for Financial Services (PDF 2.1MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Scope Specification (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Targeting Report Specification (PDF 0.6MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Threat Intelligence Report Specification (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Penetration Test Report Specification (PDF 1.4MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Remediation Plan Template (PDF 0.8MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Regulator Summary (PDF 0.6MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Threat Intelligence Maturity Assessment Guide (PDF 1.3MB) Opens in a new window
STAR-FS Detection & Response Assessment Guide (PDF 0.7MB) Opens in a new window

CQUEST
We use the CQUEST (Cyber resilience questionnaire) to gauge the cyber risk and resilience capabilities of the sector. Firms can also use it as a self-assessment tool to consider their own cyber risk and resilience maturity. It comprises 50 questions with multiple-choice answers across six domains:

governance and leadership
identify
protect
detect
respond
recover

To achieve a reliable outcome, an organisation should identify and direct a competent party with appropriate knowledge of the business to complete the CQUEST. When it is used to inform regulatory activities, supervisors might provide additional guidance and/or they could request evidence or clarifying information in response to the answers.
The latest version of CQUEST builds upon the previous one, and encompasses lessons learned from good practice frameworks and feedback from supervisors and firms.

Download the CQUEST

System-level outputs

Collective action and incident response
The Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG) leads sector-wide collective action on operational resilience. It comprises about 25 members: firms across retail, wholesale, FMIs, insurance, the financial authorities and the National Cyber Security Centre. Its co-chairs are senior executives of the PRA and UK Finance.
CMORG has three core objectives:

identify risks to the resilience of the financial sector.
develop solutions to improve the operational resilience of the sector.
share knowledge

Industry has developed CMORG-endorsed capabilities (including good practice guidance, response frameworks and contingency tools) to support the operational resilience of the UK's financial sector. The financial authorities support the development of these capabilities and efforts to improve resilience. However, their use is optional and they do not constitute regulatory rules or supervisory expectations. As such, they may not necessarily represent formal endorsement by the authorities.
Specialist subgroups support CMORG. They design, manage and deliver operational resilience improvements for the sector. Their work is voluntary. Their chairs meet regularly to discuss CMORG's activities and identify areas for more collaboration. A project management office (PMO) also supports CMORG. It is jointly resourced by us and UK Finance.

Find out more about CMORG Opens in a new window

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC) is a CMORG-led partnership. It aims to help identify, investigate and co-ordinate the response to incidents that may have consequences for the financial sector. It analyses and distributes information to produce timely outputs for the sector's benefit.

The Financial Services Cyber Collaboration Centre (FSCCC)

What happens if there is a disruption?
Firms should get in touch with their usual business or supervisory contacts at the Bank or the FCA. The sector's response is facilitated by the Sector Response Framework (SRF). It sets out how organisations across the sector and government are connected. It also explains how they may respond to incidents when the impact becomes broader than a single firm or FMI and requires co-ordination, information-sharing or collective action.
Its purpose is to:

allow firms, FMIs and the sector to make collective, timely and informed decisions in response to incidents
provide a reference to good practice, contingency tools and plans, which may be invoked as part of a sector response
include decision makers and subject matter experts
be organised on a modular basis, so that components of the SRF can respond
be recognised by the financial authorities as the principal structure by which the sector will respond to incidents
support collaborative engagement between the sector and the UK's financial authorities (see below)
be able to engage with frameworks in other jurisdictions, if required

The UK's three financial authorities are the Bank (including the PRA), the FCA and the Treasury. If disruptions could affect the whole sector, these authorities act together.

Find out about how we co-ordinate our response to the disruption of financial services

Sector exercising
The Bank works with the sector to co-ordinate and deliver exercises to strengthen the operational resilience of the UK's financial system.
The most prominent is SIMEX – a biennial, market-wide simulation conducted through a public-private partnership between industry participants and financial authorities. SIMEX performs a unique role in bringing the sector together to address the most challenging and complex risks that individual firms cannot manage alone.
These sector-wide exercises are based on our collective approach to resilience, working together with industry to identify emerging risks and build capabilities to enhance the system’s overall resilience.

SIMEX 24 – A major market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption
SIMEX 22 – A two-day market-wide simulation exercise to test the UK's financial sector’s resilience to a major operational disruption

Critical third-party oversight
The Bank, the PRA and the FCA (the regulators) are responsible for overseeing critical third parties (CTPs) to the UK's financial sector, following their designation by HMT.
Regulated firms and FMIs are increasingly dependent on a small number of third parties for the delivery of functions and services that are essential to the stability of, or confidence in, the UK's financial system. In some cases, third parties can become so critical that no single firm can adequately monitor or manage the systemic risks they pose.
The aim of oversight is to reduce systemic risks arising from the failure of, or disruption to the systemic services they provide to firms. The regulators will assess CTPs against outcomes-focused rules and expectations with the aim of ensuring the systemic services CTPs provide to the financial sector are resilient and therefore any failure of, or disruption to, those services does not threaten the stability of the UK's financial system.
The CTP regime complements, and does not replace, the existing requirements and expectations for firms on SS1/21 operational resilience and SS2/21 outsourcing and third-party risk management policy.

SS6/24 – Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
PS16/24 – Operational resilience: Critical third parties to the UK financial sector
Approach to the oversight of critical third parties

Find out more about the CTP regime:

Critical Third Parties

Cyber and operational resilience stress test (CORST)
The cyber and operational resilience stress test (formerly the Cyber Stress Test or 'CST') is a key part of the Bank’s toolkit on macroprudential operational resilience. The outcomes of cyber and operational resilience stress testing inform the FPC's monitoring of sector operational resilience and its articulation of its tolerance for disruption to vital services. The objectives of testing are to:

provide insight into sector vulnerabilities and the financial stability impacts and residual risk of severe but plausible operational disruption to vital services
explore firm and sector capabilities to respond to, and recover from operational disruption, and to mitigate its impact on financial stability
share lessons to support firms in maturing their approach to operational resilience and financial stability, including firms' roles as systemic risk managers

We invite firms to participate in CORST on a voluntary basis and they identify their own lessons and remediation actions. Actions that require cross-firm co-operation are often progressed through established collective action forums or voluntary groups.
The test aims, over time to explore all systemically important firms and provide insight into not just the impacts of disruption to the services they provide, but also the impacts to their customer firms and from their third parties. Participation may be direct, indirect through co-operation with a direct participant, or through engagement at cross-firm workshops.
The CST24 thematic letter, which provides thematic findings from the 2024 test, also provides resources to support firms’ role in mitigating potential financial stability impacts of disruption to their services.

Thematic findings from the 2024 cyber stress test
Thematic findings from the 2022 cyber stress test

FPC impact tolerance for financial stability
The FPC updated its impact tolerance for payments and settlements after CST22. This was published in the March 2023 FPC Record:

it expected the financial system to be able to complete critical payments by the end of the value date in severe but plausible scenarios; timely recovery of service delivery was the first best way firms could prevent adverse material economic impacts;
in such instances where restoring services would be harmful for financial stability, or impossible, alternative mitigating actions might be appropriate; firms should, therefore plan, prepare and test for such situations and invest so that their response could effectively mitigate any impact on financial stability until service delivery was restored; and
an example of mitigation may be providing an overdraft to a retail Banking customer, so that they can still make purchases, despite a disruption to the payment systems which may have prevented the normal 'payment' being completed

Financial Policy Summary and Record – March 2023 (see paragraphs 101-108)

In Financial Stability in Focus (FSIF), the FPC noted it would regularly review the operational resilience policy toolkit and will explore ways to continue to build system-wide resilience to operational disruption.
In addition to the tools mentioned above, the FPC does this, for example, through:

assessing potential system-wide gaps in, or risks to, operational resilience which are not adequately covered by firm-level or microprudential policies
considering whether to set impact tolerances for additional vital services beyond payments.

The committee has published its macroprudential approach to operational resilience in FSIF and sets out its priorities twice a year in its Financial Stability Report.

articles.title: Escalating Middle East tensions amplify energy supply risks | RBCCM
articles.text:
The rapid devolution of the Iran war’s second front presents escalating risks to global energy supplies as Houthi attacks intensify against Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure. In recent days, the Yemen-based fighters have launched deadly attacks on Saudi airports and targeted the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran, where Saudi Ministry of Energy officials confirmed a fire at an administrative building. The security incident comes on the heels of multiple airport attacks that claimed at least 18 lives and left over 300 injured, part of an ongoing Houthi campaign to impose a no-fly zone on the Kingdom. Over the past month, the Houthis have repeatedly targeted the country’s energy infrastructure, including the East-West Pipeline, though Aramco engineers have executed rapid repairs to prevent a more severe shock to the global energy system.
The critical question facing Washington is whether it can continue to avoid direct participation in this metastasizing conflict. While the U.S. provides intelligence and aerial refueling support, it is not participating in air operations against the Yemen-based fighters. A yearlong ceasefire between the U.S. and the Houthis remains ostensibly in effect, and in late September, Houthi leadership indicated that it would not target U.S. vessels in the Red Sea in an apparent effort to keep Washington on the sidelines. At the time, President Trump said, “the Houthis don’t want to fight us” and that they were letting most ships pass through the critical chokepoint following reports that the U.S. cancelled planned strikes on the group.
Some Pentagon officials are apparently reticent about deeper involvement in the Saudi-Houthi conflict given the substantial resources being devoted to the Hormuz oil evacuation and the Iranian campaign, as well as the deepening shortages of U.S. missiles and interceptors. The U.S. escort operation requires a significant outlay of aerial and naval assets operating in close coordination, ranging from Apache helicopters, F-35s, and aerial refueling tankers to guided-missile destroyers and amphibious assault ships. Simultaneously, around 30% of U.S. naval assets in the region are committed to the maritime blockade of Iran.
Whether Iran can continue to publicly maintain its operational distance from Houthi actions remains uncertain. Iranian officials have gone to great lengths to insist that they exercise no command and control over the Houthis, despite clear evidence of weapons and financial support to the Axis of Resistance member and the fact that Tehran is a beneficiary of the widening scope of the conflict. The apparent offer by Iranian officials to help mediate an offramp between the Saudis and the Houthis could be construed as an arsonist helping to put out a fire. The Houthis are purportedly seeking the lifting of the land, sea, and air blockade in place for nearly a decade and a substantial cash settlement — demands that seemingly mirror those made by Tehran to Washington. The recent spate of deadly Houthi attacks could strengthen the hand of the finish-the-job camp in Washington and the region.

“Oil prices are a broken barometer for measuring the geopolitical pressure building in the Middle East, and we would now include rising oil exports as well.”
Helima Croft, Head of Global Commodity Strategy and MENA Research, RBC Capital Markets

Physical crude markets have tightened amid supply disruptions and unprecedented freight costs. Platts assessed Dated Brent at around $130.52/bbl on October 13, just off its $135.74 level on October 8, which represented the highest price since the $144.42/bbl peak on April 7th. This stands in contrast to front-month paper prices around $106/bbl at that time of assessment. Despite higher volumes out of the Middle East, crude inventories — both onshore and on water — continue to fall, suggesting a continued shortage of crude. Record tanker rates are hindering the economic viability of key routes; in Europe, this has prevented the placement of grades from West Africa and the Americas, instead supporting certain local grades. Many grades have seen their arbitrage into Asia close entirely. For example, some West Africa traders have recently cited a step back from Indian interest due to the freight headwind.
Facing record diesel prices ahead of the midterms, President Trump has sought to manifest an energy ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine War, but the proposed deal already shows clear signs of failure. The recent Putin-Trump agreement to facilitate the export of Russian diesel has faced significant criticism in Washington, with easing of Russian sanctions remaining deeply unpopular on both sides of the aisle. Even so, such an agreement would be unlikely to create a meaningful impact to U.S. diesel markets. Global diesel exports in Q3 ran over 900 kb/d lower year-over-year, with Russian volumes down over 400 kb/d over the same period, driving global diesel inventories well below five-year seasonal lows.
The root cause for Russia’s export atrophy remains unresolved despite the easing of the export ban. Damage to Russian refineries has driven refinery runs to roughly 3.4 mb/d in September, down around 1.3 mb/d year-over-year. Current production levels just exceed domestic consumption, meaning that in order to meet the initial volumes outlined—300 kt immediately, 500 kt in November, and a further 1,000 kt after—by end-of-year, runs would need to recover to July levels, an increase of approximately 300 kb/d. Without such an increase in output, given domestic consumption, deal volumes would likely not be produced until mid-2027. In either scenario, the volumes represent a trickle that will have a diluted, delayed impact on markets. Furthermore, even if the volumes are drawn from inventories or runs surprise, the immediate volume would be unlikely to move the needle for pump pricing prior to midterms.
European natural gas prices have reached their highest levels since December 2022 as inventories remain critically low and uncertainty about Middle East LNG flows persists. TTF prices have broken above the €85/MWh level, last seen at the end of 2022 when prices began to climb down from highs seen after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Now, as renewed strikes in Hormuz and regional flareups increase pessimism for a durable ceasefire by year end, Europe faces a stark supply landscape with gas injections below historic levels. At the start of heating season, European storage stands at 74% full, versus 83% last year and well below the five-year average of 89% for this time of year. German gas storage further lags with injections at only 60% full, versus 76% this time last year, prompting the government to direct state-owned SEFE to buy and store an additional 8 TWh of gas by December 15.
Even as Europe seeks to shore up storage, global supply remains suppressed, with September LNG exports down 17% from January’s record highs as Qatar exports remain largely offline. Europe’s supply constraint will tighten even more this winter as the bloc’s ban on long-term Russian LNG contracts goes into effect January 1. In the first nine months of this year, Europe has imported nearly 14 billion cubic meters of Russian gas, namely from Yamal LNG, representing about 12% of total LNG imports through September. Even if El Niño brings a milder winter to the continent, without a resumption of LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz, TTF is set to remain well bid through the winter.

Helima Croft authored "Energy Flashpoints: Contagion Effect," published on October 13, 2026. For more information on the full report, please contact your RBC representative.

articles.title: Gavekal Technologies: New Energy
articles.text:
Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Most recent

Gavekal Technologies: Briefing

The State Of Chinese AI

Arthur Kroeber, Laila Khawaja
19 Oct 2026

The AI world suffered tremors last week, as doubts began to surface about the frontier labs’ revenue growth and the rising amount of high-priced debt used to finance the US’s data center building binge. The risks raise a question: when and if the American AI bubble pops, can China race ahead? Probably not.

Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Can China Export Its Nuclear Boom?

AJ Cortese
12 Oct 2026

China is the world’s biggest builder of nuclear power plants, but unlike in other energy sectors it has not become a significant exporter of reactors. While Chinese nuclear firms have figured out how to make reactors relatively cheaply, the complexity and safety needs of nuclear projects mean they will never be able to gobble up world markets through ultralow prices, as Chinese solar, EV and battery firms have done. But over the next decade it is likely China will become an important nuclear exporter.

More research

Great Tech In Search Of Profits

5 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies held its inaugural China Tech Tour with 19 institutional-investor clients. Through a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives, we examined China’s semiconductor, AI, new energy, robotics and biotechnology industries. This week’s China Tech Brief explores some of the key findings. By far the biggest theme was the gap between technological capabilities and corporate returns. China has plenty of globally competitive tech companies, but few that generate really attractive earnings.

GavekalTech On The Ground: 2026 China Tech Trip Takeaways

1 Oct 2026

On September 6-11, Gavekal Technologies made its inaugural China Tech Trip with 19 institutional investor clients. The trip offered a close-up view of China’s tech ecosystem, including semiconductors, AI, new energy, robotics, and biotech, via a dozen site visits and in-depth conversations with senior executives. This week’s Chips report summarizes our observations in the semiconductor and AI sectors.

Chinese EV Makers’ European Offensive

28 Sep 2026

Chinese EV makers have conquered their home market and are on track to export over 5mn vehicles this year, double the 2025 figure. Their next move will be to start moving production offshore, to get closer to key markets and evade tariffs. The biggest target is Europe, where half a dozen projects are under way and many more are planned.

Webinar: The State Of China Tech

25 Sep 2026

As presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping prepare for their summit meeting in Washington, China’s fast-growing technology capabilities are a major topic. The big questions at the moment are how close Chinese artificial-intelligence labs are to matching the US frontier models, and whether the two sides can start negotiating rules on AI safety. But behind those lie even bigger questions: What is the balance of technological power between the US and China? And how far can the world's two big tech powers go in pulling apart the thick webs of interdependence that tie them together?

Breaking Up Is Hard To Do

21 Sep 2026

Both China and the US have devoted intense energy to slashing their technological reliance on each other. These efforts have had some impact, but the overall lesson is that decoupling is really difficult and even as old dependencies are cut, new ones pop up. This China Tech Brief examines the underlying causes.

The China New Energy Guidebook

16 Sep 2026

Over the past year Gavekal Technologies has explored most corners of China’s vast and unique energy system, with a particular focus on how electrification is transforming China’s economy and its position in the world. We have now distilled our insights into our first annual China New Energy Guidebook. This concise presentation outlines China’s strategies for its energy and electricity systems, assesses the progress of wind, solar and nuclear deployment, and analyzes the key electricity related sectors: batteries, electric vehicles, AI and the “electrotech stack.”

articles.title: US midterm elections: fiscal gridlock on the horizon?
articles.text:
Monthly Cross Asset - Topic of the Month

US

Elections

Politics

Equity

Fixed income

21 October, 2026

14 minutes

US midterm elections: fiscal gridlock on the horizon?

EDM

Monthly Cross AssetEN

US midterm elections: fiscal gridlock on the horizon?

14 minutes

EDM

Monthly Cross AssetEN

Summary

Key Takeaways

We believe the most likely outcome is a split Congress, with Democrats taking the House and Republicans keeping the Senate, which should preserve broad policy continuity and limit the scope for major fiscal or legislative change. A Democratic sweep is also very likely. This would raise the risk of a more interventionist agenda, although still constrained by the budget deficit, while a Republican hold of both chambers is very unlikely. Markets increasingly price a Democratic sweep, but policy risks remain. A Democratic House is largely priced in, while the Senate remains the key uncertainty. A Republican rebound or more aggressive use of executive powers could still surprise markets. The midterms could reshape sector performance. Continued AI investment should support IT, with industrials and materials potentially benefitting as capex broadens. The impact on energy could be mixed, as higher energy prices remain supportive, while less opposition to renewable energy could make renewables more competitive.

US midterms: toward divided government, fiscal deadlock, and sector-specific pressure

US midterm elections will determine control of the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate. All 435 House seats are up for election, along with 33 regular Senate seats. At present, Republicans control both chambers: the House stands at 220 Republicans to 215 Democrats, while the Senate stands at 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and 2 independents who caucus with Democrats. The chamber most likely to flip is the House, given the narrow margin, while the Senate is harder to change because only one-third of seats are contested at a time.Against this backdrop, the most likely outcome is divided government, with the House going to the Democrats and the Senate remaining Republican. A divided government would constrain Trump’s policy options at home. Historically, when presidents are faced with this, they tend to focus more on foreign policy. Therefore, the US will likely become more interventionist. Recent polling also suggests that the elections may be shaped by more than normal partisan competition, with concerns about democratic backsliding – such as attempts to sway turnout or intimidate voters – which would further erode trust in US institutions and add to political uncertainty.

Macroeconomic implications

The macroeconomic consequences of the midterms are likely to be limited by the balance of power in Congress, and therefore by the degree of fiscal gridlock. Under the most likely scenario of divided government, the main implication is that it becomes harder to pass large new fiscal packages, including additional tax cuts. Existing tax legislation would largely remain in place, but the political room for fresh stimulus or broad-based tax reform would be limited. As a result, the fiscal stance is likely to remain broadly neutral to mildly restrictive over time, with elevated deficits and debt still providing the underlying backdrop.

There are likely to be differences across the three scenarios, particularly in how legislation is used to support specific parts of the economy:Consumers: supportive measures/redistribution. If the most likely outcome, divided government, prevails, there is little scope for additional tax cuts that would materially boost disposable income across household income groups. If Democrats gain more power, there may be more emphasis on redistribution, healthcare support, and benefits for lower-income households, which could support consumption at the margin but would not necessarily boost consumption. By contrast, a Republican sweep would increase the probability of further tax cuts, which could be more supportive of spending and growth, but also more deficit-expanding. In all cases, the effect on consumption is likely to be indirect and modest relative to the broader macro cycle which is currently driven by the tech/AI-related capex story.Capex cycle: the midterms could clearly affect investment conditions. We believe the expensing and bonus depreciation provisions introduced by the current administration and already in the tax code are likely to remain in place under a divided Congress, providing a meaningful support for capex. This should continue to favour eligible equipment, machinery and software, and help broaden the investment theme beyond Tech and AI to a wider range of business investments. On that basis, we expect the capex story to remain broadly intact. A split government would make fiscal deadlock the base case, increasing uncertainty around the policy environment, debt issuance and the term premium. The risk would be greater if it heightens the chance of shutdowns or debt-ceiling standoffs, and it could limit the scale of the capex cycle or expose weaknesses in the most vulnerable parts of the economy.In the context of investments, an important channel is the impact on AI-related sectors, particularly through regulation and infrastructure buildout. While the political debate around AI may become more visible at the federal level, the practical effects are likely to be felt increasingly through state and local regulation, especially in areas such as zoning, permitting, electricity access, water use, and environmental rules. That matters because data centres are a key bottleneck in the AI investment cycle. A more restrictive regulatory environment could raise costs, lengthen project timelines, and affect utilities, infrastructure, and AI-linked capital expenditure. The effect would probably be more sector-specific than economy-wide, but it could still matter for investment intentions and market valuations. It is not possible, though, to draw a very clear line between midterm scenarios: the states most exposed to AI-related regulation and infrastructure pressures are increasingly revealing a partisan tension between Democrats, who tend to favour tighter guardrails, and Republicans, who tend to prioritise innovation and faster deployment. But the issue is not purely ideological: local concerns over electricity demand, water use, zoning, and the cost of data-centre buildout can drive regulatory pushback across party lines. Thus, while a Democratic sweep could make tighter regulation more likely, this would probably focus on areas such as consumer protection, labour impacts, environmental costs, energy consumption, and local permitting. Across the broader economy, given the geopolitical priorities of the current administration, we would expect continued emphasis on innovation, competitiveness, and faster infrastructure buildout in the race for AI dominance.On inflation, the direct macro impact is likely to be very limited, but there could be some effects at the level of the inflation basket. In the event of a Democratic sweep with substantial majorities, an expansion or reintroduction of Obamacare-related subsidies would remain quite unlikely, as noted above. If Democrats nevertheless secured such measures, these could affect the healthcare-related components of CPI and PCE more noticeably, especially since medical care carries a meaningful weight in both baskets. This could introduce temporary shifts in inflation levels, although the effect is unlikely to be large enough to materially change the overall inflation trajectory in the medium term.

Bottom line

The most probable post-midterm outcome is divided government, which would constrain legislative ambition at home while leaving the executive branch largely in control of the core policy agenda. The macro significance of that outcome lies mainly in fiscal deadlock rather than a major change in policy direction, with a higher risk of government shutdowns, more budget brinkmanship, and a higher policy uncertainty premium.

What could be the impact of the midterm elections on US assets and sectors?

The IT and energy sectors have been the strong outperformers since President Trump’s second election victory. Communication services and utilities have been the underperformers, and though part of this is due to the lower beta of the sectors in a rising market, these two are also the only sectors to have recorded a negative alpha over the period. Will the winners of the first half of Donald Trump’s second term be the losers after the midterms? That is possible in certain sectors. Artificial Intelligence could face a tougher regulatory regime if Congress swings back to the Democrats, though the President has made clear his opposition to slowing down technology through regulation. We expect investment to continue, however, with technology being more of a driver than politics. This will support IT, and sectors like industrials and materials could benefit from a broadening in the investment trend. The impact on the energy sector could be mixed. Opposition to renewable energy could wane if Democrats gain ground in Congress, potentially making renewables more competitive with fossil fuels. At the same time, a more interventionist US in case of a divided government could lead to prolonged tensions in the Middle East, keeping energy prices higher for longer. Any change in direction for the energy sector would also be relevant also to utilities, given the negative correlation between the performance of the two sectors since the start of the second quarter this year. Healthcare has suffered due to President Trump’s comments on drug prices, even though the President has complained more about foreign consumers paying too little, rather than domestic consumers paying too much. We think the sector could rebound as a result. A Democrat-dominated Congress could launch investigations into the healthcare insurance sector, however, given voters’ ire over this sector. The performance of financials will depend on regulation, but also on the direction of bond yields and the cost of risk. Regulation is probably more in the hands of the Fed than of Congress, and the trend may not be affected by the midterm elections. Under a divided government, however, progress on reducing the deficit may be extremely halting. As a result, the yield curve could steepen, increasing net banking margins. It could also keep real growth strong and prevent an increase in the cost of risk, helping financials improve their performance relative to the rest of the market. By contrast, further increases in nominal interest rates are likely to continue to put pressure on the real estate sector.

Markets are pricing gridlock without relief

Pricing around the 2026 midterms does not simply reflect rising uncertainty – it reflects a repricing of the baseline. Divided government, the September consensus, has given way to a higher probability of a Democratic sweep. Markets are not just more nervous; they are starting to price a different political world.That shift has a political logic. The macro backdrop remains supportive: orderly markets, resilient growth, and a growing wealth effect. But the factors that decide midterms – purchasing power, gasoline prices, household sentiment and approval among swing voters – have not improved, and the Iran conflict has compounded these pressures. Trump's political capital looks fine in aggregate, but it is weak precisely where elections are won.A Democratic House is now close to fully priced. While prediction markets increasingly favour a Democratic sweep, our central scenario remains a divided congress, reflecting our assessment of the electoral map and the remaining uncertainty round the Senate races. A Democratic Senate would control judicial and Fed confirmations, constraining the White House in ways that go well beyond committee subpoenas.Political and policy baskets complete the picture (see chart below). Republican policy exposure has weakened dramatically, but assets sensitive to a Democratic agenda are not rallying either. Instead, markets are converging on a simpler view: whoever wins, ambitious policy is off the table. Markets already price constrained fiscal ambition, moderate trade tension and continued immigration enforcement through executive authority.Uncertainty is also visible in the options market. Implied equity volatility for the post-election expiry has risen sharply above that for the pre-election expiry, signalling a prolonged period of policy digestion after the vote. Rising rates complicate the picture, raising the cost of fiscal confrontation. Shutdowns, debt-ceiling brinkmanship, and budget gridlock under a Democratic Congress are greater risks. In prior cycles, gridlock was a relief trade. At current yield levels, it may not be.Bottom line: a House flip is largely discounted, and a sweep is increasingly in the price. The remaining market surprise is a Republican rebound – the least priced and most dislocating scenario. The larger post-election question is whether a constrained White House responds with moderation or turns to executive tools – tariffs, China policy, immigration, Fed pressure – more aggressively than markets currently assume. That is the risk not yet in the price.

articles.title: The Institute Employment Report: September 2026
articles.text: David Tinsley October 2026 Job growth softened further in September, according to Bank of America's deposit data, with growth of 1.4% year-over-year (YoY), from 1.5% in August. But falling unemployment payments in September indicate a relatively healthy overall picture. Lower-income households' wage growth remains strongest, despite a narrowing gap. After-tax wage growth eased to 4.5% YoY for lower-income households in September, while rising to 3.8% and 3.7% for middle- and higher-income households, respectively. Lower tax withholdings and a relative strengthening in the younger/lower-income end of the labor market are driving this story. Additionally, average hours have risen in some lower-paid industries, which is also boosting pay packets. Read our full analysis for a more in-depth look at these trends. articles.text:
Insights into urban and regional developmentUnderstand the consequences of global, national and local events on cities and regional economies.

Local economic audits and forecastsA core capability of our team is the production of local economic audits and forecasts. These are tailored to clients’ specific needs, but typically include demographic trends and how the economy has influenced them, labour market conditions, business statistics, productivity, wages, output and employment by sector, house prices, incomes and spending—all within the context of a macro overview highlighting global economic drivers.

Local economic planningOur projections for employment, population and household formation are widely adopted by local planners. Because of the rigourous nature of our work we can help local and regional governments make robust and defensible decisions on issues such as future land use, transport and development priorities.

Strategic analysisAs the leading practitioners in thinking about prospects and drivers of change for local, regional and city economies, we are increasingly asked to lead on strategy development.
